For Julie, and for my dad.


Julie,
   Three years ago, a few months into the rendering engine, I came out of my office
and told you I thought I was onto something. You said okay. You didn’t ask what
it was, or what it was for, or when it would be done, and you didn’t ask me for
anything I could have shown you, because there was nothing to show. There was a
program that had done something it shouldn’t have been able to do, and a man who
didn’t yet know what a Turing machine was.
   You gave me the three years anyway. The nights after the lot closed. The
weekends. The hours I was in the house and not in the house, because my head was
in a wall I couldn’t get past. Every dead end, and there were more of those than
there are pages here. You never once asked me to stop, and you never once said it
was fine when it wasn’t. You just kept giving me the next evening.
   This book is what I did with them. It’s the one thing I’ve built from nothing that
I’m sure of, because I threw out every piece of it I couldn’t prove, and what’s left
holds. I know that isn’t what you gave the years for. You gave them for me. But it’s
what I have to show, and I wanted it to be worth showing.

Dad,
    The name on the cover was yours first. I asked you before I used it and you said
go ahead. You and Mom taught me that nothing is true just because somebody says
it is. This book is that lesson, six hundred pages long. I put our name on it because I
wanted one thing in the world with that name on it that nobody handed me, that I
couldn’t have faked, and that I can stand behind in front of anyone. Here it is.
    Julie carries the name now too. So the machine has it third. This is for the two
of you who had it first.

The point

Here’s the whole book in four steps, so you know what you’re carrying. Each step is
motivated by the one before it, and the book goes up them in order.
    One: nothing becomes something for free. Take a blank cell. A square of paper with
nothing on it, a bead that could sit in either of two dips, a bit of memory nobody
has set. Now make it a 0, and keep it a 0. Something is the case now that wasn’t a
moment ago. That moment, nothing becoming something, is never free. It dissipates
by happening, in any real device, in finite time, and keeping it is paid on top, in a
merge or in room.
    Two: so what a computation makes the case is a resource. Computer science
charges a computation for two things, how long it runs and how much room it takes,
and the bits it erases have been counted too. What no model I found charges is the
moment a reading goes up and stays. The Thiele Machine is a model of computation
that does: the step that raises a reading that stays is the step that’s charged. That’s a
few events in a run, not the billions of overwrites a computer makes every second;
what they write doesn’t stay, and the toll leaves them to the erasure count and to
physics.
    Three: the structure a computation makes is made of exactly this. Structure in
general is a relation kept under the changes you choose; Part II takes that word from
the people who wrestled with it. The part a computation makes, and can’t take back,
is a distinction held in its state, and a 0 is the smallest one there is: the ways a cell
could be, sorted into piles, and one pile held. A grouping, an order, a relation a later
move leans on, a fact somebody found out and wrote down: each is a distinction
that stays, on the same bill as the 0. Insight, in the sense this book can price, is a
kept distinction. The toll charges the moment it’s raised; holding it up afterward
costs nothing more. That’s what the book’s other name, No Free Insight, means.
    Four: established is the sharpest case. Two computers can end with the same an-
swer, and only one of them checked it. The difference between them is a distinction
one of them never kept. A record that a claim was checked and closed is a 0 that
stays, with a check in front of it, and it pays the same bill. I build a machine for that
case, all the way down, because it’s the one where you can point at the kept 0 and
at what it cost. It’s the sharpest case of the bill. It isn’t the point. The point is the 0.
    Step one is where the toll gets its reason. If it breaks, the toll goes back to being
only my choice, though the latch, the window, the diagonal and the earned record


                                                     15
16   The point


                 are proved without it and would stand. So that’s where I start: the blank cell, taken
                 apart as far down as I can get before I hit something that holds or something I can’t
                 get under. I’ll tell you which.
                     One warning about how this went, because it explains the shape of everything
                 after it. Most of the time I had the hunch first and found the names later. Over and
                 over, somebody had been here before me. Sometimes that made my day. Sometimes
                 it pissed me off. You’ll see both.


                 Where a 0 comes from

                 Before any machine, the cell. What does it take for there to be a 0 at all?
                     Three things. First, something that can be more than one way. A bead in a dish of
                 water, a speck of magnetised metal, a charge on a tiny capacitor, a square of paper.
                 Nature hands you that much, and it isn’t a 0 yet. It’s stuff that can sit in a lot of
                 arrangements.
                     Second, a sorting. Somebody says which arrangements count as 0, which count
                 as 1, and which count as blank. That’s the first piece of structure Part II gets to: the
                 ways a thing could be, cut into piles. Without it there’s no 0, just a bead somewhere.
                 A 0 and a 1 aren’t things. They’re the two sides of a line somebody drew across the
                 ways a thing can be.
                     Third, a hill. A sorting that drifts isn’t a bit; it’s noise. Something has to hold the
                 bead on its side of the line: a barrier it can’t climb, a latch, a dip it can’t jiggle out
                 of. In the laboratory you’ll meet in Part I, a bead held behind a barrier eight times
                 the size of its own heat jiggle stays put for about fifty minutes, and with the barrier
                 lowered to about twice its jiggle it hops every ten seconds. A distinction that stays is
                 a hill paid for in advance.
                     Put the three together and you have what I’ll call a chair: a distinction that stays.
                 Every 0 and every 1 in every computer is one, and so is a flag that’s up, a written
                 number, a fact somebody checked and wrote down.
                     Now the moment. The cell is blank and you write a 0. Here is everything that
                 step can cost, and the rest of the book only ever adds detail to it.
                     It happens, so it dissipates. Any change a real device makes in a finite time to
                 the chances of its states, sitting in surroundings at some temperature, produces
                 entropy; slower means less, never none. That’s what dissipating means here: entropy
                 produced. Over a cycle that brings the device back to where it started it all leaves
                 as heat; within a single step the heat that leaves can even be negative, when the
                 device’s own entropy goes up.
                     If the blank could have been anything, every way it might have been now lands
                 on one way, the 0. That’s a merge, and it’s the step the physics premise puts a floor
                 under, one that survives going as slowly as you like.
                                                                                           The point   17


    If you knew the cell was blank, nothing uncertain is removed, and no new floor
is owed. The bill didn’t vanish. Somebody made the cell blank, by wiping a cell
that could have held anything, and that wipe was the merge. Or somebody is still
holding the fact that it’s blank, and that fact is itself a 0 somewhere, a chair taken,
which gets paid for when it’s wiped.
    Or you never merge at all: you write every 0 on a fresh cell and never reuse one.
That’s room, and it never comes back. An endless tape can do it forever. A real one
runs out, because a real device can tell apart only finitely many states in a bounded
place. That’s a premise about the world, not a theorem, and nobody has measured
where its ceiling sits.
    So every 0 on every tape of a machine that keeps running was bought in a merge
or in room, on top of the dissipation of the moment it was written. (A machine that
stops slips past, by having no next step at all; Part I says exactly how.) Ordinary
computing looks free because the tape was paid for before the run started, by
whoever made it blank. That’s the bottom of the book. Everything above it is the
same bill at a bigger size: a list kept in order, a measurement written down, a fact
checked and committed to. Each is a distinction that stays, and each is paid for the
way the 0 is.


Why it has to cost

Now the bill for that 0, made exact, and it’s the part I’m proudest of, because once
something stays, the choosing stops and the counting takes over. And the counting
is chairs.
    Take any machine at all. Any number of states, finite or endless, and one rule
that gives the next state. Think of the states as chairs, each one a way the whole
machine can be held, and the machine as somebody moving from chair to chair, one
step at a time. Watch one run and keep a list of the chairs it has sat in. Now look at
the next step. There are exactly three things it can do. It can land on a chair this
run has never sat in: a fresh chair. That’s room, spent now. It can come back, for
the first time, to a chair the run has used, other than the one it started on, and then
it comes from a different chair than the one that got there first. Two chairs, one
landing. That’s a merge: two different states with the same next state, and afterward
the landing can’t tell you which one it came from. Or it can go round a loop: land
back on the very chair it started from, or take a step it has already taken, which is
all a run does after its first return. A loop makes nothing new. That’s all. There is no
fourth thing a step can do, a run merges at most once, and it doesn’t matter how
many chairs there are.
    Now make the machine keep something. Pick a yes-or-no reading of the state
and make it permanent: no step ever turns a yes back into a no. Start on a chair
18   The point


                 that reads no and let some step raise it to yes. From then on the run can never come
                 back to its start, because the start reads no and the yes never comes down. So the
                 run can’t be a loop through its start, and the first time it comes back to any chair it
                 has used, that step is a merge. Either somewhere along the run two chairs share a
                 landing, or it never comes back to a chair and takes a fresh one at every step, forever.
                 Merge or room. Raising something to keep can’t be done going round a loop, the
                 only kind of step that spends neither, because the loop is exactly the step that makes
                 nothing new. Keeping isn’t the only thing that pays this, though. Any run that never
                 comes back to its start merges or takes fresh chairs, whatever it keeps; what keeping
                 adds is that coming back is ruled out. The sharper fact is about the move, and the
                 chairs below show it: when the room runs out, the move that raises a reading that
                 stays has to merge two states itself.
                     Do it with chairs when the room runs out. Draw a box on the floor, three chairs
                 inside, one chair outside by the door. Four people, one per chair: the four states the
                 machine could be in. The three inside already read yes. One step moves everybody
                 at once, each to the chair the rule sends them to. Nobody inside may leave, because
                 yes is permanent. The person by the door has to come in, because this is the step
                 that flips them to yes. Now finish the move, one person per chair. You can’t. Four
                 people, three inside chairs: somebody shares. Maybe the newcomer ends up on a
                 lap, maybe two insiders squeeze onto one chair; either way, two starting places share
                 a destination. Somebody secretly picks a starting chair, the rule moves them, and
                 you’re told only where they ended up: at a shared chair, you can’t say where they
                 started. That’s the pigeonhole principle, which is old and not mine, and the chapter
                 “Why the toll isn’t arbitrary” (Section 3) proves it with exactly three conditions:
                 finitely many chairs that read yes, a yes that stays, and one flip. No physics in it
                 anywhere. Counting.
                     (How old is it? I went looking. A French Jesuit, Jean Leurechon, used it in 1622
                 to argue that two people somewhere must have exactly the same number of hairs
                 on their heads, which is the kind of thing you can be completely sure of and never
                 check. The first name for it I can find came two centuries later, from the German
                 mathematician Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, who used it in print in 1842 without
                 naming it and in later work called it the drawer principle, the Schubfachprinzip; the
                 pigeons came later still. Benoît Rittaud and Albrecht Heeffer, who wrote a short
                 paper in 2014 on what came before Dirichlet, looked for a source for the year 1834
                 that turns up next to his name and found none, and neither have I. Is 1622 the
                 bottom? I can’t tell you. History is like that: it’s where you start digging.)
                     Now give the room endless chairs inside, numbered 1, 2, 3 and on with no end,
                 every one taken, and the newcomer still gets a seat: everybody inside moves up one,
                 from chair n to chair n + 1, and chair 1 comes free. Nobody shares. That’s David
                 Hilbert’s hotel, from a lecture in the 1920s, and it’s no trick. Look at what it took:
                                                                                         The point   19


every single person inside had to get up and move one over, into a chair that was
taken a moment before, to leave one gap, and that only works because the building
has a chair past every chair. That’s the room column, paid in full on every raise.
Richard Dedekind, the German mathematician, made it the definition of infinite in
1888: a collection is infinite exactly when it can be moved one-to-one into a proper
part of itself. So finiteness doesn’t create the bill. A keep is paid in merges or in
room whatever the size of the building, as long as every state has a next one. What
finiteness does is take room off the table, and then the bill has to come as a merge.
    Turn it around and it says the same thing from the other side. A reversible
computer, one where every step can be run backwards, never merges anything,
because a step you can undo never puts two people on one chair. So it can only
pay the keeping bill in room. Charles Bennett, at IBM, showed in 1973 that any
computation can be done reversibly if you give it room to keep its own history while
it works: that’s the room column, written out as a construction. Give a reversible
computer a finite building and it runs out. A one-to-one shuffle of finitely many
chairs always comes back around to where it started, so it can never keep a flag
up; whatever it raises comes back down, as long as every chair has a next one. A
reversible machine that stops slips past this, as Part I shows exactly, and Klaus-Jörn
Lange, Pierre McKenzie and Alain Tapp (2000) built such machines: reversible ones
that do what any deterministic machine does in the same space, up to a constant
factor, and stop with the answer, paying in time. Give it an endless tape to keep its
history on and it keeps everything, never comes back, and pays a fresh stretch of tape
at every step. And a reversible computer isn’t free either. Bennett’s own only moves
forward if it’s pushed, and at any speed above nothing the push dissipates, and in
his walker, in the long run, all of it leaves as heat. Go slower and the dissipation
per step drops, but it never reaches nothing for a run that finishes; Part I proves
that for his model (Theorem 1.8), and the physicists who study changes made in
a finite time (Tim Schmiedl and Udo Seifert for a dragged bead; Naoto Shiraishi,
Ken Funo and Keiji Saito for jump processes) find the same for any change in the
chances of a device’s states that finishes, when those states jump or drift at random
in surroundings at a fixed temperature. So in any real device of that kind every
step that actually changes something dissipates, on average. What a merge adds
is a floor under its heat that no slowness removes, and what room buys is a way
around the floor, never around the dissipation of happening. Time sets how much
you pay above the floor. Only forever makes it zero, and a step that takes forever
never happens.
    Now the physics, as an assumption with its name on it. Rolf Landauer, at IBM,
1961, said that a step that can’t be run backwards, that merges, “requires a minimal
heat generation.” That’s the rule people call Landauer’s principle: when a merge
wipes out a difference the machine really could have been holding, its heat has a
20   The point


                 floor, on average at least k B T ln 2 for every bit of difference lost, however slowly it’s
                 done. Landauer stated it for a memory whose states are alike apart from what they
                 record, a symmetric memory; when the states differ in their own entropy the floor
                 moves, and in a lopsided double well the work to erase has been measured below
                 k B T ln 2. It’s physics, it’s a premise, and no proof in this book reaches it.
                     And here’s his next sentence, which is the whole problem step four is about.
                 That heat, he wrote, “serves the purpose of standardizing signals and making them
                 independent of their exact logical history.” Ordinary machines spend their merges,
                 and their heat, on forgetting how the bits got there, on purpose, so a 1 is a 1 no
                 matter what path made it. You’ll see in step four what that does to two computers
                 that end up holding the same bits. And the very same kind of step, a merge, is what
                 it takes, on any machine whose room runs out, to make something stay for good.
                     So here’s the deepest thing I can say about keeping. Not every forgetting keeps
                 anything: wiping a scratch pad keeps nothing. But every keeping pays. On a
                 machine with finite room it pays by forgetting: the step that makes something stay
                 for good lands two states on one, somewhere, maybe not where you happen to be
                 standing, and afterward nothing can tell which one it was. With endless room it
                 can dodge the merge only by spending room it never gets back. A verdict keeps the
                 decision and lets go of the arguing.
                     Here’s where the bill can go and where it can’t, so you know exactly what you’re
                 being asked to accept. Give the machine unlimited memory and it never has to
                 merge, but it hasn’t got out of anything: it pays room, at every step, forever, on top of
                 the dissipation of every step that changes something, and the chapter “Why the toll
                 isn’t arbitrary” builds that machine and counts its room. Let the flag come back down
                 and nothing is kept, so there’s no keeping bill; the steps still dissipate when they
                 happen. Start the machine from a state you already know and Landauer’s principle,
                 in the form Part I adopts, puts no heat floor under the merge at all (Theorem 3.15),
                 because no uncertainty is wiped. It’s the known blank from a couple of pages back,
                 and the bill sits where it sat there: the step still dissipates when it happens, and
                 the difference was already being kept, by whoever knows the start. The toll I build
                 in Part I charges that step anyway, because it charges the raise, whichever way the
                 raise is paid, for every state the step could be handed. That’s a rule of the ledger, not
                 a claim about heat. The heat itself is physics. In 2012 a group in Lyon erased one
                 bit held in a tiny bead, kept in place by a laser, and found the average heat it gave
                 off coming down toward Landauer’s floor as the erasing was slowed; the principle
                 also has serious critics, the philosopher John Norton among them. So the counting
                 is proved, on any machine, the floor in heat is an assumption, and I never let those
                 two swap places. Section 1 goes all the way down: what a chair is, why writing a
                 single 0 on a blank cell is already a merge, and what the lab has measured.
                                                                                           The point   21


   So that’s the bill. An ordinary computer pays it, in merges and in heat, and keeps
nothing to show for it. What I want is a model of computation that charges for
keeping in the very step that makes something stay. That’s the Thiele Machine.


A bill the usual models don’t count
That’s step one. Step two is what it means for computing.
    Computer science has always counted what a computation costs. How many steps
it takes is time. How many cells it needs is room. Whole fields rest on those two
counts, and on the models built to make them exact: the random-access machine of
the computer scientists Stephen Cook and Robert Reckhow (1973), which charges
each instruction a unit; the cell-probe model (1981) of Andrew Yao, which counts
only the memory cells a program reads; the input-output model of Alok Aggarwal
and Jeffrey Vitter (1988), which counts only the blocks moved between a small
fast memory and a large slow one. Each of those computes exactly what Turing’s
machine computes. They differ only in what they count, and the counting is the
reason to have them. Manuel Blum gave two axioms in 1967 for any measure of
computational cost at all; they name no machine and say what every cost has to
satisfy.
    Now look at the bill from step one. Every time a computation makes something
the case and keeps it, a bit set, a list left in order, an answer written down, it pays,
in a merge or in room. That bill isn’t the time count: a slow step and a fast one can
keep the same thing. It isn’t the space count either, though room is one of the two
ways to pay it: a machine with a fixed memory pays it by merging, over and over, in
the same cells, and its space count never moves. Its merge half has been counted
before. Ming Li and Paul Vitányi (1996) took as axioms of a model of computation
that a step that can be undone costs nothing and that every bit a computation
irreversibly erases costs one unit, and Erik Demaine and three coauthors (2016) put
that count on the random-access machine, beside time and space. What none of
them charges, as far as I found, is the moment a chosen reading goes up and stays,
whichever way that keep is paid. That’s a third thing a computation does, and it’s
what this model adds. It isn’t a cost in Blum’s sense. Blum asks that “this run costs
exactly m” be decidable, and here it isn’t: a program that runs another program and
makes one mark if that one halts costs exactly one exactly when the other halts, so
deciding its cost would decide halting. (A run that never stops can also have a finite
bill, where Blum leaves the cost undefined, but that alone isn’t a violation; it’s the
decidability that fails.)
    So here’s the Thiele Machine, all of it. It’s a model of computation, math you
can reason about, the way Turing’s machine is. It has five parts and one rule. A set
of states. A set of moves. A step that takes a state and a move to the next state. A
22   The point


                 price on each move, a whole number of marks. And a reading of the state, yes or no.
                 The rule, which I call the toll: a step that turns the reading from no to yes costs at
                 least one mark. The toll sits on the raise, not on the merge, so it charges the keep
                 whichever way it’s paid, merge or room. Two more pieces come in when a result
                 needs them: a counter in the state that adds up the marks and only climbs, which is
                 the ledger, and a window, what an outside observer gets to see. The toll’s first name,
                 the one I gave it before I understood it, is No Free Insight.
                     It computes nothing new, any more than the cell-probe model does. What it adds
                 is a place, in the step itself, for what a computation made the case and what that
                 cost. Which reading? Any yes-or-no reading at all; the toll charges every step that
                 turns it on. The readings this book cares about are the ones that, once yes, stay yes,
                 because those are the kept distinctions and keeping is what the bill is for. The blank
                 cell’s “it’s a 0 now” is one. “This list has been put in order” is one. “This claim was
                 checked and closed” is one. The model doesn’t care which, and for readings that
                 stay, Part I derives the toll from the bill, on stated premises. A reading that flips back
                 and forth isn’t a record of anything: Part II calls it a toggle and proves it’s the latch
                 of no event (Section 10).
                     One what, and why one? One mark, in the model’s own count. One because
                 it’s the least a whole-number count can charge and still not be free, and the toll
                 only says not free. A mark isn’t a joule. What ties it to heat is Landauer’s principle,
                 named, and nothing else.
                     And here’s the thing to hold on to through the whole book, because it’s where
                 readers go wrong and where I went wrong for a long time. The ledger is a count,
                 not a lock. It doesn’t stop anybody from doing anything. It adds up the prices you
                 chose for the moves that ran, writes the sum down where the machine can’t lose it,
                 and the toll makes each raise of the reading you chose cost at least one. It doesn’t
                 measure merges, room or heat: a merge that keeps nothing can cost no marks, room
                 is spent at every step and charged at most once, at the raise, and where a merge
                 raises nothing, a bill of one mark per raise leaves that merge out. What ties the
                 count to the bill is a theorem, not a reading of a dial: on a machine with finitely
                 many states reading yes, any price list that charges merges has to charge each raise
                 of a reading that stays at least one. What a kept reading means, whether a reading
                 that’s up stands for anything, is a separate question with a separate answer, and
                 Part III gives it for one case: an order the step enforces, which is the lock. A lock
                 would work at a price of zero. The price isn’t there to make the lock work. It’s there
                 because, on a machine where every state has a next one, the raise of a reading that
                 stays merges or takes room, whether anybody writes it down or not.
                                                                                           The point   23


What I found, what I assumed and what I chose
I didn’t invent a machine. I found one. That’s how I see this work, and I’ll be straight
about the difference between that conviction and a theorem before I do anything
else.
    That sentence walks straight into one of the oldest fights in mathematics, so
here’s a short trip into it first. G. H. Hardy, a Cambridge number theorist who wrote
A Mathematician’s Apology in 1940 to defend doing mathematics for its own sake,
came down on the found side about as hard as anyone ever has: mathematical
reality, he wrote, lies outside the people who study it, and the theorems they like
to call their creations are really just notes on what they saw there. The German
mathematician Leopold Kronecker supposedly split the difference: God made the
whole numbers, and everything else is the work of people. Supposedly, because push
on that line and it gets thin fast. It comes down through Heinrich Weber, another
German mathematician, in a memorial piece written after Kronecker died, pointing
back to a lecture from 1886, and that’s the only source I could find anybody citing.
A great line with one witness. (The record chapter of Part I, Section 2, stops early
on to ask how many witnesses a claim ought to need. The answer is more than
one.) So does any of this settle whether I found the Thiele Machine or made it
up? No. A proof doesn’t settle it either: showing what follows from the premises
doesn’t decide whether you found the theorem or made it. That’s why it’s labelled a
conviction. What it changes is how I hold the thing: like something that was already
there, which means I can be wrong about its shape and the shape won’t care. And to
be exact about what “found” covers: the parts the counting forces on you, the latch
shape and the merge or the room. The event to record, the price list, and putting
the count inside the step are choices, mine, and the three lists below say which is
which.
    Here is the line between what nothing let me choose, what I had to assume, and
what I did choose, because everything after this depends on where it falls. Read the
first list as the ground, the second as what the ground is taken to stand on, and the
third as the model built on it.
    Found: what counting forces on any machine.
• Run a machine that gives each state exactly one next state. It takes fresh states
  until it first comes back to one it has used; that return lands on its start or is a
  merge, two states with one next state; and after it the run only repeats steps it
  already took. There’s no fourth thing a step can do, and a run merges at most
  once (Theorem 1.1).
• So any run that never comes back to its start merges somewhere or takes a
  fresh state at every step. A reading that goes from no to yes and never comes
  back rules the return out, so every run that raises it merges or takes fresh states
24   The point


                   (Proposition 3.4). The sharper fact is about the move: when only finitely many
                   states read yes, the move that raises the reading merges two states (Theorem 3.1
                   for a finite machine, Proposition 3.3 when only the yes-states are finitely many).
                   A machine that can stop, with a state that has no next state at all, slips past this,
                   and Part I says exactly how (Theorem 1.2). That’s counting. No physics.
                 • Over any machine at all, a record that the computation drives and that never
                   comes down is a latch on one event: it switches on the first time something
                   happens and nothing switches it off (Observation 10.1). That’s counting too,
                   given the two conditions in it.
                   Assumed: what the found list is taken to stand on, in the world.
                 • A merge of states the machine really could have been in has a floor under its
                   heat, on average, however slowly it’s done, in a memory whose states are alike
                   apart from what they record. That’s Landauer’s principle, the premise from
                   thermodynamics, named and assumed and never proved here, with its critics
                   named.
                 • A real device can tell apart only finitely many states in any bounded place, so
                   room runs out. Nobody has measured where that ceiling sits.
                 • The clean start. A raised record means the event happened only because the
                   record was down at the start, and that start is put in by hand. It’s a past hypothesis
                   in miniature. The past hypothesis, the philosopher David Albert’s name (2000)
                   for an assumed low-entropy beginning of the universe, is an idea that goes back
                   to Boltzmann; several accounts of why records point to the past lean on it, and
                   every theorem here about records gets its arrow from an assumed clean start
                   (Section 10).
                   Chosen: what the model adds, each of which could have gone another way.
                 • To put the account inside the step, as part of what a step is. Two things go there.
                   That the record stays and the computing can’t reach it has to: a rule kept by the
                   step holds of every program, and a log a program keeps holds of that program
                   only. The count can go there or not: it’s the sum of the prices along the run, so a
                   log of the run holds the same number. I keep it in the step so every state carries
                   its own bill, and that part is presentation, not necessity. On the certified machine
                   of Part III the step also keeps the order, check, then commit, then certify, for the
                   same reason.
                 • The toll itself: a whole mark, at least one, on the step that raises a reading,
                   whichever way the keep is paid. On a finite machine it follows from a price on
                   merging, and that price is a choice too; on a machine that pays in room, the toll
                   is simply declared.
                                                                                            The point   25


• Which readings matter: the ones that never come down. The toll charges any
  reading’s rise; permanence is what makes the rise a keep, and it’s a choice. So is
  one next state for every state, the condition the stopping hole gets around.
• Which event gets a record, and what price list the record pays. The latch leaves
  both free. And on a machine that pays in room, where the write merges nothing,
  the record stays up because I declare that it does (Theorem 10.3).
• On the machine of Part III, where its ordinary computer ends and its record
  begins, and the form of its certifying move: it treats the rest of the state the same
  whichever way the flag reads, so it keeps no copy of the old reading. The merge
  is not a second choice. Given that form, the flag’s two readings go to one, and
  the state with the flag down and the same state with it up land together. A record
  kept as a list that only grows keeps the copy, raises its reading with no merge,
  and pays in room instead.
   The machine Part III builds is one worked demonstration of the third list, on one
reading. Nothing in the first list needs it.


What structure is made of
Step three. A 0 is the smallest structure there is, and the rest of structure is the same
thing at a bigger size.
     What’s a sorting of a pile into groups? A distinction: these go together, those
don’t. Keep it and it’s a chair taken, on the same bill. What’s an ordering? Every
pair compared, and the answers kept. What’s a fact somebody found out and wrote
down? A distinction between the ways things could have been and the way they
were, kept. A machine can carry any of those in its state and in its rules, and each
one it keeps is paid for the way the 0 is. Part II goes through the people who wrestled
with the word structure, from Pythagoras to category theory, and comes out at that:
structure is distinctions held in a state.
     That gives insight an exact meaning, a narrower one than you might want, and
I’ll be honest about how narrow. Finding something out doesn’t have to pay the
merge. Bennett showed that you can write down what you see on a blank page
without merging anything, so Landauer’s floor isn’t owed; the page is what you
spend, and it can be handed back while the original is still there. Making it stay is
what pays. Learning borrows, committing pays. The insight the toll prices is the
committed kind: a distinction made to stay. Whether that narrower thing deserves
the word is a fair thing to argue about, and Part I argues it, where learning and
committing get pulled apart.
     Then Part II asks what follows, on any machine, once a distinction is kept and
the keeping is charged. The ledger is a chair too: a number that only climbs takes a
26   The point


                 fresh value for every mark. A window that shows only part of a state can hide the
                 very distinction that was paid for, and when it hides it, no bill read off the window
                 can be exact. A later step can be entitled to something because a distinction stayed,
                 and the entitlement has an exact count. Over any machine at all, a reading the
                 machine’s own steps turn on and nothing turns off is a latch, the blank cell’s 0 one
                 level up. And there’s a wall no level gets past: no state codes every question about
                 the states.


                 Established

                 Step four, the sharpest case, and the one I build a machine for.
                    Two computers each get the same messy list and each end up holding it sorted.
                 One sorted it. The other was handed the sorted list and copied it in. Same bits
                 in memory, byte for byte. Ask me which is which and I can’t tell you, and neither
                 machine can tell you either. The difference was real: one of them ran a check that
                 could have come out no. It just wasn’t kept. Nothing in an ordinary computer’s
                 end state holds “this was checked.” Ordinary computers spend their merges on
                 forgetting how their bits got there, on purpose, so that a 1 is a 1 whatever path
                 made it. That’s step one’s bill, paid, with nothing kept for it.
                    Established is the name for the difference. An answer is established when a check
                 that could have said no said yes, about that very answer, and the result was made to
                 stay. That last part is a kept distinction, a 0 in some cell that says “checked,” and it
                 pays the same bill as every other 0. Part III opens by taking that apart (Section 14):
                 what “could have said no” means, what settling a question is, and why the people
                 who thought hardest about knowledge kept landing near it.
                    Then it builds the machine, in two layers. Underneath is an ordinary computer,
                 as small as I could make it: two counters that add one and take one away, which
                 Marvin Minsky proved can compute anything a Turing machine can. Its own merges
                 are an ordinary computer’s merges, and the ledger leaves them alone. On top sits
                 a record layer whose flag is the blank cell. Raising the flag is the write of a 0: the
                 state with the flag down and the same state with it already up both land on one
                 state. That’s a merge, the one step one is about, and once merges in that layer are
                 priced, the toll on the flag follows as a theorem (Theorem 3.17). The machine’s toll
                 charges the 0 in the step itself.
                    What makes a raised flag mean something is the lock, and it’s one rule: no flag
                 without a commitment, and no commitment without a check of that same claim
                 that passed, with the thing checked untouched since (a counter’s edition is how
                 many times it has been written, so “untouched” means the edition hasn’t moved;
                 the machine of Part III calls it the counter’s version). The rule is in the step, so it
                 holds of every program anybody can write for the machine, buggy and hostile ones
                                                                                             The point   27


included. A log a program keeps tells you about that program. A rule in the step
tells you about all of them.
    How far the machine reaches, to other models of computation and to universal
machines that run it as a guest and earn its flag again, is proved too; Part III states it
(Section 16) and the appendices build it. That’s the reach of the case, not what the
book is about.


What’s proved, what’s argued, and what I just believe
Every claim in this book has a status and I’ll tell you which, every time. Here’s the
whole list at once, in the order of the four steps, so you know what I’m on the hook
for.
    Proved, step one, on any machine with one next state for every state, finite
or endless: every step lands on a fresh state, merges two states into one, or goes
round a loop, and a run that keeps a reading up can’t be on a loop through its start,
so it merges somewhere or spends fresh room at every step. Heat or room. On
finitely many states, a noisy step that keeps the even spread and a quantum step that
keeps lengths can’t raise a reading that stays up either. And a coarse merge forces
something at every finer zoom it’s exact about (when a coarse picture merges, a
finer picture it’s exact about merges too, steps out of the states the picture describes,
or has no end), and for a bounded memory the room runs out at an exact count.
With finitely many states reading yes and a reading that never comes down, every
move that raises it merges states, which is the chairs. That a merge carries a heat
floor is Landauer’s premise, and that every change a real device makes in a finite
time dissipates is cited physics; neither is proved here.
    Proved, step two: with finitely many states reading yes, every schedule that
prices merges charges the move that raises a kept reading, which is the toll, derived;
and anything that obeys the toll pays at least one mark every time its reading goes
from no to yes, which is the universal floor. Finding out doesn’t have to merge: copy
what you see onto a blank page and you learn something with no two states landing
on one, so a price list on merges can charge it nothing. It isn’t free. It borrows room,
the blank page, and the copy can be handed back while the original’s still there. A
commitment can’t be handed back, so the toll lands on committing. Put a number
on that, on a finite machine whose price list charges every bit a move removes, and
it’s the certainty bill: what anyone learns about where a machine started is either
still held in its state or was paid for in marks, at most one bit a mark.
    Proved, step three: a window that shows a step raising a kept reading and a quiet
one alike, before and after, can’t price the raise exactly, however clever it is. Over
any machine, a reading the machine’s own events turn on and nothing turns off is a
28   The point


                 latch on one event, with two choices left free: the price list and which event. And
                 no state codes every question about the states.
                     Proved, step four, inside its one case, on the smallest machine I could build, six
                 instruction kinds on two counters: for every program anybody can write, from a
                 clean start, a raised flag always went through a passing check, then a commitment,
                 then a certificate, of exactly the same claim about exactly the same edition, with
                 claims about any property that comes with a checker proved to mean it and an
                 exact test for telling properties apart, “sorted” included (Section 15). Every such run
                 incurred at least three marks, and three is reached. The machine meets a definition
                 I call certified Thiele-complete, which asks that the record be earned, on top of
                 everything the bar below asks.
                     Defined, and proved about, over any base and any event: a machine is Thiele-
                 complete when its computing is universal, costs no marks and can’t touch the
                 record, the record stays, starts are blank, and some run’s record tells two starts
                 apart (Section 10.8). A clock fails it, every machine that meets it hides its record
                 and its ledger from its own window, and any universal base becomes one by adding
                 marks, all by theorem. Certified Thiele-complete is exactly Thiele-complete with
                 clean starts, an earned record (the chain, a checker proved sound, claims that stay
                 true while what they’re about is unchanged) and a claim that could have failed
                 added (Theorem 15.18).
                     Argued only: that the structure a computation makes is kept distinctions, priced
                 by the toll, while a reading that undoable moves keep never rises and is never
                 charged; that’s a choice of what to price, and on a finite machine the second half is
                 proved.
                     Argued only: that an account of computation should carry what a computation
                 made the case, and what it cost, in how it steps. The proofs show that it hangs
                 together, what it follows from, and what it costs; whether it ought to be adopted is
                 a claim about what matters, which no theorem decides.
                     Guessed at, with the ways to kill it written down, and only about step four: that
                 among kept distinctions the one most worth recording is certification, because its
                 records are the ones that get copied and relied on all over the place by parties who
                 didn’t produce them (the pointer thesis, Part III).
                     Not proved, and I’ll say so every time it’s tempting: any physical price for one
                 mark, anything about a physical device running any of this, or anything about which
                 problems are hard.
                     Which of the proved part is new? Not one big thing, and I’d be suspicious of me
                 if I said otherwise. By my own sorting at the back (Appendix C), each piece has
                 its neighbours standing right there. Start from the top. The small machine and its
                 universal programs carry the reference monitor’s every-program move (Anderson
                 in 1972) to a record that’s priced and earned; the two-player game check in the
                                                                                             The point   29


appendices (Appendix H) is careful engineering on known mathematics. The latch
has the 1918 flip-flop and write-once memory for neighbours. The window fact is
an old fact about functions, from Edward Moore’s 1956 thought experiments and
Rudolf Kalman’s observability, with a price put on it. The toll derived from finiteness,
permanence and a price on merging is a ledger form of the core underneath. And
that core, step one’s bill, is old mathematics: the pigeonhole principle, Dedekind’s
1888 definition of infinite and the finite heart of Ernst Zermelo’s 1896 recurrence
argument, with Landauer and Bennett on merging and Thomas Ouldridge and David
Wolpert’s 2023 price in entropy on the merges a finite automaton can’t avoid. For
deterministic machines the arrangement is old too: Ming Li and Paul Vitányi (1996)
wrote that a bounded memory forces erasure in the long run, and Demaine and
his coauthors (2016) that extra room only postpones it. What I’d defend most is
there, at the bottom, in the form I didn’t find: one law with three columns and no
fourth, stated alike for deterministic, noisy and quantum steps, with two small exact
lemmas, the chair count and the bill at every scale, and a toll on a reading that stays,
which charges the keep whichever column pays it.
   What this book is not. Not a solution to P versus NP, and not a complexity-class
separation of any other kind. Not a theory of everything. Not a claim that compu-
tation is physics, or that physics is computation. Not a physics result: Landauer’s
principle enters only as a premise with its name on it, and nothing here derives it.
Not a quantum computer; its theorems about quantum strategies are mathematics
about vectors and matrices. Not a chip or a device of any kind. Not a claim to
priority on the ideas it builds from. Not closed on every question: the ones I couldn’t
settle are listed at the end of the claim ledger (Section 21).


How the book goes

Part I is the bill. What a chair is, and what every step of every machine does to the
chairs it has; the smallest thing that writes the bill into its own step, as one rule, the
toll; whether the rule is forced, and on which premises; and why finding out only
borrows, where committing pays. If the book breaks, I’d bet it breaks there, so that’s
where to aim first.
    Part II is structure, as kept distinctions: the word itself, from the people who
wrestled with it, and then what follows on any machine once a distinction is kept
and the keeping charged. The ledger, the window, entitlement, the latch, and the
wall no level gets past.
    Part III is the sharpest case. What established means, the machine that keeps it,
how far the machine reaches, five real systems that keep records and whether they
price the write, the thesis about which kept distinction is worth paying for, and what
its counter has to do with heat.
30   The point


                    Part IV is where you aim at all of it: how to break each claim, the ledger of what’s
                 proved and what isn’t, the fence around what I’ve shown, and the conclusion. After
                 that, how I got here, for anyone who wants the story; then the appendices, which
                 carry the full constructions the main text only states.

         Part I is step one, and the rule step two needs. It starts at the smallest structure
     there is: a cell that’s blank, and then a 0. First the bill itself, before any price list:
     what a chair is, what every step of every machine does to the chairs it has, and what
     it costs for something to go from nothing to something and stay. Then the smallest
