CHAPTER 1




What a chair is

A cell can be blank, or 0, or 1, and somebody has drawn the lines between those.
Write a 0 in it and it stays a 0. That’s the event this whole book is about, nothing
becoming something, and this chapter is its bill, before any machine and before any
price list.
    A chair is a distinction that stays. A cell on a tape that reads 0, and not 1, and not
blank. A bead sitting in the left well and not the right. A flag that is up. Anything
the world can tell apart from something else and keeps telling apart. It takes three
things: something that can be more than one way, a sorting of its ways into piles,
and a hill that keeps it in its pile. The point said so in pictures (“Where a 0 comes
from”). Here I want two things exactly: what every step of every machine does to
the chairs it has, and what it costs for a chair to be filled at all. Both answers are
proofs, and every one of them is short enough to follow on the page. Nothing in this
chapter needs a price list, and the toll, named up front, is stated exactly only in the
next chapter, which writes this bill into a machine’s step; the one after asks whether
it had to.


1.1 Every step does one of three things
Forget the cell for a moment. Forget finiteness. Take any machine at all, with any
number of states and any rule that gives each state exactly one next state, and watch
it run from any start. Keep a list of the chairs it has sat in. Now look at one step, the
next one. There are exactly three things it can do.
    It can land on a chair nobody in this run has sat in. A fresh chair. That’s room,
spent on this step. The only way to get it back is to go back to where you were, and
a run that does that has kept nothing.
    It can come back, for the first time in the run, to a chair somebody sat in before,
and not the chair the run started from. Then it came from a different chair than the
one that first got there. Two chairs, one landing. That’s a merge, and a merge is a
literal collision: two different states with the same next state. Under Landauer’s
premise a merge of states that were really possible carries a floor of heat, and no
amount of going slowly lowers it.
    Or it can land back on the very chair it started from, or take a step the run has
already taken. Then the machine is going round a loop. Not “might be.” Is. A

                                                   33
34   1 What a chair is


               machine with one rule for the next state, once it stands where it stood before, does
               again what it did before, forever. Every later state is one it already had, and every
               later step is one it already took. It is computing nothing new.
                  That’s all. There is no fourth thing a step can do, and every run has the same
               shape: fresh chairs, then at most one return, and after it nothing but steps already
               taken. The proof is one line: the first time a run comes back to a chair, either it
               came back to its very first chair, which is a pure loop from the start, or the step that
               brought it back shares the chair with the step that first got there, which is a merge.
               So a run merges at most once; going round the loop it settles into doesn’t merge
               again.


               Theorem 1.1 (The step law). Let a step give every state of a set exactly one next
               state, where the states can be told apart, and run it from any start x0 , writing
               x0 , x1 , x2 , . . . for the run. Either every step is fresh, landing on a state the run has
               not visited, or there is a first step that lands on a visited state, from xn to xn+1 = x j
               with j ≤ n, and then: every step before it is fresh; it lands on the start (j = 0), or
               it is a merge, coming from a different state than the one that first reached x j , so
               that two distinct states share a next state; and from x j on the run is periodic, so
               every later state is one the run already had and every later step, from xk to xk+1
               with k > n, is a step the run already took. In a run at most one pair of distinct states
               shares a next state, x j−1 and xn , and the step that first joins them is the only merge;
               later laps retake it.

               Proof. If no state repeats, every step is fresh. Otherwise take the first step that
               lands on a visited state, from xn to xn+1 , and the position j ≤ n with x j = xn+1 ;
               it is unique, because x0 , . . . , xn are all different. Every earlier step is fresh, by the
               choice of n. If j > 0, compare x j−1 , which first reached x j , with xn : both land on x j .
               They differ, because xn = x j−1 with j − 1 < n would be an earlier repeat. So two
               distinct states share a next state: a merge. Either way, since one rule gives the next
               state, xn+1 = x j gives xn+1+k = x j+k for every k, so the run repeats with period
               p = n + 1 − j from position j on. For k > n the step from xk to xk+1 is then the step
               from xk− p to xk− p+1 , taken earlier, and every later state is one of x j , . . . , xn . No later
               step merges: it lands where an earlier step from the same state landed, and the only
               two distinct states with a shared next state in the run are x j−1 and xn .
                   So here is “nothing is kept for free” as a theorem with two hypotheses: you can
               tell states apart, and each state has one next state. The only step that pays neither
               room nor a merge is a step on a loop, and a loop makes nothing new. Anything new
               is a fresh chair or a shared one. That’s the bill for keeping. There’s a second bill on
               top of it: a real step that changes a device’s state in a real amount of time dissipates
                                                                1.1 Every step does one of three things   35


just by happening. That one is time’s bill: I prove it below for Bennett’s walker,
and the physicists have it for devices sitting in surroundings at a temperature. The
reading that stays up is the way to force “new”: a reading that was no and is now
yes can never come back to the chair it started on, so the run can’t be a loop through
its start. Its first return to any chair it has used, if it ever has one, is a merge; if it
never has one, every chair it takes is fresh. Two chapters on, that’s the first part of
Proposition 3.4, where the room gets counted exactly. (After a merge the run can
settle onto a loop among chairs that read yes and idle there, making nothing new.
The keep was paid at the merge.)
    One hole, and it’s worth seeing exactly. A machine that stops. Two chairs. The
first reads no, the step takes it to the second, which reads yes, and the second has
no next step at all. Reading raised, no merge, no fresh chair after that, nothing. The
step law assumed every state has a next state, and a machine that stops its clock
dodges it. Close the hole either way and the bill comes back. Say the halted state’s
next state is itself, which is the usual way to give a stopped machine a step, and
the halt is a merge: the moving state and the halted state both land on the halted
state. Or keep the machine physically stopped, and something has to hold it there, a
barrier, a hill, a latch, which is a chair paid for before the run began. The cost of
halting hides in holding.



Theorem 1.2 (Halting). A partial step, one that may have no next state, can raise a
permanent reading on two states with no two states sharing a next state. Totalising
it, with the halted state stepping to itself, makes the raise a merge: the halted state
and the state that steps onto it share a next state. In general, once every halted state
steps to itself, any other state that steps onto a halted state shares that landing with
it.

Proof. States a and b, reading no on a and yes on b; a steps to b and b has no next
state. No two states step to the same state, because only a steps at all. Totalise:
b steps to b, and now a and b both step to b, a merge of two distinct states. The
general case is the same two lines: if c ̸= h steps to the halted state h and h steps to
h, then c and h share a next state.
   Stepping the halted state to itself is one way to totalise. Step it to a fresh sink
state instead and the sink is the held chair of the paragraph above, paid for before
the run began; let it tick a counter instead and the counter is room. The bill moves
columns. It doesn’t go away.
36   1 What a chair is


               1.2 A chair is a distinction that stays
               Now the cell. A blank cell could be anything. Write a 0 in it and it is a 0, and it stays
               a 0. That moment, nothing becoming something, is an event, and like every change
               a real device makes in a real amount of time, it dissipates when it happens. Time’s
               bill, below, says how much. And if the blank could have been anything, fixing it to a
               0 also wipes out what it might have been, and that part carries a floor no slowness
               takes away: it’s the merge I’m about to show you. Here I want the other part of the
               price, the part for keeping it, from the step law and nothing else.
                   And the cell isn’t a floor. Describe whatever holds it, a bead in two dips, the
               molecules that jostle the bead, whatever holds those, and you’ve described states
               that can be told apart and a way they change: a machine of the same kind, on
               the same bill, because a merge one level up forces a merge or room one level
               down, as long as the level below stays among the states the one above describes
               (Theorem 1.9). Every level you can describe is one of these. Under all of them
               there’s nothing told apart at all, and that’s the nothing a blank cell stands for.
                   Three states: blank, zero, one. The reading is “the cell is definite,” no on
               blank and yes on the other two, and a written cell stays written, so the reading is
               permanent. The move is “write a 0,” which takes blank to zero and leaves a written
               cell alone. Now look. Blank lands on zero, and zero lands on zero. Two chairs, one
               landing. Writing a 0 on nothing is, by itself, a merge. When you don’t know whether
               the cell was blank or already 0, that merge owes Landauer’s floor on top of the
               dissipation of happening, and no slowness removes it. When you know it was blank,
               the floor goes where the knowing is, as you’ll see below. The history in which the
               cell was blank and the history in which it already held a 0 are now the same history.
               That’s not an analogy to the step law. It’s the step law with three states filled in.
                   The obvious way round it is a fourth state that remembers: “0, and it was
               blank before.” Now blank goes somewhere fresh. But the remembering state
               has to go somewhere on the next write too, and it’s written, so it has to stay
               written. Every written chair is already taken: zero and one land on themselves,
               and the remembering state is where blank landed. So it shares. In the smallest
               version it lands on itself, and then blank and the remembering state share a chair.
               No finite extension of the cell gets out of the merge, and the reason is counting
               (Proposition 3.3, two chapters on), not bad luck. The only way to write with no
               merge, once every state has a next one, is endless room: a fresh state for every
               write, forever, such as a new cell of an endless tape for each one (it comes back two
               chapters on, as the first of three doors out of a theorem, Door one). That isn’t getting
               out of the bill. It dodges the floor by paying room, without limit, and each write still
               dissipates when it happens. Or, in a form I need below, a tape that stretches both
               ways with the machine stepping one cell along it. Every cell has one before it and
                                                               1.2 A chair is a distinction that stays   37


one after it, nothing ever shares, the reading “past the start” goes up on the first
step and never comes down, and the machine never returns. That’s the bilateral
shift, and it pays room at every step.


Theorem 1.3 (The write of a 0 merges, and only room avoids it). (1) On the three
states blank, zero, one, with reading “definite,” writing a 0 is permanent, raises the
reading from blank, and merges blank with zero. (2) Adding a fourth state that
remembers the cell was blank, with written cells staying written, does not avoid
the merge: on the four states the write still merges two distinct states. The same
holds on any finite set of states. (3) On an endless tape, writing adds one cell and is
one-to-one; on the integers, the step “one cell along” is a bijection, raises “past the
start” on the first step, keeps it up, and after any positive number of steps is away
from where it started.

Proof. (1) Blank and zero both step to zero, and blank is not zero; zero and one step
to themselves, so a written cell stays written. (2) Blank steps to the remembering
state, and permanence sends each of the three written states, zero, one and the
remembering state, to a written state. So four states land among the three written
ones, and two of them share a landing. On any finite set of states the same count
works: permanence sends the finitely many written states among themselves, blank
lands among them too, so one more state lands among them than there are, and
two share a landing (Proposition 3.3, two chapters on, states it in general). (3) “Add
one” on the counting numbers is one-to-one and never returns to zero; “add one”
on the integers is one-to-one and onto, sends 0 to 1, sends every number that is at
least 1 to one that is at least 1, and after k > 0 steps has moved by k.
   One thing the theorem leans on, and I want it in the open. The write is a move
defined on every state of the cell, written ones included, and a written cell stays
written, so the state blank merges with is a cell that was already written. A write
defined only on blank, with the machine simply stopping when it meets a written
cell, merges nothing. That’s the stopping hole above (Theorem 1.2): it buys the 0
by having no next step at all.
   Here is what the theorem buys. A fact is a distinction that stays, and a kept
distinction is a chair you can’t give back. The machine is the thing whose state
includes the chairs it can’t give back.
   It doesn’t stop at the cell. The tape is a set of distinctions that stayed. So is the
rule for the next state, and so is the question you ask of a chair. Each of the five
parts of the model is itself a definite thing where there could have been anything;
the model doesn’t charge for them, but they’re the same kind of thing it charges for.
And the model can run itself: a host that pays the toll and runs a guest move for
38   1 What a chair is


               move pays at least a mark in its own ledger for every step where the guest’s record
               went up, and Part III states one (Section 16; Appendix D builds it). The tower is the
               same kind of machine above and below. What no level does is hold all the questions
               you can ask of it: for any way of coding readings as states, there’s a reading no
               state codes, the one that answers each state with the opposite of what that state’s
               own coded reading says of it. That’s Cantor’s diagonal, the shape of Russell’s 1902
               letter to Frege (Section 5), and the subject of Section 13. Put the two together and
               you have the regress exactly: every level runs the one below and pays again, in its
               own ledger, for every rise of the lower level’s record, and no level ever holds every
               question about itself.


               Theorem 1.4 (No level holds its own questions). For any set of states and any
               assignment of a yes/no reading to each state, some yes/no reading on the states is
               assigned to no state.

               Proof. Take the reading that says, of each state, the opposite of what that state’s
               assigned reading says of the state itself. If some state were assigned it, that state
               would answer itself both ways.
                  The regress has a price too. Write a 0 on a cell you know is blank and Landauer’s
              premise sets no floor: the entropy before and after are both zero (Theorem 3.15,
              two chapters on, does the arithmetic). The write still dissipates when it happens.
              What’s missing is a floor that survives going slowly, and it’s missing only for a writer
              built for this one cell, knowing it’s blank. A writer that writes 0 on whatever it’s
              handed, blank or 0, keeps a floor on the worse of the two however slowly it goes
              (Section 3.7 says how much). So where did the floor go, for the writer built knowing?
              Into the knowing. “This cell is blank” is a distinction that stays, a record, and the
              entitlement count of Section 8 says how much a record like that has to say: at least
              the rounded-up logarithm of how many possibilities it picks among, one yes-or-no
              question per halving. Blank among three possibilities is two questions. Blank among
              “it could have been anything” is as many as you like. Whoever knows the cell is
              blank is keeping that distinction, and the bill for it was paid in the knowing, or will
              be paid when that record is wiped. And the chair the 0 sits in was paid for before
              the run, by whoever built the cell.


               1.3 A reversible machine keeps nothing

               Bennett’s reversible machine never shares a chair; that’s what reversible means. Put
               one on a finite building and watch it. It has to revisit a chair within as many steps
               as there are chairs, by the pigeonhole. The step law says the first revisit is a merge
                                                                                 1.4 Noisy chairs   39


or a return to the start, and a merge is impossible for it. So it returns to its start.
And once it’s back at its start it does everything again. Any reading it raised has
come back down. A reversible finite machine with a next state for every state keeps
nothing. Not as a slogan: as a theorem. One that stops slips past, as the stopping
hole above says, and keeps what it halted on. It is the recurrence Zermelo threw at
Boltzmann (Section 3 tells that story), in its finite form, proved from the step law
and the pigeonhole and nothing else. What Bennett’s machine keeps is the room
it’s handed: on an endless tape it can keep its whole history and never come back,
taking a fresh chair every step, and the tape was paid for before the first step by
whoever built it. A reversible machine dodges the merge and its floor. A real one,
in contact with its surroundings, doesn’t dodge the dissipation of happening: run
slowly it’s cheap, never free, and it pays room besides.


Theorem 1.5 (Reversible keeps nothing). Let a one-to-one step act on finitely many
states. From any start the run returns to the start after some positive number of
steps, and any reading that is no at the start and never goes from yes to no is no at
every step.

Proof. Among the first (number of states) plus one states of the run, two are equal,
by the pigeonhole. Take two equal positions and cancel the one-to-one step back
from both the same number of times, until the earlier one reaches the start; the later
one then equals the start. So the run returns to the start after a positive number of
steps, and from then on repeats. If the reading were yes at some step, it would stay
yes from there, in particular at a later multiple of the period, where the state is the
start, which reads no.


1.4 Noisy chairs

Real chairs are noisy. The bead hops on its own. So take the step to be a table
of chances: from each chair, the chance of landing on each chair next, every row
adding to one. A permanent reading is a set of chairs you never leave once you’re in
it. And “no merge” has an exact noisy meaning: the step preserves the even spread.
Start with everybody spread evenly over the chairs, take one step, and they’re still
spread evenly; which is to say every column of the table adds to one as well as every
row. That’s a step that squeezes nothing on average.
    Then the cell’s count goes through with chances in place of people. A step that
preserves the even spread cannot raise a permanent reading from any chair outside
it, not with small chance, with none. Count the chance flowing into the yes-chairs
from everywhere. Column by column that’s one per yes-chair, so it equals the
40   1 What a chair is


               number of yes-chairs. The yes-chairs alone already send exactly that much, because
               they never leave. What’s left over for the outside chairs is zero, and it’s a sum of
               chances, so each is zero.
                  And it runs the other way too. A step that can raise a permanent reading does
               not preserve the even spread, so after one step from the even spread the crowd is
               more bunched up than it was. Two ways to say “bunched”: the chance that two
               independent draws land on the same chair goes strictly up, which is arithmetic
               and needs no logarithm; and the Shannon entropy goes strictly down, which is the
               quantity Landauer’s premise puts a floor of heat under. Both are proved. And a step
               that preserves the even spread never raises the chance of a double landing, from
               any spread at all, by Cauchy’s inequality one column at a time.


               Theorem 1.6 (Noisy chairs). Let a step on finitely many states be a table of chances
               with rows adding to one, and let a set of states be closed: from inside, the chance
               of leaving is zero. (1) If every column also adds to one, the chance of entering the
               closed set from any state outside it is zero. (2) If some state outside can enter the
               closed set with positive chance, then some column does not add to one, and one
               step from the even spread strictly raises the collision weight, the sum of the squared
               chances, which is least for the even spread, and it leaves a Shannon entropy strictly
               below the logarithm of the number of states. (3) If every column adds to one, one
               step never raises the collision weight of any spread.

               Proof. (1) is the count above. (2) The first half is the contrapositive of (1), decided
               on the finite table. For the collision weight, with column sums c j adding to the
               number of states N, ∑ j (c j − 1)2 = ∑ j c2j − N, the left side is a sum of squares, and
               it is positive as soon as some c j differs from 1. For the entropy, the stepped spread q
               has q j = c j /N, so it is not the even spread. The gap between ln N and the entropy
               of q is its relative entropy to the even spread, ∑i qi ln( Nqi ), the sum taken over the i
               with qi > 0. Each such term is at least qi − 1/N, by ln y ≤ y − 1 at y = 1/( Nqi ),
               with equality only when qi = 1/N; each i with qi = 0 contributes 0 > −1/N. So
               the gap is more than ∑i (qi − 1/N ) = 0 unless every qi is 1/N, and here they are
               not. (3) For each column, the stepped chance is a weighted mean of the old chances
               with the column’s entries as weights adding to one, and a weighted mean squared is
               at most the weighted mean of the squares, the difference being a weighted variance;
               summing over columns and using that the rows add to one gives the bound.
                                                                                1.5 Quantum chairs   41


1.5 Quantum chairs
The same theorem holds for quantum states, and the proof is three lines, so here
they are. States are vectors; the step is a unitary, which is the quantum word for a
step that never squeezes, every length and every angle kept. A permanent reading is
a subspace the step maps into itself: once the state is in it, it stays. Finite dimension.
Claim: no state outside the subspace, orthogonal to it, ever gets in.
   Line one: the step is one-to-one and the subspace is finite-dimensional, so the
step maps the subspace onto itself, not just into it. Line two: then the step’s inverse
maps the subspace into itself as well, because anything in the subspace is the step
applied to something in the subspace. Line three: take a state orthogonal to the
subspace and any vector in it; the overlap of the vector with the stepped state
equals the overlap of the inverse-stepped vector with the state, which is zero. So the
stepped state is still orthogonal, and it never reads yes.
   Finite dimension was used exactly once, in line one, for “onto.” Drop it and the
bilateral shift, which is unitary on an endless ladder of states, raises “past the start”
on the first step and keeps it forever, taking a fresh rung every time. A reading that
stays, which no unitary step can raise in finite dimension, is paid either by room, a
ladder of states that never comes back around, or by a step that squeezes the even
spread, which, when the squeezed states were really possible, owes Landauer’s floor.
Not every step that fails to be unitary squeezes: one that keeps the even spread,
as pure dephasing and an unread measurement do, can’t raise a reading that stays
either. Two lines show it: such a step takes the fully mixed state to itself, so if it
keeps the yes-subspace inside itself it takes that subspace’s projector to something
no bigger with the same trace, which is the projector itself, and then it keeps the rest
in place too, so nothing outside ever gets in. The finite building forbids a keep with
neither. Which way a quantum measurement pays when its outcome is kept isn’t
settled here. The collapse models people test keep the even spread too, so the heat
the experiments look for is the heat of the noise those models add, not a Landauer
price on a kept outcome; I come back to them below.


Theorem 1.7 (Quantum chairs). On a finite-dimensional space, let a unitary map
a subspace into itself. Then it maps the orthogonal complement into itself: a state
orthogonal to the subspace remains orthogonal after every step.

Proof. The three lines above. In matrix form, with P the projector on the subspace
and Q = 1 − P: the invariance is QUP = 0, so UP = PUP, and its adjoint gives
PU † = PU † P. With V = PUP one gets V † V = P and (V + Q)† (V + Q) = 1; in
finite dimension a left inverse is a right inverse, so (V + Q)(V + Q)† = 1, which
gives VV † = P. Then PUQ = VV † UQ = V PU † UQ = V PQ = 0.
42   1 What a chair is


               1.6 Time has a bill
               Everything so far was the bill for keeping. Here’s the bill for happening, which no
               device in contact with its surroundings dodges. Bennett’s own reversible computer
               is a walker on a line that is pushed forward a little: at each tick it steps forward
               with some chance and back with the rest. Its speed is the difference. Every step it
               takes is one-to-one; it merges nothing and owes no floor. The entropy it gives off
               per tick is Schnakenberg’s formula for a biased walk, the speed times the logarithm
               of the forward-to-backward ratio, and that number is strictly positive at any speed
               other than zero, because both factors have the same sign. The only walker that gives
               off nothing is the one with no drift, as likely to step back as forward. That’s “slow
               isn’t free” as a theorem: at any speed you actually run it, every tick gives off heat on
               average.
                   And the exchange rate has a floor. Heat per net step forward, counted in units
               of kT, is the logarithm of the forward-to-backward ratio, and that logarithm is at
               least the speed. So walking a distance costs at least distance times speed in heat
               and takes distance over speed in time, and heat times time is at least the distance
               squared. At low speed, halve the speed and the heat roughly halves while the time
               doubles; the product never drops below the square of how far you went. Going
               slowly shrinks the heat toward zero. It never gets there for a walk that finishes,
               because zero heat takes infinite time, and a walk that takes forever never arrives.


               Theorem 1.8 (Time’s bill). For a walker stepping forward with chance p and back
               with chance 1 − p, with 0 < p < 1, the entropy it hands to its surroundings per
                                  p
               tick, (2p − 1) ln 1− p , is zero at p = 12 and strictly positive otherwise. With speed
               v = 2p − 1 in (0, 1) and distance N ≥ 0, the heat in units of kT, N ln 11+ v
                                                                                        −v , times the
               time N/v is at least N 2 .

               Proof. For p > 12 both factors are positive and for p < 12 both are negative, by
               the monotonicity of the logarithm; at p = 12 the first factor is zero. For the floor,
               ln(1 + v) ≥ 0 and ln(1 − v) ≤ −v since ln y ≤ y − 1, so ln 11+ v
                                                                            −v ≥ v, and the product
               is N 2 times that logarithm divided by v.
                  That is the surroundings’ share of the entropy production. The whole of it adds
               the change in the walker’s own spread, which on a line keeps growing but ever more
               slowly, so per tick that share goes to zero and the long-run rate is the heat’s.
                  The sharp floor is twice that. The difference ln 11−+v − 2v is zero at v = 0 and its
                                                                       v
               derivative, 1−2v2 − 2, is never negative on (0, 1), so the logarithm is at least 2v and
               the product is at least 2N 2 . I state N 2 because the one-line bound gives it and the
               factor isn’t the point. The square is.
                                                                               1.6 Time has a bill   43


    The walker is the one case I prove, but it isn’t special, and the physicists have
the general form. Drag a bead held in a spring-like trap through water from one
place to another in a set time and the least work you can get away with is the drag
times the distance squared, divided by the time plus twice the drag over the stiffness,
which at long times is the drag times the distance squared over the time (Schmiedl
and Seifert, 2007, who worked out the best protocols for doing it in finite time).
Change any spread of chances into another in a set time and the entropy produced
is at least a fixed fraction of the square of how far apart the two spreads are, divided
by the time and by how mobile the states are: the diffusion, for a bead that drifts
(Aurell, Mejía-Monasterio and Muratore-Ginanneschi, 2011), and how busy the
jumping is, for states that jump (Shiraishi, Funo and Saito, 2018). Those are their
results, and I cite them as physics. Put them next to the step law and the whole bill
reads like this. Every change a device makes to the spread of its states in a finite
time dissipates, merge or no merge, reversible or not; time sets how much, and
only infinite time makes it zero. That’s for a device sitting in surroundings at some
temperature, and it’s dissipation, entropy produced, not heat given off step by step:
a step that leaves the spread exactly as it was owes nothing on these bounds, and
the heat a single step gives off can be negative when the device’s own entropy goes
up. An idealised machine cut off from everything, frictionless billiard balls bouncing
their way through a computation (Edward Fredkin and Tommaso Toffoli’s, 1982),
could in principle run without dissipating at all; Bennett (2003) wrote that such
ballistic machines compute at constant velocity without dissipating any energy, and
that they must be kept isolated from heat baths and noise. Keeping one on course
against noise means correcting its errors, and whether that brings the bill back I
don’t settle here; in 2003 Bennett called the thermodynamics of error correction a
subject that appears to be in its infancy. The bead of Jun, Gavrilov and Bechhoefer
(2014) shows the other half. Put through the same moves as an erasure but with
no tilt, so nothing is squashed, its work extrapolated to the slow limit came out
at 0.05 ± 0.03 kT, within two error bars of zero: no floor under it, which is what
the premise says. Keeping something costs, on top of that, a merge, which under
Landauer’s premise owes a floor of kT ln 2 per bit that no slowness removes, or a
fresh chair of room. Room dodges the floor and never the dissipation of happening.
And a finite building, where every state has a next one, forces the merge.
    I also simulated the bead. Bérut, Arakelyan, Petrosyan, Ciliberto, Dillenschneider
and Lutz (2012) erased one bit held by a glass bead in a laser double well, and found
the heat falling toward Landauer’s number as they slowed the erasure, with the
excess going like a constant over the time taken. I wrote their protocol as described,
barrier down over a second, tilt ramped over the protocol time, tilt stopped, barrier
up over a second, as overdamped Brownian motion in a quartic double well with
their numbers, and added up the heat the way they do, the force times the bead’s
44   1 What a chair is


               displacement along each path. I set the tilt at each protocol time from a scan so
               that it erased about nine times in ten (between 88 and 92 times in a hundred across
               the six protocol times, two seconds to eighty; they took the smallest that erased
               ninety-five times in a hundred), and fitted the heat against the time. Averaged over
               every run, the fit’s floor is 0.56 kT. That’s above the floor for an erasure that comes
               off only about nine times in ten, ln 2 less the uncertainty left in the outcome, about
               0.37 kT, which is the formula the Bérut paper gives for an erasure that sometimes
               fails; it’s the honest floor for all the runs. Averaged over the successful erasures
               alone, the fit is 0.694 kT plus 3.64 kT · s divided by the time, and ln 2 is 0.693. The
               fit is good to about 0.015 kT, so the third decimal is luck, and I have no argument on
               the page that ln 2 has to be the floor for the successful runs taken alone; it’s where
               the fit landed. The slowest point, at eighty seconds, came in at 0.674 kT, a little
               under ln 2, so the fitted number isn’t a floor the successful runs stay above. The floor
               that holds is the one for all the runs. The script is scripts/bead_erasure_sim.py
               in the repository, and it prints all of those numbers. My excess constant isn’t theirs,
               which was 8.15; the shape is. Nothing in that model but a particle, a well and
               noise, and the heat came down toward a floor as the erasure slowed, with the
               one-over-time excess on top of it. That’s the floor and time’s bill together, in a
               simulation of their bead.

                  Everything that has been measured agrees with the floor, stated for a symmetric
               memory, and with time’s bill at the measured rates, and nothing measured has kept

               room’s ceiling, and it’s the one I lean on least: every memory anyone can buy fills,

               1.8 The same bill at every scale
               One more question, and it’s the one that decides whether any of this is about the
               world or only about my pictures. A chair is a description. The dial on a lab bench is
               a chair, and so is each atom in it, and so is each atom together with the light it gave
               off. Describe the same thing coarser or finer and you get different chairs. Does the
               bill change with the zoom?
                   It doesn’t, and here’s why in one picture. Draw the fine chairs, and draw a fence
               around each group of them that counts as one coarse chair. Say the coarse picture
               merges: two coarse chairs send everyone to one coarse chair. Then on a finite floor,
               the fine chairs can’t all be keeping their distance either. Count them. If the fine step
               sent different chairs to different chairs and nobody left the fenced floor, it would be
               a reshuffle of the fine chairs, every chair filled exactly once afterwards. But some
               fenced group is now empty, because the coarse step missed a coarse chair (two
               coarse chairs went to one, so on a finite floor some coarse chair gets nobody), and
               the chairs in that group got nobody. A reshuffle can’t empty a chair. So something
               gave: the fine step merges too, or some fine chair stepped off the fenced floor, or
               the floor has no end. Three ways again, one level down, though stepping off the
               floor isn’t room: it’s where the coarse picture stops tracking the fine one.


               Theorem 1.9 (The same bill at every scale). Let a fine machine have one rule F on
               a set X of states, let A be a set of its states, and let a coarse description be a map
               π from X to a set S of coarse states that takes A onto S, with a coarse rule f on S
               such that π ( F ( x )) = f (π ( x )) for every x in A. If the coarse rule merges two coarse
               states, then at least one of these holds: F merges two states of A; F takes some state
               of A outside A; or A is infinite.

               Proof. Suppose none holds: A is finite, F keeps A inside A, and F sends different
               states of A to different states. A one-to-one map of a finite set into itself is onto,
               so every state of A is F of some state of A. For each coarse state c write Ac for the
               states of A that π sends to c; each is non-empty, because π takes A onto S, and S is
               finite because A is. The rule π ( F ( x )) = f (π ( x )) says F sends Ac into A f (c) . The
               coarse rule merges, so it is a map of the finite set S to itself that isn’t one-to-one,
                                                               1.9 The bill, and where the toll comes in   47


and so it misses some coarse state d. No Ac is sent into Ad , so no state of A is sent
into Ad , which isn’t empty. That contradicts F being onto A.
    Put it next to the permanent flip. On a finite coarse picture, a reading that goes
up and stays up is raised by a merge (the cell above, on three states; Theorem 3.1,
two chapters on, in general). By this theorem, at every finer description that the
coarse one is exact about, that keep is a merge again, a step off the described states,
or an endless floor. The dial and its light are the example. In the dial’s own picture,
two blends of readings decay to one either-or, a merge (Section 18). In the picture
of dial and light together, the step is one-to-one, and it’s the second case: the light
starts blank and leaves carrying the copy, so the fine step leaves the set of states
where the light is still blank. At the fine scale nothing merges; the step leaves the
states the coarse picture describes. And the heat floor sits where the merge really
is. Landauer’s premise charges the scale whose step merges states that were really
possible; a description that merges only because it stopped looking at the light owes
that floor nowhere, and owes the room instead.


1.9 The bill, and where the toll comes in
So that’s the bill, all of it, before anybody writes a price on anything. The toll, which
the next chapter states, is that bill written into a step. It’s the price of something
being the case: a reading that goes from no to yes and stays is a distinction that
stays, and a distinction that stays is a chair you can’t give back. Anything whose
state includes chairs it can’t give back pays the bill the toll prices: the bead, the cell,
the memory bit, a world with a past. Give one a price list that obeys the toll and it’s
a Thiele machine, and when the cell could have held anything, Landauer’s premise
puts a heat floor under that raise, because on a finite cell the raise is a merge. That’s
the toll’s shape, paid in heat instead of marks. And the bill, deterministic or noisy
or quantum, is this: in any real device every change that finishes dissipates, more
the faster it goes, which I prove for Bennett’s walker and cite the physicists for
wherever a device’s states jump or drift at random in surroundings at a temperature;
keeping something costs on top of that either a merge, with Landauer’s floor when
the merged states were really possible, or a fresh chair of room; and a finite building,
where every state has a next one, forces the merge. The step law, the noisy chairs and
the quantum chairs are proved, and the table above says how near the laboratory
has come to each; the heat is physics.
   That’s also why the rule sits on the raise and not on the merge. The toll charges
the keep whichever column pays it, merge or room. A price on merges charges only
the merge column, so it misses a keep paid in room: the endless strip of Door one,
two chapters on, raises its reading at zero marks under it. And it charges merges
that keep nothing, like the reset that lowers a flag. That reset costs no marks on
48   1 What a chair is


               my ledger and still merges two states, so in a real device it owes Landauer’s floor
               whenever the bit it lowers was really unknown; the ledger leaves that to physics,
               the same as the dissipation of happening.
                  Next, then, the smallest machine that keeps that bill on its own ledger: two boxes
               on a sheet of paper, a tally, and one rule.
CHAPTER 2




A record and a toll

The last chapter found the bill and kept no count of it. Now give the bill a ledger.
Take a record with two positions, no and yes, and build the smallest thing that could
carry a charge for its change, on paper, with a pencil. Write the charge into its rules
and see what follows. Keeping it this small is what lets you see which part of the
construction does which part of the work.
    The usual models charge a computation for two things: how long it runs and
how much space it uses. The bits it destroys have been counted too, as the opening
said, by Li and Vitányi and by Demaine and his coauthors. What this part charges is
something else: what the computation keeps and can’t take back. This part is about
that charge. It gets paid in a merge, which carries a heat floor when the merged
states were really possible, or in room, and the last chapter showed it can’t be talked
down to zero. The record built below is the smallest thing that can carry the charge,
and the tally next to it counts every time the record goes up. Whether a machine
has to charge it as a mark, and on which premises, is the next chapter.
    One thing about what a flag stands behind, because it stays out of the picture
a while. What I’m about to build prices vouching for anything at all: a flag goes
up, and the rule doesn’t ask what the flag is standing behind. A sorting of a pile
into groups, the kind of structure Part II starts from (Section 5), is the first kind of
claim I care about. It isn’t the only kind, and the book comes back to what a flag
stands behind in Section 8, and on a machine in Section 15, where a flag stands on
a checked claim. Until then nothing leans on groupings. The floor in this section,
the reason for it in the next, and the latch in Part II all work whatever the reading
is about, partition or no partition. When groupings come in, in Section 8, it’s as a
theorem: a reading that says a grouping has been checked and committed sees the
grouping only through its partition, and what it entitles is exactly the groupings that
refine it (Theorem 8.5). So the grouping gets a job, and an exact one.
    But first the word, because I’ve got a new one and I don’t trust it either. Record.
Receipt. Certificate. Vouch. People have been making marks that other people are
supposed to rely on for a very long time, and I wanted to know what they thought
they were doing, and what it cost them, and whether any of them ever said the
thing I need said. So here’s what I could reach, pushed on with you, and I’ll tell you
where the search ran out.


                                                  49
50   2 A record and a toll


               2.1 Clay, seals, and seven witnesses
               Start a little over five thousand years ago, in the Near East, with people who counted
               sheep with little clay tokens. To send a count across a distance without the courier
               changing it, they put the tokens inside a hollow clay ball, pressed the shapes of the
               tokens onto the outside while the clay was soft, and sealed it. The archaeologist
               Denise Schmandt-Besserat has spent a career on these, and she puts the practice at
               around 3300 BC; the ball is called a bulla. Here’s the push, and you can do it with a
               cookie tin, with a paper seal glued across the lid and rim. Let it dry, then try opening
               the lid without tearing or disturbing the seal. The bare lid would come straight off;
               it is the seal that makes this a test. A substitute seal could fool you, so this little trial
               shows a disturbance, not an unforgeable history. In the clay ball, the outside shows
               the count inside and opening the ball breaks it. That is the property the tin and seal
               are trying to reproduce. That’s a real idea and it will show up again in a form you
               won’t expect: a record is worth something only if it can’t be silently undone.
                   Now law, which is where people get serious about who’s allowed to say what
               happened. The book of Deuteronomy, chapter nineteen: nobody is convicted on
               the word of one witness; it takes “two or three.” The Roman jurist Gaius, writing
               in the second century, says a will the praetor will honour is one sealed by seven
               witnesses. Seven. Why seven? Gaius doesn’t say. The legal historian Henry Maine,
               in 1861, had an answer: the older Roman will was a mock sale, done in front of five
               witnesses, a man holding the scales, and the buyer of the estate, seven people in
               all, and when the ceremony fell away the seven seals kept the count. Maine’s is the
               only account of it I found, so treat it as his. Gaius’s own text does show they kept
               those old formalities around a will, and it isn’t hard to see why anyone would: one
               person can lie, and a will moves a fortune, and the dead man can’t object. So the
               record isn’t the paper. It’s the number of independent people who have put their
               own seal, their own name, their own risk, next to the claim. Try it: write “paid five
               dollars, signed A” on a napkin and ask a friend to forge it. Takes them ten seconds.
               Now require two other people to initial it at the moment of payment and each keep
               a copy. Your forger needs two accomplices or has to match two copies held in two
               other pockets. The claim didn’t change. What stands behind it did.
                   Which brings me to seals, and the medieval historian Michael Clanchy, whose
               book is called From Memory to Written Record. England between the Norman
               Conquest and the early 1300s was learning to trust writing. Until then it had trusted
               people who remembered. The lesson was painful: seals were forged, charters were
               forged, and historians today have a whole craft of telling real charters from fake
               ones because the fakes are so many. A seal is only as good as whoever holds the
               stamp. Keep that one too, because in 2011 a certificate authority called DigiNotar
               found out, at the cost of its existence, that a mathematically perfect signature is
                                                                       2.2 Two columns and a stamp   51


worth exactly what the custody of the key is worth, and intruders had taken control
of the machines that signed. Nine hundred years, same failure. I find that oddly
comforting.
    And then the obvious next question: if seals could be forged, what caught the
forgeries? Not the seals. The most famous forged record in European history is the
Donation of Constantine, a document in which the emperor Constantine supposedly
handed rule over Rome and the western empire to the Pope. It was most likely
written in the eighth century, some four hundred years after Constantine died, and
it was leaned on for centuries. Around 1440 a scholar named Lorenzo Valla took it
apart by its Latin: the language belonged to a much later age, and it used words,
“satraps” among them, that no Roman of Constantine’s day would have used for
his officials. (Valla wasn’t even first. Nicholas of Cusa, a German churchman and
philosopher who later became a cardinal, had already called it a forgery in 1433, in
De concordantia catholica, a long book on how the Church and the empire ought to
hang together. I know that from the reference works, and I haven’t read the book.
Valla’s is the version people remember, which is a pattern that keeps turning up.)
Look at what kind of check that was. The question wasn’t “is the stamp real.” It was
“could these words have been written when they say they were.” A record can pass
the first and fail the second, which is a hint that what I keep calling one thing, a
record, is doing more than one job.


2.2 Two columns and a stamp

Here’s the one I’d never have guessed mattered. Bookkeeping. Around 1300, the
ledger of a Florentine company called Farolfi, kept at its branch in Provence, shows
the earliest complete example anyone has found of a trick merchants were working
out: write every transaction twice, once where the money came from and once
where it went, and the two columns have to balance. The treasurers of the city of
Genoa kept their ledger for 1340 that way, and accounting historians still count
it among the most famous government account books of the Middle Ages kept in
double entry. And in 1494 a friar named Luca Pacioli printed the method in a
mathematics book, and it spread. That’s double-entry bookkeeping, and it’s easy to
take it for just a tidy habit.
    Do it for one day. Keep two columns of every dollar that moves, and total them
at night. Now have a friend secretly change one entry in one column. The totals
disagree; you catch it. Now have them change the matching entry in both columns.
The totals agree. You’ve caught nothing. Push on that and you’ve found what double
entry actually is: a trap for slips. A careful liar walks straight through it. Did Pacioli
see that? I can only get at it secondhand. The scholar Forrester, in a paper on the
University of Strathclyde’s accounting-history pages, reads him as reporting that in
52   2 A record and a toll


               many places the books were taken to the local consul to be authenticated before a
               single entry went in. The stamp is a witness again, from outside. The two columns
               are the discipline; the stamp is the claim that someone other than you will stand
               behind the fact that these are the books. No other set gets that stamp. Keep both
               halves separate in your head. One is a method. The other is a commitment.
                   And then I found the place where this got turned into a motto. The Royal Society,
               founded in London in 1660 and still running, picked as its motto Nullius in verba:
               take nobody’s word for it. (Where did they get it? From somebody’s words, naturally.
               It’s half a line of the Roman poet Horace, from a verse letter to his patron, saying
               he isn’t bound to swear by the words of any master. So the society that takes
               nobody’s word for it took its motto from a poet and cut the line to fit. That’s not a
               contradiction, and it’s a nice picture of the method: borrow what’s useful, say whose
               it was, and don’t swear by it.) The historian Steven Shapin wrote a paper about
               what that meant in practice, and the answer is more interesting than the slogan.
               Robert Boyle, pumping the air out of a glass globe to see what happens to a candle
               or a bird, had three problems: the machine, the report, and the witnesses. He solved
               the third by having gentlemen present who’d sign their names, and the second by
               writing the report so richly that a reader who wasn’t there could picture the scene
               and count as a witness anyway. Shapin calls that virtual witnessing, and he notes,
               dryly, that the air pump was very expensive, seventeenth-century big science. So
               there was a cost. It just wasn’t a cost of declaring the fact. It was the cost of the
               instrument and of getting enough people into the room. Hold on to that distinction.
               The rest of the book hangs on it.


               2.3 A demon, and the step that pays

               Now the strangest entry, and the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist James
               Clerk Maxwell, in a letter to his friend the Scottish physicist Peter Guthrie Tait,
               imagined a “very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at a tiny door between
               two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and slow ones
               the other, so that one side heats up and the other cools with no work done, which is
               supposed to be impossible. The being got called Maxwell’s demon, and physicists
               have been arguing about it for a hundred and fifty years, which should tell you
               something.
                  In 1929 Leo Szilard, a young Hungarian physicist working in Berlin, cut the
               demon’s box down to a single molecule, and that made information part of the
               accounting. The tempting move, and the one Szilard’s own accounting made, is to
               put the whole bill on finding out which side the molecule is on. Bennett separated
               finding out from restoring the memory for another round: measuring onto a blank
               record can, in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting an unknown
                                                                 2.3 A demon, and the step that pays   53


record is a different operation. That does not make a real measuring device free to
build or run. It says that learning and resetting do not carry the same unavoidable
entropy cost, and I’m about to pick a step to charge, so I need that distinction before
I do.
    Bennett’s version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must
cost is “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.” Erasing, or
taking two possible situations and making them one. And in the same paper he
lists copying unknown data onto a blank place to write among “the most important
logically reversible operations,” the kind he says can, at least in principle, be run
thermodynamically reversibly. So, in the one place in all of this where a record is
priced by physics, the unavoidable erasure charge belongs to forgetting the unknown
record. Making a record on a blank place carries no such charge of its own. It does
use up the blank place, which is room, and that place gets paid for in heat when it’s
wiped to be used again. Read that twice. It’s not what I expected either.
    Making a record on a blank place is one operation. Landauer’s 1961 paper names
another: set a bit to one whatever it held. If that bit is the whole state, down goes to
up, up stays up, and two possible states become one. Landauer called this “restore
to one.” On an uncertain input it removes information; a heat bound then needs the
thermodynamic premises.
    A larger machine has more state than its flag. Two starts can both finish with
the flag up while remaining different elsewhere. The next chapter proves that, on a
finite machine whose reading is permanent, any instruction that raises it must merge
some full states. It does not say the state whose flag just rose is one of that pair. Put
one chair outside the room that reads yes and two inside. Send the outsider to the
first inside chair, and both insiders to the second. The flag rises for the outsider, but
the two insiders are the states that merge. These arrows describe alternative starts,
not three things happening in one run.
    That is the distinction the one-bit picture hides. The instruction has a collision
somewhere; the actual distribution of starting states determines whether that col-
lision removes uncertainty. A known starting state loses none under the entropy
premise, even when its flag rises (Theorem 3.15, next chapter). That isn’t a way
around the bill: whoever knows the start is already holding the distinction, and the
bill was paid in that knowing, or gets paid when that knowledge is wiped. The ledger
can still charge the instruction under merge pricing. A ledger charge, information
loss and a device’s heat are three quantities to keep apart.
    I’ll put the rest of the lineage quickly, because it all points the same way. Regu-
lators who make brokers keep records on media that can’t be rewritten (the SEC
required exactly that, write once and read many, from 1997 until 2022, when it
allowed an audit trail as the other way to comply) are pricing the hardware. The
rule puts no charge on the act of writing. Haber and Stornetta in 1991, the times-
54   2 A record and a toll


               tamping that Bitcoin’s footnotes lead back to (Section 14 follows them), chained
               time-stamped records together with hashes so that changing an old entry breaks
               every entry after it (and Ralph Merkle’s hash tree, from his 1979 Stanford thesis on
               secrecy and authentication, lets one short value vouch for a great many records); try
               the dependency with five entries, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, adding each to the running total: 1, 3,
               6, 10, 15. Keep that sheet and make another with the second entry changed to 3. Its
               totals are 1, 4, 7, 11, 16. The change travels down the chain. Now lower the third
               entry to 2: the last total is 15 again. Simple addition can be fooled by compensating
               changes. A cryptographic chain needs a stronger function, and someone must retain
               a trusted value to compare against. This trial shows the dependency between entries;
               it supplies neither that function’s security nor a price on the record. Proof-of-work,
               which the computer scientists Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor proposed in 1992 to
               make junk mail expensive and which Bitcoin later chained, is the one framing where
               a record genuinely costs, and what it charges for is a search: how many tries it
               took to find a lucky number. An empty block costs the same work as a full one. So
               the work prices the search. Proof-of-work charges nothing extra for the moment
               anything becomes certified. Robert Floyd and Tony Hoare, two computer scientists
               asking how you’d prove a program does what it’s supposed to, attached claims to
               points in a program in 1967 and 1969 (“whenever you get here, this is true”), and
               the claim is backed by a proof that’s paid for off the machine. And the certificates of
               complexity theory, which go back to Stephen Cook’s 1971 work on NP, are strings
               designed to be cheap to check: hand me the certificate and I can confirm the claim
               quickly. Whether they’re also expensive to find is the famous open question of the
               field, P versus NP, and nobody knows; what’s settled is only the cheap half. That’s
               the opposite of a price on vouching: the whole design goal is that checking a claim
               costs nearly nothing. And from statistics, a ledger that runs the other way: Dean
               Foster and Robert Stine’s alpha-investing (2008) runs a long string of tests against
               a budget of allowed false alarms, where every test spends some of the budget and
               every discovery, a rejection that stands, pays some back. That’s the other way round
               from a toll on vouching: the test pays, and a discovery that stands gets paid.


               2.4 What they all agree on, and who they rule out

               Lay them down, and this time what shows through is not one thing. It’s five different
               jobs that the word “record” has been doing, and I’d been letting one word carry all
               five. Most of them have a corpse next to them, and the corpses are different too.
                   Durability: the record can’t be silently undone. The bulla, the write-once disk,
               the hash chain, Bennett’s card that has to be wiped. The corpse is the editable
               log, and the company that kept its debts off the books: Enron hid its debt in side
               entities set up to keep it off the balance sheet, which is how the Justice Department
                                                    2.4 What they all agree on, and who they rule out   55


described the scheme in 2002, and its auditor, Arthur Andersen, shredded the paper.
Andersen was convicted for the shredding that year, and the Supreme Court threw
the conviction out in 2005 over how the jury had been instructed; either way, the
books concealed debts they should have shown. But notice this job doesn’t need a
witness at all. A copy will do: a hash chain nobody signed is still hard to change
quietly, so long as somebody else holds the latest link, because a chain with no copy
anywhere can be rewritten from end to end and recomputed, and nobody would
know.
    Authenticity: the record came from who it says it came from. Seals, the signature
only a key-holder can make, the consul’s stamp. The corpse is the forged charter
and DigiNotar. This job is about custody of a stamp, and it’s a different job from
durability; a perfectly authentic entry can still be erased, and a perfectly durable
one can still be a forgery.
    Evidence: enough independent people stand behind the claim that lying is
expensive. Two witnesses, seven seals, Boyle’s gentlemen. It rules out anonymous
assertion, and it rules out “the universe keeps the receipt”: information spread into
the environment is not a record anyone can read or rely on. This one is about
numbers of people and their risk. Paper has nothing to do with it.
    Accounting: the record checks itself for slips. The two columns. And here’s
a thing to keep straight: the second column is not an outside witness. It’s you,
checking you. It catches a dropped digit. A careful liar gets past it, as you saw. It
belongs on this list as its own job, separate from the seven seals.
    Cheap checking: a record whose correctness can be confirmed for much less than
it cost to make. Cook’s certificates, the signature, the hash. This one isn’t universal,
and I thought it was. Whether checking needs to be cheaper than making depends
on who you’re worried about and how much a wrong record costs you; plenty of
records are checked by redoing the whole thing, and that’s fine when the thing is
small.
    Now the thing none of them says. Not one of these jobs is pricing the moment a
record goes up and stays. Bennett prices merging and erasing, which that moment
might or might not be. Proof-of-work prices a search the designer chose. Book-
keeping prices a discipline. Witnesses and seals price showing up and guarding
the stamp. I looked, with everything I had, and that’s where it ran out. If the bill
exists as a bill for that moment, nobody in this lineage wrote it down, and that’s
either because it isn’t there or because the one person who did write it down is on a
shelf I never found. The literal one-bit reset already has a thermodynamic analysis:
Landauer’s restore to one. The question here is which premises force an instruction
that raises a record to merge full states, and which further premises put a price on
that loss. So I’m going to have to try it myself, on the smallest thing I can build, and
56   2 A record and a toll


               let you watch. And I’ll have to be honest about which of the five jobs the small thing
               even attempts, because the answer is going to be none.


               2.5 The smallest thing that could carry the bill
               Take a sheet of paper. Draw two boxes and label them NO and YES. That’s the
               reading, a single yes-or-no question asked of the state, and I’m going to be careful
               about what the question is, because after five thousand years of seals and witnesses
               the word “vouch” is carrying a lot and this toy carries almost none of it. The question
               is only: “has the designated flag been set.” Not “is some claim about a grouping
               true.” Not “did anyone check.” There is no claim in this toy, no evidence, no checker,
               nobody standing behind anything. There is a flag. Whether a flag can ever be made
               to mean that something was checked and can be relied on is a real question, and it’s
               not this section’s; I’ll build toward it later, and until then please read YES as “the
               flag is up” and nothing more. Where the state is: which box you’re in. That’s the
               whole state, one bit. Then draw a line under the boxes for tally marks. The marks
               sit outside the state. They’re the running total you keep beside it as you play, the
               way you’d keep score beside a board game.
                   Now give yourself three moves. STAY: you don’t move, no mark. WORK: you
               don’t move either (it’s a stand-in for every ordinary step a machine takes), no mark.
               VOUCH: from NO you move to YES; from YES you stay in YES; either way you make
               one tally mark, because in this toy the price belongs to the move’s name; where you
               were standing doesn’t enter into it. Play. Start in NO, make any sequence of moves
               you like, and stop in YES. Count the marks. Now try to reach YES with zero marks.
               You can’t, and you can see exactly why: the only move that crosses from NO to YES
               is VOUCH, and VOUCH makes a mark. Now erase the mark from VOUCH’s rule and
               play again. YES at no marks, every time. That’s the entire content of what I’m about
               to call a rule, and I want you to see how little it is before I dress it up: I’ve decided
               that the move which crosses the line makes a mark. Nothing in the toy’s rules forces
               the mark. VOUCH does merge, NO and YES both landing on YES, which is what the
               last chapter says a kept raise on two chairs has to do; what nothing yet says is that a
               merge has to cost a mark. Here it’s a choice, the last chapter’s bill written down as a
               rule. The next chapter is about when a machine has no choice.
                   Why tally marks, by the way? Because they’re about the oldest receipt there is.
               The real ones, the English treasury’s notched sticks split down the middle, get their
               own story in Part II (Section 6), fire and all. The tally on your paper is nothing like
               those. Nobody holds the other half. You keep it, beside the board, and you could
               rub a mark out and nobody would ever know. Hold on to that, because by the end
               of this section it’s the reason the toy does none of the five jobs a record does.
                                                       2.5 The smallest thing that could carry the bill   57


    Here is the same toy, stated once, carefully, because this is the one place in the
book where I state it exactly and everything later points back here. The point listed
the five parts in a sentence; here they’re pinned down. The thing on your paper has
five parts.
    A set of states. (Here: NO and YES, and nothing else.)
    A set of move names. (STAY, WORK, VOUCH.)
    A step: for each state and each move name, where you land.
    A cost for each move name: a whole number of marks, zero or more. (Zero, zero,
one.)
    A reading: for each state, yes or no.
    That’s it. Add the one rule below and I’ll call it a Thiele machine. And I want
to be exact about what’s not in it. There’s no counter stored inside the state that’s
forbidden from going down; the marks are the side tally from the board game, and
the tally only ever grows because the costs are whole numbers, zero or more. (A
machine could keep the total inside its state too; that’s an extra part beyond the
five, and Section 6 builds it.) There’s no window, no observer who sees only part of
the state; that’s a later question and it gets its own section. And the cost depends
only on the move’s name; where you are when you make it doesn’t matter. That’s on
purpose: the charge is on the attempt, so you pay for making the move, whatever
it turns out to do. It’s also a real simplification, and where a result needs a price
that depends on where you are, Section 7 says so and uses one. Last, the step gives
every state and every move exactly one place to land. A choice becomes a move
name. A machine that has stopped steps to itself. A step that can land in several
places by chance is a different picture, and the noisy chairs in Section 1 take it
up. One landing place for each state and move is what the step law there and the
heat-or-room argument in the next chapter need.
    One rule, which I’ll call the toll. For every state and every move: if the reading is
NO before the move and YES after it, the move’s cost is at least one mark. That’s all.
It says nothing about any other move. It says nothing about how big a mark is in
anything you could measure. One mark is one mark; what a mark is worth, why
the smallest charge is one (why not two, or a half?), and whether I had any right
to decide that, come next. The middle question has a short answer I’ll give away
now. What the next chapter forces, on its premises, is that a raise that stays up, with
only finitely many yes-states, merges two states, so any price on merges lands on
it. Costs here are whole numbers of marks, which I chose so the ledger counts acts,
and the least whole number above nothing is one. That’s where the “at least one”
comes from.
    And one theorem, which is the only thing the toy actually proves, and you’ve
already proved it by playing. Take any run of moves that starts in a NO state and
ends in a YES state. Then the marks it made add up to at least one. Here’s the
58   2 A record and a toll


               argument in words, and it’s short enough that you can hold the whole thing. Walk
               the run move by move, reading the box at each step. It read NO at the start and YES
               at the end, and every move either leaves the reading alone or flips it, so at some
               move it went from NO to YES. The toll says that move cost at least one. Every other
               move cost zero or more. Add them up: at least one. Notice what the argument did
               not need. It didn’t need the reading to stay YES afterward; if a later move flipped it
               back to NO and another flipped it to YES again, that’s two tolls, and the argument
               still goes through. It didn’t need the machine to be finite. It didn’t need to know
               what any move does besides what the reading says before and after. It needed
               exactly one thing: the toll.
                   That’s the whole theorem. Here it is once more in the exact form, because from
               here on the book carries two layers side by side: what I mean, in words, and what’s
               stated and proved, in symbols you can hold me to. The symbols are few. N is the
               whole numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. S and I are just names for “the set of states” and
               “the set of move names.” Writing step : S × I → S means “hand it a state and a
               move name and it hands back a state.” A run is a list of move names, t = [i1 , . . . , in ],
               played from a start s0 , one after another. The double arrow =⇒ reads “then”: the
               thing on its left forces the thing on its right. And “by induction on the run,” in the
               proof, is the formal name for the way you’d check it by hand: settle the empty run,
               then show that one more move at the front can’t break what you’ve settled.

               Definition 2.1 (Thiele machine). A Thiele machine consists of a set S of states, a
               set I of move names, a step function step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a
               reading cert : S → {no, yes}, subject to one rule, the toll: for every state s and move
               i,
                              cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes =⇒ cost(i ) ≥ 1.

               The run of t = [i1 , . . . , in ] from s0 ends at run(t, s0 ), the result of applying the steps
               in order, and its total cost is cost(t) = cost(i1 ) + · · · + cost(in ), with the empty run
               costing 0.

                  The formal files, the proof-assistant versions of these arguments (Appendix M
               says what they are and aren’t), call this definition CertificationSystem, after one
               reading it can carry, and they call the reading cert, which is the name I keep for it in
               the formulas. The book calls the whole thing what it is.
                  A word on the label before the first result. I call a result an observation when its
               proof does little more than unfold the definitions, and in an axiomatic cost model
               that’s what the definitions are meant to do: the work is in choosing them, so the
               results that follow from them in a few lines are labelled that way and the theorems
               with more in them stand out.
                                                          2.5 The smallest thing that could carry the bill   59


Observation 2.1 (The universal floor). In any Thiele machine, every run that starts
at a state reading no and ends at a state reading yes has total cost at least 1: if
cert(s0 ) = no and cert(run(t, s0 )) = yes, then cost(t) ≥ 1.
Proof. By induction on the run. If t is empty, the run ends where it starts, at a
state reading no, so the hypothesis “ends at yes” can’t hold and there’s nothing to
prove. Otherwise t = i :: t′ (the first move, then the rest); let s1 = step(s0 , i ). If
cert(s1 ) = yes, the first move is a crossing, the toll gives cost(i ) ≥ 1, and the rest cost
at least 0, so cost(t) ≥ 1. If cert(s1 ) = no, the rest of the run starts at no and ends at
yes, so by the induction hypothesis cost(t′ ) ≥ 1, and cost(t) = cost(i ) + cost(t′ ) ≥ 1.
Nothing else is used: not finiteness, not that the reading stays yes, not what any
move does beyond the reading before and after.
    The theorem is about every Thiele machine, a system with the toll among its
conditions, and about no system without it. One edge matters: the theorem does
not assume that a YES state exists. If no state ever reads YES, no run meets the
theorem’s hypothesis, so it’s true of every run and tells you nothing about any of
them, which is a mathematician’s way of saying it’s true and useless. The toy on
your paper has a YES box, so it isn’t useless there. It would be natural to assume the
system has to have at least one NO state and one YES state; the statement has no
such clause, and that’s on purpose, because a theorem that applies to no run is still
a theorem and the toy is where you supply the runs.
    The theorem also runs backwards, and that direction is one line. Suppose every
run from a state reading no to a state reading yes costs at least one, whichever state
you start from. A single move is a run of length one, so a move that takes no to yes
costs at least one, which is the toll. The floor from every start and the toll are the
same rule, and nobody has to choose between them. From one fixed start that reads
no, the floor asks for the toll only at the crossings you can reach without paying
anything; a crossing you can only reach by paying has already cost at least one by
the time you get there.
    And the bound of one is the smallest case of a count.
Observation 2.2 (One mark per crossing). In any Thiele machine, a run costs at
least the number of its steps that take the reading from no to yes, with no permanence
assumed. Conversely, a system in which every run costs at least its number of such steps
obeys the toll. And the bound is reached for every count: on the one-bit machine with a
set that costs one and a reset that costs no marks, setting and resetting n times from no
crosses n times and costs exactly n.
Proof. Each crossing step costs at least one by the toll, every other step costs at least
zero, and each step is counted once, so the total is at least the number of crossings.
Conversely, a single move that crosses is a run with one crossing, so it costs at least
60   2 A record and a toll


               one, which is the toll. On the one-bit machine, each set from no is a crossing costing
               one and each reset costs no marks, so n rounds cost n and cross n times.
                   And one more edge, because it’s the first thing to bite when you ask a machine
               to stand behind more than one thing. The definition has one reading in it. One
