               question, one flag, one toll on its crossing. Once the flag is up, a second claim has
               nowhere to go: raising a flag that’s already up doesn’t move anything. So a second
               claim needs a reading of its own, and a third claim a third: one reading per claim,
               each with its own crossing. Part II builds that properly, as a family of flags, one per
               threshold, with a step that raises any of them charged at least one (Theorem 10.11).
               A step that raises three at once still owes at least one, and nothing in the toll makes
               the charges add up flag by flag. Charges that add need the composition assumptions
               for independent machines (Appendix F). The same theorem has a count in it that
               is the bill for finiteness. Picture the record as a row of switches that only ever get
               turned on. Ten switches can change at most ten times in one run, one switch per
               change, and then the row is full. (Across different runs the row can end in any of
               its thousand and twenty-four settings; along any one run it climbs through at most
               eleven.) A finite machine can keep only so many things up for good in its whole life.
               That’s “you can’t keep all of it,” which Section 14 says of a full trace, turned into a
               count.


               2.6 What this does and doesn’t buy
               I want to be very plain about how small this is, because the temptation is to look
               at the word “theorem” and feel something has been established about the world.
               Nothing has. What’s been established is that if you adopt the toll, then the flag can’t
               be raised without a mark, in any system with those five parts that obeys it, no matter
               what the states and moves are. The “if” is doing all the work. In the toy I chose the
               rule. The reason I wanted it is the last chapter: a reading that goes up and stays up
               is a chair filled, and a filled chair is paid for in a merge or in room. Whether that
               reason makes a machine charge a mark, rather than just making me want it to, is
               the next chapter, and until then the toll is a rule I wrote down.
                   Notice also what it doesn’t ask about how strong the thing is, in either direction.
               A system is Turing-complete when it can imitate a Turing machine, and no stronger
               than one when a Turing machine can imitate it. The theorem asks neither. Stronger
               than a Turing machine, weaker, dead even: none of it reaches the floor. Bring the
               five parts, charge the toll on the crossing, and you’re in scope. The floor doesn’t
               check what you can compute, because it was never about what you can compute.
               It’s about what a move is allowed to do without a mark.
                   Which brings up the objection a theorist makes in about four seconds, so I’ll
               make it first. The toll is a floor, and a floor is easy to meet. Charge one mark for
                                                                  2.6 What this does and doesn’t buy   61


every move, whatever it does, and the toll holds for any reading you like, since every
crossing is a move and every move costs one. So any computer with a step counter
beside it, and any yes-or-no question at all about its state, is a Thiele machine.
A clock passes. Nothing about that is a loophole. It’s what the definition says,
and it means the definition, on its own, doesn’t tie the marks to anything kept or
certified. It only says a crossing can’t go unpriced. (It’s also why “a base that can
compute anything plus a flag that obeys the toll” would be a cheap thing to call
Thiele-complete, and why the definition that gets that name, at the end of Part II,
asks for computing that costs no marks and a record that tells starts apart, which no
clock meets; Section 10.8.) Three things later in the book tie them down. The first
is that bar: computing at no marks, marks at one, and a record that tells starts apart.
The second is a ceiling: demand that a run’s total never exceed the number of times
the flag went up. With a price that can depend on where the step starts, that and the
floor leave exactly one bill, one mark per raise and nothing else (Sections 6 and 7).
With a price per move name, as in my definition, no system whose flag ever rises
meets both, because the raising move, played again from yes, raises nothing and still
costs one. A clock fails the ceiling the first time it charges a step that raised nothing.
The third is order, on the smallest machine I build, and it’s the certified case: there,
from a clean start, the flag can’t go up unless a passing check of a claim came first,
then a commitment to that same claim, and a clock can’t fake that, because it’s about
which moves happened, and a clock only makes marks (Theorem 15.9).
    And why the ledger doesn’t bill heat. In any real device every step that changes
something dissipates as it happens. A ledger that billed that would charge every
step, and that’s the clock: it can’t tell a run that kept something from a run that only
ran. So the ledger leaves the dissipation of happening to physics and counts one
thing, the rise of a reading that stays. A step that costs no marks still dissipates. It
just raises nothing the ledger prices.
    And the other side of that: nothing is in scope just for being a computation. A
Turing machine’s run isn’t an instance of this theorem because it’s a run. It becomes
one when somebody supplies all five parts for it, says which states read yes, and
proves the toll for that cost. Until then the theorem says nothing about it, and I
won’t pretend it does. That’s the toll’s scope. The bill has none to supply. Every
run of anything with one next state per state takes a fresh state at every step, joins
exactly one pair of its states into one, or goes round a loop through its start and
keeps nothing (Theorem 1.1). The reading this isn’t the state I started in rises at the
first step and stays up exactly on the runs that never come back to their start, the
first two kinds, and those pay, in room or in their one merge.
    That’s also where the hunch this book started from ended up, once I checked it:
the night a video about Flatland convinced me there was another axis, a direction
ordinary computing is blind to (the Afterword, Section 24, tells it). It isn’t a direction
62   2 A record and a toll


               an ordinary computer can’t reach. Hand a Turing machine a reading, charge the toll
               on its crossing, and it’s in scope like anything else. The possibility was always there.
               What the usual rules leave out is the price.
                   The same goes for a system with no reading at all. If nothing in it answers “is
               the flag up,” then nothing in it can say, from the inside, that anything is entitled to
               be relied on. Whatever entitlement it ends up with gets carried in from outside, by
               somebody who signs their name to it, and nothing in the system priced it. Smuggled
               entitlement isn’t entitlement for the system, no matter whose name is on it. Be
               careful which way that cuts, though. Whoever reads the signature can be perfectly
               entitled on their own account; that’s what an auditor has, and it’s honest as long as
               it’s called the auditor’s. It isn’t the system’s. On the smallest machine I build later,
               the reason to believe its checker says yes only when the claim is true is exactly that
               kind: a proof, done outside any record the machine keeps, and I’ll say so when I get
               there (Section 15). What outside entitlement never is, is something the system itself
               earned.
                   And here’s a question I’ll only start on here: bolt two Thiele machines together,
               and do you get one? Run them side by side, each move being a move of one or the
               other, and add up the marks. It depends on the reading you give the pair. Take a
               reading that can only go up when one of the parts’ readings goes up, like “either flag
               is up” or “both are”: then any crossing of the pair is a crossing of a part, that part’s
               toll charged it, and the pair obeys the toll. Take “the first flag is up and the second is
               down,” and it doesn’t: that reading turns on when the second flag falls, and nothing
               charges a fall. The first two readings are proved in Appendix F: read through “either
               flag is up” the pair is a Thiele machine whose floor is one. Read through “both are,”
               a run that starts with both flags down and ends with both up costs at least two, and
               two is reached when each part can raise its own flag for one. From a start with
               one flag already up, one raise is enough, so two is a floor for the clean start only.
               The third needs nothing beyond the one unpriced fall above. A related composite is
               proved too, a host machine running a guest, read through “the host’s own flag or its
               copy of the guest’s” (Theorem D.13). Whether every way of building one machine
               out of others keeps the toll is a bigger question, and Appendix F takes it as far as I
               could: some ways do, some provably don’t, and it says which.
                   So why bother with the toy at all? Not because the lineage was looking for it.
               The bulla was after durability, the seven seals after evidence, the consul’s stamp
               after authenticity, the two columns after catching slips; none of them was trying to
               put a price on the moment a flag goes up, and I shouldn’t pretend they were. The
               reason is narrower. Everywhere in that lineage where somebody did locate a cost,
               it sat on a step next to the flag. The flag itself went unpriced as a flag: Szilard on
               the measurement, Bennett on the wiping, proof-of-work on the search, Boyle on
               the instrument and the room, Foster and Stine on the test. One entry prices the
                                                                  2.6 What this does and doesn’t buy   63


crossing’s own shape, and I put it beside the toll on purpose: Landauer’s restore to
one, the literal two-state version of the crossing, whose heat bound depends on the
input uncertainty and the thermal premises. The flag’s job never came into it. The
toy is the first thing I could build where the cost sits on the crossing itself, and it
proves that if you price that step, the floor follows everywhere, for any machine
with the five parts. That’s not an answer. It’s the question made exact enough to be
wrong. And of the five jobs a record does, the toy attempts none of them. Not even
durability: the flag can be lowered by any move you care to write, and the marks
that don’t go away are kept by you, the scorekeeper, beside the board. The machine
keeps none of them. What the toy has is a scorekeeper’s receipt for the crossing.
Whether the machine can be made to keep that receipt itself, where a step could
reach in and change it, is Section 6’s question. Authenticity, evidence, accounting,
cheap checking: none of them is in here, and I’ll say so again when it’s tempting to
forget.
   And here’s what I’ll owe you by the end. Whether the toll is a choice or a
necessity: the next section, and I’ll tell you now that the answer surprised me. What
a mark is worth in anything physical: later, and only partly. What an observer who
sees only a window can and cannot recover, including whether they can even tell
which step paid: its own section. And whether a full-size machine, the kind you
could actually run a program on, can be made to obey the toll without cheating,
and what that machine looks like, and what it costs to vouch for structure in it: that
waits for Part III, on purpose, and takes most of it.
   For now you have a sheet of paper with two boxes, three moves, one rule that
writes the last chapter’s bill into the step, and one theorem you proved yourself in
about a minute. Don’t let go of it. It’s the smallest version of everything that follows,
and if it’s wrong here, it’s wrong everywhere.
CHAPTER 3




Why the toll isn’t arbitrary

The first chapter of this part proved the bill with chairs: a run that raises a flag and
keeps it up either shares a chair somewhere or never repeats one, so keeping is paid
in a merge or in room; and in any real device every step that changes something
dissipates on top of that, by happening. The merge-or-room part needs no premise;
the heat is physics, which I proved for Bennett’s walker with Schnakenberg’s formula
taken as the model, and cited for devices whose states jump or drift at random in
surroundings at a temperature. This chapter counts the room exactly, and asks what
it takes to turn the bill into a mark on a ledger. The flag I built is one thing that
stays; the result is about anything that stays.
    The last chapter wrote that bill into a toy as one rule, and in the toy the move
that raises the flag makes a mark because I said so. If that’s all it is, the ledger is
a long way of describing a preference, and you should treat it the way you’d treat
someone telling you their favourite colour is a law of nature. So this chapter is
me trying to find out whether a machine has to charge it. I’ll tell you the shape
of the answer up front, because I don’t want you reading forty paragraphs to find
out whether there’s a point. The bill itself needs no “if”: on any machine, keeping
something is paid in a merge or in room, and in any real device that comes on top of
the dissipation of every change, with time setting how much; that’s the paragraph
above. Getting from that bill to my rule, a mark on the ledger for the step that
raises the flag, takes three “ifs”: there are finitely many states that read yes, so room
runs out; the flag, once raised, stays up; and the ledger charges every move that
forgets. Then the move that raises the flag has to forget something, two of the states
it acts on landing on one, and pays. Forgetting is also the step Landauer’s principle,
my premise, puts a heat price on, when what’s forgotten wasn’t already known;
when somebody already knew, that knowing is where the bill went, and I’ll show
you that too. Each of the three “ifs” is a door out of the theorem, and I’m going
to walk through each one, because what’s on the other side of each door is where
the content is. None of them is a door out of the bill. Behind the first, the machine
pays in room. Behind the second, the flag comes back down, so nothing is kept and
there’s nothing to bill. Behind the third, the step still forgets, and only the ledger
looks away.




                                  64
                                                              3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   65


   One more thing before the doors, and it comes first on purpose. Nothing in the
argument uses the word certify. It uses a reading that can go from no to yes and
never back. A fuse that has blown is one. So is a seal that has been broken, a bit in
write-once memory, a block a chain has finalized, a measurement somebody wrote
down and won’t take back. The argument below sends the bill to whichever of them
you point at, and the latch chapter (Section 10) proves it doesn’t matter which one
you pick. Certification is the instance I build, for reasons I give in Section 18 and
don’t claim to have proved. So read this section as being about anything that stays.
The flag is only the one I keep on the table.


3.1 A closed room with no spare chair
Do this one with real objects, because the whole section rests on it and it’s about
ninety seconds of work. Draw a box on the table and call it the yes room. Put three
chairs inside the box and one chair outside, by the door. Four people, one per chair;
the people are the states your machine could be in, and the three inside are the
ones whose flag is already up. One move of the machine moves everybody at once:
each person stands up and goes to the chair the rule sends them to. Two rules. First:
nobody inside the room may end up outside, because the flag, once up, stays up.
Second: the person by the door must end up inside, because this move is the one
that raises their flag.
    Now try to finish the move with one person in each chair.
    You can’t. Three people start inside and have to stay inside, so they take the
three inside chairs between them, with nobody left out, because nobody may leave.
The person from the door has to come in. There is no fourth chair inside. Somebody
shares. Two of the machine’s possible states land on one state. Now use the chairs
as a guessing game: secretly choose one starting chair, apply the rule, and report
only the finishing chair. If two arrows end there, the report cannot tell your partner
which start you chose. Watching the people move would tell them; that would keep
information outside the finishing chair. The chair alone has forgotten something.
    That’s the whole argument, and I want to name the piece of mathematics that
did the work, because it’s old and it’s not mine. If you put things into fewer boxes
than there are things, some box gets two. People call it the pigeonhole principle; it’s
the one from “The point,” where Jean Leurechon used it in 1622 to argue that two
people somewhere have the same number of hairs, and the first name for it I could
find came from Dirichlet, who used it in 1842 and later called it the drawer principle.
It’s the kind of fact a child accepts and a mathematician spends a career finding
new uses for. Here the use is: a step that forgets nothing is a one-to-one shuffle, a
one-to-one shuffle of a finite set of chairs hits every chair, so the inside chairs are
all taken by insiders, so there’s no room for the newcomer. Finite. Permanent. Flip.
66   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               Those three force a collision in the instruction’s map. The two starts that collide
               need not include the outsider: send the outsider to one inside chair and send two
               insiders to another. A run from a known outside chair can still have a uniquely
               identifiable start. The collision is a fact about the instruction over possible states.
                   The precise statement of the chairs argument is a theorem a few lines down, and
               it needs one word first. “Injective” is the mathematician’s word for “forgets nothing”:
               a step is injective when two different starts always give two different ends. The
               theorem says exactly what the chairs said and takes exactly the three premises: a
               duplicate-free list that names every state (finite), a reading that no step ever turns
               off (permanent), and one state that reads NO before the step and YES after it (the
               flip). There is no price in it anywhere. It is pure counting. I’ll come back to what
               counts as physics, but notice that nothing so far has been.
                   Here are the words, exactly. For this whole section the setting is the five parts
               from Section 2 without the toll: states S, move names I, a step, a reading, and
               (later) a cost.

                Definition 3.1 (Finite, permanent, injective). The machine is finite when there is
                a list of states with no repeats that contains every state. The reading is permanent
                when no move ever turns it from yes back to no: for all s and i, cert(s) = yes implies
                cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is injective (forgets nothing) when different starts
                give different ends: step( a, i ) = step(b, i ) implies a = b. A move that is not injective
                merges.



                Theorem 3.1 (A permanent flip merges). On a finite machine with a permanent
                reading, if cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then the move i merges.

                Proof. Suppose i were injective. Let C be the list of states that read yes: go down
                the list of every state and keep the ones that read yes. It has no repeats. (That is the
                only use of finiteness: all the proof needs is a duplicate-free list of the yes-states.)
                By permanence, used only for the move i, step(·, i ) sends every member of C into C.
                Being injective, it sends the members of C to members of C with no two landing on
                the same one, so its images are as many as C itself, and a list of that many distinct
                members of C is all of C. So the yes-state step(s, i ) equals step(c, i ) for some c in C,
                and injectivity gives s = c, so s reads yes. It reads no. That’s the contradiction, and
                it’s the chairs.
                   A list with no repeats, as long as the set it draws from, contains the whole set.
                Leave one member of the set out and you have packed the list into one place fewer
                than it has members. That can’t be done: take away one occupied place and the
                                                                3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   67


member sitting in it, and the list is still one too long for the places left, and it stays
one too long until there are no places left at all. This is the pigeonhole in the form
Leurechon would recognise.
    Is that new? No. It has been sitting in two places for a long time, one in physics
and one in the theory of automata, and a physicist will recognise it on sight, so start
there. In 1876 Josef Loschmidt pointed out, against Ludwig Boltzmann’s account
of how a gas settles down, that the laws of mechanics run just as well backwards:
reverse every molecule’s velocity and the gas retraces its steps, so mechanics alone
can’t make entropy only ever climb. Twenty years on, in 1896, a young assistant of
Max Planck’s in Berlin pushed harder. He took Henri Poincaré’s recurrence theorem
of 1890, which says that in a system preserving a finite measure of its accessible
states, almost every starting state returns arbitrarily close to itself, again and again,
and used it to argue that nothing in such a system can climb forever: give it time
and it comes back down. The assistant was Ernst Zermelo, the same Zermelo who’d
put set theory on axioms twelve years later, axioms that keep out the paradox that
had sunk Frege’s foundations of arithmetic (Section 5 tells that one). Boltzmann
answered the same year, not very politely, that the times you’d have to wait for a
return are so enormous that nobody would ever see one. (Jos Uffink, who wrote
the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on Boltzmann’s statistical physics, calls that reply
drenched in sarcasm and bitterness, and calls Zermelo’s own paper a careful logical
argument.)
    Now look at the chairs again. A step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, is a
reshuffle: it moves everybody around in loops, and every loop comes back to where
it started. A flag that goes up and stays up is exactly a quantity that climbs and
never comes back down. So a reshuffle can’t carry one, which is Zermelo’s objection
with the infinities taken out. On a finite set the loops are enough, and Poincaré’s
theorem isn’t needed. And the wait is at most as many steps as there are chairs.
Nothing enormous. Zermelo was aiming it at the second law. Flags never came into
it. A quantum recurrence result came in 1957, when P. Bocchieri and A. Loinger
proved returns arbitrarily close to the initial state under their conditions on a closed
quantum system. That is a neighbouring recurrence argument, not this finite-state
proof: even a finite-dimensional quantum system has continuously many states.
Applying it to a physical record requires saying how that record is read and how
robustly it distinguishes nearby states.
    The second place stings more, because it’s in computer science. Somebody got
here first, again. Picture a finite machine that reads letters, one move per letter.
If every letter just reshuffles the states one for one, automata theorists call it a
permutation automaton, and the sets of inputs such machines can pick out are called
group languages. Jean-Éric Pin’s 1992 paper on reversible automata, machines
whose letters act as one-to-one maps, sorts out exactly which languages those
68   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                machines recognise, and in that world the chairs are folklore. Here’s the short
                version. Start at a state that reads no, and collect every input that ends at a yes.
                Because yes is permanent, adding letters to the end of a collected input keeps it
                collected. A group language with that property is either empty or everything, and
                everything would include the empty input, which ends where it started, at no. So
                it’s empty: no run of reshuffles raises the reading. That’s Theorem 3.1 with the
                moves as letters. Pin’s paper is where I’d send you to check the automata side. It
                isn’t about flags or prices, and I’m not claiming it says anything about them.
                    And if you like your facts in the most general clothes going, category theorists
                have this one too. Treat the moves as a monoid acting on the states, and a permanent
                reading as a set of states the moves never leave. In the topos of that monoid’s actions,
                the truth value of “reads yes” at a state is the set of move sequences that carry it
                into the yes-states. Every move can be undone exactly when the monoid is a group,
                and exactly then is that topos Boolean, which makes every such truth value all or
                nothing. Morgan Rogers lays out that fact in his 2019 and 2021 papers on toposes
                of monoid actions. On a finite set, a move that merges nothing can be undone, so
                it’s the chairs again, in a third language. Does it change anything here? No. It’s the
                same fact wearing a bigger coat, and I mention it so nobody thinks the chairs are
                mine.
                    Going quantum doesn’t get around the automata version either. Alex Brodsky and
                Nicholas Pippenger (2002) showed that a quantum finite automaton that measures
                only once, at the very end, accepts with bounded error exactly the group languages,
                the reshuffle kind. One that’s allowed to measure after every letter, and to stop on
                what it sees, does better: it accepts every piecewise testable language, and “has
                seen a b somewhere” is one of those. A measurement that can stop the machine is a
                record that stays, and it’s the extra thing that lets the bigger class in.
                    The third place is the closest, and it isn’t old at all. In 2023 Thomas Ouldridge
                and David Wolpert derived the thermodynamics of a finite automaton built the way
                real computers are: the same physical step run again and again, each time touching
                only the part of the machine that changes. They sorted languages into two kinds by
                the smallest automaton that recognises each one. If that automaton has a letter that
                sends two states to one, every automaton for the language has such a letter too, and
                on their derivation recognising the language on a device like that produces entropy,
                waste no cleverer design gets back, unless the inputs are so finely arranged that
                only one of the merged states ever actually turns up. If the smallest automaton only
                reshuffles, they find the language can be recognised with no unavoidable entropy
                production at all. One of their worked examples is the strings with no b in them,
                which is my flag turned inside out: the runs that raise it are exactly the strings that
                have seen a b. So the chairs, a real price on them, and the case when you already
                                                                 3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   69


know which chair you’re in are all in their paper, three years before this book. Their
price is derived from the physics of the device. Mine is assumed.
    There’s a fourth neighbour, and I’d call it a cousin, because it speaks another
language. Constructor theory is David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto’s programme for
stating physics as which transformations a device that runs in a cycle can and can’t
bring about, and in it a task is irreversible when it’s possible and its inverse isn’t.
Marletto’s version of thermodynamics (posted in 2016) leans on exactly that: tasks
that are possible while their transposes aren’t. Marletto, the physicist Vlatko Vedral
and coauthors (2022) made an irreversible task out of the quantum homogeniser, a
machine of reservoir qubits that interact by partial swaps, and ran it with photons.
Maria Violaris and Marletto (2022) then argued that the same machine, run in a
cycle, can turn a pure qubit into a mixed one and can never turn a mixed qubit
back into a pure one, even though every interaction in it is reversible, and that this
suggests erasure may cost something beyond Landauer’s bound. The chairs are a
classical, finite, exact cousin of that sentence: a set of states a step can’t leave, a task
that’s possible, and no way back. Theirs is quantum and approximate and aimed at
physics’ price; mine is counted, and assumes its price. Deutsch and Marletto’s paper
on information (2015) has a neighbour of the chairs argument in its section 8.6:
measuring one observable disturbs another irreducibly, and nothing can undo the
disturbance afterwards while the outcome stays in an information variable. That’s a
second, theory-independent way of saying that a record that stays makes the step
irreversible.
    So what I can claim here is narrower again, and I’d rather say exactly how. Is
even the pricing form Ouldridge and Wolpert’s? In physics, on their derivation,
yes: a merge the language can’t avoid costs entropy. A price assumed rather than
derived isn’t mine either: Li and Vitányi (1996) took a unit charge for every bit
irreversibly erased, with steps that can be undone priced at zero, as axioms of a
model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) put a price on named
instructions that destroy bits, a unit for an AND or an overwrite. What I didn’t
find anywhere I looked is what a price on merging moves forces on a reading that
stays, charged on a ledger whether or not anybody’s physics is right (put a price
on merging and the flip has to pay it, which is the next subsection), and what I get
out of that: the toll, as a theorem about the ledger, the merge-or-revoke split for
a single move, the exact match between “forced to be priced” and “merges” when
move names can be decided equal or different, the squeeze bound counted in whole
marks and its entropy form, a built machine walking out of each door, and every
proof on the page. Those are the forms I didn’t find stated anywhere I looked, and
Appendix C sorts them the same way: the counting core classical and somebody
else’s, the pricing form only partly mine. The core move is older than the computer,
it had two homes before it got to mine, and its physical price had a third.
70   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                3.2 Now charge for forgetting, and the toll falls out
                Here’s the step I’d been circling since the chairs. In the last chapter I told you
                Bennett’s rule as he states it: what has to cost is erasing a bit or merging two paths
                a computation could have taken. I didn’t ask you to believe it. I’m not going to ask
                you now either. I’m going to write it down as a rule you can accept or refuse, in the
                smallest form that does any work: any move that forgets something costs at least one
                mark. Any move that is not injective has cost at least one. That’s it. Note what it
                does not say. It says nothing about certifying. It says nothing about flags. It’s a price
                on forgetting and only on forgetting.
                    Put the two together. The room says: on a finite machine with a permanent flag,
                the move that raises the flag forgets something. The price says: a move that forgets
                something costs at least one. So the move that raises the flag costs at least one. That
                is the toll, the rule the toy was handed because I said so, and now a machine has to
                charge it. The proof is two lines: the first theorem says the flipping move merges,
                the premise says merges are priced, done. I’ll keep saying “premise,” because that’s
                what it is, and because a section further on (Section 4) is about what happened to
                some very smart people who put a price where a premise goes and then treated it as
                a law of nature, and about half of this one is me trying not to do that.

                Premise 3.2 (Merge pricing). Every move that merges costs at least one: for all i, if
                i is not injective then cost(i ) ≥ 1.
               Observation 3.2 (The toll from finiteness, permanence, and merge pricing). On
               a finite machine with a permanent reading whose cost satisfies merge pricing, every
               move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. That is, the machine
               with that cost is a Thiele machine in the sense of Definition 2.1, and the universal floor
               (Observation 2.1) applies to it.
                Proof. A move that flips the reading merges, by Theorem 3.1; merge pricing charges
                it at least one.
                    The theorem asks for more than it uses. Only the yes-states need to be finitely
                many: with a permanent reading and finitely many states reading yes, the rest of the
                machine as large as you like, merge pricing still gives the toll. With infinitely many it
                can fail: Door one below builds a machine that raises a permanent flag at zero marks
                while charging every merge. That machine hasn’t got out of the bill. It pays in room,
                and a price list that charges only merges never looks at that column. And merge
                pricing asks for more than the toll needs. Under those same two conditions the
                toll holds exactly when every move that flips the reading somewhere and merges is
                priced. Merge pricing gives that, and the eight-state machine described later in this
                section, with its jump repriced at no marks, meets the toll without merge pricing.
                                                       3.3 Door one: keep everything, and pay in room   71


   One more way to see the same thing, because it answers a rival I’d otherwise owe
you. The rival says: leave certification alone. Price erasure, and keep an honest flag
that reports when something was erased. Fine; but a system can set its certificate at
cost zero with its erasure flag reporting nothing, exactly because the certifying move
merged two states and the flag didn’t say so. Make the erasure flag honest, so that it
reports every move that forgets, and on a finite machine with a flag that stays up the
erasure law sends the same bill the toll does. The toll isn’t a rival to honest erasure
accounting. It’s what honest erasure accounting says about the certifying move.
   So, is the toll arbitrary? Here’s the honest version. The toll is a consequence of
three things: finitely many states that read yes (a finite memory is plenty), a flag
that stays up, and a charge on forgetting. If you accept all three, you don’t get to
refuse the toll; it’s forced. If you refuse any one of them, the toll on my ledger goes
back to being my preference. The bill stays where it was; what’s gone is the proof
that my ledger has to send it. So the question “did I have to pick it” has turned
into three smaller questions, which is what progress usually looks like: a better
set of things to argue about. Let me take the three doors in order, and for each
one, build the thing that walks out through it, because a premise you can’t see the
counterexample to is a premise you’re taking on faith.


3.3 Door one: keep everything, and pay in room

Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine’s whole state is the
strip. Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any
box has a 1 in it. Check the three premises. Permanent: once there’s a 1, there’s
always a 1. Flip: the empty strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. Forgets
nothing: every move can be undone by erasing the last 1, so two different strips
never become the same strip. So here is a machine that raises a flag, keeps it up,
and never merges anything. The chairs theorem has no grip on it, and a price list
that charges only merges doesn’t charge it. But look at what each move does: it
writes in a box nobody has written in before. The raise takes a fresh box, and so
does every step after it, forever. It hasn’t got out of the bill. It’s paying in the other
column, room, and a price list that only charges merges just isn’t looking at that
column. (Each write still dissipates when it actually happens, like any change; what
the strip dodges is the floor a merge would add on top.) In the exact form its state
is a row of 1s of any length, which is how you say the strip has no end.
    If the endless strip feels like a cheat, it’s a famous one. David Hilbert, in a lecture
course in the winter of 1924–25, told a story about a hotel with infinitely many
rooms, every one of them taken, where a new guest still gets a room: everybody
moves from room n to room n + 1, and room 1 comes free. That’s the room column,
told as a joke about a front desk: nobody shares, and every guest in the building
72   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               packs up and moves one room along, into a room that’s occupied as he moves, by a
               guest who’s moving on at the same moment, so that one room at the front comes
               free. The guests go one-to-one into a part of the hotel, with a gap left over. And
               here’s the part worth checking: Hilbert never published it. The hotel became famous
               because George Gamow put it in a popular book in 1947, and for a long time it
               wasn’t clear Hilbert had told it at all. The historian of science Helge Kragh first
               guessed that Gamow had made it up. Then Tilman Sauer, a historian of science who
               had co-edited a volume of Hilbert’s lectures on the foundations of physics, pointed
               him to Hilbert’s lecture notes, which had just been printed in 2013, and in 2014
               Kragh took his guess back in a paper called “The True (?) Story of Hilbert’s Infinite
               Hotel.” Keep the question mark. Even Kragh’s own paper puts the lecture in January
               1924 in one place and January 1925 in another. Still, this time a story everybody
               repeated turned out to have a real lecture behind it. I’ve learned not to count on
               that happening. Bring it back to the table. In the room, the person from the door
               had nowhere to sit because the chairs ran out. In Hilbert’s hotel they never do, so
               everybody shifts one over and nobody has to share. The strip machine is that hotel.
               The argument stays the same. What the hotel shows you is that it was about running
               out of chairs all along.
                   What walked out the door is the finiteness premise. Now cut the strip to eight
               boxes and run it for real: eight boxes, nine moves. On the ninth move there’s
               nowhere to write. To keep going you have to reuse a box, and the moment you reuse
               a box two different histories end on the same strip, and you’re back in the room
               with a shared chair. Keeping the whole history is exactly the move Bennett made in
               1973, when he showed that any computation can be done without forgetting if you
               let it keep a copy of everything it did; Landauer, back in 1961, had already written
               that for a machine able to run a program that doesn’t stop, the space to hold every
               intermediate result “cannot be there.” Keeping the history is a real way to pay. It
               costs a memory that never fills, and every machine you can buy has a memory that
               fills.
                   Bennett wasn’t the first there, or the last. Yves Lecerf, in a short note to the French
               Academy of Sciences in 1963, had already shown that reversible Turing machines
               can simulate arbitrary ones, and the note went largely unnoticed. The computer
               scientist Tommaso Toffoli (1980), and Edward Fredkin and Toffoli together (1982),
               both then at MIT, built reversible logic: gates and circuits that compute any function
               and lose nothing, by carrying constant inputs in and extra outputs out. Their basic
               gate wasn’t new even then. Landauer’s own 1961 paper writes down a three-bit
               device that replaces r by p · q when r is 0 and by the negation of p · q when r is 1,
               calls it logically reversible and capable of an AND, and says each AND then needs its
               own supplied ZERO and leaves its extra outputs behind. He doubted such a machine
               could be useful. What Toffoli added was the proof that it computes everything. And
                                                       3.3 Door one: keep everything, and pay in room   73


the computer scientist Kenichi Morita (1996) proved that reversible two-counter
machines are universal, so even a machine as small as the one Section 15 builds can
compute everything with every move one-to-one. Every one of them keeps what it
doesn’t forget somewhere: a history, garbage outputs, a counter that codes the past.
The strip is that.
    There are three separate claims here, and I need to keep them apart. The strip
machine is permanent and forgets nothing. It also has infinitely many states: no
finite list holds every finite strip. Neither of those involves a cost. The third does: the
strip can raise its reading at zero marks. Count the strip’s length as a whole number
and let each move add one at a price of zero. Nothing merges, merge pricing holds,
and the toll fails. That’s what a price list that charges merges and nothing else looks
like on a machine with endless room: the raised reading shows up at no charge on
the ledger because the column it’s paid in isn’t on the bill.
    Here’s the same thing for one move instead of a run, and it says exactly how
much room it takes.


Proposition 3.3 (A raise with no merge takes endless room). Let a move never turn
a reading from yes to no, let it raise the reading at some state s (no at s, yes where
the move sends s), and let it send no two different states to the same state. Then
it sends the states that read yes one-to-one into a part of themselves that leaves at
least one of them out: the state the move sends s to. So there are infinitely many
states that read yes. With finitely many, the raising move merges two states.

Proof. The move sends every yes-state to a yes-state, because it never turns yes
to no, and it sends different states to different states. It sends s to a yes-state. If
some yes-state c were also sent there, the move would send s and c to one state,
so s = c; but s reads no and c reads yes. So the yes-states are sent one-to-one into
the yes-states with that one left out. If there were only n yes-states, that would put
n things one-to-one into n − 1 places, which the pigeonhole forbids. So there are
infinitely many.
    That’s Hilbert’s front desk as a theorem, and it’s also exactly how Richard
Dedekind defined an infinite collection in 1888: one that can be matched one-
to-one with a part of itself that leaves something out. So with no merge, every raise
has to send the kept things one-to-one into a part of themselves with a gap left over,
and only endlessly many of them have a gap to spare. Room isn’t the absence of a
bill. It’s the other way of paying it, and only an endless building can keep paying it.
    Which state is being counted. Whether a move merges depends on what the state
keeps. The strip keeps its history, so nothing merges; cut it to eight boxes and the
reuse merges. Section 19 proves the general form (Theorem 19.3): keep the list
74   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                of every earlier state alongside the current one and every fixed-instruction step is
                one-to-one. (Keeping only the one state before isn’t enough: two states that differ
                only in what came before them still land together.) So a merge price is a fact about
                a move on a stated state space. Each price derived in this book is derived on the
                whole state its definition gives, and three things go with it: which state that is, what
                lies outside it (nothing outside it is charged), and whether the move is one primitive
                instruction or a composite run of several. Relabelling the states one-to-one changes
                no price, since it sends merges to merges and one-to-one moves to one-to-one moves.
                Adding history to the state, or projecting part of the state away, changes the machine
                being modelled, and the price can change with it.
                    Door one deserves a number, because “a memory that never fills” is doing all the
                work and I’d rather see the bill than take it on trust.


                Proposition 3.4 (Heat or room). (1) Let a machine run by one rule, so that every
                state has exactly one next state, and let its reading never go from yes back to no.
                Take any run in which the reading goes from no to yes. Then either some step of the
                run merges two of its states (two different states of the run have the same next state),
                or the run never visits the same state twice. So on a machine with M states, a run
                that keeps a record and never merges has fewer than M steps. (2) Let an operation
                send every value to one fixed value and leave that value alone. Take a machine
                with M states run by one rule, a reading of its states, and N different starting states,
                exactly one of which already reads the fixed value, such that from every start each
                of the next T states reads the fixed value. If no two different states among those the
                runs sit in at steps 0 to T − 1 have the same next state (the operation is carried out
                through T repetitions without merging), then M ≥ 1 + ( T + 1)( N − 1). A bounded
                memory delays the merge and does not avoid it.

                Proof. (1) Suppose no two different states of the run share a next state, and suppose
                the run still sits in some chair twice, once early and once later. Walk the two visits
                back together, one step at a time: two equal states whose predecessors are both in
                the run had equal predecessors, because nothing merged. The early visit gets back
                to the start first, and the later visit is then on the start’s chair too. So the run comes
                back to its start after some number p of steps, and since one rule gives the next state,
                it comes back again after 2p, 3p, and so on forever. The start reads no: a yes there
                would stay yes all along, and the reading does go from no to yes. Some of those
                returns come after the raise, where the reading is yes and stays yes, and each of
                them is the start, which reads no. So the repeat was impossible. A run that never
                shares a chair takes a fresh chair at every step, and with M chairs that’s at most
                M − 1 steps. (2) Run the chairs along paths. Walking two equal states back together,
                                                       3.3 Door one: keep everything, and pay in room   75


as in (1), is allowed at any step from 1 to T, because the states one step earlier
are at steps 0 to T − 1. Each of the N − 1 starts not already in the fixed reading,
followed through T repetitions, occupies T + 1 chairs, and none twice: a repeat
would walk back to the start equalling a later state of its own path, and every later
state reads the fixed value while the start does not. Two of those paths cannot share
a chair either: walk back to the earlier time, and either two different starts sit in
one chair, or a start sits in a chair that reads the fixed value. That is ( T + 1)( N − 1)
chairs. The start that already reads the fixed value, followed through T repetitions,
ends in one more: if that chair were on one of the paths, walking back would again
put a start in a chair that reads the fixed value. One more is all that start is owed,
not T + 1: every state on its own path reads the fixed value, so walking back along
it finds no contradiction, and the path may fold onto one chair, as it does in the
building below.
    The number is exact, not only a floor, and you can build the building that reaches
it. One chair for the start that already reads the fixed way; the operation leaves it
sitting there. For every other start, lay out a row of chairs, one chair longer than
the number of repetitions you want to survive. The first chair in the row reads the
way that start reads, the rest read the fixed way, and the operation walks the row
and parks on the last chair. Count the chairs: one, plus a row for each of the other
starts. For as many repetitions as you asked for, nobody shares a chair. On the next
repetition somebody does, because the last chair in every row now lands where the
chair before it lands. A single fixed reading isn’t needed either. If the operation sends
everyone to one of a few parking spots and leaves each spot alone, and every spot is
one of the starts, the same walking back counts the same rows inside each spot’s
own catchment. The total comes to one chair per start, plus, for every repetition,
one more chair for each start that isn’t a parking spot. With one spot that is the
bound in the proposition, and the same rows in each catchment show it exact. In the
exact form: N starts, L of them spots, T repetitions, at least N + T ( N − L) chairs,
and that many are enough. In bits: a memory of B bits has at most 2B states, so
                                                                                  
surviving T repetitions with one spot takes B ≥ log2 1 + ( T + 1)( N − 1) . The
room grows with the logarithm of how long the history is kept; a fresh state at every
step isn’t a fresh cell at every step.
    So the strip pays in room for as long as it has room to pay. Cut the strip anywhere
and part (1) says how many moves are left before a box gets reused. Room is not
the only other cost. Bennett (1989) showed that a computation can run without
ever forgetting, but then its space grows with the run, or it spends time undoing and
redoing its own work to keep the space small. Part (1) says what that time buys: a
run that never sits two in one chair needs a fresh chair at every step, so a building
of chairs runs out one step before the number of chairs. Redoing work slows down
76   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                how fast you go through the chairs. It doesn’t add any. And the time has its own bill.
                Bennett’s review (1982) gives the rate for his Brownian computer: the heat per step
                is proportional to the speed, so at any speed the machine actually runs at, every
                step gives off heat. Going slower shrinks that heat toward zero and never gets there,
                because only a step that takes forever gives off none, and a step that takes forever
                never happens. The first chapter of this part proved that as time’s bill, Theorem 1.8.
                So two bills are running. Anything that changes a device’s state dissipates, and time
                sets how much. Keeping something adds a second bill on top: a shared chair, which
                carries a floor of heat that no slowness removes, or a fresh chair, which is room. A
                reading that stays up pays that second bill, heat floor or room, and it lands on the
                move that raises it. Which one a device pays is physics. That it pays one of them is
                counting.


                3.4 Door two: let the flag come back down
                Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is
                undoable (turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads: that’s a
                flip, NO to YES. And heads goes to tails: the same move takes the flag back down
                somewhere else. Two states, finite as it gets, and the move that raises the flag
                forgets nothing, so a schedule that charges only for forgetting is allowed to charge it
                nothing. The move is injective and can switch the reading both on and off. Pricing
                the turn at zero meets merge pricing, since no move merges, and fails the toll. The
                thing that walked out the door is permanence.
                     Now here’s a fact sharper than the premise it replaces, and it was the thing in this
                section that surprised me. Drop permanence entirely. Keep only finiteness. Take any
                move that raises the flag anywhere. Then one of two things is true: the move forgets
                something, or the same move lowers the flag somewhere else. There’s no third
                option, and the proof below is a search: go through the finitely many YES states
                looking for one this move turns to NO. Find one, and that’s the revocation; find
                none, and the move is permanent at least for itself, which is all the room argument
                needs. So a flag that goes up without a merge is a flag the same move can take back.
                A flag that nothing takes back is paid for. You can’t have a raise at zero marks that
                stays raised, not on any finite machine, not with any price schedule that charges for
                forgetting. That’s a narrower sentence than “every certificate costs.” It’s true, and
                I’ll take it. The broad one would only be mine.


                Theorem 3.5 (Merge or revoke). On a finite machine (no permanence assumed),
                if cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then either i merges, or there is a state t
                with cert(t) = yes and cert(step(t, i )) = no.
                                                          3.4 Door two: let the flag come back down   77


Proof. Check every yes-state on the finite list for one that i sends to no. If there is
one, that is the second alternative. If there is none, then i keeps every yes-state at
yes, which is permanence for the single move i; the argument of Theorem 3.1 uses
permanence only for the move it is about, so it applies, and i merges.
    I’ll give you the three-card version too, because it shows that a move can be
forced to be priced without writing anything permanent, and I don’t want you to
think the picture is tidier than it is. Three cards, T0, T1, T2, with a star on T1. The
rule: T0 goes to T1, T1 goes to T2, T2 goes to T1. T0 gains the star (a flip). T1 loses
it (a revocation). T0 and T2 both land on T1 (a merge). So this move is priced,
by the forgetting rule, and yet it writes nothing permanent; it takes a star away in
the same breath. “The priced moves are exactly the permanent records” is false,
as the three cards just showed. What’s true is one direction: on a finite machine
whose move names can be decided equal or different, every permanent raise is a
priced move. The other direction has the three cards standing in it. And “priced”
here has an exact meaning worth one sentence: a move is forced to be priced when
every schedule that charges for forgetting charges it, and that holds exactly when
the move forgets something, with no finiteness needed at all. A way to tell two
move names apart is enough.

Definition 3.3 (Forced to be priced). A move i is forced to be priced when every cost
function satisfying merge pricing (Premise 3.2) charges i at least one.



Theorem 3.6 (Forced price is merging). If any two move names can be decided
equal or different, then a move is forced to be priced exactly when it merges. No
finiteness is needed.

Proof. If i merges, merge pricing charges it at least one, whatever the cost function.
If i does not merge, define the cost that is 0 on i and 1 on every other move (this
is where telling move names apart is used). It satisfies merge pricing, since every
merging move is some move other than i and costs one, and it charges i nothing, so
i is not forced.



Corollary 3.7 (Permanent records are forced). On a finite machine whose move
names can be decided equal or different, a move that never turns the reading off
and turns it on somewhere is forced to be priced. (By Theorem 3.5 it merges; by
Theorem 3.6 it is forced.) The converse fails: the three cards are forced, because
they merge, and they revoke.
78   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                3.5 Door three: don’t charge for forgetting
               The third door is the easiest to describe and the hardest to argue about, so I’ll
               describe it and then spend the rest of the section on the argument. Take a sheet of
               paper and let its reading be just BLANK or STAMPED. One move: stamp it if blank,
               and leave it alone if already stamped. Finite, two readings. Permanent: STAMPED
               stays STAMPED. Flip: BLANK goes to STAMPED. Both possible readings now end at
               STAMPED. The paper’s fibres, the ink and your memory are outside this two-state
               description; the merge is a loss from the reading, not the disappearance of every
               physical trace. Everything the room argument needs is here, and the move merges.
               Now set the price of that move to zero. The toll fails, and you can watch it fail: the
               flag went up at zero marks. What walked out the door is the charge on forgetting.
               (A price of one on that move satisfies all three premises, so the premises can hold
               together; door three is about whether they must.) Nothing in counting stops you
               from setting that price to zero. Only a claim about the world does. The nearest
               such claim is Landauer’s, and I have to be exact about the gap between the two: the
               premise as written charges every forgetting move, whether or not you knew which
               state you were in, and Landauer’s own heat, as the coin under the cup below will
               show, is owed only for what you didn’t know. Merge pricing keeps only a yes-or-no
               distinction: whether any pair can merge. The one-bit reset is where it comes from,
               and it measures neither the full worst-case entropy loss nor the heat of any particular
               preparation. The counting needs only that rule.
                  Here is what Landauer said, in 1961, as exactly as I can put it. I went past the
               summaries and read the paper itself. A logical operation with no single-valued
               inverse (a step that forgets, in this book’s words) must produce heat, “typically
               of the order of kT” per operation, where k is Boltzmann’s constant and T is the
               temperature; and for the specific case of resetting one bit whose value you don’t
               know, the minimum is kT times the natural log of 2, about 0.69 kT. I want you to
               hear two things in that. First, “of the order of”: he was not handing out a number
               to three decimals. Second, and this surprised me, he did not measure anything.
               The paper is argument, with models. He writes that he can “show, or at least very
               strongly suggest” the conclusion, and that his reasoning gives “no guarantee that
               this minimum is in fact achievable.” That’s the founding paper of the whole subject,
               and it’s a careful man saying “I think this is right and here’s why.” I like him more
               for it.
                  Was it measured, eventually? Yes, and only recently. In 2012 a group at the École
               Normale Supérieure in Lyon, Antoine Bérut and Sergio Ciliberto’s lab working with
               Eric Lutz, trapped a single glass bead, two millionths of a metre across, in a double
               well made of laser light, and used the two wells as the two values of a bit. Then they
               erased the bit, by lowering the barrier, tilting the trap, and raising it again, many
                                                          3.5 Door three: don’t charge for forgetting   79


times over, slower and slower, and measured the heat each time. The average heat
came down toward Landauer’s kT ln 2 as the erasure got slower, closer the slower it
went, and never under it. On average. Single runs went under it; the bound is about
the average, and any one erasure can beat it. And if you only succeed in erasing
half the time the floor drops to zero, which the paper’s formula shows and which I
think is the most honest line in it. Others have done it since with different devices.
So: predicted in 1961 by argument, seen in a laboratory fifty-one years later.
    And is it settled? No, and I’d be lying by omission if I left that out, because the
people who doubt it are not cranks. John Norton, a philosopher of physics, has
argued since 2005 that the usual proofs of the principle quietly assume what they’re
trying to prove, and that the kinds of process they assume, combined, could be made
to break the very law the principle is supposed to guard. An earlier objection, made
in 1998–99 by Norton and his Pittsburgh colleague John Earman, also a philosopher
of physics, was that the principle can’t be independent of the second law. Charles
Bennett, who did more than anyone to build the subject, rated that one “in my
opinion the one of greatest merit,” and then disagreed with it. Others replied to
Norton; Norton replied back. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on the topic, written
by a philosopher of physics who works on exactly this, ends without a verdict. I’ve
read what I could of both sides and I’m not qualified to referee them, and I’m not
going to pretend the laboratory settles a question about what the principle means in
general, because measuring one bead doesn’t do that.
    So here’s what I did with it, and I think it’s the only honest thing to do. The
charge on forgetting is written into this book as a named premise. It’s a definition
the theorems take as an assumption, and nowhere is it proved as a general fact,
because it isn’t provable from counting; for a particular machine with a particular
price list you can see it hold (the stamp at cost one, above), which is a different
thing. If Norton turns out to be right, every theorem in this section still holds; they
just have one premise fewer that the world agrees to. If Landauer’s side turns out to
be right, it supports a thermal price under its conditions; the whole-number charge
on every merging move is still the ledger rule stated here. Either way, nothing in
this section says a device does anything until someone measures the device. The
counting is mine to prove. The physics is a door I’ve labelled, and what opens it is a
measurement. A proof can’t.
    Labelled, though, isn’t the same as unplaced, and a hedge isn’t a position, so
here’s mine. Earman and Norton’s objection is a dilemma. Either an information-
theoretic exorcism of the demon assumes the second law, which they call the sound
horn, and then it adds nothing the second law didn’t already give; or it rests on
a new principle tying information to entropy, the profound horn, and nobody has
given that principle independent grounds. A named premise is the sound horn, on
purpose. That’s where Bennett ended up in 2003, and Norton’s “Too Good to Be True”
80   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               (written in 2025, published in 2026) says the careful literature almost always accepts
               that horn, and argues that whatever succeeds there is ordinary thermodynamics
               relabelled. I’ll take that. Ordinary thermodynamics, relabelled onto a ledger, is all
               this section asks of the physics. And on the counting I’m on Norton’s side outright.
               His 2018 paper “Maxwell’s Demon Does Not Compute” exorcises the demon with
               Liouville’s theorem and nothing else, no information and no computation: dynamics
               that keeps every patch of states the same size can’t crowd a big set of states into a
               small one. The counting core of this section, that a step losing nothing can’t carry
               a no-state into a set that stays up, is that point in finite, discrete form. And if you
               want the best case for the premise itself, the one I found is James Ladyman, Stuart
               Presnell, Anthony Short and Berry Groisman (2007): from one of the standard
               statements of the second law, the one named for Kelvin, they derive that a logically
               irreversible operation can’t be carried out thermodynamically reversibly by any of
               their L-machines. That’s a physical argument under their stated model of a machine.
               It deserves to be argued with on those terms; it does not by itself establish the book’s
               whole-number ledger charge.
                   One question a physicist asks before any of that, and it’s a good one: the laws
               underneath never merge anything. Classical mechanics carries each exact state
               forward to exactly one next state and could carry it back again, and Liouville’s
               theorem adds that a patch of states keeps its size as it moves; quantum mechanics is
               unitary, which is one-to-one too. So when this section says a step merged two states,
               where did the difference go? Out of the machine. The merge is in the machine’s own
               description, the states its reading is about. The machine together with everything
               around it still runs one-to-one, and the distinction the machine forgot survives. It
               gets pushed out into the surroundings. The surroundings are Door one’s endless
               strip: the room column, which the universe as a whole may have to spend and
               the machine doesn’t, because the machine isn’t the universe and its memory fills.
               Pushing a distinction out isn’t yet heat: another memory could keep it as a readable
               record. It’s heat when the reset removes real uncertainty into a thermal reservoir,
               and then Landauer’s premise bounds the mean heat handed over. None of that
               heat has to be heat wasted. Takahiro Sagawa’s 2014 analysis says that erasure can,
               in principle, approach a process that produces no entropy overall: the reservoir’s
               entropy goes up by what the machine’s goes down. A positive mean heat transfer
               can then be unavoidable without being wasteful. A known input has no uncertainty
               to remove, and this entropy-loss premise alone sets no positive heat floor for it. The
               reset still dissipates when it actually happens in a finite time, and a reset device that
               wasn’t built for that one input keeps a floor that survives going slowly (Section 3.7).
                   Ladyman and his coauthors and Sagawa aren’t disagreeing. They use “reversible”
               for two different things. Ladyman’s L-machines are devices, and a device counts as
               reversible only if it produces no entropy on every input it’s fed, each one known
                                                     3.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze   81


(their section 4: “the L-machine is thermodynamically reversible if and only if”
every one of its processes, one per input, produces no entropy). Sagawa’s reversible
erasure is a process on one given spread of inputs, with the device tuned to that
spread. The standard eraser is reversible in Sagawa’s sense and not in Ladyman’s:
on an even mix of 0 and 1 it produces no entropy, and on each known input it
produces k B ln 2. One identity holds the two together. For a fixed device that sends
every input to one output, and any spread q of its inputs, the average over inputs
of the entropy produced on each known input equals the entropy produced on the
spread q, plus k B times the Shannon entropy of q. Here’s why. The heat is the same
average either way, because the device is fixed. The output is the same either way.
The only difference is at the start: the spread’s own entropy includes k B H (q) for
not knowing which input it is, and each known input’s doesn’t. Sagawa makes the
first term on the right zero; Ladyman reads the left side, which is then k B H (q), and
more than zero.


3.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze

The toll says “at least one mark.” That’s a floor for raising one flag. The room
argument says more if you let it. Say there are m people already inside and k
more come in through the door in one move. (That’s a different k from the one in
Landauer’s kT; when the two meet, below, Boltzmann’s constant gets a little B hung
under it, k B , so you can tell it from a head count.) All m plus k of them end up in m
chairs. That’s a squeeze, by a factor of (m + k) over m, and if you accept a slightly
stronger version of the forgetting price, that each mark pays for at most one halving
of the number of distinguishable states, then the move costs at least the number of
halvings in that squeeze, which is the base-two logarithm of (m + k)/m.
    Back to door three’s stamp, but give the reading four possible values this time: A,
B, C and YES. Write them on four cards. Choose one secretly, then cover its face with
an identical opaque YES label. Read only the new face: all four possibilities now
give YES. Before the move, identifying the original face took two yes-or-no questions
(one of the first two? then which one?); afterward there is only one possible face to
report. Two bits gone from that reading. Two halvings. Peeling the label off would
recover the old face, so this tabletop version models the loss from the reading; it
does not demonstrate physical erasure. So that move costs at least two marks, and
two marks is enough: a cost of exactly two satisfies the halving rule. The general
statement is m + k at most 2 to the cost times m, and there is also a logarithm form
that rounds both logarithms up and is weaker for it (three states and one newcomer
round to the same two bits on both sides, and the rounded form says nothing). The
halving premise, like the one before it, is a definition used as an assumption. The
82   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                units are halvings. To turn a halving into joules of heat you multiply by k B T ln 2,
                and that multiplication is physics; the counting stops before it.
                    That little k B deserves a short trip of its own, because it sits exactly where count-
                ing turns into physics, and its name is a small history lesson. Ludwig Boltzmann’s
                grave in Vienna has S = k log W carved on it (that k is the same k B , before anyone
                hung a B under it): entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of ways
                the parts could be arranged. The idea is his. The constant, and the equation written
                that way, came from Max Planck, in his work on radiation around 1900. In his
                Nobel lecture in 1920 Planck said the constant “is frequently termed Boltzmann’s
                constant, although to the best of my knowledge Boltzmann himself never introduced
                it,” and guessed that Boltzmann never believed anyone could measure it accurately.
                I’d assumed Planck named it after Boltzmann. His own words point the other way:
                it was other people calling it that, and who first did, I couldn’t pin down. So the
                most famous constant in this corner of physics wears the name of a man who didn’t
                write it down. Does that change the bill? No. But look at the job the constant does
                in that equation. Take it away and what’s left is the logarithm of a count, which is
                a number of halvings, which is what the squeeze bound hands you. The constant
                is the exchange rate, and whether the world honours that rate for a merge is the
                premise. No theorem here settles it.
                    Exactly, with one new piece of notation: for a list D of states, write | D | for how
                many it has, and imgi ( D ) for the number of different states the move i sends them
                to.

                Premise 3.4 (Halving price). Each mark pays for at most one halving: for every
                move i and every list D of states with no repeats, | D | ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ( D ). (It
                implies merge pricing, since a merge sends two different states to one and so needs
                cost(i ) ≥ 1.)

                    There’s a plainer way to read that premise, and it’s worth having because it says
                what the premise is about. Look at one landing spot of a move and count how many
                states land there; call the biggest such count the move’s worst pile-up. The premise
                holds exactly when the cost covers the worst pile-up in halvings: a cost of one allows
                piles of two, a cost of two allows piles of four, and a pile of three already needs a
                cost of two. One direction: hand the premise one whole pile. It lands on a single
                spot, so the premise says the pile has at most that many members. The other: any
                list of states splits by where its members land, each part sits inside one pile, so the
                list is at most the number of landing spots times the worst pile-up, which is what
                the premise says. So the halving price asks a move to pay for the worst it could
                ever do, whichever state it’s actually handed. That’s worst case on purpose, and it
                has a home in physics. In the branch of thermodynamics that prices a single run
                                                     3.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze   83


that has to succeed every time, with no averaging over many runs, Philippe Faist,
Frédéric Dupuis, Jonathan Oppenheim and Renato Renner derived in 2015, in that
framework, what they give as the least work any logical process needs, and when
every input might occur and no error is allowed, their bound comes to k B T ln 2 times
exactly that logarithm. Take an AND gate as the example: three inputs land on 0,
so it needs at least log2 3, about 1.6, halvings’ worth of work (two marks, in whole
numbers). The premise asks for that bound of a device that has to work whatever
it’s handed, and it counts it in marks. Joules don’t come into it.


Theorem 3.8 (The squeeze bound). On a finite machine with a permanent reading
and a cost satisfying the halving price, let m be the number of states that read yes,
and let a move i turn k different no-states to yes. Three numbers, then: m counts
every yes-state of the machine, reachable or not; k counts a list of distinct no-states
that the move turns to yes, and the move may turn others too; and cost(i ) is the
price the cost assigns to the move. Then
                                                                           m+k
      m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · m,     and, when m ≥ 1,         cost(i ) ≥ log2       .
                                                                            m
When m ≥ 1 the two displayed bounds say the same thing. (When m = 0 there is
nowhere for a newcomer to land, so k = 0 too.)

Proof. Put the m yes-states and the k newcomers in one list; it has m + k different
members. By permanence every yes-state lands on a yes-state, and by hypothesis
every newcomer does too, so all m + k land among the m yes-states: imgi ≤ m. The
halving price gives m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ≤ 2cost(i) · m.
    The four card readings are the case of one yes-state and three newcomers, where
the bound is reached. With one newcomer the bound says the move costs at least
one, which is the toll again. The counting argument also shows that at least as many
states collapse as there are newcomers, without any price premise.
    The bound is reached, whatever the numbers. Pick how many states already
read yes and pick a cost. As long as the old yes-states and the newcomers together
fit under that cost’s pile-up allowance (a cost of one allows twice the yes-states, a
cost of two allows four times), there is a finite machine with a permanent reading
and the halving price that has exactly that many yes-states and a move of exactly
that cost turning those newcomers to yes. The move turns every other no-state of
that machine to yes as well, filling the allowance to the brim. No cost meeting the
halving price on that machine charges the move less. So the least whole-number
cost that meets the bound is exactly the rounded-up logarithm, ⌈log2 mm+k ⌉.
84   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                  Four more facts about the halving price, and the last one is a limit. First, the
               plainer reading above is a theorem on a finite machine: the halving price holds
               exactly when no move has a landing spot with more than 2cost(i) states landing on it.
               Second, for the eight-state machine described later in this section that’s a theorem
               about its own price list: no move has a larger pile-up than 2cost , so the halving
               price holds, and the toll follows from it; and the price list is the least that meets the
               halving price, since any price list that does charges every move at least what this
               one charges. Third, the squeeze bound is met with equality there: its stamp turns
