               on the four states whose flag is down, beside the four whose flag is already up, and
               4 + 4 = 21 · 4. Fourth, and this is the limit, the small machine of Part III (Section 15)
               as a whole does not meet the halving price, whatever procedure you use to decide
               whether two of its states are equal, because one of its zero-price moves, the one
               that takes one off a number the machine holds, lands two different states of the
               whole machine on the same state (the pair is in Theorem 15.30), and a pile of two
               at price zero is all it takes to break the halving price. What does hold there is merge
               pricing asked of the record layer alone, and it gives the toll on that machine too
               (Theorem 3.17, below).


                3.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero

                There’s one more way to say all this, and I include it because it’s the way physicists
                say it and because it hands you the two cases where the bill is exactly zero, a move
                that forgets nothing and a move on a state already known, and the second I find
                more instructive than any case where it isn’t.
                    Claude Shannon, in 1948, gave a number to “how much you don’t know”: if
                something could be in any of n states and you have no idea which, your uncertainty
                is log base two of n bits, and that’s the most it can be for n states. If you push your
                uncertainty through a step that forgets nothing, it stays the same; through a step
                that merges two states you might have been in, it drops. Now run the room. Before
                the move, you might be in any of the m + k states in play. After it, you’re in one
                of m. So your uncertainty afterward is at most log2 of m, whatever you believed
                before. If you started with no idea at all, every one of the m + k states equally likely,
                your uncertainty was exactly log2 of (m + k), and the move removed at least log2
                of (m + k)/m bits: the same number as the halving count, now in Shannon’s units.
                Landauer’s principle, in the form physicists write it, then says a step that removes
                that many bits from the state gives off at least k B T ln 2 of heat per bit. Put the two
                together and the flip gives off heat, and the exact statements below say how much
                and under which side conditions, one of which (the temperature has to be taken as
                zero or above) is easy to skip and shouldn’t be.
                                                        3.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero   85


    Why does Shannon’s number share a name with the physicists’ entropy at all?
There’s a story about it. Shannon wanted to call it uncertainty, and the mathemati-
cian John von Neumann told him to call it entropy instead, for two reasons: the
same formula already lived in statistical mechanics under that name, and nobody
really knows what entropy is, so in an argument he’d always have the upper hand.
It’s a great story. It comes from Myron Tribus, who spent years tying information
theory to thermodynamics, who said Shannon told it to him in 1961, and who
printed it, with Edward McIrvine, in Scientific American in 1971. Then in 1982 an
interviewer, Robert Price, asked Shannon about it, and Shannon said he didn’t think
von Neumann had told him any such thing. So it’s a legend with one witness, and
the person the witness quoted doesn’t remember saying it. What doesn’t hang on the
story: the two formulas really do have the same shape, and it still takes Landauer’s
premise, a named assumption, to turn a count of bits into heat.
    Exactly, with the notation built first. A spread (probabilists say distribution) is
a way of giving each state a chance p( x ) ≥ 0, with the chances adding to 1. Its
Shannon entropy, in bits, is

                         H ( p) = −      ∑          p( x ) log2 p( x ),
                                      x: p( x )>0

where the big sigma means “add up, over every state x with a chance above zero,”
and each term is a state’s chance times the bits it would take to single that state
out. That comes to log2 n when n states share the chance evenly and less when the
chance is lopsided. Pushing a spread through a move i gives the spread of where
you land: q(y) = ∑ x: step( x,i)=y p( x ). The bits the move removes are H ( p) − H (q).
   Try four equally likely cards, A, B, C and D. Send A and B to a box marked X, C
to Y and D to Z. Beforehand each card has chance 1/4, so the four terms in the sum
are each 1/2: two bits. Afterward the box chances are 1/2, 1/4, 1/4, and the three
terms are each 1/2: one and a half bits. Half a bit was lost on average. You can see
where: half the time the box is X and leaves one binary question unanswered—A or
B? The other half of the time Y or Z tells you the starting card exactly. An actual draw
never loses half a card; the half belongs to the average uncertainty over repeated
draws.
   Start with the half of the claim that removes no bits, Bennett’s half. A move
that forgets nothing sends each state somewhere different, so the chances just get
carried to new addresses, one for one. Nothing piles up and nothing spreads out.
The uncertainty is the same number before and after.
86   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary




                Theorem 3.9 (A move that forgets nothing removes no bits). Let the states be finite,
                listed once each, and let f send states to states with f ( a) = f (b) only when a = b.
                Then for every assignment of chances p, the pushed spread q has H (q) = H ( p).

                Proof. An injective map on a finite list of distinct states is a reshuffle of that list:
                every state is hit exactly once. So q( f ( x )) = p( x ) for every x, and the sum defining
                H (q) is the sum defining H ( p) with its terms in a different order.
                   That’s why a price on removed bits can leave every reversible move at zero marks,
                which is the shape the toll needs: the ledger’s bill lands only where something was
                forgotten.


                Theorem 3.10 (Entropy after a permanent flip). On a finite machine with a per-
                manent reading, let m be the number of states that read yes, and let a move i turn
                k ≥ 1 different no-states yes. For any spread p whose chance lies on those m + k
                states, the spread after the move has H (q) ≤ log2 m. For the even spread on the
                m + k states, the move removes at least log2 mm+k bits.

                Proof. After the move, all the chance sits on the m yes-states (permanence for the
                old ones, the hypothesis for the new). There is at least one yes-state: the image of
                a state that flips. So m ≥ 1. Write q1 , . . . , qr for the positive output probabilities,
                where r ≤ m and their sum is 1.
                    For y > 0, ln y ≤ y − 1: the derivative of y − 1 − ln y is 1 − 1/y, so its minimum
                is 0 at y = 1. Apply this with y = 1/(mq j ), multiply by q j , and add:
                                          r              r
                                − ln m − ∑ q j ln q j ≤ ∑ (1/m − q j ) = r/m − 1 ≤ 0.
                                        j =1            j =1

                Dividing by ln 2 > 0 gives H (q) ≤ log2 m. The even input spread has m + k
                probabilities each 1/(m + k), so H ( p) = log2 (m + k). Subtracting the output bound
                gives the claimed loss log2 ((m + k )/m).

                Premise 3.5 (Landauer’s principle, as a premise). For the chosen physical memory
                and its input distribution, assume that a step lowering its logical-state entropy by
                ∆H bits transfers mean heat Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H to a bath at temperature T, where
                k B is Boltzmann’s constant. Here Q is an average over that preparation, not a bound
                on each individual trial. Applying this premise requires a physical model in which
                the logical entropy loss has this thermodynamic meaning; a bare state-transition
                                                   3.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero   87


table does not supply one. In particular the memory is symmetric, its logical states
alike in their own entropy, as Landauer assumed; for a memory whose states differ,
the floor changes (Maroney 2009), and erasure work in an asymmetric double well
has been measured below k B T ln 2 (Gavrilov and Bechhoefer 2016).



Corollary 3.11 (Heat floor of a permanent flip). Under Premise 3.5, with k B T ≥ 0,
the flip of Theorem 3.10 from the even spread gives off at least k B T ln mm+k ; with
k B T > 0 that is strictly positive.

Proof. Theorem 3.10 gives an entropy loss of at least log2 ((m + k)/m) bits. Multiply
by the nonnegative factor k B T ln 2 and use Premise 3.5. The identity ln 2 log2 x =
ln x gives the displayed floor. Here m > 0 and k > 0, so (m + k)/m > 1 and its
logarithm is positive; if k B T > 0, the heat floor is strictly positive too.
    How big is that? Take the case where the squeeze is two, one state flipping in
beside one that was already yes, and the floor is k B T ln 2. At room temperature,
about 300 kelvin, that’s roughly three zeptojoules: three thousandths of a billionth
of a billionth of a joule. And that’s the biggest bill a one-state flip gets from this
corollary. With one newcomer the floor shrinks as more states already read yes,
because the squeeze gets thinner: with a thousand of them it’s about a thousandth
of k B T, some seven hundred times less than the case of two. So, for an even spread
over the states in play, one mark is not one halving. It’s one halving exactly when
the squeeze is two; for any thinner squeeze and an even spread, the physics asks for
less than a halving, and the toll still charges a whole mark, because marks come in
whole numbers (that’s the rounding the entropy road to the toll leans on, a little
further down). Read in the worst case over what the machine might be holding, the
way the halving price reads a move, it’s at least a full bit every time. A permanent
flip merges two states (Theorem 3.1); put half the chance on each, and the move
removes a full bit, however many states already read yes. So the gap between the
mark and the bits is a fact about the even spread. In the worst case the flip removes
at least the full bit the mark pays for. Whatever the size, it’s a bill only if you grant
the premise; nothing on this page measured anything. And even granted, it’s a bill
nobody will ever see on a meter: real logic gates spend many thousands of times
more than this on every switch, even the frugal ones. One 2023 tally of the numbers
puts switching a single CMOS gate at a hundred attojoules at the low end, over
thirty thousand times this. The point of the number isn’t that a permanent flip is
expensive. It’s that, on the premise, it isn’t zero.
    A related logarithm appears in a different physical question. Yûto Murashita,
Ken Funo and Masahito Ueda (2014) study processes whose reverse histories can
88   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                include ones with no forward counterpart. They call this absolute irreversibility. If
                the reverse histories with no forward partner carry some share of the probability,
                their bound on mean entropy production picks up the logarithm of one over what’s
                left. In their free-expansion example, gas that starts confined to a tenth of a box
                gives the logarithm of ten.
                    Make the confined fraction the old yes-states’ share of the pile, the yes-states over
                the yes-states plus the newcomers, and out comes the same logarithm as the squeeze
                bound. That numerical match does not identify two physical processes. The arrows
                specify neither a thermodynamic reverse experiment nor its path probabilities, so
                they don’t determine that share of reverse histories. The state count alone says noth-
                ing about absolute irreversibility, its absence, or a heat equality. Gonzalo Manzano,
                Gülce Kardeş, Édgar Roldán and David Wolpert (2024) study such trajectory-level
                questions for computations with one-way transitions and random stopping times.
                Their physical premises are additional to the counting done here.
                    The even spread is the easy case, and you might worry the heat depends on
                picking it. It doesn’t. Any spread that gives a real chance to every yes-state and to
                the state that flips will do.


                Corollary 3.12 (Positive heat for any full spread). On a finite machine with a
                permanent reading, let move i turn a no-state s yes. Take any spread p that gives
                positive chance to s and to every yes-state. Under Premise 3.5 with k B T > 0, the
                heat the move gives off is strictly positive.

               Proof. After the move, s and the yes-states all land among the yes-states, and there
               is one more of them than there are yes-states, so two distinct states with positive
               chance land on the same state. That merge removes a positive number of bits
               (Theorem 3.16 below), and a positive temperature times a positive number of bits is
               positive heat.
                   There’s a third road to the toll here too, and it’s the same shape as the merge
                road, with bits in place of marks for forgetting.

                Definition 3.6 (Entropy-priced). On a finite machine, a cost is entropy-priced when,
                for every move i and every spread p, the cost of i is at least the bits the move
                removes: cost(i ) ≥ H ( p) − H (q), where q is p pushed through i.
                                                       3.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero   89




Theorem 3.13 (The toll from entropy pricing). On a finite machine with a perma-
nent reading and an entropy-priced cost, every move that turns the reading from
no to yes costs at least one. So the machine with that cost is a Thiele machine
(Definition 2.1), and every run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least one.

Proof. Let move i turn s yes, and let m be the number of yes-states; m ≥ 1, since
step(s, i ) is one. Take the even spread on the m yes-states and s. By Theorem 3.10
with k = 1, the move removes at least log2 mm  +1 > 0 bits, so the cost of i is a whole

number above a positive number, which makes it at least one. The run-level floor is
the universal floor (Observation 2.1) applied to that system.
    There are three roads to the toll, with two different strengths. Entropy pricing
and the halving price are equivalent: the most bits a deterministic move can remove
is the base-two logarithm of its largest pile of starts sharing a destination. Merge
pricing asks only for at least one mark whenever any pair collides. It is the two-state
restriction of the stronger conditions.
    Try eight equally likely cards all sent to one box. The loss is three bits. A charge
of one meets merge pricing but fails entropy pricing and the halving price, which
require at least three. All three conditions give the permanent-record toll; only the
stronger two give the full squeeze bound.


Theorem 3.14 (Entropy pricing, halving, and pairwise merge pricing). Take a finite
machine whose states can be decided equal or different, and a move i. (1) If no state
has more than K ≥ 1 states landing on it under i, every spread loses at most log2 K
bits through i; and if some state has exactly K states landing on it, the even spread
on those K loses exactly log2 K bits. (2) A cost is entropy-priced (Definition 3.6)
exactly when it satisfies the halving price (Premise 3.4). (3) A cost satisfies merge
pricing (Premise 3.2) exactly when it satisfies the halving price for every list of at
most two different states, and exactly when it satisfies entropy pricing for every
spread whose chance sits on at most two states. The first of those two equivalences
uses no finiteness, only the test for equal states.

Proof. (1) Split the bits removed into one term per state, as Theorem 3.16 below
does, and bound each term with ln y ≤ y − 1 at y = q(step( x, i ))/(K p( x )). Adding
up, the total is at most log2 K plus a positive multiple of K1 ∑ x: p( x)>0 q(step( x, i )) − 1,
and that sum counts each landing spot’s chance once for every state that lands there,
at most K times, so the sum is at most K and the extra part is at most zero. For the
even spread on a pile of K, the chance starts on K states, log2 K bits, and ends on
90   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                one, which is zero bits. (2) If the cost is entropy-priced, take the even spread on any
                pile: by (1) the cost is at least log2 of its size, and a whole number c at least log2 n
                has n ≤ 2c . That every pile is at most 2c is the halving price (the plainer reading
                above). The other way, (1) with K = 2c says no spread loses more than c bits. (3)
                Two different states that land together have one image, so the halving price for that
                pair reads 2 ≤ 2cost(i) , which is cost(i ) ≥ 1; a pair that doesn’t land together, or a
                single state, asks nothing. A spread on two states loses at most one bit, and none
                unless they land together; the even spread on two that do loses exactly one.
                    So merge pricing is weaker than full entropy pricing, though both force the
                one-mark toll under the permanence and finiteness premises. The prices are rules
                on moves. Reading one as physics takes Landauer’s premise for the actual spread
                and a stated exchange rate from bits or marks to heat.
                    Now the zero. Toss a fair coin under a cup without looking at how it lands. Rule:
                set it heads up. You might have had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you
                didn’t know is gone, and that’s the bit the principle charges for. Now lift the cup,
                see heads, put the cup back, and apply the rule again. Nothing you didn’t know
                changed. No bit was lost. And the principle, applied to a state you already knew,
                demands nothing: the premise holds exactly when the heat is zero or more, which is
                to say it sets no positive floor. Setting a coin you know is tails to heads still dissipates
                when you do it in a finite time, as any change in a real device does (time’s bill);
                setting one you know is heads changes nothing. What the premise gives up either
                way is a floor that survives going slowly. Whether the hand that sets the coin keeps
                one is a question about the hand, and I come to it below. And that isn’t a hole in
                the premise’s bill. When you lifted the cup, which side was up got written down
                somewhere: in you. That’s a distinction that stays, kept by whoever knows, on a
                page that was blank before you looked, and the page gets paid for in heat when
                it’s wiped to be used again. The bill moved to the one who knows; it didn’t vanish.
                The entropy-loss bound depends on the preparation and on what the move does
                to it. Here “known” means a preparation concentrated on one logical state, or a
                conditional ensemble whose side information is explicitly included in the account.
                Merely telling a spectator which way the coin landed does not change an unchanged
                device’s heat. This is the generalized form of Landauer’s principle, worked out by
                Owen Maroney in 2009, in a paper he wrote at the Perimeter Institute in Canada (he
                has been a philosopher of physics at Oxford since 2011), and by Sagawa in 2014,
                and Landauer himself had the seed of it in 1961: for a row of bits all already ONE,
                he wrote, there’s no need to carry out any operation, so no entropy changes and no
                heat is given off, and resetting a row all ZERO to ONE involves no entropy change
                either, because neither row carries any information.
                                                 3.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero   91




Theorem 3.15 (A known state gets no heat floor from the premise). On a finite
machine, if the spread puts all its chance on one state s, then any move removes
zero bits, and Premise 3.5 for that move holds exactly when Q ≥ 0.

Proof. A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on
one state. So ∆H = 0 and the premise reads Q ≥ 0.
    Be careful with that one, because it’s easy to overread. “The premise sets no heat
floor for a known state” does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-blank
sheet dissipates nothing. It dissipates every time the stamp actually comes down in
a finite time, known input or not, since the stamp changes the sheet: that’s time’s
bill, proved here for Bennett’s walker (Theorem 1.8), found for a dragged bead by
Schmiedl and Seifert and for any classical jump process by Shiraishi, Funo and Saito,
and how much depends on the device’s physical implementation, its control protocol
and how fast it goes. What the theorem says is only that the premise sets no floor
there. The floor comes from what you didn’t know. That’s a sentence about the bill.
The device is a separate matter. And notice that the toll still charges the known-state
stamp one mark, because the toll is a rule about the move, and the move doesn’t
know what the observer knows. That’s the worst-case gap from door three showing
up again, and it’s the price of having a rule a machine can follow without asking
who’s watching.
    The physics of all this has a standard review, the physicists Juan Parrondo, Jordan
Horowitz and Takahiro Sagawa’s “Thermodynamics of information” (2015), which
sets Landauer’s bound, its generalized form and the costs of measurement and
feedback side by side. And the gap between a device and the spread it runs on has a
physicist’s number on it. Artemy Kolchinsky and David Wolpert (2017) showed that
a fixed process built to dissipate as little as possible for one spread over its states
pays extra when it runs on another, and the extra is how much closer the process
brings the two spreads, measured in relative entropy; the extra was later named
mismatch cost. That’s the worst-case gap again, priced for an actual spread, where
the toll prices the move.
    Run a known input through a fixed device and a floor comes back, from the
device this time. Take K inputs the device sends to the same output, and spread your
chances evenly over them. The identity of Section 3 that ties Ladyman’s reading to
Sagawa’s says the average, over the K, of the entropy the device produces on each
one known equals the entropy it produces on the even spread, plus k B ln K. The
second law makes the entropy produced on the spread zero or more. So the average
is at least k B ln K, and the worst of the K is at least the average: on some one of
them the device produces at least k B ln K of entropy, which is at least k B T ln K of
92   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                dissipated work, however slowly it runs. Kolchinsky and Wolpert’s formula says,
                under their conditions, which input pays: the one the device’s own best spread gave
                the least chance. A device can make one input cheap only by making another dear.
                Only a device chosen knowing the input gets it to nothing, and then the device is
                where the knowing is kept. So the floor sits on the merging move, on its worst input,
                whatever anyone knows, and that’s the shape of the toll. The bound on a device left
                to relax from a known start, in the next subsection, is one more floor of this kind.
                   There’s a second piece of fine print on Theorem 3.15, and it’s about who works
                the controls. The entropy-loss bound supplies no positive floor for a known input.
                Whether a device can approach that floor also depends on its controls: lower this
                barrier, tilt that well, raise the barrier again. Those operations have a timing and a
                physical implementation. The entropy calculation alone does not price either.
                   Paul Riechers, Alexander Boyd, Gregory Wimsatt and James Crutchfield (2020)
                analyse metastable memories under time-symmetric control: the prescribed control is
                the same played forwards or backwards, with the relevant time-reversal conventions.
                A symmetric clock pulse can meet that restriction; an arbitrary clocked pulse need
                not. For memory states unchanged by time reversal, their low-error result singles
                out the memory states that the desired logical map, applied twice, fails to bring back
                to where they started. They call those transitions nonreciprocal. With equal local-
                equilibrium free energies, the leading minimum-work term as the error allowance ε
                tends to zero is proportional to
                                                                            
                                             k B T ln(1/ε) Pr C (C (m)) ̸= m .

                The probability is over the initial memory states. This is a low-error scaling with
                physical premises, not an exact finite-error heat charge on every execution.
                   A permanent flip from no to yes is nonreciprocal at that no-state: a second
                application cannot return it to no. A known input at that state can then face the
                extra work cost in their restricted control setting, even though its initial logical
                entropy is zero. Their class also includes a three-state cycle, which merges nothing.
                The distinction is about the permitted controls as well as the logical map. It neither
                changes Theorem 3.15’s entropy calculation nor identifies the book’s abstract merge
                price with a universal physical bill.
                   A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step, so
                the premise sets no floor under any of its steps; each that changes something still
                dissipates when it happens in a finite time, and a fixed device keeps the floor above
                on each step that merges. One more limit, about which states collide. The chairs
                guarantee a collision among the already-yes states together with the entering no-
                state. They do not guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision. Take
                four chairs with only the first reading no, and a move that walks the first chair to
                the second, the second to the third, and leaves the third and fourth where they are:
                                                    3.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero   93


the second and third both land on the third, and the first never shares with anyone.
For an input distribution supported only on no-states, this counting argument alone
forces no positive entropy loss. Whether other states in that support merge depends
on the move. The operation-level ledger toll still follows under merge pricing.
   So here’s what this section actually earns. A finite machine’s permanent flag-
raising instruction has two allowed starting states that land on one state. Prepare
those two with equal chances: that instruction removes one bit, and under the
adopted physical premise its mean heat is at least k B T ln 2. That is a worst-case
preparation, not a positive charge on every execution. A known start gives no
positive entropy-loss floor. It still dissipates whenever it runs in a finite time, and
how much depends on the device’s dynamics, controls and speed; a fixed device
that merges K inputs produces at least k B ln K of entropy on its worst one, however
slowly it runs. The ledger charges the merging move whatever the preparation,
because merge pricing says so. The counting proves a collision, the preparation
determines the uncertainty removed, and the physical premises connect that removal
to heat.
   Here’s the general case, and it’s the one that shows you where the bits go. Split
the bill state by state. Each state x you might be in carries its chance p( x ) along
to where it lands, step( x, i ), and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If
nobody else landed there, its term is zero. If others did, its term is the difference
between how crowded its landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.


Theorem 3.16 (The bits removed, one term per state). On a finite machine, for any
move i and any chances p( x ) ≥ 0, with q the pushed spread,

                              ∑ p(x) log2 q(step(x, i)) − log2 p(x) .
                                                                    
         H ( p) − H (q) =
                               x: p( x )>0

Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states x ̸= x ′ ,
both with positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.

Proof. Group the sum for H (q) by where things land: the chance q(y)
at a landing spot is the sum of the p( x ) that land there, so H (q) =
− ∑ x: p(x)>0 p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )). Subtract from H ( p) term by term. Each
term is non-negative because the landing spot holds at least what x brought,
q(step( x, i )) ≥ p( x ), and the logarithm keeps order. If x and x ′ share a landing spot,
that spot holds at least p( x ) + p( x ′ ) > p( x ), so the term for x is strictly positive.

                3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not
                Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and what is still a door?
                    You’ve earned this first, and it needs no premise at all: on any machine, finite or
                endless, a run that keeps a reading up either merges two of its own states or never
                repeats one, and a single move that raises a kept reading without merging anything
                has to send the kept states one-to-one into a part of themselves with a gap left over,
                which takes endlessly many of them. Heat or room. You’ve earned this: on any
                machine with finitely many states, a move that raises a flag either forgets something
                or takes a flag down somewhere else. Pure counting, no physics, no premise beyond
                finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down is the four chairs. You’ve
                earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up, then raising it has a
                collision somewhere. If it raises several no-states at once, the yes-states together
                with those newcomers land on at least that many fewer spots than there are of them.
                This does not say that each newcomer shares its destination. Counting again. And
                you’ve earned this: if forgetting is charged for, the toll follows, and if forgetting is
                charged per halving, the size of the toll follows too; each of those derivations hands
                back a system with the five parts and the toll, so Section 2’s floor applies to it as it
                stands. That’s the rule from Section 2, now derived, with every premise named, for
                any finite machine with a flag that stays up. In that section I only declared it.
                    Here’s what you haven’t earned. I’m listing it so you don’t assume it. You haven’t
                earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that’s Landauer, it’s measured for
                beads and argued over for the general case, and in this book it’s an assumption with
                a name. And even granting it, Landauer’s entropy-loss bound demands no positive
                heat from a run whose state is known (the lifted cup), so what the physics forces is
                a floor on a device that has to work whatever it’s holding. Any one run can come
                in under it, and when it does because somebody knows its state, that somebody is
                holding the bill. You haven’t earned that any machine you’d actually want to build
                is of this kind, either, and there are two easy ways to miss. A machine that keeps its
                running total inside its own state, as a number with no ceiling, has infinitely many
                states, so the finite premise fails for it as a whole. And you can’t patch that by giving
                the total a ceiling. A total that only climbs, held in finite memory, eventually either
                stops at its top, and then two different histories leave the same top value, which is a
                merge, or rolls back over to zero, and then it doesn’t only climb. So any running
                total a finite machine keeps for itself has a horizon: it’s honest up to its width and
                no further. And a machine whose price list charges the step that raises the flag, but
                lets some other step merge two states at zero marks, raises the flag honestly and
                still doesn’t charge for forgetting in general, so the merge-pricing premise fails for it.
                Either one puts a machine outside these theorems as stated, though a finite piece
                of it can still sit inside. The machine I build later (Section 15) misses in both ways.
                                                      3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   95


It keeps counters with no ceiling, so it’s infinite outright, and some of its ordinary
steps, counting a counter down among them, can land two different states on one
at no charge on the ledger. So the chairs, as stated, don’t reach it: they force the
toll only on machines with finitely many yes-states that price every merge, and it is
neither. It doesn’t need the chairs, though: the moves that raise its flag merge states
themselves, so the same bill lands on them directly (Theorem 3.17).
    A finite piece can still sit inside, and here’s the smallest one I could build where
every premise can be seen to hold. None of them is left as a hypothesis. Four slots
times a flag, eight states. Three kinds of move: stamp (set the flag, go to the next
slot, cost one), jump to a chosen slot (cost two), next slot (cost zero). It’s finite
and permanent; the next-slot move forgets nothing; the stamp and the jump merge;
merges are priced, and priced per halving. So this section’s two conclusions hold on
it outright. The counting lemma underneath, that a duplicate-free list in which no
landing spot is hit by more than a set number of members has at most that many
times as many members as landing spots, is the plainer reading of the halving price
above. Merge pricing alone would take any price of at least one for the jump. The
jump’s price of two is what the halving price asks, since the jump squeezes four
states into one. One more fact about it: each move’s price is exactly the number of
halvings in its largest squeeze. A move that costs one has no spot hit by more than
two states, a move that costs two has none hit by more than four, and some spot is
hit by exactly that many (stamp squeezes at most two states into one, jump to a slot
squeezes four, and next-slot squeezes nothing).
    The machine Part III builds runs this eight-state machine. Seen through a window
that shows only a line number, read modulo four as the slot, and a flag, a short
program of that machine, once a two-instruction setup has run, does what the
eight-state machine does, one move at a time, and pays exactly what the eight-state
machine charges (Section 15.14 has the construction and the exact statements).
The machine as a whole prices its record layer and not every merge: some of its
zero-price steps merge states, and whatever those merges cost the hardware is off
the ledger, so the finite piece is a piece. The toll on the whole machine comes from
the record layer (Theorem 3.17).
    Finiteness did one job in the chairs. It forced the step that raises a permanent flag
to merge two states. On the machine of Part III no count over the whole machine
has to force that, because the merge is in plain view. Its record moves are the check,
the commitment and the raised flag that the opening’s lock puts in order, and it
names them CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY: COMMIT names a checked claim in
a slot called the channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. CERTIFY takes a state with
the flag down and the same state with the flag up to one place, since a flag that’s
already up just stays up. Its COMMIT overwrites the channel, so two states that
differ only in what the channel names land on one state. Part (1) of the theorem
96   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                below shows both. So any price list that charges every merge of that machine’s own
                step charges the flag-raising step, with no premise that the machine is finite. It isn’t:
                its versions and its ledger grow without bound.
                    Finiteness is still there, in the smallest place it can be. Hold every part of the
                state but the flag fixed, and the flag has two readings, down and up. CERTIFY sends
                both to up, and it does the same to everything else from either, so the two states
                land together. That is the counting of Theorem 3.1 on a set of two. So the choice I
                made in the opening’s list isn’t the merge. It’s that CERTIFY treats the rest of the
                state the same whichever way the flag reads, which is to say it keeps no copy of
                the old reading. Make CERTIFY trap instead when the flag is already up, and the
                merge moves rather than goes away: the state it traps lands with the state that was
                trapped already, since a trapped machine only pays. The one way out is to write the
                old reading somewhere, a ledger that counts a raise and a re-raise differently, say,
                and that is room, the other column.
                    That leaves the other miss, the unpriced merges. Clause (c) of certified Thiele-
                complete (Definition 15.7, in Part III) asks for base moves at zero, and a base move
                merges (DEC, counting a counter down, lands two states on one), so full merge
                pricing and clause (c) can’t both hold on that machine. They don’t have to. Split a
                state into its base part, which is what a two-counter machine would show (the line
                number and the two counters), and its record part, which is everything else: the
                versions (each counter’s count of how many times it has been written), the table
                of facts, the channel, the trap latch (which goes up when a record move fails, after
                which nothing moves), the ledger and the flag. Then price only the merges the
                record layer makes.

                Premise 3.7 (Record-layer merge pricing). A move that sends two different states
                with the same base part to one state costs at least one.

                    The merges among base parts are the ordinary computer’s business, the ones any
                two-counter machine makes, and whatever heat they cost is the ordinary computer’s
                heat. The premise prices only merges between states with the same ordinary-
                computer part. A step like DEC, which changes that part, can lose a version number
                with no mark, and the premise doesn’t object. Merge pricing implies this premise, so
                it asks less, and on the record distinctions it is still an assumed operation-level price;
                identifying it with heat needs a physical model. And it is a price on this machine,
                not a source of the toll on any machine. A certifying move whose effect on the
                base read the flag, say one that moved a counter up when it raised the flag and left
                the counter alone when the flag was up already, would raise the flag and send no
                two states with the same base to one state, and the premise would have nothing to
                charge; the counter’s extra step is the copy of the old reading, paid in room. The
                                                     3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   97


small machine’s record moves treat the base the same whichever way the flag reads,
which is why the premise does its job there, and the theorem below is stated for that
machine and no other.


Theorem 3.17 (The toll on the machine I built). For the small machine of Section 15,
with no finiteness premise: (1) CERTIFY merges, and so does COMMIT of every
claim, and each joins two different states with the same line and counters. (2) Every
cost that satisfies merge pricing for that machine’s step charges CERTIFY and every
COMMIT at least one, and obeys the toll, so the machine with that cost is a Thiele
machine. (3) No INC, DEC or HALT sends two different states with the same line
and counters to one state. So the machine’s own prices, base moves at zero and
each record move at one, satisfy Premise 3.7, and merge pricing fails for them. (4)
Every cost that satisfies Premise 3.7 obeys the toll, so the machine with that cost is a
Thiele machine.

Proof. (1) Take a state whose channel holds a commitment, once with the flag down
and once with it up. CERTIFY raises the first, leaves the second up, moves both on a
line and charges both one, so they land together. For COMMIT, take a table holding
the claim about the current version, once with an empty channel and once with the
channel already naming that claim; COMMIT writes the same name in both. (2)
Only CERTIFY raises the flag, and it merges. (3) A base move keeps the table, the
channel and the trap latch, adds nothing to the ledger and leaves the flag alone, and
when it writes a counter it moves that counter’s version up by one; so two states
that agree on line and counters and land together agree on everything. A base move
leaves a state with the trap up exactly as it is, and never sets the trap, so a trapped
state and an untrapped one never land together. Merge pricing fails because of the
zero-price DEC of Theorem 15.30, whose two states differ in a counter. (4) Only
CERTIFY raises the flag, and by (1) its merge is a record-layer merge.
    So this section reaches the machine I built. On that machine the toll follows from
record-layer merge pricing, and the machine’s own price list, clause (c) included,
satisfies that premise. This is a result about its ledger, not a heat bound. There’s a
second way to settle the clash, which I note and didn’t take. Morita’s reversible two-
counter machine, from the history earlier in this chapter, runs every step backwards
and is still universal: with its input encoded, it computes anything a Turing machine
can. Put the record layer on a base like that and every base move is one-to-one, and
full merge pricing permits those base moves to cost zero. Choosing that schedule
would meet clause (c); the lower-bound premise alone does not require zero charges.
That base wouldn’t be getting anything for nothing: what it doesn’t forget it keeps
in its counters, which is the room column again. I haven’t built that machine.
98   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                   And you haven’t earned anything about what the flag means. Four chairs don’t
               know what they’re certifying. The bill is for raising a flag that stays up. Whether
               raising that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural fact, the “vouching” I
               keep promising and keep not delivering, is a question for the machine of Part III,
               and here it has moved exactly this far: on a finite machine that charges for every
               merge, if that flag stays up, it was paid for.
                   One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the premises,
               but the premises were chosen, and “permanent” in particular was chosen by me.
               Why should a flag stay up? Why not let it come down, pay no mark, and be honest
               about it? That’s a fair question, and merge or revoke is the start of an answer (the
               three-card machine only showed that the converse of Corollary 3.7 fails): on a finite
               machine that charges for every merge, a flag that goes up at zero marks is a flag the
               same move takes back somewhere, and a record that can be silently taken back is
               the thing the bulla and the hash chain and the write-once disk were all built against.
               “Permanent” here is exactly that: the flag can’t be lowered. The toy in Section 2 has
               it only because none of its three moves happens to lower the flag, and it does none
               of a record’s five jobs; the lineage in that section, the bulla and the write-once disk,
               was built around this one, durability; I chose it. Whether that was the right job to
               pick out of the five is something you can argue with me about, and I’d want you to.
                   And “permanent” is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does.
               No physical record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at
               some rate, however slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is
               Zermelo’s point from the chairs (Theorem 1.5 is the finite form). The toll theorems
               in this section, the ones that start from a flag that stays up, need permanence on
               every state, including states the machine never visits, forever; merge or revoke does
               without it. Weaken that to “the flag stays up on the states that actually turn up, for
               as long as anyone cares,” and merge-or-revoke tells you what goes wrong: the move
               could take the flag down somewhere nobody ever looks, and then it isn’t forced to
               merge at all. A version of the toll stated in chances is the noisy chairs of Section 1: a
               step that squeezes nothing on average can’t raise a reading that stays, and one that
               can strictly bunches the even spread. A version stated in time spans is a different
               theorem, and what I have of it is below.
                   One piece of it I can hand you, and the step law of Section 1 is its general form.
               Take one move and repeat it from one start, forever. On a finite machine the states
               that run passes through are finitely many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot
               nothing on those states, it would be a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every
               one of them back around, the start included, where the flag was down. So if the
               flag goes up along that run and stays up from some point on, the move merges two
               states the run itself visits. The shared chair is one the machine actually sits in. And
               it doesn’t touch the known-state point above: a merge among states the run visits
                                                    3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   99


still receives no positive lower bound from the entropy-loss premise when its state is
known. The argument holds for any map iterated from a start whose flag is down,
with the flag up at every step from some point on; no permanence premise is used.
    Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to
give here. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at all, the answer is
no. Take two states, one reading no and one reading yes. One move swaps them;
the other does nothing. Run the swap once and then the do-nothing move forever:
the flag goes up at the first step and stays up for good, and neither move merges
anything anywhere. The swap would take the flag down from the yes-state if it ever
ran there; on this run it never does, and that’s exactly the weakened permanence
this paragraph is about. But if the machine is closed, picking its next move from its
own state, the run is the orbit of one map, the step with whatever move the state
picks, and the single-move argument applies to that map as it stands. Now say the
moves come in a pattern that eventually repeats, one phrase of moves played over
and over. Suppose the flag is down at some step after the repeating starts, and goes
up and stays up after that. Count the repetitions from a step where the flag was
down (start the phrase at that move if you have to) and run the same argument on
the whole phrase treated as one move, at the states where each playing of it begins.
It merges two of those states, both visited; follow the two through the phrase, and
the first move where their paths meet merges two states the run visits at that move’s
place in the pattern. So: moves picked from outside, no; a closed machine or a
repeating program, yes.
    There is also a limited statement about how long a noisy record lasts, using a
different quantity: total entropy production during relaxation. Take a device with
no outside hand: a random process hopping among finitely many states at rates that
never change, with a reverse for every hop and local detailed balance, able to get
from any state to any other. Require at least one up-state and one down-state. Left
to run, it settles into a long-run spread π. Measure each up or down stretch from
its entrance, with entrances sampled in the stationary process, and call the mean
lengths Tup and Tdown . Start the device in a known no-state s. The total entropy it
produces over relaxation is at least ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ), in units of k B .
    The argument is three lines once the pieces have names. With fixed rates, total
entropy production is at least the drop in relative entropy to π; that follows from
Massimiliano Esposito and Christian Van den Broeck’s split of entropy production
(2010). A known start s has relative entropy − ln π (s), at least − ln π (no), and the
relative entropy runs down to zero as the device settles. The stationary chances of
up and down have the ratio of their mean stretch lengths, because crossings up and
down balance. So − ln π (no) = ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ).
    For a large up-to-down ratio, doubling that ratio raises this lower bound by about
k B ln 2. Making both stretches longer by the same factor leaves it unchanged. Across
100   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               a family of devices whose ratio tends to infinity, the bound diverges; no single
               finite irreducible device in this class keeps its flag up forever. This is a relaxation
               bound, not a heat charge on each flip. It uses neither a thermodynamic reverse-path
               construction nor time-symmetric control, so it does not identify the quantities in
               those other results. It also leaves the known-input case of the deterministic entropy-
               loss bound where it was: this noisy evolution and its total entropy production are a
               different question. The entropy is added up over one whole relaxation, from the
               known no-state s until the device has settled, and local detailed balance is what
               ties it to heat exchanged with the reservoirs. Total entropy production includes the
               change in the device’s entropy too; it is not heat alone. It also isn’t the permanence
               of the finite-state theorems on a noisy device: on this device the flag comes back
               down, and Tup and Tdown are average stretches.
                   Here is the core of it for a chain that ticks, worked out, in the case where
               the long-run spread π gives every state a positive chance and satisfies detailed
               balance: in the long run as much weight flows from x to y in one step as from y
               to x, π ( x ) P( x, y) = π (y) P(y, x ), where P( x, y) is the chance of stepping from x
               to y. Count the entropy produced in one step as the change in the device’s own
               entropy plus what goes out to the surroundings, which for a hop from x to y is
               ln( P( x, y)/P(y, x )). Detailed balance turns that ratio into π (y)/π ( x ), and the sum
               collapses: the entropy produced in one step is exactly the drop in relative entropy to
               π. It’s never negative, because a step that leaves π where it is can’t make any other
               spread harder to tell from π (that’s the data-processing inequality, a standard fact of
               information theory). Add the steps up and the sum telescopes. A known start s has
               relative entropy − ln π (s), so the entropy produced in the first T steps is − ln π (s)
               minus the relative entropy left at step T: it never exceeds − ln π (s), and it reaches it
               in the limit exactly when that remainder goes to zero. Next, − ln π (s) ≥ − ln π (no),
               because s is one of the no-states and so carries at most their total chance. The flow
               from the no-states to the yes-states equals the flow back, because in the long run the
               weight on the yes-states doesn’t change, so what flows in equals what flows out. Last,
               take each mean stretch as its mass over that flow; then Tup /Tdown = π (up)/π (no),
               and since the two chances add to one, − ln π (no) = ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ).
                   Try the stretches with a bag of ten counters: nine marked YES and one NO.
               Draw, record the answer, replace the counter and mix again. Each draw gives
               YES with chance 9/10, whatever the last answer was. A YES stretch ends on the
               next draw with chance 1/10, so its mean length is ten draws: the mean L obeys
               L = 1 + (9/10) L. A NO stretch similarly averages 10/9 draws. Their ratio is nine,
               just like the ratio of YES to NO counters. In a long record, count all the YES entries
               and divide by the number of YES stretches; that is the measured mean stretch length.
               Divide both counts by the total number of draws and you have mass divided by flow.
                                                     3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   101


    For this rule the long-run flow from NO to YES is (1/10)(9/10) = 9/100 per
draw, and the reverse flow is the same. A start known to be NO has relative entropy
− ln(1/10) = ln 10 against the long-run spread; after one draw the spread is already
1/10, 9/10, so none of that relative entropy remains. This bag shows the probability
accounting. The entropy-production interpretation still needs the stated physical
model; shaking counters in a bag does not measure that heat.
    Two things need establishing for a general device: that it actually settles, and
that “mean stretch length” means what it sounds like. Here is what each says, and
why it holds.
    Settling first. A chain doesn’t have to settle. It can get stuck in a corner, or cycle
round forever. What rules that out here is a condition named for Wolfgang Doeblin,
a German-born French mathematician, son of the novelist Alfred Döblin, who took
his doctorate at the Sorbonne in 1938 for work on chains like this one and died
in June 1940, at twenty-five. In words: from wherever the device is, its next step
lands on each state with at least some fixed fraction δ of that state’s long-run chance.
No state is ever out of reach in one step, and none is favoured so heavily that the
others starve. Under that condition each step shrinks the distance between where
the device is and where it’s going by the factor 1 − δ (the distance here is the total
of the differences in chance, state by state). Here’s why. Split each step in two: with
chance δ, forget where the device was and draw a fresh state from π; otherwise,
move by whatever is left over, and the condition is exactly what makes the leftover
a genuine set of chances. The fresh draw puts the device’s spread and π in the same
place, so only the other share, 1 − δ, can keep them apart, and no step pushes two
spreads further apart than they were. So the distance dies off geometrically and the
spread converges to π at every state. Here’s the payoff for the bound. The entropy
produced from the known start stays under − ln π (s), and it also gets there: after T
steps it falls short by at most (4/πmin )(1 − δ)2T , where πmin is the smallest long-run
chance of any state. The shortfall is the relative entropy left, and ln y ≤ y − 1 once
more puts that under the sum of ( p( x ) − π ( x ))2 /π ( x ), which is at most the square
of the distance over πmin ; the distance starts at no more than 2 and shrinks by 1 − δ
a step. So − ln π (s) is the exact total entropy production of the whole relaxation, in
units of k B , and the bound − ln π (s) is reached.
    For rates satisfying detailed balance with π, the same equality holds when the
device hops at random moments, with no clock ticking. Write out how fast the
relative entropy to π changes and pair each hop with its reverse. Detailed balance
makes each pair’s share minus (the flow one way minus the flow back) times the
logarithm of their ratio, and that is exactly the pair’s share of the rate entropy is
produced; a difference times the logarithm of the same ratio is never negative. So at
every instant the relative entropy falls at exactly the rate entropy is being produced,
and that rate is never negative; add the rate up between two times and you get
102   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               exactly the drop in relative entropy between them. For settling, Doeblin’s condition
               becomes a condition on rates: the rate of hopping from any state x to any state y
               is at least c times π (y), for some fixed c > 0. Split the rates in two again: a part
               that, at rate c, forgets where the device was and redraws it from π, and the rest,
               which still satisfies detailed balance. The production rate adds over the two parts,
               because with detailed balance it’s the rates times quantities that don’t depend on
               the rates. The rest produces nothing negative, and the redraw part alone produces
               at least c times the relative entropy still left. So relative entropy falls at least as fast
               as e−ct . One wrinkle needs its own line. A known start puts all its weight on one
               state and none anywhere else, and the logarithms in the relative entropy go bad at
               zero. The relative entropy is still continuous at the starting instant, because each of
               its terms has the form u ln(u/π ), and u ln u goes to zero as u does. So adding up
               the production from the start out to infinity gives exactly − ln π (s).
                   I should say what Doeblin’s condition costs. It asks for every hop to be possible
               directly, in one step or at a positive rate. A device whose states reach each other
               only through other states can still settle, and the standard theory of these chains
               says when: always, for a device that hops at random moments and can get from any
               state to any other; and for a chain that ticks, as long as it also doesn’t march round a
               cycle. Those devices meet the condition for some fixed stretch of time or number of
               steps instead of one, and the same argument runs on blocks of that length, because
               the relative entropy never goes up in between.
                   Then the stretches. The bound used the fact that the long-run chances of up and
               down stand in the ratio of the mean stretch lengths, and I took the mean length of a
               stretch with the flag up to be the long-run weight of the up-states divided by the
               flow into them. Here’s why that’s right for a chain that ticks. Start each stretch the
               way the flow starts them, count the steps until the chain leaves the up-states, and
               the average is exactly π (up) over the flow. Look at the long-run weight that has
               been up at each of the last k + 1 ticks. It splits in two: the part whose stretch began
               exactly k ticks ago, which is the flow times the chance that a fresh stretch lasts more
               than k ticks, and the part that was up one tick earlier still. Add those splits from
               k = 0 up to some K and the sum telescopes: π (up) is the flow times the sum of
               those chances, plus the weight that has been up for more than K ticks. The sum of
               the chances that a stretch lasts more than k is its mean length. Doeblin’s condition
               makes the leftover die: from any up-state the next step lands in the down-states
               with chance at least δ π (down), so the weight that has stayed up for K ticks is at
               most (1 − δ π (down))K .
                   With the stretches measured in seconds, when the device hops at random mo-
               ments, it comes out the same, by a different route. Ask, for each up-state, how
               long on average the device takes to leave the up-states from there. Call that its
               leaving time. The leaving times are finite: from every up-state the device hops
                                                      3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   103


into the down-states at a total rate of at least c π (down), so the chance a stretch
is still running at time t falls at least as fast as e−c π (down) t , and no leaving time is
more than one over c π (down). And they obey one plain rule, which you get by
asking what happens in the first instant: from any up-state, the rate out of it times
its leaving time, minus the rates into the other up-states times their leaving times,
comes to exactly one. (Per second times seconds: a pure number.) Average the
leaving times over the way the flow starts stretches, multiply by the flow, and the
rule plus the balance of the steady spread (as much weight flows into each state as
out of it) rearrange the sum into exactly π (up). Mass over flow, in seconds. Both
of the bound’s premises are proved now, in steps and in seconds, under Doeblin’s
condition.
    One chapter remains in this part, and it’s about a different door entirely. Forget-
ting has had its chapter; the question after that is whether finding out costs, because
the demon’s whole trick was that it knew which way the molecule was going, and I
owe you a straight answer on what knowing costs.
CHAPTER 4




Learning borrows, committing
pays

I ended the last chapter owing you an answer about knowing. The keeping part of
the bill so far sits on forgetting: under merge pricing, a finite machine’s permanent
flag-raising instruction was paid for because it merges two states somewhere. But
there’s a thing that looks like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it ought to
cost at least as much, probably more. Finding out. Every time a machine rules out
a possibility, it knows more than it did. If forgetting a bit costs, does learning one
cost too? I had a strong feeling about this, and you probably have it too, so here
it is first: learning is the expensive part. Most physicists had that feeling as well,
for a long time. It’s why the demon took a hundred and fifteen years to exorcise.
Or didn’t. “Exorcise” is the word the people who think it worked like to use. John
Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the last chapter, called their two-part
paper on it “Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell’s Demon,” and I read that Roman
numeral as a joke about how many times the demon has been declared gone. So
hold the word loosely. This section is me finding out where the feeling goes wrong,
and where it’s right. Here’s the answer up front. Looking, like every change a real
device makes, dissipates when it happens. But it doesn’t have to merge anything, so
it owes no floor, and a ledger that charges merges can leave it at zero marks. What
it does use up is a blank page to write on. Learning borrows that page. Wiping the
page to use it again is a merge, and that’s where the floor gets paid. Committing,
making a record nobody can hand back, is paying for good. I’m going to tell you the
version where the exorcism worked, Charles Bennett’s, because it’s the version that
says where the bill goes, and the door I labelled Landauer’s in the last chapter stays
open behind it.


4.1 Somebody got there first, goddamn it

I’d been sitting on this idea that committing, making a result stay so it can’t be
handed back, is what pays, and learning, writing on a blank page you could hand
back, only borrows, and I thought: this one’s mine, I finally had an original thought.
Then I found Carlo Rovelli’s 2024 paper, “The Thermodynamic Cost of Choosing.”


                                 104
                                                                    4.2 A small being at a small door   105


Nope. Somebody got there first, goddamn it. A real physicist, with a real paper,
saying that making a choice that sticks dissipates at least the energy Landauer
charges for erasing a bit. He even quotes a German saying, Wahl ist Leiden, to choose
is to suffer, and at that point what are you going to do but laugh.
    And then, taking him apart properly, it got good, because he seems to contradict
Bennett. Bennett says measuring owes no floor; Rovelli says any measurement costs.
So which is it? Look at what Rovelli calls a choice. A coin in the air hasn’t chosen
anything; it has to hit the ground and stop. And then the sentence I’d put on my
wall: “stabilization must be irreversible, otherwise it is not stabilization.” Bennett’s
floorless measurement is one that could still be undone; that’s why it owes no floor.
It only borrows the page. Rovelli’s choice is one that’s been made to stay; that’s why
it costs. The way I read them, they’re standing on opposite sides of the same door:
learning, which borrows, on Bennett’s side; committing, which pays, on Rovelli’s.
(Bennett’s demon still pays in the end, when it wipes the page.) Neither of them
puts it that way, so push on it. But if it holds, it’s the best sign I’ve got that the line
I’m drawing between finding something out and making it stay isn’t something I
made up.
    Push on it with his paper open and it gives in four places, which I go through at
the end of this chapter, once the demon has been built. So the two-sides-of-one-door
picture is my reading, not his, and the piece of it that’s really his is the one sentence
about stabilizing. That sentence I’ll still put on my wall.
    So he’s my closest neighbour, and here’s the difference, exactly. His is physics: a
dissipation bound, at least kT ln 2 at the temperature of the recording parts, with no
outside heat bath, for a choice that sticks. Mine is a rule in a model of computation:
a charge in the machine’s own count, on the step that flips a permanent reading on,
with no temperature anywhere in it. Same instinct, different place. I’ll take it. It’s
annoying to be second. It’s worse to be alone and wrong. And he’s the closest only
on choosing. On copying there’s an older neighbour, in the chemistry of copying
molecules, and the end of this chapter gets to it.


4.2 A small being at a small door
You met Maxwell’s demon briefly in Section 2. It gets a whole section here, because
the step it seemed to pay for and the step it actually pays for are what this section is
about.
    In December 1867 James Clerk Maxwell, who had published his equations for
electricity and magnetism two years before, in 1865, and to my mind had as good a
claim as anyone to being the most important physicist alive, wrote a letter to his
friend Peter Tait describing a problem he couldn’t get rid of. Take a box of gas at one
temperature, with a wall down the middle and a tiny door in the wall. Now imagine,
106   4 Learning borrows, committing pays


               he said, a “very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at the door, who can see
               individual molecules coming. When a fast one approaches from the left, it opens
               the door and lets it through. When a slow one approaches from the right, same.
               Otherwise it keeps the door shut. It never pushes anything; it only opens and closes
               a frictionless door at the right moments. After a while the right side is hot and the
               left side is cold, and you’ve got a temperature difference you could run an engine
               off, made out of nothing but looking. That’s supposed to be impossible. It’s the thing
               the second law of thermodynamics says can’t happen, and the second law is the law
               physicists are least willing to give up; Arthur Eddington, the English astronomer,
               wrote in a 1928 book of popular lectures that a theory found to contradict it has
               nothing for it but to collapse in deepest humiliation, and nobody has had to test that
               yet.
                   Maxwell put it in his textbook in 1871, and it got named Maxwell’s demon,
               though not by Maxwell. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, called it a demon
               in Nature in 1874, and Maxwell, in an undated note to Tait headed “Concerning
               Demons,” tried to take the name back: “Call him no more a demon but a valve . . . ”
               Nobody listened, which is probably for the best, because “Maxwell’s valve” would
               not have lasted a century. But keep his correction, because it’s exactly right and it’s
               the whole problem: the being does no work. It opens and shuts a door. So physicists
               spent the next century trying to find where the being was cheating. I want you to
               feel the pull of the obvious answer, because I felt it and so did most of them: the
               being has to see the molecules. Seeing costs. Case closed. In 1929 Leo Szilard built
               a one-molecule version of the box and did the arithmetic, and said the second law
               survives if finding out which side the molecule is on costs at least as much entropy
               as the being gains. In 1951 the French physicist Léon Brillouin made it concrete:
               to see a molecule you have to bounce light off it, and the way the philosopher of
               physics Jeffrey Bub sums up the result, finding out that way costs at least k ln 2 of
               entropy for every bit, which is kT ln 2 of heat, Landauer’s number before Landauer,
               and there was your toll on looking. For thirty years that was the answer. Information
               costs because getting it costs.
                   That’s a price on one way of looking, and it doesn’t show that every possible way
               of making a record has to pay it. A device can burn energy without that being a law.
                   Szilard is worth one more minute, for a reason that has nothing to do with the
               demon. Four years after the one-molecule engine, in September 1933, by his own
               later telling, he was waiting at a traffic light on Southampton Row in London, having
               just read a newspaper report in which Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who had
               announced the atomic nucleus in 1911, called the hope of getting power out of
               atoms moonshine, and as the light changed it occurred to him that an element which
               gave off two neutrons when it swallowed one could keep a reaction going by itself.
               That’s the nuclear chain reaction, thought up crossing a street. It’s his memory of
                                                                       4.3 Bennett moves the bill   107


himself, and Richard Rhodes’s history of the bomb opens with it, in a first chapter
called “Moonshine,” which is where most people meet it, so hold it as the man’s own
story, not a record made at the time. Does it change anything about the demon? No.
What it adds is a picture of the man: the same mind looked at one molecule in 1929
and one neutron in 1933, and both times the question was what a single small step
forces downstream.


4.3 Bennett moves the bill
In 1982 Charles Bennett, who’d already shown in 1973 that computation can be
done without forgetting if it keeps its whole history, paying in room instead, took
the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks at a molecule and writes down
which side it’s on. Is writing that down a merge? Picture the being’s notepad, which
starts blank. After looking, the notepad says “left” or “right.” Two possible worlds
before (molecule left, pad blank; molecule right, pad blank). Two possible worlds
after (left, “left”; right, “right”). Nothing merged. Two in, two out, and you can read
the before off the after. Copying what you see onto a blank page forgets nothing, and
a step that forgets nothing owes no floor under Landauer’s premise. It still dissipates
when it happens, like any change a real device makes, and going slowly shrinks that
as far as you have patience for. But it isn’t free, because it used something up: the
blank page. Before the look, the pad was blank and ready; after it, the pad is full.
Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking (bouncing light) and took it as
the price of getting information at all. Bennett gave a way of looking that, on his
account, doesn’t pay that price. It borrows a page instead.
    So where is the bill? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules. After
the first molecule the page is full. To do the next one it has to wipe the page. And
wiping takes two possible worlds (pad says “left”; pad says “right”) to one (pad
blank). That’s the merge. That’s the step with no way back. The demon pays every
cycle, and what it pays for is making room to see again, and the amount it pays
is at least what it gained, and the second law sleeps soundly. That’s the rule from
his 2003 notes I quoted in Section 2: erasing and merging carry the unavoidable
charge, and copying onto a blank place to write doesn’t. The look borrows the page.
The wipe pays the page back, with the floor’s worth of heat. And the blank page the
being started with was itself a distinction somebody paid to set, because writing a
blank is a write, and Section 1 showed what a write on a finite cell is: a merge.
    Section 2 separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see exactly
which step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking feels like
the active part. It’s the thing the being does. Wiping feels like housekeeping. The
housekeeping is where the floor gets paid. If there’s a sentence in this section I’d
want you to carry out of it, that’s the one, and the idea in it is Bennett’s.
108   4 Learning borrows, committing pays


               4.4 Two different things called “narrowing”
               Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense,
               and I’ll give it to you as a picture because that’s how I eventually got it.
                   Draw the machine’s possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row
               above it: the dots that you, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are
               two different rows. The first is a fact about the machine. The second is a fact about
               you, about what you’ve seen and what you’ve ruled out. Both rows can shrink. They
               shrink for different reasons, and only one of them costs.
                   The machine’s row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state. That’s
               a merge. That’s what the price charges. Under the halving rule from Section 3, a
               run can’t shrink the machine’s own row by more halvings than it paid for. That’s the
               theorem just below, and it’s that section’s halving price run forward along a whole
               program. That section took it one step at a time. No new idea; the same chairs.
                   Exactly. Write ⌈log2 n⌉ for the index-bit count of n: the smallest whole number k
               with 2k ≥ n, the fewest yes-or-no questions that can guarantee identification among
               n things when arbitrary binary splits are allowed. It is 0 at n = 1, and I set it to
               0 at n = 0 too, a convention for empty lists, since the logarithm of zero isn’t a
               number. Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without the rounding, its argument
               is positive. For a run t and a list D of starting states, let imgt ( D ) be the set of states
               the run can end in, starting from somewhere in D, and write |imgt ( D )| for how
               many there are (in Section 3 the symbol for one move already meant the count;
               here I need the set and its size both). Let cost(t) be the run’s total cost.


               Theorem 4.1 (The machine’s own narrowing is priced). If the cost satisfies the
               halving price (Premise 3.4), then for every run t and every list D of starting states
               with no repeats,
                                      ⌈log2 | D |⌉ ≤ cost(t) + ⌈log2 |imgt ( D )|⌉.

               Proof. By induction on the run. A single move of cost c shrinks a list with no repeats
               by at most a factor 2c (that’s the halving price), which costs at most c in rounded
               logarithms; the states reachable after the rest of the run from the shrunk set are
               exactly those reachable after the whole run from the original. Add the costs.
                   The run itself is the witness; nothing else is handed in. That will matter in
               Section 8, and I’ll say why at the end of this section.
                   Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn’t
               have shown you. You cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the machine.
               It didn’t merge anything; it didn’t know you were watching; it would have done
               the same thing with nobody in the room. The physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name
                                                                 4.5 The demon on a sheet of paper   109


for mixing these up, and I think it’s one of the most useful names in all of science:
