the part that compresses, the part where the “th” tells you about the “e,” and most
information and most structure are different things. Hold that one tightly, because if
you built something that charged for information, you’d be charging for the wrong
thing, and for a while I wasn’t sure which one I’d built.
    And now notice that the word just changed meaning on you, and on me. I’m
pointing at it so it doesn’t slide past. Shannon and Rissanen and Vereshchagin mean
regularity: a pattern that lets you say something shorter. Tarski, a few pages back,
and Paul Halmos, a Hungarian-American mathematician whose short textbook on
sets is coming up, mean a set with named relations on it, and those two are not the
same thing. Here’s the test, and you can run it: number a thousand objects, flip a
coin for each, heads goes in group one, tails in group two. That’s a perfectly good
sorting in the set theorist’s sense, every object in exactly one group. And the list of
who went where is a thousand coin flips, which is to say it compresses about as well
as a thousand coin flips, which is to say not at all. Feed it to a code built like the
little one, with the fields widened to fit a thousand, and you get the coin-flip row
again, only longer: typically most of the assignment still has to be written down.
A lucky pattern can save some of it; the coin tosses alone do not guarantee there
is none. By the set theorist’s rule, the sorting is the structure, and it’s every bit as
much a sorting as “evens in one group, odds in the other,” which compresses to
almost nothing. Same kind of object, wildly different description lengths. So the two
meanings don’t even rank things the same way: one asks “is there a sorting?” and
the answer is yes for both; the other asks “does a short rule say who went where?”
and the answer is yes for evens and odds and no for the coins. Structure in the set
theorist’s sense, none in Rissanen’s. I’ll keep both meanings, and I’ll try to say which
one I’m using, and when I slip you’ll know what to look for.
136   5 What structure is


               5.13 The four parts of every computer
               In 1936 Alan Turing described the machine that every computer you’ve ever touched
               is a version of, and he did it before any of them existed. It’s a clerk with a pencil, fol-
               lowing a rulebook, written down as a machine (that clerk comes back in Section 14).
               Write down its parts; there are four. A tape, divided into squares. A head that reads
               one square at a time and can write on it and move left or right. A finite list of states
               the head can be in. A table of rules: in this state, reading this symbol, do this. That’s
               all, and two different things are true about it that get run together. Every other
               recipe anyone has proposed as a general formalization of “a procedure,” before or
               since, computes exactly what this one does; those are theorems, proved one pairing
               at a time, and Turing himself sketched one of them, the pairing with the logician
               Alonzo Church’s lambda calculus, in an appendix to the 1936 paper. That it also
               captures everything a person could ever carry out by rote, everything “computable”
               in the plain-English sense, is a claim, called the Church-Turing thesis, and nobody
               has proved it, because the plain-English side isn’t a mathematical object. Turing
               himself kept those two apart in the 1936 paper, and so will I. There’s a third claim
               that gets stacked on top, and it’s a different kind again: the physical Church-Turing
               thesis, that every device you could build out of real stuff computes no more than
               this machine does. That one is a claim about physics. No mathematical proof can
               settle it. Nobody has built a device that breaks it. Your laptop, your phone, every
               server in every data center compute nothing a Turing machine can’t; what differs
               between them is speed, space, energy, and cost. Hold on to that last word. Cost is
               where this book lives.
                   Now do the thing I did, and do it honestly. Look through those four parts for a
               place that says “these squares belong together.” There isn’t one, and that’s not me
               failing to look. Everything the machine is at any moment is which state it’s in, where
               the head is, and what’s on the tape, and the table says what happens next. That’s
               the full list. So any grouping has to live in the states and the table, as a rule, or on
               the tape, as marks, which is to say as bytes like any other bytes. The machine can
               hold a grouping. It just has no place where holding one is different from holding
               anything else.
                   In 1972 David Parnas, a software engineer, wrote a short paper that every
               programmer should be made to read and most haven’t, on how to cut a program
               into modules. He took one small program and cut it two ways. Both worked. But
               one was easy to change later and the other wasn’t, and the easy one could be “much
               less efficient” if talking between modules cost anything. His point: a module is “a
               responsibility assignment,” a decision about who answers for what, and how you
               cut decides what every later change costs. If you’ve ever maintained someone else’s
               code, you’ve paid Parnas’s bill, probably at two in the morning. What survives the
                                                                         5.14 Laying them all down   137


push: a division is a commitment. It changes what the work costs. It is no caption,
no label stuck on afterwards. I’d like to say the thing I built understood that from
the beginning. It didn’t. I did, eventually.


5.14 Laying them all down
Now lay every one of those on top of the others and see what shows through. Here
are the seven things I see. They’re my overlay, the places where I see the sources
agreeing. The sources never proved it together; some of them never met, and some
of them disagree (Bourbaki left out the maps that Eilenberg and Mac Lane built
everything on; Shannon’s structure and Tarski’s are two different words, as I just
showed you). You’ve pushed on each source yourself by now, so you’re in a position
to tell me if I’m seeing things.
    A list of seven slogans would be easy to nod at and impossible to check, so I’m
going to carry one thing through all seven and let you watch each one add to the
one before it. The thing is the square you drew for the Pythagoreans, side, diagonal
and all. Draw a few more on the same sheet: one small, one big, the small one again
but tilted, and one stretched out into a long rectangle. You’ll want a pile.
    Structure is about relations among things. The things themselves aren’t it. The
diagonal, the bronze, Leibniz’s room, Bourbaki’s unspecified elements, Tarski’s
named relations, the arrows. On your sheet, what makes a square a square was
never the ink. It’s that the four sides match and the corners are square, and that the
diagonal stands to the side the way it does whether or not any number names it.
Every one of those is a relation among parts. But on its own this first thing is too
loose to use, because a sheet of paper is drowning in relations: this square is left of
that one, this one is nearer the coffee ring. Which relations count?
    Structure is what stays the same under a chosen set of changes. Euclid’s triangles
laid together, Klein’s allowed moves, Noether’s symmetry, Frege’s direction that every
parallel line shares. That’s the answer the first thing was missing. The relations that
count are the ones that survive the moves you’ve decided to allow. Slide the small
square across the sheet, turn it, and the diagonal still stands to the side exactly as
before; “left of the coffee ring” doesn’t make it across. The second thing is a filter on
the first.
    The same structure can be carried by different stuff. The statue in marble. Two
sets that answer the same vocabulary the same way. This is the second thing again
with one more change allowed: swap the material. Cut the square out of cardboard,
or lay it out in string on the table, and if the relations survive, it’s the same square in
every way you agreed to care about. Aristotle’s bronze is one more thing you agreed
not to look at, and the wooden sandwich is what happens when the material was
never on that list.
138   5 What structure is


                   The first act of structure is a sameness that sorts a pile you were already given.
               Euclid’s first common notion, Frege’s direction, Tarski’s one question, and Russell’s
               letter, with Zermelo’s repair that you must start from a pile. This is where the overlay
               stopped being a list for me and turned into a shape, so slow down here with me.
               Look at your pile of drawings and say: two of them count as the same when an
               allowed move, for now a slide or a turn, carries one exactly onto the other. Watch
               what happens to the pile. It falls into groups. The small square and its tilted twin
               go together; the big one sits on its own; the rectangle sits on its own. And it falls
               cleanly, nothing half in one group and half in another, for a reason you can check.
               Klein’s allowed moves always come with three guarantees: doing nothing counts as
               a move, every move can be undone, and two moves in a row is again a move. Those
               three are, in different clothes, “everything is the same as itself,” “if this matches
               that, then that matches this,” and “if this matches that and that matches a third,
               then this matches the third.” Put the last two together and you get Euclid’s first
               common notion, “things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one
               another.” So the second thing, sameness under chosen moves, is a sorting of the pile
               the moment you ask which drawings it calls the same. Frege did it with lines and
               parallels. Tarski’s one question does it in the crudest way there is, by cutting the pile
               in two. And the pile has to be there first, because a sameness has to be a sameness
               among something; that’s Russell’s letter, and Zermelo’s repair.
                   Adding structure rules possibilities out. Every one of Euclid’s postulates is a
               door closed. Half of English is already decided. A conserved quantity limits where
               a system can go. On your sheet: once the small square and its tilted twin are in
               one group, you’ve given up the right to answer any question the moves respect
               differently for the two of them. Tell me the side of one and the diagonal of the other
               isn’t an open question any more. A sorting is a bundle of doors closed at once.
                   Held structure gets used without re-deriving it. Shannon’s saving in time. Rissa-
               nen’s compression. Parnas’s one-module-at-a-time. Leibniz’s analysis of situation,
               reasoning about where things are straight from their relations, with no coordinates
               laid down first. This is the fifth thing paying out. The doors you closed are doors
               you never have to check again: know which group a drawing is in and you know
               everything the group shares without getting the ruler out, the same way the row of
               01 never needed writing out. With one catch that I’ll need a whole section for: it
               only pays if you kept the sorting somewhere you can read it back.
                   And structure is always relative to a chosen frame. Klein’s group. The vocabulary.
               The code you compress against. Parnas’s criteria. Nobody gets to say “the” structure
               of a thing without saying from where, and I do it constantly, so watch me for it. On
               your sheet: allow stretching as one of the moves and the rectangle walks over and
               joins the squares; allow only slides and turns and it doesn’t. Same pile, same ink,
                                                                          5.15 The smallest piece   139


different groups, because I chose different moves. The groups were never in the
paper. They were in the paper and the choice, together.
    So here’s how I think they hang together. Relations are what structure is made
of. The chosen moves pick which relations count, and a change of material is just
one more move. Asking which things the moves call the same sorts the pile. The
sorting closes doors, and closed doors are what you get to skip later. And because
the moves were chosen, all of it is relative. Read that way, the fourth thing sits in
the middle: it’s where the first three turn into something you can write down, and
where the last three get their start.
    That’s my reason for starting the next subsection with a sorting, and I want to be
exact about what kind of reason it is, because it’s mine. None of these people said
“start with a partition.” Klein would tell you to start with the moves, Eilenberg and
Mac Lane with the arrows, Shannon with the probabilities. What I can actually point
at is narrower. In the framings about when two things are the same shape or the
same kind (Euclid laying one triangle on another, Klein’s moves, Frege’s directions,
Tarski’s question) there’s a moment where somebody decides what counts as the
same, and that decision, written down, is a sorting of a pile. In Shannon, Rissanen
and Noether I can’t find that moment as cleanly, and I’m not going to bend them
until I do. So the overlay doesn’t prove that a sorting comes first. It shows me where
the framings I trust most keep putting their first foot down, and I’m putting mine
there too.
    I looked for a framing that denies any of the seven and didn’t find one, which
could mean there isn’t one or could mean I didn’t look where it lives. If you know of
one, I’d like to see it.


5.15 The smallest piece

Now the sentence I wanted to say at the top and had no right to until here, and even
here I have to split it in two, because half of it is a textbook fact and the other half
is me. The piece of structure I’m going to start from is a partition.
   The textbook half: a partition and an equivalence relation are the same object.
That’s Paul Halmos, Naive Set Theory, 1960, section seven, and you could read that
section before dinner. Here it is in words. Take any pile of things. An equivalence
relation on it is a way of saying “these two count as the same” that behaves the way
sameness should: everything is the same as itself; if a is the same as b then b is the
same as a; and if a is the same as b and b the same as c, then a is the same as c.
Every such relation sorts the pile into groups, the things that count as the same go
together, and every sorting into groups hands you back a relation, “same group.” Do
one and then the other and you land where you started, in both directions. So a
partition and an equivalence relation are one object seen from two sides, and that’s
140   5 What structure is


               the fourth thing on the overlay, the sorting of a given pile, now with a name and a
               page number.
                   Here it is in the exact form, since this is the first place the book uses one. A
               set is a pile, x ∈ X means “x is in the pile X,” and a relation on X is any rule ∼
               that, for each pair of things, says whether x ∼ y holds. A few more marks show
               up below, and each is a word in disguise. The buckets are written S j , with j saying
               which bucket (finitely many buckets in every example here, though nothing below
               needs that). A cap, S j ∩ Sl , is “what the two buckets share,” and ∅ is the empty pile.
               And curly braces with a colon, { y ∈ X : y ∼ x }, mean “the pile of every y in X for
               which y ∼ x holds”; the theorem writes that pile [ x ], the things that count as the
               same as x.

               Definition 5.1 (Equivalence relation, partition). A relation ∼ on a set X is an
               equivalence relation when it is reflexive (x ∼ x), symmetric (x ∼ y implies y ∼ x),
               and transitive (x ∼ y and y ∼ z imply x ∼ z). A partition of X is a collection of
               non-empty subsets of X, the blocks, such that every member of X lies in exactly one
               block. Spelled out, with the blocks written S j : each S j is non-empty, no two share
               a member (S j ∩ Sl = ∅ when j ̸= l), and together they cover everything (every
               member of X lies in some S j ).



               Theorem 5.1 (Sameness and sorting are one object). Every equivalence relation
               on X determines a partition, whose blocks are the classes [ x ] = { y ∈ X : y ∼ x };
               every partition determines an equivalence relation, “x and y lie in the same block”;
               and the two constructions undo each other.

               Proof. The classes are non-empty (x ∈ [ x ] by reflexivity) and cover X. If z lies in [ x ]
               and in [y], then z ∼ x and z ∼ y, so x ∼ y by symmetry and transitivity, and then
               [ x ] = [y] by symmetry and transitivity again (anything the same as x is the same as
               y, and the other way round); so two classes either coincide or don’t overlap. “Same
               block” is plainly reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Going relation to partition to
               relation returns “x and y share a class,” which holds exactly when x ∼ y (if x ∼ y
               then x and y both lie in [y]; if both lie in [z] then x ∼ z and, by symmetry, z ∼ y, so
               x ∼ y), so it is the original relation. Going partition to relation to partition returns
               the original blocks, because the class of x under “same block” is exactly the block
               that contains x.
                  This is textbook mathematics (Halmos, section 7), and the book uses it as a
               foundation. I’m claiming nothing new in it.
                                                                                      5.16 Buckets   141


    And the smallest structure that sorts, by my ruler in Tarski’s setup, the one
question, is the same object a third time. Put a yes-or-no question to every thing in
the pile. The ones that say yes are one group and the ones that say no are the other.
Going the other way, a two-group partition becomes a question the moment you
point at one group and call it “yes.” The only thing a question has that the partition
doesn’t is which group got the label. So the set theorist’s first step and the logician’s
first step are the same step, and nobody has to pick a side, which is a relief, because
it’s an argument you can lose with yourself for a long time.
    That’s the textbook half. Now mine, and hold it looser, because Halmos says
nothing about “smallest” or “first” and I’d be lying if I let his page number carry my
sentence. In what I’m going to build, the order goes: a pile, then groups in the pile,
then whatever connects one group to another, and the groups come first because a
question needs something to be about and a connection needs somewhere to land.
That’s an order for my construction. It is not a law that every account of structure
has to start by sorting. You could start with an ordering instead (“this one comes
before that one”), or with arrows between the things themselves and no groups
at all, and people do, and nothing I’ve shown you rules that out. So the honest
sentence is: a partition is where I chose to start, it is the smallest start by the ruler I
gave you, and I chose it because it’s the first thing that can be right or wrong about
a pile and the last thing I could take away without everything I build on it coming
down. If you have a smaller start by a ruler you can state, I want to see it. It would
change this book.


5.16 Buckets
So here’s the smallest piece, done once, for real. Take everything in front of you
and sort it into buckets: nothing in two buckets, nothing left on the floor. That’s
the whole of the definition. It’s the thing you do with a kindergartner and a pile of
blocks, and I am aware that I’ve just marched you past Pythagoras, Plato, Euclid,
Frege and Noether to arrive at a pile of blocks. Keep the blocks anyway. They’re
about to cost you something.
    Ten blocks. Red ones in one bucket, square ones in another, everything else in
a third. Now a red square turns up, as they do, and you’ve got your first crisis: it
belongs in two buckets and the rule says one. So this isn’t a partition yet, and you
have to decide which bucket wins. That decision is the whole thing. A partition is a
pile of small rulings like that one, and once you’ve made them all, the pile is holding
a fact it wasn’t holding a minute ago. The formal version says the same thing with
fewer words and more squiggles, and you’ve already seen it: it’s the definition of a
partition in the last subsection (Definition 5.1). Non-empty buckets, nothing in two,
nothing on the floor.
142   5 What structure is


                   Here’s the part that isn’t kindergarten. Why would that fact cost anything? Watch
               what it does to one question. Before the buckets, “are these two in the same group?”
               means working it out: go find the first one, go find the second one, apply the
               rule to each, compare. After the buckets, it’s a glance: read the first one’s bucket,
               read the second one’s bucket, done. And the glance costs the same when the pile
               goes from ten blocks to a billion. That’s Shannon’s saving in time and Parnas’s
               one-module-at-a-time, the sixth thing on the overlay, showing up in a kindergarten.
                   Now push on it, because that paragraph sells more than it should, and I want you
               to see where. The partition didn’t give you the glance. A table gave you the glance:
               a written-down line for each block saying which bucket it went in. The partition
               is the fact; the table is one way of holding the fact so it can be read back fast, and
               you had to build the table, and you have to store it, and it has to be the kind of
               thing you can read in one look (a bucket number, say; a list of every block in the
               bucket would have you searching through it again). Anybody who’s used a database
               has met this table; it’s what an index is, and an index is a thing you build, store,
               and keep up to date, and none of that comes free. Take the table away and keep
               the partition and you’re back to working it out. And sometimes there was never a
               search to save: if the rule is “evens here, odds there,” you can answer “same group?”
               by looking at the last digit of each, no buckets needed. So here’s what survives:
               holding a sorting in a form you can read back is worth something, and building that
               form cost something, and those are already two different events. Building the table,
               storing it, checking that it’s right, and deciding to rely on it are four different things.
               The first cost question I want to put to that structure lives in the gap between the
               third and the fourth. Nothing in the kindergarten has shown a charge in that gap. It
               has separated the acts well enough to ask.
                   So who, in everything I read, says what the bill is? I found three answers that
               come close, and I’ll be exact about how close, because this is the edge of what I know.
               Rolf Landauer, in 1961, and Charles Bennett after him, say that any step which takes
               two possible situations and makes them one, erasing a bit or merging two paths a
               computation could have taken, has a heat floor when it removes uncertainty under
               their thermodynamic assumptions. That is a physical claim about how the device
               and its surroundings are prepared, Landauer’s principle, and in this book it is always
               a premise, never something I prove. It’s the place, of all I’ve found, where a fact
               about information turns into a fact about heat, though at room temperature the
               amount for one bit is far too small to show up on anybody’s electricity bill. In 2012 a
               lab in Lyon erased one bit, held in a single tiny bead, and measured the average heat
               it gave off coming down toward Landauer’s floor as the erasing was slowed, and
               other labs have found the same since. Not everyone accepts the principle in general,
               and I’ll come back to the people who don’t. Is sending blocks to buckets a step of
               that kind? Push, because it depends on what you keep. If you keep each block and
                                                                                 5.16 Buckets   143


write its bucket next to it on a spot you knew was blank, you’ve merged nothing;
you can read the block right back off the pair. You have spent something, though:
the blank spot the label now sits on, which is room, and the writing dissipated
when it happened, like any change a real device makes. Bennett’s whole point in
his 1973 paper was that a computation which keeps its inputs, and keeps enough
of its working to retrace its steps, can be run without any merging step at all, and
it pays for that in room. If instead you throw the block away and keep only the
bucket label, then two different blocks can leave the same label behind, and that
is a many-to-one step, the kind Landauer charges for. Both are things people call
“sorting into buckets.” Only the second loses a distinction. So the bucket by itself
doesn’t hand you a Landauer bill. The forgetting does, when there is forgetting, and
keeping instead is paid in room. Whether a given machine forgets is a question
about that machine. It has to be answered on the page, and I won’t wave at it here.
Rissanen says a model is paid for in the bits it takes to state, and Grünwald says
the price depends on the code. Parnas says a bad cut is paid for later, at two in the
morning. And that’s where it stops. Rovelli, back in Section 4, prices a choice that
sticks, and his choice is one nobody could predict, which that section showed is
a different act. I couldn’t find anyone who says that the moment you vouch for a
grouping, the moment you stand behind “these belong together,” has a price of its
own. Just arranging them that way is a different act. That could mean nobody says
it. It could mean I didn’t find the person who does. I honestly can’t tell you which.
    So that’s where I am at the end of one word. A grouping, the act of making it, the
information kept about it, and a commitment to rely on it are different things. The
blocks let you separate them with your hands. Now take them down to the smallest
case there is. A bucket with two sides, one block, and a ruling that sticks: that’s a
cell going from blank to 0, the case Part I started from and put a bill on. So this is
where the word lands. Structure is distinctions held in a state, every one of them a
ruling that sticks, and holding one is on the same bill as the 0: a merge or room.
Klein’s invariants are kept by every move you choose, so they never rise, and the
toll never charges them. On a finite machine Part I proved more: a step that loses
nothing can’t raise a reading that stays. What the toll charges is the other kind, a
distinction a computation made and holds. The rest of this part asks what follows,
on any machine, once that bill is kept.
CHAPTER 6




The counter

Everything so far has kept the marks on the side of the page. You played Section 2’s
toy, you made a tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand. The machine
never saw it. A tally is a row of chairs filled one at a time and never emptied, and
putting it inside the machine doesn’t change that; it only makes the machine the
one paying for the room. That’s fine for a toy. For anything that’s going to run on its
own, with nobody tallying, the total has to live somewhere the machine can reach,
which means the machine can, in principle, write it. So this section is about what a
counter has to be before you’re allowed to call it a receipt. I mean the counter of
any machine whose state carries a running total that every step bumps by whatever
a price list says that step costs. Section 2’s five parts don’t need one (there the total
was a sum you did on the side), so this is one piece added to the five, and the facts
below are about anything that has it. I’ll give you the answer first, because it’s short,
and then spend the section on why each word is there: a receipt is a total that lives
in the state, that only climbs, that equals the sum of what was charged, and that
nothing else could have been.


6.1 A stick, split down the middle
The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about
1100, under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was
owed on tally sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (the
treasury’s own handbook from around 1180, the Dialogue of the Exchequer, gives
them: a thumb’s width for a hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound,
a bare cut for a penny), then split lengthwise so that each half carried the same
notches. The payer kept one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the
word stockholder comes from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to
settle, you laid the two halves together, and only the two original halves fit, because
wood splits along a grain nobody can copy. Add a notch to your half and the other
half shows a gap where the partner should be. Try to remove a notch and you find
that wood can’t be uncut. When they finally stopped using them, the clerks burned
centuries of old tallies in the furnaces under the House of Lords, overheated the flue,
and burned down the Palace of Westminster, which I mention because it’s the best
fact I picked up for this book and because it tells you how many of them there were.

                                  144
                                                                          6.2 Why it has to climb   145


    Do it: draw a border round a strip of card, notch it once for every coin you hand a
friend, then split it lengthwise through the notches and keep half each. No trimming
the edge, no swapping in a fresh strip. Now add a notch to one half and put them
back together. You’ll see the mismatch straight away. And you can’t put a cut back:
a patch is just one more thing to look at. The total is the notches, one per coin, and
under that rule the count only climbs. Both halves started with the same count, so if
they disagree now, somebody changed one. The mismatch won’t tell you who. What
the stick gives you is a comparison you can make, not an object nobody can forge
and not a verdict on who cheated.
    Economists read the same stick another way, and they’re not wrong either. Alfred
Mitchell-Innes (1913) made the exchequer tally his star witness that money is credit:
the crown paid the people it owed by “raising a tally” on some branch of its revenue,
a wooden acknowledgment of debt. A receipt to me, money to him, and it’s the same
piece of wood. Narayana Kocherlakota (1998) later proved a version of his point: in
a wide class of economies where nobody can be held to a promise, anything money
lets people do, a memory of everyone’s past dealings lets them do too. His title says
it in three words: money is memory.


6.2 Why it has to climb

Start with the second property, because it’s the one that does the most work and the
one people fight hardest. Why can’t the counter ever go down?
    Because of what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section 2, says a run
from NO to YES costs at least one. That sentence is a floor: it says the run paid
at least this much. If the counter could come back down, a run could pay the toll,
get its flag, and then take the payment back, and the floor would be a floor on
nothing; “this run cost at least one” would be true of a run that ended having cost
nothing. So a counter that can fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise the
books, and a floor stated in terms of it isn’t a floor. The counter only climbing
is not a flourish. It’s what makes “at least” mean something. This ledger records
cumulative charges, each a whole number of marks and none negative, so it never
decreases. A refundable balance, one that pays money back, would be a different
accounting object with a different invariant, and the floor here says nothing about it.
(In Section 2’s abstract theorem the total is a sum of whole numbers and climbing is
automatic; this paragraph is about why a total stored in the state, where a step could
in principle write it, has to be designed so that no step ever lowers it.)
    The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other,
pointing in opposite directions, and that’s a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie
Lamport asked how a set of computers that pass each other messages, with no shared
clock, could ever agree on what happened before what. His answer is a counter
146   6 The counter


              per machine with two rules: add one before you do anything, and when a message
              arrives carrying the sender’s count, jump your own counter above it (never below
              your own). Those counters, he showed, respect cause and effect: if this caused that,
              this has the smaller number. And they do it “with no actual timing mechanism,” his
              words; they’re clocks only in name. Try it with three people passing notes and you’ll
              see it work in two minutes, and then let one of them reset their counter to zero after
              reading a note, and watch a reply come out numbered before the note it replies to.
              A counter that goes down can’t be leaned on for order.
                  Where did Lamport get it? In the notes he keeps on his own papers, he says the
              timestamps came from an earlier note by Paul Johnson and Bob Thomas on keeping
              copies of a database in step, whose algorithm wasn’t quite right: it let things happen
              in an order that broke cause and effect. What let him see the fix, he says, was special
              relativity, which teaches that the one order of events everybody agrees on is the
              order of what could have caused what. And he passes on a line from Jim Gray, the
              database pioneer whose commit comes back in Section 14: Gray had heard two
              opinions of the paper, that it was trivial and that it was brilliant. Lamport’s answer
              is that he can’t argue with the first and isn’t inclined to argue with the second. His
              account stops at relativity, so the chase does too. The picture it leaves is a good one:
              a number that’s allowed to climb and never to fall is enough to write “this came
              after that” with no clock anywhere.
                  Now the other direction. In 1949 Alan Turing, and in 1967 Robert Floyd, each
              asked how you prove a program stops. The answer, both times: find a quantity that
              goes down on every step and can’t go down forever (a whole number that can’t go
              below zero, say). If every step lowers it and it can’t fall forever, the steps can’t go on
              forever. Up-only gives you order. Down-only gives you stopping. They’re different
              rules (one needs the jump-above-the-message step, the other needs a floor it can’t
              fall below). They have the same shape, seen from the two ends: a one-way quantity
              is something you can build on, and a two-way quantity is a number that happens to
              be written down somewhere.
                  And the real-world case where a counter was allowed to go down, and got gamed
              exactly there: Ethereum, one of the largest blockchains, charges “gas” for every
              step of a program, and for years it refunded gas when a program freed up storage.
              Someone noticed you could fill storage when gas was cheap, hold it, and cash the
              refunds when gas was dear, and a token was built to do exactly that, and the real
              work in a block could reach nearly twice the block’s stated limit. In 2021 a change
              called EIP-3529 cut the refunds sharply (none for self-destruct, a smaller one for
              clearing storage, and a cap of one fifth of the gas used). The written reasons are the
              gas token and those overfull blocks. I read both as the same lesson: a counter that
              goes down was being leaned on at the place where it went down. Ethereum’s gas
              comes back in Section 17 as one of five small models of systems people actually run,
                                           6.3 Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else   147


and it’s the only one of the five that takes a fee at the moment of the write, and it’s
instructive that the part they had to fix was the part that could fall.


6.3 Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else
The third property is the plainest one. The counter after a step is the counter before
plus what that step was charged. Add up a whole run and the middle values cancel
out, the way a sum of differences collapses to last minus first, and the total is the
sum of the per-step charges. Why state it?
    Because it’s the property that fails quietly. Say a machine charges one for raising
a flag, and also, somewhere in its error handling, forgets to add the charge when the
step fails halfway through. Or charges two in one code path and one in another for
the same move. Or has one step that writes the counter directly. Then the counter is
mostly the sum of the charges, and “mostly” is the whole gap between a receipt and
a note that says “trust me, about this much.” Conservation is the sentence that there
is no “mostly”: every step, every outcome, every error, adds exactly its charge, and a
step that fails is charged the same as one that succeeds, because the charge is on the
attempt. For a machine built the way I’m describing, that sentence is the rule the
counter is updated by, so it can’t fail by definition. What can fail is the claim that a
real machine is built that way, and checking that means going through every move
it has, the failure branches included, one at a time, which is dull and is the whole
job. The run-long form, counter at the end equals counter at the start plus the sum
of the charges, then follows from the one-step rule by the cancelling sum; it’s below.
It’s the kind of theorem that looks boring and is the one you’d most want if you
were going to rely on the number. One thing it doesn’t say: that every mark bought
something. The ledger is exact about what was spent. What the spending was worth
is another question, and whether a mark bought a real narrowing is Section 8’s
question, and it needs a witness on top of the ledger entry.


6.4 Only one honest count
Here’s the property that surprised me by being provable at all. Suppose you fixed
the schedule: this move costs one, that move costs zero, and so on, for every move.
And suppose someone else keeps their own books: their own function from states to
totals, which starts at zero and, on every step, goes up by exactly what the schedule
says. Could their books disagree with the machine’s counter, somewhere, on some
state you can actually get to?
   No. And the proof is the tally stick. Both totals start at zero. On every step both
go up by the same amount. So on every state you can reach by steps from the start,
they’re equal. That’s it; it’s an induction, the one-step-at-a-time argument from
148   6 The counter


              Section 2’s floor. The mathematician’s word for this is initiality: the counter is the
              one bookkeeping that all the others, if they’re honest about the schedule, turn out
              to be. Given the schedule, the count is forced. Two things about that sentence I had
              to be careful with, and they’re worth saying before the symbols. It doesn’t assume
              the other books climb: climbing follows from the schedule, since the schedule never
              charges a negative amount, so “only one honest count” and “it only climbs” aren’t
              two separate demands on the other bookkeeper. And it holds on reachable states
              only. A state you can’t get to from the start is one where it says nothing about
              whether the other books agree, which is the right thing for a receipt to say.
                 Here are the properties exactly. First the piece being added to Section 2’s five,
              a counter and a price list, and then the two facts about it. A counter machine here
              means a machine that keeps this ledger. It isn’t Minsky’s counter machine, the
              two-counter base Part I mentioned; same word, different thing, and Section 15
              keeps the two apart. The counter gets the Greek letter µ (mu), which is the letter
              the machine in Part III uses for it (Theorem 15.5).

              Definition 6.1 (A counter kept by a price list). A counter machine has a set of states,
              a set of moves, a step function apply that takes a state and a move, a start state sinit ,
              a schedule c giving each move a cost in N, and a counter µ from states to N, such
              that µ(sinit ) = 0 and µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + c(i ) for every state s and move i, with
              no exceptions. A run of a list t of moves from s applies them in order, and c(t) is
              the sum of their costs. A state is reachable when it is the start or is apply(s, i ) for a
              reachable s and some i.



              Theorem 6.1 (Conservation). In a counter machine, for every state s and every
              list t, µ at the end of the run of t from s equals µ(s) + c(t). In particular µ never
              decreases along a run.

              Proof. Induction on t. For the empty list both sides are µ(s). For a list i followed by
              t′ , the one-step rule gives µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + c(i ), and the induction hypothesis
              from apply(s, i ) adds c(t′ ). Since every c(i ) ≥ 0, the counter never falls.



              Theorem 6.2 (Only one honest count). In a counter machine, let B (for “books”)
              be any function from states to N with B(sinit ) = 0 and B(apply(s, i )) = B(s) + c(i )
              for all s and i. Then B(s) = µ(s) for every reachable state s.
                                                                         6.4 Only one honest count   149


Proof. By induction on why s is reachable. At the start both are 0. If s = apply(s′ , i )
with B(s′ ) = µ(s′ ), then B(s) = B(s′ ) + c(i ) = µ(s′ ) + c(i ) = µ(s), the last step by
the counter’s rule.
    One thing follows that’s easy to miss. If a run comes back to a state it has already
visited, the counter is the same both times, so the moves on that loop cost no marks
in total. A machine that keeps its counter inside its state can go round a loop only at
no marks, and every paid move lands on a state the run has never been in, because
the counter is higher there than anywhere before. So a counter that only climbs is
itself paid in room: it needs a fresh number for every mark, and it never gets one
back.
    Those two proofs are the whole of it, and they’re about any counter machine.
They’re on the page, where you can check every line. The machine I build later
is one of these, and on it the run form is a theorem: the ledger after any list of
instructions is the start plus the sum of their costs (Theorem 15.5). The uniqueness
half holds even with the books’ rule asked only of reachable states.
    I want to flag what initiality does not do, because the fact is smaller than the
word. It doesn’t pick the prices. The schedule is an input: somebody decided that
raising the flag costs one and adding two numbers costs zero, and nothing here says
that decision was right (Section 3 is where I argued the floor isn’t arbitrary; the rest
of a schedule has to be defended by whoever writes it). It doesn’t turn marks into
anything physical. And it isn’t the category theorist’s “initial object,” though the
word is borrowed for a related reason.
    There is a universal property nearby, and I’ll say exactly how far it reaches so the
borrowed word doesn’t reach further. Take any other machine that understands the
same moves (call it the target), and pick a state of it to start from. Walking a list of
moves through it, one at a time, is the one and only way to send lists to its states
that starts where you said and keeps in step as the list grows by one. Programmers
call that walk down a list, one item at a time, a fold, and I’ll borrow the word. That’s
an induction on the list from its end, the same shape as the proof just above, and it
never looks at the other machine’s reading or its prices, which tells you how much
the toll is doing here: nothing. It’s a fact about lists of moves; states haven’t come
into it yet.
    Coming down from lists to the states of the machine running them is where it
gets interesting, and where the borrowed word stops. Two different lists can leave a
machine in the same state. If they leave the target in two different states, there’s no
single place to send that state. That’s the whole obstruction, and it’s exact: the map
from states exists on the reachable ones precisely when equal states always come
from lists that agree on the other side. Call that the descent condition, because it’s
what lets the fold come down from lists to states. A toll doesn’t force it. Take the
150   6 The counter


              one-bit machine whose set costs one and whose reset costs no marks. It obeys the
              toll, yet a single set and a reset followed by a set leave its bit in the same state. A
              target that keeps its whole history as its state tells those two runs apart, so nothing
              comes down. So the fold is unique on lists, and that’s what the word “initial” earns.
              It doesn’t make anybody’s states initial among everything that obeys the toll, and I
              won’t say it does. All three facts hold over any machine, by the arguments above:
              the fold is the one such map (the induction on the list), descent holds exactly when
              each reachable state goes to one target state, and a map the fold factors through
              gives descent (equal states have one image); the history-keeping machine is the
              example that shows where descent fails.
                  And the borrowed word has a home. I didn’t build it, so I’ll point at it. That lists
              of moves are the starting object, and that a machine’s behaviour factors through
              its reachable states exactly when a condition like descent holds, is the theory of
              minimal realization. Joseph Goguen put it as a universal property in 1972, in a
              paper whose title says it outright, “Realization is universal,” and Thomas Colcombet
              and Daniela Petrişan redid automata minimization in the same functorial terms in
              2020. Their machines can have any output at all, which is the honest point: the fold
              and the descent condition never use the record, so the toll is doing nothing here,
              just as I said.
                  The nearest classical parallel to “only one honest count” is in thermodynamics.
              The mathematical physicists Elliott Lieb and Jakob Yngvason showed in 1999 that
              once you fix which states of a system can be reached from which by adiabatic
              processes, and that relation meets a short list of axioms, there is an entropy, a
              function that goes up exactly along the relation, and it is unique once its zero and its
              unit are chosen. Their uniqueness, like this one, comes after the fixing: the order is
              the input there, the price list is the input here, and in both the count is forced by it.


              6.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name
              Now a thing I first took as a let-down. It would be nice to have a new kind of cost
              argument. This isn’t one. The toll is a case of a technique that algorithm people
              have used since 1985 and that a mathematician studying the stability of motion had,
              in a different costume, in 1892. I’m telling you it’s old so you don’t think I invented
              it.
                  The trick is called the potential method, and here’s the whole of it. Give every
              state a number, call it the potential, that measures how much “owing” is stored
              up in that state. Then look at each step and ask: does the cost of the step, plus
              the change in potential it causes, ever come out negative? If it never does, you’ve
              got a bound: any run costs at least the amount the potential dropped from start to
              finish, because the drop had to be paid for by the steps along the way. The computer
                                                        6.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name   151


scientist Robert Tarjan set it out in 1985, crediting the potential view to Daniel
Sleator. Tarjan’s use goes the other way (potential as prepaid credit, to bound a run
from above): he used it to analyse data structures that are occasionally expensive
and usually cheap; and the decreasing-function idea underneath it is the one the
Russian mathematician Aleksandr Lyapunov used in 1892 to prove that a system
settles down. Do the coin version, which runs Tarjan’s way, as a ceiling: a stack
of coins, PUSH adds one and costs one, POP-ALL removes them all and costs as
many as it removed, potential equals the number of coins. PUSH costs one plus one
potential; POP-ALL of k coins costs k and drops the potential by k, net zero. So any
sequence from an empty stack costs at most twice the number of pushes, however
many expensive pops are in it. That’s the method. Three lines.
   Push on that 1892 for a second, because a date like that hides a lot. Lyapunov
wrote the idea up as his doctoral thesis, in Russian. A French translation came
out in 1907, made by a French naval engineer, Édouard Davaux, and corrected by
Lyapunov himself. The English one came out in 1992, a hundred years after the
original, and it was translated from the French: a translation of a translation. So for
most of the twentieth century a reader with only English met the idea secondhand
or not at all. Did the algorithm people of 1985 get it from him? I can’t tell you, and
nothing here needs them to have. Whether anybody walked from one to the other
on purpose is a question I’d like answered. What I do have is a picture: the same
idea, a number that only goes one way along a run, turned up in a thesis about
whether a moving system settles down and in a paper about data structures, close
to a century apart.
   Now point it at the flag. Potential: one if the flag is down, zero if it’s up. A step
from down to up drops the potential by one, so for the step’s cost plus potential
change to be non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That’s the toll, exactly,
and the two are the same statement: the toll holds for a machine if and only if every
step has non-negative amortized cost under the flag potential (“amortized cost” is
just that sum, the step’s cost plus the change in potential). Then the universal floor
from Section 2, “any run from NO to YES paid at least one,” is just the potential
method’s standard conclusion, the drop in potential from one to zero, and every
system with the five parts that obeys the toll is an instance, which is exactly what
a Thiele machine is. Two more facts fall out of the same picture. Under the toll,
a run raises the flag at most as many times as its total cost; each raise uses up a
unit and a unit isn’t used twice. And if you demand the upper-bound version too,
that the potential before a step covers its cost plus the potential after, then the two
together say every step’s cost is exactly the potential it drops. Go through the four
cases. Down to down and up to up drop nothing, so they cost zero. Down to up
drops one, so it costs exactly one. Up to down would have to cost minus one, and
no step costs less than nothing, so the flag never comes down. So the two together
152   6 The counter


              hold exactly when raising the flag costs exactly one, everything else costs zero, and
              the flag never comes down. That’s rise-only pricing in its tightest bill, and I’ll call
              it the exact schedule. Notice that Section 2’s toy doesn’t meet it: the toy’s VOUCH
              move, played from YES, makes a mark although it raises nothing, which the floor
              allows and the exact schedule forbids. The small machine of Part III (Section 15)
              doesn’t meet it either, and on purpose: its CHECK and COMMIT, the check and the
              commitment that must come before its flag goes up, cost one each and raise no flag.
              It charges every instruction a fixed listed price, which is a different job for the word
              exact (instruction-exact pricing), and it breaks no rule. (These two facts hold even
              if the price depends on the state as well as the move’s name, which is wider than
              Section 2’s per-name cost; a per-name cost is a special case, and there the floor and
              the ceiling together are out of reach for any system whose flag ever goes up.) Two
              older tools sit beside these. Run a list of moves in a “writer,” a wrapper that adds up a
              number as it goes, and you get back the final state and the run’s cost; and a per-move
              schedule is a “grade,” fixed before the run. I’m borrowing those two and no more:
              neither brings along the full type systems they come from. The writer is the move
              the programming-language researchers Norman Danner and Daniel Licata make in
              their cost semantics, a translation that carries a cost alongside a program’s result
              (Danner, Licata and Ramyaa, ICFP 2015; Danner and Licata, Journal of Functional
              Programming, 2022). The grade is Shin-ya Katsumata’s: a computation carries its
              resource as a grade, and the grades compose as the computations do (“Parametric
              effect monads and semantics of effect systems,” POPL 2014). Dominic Orchard,
              Vilem Liepelt and Harley Eades put grades into the types of a working language
              (“Quantitative program reasoning with graded modal types,” ICFP 2019). And the
              potential method went into types before any of those: the computer scientists Martin
              Hofmann and Steffen Jost (POPL 2003) gave a type system that attaches potential
              to data and predicts, before a first-order functional program runs, how much heap it
              can use, which is where type-based amortized analysis begins; the multivariate work
              of Jan Hoffmann, Klaus Aehlig and Hofmann (2011) carried it further. Read against
              them, the counter is a grade carried in the state by the step rule. No type carries it.
              And what does that difference even mean? A cost that lives in a type gets checked
              before the program runs, by whoever checks the types; a cost that lives in the state
              gets written during the run, by the step itself. Same number, different moment of
              truth.
                  So is mine an embedding of their frameworks, or something weaker? Half of it is
              exactly theirs, and the other half is left out on purpose. The counter is their writer:
              a step that moves the rest of the state without looking at the counter, hands back its
              cost, and has the cost added on is a computation in the writer over whole numbers
              with addition, and running a list of moves in that writer gives back the final state
              and the total cost, nothing more and nothing less. Every system in this book whose
                                                       6.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name   153


step never reads its own counter has that shape. What doesn’t come along is the
part of their frameworks that works before anything runs: the type systems that
carry grades, Danner and Licata’s bounding relation and the recurrences they extract
for a program’s cost. That isn’t a hole waiting for a patch. It’s the moment-of-truth
difference I just named. Putting the count in the step is choosing the other moment,
so the grade here is written by the step at run time and never checked ahead of it.
    How close do the two moments come? Close enough to say exactly, in a limited
form. Take a small structured language over a machine with this kind of counter:
sequencing, branches whose two arms carry the same grade, and paid acts each
graded with their charge, and grade every program the way Katsumata’s discipline
does, adding grades along the program. On loop-free programs the two agree on
the nose: on every run that doesn’t trap, the counter rises by exactly the grade. The
argument is conservation set beside the grade rule; the counter’s rise is the sum of
the charges along the run, and the grade rule adds the same charges in the same
order. Loops break the agreement, and in one direction only. A loop that runs a
paid check once for every unit in some register, where the check always passes and
is charged one, costs that register’s value on entry, and no fixed whole number is
an exact grade for it; a grade that’s a function of the inputs, the kind cost-aware
type theories like calf (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022) allow, gets exactness
back. So the counter is their writer exactly, agrees with fixed grades wherever a
fixed grade can be exact, and where a run’s cost depends on its data it holds the
exact number that a fixed grade can only bound. What has no counterpart in the
step is the checking ahead of time: a type checker turning a program away before it
runs.
    There’s one more neighbour, closer than any of those, and I’ll name it before
somebody names it at me. A number the step keeps up to date and nothing else
ever reads is what program-proof people call an auxiliary variable, or ghost state.
Susan Owicki and David Gries added auxiliary variables to parallel programs in
1976, because some true facts about such a program can’t be proved without one,
under the rule that an auxiliary variable never steers the program. Jean-Christophe
Filliâtre, Léon Gondelman and Andrei Paskevich, in 2014, worked out when ghost
code can be erased without changing what the program computes. By that test
this section’s counter is ghost whenever no step consults it, and Section 10’s base-
driven records are built exactly that way: the base moves the same whatever the
ledger and the record say. So what does putting it in the step buy, if the number
is ghost anyway? Two things, as far as I can see. The number is there while the
machine runs, where a window can show it (Section 7), and not only inside a proof
somebody wrote afterwards. And the rule that keeps it is one rule for every run of
every program. An annotation covers only the one program somebody happened to
prove. Whether a record stays ghost depends on what else the step does with it; the
154   6 The counter


              machine in Part III has a part that isn’t ghost, its table of checked facts, because the
              step reads it and refuses on it, as the opening section said. One last relative, from
              the graph side: Section 2’s floor is a cheapest-path bound in a system with weights
              on its moves. Every path from the no-states to the yes-states crosses the line between
              them, and every edge across that line weighs at least one. Weighted automata go
              back to Marcel-Paul Schützenberger in 1961, and priced timed automata, which
              add clocks, were set out in 2001. The floor is about the smallest case of what they
              compute.
                 Exactly, for any Thiele machine with states S, moves I, step, per-name cost, and
              reading:

              Definition 6.2 (Potential, amortized cost). A potential is a function Φ : S → N. A
              step has non-negative amortized cost under Φ when cost(i ) + Φ(step(s, i )) ≥ Φ(s).
              The flag potential is Φcert (s) = 1 if cert(s) = no and 0 if it reads yes.



              Theorem 6.3 (The toll is the potential method). (1) The toll holds exactly when
              every step has non-negative amortized cost under Φcert . (2) For any Φ with non-
              negative amortized cost and any run t from s, cost(t) + Φ(run(t, s)) ≥ Φ(s). (3)
              So, under the toll, a run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least 1 − 0 = 1.

              Proof. (1) Check the four combinations of the reading before and after: only no-
              to-yes has Φcert dropping, by one, so the inequality there is exactly cost(i ) ≥ 1; in
              the other three it holds for any cost. (2) Induction on the run, adding the per-step
              inequalities so that the middle potentials cancel. (3) Apply (2) with Φcert , which is
              1 at the start and 0 at the end.
                  So what’s new, if the method isn’t? Only where it’s pointed. The potential method
              is a way of proving things about costs. What this book adds is a claim about which
              potential, the flag, and about what happens to that claim when you can only see a
              window of the state. The method is Tarjan’s and Sleator’s. The reading is mine, and
              I’m about to find out what it can and can’t survive.
                  The flag potential has relatives in physics-flavoured mathematics too, which I
              found after the fact. Resource theories study what you can turn into what when
              some operations are free: Bob Coecke, Tobias Fritz and Robert Spekkens gave the
              general definition in 2016, Fritz worked out its algebra in 2017, and Tomáš Gonda
              and Spekkens catalogued the numbers that never go up under free operations, which
              they call monotones, in 2023. Read with the raised flag as the resource and one
              mark as the currency, the flag potential is the kind of cost monotone they build,
              measured in that currency, and the floor is its simplest case. Does that make the toll
                                                                 6.6 What the counter is, said once   155


a resource theory? Only as the smallest example of one: it says a run from no to yes
costs at least one mark. To say yes costs exactly one mark you’d also need a run that
gets there for one. It’s a neighbour to know about. I don’t count it as a result.


6.6 What the counter is, said once
A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges
on every path including the failures, and is the only such total, on the states a run
reaches, for its schedule. Each of those had a home before this book: the stick for
a total that lives in the state, Lamport’s clocks for climbing, Turing’s and Floyd’s
ranking functions for the same one-way rule run downward, the telescoping sum
for conservation, the induction for the single honest count. None of them is physics.
None of them says what the charges should be. What they say is that once you’ve
chosen the charges, the counter is the arithmetic. It’s no second opinion. And the
toll on top of it is the potential method with the flag as potential, which is to say a
trick from 1985 wearing the question from Section 5.
    Here’s one thing the counter can’t do just by existing: if you can only see part of
the state, can you tell what the counter is? Can you even tell, from outside, which
step paid? The stick works because you can lay the two halves together. What if
you’re only ever shown one half, through a window, and the window doesn’t show
the notches?
    One piece of that has a short answer, and I’ll give it now so the next section can
start from it. A window, for now, is just the part of the state an outside observer is
shown (Section 4’s display was one, and Section 7 is about windows in general).
Call a window counter-complete when some rule, applied to what the window shows,
returns the counter on every state; flag-complete likewise for the flag. Say a window
forgets the counter when changing the counter and nothing else never changes what
the window shows, and likewise for the flag.
    The short answer: a window that forgets the counter is never counter-complete,
whatever else it shows, and a window that forgets the flag is never flag-complete.
Take any state and make two copies of it, one with the counter set to 1 and one with
it set to 2, everything else held still. The window shows the same thing for both,
so any rule gives the same answer for both, and one of the two answers is wrong.
The flag is the same argument with yes and no. On the stick: a window that shows
you the wood’s colour and its length, and hides the notches, can’t tell you what’s
owed, and staring harder at the colour won’t help. (The argument needs a state
space where the counter can be changed on its own, the rest held still; that’s what
“forgets” quietly assumes. The machine I build later is such a space, and it has a pair
of its own, written out move by move: two runs with the same window, one paid
and one not (Theorem 15.14).)
156   6 The counter


                 Be careful what that doesn’t say. It says neither part can be dropped. It doesn’t
              say a window showing both is the smallest window that works, because nothing here
              orders windows, so there’s nothing for it to be smallest in. And it’s about reading
              the counter back. Which step paid is the harder question, and it’s the next section’s.
CHAPTER 7




Windows and shadows

Every chair a machine keeps is a distinction, and a look from outside can show some
of them and drop the rest. That look is a window. I left you with the stick split in
half and asked what happens if you can only ever see one half through a window
that doesn’t show the notches, and with a harder question under that one: can you
tell, from outside, which step paid? This section is about windows. It’s a section
where the mathematics is so small that I’m going to state it in full and then spend
most of the pages on what it’s not, because the smallness is the trap: the fact is
a one-liner and it’s tempting to climb over it with cleverness, and you can’t, and
seeing why you can’t is the content.


7.1 A cave, and the people who got good at it
This one is Plato’s, and the part I need is near the end. In the seventh book of the
Republic, Plato has Socrates, the main speaker of the dialogue, describe prisoners
chained in a cave since childhood, facing a wall, with a fire behind them and people
carrying objects along a walkway between the fire and their backs. All the prisoners
have ever seen is the shadows on the wall. To them, Socrates says, the truth would
be nothing but those shadows. Further on, Socrates reads the story out himself: the
cave is the world of sight, and the climb out of it is the soul’s climb toward what’s
really there. So a real world hidden from anyone who only looks is in the story on
purpose, and Plato put it there. It still isn’t the part I need.
    What I need comes a little before that reading, when one prisoner, freed and
taken up into the daylight, thinks back to the cave. The prisoners, Socrates says,
hand out honours to whoever is quickest at spotting the shadows as they pass and
best at guessing which comes next. Read that again. The prisoners get good at it.
They build a whole science of shadows, with experts and prizes, and it works, on
shadows. What they can’t do is say anything about a carried object that leaves no
mark on the wall. Not because they’re stupid. Because the information isn’t on the
wall. Skill inside a window doesn’t reach past the window, no matter how much
skill. That’s the fact. Plato dressed it as a lesson about education, and it is one, but
strip the dressing and it’s a sentence about functions, and it’s going to be the whole
section.
