               or it’s testimony from outside, and a run that leans on testimony hasn’t earned it
               itself. It can inherit it, but only as far as the copy it leans on is genuine, which is
               Section 7’s problem of a record shown from outside.
                   Robert Brandom, a philosopher at the University of Pittsburgh, built a whole
               account of language on two words this book leans on, commitment and entitlement,
               and his Making It Explicit (1994) is where I’d send anyone who suspects I invented
               the pair. In his picture, as I read it and as his reviewers describe it, people talking
               keep score on each other: what each speaker is committed to, what they’ve put
               themselves on the hook for, and what each is entitled to, what they’re licensed to
               claim. You can be committed without being entitled (a reckless assertion), many
               claims count as entitled by default until someone challenges them, and entitlement
               can be borrowed: I can claim a thing on your say-so and defer to you when I’m
               challenged. Lay mine beside his and the differences are the content. His score is
               kept by the other people in the room; here it’s a reading in the state. His entitlement
               often comes by default; here it’s an event that has to happen and is charged. And
               his deferral is my testimony, which I’ve just let back in on a leash: borrowed
               entitlement is only as good as the copy is genuine. The leash has an older formal
               cousin, the jurisdiction rule of Burrows, Abadi and Needham’s logic of authentication
               (Section 7), where you take a statement on an authority’s word only if you already
                                                                          8.3 The shape, said once   183


believe the authority has jurisdiction over it. It came first, presented in 1989 and
printed in 1990, years ahead of Brandom’s book of 1994, and its words are believes
and jurisdiction where his are commitment and entitlement.
    There’s a whole field that would want a word here too, the logic of belief revision,
which asks how a reasonable mind should change what it believes when something
new comes in. Its nearest neighbours are worth naming, and I couldn’t keep them
apart until I put them back on the table with the cups. Your friend believes the coin
is under cup one. They can learn something that doesn’t clash with that, say cup two
is empty, and just add it. They can lift cup one, find nothing, and have to change
their mind about a table nobody touched. Or you can tell them you moved the coin.
The last two felt alike to me at first. They aren’t. In one the friend was wrong. In
the other the friend was right, and then the table changed.
    Krister Segerberg, a Swedish logician at Uppsala, built a logic of irrevocable
revision in 1998: accepting something so that it can’t be given up. That’s the
firmness question taken to its end. Isaac Levi, a philosopher at Columbia who spent
a career on how beliefs get fixed and unfixed, split adding a belief into a deliberate
kind and a routine kind (I cite his 1991 book; the split goes back to his 1980 one).
Deliberate is reasoning your way there. Routine is where you take on whatever a
procedure you committed to in advance hands you, the way you’d accept a reading
off a thermometer you’ve already decided to trust, or what’s under a cup when you
lift it. What I think the split rests on is when the trust goes in: once, before the
data comes. A passing CHECK, the test move of the small machine in Section 15, is
routine in exactly that sense, with a checker proved honest once, outside every run.
    Neil Tennant, a logician at Ohio State, and Gösta Grahne, a computer scientist
trained at Helsinki, I first filed as two separate complaints. They’re one move
made from opposite sides. The target is the best-known impossibility in that field,
the Swedish philosopher Peter Gärdenfors’s 1986 theorem that a natural rule for
conditionals, the one his paper calls the Ramsey test, can’t live with rational revision.
Tennant argued in 2008 that it goes through only by treating some additions as
revisions: the friend who learned cup two was empty gets counted as having changed
their mind. Grahne, working on updates and counterfactuals, argued in 1998 that
Gärdenfors’s theorem bites only revising, so the friend whose coin was moved is out
of its reach. Side by side, they squeeze the theorem from both ends into one case:
being wrong about a table nobody touched.
    The line this book leans on hardest is between two kinds of change. Revising is
changing what you believe about a world that stayed put. Updating is changing it
because the world moved. Two computer scientists, Hirofumi Katsuno and Alberto
Mendelzon, drew that line for knowledge bases in a 1991 paper on the difference
between updating a knowledge base and revising it; database researchers had
been working on updates with incomplete information since the mid-1980s, Arthur
184   8 Structural entitlement


               Keller and Marianne Winslett among them. Grahne’s result stands on it. And look
               at what the friend sees: an empty cup one is the same empty cup whether they
               misremembered or you moved the coin. The evidence alone can’t tell revising from
               updating; that’s a fibre. What tells them apart is a count of how often the cups were
               touched. The machine in Part III keeps that count as an edition number for each
               thing, and its version rule treats every write as an update: a write moves the edition
               number, so every fact about the old edition stops counting for the new one.
                   And Alexandru Baltag, Bryan Renne and Sonja Smets, three logicians at Am-
               sterdam, gave a logic in 2014 that keeps apart three things Gettier’s cases blur:
               justified belief, explicit knowledge and conclusive evidence. The friend who watched
               has justified belief; the friend who lifted the cup has conclusive evidence. Explicit
               knowledge I read as knowing with the justification written out beside it, the way the
               record keeps its check, and I’m less sure of that one. Put them together and they say
               something exact about this book’s record. A record that’s never wrong and never
               corrected would be a dogmatist’s dream if its sentences were about the present.
               They aren’t. Each says a property held of a thing at one edition, and that sentence
               stays true after the edition number moves on. The record can be infallible and never
               corrected only because its sentences are edition-stamped. Strip the stamps, and the
               first write would turn it into a liar that can’t take anything back.
                   Push on that and it gives twice. The record is Segerberg’s irrevocable acceptance
               every time, with no revising in it. If a check was dishonest, the only fix that fits a
               record like this is a second record on top saying “withdrawn,” the way a revocation
               list works, so the infallibility leans on the checker, proved once, outside. And the
               record is never wrong partly because it only talks about past editions. Whoever
               reads it wants now, and getting from “held at that edition” to “holds now” crosses
               every update since. The record doesn’t make that step for you.
                   And the logicians who taught the logic of knowing to count, whom Section 14
               names again in passing. Here they are properly, and this time I want to see what
               each price rests on. Ho Ngoc Duc, in 1997, gave the logic of knowing an operator
               for “true after some train of thought”: an agent doesn’t know every consequence of
               what it knows now. It can come to know any of them by taking steps of reasoning.
               Steps. I took that at first for the thing I was after, until I saw which way it points.
               His operator points forward, at what the agent could come to know. A record
               points back, at what was checked. One arrow, read from opposite ends. And Sergei
               Artemov and Roman Kuznets, in 2014, turned logical omniscience into a question
               of cost: a logic escapes it when every valid claim that something is known comes
               with a proof whose size is bounded by a polynomial in the size of the claim. The
               usual modal logics of knowledge can’t pass that test unless NP equals coNP, which
               most people would bet against, and justification logic passes it for knowledge stated
               together with its justification, because the size of the justification pays for the search.
                                                         8.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals   185


That last clause took me a few reads. What I think it means is Cook’s certificate
from the proof-carrying-code paragraph above: put the justification inside the claim,
and the hard part, finding it, was paid before the claim was written. Their price
rests on an open bet, and it’s a price on looking. A price, of a sort. Steps and a price
are both there, then, in their own form. What I still don’t find in them is the one I
care about: a single act that closes a question for good and is charged as that act.
Their steps are steps of reasoning, and their price is on finding a proof. Neither is on
settling. I couldn’t get past the journal’s paywall to Artemov and Kuznets’s paper, so
my account of it comes from how other people describe it.
     Push on mine the same way and it gives. A check is one of Duc’s trains of thought,
so my act is the last step of his train, where the walking stops. What I’ve added is a
direction and a charge on stopping. Where the charge sits rests on a choice: I put it
inside the step, and nothing forced me to.
     Three things entitlement is not. It isn’t permission: an access control system says
who may write to what, and that’s granted from outside and says nothing about
truth; a process with permission to write the note still has no entitlement. It isn’t
“it’s true, so I can use it”: that’s the cups. And it isn’t “sound by luck”: a shortcut
that gives the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate is the stopped
clock. The count below has one condition aimed at it, and I’ll tell you what the
condition says and how much it actually catches.


8.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals

Now the number, because a book about a bill has to say how much. Here’s the idea
in a form you can do with three playing cards. Shuffle cards marked 1, 2, 3 face
down. Sort them using only questions of the form “is this one bigger than that one?”,
and count the questions. There are six orders the cards could be in. Each question
has two answers, so after one question you’ve split the six into at most two piles,
after two questions at most four, and you need to get down to one. Four is less than
six, so two questions can’t always do it, and three can, and you can draw the tree of
questions on paper and see it: six leaves, three deep. The number of questions you
need is at least the base-two logarithm of the number of possibilities you started
with, rounded up: that’s log2 of 6, which is a bit under 3, rounded to 3. Donald
Knuth, a computer scientist at Stanford, gives this, in the volume on sorting of his
The Art of Computer Programming, as the lower bound for all comparison sorting,
and the shape of the argument is just: a tree f questions deep has at most 2 f leaves,
so it can’t tell apart more than 2 f cases.
    And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards.
There are 120 orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven
questions, and seven is enough, though not by the obvious method. Finding the
186   8 Structural entitlement


               way is a good evening with a deck of cards (Knuth has it, under the name merge
               insertion, from the mathematicians Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in 1959). Now
               twelve cards. They can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8, so the
               count says at least 29. Ford and Johnson’s method takes 30, and in 1965 Mark Wells,
               a mathematician at Los Alamos who built a programming language for exactly this
               kind of combinatorial search, showed by a computer search that nothing does better:
               twelve cards need 30. The floor was 29. The price is 30. So the count is a floor and
               only a floor; it never promises the floor can be reached, and the bound later in this
               section has to be read exactly the same way.
                   Ralph Hartley, an electronics researcher at Bell Labs, writing in the Bell System
               Technical Journal in 1928, before Shannon, measured information exactly this way:
               the logarithm of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count. That’s the
               measure here, and I’ll say plainly it’s Hartley’s. Shannon’s would need a distribution
               over the list, and there isn’t one. There’s just the list’s length.
                   Here’s the same count with something you can hold. Put three coins under three
               cups. Each coin is heads or tails, so there are eight possible rows under the cups.
               Someone hands you two answers: heads under the first cup, tails under the second.
               Lift the first cup and compare. A matching answer leaves four possible rows. Lift
               the second and compare. A match leaves two. The last coin can still be either way.
               The list really shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that count needed a claim about
               which way the last coin faces.
                   This is a parlour game, and an old one. In A Christmas Carol, in 1843, Scrooge’s
               nephew Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks
               of something, and everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no.
               He’s thinking of an animal, a disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and
               lives in London, and the answer is Uncle Scrooge. Most people know the game as
               twenty questions, and twenty is a good number for it: a balanced question splits
               the remaining field in half, and twenty such questions can guarantee identification
               among 220 = 1,048,576 possibilities. A lucky answer to “is it this one?” can finish
               immediately; the count is about handling every possible answer. Push on that,
               though. The halving only happens because Fred answers truthfully about what’s
               actually in his head. Lie once and the count still shrinks; it shrinks around the wrong
               animal. That’s the cups again: the four and the two are real because you lifted the
               cup and compared. Being told what was under it wouldn’t have made them real.
                   Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are “still on the
               table,” the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior
               and the second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as a list you could print.
               They aren’t “the space of possible worlds.” Picture the ruling-out as observations,
               each observation that ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like
               the card tree. And here’s the claim: if that tree is no deeper than the number of
                                                         8.5 What “narrower” buys: a stronger test   187


paid steps the run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover the narrowing in a
way I’ll spell out in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of the prior’s
length, rounded up, minus log2 of the posterior’s length, rounded up. At least as
many marks as index bits the list lost, where the index bits of a list are the yes/no
questions it takes to point at one entry of it, the card count again. That’s the bound.
    “Paid step” needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least
one for. In a Thiele machine the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading
is one; a price list is free to put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send,
a check), and the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape,
branches and leaves with nothing written on them, and “no deeper than the number
of paid steps” is a count along the run that happened. It isn’t a walk down the tree.
A paid step doesn’t have to have asked any question at all.
    Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn’t say about the run. It takes the two
lists, the tree and the covering as given. It doesn’t say the run produced the posterior
from the prior; nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given
lists, a tree and a covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover
the rounded drop in list length. That’s Section 4’s warning come due: watching can
narrow without a mark, so the payment can’t be dug out of the narrowing. It goes
in as a premise, the tree’s depth against the paid steps, and I’ll keep calling it one.
Later in this section the run makes the posterior itself, from a prior and the tests it
passed (Theorem 8.4), and then the premise is a share each test keeps.


8.5 What “narrower” buys: a stronger test

Before the count, one link that’s pure logic, and Plato’s third account is the whole
of it. Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each
candidate looks like from outside. The list’s membership test accepts an observation
when some candidate on the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get
pickier: anything the short list’s test accepts, the long list’s accepts too. The word
for that, and it runs backward from English, is stronger: the stronger test is the one
that lets fewer things through.
    Pickier, though, isn’t the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap.
Take all six orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left
of card 2: 1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: “is 1 left of 2?” Every survivor
says yes, and the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior’s test accepts yes and no, the
posterior’s only yes. Strictly stronger. Second observation, same two lists: “is the
first card a 3?” Now 3-1-2 says yes and the other two survivors say no, and among
the removed orders 3-2-1 says yes and 2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept yes and no.
Same strength, even though three orders are gone. What made the difference is a
removed candidate whose observation no survivor shares. That’s Plato’s mark, the
188   8 Structural entitlement


               thing that sets this case apart from everything it could be confused with, turned into
               a function. Narrow the list and keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and the
               test is strictly stronger; narrow it without one, and the test may not have moved at
               all.


               8.6 The count, exactly

               Here are the words and the count, for any system with Section 6’s counter. A list is a
               finite list of candidates, repeats allowed, and |Ω| is the length of the list Ω, repeats
               counted. ⌈log2 x ⌉ is the base-two logarithm of x rounded up: the smallest k ∈ N
               with 2k ≥ x. At x = 0 it is 0, the convention for empty lists set in Section 4. And
               a −̇ b is subtraction on whole numbers that stops at zero, so 3 −̇ 5 = 0.

               Definition 8.2 (Decision tree). A decision tree is a leaf, or a branch with two subtrees.
               Its depth is 0 for a leaf and one more than the deeper subtree for a branch; its leaf
               count L( T ) is 1 for a leaf and the sum of the two counts for a branch. Nothing is
               written on a tree: no question, no answer, no candidate.



               Lemma 8.1 (A tree is no wider than two to its depth). For every decision tree T,
               L( T ) ≤ 2depth(T ) , and so ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ).

               Proof. Induction on the tree. A leaf has one leaf and depth 0, and 1 ≤ 20 . A branch
               with subtrees of depths d1 , d2 has at most 2d1 + 2d2 ≤ 2 · 2max(d1 ,d2 ) leaves, which is
               2 to its own depth. The second half: L( T ) ≤ 2depth(T ) means depth( T ) is one of the
               k with 2k ≥ L( T ), and the rounded-up logarithm is the smallest of them.
                   Nothing about any machine is in the definition or the lemma. They’re about trees,
               a leaf or a branch, and nothing else.


               Theorem 8.2 (Paid narrowing, counted). Take a system with a counter µ and a price
               list c that obey conservation (Theorem 6.1): each step raises µ by exactly its charge.
               Let Ω and Ω′ be lists with |Ω′ | > 0, let T be a decision tree with |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |
               (the tree covers the narrowing), and let t be a run from s ending at s′ in which at
               least depth( T ) steps are charged at least one each. Then
                                     ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(s′ ) − µ(s).
                                                                            8.6 The count, exactly   189


Proof. The rounded-up logarithm respects order, so the covering gives ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ ≤
⌈log2 ( L( T ) · |Ω′ |)⌉. It is also subadditive on products of positive numbers,
⌈log2 ab⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 a⌉ + ⌈log2 b⌉, because 2⌈log2 a⌉ · 2⌈log2 b⌉ ≥ ab. So
               ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ),
the last step by Lemma 8.1. By hypothesis at least depth( T ) steps of the run were
charged at least one, and no step is charged less than zero, so the sum of the charges
is at least depth( T ). By conservation that sum is µ(s′ ) − µ(s).
    Two arguments are stuck together in that proof, and they come apart. The tree
half (the covering and the lemma) bounds the index bits by the sum of the charges
of the run, on any price list at all. Conservation is only what turns that sum into the
counter’s rise. So the bill form, with the sum of the charges in place of the counter,
holds in any Thiele machine, and it’s part (3) of Theorem 8.3 below. Notice what’s
missing from the hypotheses: anything tying the lists to the run. That’s the shape of
the bound.
    Three honest small prints, all of them visible in the statement. Both logarithms
round up separately, and the subtraction stops at zero, so when the prior and the
posterior round up to the same number of index bits (four candidates narrowed
to three, say) the bound says nothing. The lists are plain lists, repeats allowed, so
“index bits” is a difference of rounded list lengths with repeats counted; a list can get
shorter by dropping a duplicate without losing a single candidate, and “a candidate
was ruled out” and “the list got shorter” are two different claims. And the difference
isn’t the number of questions anyone asked.
    The covering condition, |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |, is the nearest thing the count has to
an anti-stopped-clock clause, and I have to be exact about how near. Picture each
survivor standing for a little crowd of the prior’s candidates, a crowd no bigger than
the tree has leaves. The condition says the crowds have room for the whole prior:
share the prior’s candidates out among them and none overflows. That limits how
much can be deleted per leaf you paid for. It doesn’t say why anything was deleted.
So the condition rules out deleting too much for the tree you’ve paid for. It doesn’t
rule out deleting for no reason. A run can satisfy every hypothesis of the count and
have ruled nothing out on purpose; the count prices the size of the drop. It says
nothing about the honesty of it. And the covering can’t just be dropped. On the
small machine of Part III (Section 15), whose record moves CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY cost one mark each, take the sixteen starts with A at 0 through 15, and
the run CHECK “A ≥ 15,” COMMIT, CERTIFY from the start with A at 15. One
yes-or-no question with a big constant in it narrows sixteen candidates to one, four
index bits, and the run has three paid steps, a ledger of three. A tree no deeper than
three has at most eight leaves, and eight times one survivor is less than sixteen, so
190   8 Structural entitlement


               the covering fails, and without it the bound would say 4 ≤ 3. More candidates only
               widen the gap: 2n starts and the constant 2n − 1 give n index bits for the same three
               marks (Section 15.14, Proposition 15.34).
                   Here’s a side trip worth taking, because it looks like it breaks the count and
               doesn’t. Two information theorists, Rudolf Ahlswede and Gunter Dueck (1989),
               noticed that asking “is it this one?” is a different job from asking “which one is it?”
               If each receiver only wants to know whether the message is theirs, a noisy channel
               used n times can serve a number of receivers that grows like two raised to two to
               the nC, with C the channel’s capacity, where naming the message only gets you two
               to the nC. That’s identification, and on its face it says checking can be exponentially
               cheaper than naming. But their tests are allowed to say yes wrongly once in a while.
               Make the yes sound, a test that never says yes to the wrong message, which is the
               only kind of check this book lets raise a record, and the double exponential collapses.
               The argument is two lines of pigeonhole, and here they are. Each receiver’s test, to
               be any use, says yes on some output its own message can produce, and soundness
               means no other message can produce that output; so those outputs are all different,
               one per receiver, and there can’t be more receivers than outputs, |Y |n for an output
               alphabet Y. Single exponential, the same order as naming. So for a check that never
               lies, the card count is the right scale after all, and the cheap trick needs a check that
               can be fooled.


               8.7 What you’ve got

               A paid flag is not a true claim; Section 7 left it at “a paid flag is a paid flag,” and
               Section 9 will say it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation
               behind it gives you is entitlement: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as
               established, and can point at the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing
               in the five parts makes the system itself read the flag; I said that above and I’m
               saying it again because it’s the sentence most likely to get lost.) Entitlement costs
               at least the index bits of narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree and a covering
               somebody supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree’s depth. The cups say why
               entitlement and truth are different. Plato says what the checked relation has to do:
               distinguish. Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.
                   Put the three pieces on one hypothesis list (narrow the list with a test that
               separates, find the paid event, count the bill against a tree the run paid for) and
               you get a single statement, structural entitlement, once over any Thiele machine
               and once, under the longer name structural entitlement represented, for every
               certified Thiele-complete machine, the small machine included (Theorem 15.31).
               The machine version asks the same things with two changes: the run starts clean
                                                                            8.7 What you’ve got   191


instead of merely at no, and the paid steps are the run’s own record moves, CHECK,
COMMIT and CERTIFY, at exactly one mark each. The first one reads as follows.


Theorem 8.3 (Structural entitlement, over any Thiele machine). Take a Thiele
machine (Definition 2.1), a state s that reads no, and a run t from s that ends in a
state that reads yes. Take a type of candidates, a type of observations with an exact
equality test, an observation obs of each candidate, and a decoder d that turns a run
into an observation (what its record shows). Take lists Ω and Ω′ of candidates and
a decision tree T such that: (H1) Ω′ strictly narrows Ω: every member of Ω′ is in Ω,
and some member of Ω isn’t in Ω′ ; (H2) some dropped candidate w, in Ω and not
in Ω′ , shows an observation different from every survivor’s; (H3) the decoded run
d(t) is shown by some survivor; (H4) |Ω′ | > 0 and |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |; (H5) at least
depth( T ) steps of the run are charged at least one each. Then (1) the membership
test of Ω′ is strictly stronger than the membership test of Ω; (2) some step of the
run took the reading from no to yes, and that step was charged at least one; and (3)
the sum of the charges of the run’s steps is at least ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉.

Proof. (1) is the cards’ argument: the dropped w shows something no survivor
shows, so the posterior test says no where the prior test says yes, and every survivor
was in the prior, so nothing the posterior accepts is refused by the prior. (2) The run
starts at no and ends at yes, so at some step the reading goes from no to yes, and
the toll charges that step at least one. (3) is the proof of Theorem 8.2 with the sum
of the charges in place of the counter’s rise: the covering and Lemma 8.1 bound the
index bits by depth( T ), and the sum of the charges is at least the number of steps
charged at least one. On a system that obeys conservation the sum of the charges is
the counter’s rise.
   Theorem 8.2 is the same count with the counter’s rise, so for a system that obeys
conservation it’s the special case. Three things in the hypotheses feed nothing, and
I’m naming them here so you don’t have to find them: (H3) isn’t used by any of the
three conclusions; from (H1) only the inclusion is used, and the gap goes unused;
and in (H2) the words “not in Ω′ ” go unused, since a candidate whose observation
differs from every survivor’s can’t be a survivor itself. And (H4)’s |Ω′ | > 0 is used
in that proof but can be dropped too: the covering forces it once the prior has a
member.
   A statement like that is true by packaging: it takes the hypotheses in and hands
the conclusions back, and the right word for it is a checklist. A checklist for leaning
on a claim. It discovers nothing about leaning. The version in which the run itself
does the narrowing, Theorem 8.4, comes later in this section.
192   8 Structural entitlement


                   And a checklist isn’t nothing. On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field, northeast of
               Dayton, Ohio, the Army was evaluating Boeing’s new four-engine bomber, the Model
               299. Shortly after take-off it plunged back onto the field and caught fire; that’s how
               the wire report of that day has it, and the later histories add that it pitched up and
               stalled first, which is what elevators locked in a raised position would do. Two men
               died of their injuries, the Army’s pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and Boeing’s chief test
               pilot, Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks on, a
               locking mechanism worked from inside the cockpit that holds the control surfaces
               still while the plane sits on the ground. There’s a famous line that a newspaper
               called it too much airplane for one man to fly. I couldn’t find that line in any paper
               from 1935; the earliest place I could find it is a New Yorker article from December
               2007 by Atul Gawande, a surgeon who writes about how people get complicated
               work right, and he names no newspaper, so take it as a lead. What I can find is what
               came after. The answer was a card: a list of things to check, in order, every time,
               and the crews of the airplane worked through written checklists for each phase of
               flight. The most careful history of it I found is by Walter Boyne, a retired Air Force
               colonel and a former director of the National Air and Space Museum. By his account
               it wasn’t the first written routine for a pilot; those go back before the First World
               War. And it’s this crash, he says, that made the checklist the way a crew flew. The
               airplane went on to be the B-17. Nothing on that card was a discovery. Every item
               on it was something the pilots already knew. What the card did was make sure none
               of it got left out when it mattered. That’s what putting entitlement’s hypotheses
               on one list does: it finds nothing new about leaning on a claim, and it makes the
               hypotheses impossible to drop quietly.


               8.8 When the run does the narrowing

               Theorem 8.3 takes the lists in. Here is the version where the run makes the posterior,
               and the count stops being an item on the list and becomes a consequence. It needs
               one thing a bare Thiele machine doesn’t have: which steps are tests, and what each
               asks. So a reading names them. For each instruction it gives either nothing or a
               yes-or-no question about the state the run is in when it gets there, and a test step
               passes when its question says yes there. The candidates are states the run could have
               started from. A passed test is asked of a candidate by running the same moves from
               the candidate up to that step and asking the same question there. The posterior is
               the candidates that pass every test the run passed, asked that way, in the order the
               run asked them.
                                                              8.9 A grouping, checked and committed   193




Theorem 8.4 (Structural entitlement, with the narrowing made by the run). Take
a Thiele machine and a reading that names its test steps, every test step charged
at least one. Take a state s that reads no, a run t from s that ends in a state that
reads yes, and a list Ω of candidate starts that contains s. Let Ω′ be the posterior t
makes from Ω, and let bi and ai be the numbers of candidates standing just before
and just after the ith test t passed. Then (1) Ω′ sits inside Ω and contains s; (2)
every candidate of Ω that isn’t in Ω′ fails, asked that way, a test t passed; (3)
|Ω| · ∏i ai = |Ω′ | · ∏i bi ; (4) if every test t passed keeps at least a 2−k share of the
candidates standing before it, bi ≤ 2k ai , then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is at most
k times the number of tests t passed, that number is at most the number of steps
charged at least one, and the index bits are at most k times the sum of the charges;
and (5) some step of t took the reading from no to yes and was charged at least one.

Proof. (1) The run passes its own tests from s, and a candidate is kept only if it
passes them all. (2) A candidate dropped failed one of them. (3) Each test turns a
standing list of bi into one of ai , and the products telescope. (4) Each test keeps at
least bi /2k , so |Ω| ≤ 2kn |Ω′ | with n the number of tests passed, and the rounded
logarithms follow as in Theorem 8.2. Each test passed is a test step, charged at least
one. (5) is Theorem 8.3(2).
    Part (3) is the exact count: take base-two logarithms and log2 |Ω| − log2 |Ω′ | is
the sum, over the tests the run passed, of log2 (bi /ai ), the bits each one took. Part (2)
answers the complaint I made about the covering, that it doesn’t say why anything
was deleted: here everything deleted was deleted by a test the run passed and paid
for. Two premises stay, the prior list and the share. The share is needed. On the small
machine one CHECK of “A ≥ 15,” asked of sixteen candidates, keeps one, a 2−4
share, and narrows by 4 index bits on a run of 3 record moves (Proposition 15.34);
with k = 1 part (4) would say 4 ≤ 3. The same statement on every certified
Thiele-complete machine, where the tests are the CHECK moves and the bill is the
ledger, is Theorem 15.33.


8.9 A grouping, checked and committed

Section 5 ended on buckets, and the toll of Part I never needed them: it prices any
yes-or-no reading. This is where the word in this section’s title gets attached to a
partition in a theorem. Take a pile, a finite list of items, and a grouping, a bucket
label for each item. Its partition is “same label,” and the classes of that relation are
a partition in the sense of Definition 5.1. The data is a key for each item, drawn
from any type you like (a grouping’s own labels can serve as a key), and a grouping
194   8 Structural entitlement


               is sound for a key when any two items it puts in one bucket have the same key.
               The grouping says “these belong together,” and the key says whether they do. One
               grouping refines another when every bucket of the first sits inside a bucket of the
               second.
                   Put two red buttons and two blue buttons on the table, numbered 1 through
               4, with 1 and 2 red. Let the key be colour. Circles round {1, 2} and {3, 4} give a
               sound grouping: every pair inside a circle has the same colour. Split the red circle
               into two singletons and it stays sound; splitting cannot introduce a mismatched pair.
               Join 1 and 3 instead and it fails. Changing the circles’ names from A and B to North
               and South changes none of these checks. That is why the reading below uses the
               partition, not the spelling of its labels.
                   Now the rule for the record. Put a tick beside a grouping only after comparing the
               colours within each circle. Copy that ticked grouping onto a separate commitment
               card, then place the card in a record envelope; charge one tally for each of those
               three acts. Change a button’s colour between the check and the copy, and the old
               tick must no longer authorize the copy. The machine’s SET rule below does that by
               clearing the current table and channel. A record already kept remains about the old
               colours, which it keeps with the grouping.
                   The bucket machine holds a key, a table of checked groupings, a channel, a record,
               a trap latch and a ledger. SET costs no marks; it replaces the key and throws away
               the table and the channel, which were checked against the old key. CHECK g costs
               one and passes when g is sound for the current key, and, when it passes, writes g in
               the table. COMMIT g costs one and passes when the table holds a grouping with the
               same partition as g, and puts g in the channel. CERTIFY costs one and passes when
               the channel holds a grouping; if the record is still down it then keeps that grouping
               with the current key, the key a grouping with its partition was checked against, and
               a record already kept is left as it is. A CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY that fails traps,
               and a trapped machine only pays. The reading for a grouping g is: the record holds
               a grouping with g’s partition. That’s the reading “this grouping has been checked
               and committed.”


               Theorem 8.5 (A committed grouping entitles exactly its refinements). (1) The
               classes of “same label” under any grouping form a partition. (2) Two groupings with
               the same partition of the pile have the same reading at every state of the bucket
               machine. (3) For groupings g and h of the pile, soundness of g for a key gives
               soundness of h for that key, for every key, exactly when h refines g. (4) On every
               run from a clean state (table and channel empty, record down, trap down), if the
               reading for g is up, the record holds a grouping and a key for which g is sound, and
               so is every grouping that refines g; and for every grouping h that doesn’t refine g
                                                           8.9 A grouping, checked and committed   195


there is a key for which g is sound and h isn’t. (5) The bucket machine pays the toll,
and a run from a clean state that ends with the record up has raised the ledger by at
least three.

Proof. (1) “Same label” is an equivalence relation, so Theorem 5.1 applies. (2) The
reading asks only for a grouping with the same partition, and having the same
partition is symmetric and transitive. (3) If h refines g, two items h puts together g
puts together, and soundness of g gives them the same key. Conversely, take g itself
as the key: g is sound for it, so h is, and that says h refines g. (4) Along any run,
every grouping in the table is sound for the current key, the one in the channel is
too, since it has the partition of one in the table, and the one the record keeps is
sound for the key kept with it; SET empties the table and the channel when the key
changes. Then (3), and its converse with g as the key. (5) Only CERTIFY raises the
record, and it costs one. A raised record needs a passing CERTIFY, which needs a
grouping in the channel, which needs a passing COMMIT, which needs a grouping
in the table, which needs a passing CHECK.
    So “structural” has a theorem under it. The reading sees a grouping only through
its partition, which is item (2). If the recorded circles are sound, so is any way of
cutting them smaller, whatever the key is. A grouping that isn’t a cutting-smaller can
still happen to be sound for this key (paint all four buttons red and every grouping
is sound), but nothing in the record promises it: for some key it fails. Item (3) and
item (4) say exactly that much, and that’s all the record buys. It’s the three parts
of entitlement from the start of this section in their smallest case: the object is the
grouping, the checked relation is soundness for the key, and the paid event is the
CERTIFY, on top of a CHECK and a COMMIT at one mark each. What it doesn’t do
is make a later move read the record. Like everything in this section, it says what
someone auditing the run may conclude.
    Before the machine of Part III, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the
“insight” in “No Free Insight” (Section 4), because I’ve been using it as if it meant
one thing.
CHAPTER 9




What insight is

I named the rule in this book “No Free Insight,” and the name ran ahead of any
careful account of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not
learning (Section 4), not looking, not copying. Part I already says where to look:
learning borrows and committing pays, so the part of insight a toll can price is the
part that stays. It’s time to say what that is, and to say it in a way that someone who
studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn’t laugh at. So who are those people,
and what did they find? Here’s what I ran into, pushed on as I go. Where a story
reached me secondhand, I treat it as a lead to check.


9.1 Sultan and the sticks
In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station
with a colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until
1920, five years longer than planned, with the chimpanzees to watch. The famous
one is Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each
too short, but one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks,
plays with the sticks, and then, by Köhler’s account, at a moment you can see, joins
them and reaches the food. Köhler’s words were Einsicht and einsichtig, which came
into English as “insight,” and the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the
Gestalt school, said that’s what thinking is: a restructuring, the moment two sticks
stop being two sticks and become one tool. Stacking up tries until one works was,
for them, something else. Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935
and in English in 1945, five years after he died at thirty-seven; he’d spent his last
years working with Köhler at Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a
box of tacks, matches, and the task of fixing the candle to the wall. Almost nobody
sees that the box is a shelf, until they do. And then he found that if you hand people
the box empty, with the tacks poured out beside it, they solve it far more readily.
Same objects. What changed was which relation among them was on the table.
   I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn’t add an object. Sultan
had both sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived
was a relation, which is to say a piece of structure in Section 5’s sense, and the
arrival was sudden. Hold that, because the thing the toll prices also arrives in one
step, and at its best it’s also a relation.

                                  196
                                                                             9.2 It isn’t a feeling   197


9.2 It isn’t a feeling
But here’s the finding I’d hand anyone who thinks insight is a feeling, and it comes
from someone who measured it. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked
people to solve problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how “warm” they felt,
how close to the answer. On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth
climbs steadily and peaks at the answer, which is what you’d expect. On insight
problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then
the answer arrives, and if anything the people who felt warmest beforehand were
more likely to be wrong. She put that last finding in the title of a 1986 paper:
premonitions of insight predict impending error. The feeling of being close is not a
gauge of being close. Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen
seconds while doing a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.
    And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well.
Archimedes, a mathematician who died in 212 BC, asked by Hiero, the king of
Syracuse, whether a goldsmith had cheated him on a crown, gets into a bath, sees
the water rise, and runs home naked shouting “eureka,” I’ve found it. That comes
from Vitruvius, a Roman writer on architecture, writing about two centuries later. Is
it true? Galileo Galilei, then a young Italian mathematician, at twenty-two, in 1586,
took it as known that Archimedes caught the goldsmith. What he didn’t buy was
the method. Water spilling over the side, as Vitruvius tells it, was to him “a crude
thing, far from scientific precision,” and he guessed some writer had set down a
rumour. So he wrote a little tract, La Bilancetta, proposing a balance weighed in
air and in water instead, which he thought was probably what Archimedes actually
did, since it rests on Archimedes’s own results. Whether there was ever a bath, or a
shout, nobody can check now. What survives is a story two centuries late, wrapped
around a real man and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept: the
bath, the shout, the running home naked. The feeling. What it left shaky is the part
that would count as the check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith. The
bit everybody remembers is the bit that tells you least.
    So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the “aha,” is keyed to
something that the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn’t the feeling of
having it. That’s a relief, because a system of states and moves doesn’t have feelings,
and a word that only meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The
version this book can price has to be keyed to an event, and the question is which.
198   9 What insight is


               9.3 What happens when a computation learns
               Here’s the split, and I’ll say what the toll does with each part, and then I’ll say who
               decided the split. Keep Section 2’s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box, the
               YES box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.
                   The first thing: raw observation. Something comes in and gets written down. A
               counter ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting
               on it, and the reading doesn’t move because of it. Later moves can read what it
               wrote, but that reading is a move of its own. This is the demon’s pad in Section 4,
               and it’s what the statistician Dennis Lindley measured in 1956 as the information
               provided by an experiment, the words of his title, and defined as the expected drop
               in your uncertainty: a real quantity, and a quantity about what was seen. It can cost
               nothing on the ledger. The toll says nothing at all about a move that doesn’t cross
               from NO to YES, so a price list may charge it zero: on the paper, STAY and WORK
               cost no marks, and Section 4’s watcher narrowed a whole row of candidates without
               paying a mark. “Can” is the word that matters. A price list is allowed to charge for
               looking anyway. And in the physical world a look isn’t free either: copied onto a
               blank page it merges nothing and owes no floor under Landauer’s premise, but it
               still dissipates when it happens, in any real device, and it uses up the page, which is
               room, borrowed until the page is wiped (Section 4).
                   Lindley’s measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good,
               who was Alan Turing’s main statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in
               1979 that Turing had worked out the expected weight of evidence an experiment
               would give, to judge one of the codebreaking procedures before running it, and so
               partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work that stayed secret. Turing
               measured evidence in bans, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth of one called a
               deciban, and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of
               the sheets used in that procedure were printed. It’s the same base-ten unit other
               people call the hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that
               Turing didn’t know the logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in
               a paper by Charles Sanders Peirce, the same Peirce from Section 5, who’d called
               it the weight of evidence. Peirce is as far back as Good takes it. What it changes:
               nothing in the argument, but it shows how well trodden this first kind of thing is.
               For a century and a half careful people have measured what an observation tells
               you, and every one of those measures is about what was seen. That’s the side of the
               line the toll leaves alone.
                   The second thing: the raise. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES. Here
               is where the toll lives. In any system with the five parts that obeys the toll, that
               move costs at least one mark, and every run that starts at NO and ends at YES pays
               at least one somewhere along the way, which is Section 2’s universal floor. What’s
                                                       9.3 What happens when a computation learns   199


being charged for, at its best, is exactly the Gestalt thing: a relation, committed to.
One tool, claimed, out of two sticks. “At its best,” because Section 2 was careful
about what YES means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A crossing that writes
down which relation it’s committing to carries Sultan’s tool with it. A bare crossing,
VOUCH on the paper, commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the same.
     The third thing isn’t a kind of event. It’s an observation about the price: it’s
flat, whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep
relation, a result nobody could have guessed, Sultan’s two sticks become one tool.
The toll charges the crossing at least one. It doesn’t charge the striking crossing
more, because the floor’s proof never looks at anything but the reading before and
after. On the paper: VOUCH from NO makes one mark whether you were thinking
of Duncker’s box or of lunch. Meaning is not cost. The depth of what’s certified adds
meaning. It doesn’t add a mark.
     The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In
1962 the psychologist Sam Glucksberg ran Duncker’s problem with money on it:
some people were told they could win five or twenty dollars depending on how
fast they solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people chasing the money did
worse than the people who weren’t. With the box empty the problem was easier for
everybody, and the accounts I’ve read don’t agree on what the money did there, so
I’ll leave that half alone. Paying more didn’t buy the insight, and on the hard version
it got in the way. That’s a fact about heads. It says nothing about records, and I
won’t push it further than that. But it’s a nice mirror for the paper. On the paper a
deeper crossing isn’t charged more, and in Glucksberg’s room a bigger prize didn’t
bring the crossing sooner. In neither place does the price measure the depth.
     Here they are, exactly, for any Thiele machine (Definition 2.1). Runs are written
as lists, the way Section 2’s proof wrote them: [ ] is the empty run, and i :: t is the
run that starts with move i and carries on with the run t.

Definition 9.1 (Raise, non-raising move). In a Thiele machine, a step from state s by
move i is a raise when it turns the reading on: cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes.
A move i is a non-raising move when no step by it, from any state, is a raise. Raw
observation, the first thing above, is one kind.

Remark 9.1 (What the toll prices, and what it doesn’t). All three read straight off
Definition 2.1 and Observation 2.1, with Section 2’s board as the example. (1) The
toll puts no bound on the cost of a non-raising move; on Section 2’s board STAY and
WORK are non-raising moves and cost 0. (2) Every raise is charged at least 1, by the
toll, and every run from a state reading no to one reading yes has total cost at least
1, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat: the floor’s proof uses nothing about the
end state but its reading, so it gives the same floor of 1 whatever else the end state
200   9 What insight is


               shows. A higher floor needs more hypotheses than the toll, and those hypotheses do
               the work. A system that wants to charge more for a deeper certification has to write
               that into its price list, move by move; the toll doesn’t do it for anyone.

                  So the account comes down to two facts and a warning. Looking can stay off
               the ledger. Turning the reading on can’t. The toll alone does not charge more for a
               remarkable claim; another pricing rule or an additional requirement could.
                  Who decided the split? Not the costs alone. The toll prices exactly one thing, the
               crossing. A price list is free to put a floor under more moves than that (a look, a
               send, a check) and free to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into non-raising
               moves and raises is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is this book’s.
               The part that’s forced is the floor under the crossing, once you grant a reading that
               stays up, finitely many states that read yes, and a price on every merge; Section 3 is
               the argument; anything a price list charges beyond that is a choice, and any concrete
               machine owes you its whole table so you can see which choices it made.


               9.4 Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first

               The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being exposed: you
               make a conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for
               something, where “real” means the test could have failed. His word for that earned
               credit is corroboration. I lean on that idea all through this book (Section 14 gives it
               its full due), and here’s where a Thiele machine has a version of it, and here’s where
               the version is weaker than Popper and I have to say so.
                   Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin
               under a cup, a formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail,
               and it doesn’t move the box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt,
               pass or fail, fits Popper, because what made his test count was that it was really run
               and could have failed. That’s the test. It’s a non-raising move in the sense above,
               because it never turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest protocol
               is two moves: test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the checking
               work and one for the crossing.
                   But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step
               is handed the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the
               reading crossed. Play VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you
               land in YES and make one mark, the same box and the same mark as the player who
               checked first. The two tally lines differ by exactly what the CHECK was charged,
               and if you charged it nothing they don’t differ at all. The mark for the crossing is
               the same mark either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid for. It does not
               say it was earned. Popper’s corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn’t.
                                                                        9.5 What the word means   201


    You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in
the state when it passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark
is there. That’s a design, written into the step function, and it’s a perfectly good one.
Nothing in the five parts or the toll asks for it. That’s a real gap between the word
and the bare system, and I’m leaving it in plain sight: the toll prices the commit,
and whether the commit was preceded by a test is a fact about the run, or about a
design somebody chose. The five parts don’t guarantee it.

Remark 9.2 (Nothing makes the crossing wait). Read off Definition 2.1. The toll
constrains cost(i ) for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any
function of the current state and the move. So a Thiele machine may have a move
that crosses from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section 2’s
board extended with CHECK, the run [VOUCH] from NO crosses with one mark, and
[CHECK, VOUCH] crosses with one mark for the crossing plus whatever CHECK was
charged, one mark in all if CHECK is priced at zero. Making a crossing depend on
an earlier check is a condition on the step function, which a particular system can
impose and the definition does not.


9.5 What the word means

Insight, in the sense this book prices, is a distinction made to stay: a move that
flips a reading from off to on, for good, and that move costs at least one mark, in
any system with the toll, whatever the reading is about and whatever its depth. At
its best the reading is a relation committed to, a claim checked and closed; a bare
crossing that commits to nothing pays the same mark, and the toll doesn’t tell the
two apart. Part III’s certified machine is one way to make sure a crossing is the
first kind. Three boundaries, each from a different place. From Metcalfe: it isn’t a
feeling, and a system’s version has to be an event. From the proof: the price is flat;
a shallow commit and a deep one both cost at least one, and cost is not depth. A
system can pay heavily to check a trivial claim, and Duncker’s box, a real insight, is
still one small commit. And from the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing
on its own. Price and correctness are separate books.
    Which leaves a suspicion I’d have in your place. Everything so far has been one
reading on one sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the
shape of that record something I picked, or is it what any base-driven record has
to look like, on any machine at all? That’s the next section: take any machine that
steps, bolt a record onto it, and see what shape it’s forced into. How a concrete
machine hangs actual claims on its parts, a checked property of one counter at one
edition, and where those sit in the state, comes in Part III (Section 15).
CHAPTER 10




Records over any base: the latch

This is the blank cell again, over any machine: a reading that goes from no to yes
because the machine did something, and stays. For the whole book so far I’ve been
building up a thing with a flag and a counter, and you’d be right to suspect that the
whole apparatus is special pleading for one machine, the one I keep promising to
build. So here’s the section that answers the suspicion with no particular machine
in it at all, and sees what’s left. Take any machine that steps deterministically: a
Turing machine, a register machine (a few numbered boxes that each hold a whole
number, and a program that adds, subtracts and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo
Church’s way of computing by nothing but plugging expressions into expressions;
Section 13 builds one), anything. Call it the base. Now bolt a record onto it, under
rules I’ll state, and ask: what can the record be?
    The answer is one shape, and I’ll show you the shape first because it’s a thing
you can build from a cup and a die.


10.1 A cup and a die

Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule: the first time a coin lands in front of
it, turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and
put a coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. If a six appears, the cup turns over
on the first one and stays turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number is
where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record. If no six appears,
the cup stays down; a reachable event need not occur on every trial.
     For the deterministic base in the theorem, write the rolls down first and replay
them. The base state is the fixed list and a finger pointing to its next entry; a step
moves the finger one place, regardless of the cup. The event asks whether that entry
is six. Nothing about the cup changes which entry comes next.
     That’s a latch. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two
British physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer,
and Frank Jordan, applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds
whichever state you last put it in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and
caches in the device you’re reading this on descend from it. Cut its reset wire and
what’s left has one input, “set,” and the rule new state = old state or set: once set, it
stays set. The cup is that circuit: a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

                                  202
                                                              10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   203


    (Eccles and Jordan didn’t call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a trigger
relay. Where the newer, sillier name came from I can’t source, so I’ll leave it at that.)
    Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build
one on purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that’s very close to this book’s. In
the mid-1950s Wen Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American
Bosch Arma Corporation in Garden City, New York, was asked by the United States
Air Force, in the accounts of his career I could find, for a more flexible and secure
way to hold the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer
of the Atlas missile. What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented
(filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the plain title “Storage matrix”) was a grid
with a connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by taking out the
connections you didn’t want, physically or by burning them out with too much
current. The word burn is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a
chip. The descendants are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and
a fuse blown in one stays blown: there’s no current you can send to grow it back.
A whole memory built out of cups with no reset wire, because somebody wanted
numbers nobody could quietly change later. Does that prove anything here? No.
The theorem below doesn’t care what a cup is made of. But it’s good to know the
shape wasn’t invented for a sheet of paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a good
deal higher than a die.
    Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: every base-driven record, over any
base, is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.


10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean
Here’s where the content is, and I’ll give you the five rules, because the theorem is
only as strong as they are.
   A machine extends a base when there’s a map from the bigger machine’s states
down to the base’s, and that map starts in the base’s start states, reaches every one of
them, moves in step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through
the map), and agrees about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden
state as it likes beyond the base. That’s the “any base” part: the base doesn’t get to
see the extension, and the extension doesn’t get to change what the base does.
   The extension carries a record, a yes/no reading, and a ledger, a counter. It’s
a base-driven record when five things hold. One: the record’s next value depends
only on the base’s current state and the record’s current value. (I’ll call this driven
by the computation. It says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A
clock on the wall or someone’s hand doesn’t get a say.) Two: the ledger never
goes down (Section 6). Three: the step that turns the record on costs at least one;
that’s the toll (Section 2). Four: once on, the record stays on; that’s permanence
204   10 Records over any base: the latch


               (Section 3). Distributed-systems people have a name for a predicate like that. The
               computer scientists K. Mani Chandy and Leslie Lamport, in their 1985 paper on
               taking a consistent snapshot of a distributed system, called a property stable when
               once it holds it holds forever after, and stable properties are the ones a snapshot can
               be trusted to detect. Five: some run from a start state actually reaches a step that
               turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.
                  Here are the words exactly. On/off is true/false, ∨ is “or” (on when either side is
               on), and nextk is k steps.

               Definition 10.1 (Base, record-carrying machine, cover). A base B is a set of states
               with a step function nextB , a set of starting states, and a halting predicate. A record-
               carrying machine M is a set of states with a step function next M , a set of starting
               states, a record rec from states to Booleans, a ledger µ from states to whole numbers,
               and a halting predicate. The cost of a step is cost(m) = µ(next M (m)) −̇ µ(m). A
               cover of B by M is a map π from states of M to states of B that sends starting states
               to starting states, has every starting state of B as the image of some starting state
               of M, commutes with the steps, π (next M (m)) = nextB (π (m)), and agrees about
               halting: m halts exactly when π (m) does.


               Definition 10.2 (Base-driven record, latch). M with cover π is a base-driven record
               over B when (R1, driven by the computation) there is one function f such that, for
               every state m, rec(next M (m)) = f (π (m), rec(m)); for every state m, (R2, ledger)
               µ(m) ≤ µ(next M (m)); (R3, toll) if rec(m) is off and rec(next M (m)) is on, then
               cost(m) ≥ 1; (R4, permanence) if rec(m) is on, so is rec(next M (m)); and (R5, a
               reachable write) some starting state m0 and some k have rec(nextkM (m0 )) off and
               rec(nextkM+1 (m0 )) on. An event is a function h from base states to Booleans, and its
               latch is the step (b, r ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b)). M factors as the latch of h when, for
               every state m (reachable or not),
                      (π (next M (m)), rec(next M (m))) = (nextB (π (m)), rec(m) ∨ h(π (m))).
                  Now the theorem. Under those rules, the base state and the record move exactly
               as a latch: the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds,
               and never off, and the event is read off the extension’s own rule by asking it what it
               does when the record is off (stated exactly below). That’s a statement about what
               the base and the record do together. The hidden state the extension carries can’t
               push the record anywhere (R1) doesn’t allow, since the record’s next value is a
               function of the base state and the record’s own value. The theorem doesn’t say the
               whole extension is a bare latch machine, and it doesn’t make hidden state show
               up anywhere in particular: an extension can carry a field that touches neither the
               record nor the ledger. And the event is pinned down only on base states that some
                                                                10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   205


state with the record off covers; on a base state with no such state above it, f (b, off)
is whatever (R1)’s function says, and nothing in a run ever consults it.
     I promised the content was in the definition, and here’s what that means: the
proof is a short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only two
of the five rules, “driven by the computation” and “permanent.” The ledger, the
toll, and the reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A latch is what you get from
“answers only to the base” plus “never comes back down,” full stop. The other three
rules matter for the converse: for any base and any event the base can reach, the
latch of that event, priced at one unit per write, is a base-driven record. The event
can be one that holds everywhere. Then its latch is up after one step from every
start and tells no two starts apart. It’s still a latch and still base-driven: the converse
doesn’t ask the record to distinguish anything. A record that tells two starts apart
at some step has to latch an event that has held along one run by then and not yet
along the other, and the latch tells them apart for as long as that stays so. Put the
two together and you’ve got: base-driven records are exactly latches. One shape, no
others, over any base.
Observation 10.1 (The record is a latch). Let B be any base, π a cover of B by
M, and suppose M’s record is driven by the computation (R1), through a function
 f , and permanent (R4). Then M factors as the latch of the event h(b) = f (b, off).
In particular every base-driven record factors that way; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are not
hypotheses.
Proof. The base half of the equation is the cover’s step clause. For the record, split on
rec(m). If it is on, permanence (R4) makes the next value on, and on ∨ h(π (m)) is
on. If it is off, (R1) makes the next value f (π (m), off) = h(π (m)) = off ∨ h(π (m)).
Only (R1), (R4) and the cover are used; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are discarded.
   The latch’s nearest neighbours are in verification, and they’re old. The computer
scientists Martín Abadi and Leslie Lamport, then at Digital’s research lab in Palo
Alto, added history variables to specifications in 1991: extra state that records what
has happened and never steers the system, used to prove that one specification
implements another. A history variable that only ever turns on is the cup. Temporal
logic has the same record as an operator. In the past-time temporal logic that Orna
Lichtenstein, Amir Pnueli and Lenore Zuck set out in 1985, “once h” holds now
exactly when h has held at some point so far, and a runtime monitor keeps it in one
bit with the update r ′ = r ∨ h. Klaus Havelund and Grigore Roşu, two computer
scientists working on runtime verification, synthesized monitors of exactly that
kind for safety properties written in that logic in 2002. That update is the latch of
Definition 10.2, word for word. What the observation adds is the other direction: a
record driven by the computation that never comes down can’t be anything else.
206   10 Records over any base: the latch


                   One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways. It
               never asks what the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down
               is base, and the record’s rule is allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is
               extension, and (R1) keeps the record’s rule from reading it. Draw the line low, so
               the base is only the computation’s own working state, and (R1) is a real demand.
               Draw it high, put every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1) is easy
               to meet, and the latch shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds
               wherever you draw the line, and that’s exactly why it can’t tell you where a record’s
               meaning lives. The meaning lives in what the event h reads, and that’s in the base
               by construction. On the small machine of Part III (Section 15), the checks that give
               the flag its meaning sit in the base its cover picks out. So when that machine arrives,
               ask it first which parts it puts above the line.


               Theorem 10.2 (Every reachable latch is a base-driven record). Let B be any base
               and h any event. Let Latchh have states (b, r, x ), starting states (b, off, 0) with b
               starting in B, step (b, r, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), x + δ) with δ = 1 when r is off
               and h(b) is on and δ = 0 otherwise, record r, ledger x, halting as b halts, and cover
               (b, r, x ) 7→ b. Suppose some starting b0 and some k bring Latchh from (b0 , off, 0), in
               k steps, to a state whose record is still off and whose base state satisfies h. Then
               Latchh is a base-driven record over B.

               Proof. (R1) holds with f (b, r ) = r ∨ h(b). (R2): each step adds 0 or 1. (R3): a step
               that turns the record on has r off and h(b) on, so it adds 1. (R4): on ∨ h(b) is on.
               (R5) is the supposition. The supposition asks for the first time h holds on some run;
               any run from a start that reaches an h-state has such a first time.
                   What about a base that never merges, a reversible one? It can carry a record,
               and the next theorem says exactly what it pays. Keep every earlier record value
               in a history beside the latch, one more entry on every step, and the whole step
               merges nothing either. But that history needs a fresh slot at every step, forever, so
               the machine never comes back to a state it has been in. That’s the room column. On
               a finite state space there’s no such room, and a permanent record can’t be written
               by a step that merges nothing at all. A step that merges nothing is called injective:
               no two states go to the same next state. And r :: H is the history H with r put on
               the front, as in Section 9.


               Theorem 10.3 (Records on reversible machines). (1) Let B be a base whose step
               is injective. The machine with states (b, r, H, x ), step (b, r, H, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨
               h(b), r :: H, x + δ) (δ as in Theorem 10.2), starting states with r off, H empty and
                                                              10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   207


x = 0, has an injective step, never visits the same state twice on a run (the history
gets one entry longer on every step), and under the supposition of Theorem 10.2
it is a base-driven record over B. (2) On a finite state space, a single injective step
with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off to on.

Proof. (1) Equal images have equal base parts, so equal base states by injectivity;
equal histories r :: H, so equal records and histories; and equal ledgers once the
equal δ is subtracted. Each step makes the history one entry longer, so no state of a
run comes round again. That it is base-driven is the proof of Theorem 10.2 with the
history carried along. (2) is Theorem 3.1 of Section 3 with a single move.
    So a base that never merges can carry a record only by paying room: a history
that grows by one entry every step and never ends. A machine with finitely many
states hasn’t got that room, so it can’t carry one without merging: on a finite
machine an instruction that first raises a permanent reading must merge some
possible states. The entering state need not belong to the colliding pair; Section 3
prices the instruction under merge pricing.
    Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent
Danos and Jean Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin
down what a transaction is. In 2004 they had built a reversible version of CCS,
Robin Milner’s calculus of processes that talk to each other, where every step can
be rolled back, and in 2005 they modelled a transaction in it as a process that
wanders freely through everything that can be undone until it performs an action
declared irreversible, which is the commit. The way I read it, they start from steps
that all come undone and ask what has to be added before anything sticks, and the
theorem above starts from a record and asks what the step under it must be. In their
calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect needs a step with no way back, and
