the calculus has to say which steps those are. The word I tripped on was declared.
Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out by counting, since on a finite
machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it. Push on that and it gives. I
choose the event h, and on a base that grows its history forever the write merges
nothing, because it pays in room instead (Theorem 10.3), so there my permanence
is declared too.
    There’s an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from,
because I put it there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That’s the
only reason a raised record means the event happened: it was down at the start,
and only h lifts it. Turn the cup up before the first roll and it tells you nothing about
the die. So the clean start is an assumed ready state, a past hypothesis in miniature.
The past hypothesis is David Albert’s name for an assumed low-entropy beginning
of the universe, which several of the accounts below lean records on. Whether every
trusted record leans on it is their argument, and I’m not settling it. Nothing in this
208   10 Records over any base: the latch


               book derives one; every theorem here about records assumes its small version and
               starts from there.
                   When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got
               five papers that read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each
               one the same thing: what does the cup being down at the start rest on? There are
               two places to put it. You can put it at the beginning, as a fact about how things
               started. Or you can put it in the structure of what causes what. David Wolpert,
               then a physicist at Los Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem
               (Appendix C), sorted memory systems in 1992, and one of his kinds works only
               because it begins in a prepared state set up by a process that runs one way, which is
               how it leans on the second law. That’s the cup put down by somebody before the
               game, at the first place. Wolpert and Jens Kipper, a philosopher at Rochester, put in
               2024 that sorting on a formal footing, and they say plainly that they have no formal
               proof this kind can only remember the past. I trust them more for that sentence.
               What I think they’re saying is that a prepared start buys you a memory, and getting
               its direction too takes something they can’t yet prove.
                   Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who
               works on the theory of general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the
               Australian National University, built in 2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past
               hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of the past and none of the
               future. As I read their route, the clean start doesn’t go straight to the records. It
               goes through a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas
               Blanchard, a philosopher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness
               of knowledge out of the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure.
               So Blanchard starts at the second place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter’s
               road. That took me a while to see, because one is a toy world and the other is
               philosophy of causation. They go from the start to causes to records; he goes from
               causes to records. The fit is my reading, and it’s mine to defend. And Carlo Rovelli,
               two years before his paper on the cost of choosing from Section 4, studied traces in
               “Memory and entropy” (2022) and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into
               available information. He’s at the first place, and he says what the beginning gets
               spent on. Read against the latch, that’s the blank the record uses up: the flag can
               say yes once because it started at no.
                   So does the latch explain why records point backwards? No. I’ll say that plainly,
               so it doesn’t look like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start clean, and
               a theorem built on those two can only hand the arrow back. Push further and it
               gives in a second place. The history that grows forever looked like a way around the
               clean start. It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank. Under a step that forgets
               nothing, on a finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past or future,
               which is Zermelo again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with Wolpert
                                                              10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   209


and Rovelli, and it sits there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least imposed
their start on a world with its own dynamics and watched what came out. I wrote
mine into the definition.
    Constructor theory, which Section 3 brings in as a neighbour of the chairs, has
a paper on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated as which
transformations a device can and can’t bring about can’t mention time at all, so
duration has to come from relations between physical systems, clocks, that have their
own dynamics. What I think they’re saying is that whenever you want a duration
you point at a second system and count what it did. That’s the position this book
is in by construction. The step count is the only time in it, and it comes from the
machine’s own steps. The next subsection has a record turned at the fifth tick of a
hidden clock, and (R1) throws it out, which read beside them is a rule about which
system may be the clock: the one being recorded. Push on it, though. Their laws
have no step in them, and the paper’s work is getting duration and dynamics out of
clocks and timers. I put a step, nextB , into the definition of a base. So I’m in their
position only at the far end of their argument, where a clock already exists. The
base is my clock, and I assumed it.
    Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it
behaves the way the last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is
where the cup puts what it forgets, since a closed quantum system with separate
energy levels comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger, Section 3) and the theorem left
only two ways to pay for a record that stays: room, which here means a history that
never ends, or a merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH Zurich, wanted
a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in 1972 a particle
that flips spins in a long chain as it passes, now called the Coleman-Hepp model (I
know Hepp’s paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975) took it apart:
the record is exactly definite only for an infinitely long chain, which is the room
column above, a history that never ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan Halliwell, a
theoretical physicist at Imperial College London, used in 1999 a two-state detector
that flips once when a particle crosses a point and is kept from flipping back by a
large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the history. His
abstract calls it effectively irreversible, and I like that he puts the word effectively
right there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the physicist who named
the quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa Barbara, gave
in 1995 the property a name inside their framework of decoherent histories: the
permanence of the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story is extended
into the future. They name (R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to others. So
Hepp’s chain, as Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and Halliwell’s detector is finite
and only effectively permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once, and
it gets there by letting the first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never say
210   10 Records over any base: the latch


               where the merged state goes. Hepp’s chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to put
               his in an environment. Mine just goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter. That’s
               fine in a model of computation, and it’s exactly where this stops being physics.


               10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp
               A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each
               hypothesis dropped, and it does, and they’re the two ways a record goes wrong in
               the world.
                   Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every
               step: on, off, on, off. It’s driven by the computation; it’s not permanent; and it’s not
               a latch of any event. This is a toggle, a piece of working state. A record you can
               revoke is working state wearing a record’s clothes, and if a revocation has to stick,
               that’s a second latch (“revoked”), which is how certificate revocation lists actually
               work: you add an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer
               scientist then at MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built append-only authenticated
               sets and dictionaries for transparency logs, and revocation fits that shape exactly:
               a revocation goes in once and stays. The pair lemma (stated below) covers two
               latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the second only
               turns over on an even roll if the first is already up, and you’ll see the second can
               never turn before the first.
                   Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each
               speaker a row of cups, one for every claim they’ve made. Everybody I read in this
               field is answering two questions about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can
               they come back down. C. L. Hamblin, an Australian philosopher and logician who
               also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote Fallacies (1970),
               and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a commitment store,
               a list of what they’re on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue update it. The
               speaker doesn’t. I know that chapter from other people’s accounts of it. That’s an
               answer to the first question, and it’s (R1) for arguments: the cup answers to what
               happened in the dialogue, and the speaker’s hand is kept off it. Henry Prakken, who
               works on AI and law at Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for argumentation
               on stores like that and made commitments sticky: a claim can be retracted only
               when it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking carry a price. He also
               floats a convention that once a player has retracted a proposition, that player can’t
               take it on again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way an entry on a
               revocation list does. That’s an answer to the second question, and it took me a
               second pass to see that it’s two answers. A cup can come down, and coming down
               costs. And once it has, the taking-back is itself a cup that stays up. Erik Krabbe,
               an argumentation theorist at Groningen, names in 2001 the awkward part of that:
                                               10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp   211


retraction is frowned on, and yet resolving a dispute takes somebody retracting a
doubt or a point of view, so the rules have to say when taking a commitment back is
allowed. As I read him, he’s standing between the two ends of the second question.
A store that never gives can’t settle a dispute. A store that gives freely isn’t a store.
The part of all that I’d keep is Hamblin’s, that the store belongs to the rules. It
doesn’t belong to the speaker. Take the pen away from the program. And this book
answers Krabbe with a price: a take-back is a second cup, “revoked,” and turning
it costs at least one like any other write, so a retraction is allowed, permanent and
paid for. That’s Prakken’s convention with the toll attached. Where mine gives is
his first condition. He lets a claim come down only when it’s been challenged, and
nothing in my latch asks why the second cup turned. The pair lemma lets the second
cup’s event read the base and the first cup, and nothing in it requires a challenge to
be there.
    The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumen-
tation of Phan Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology
in Bangkok (1995), arguments attack one another, and the grounded semantics starts
from the arguments nobody attacks and keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at
how it’s built: things go in and never come out, which is a row of cups turned one
at a time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia, introduced in 2007,
and Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, strong admissibility: a
set is strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the
set that don’t lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. That’s the argumentation
form of an earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is in by default, which puts
it at the far end from Burge’s default on the testimony map in Section 7. Caminada
argues it plays a vital part in the dialogue games that decide grounded acceptance.
I’ve read Caminada’s paper; Dung’s and Baroni and Giacomin’s I know through
what later papers say about them. Notice the bottom, though. An argument nobody
attacks gets in on a check that can’t fail, and this book says a check that can’t fail
establishes nothing (Section 14). Now turn that on my own cups, because it lands.
My first write needs only that h holds, and what h reads sits in the base, where the
latch theorem doesn’t look. I charge a unit for it. A unit is a price. It isn’t a check.
So my earned records bottom out the way Dung’s do, in something let in without an
argument, and the one difference is that mine pays to get in. Whether a machine’s
earned record certifies exactly the strongly admissible sets is the kind of statement
I’d have to prove before I said it, and I haven’t.
    A record that’s allowed to change its mind isn’t lawless, though. It’s somebody
else’s subject. Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down
to up, is the latch. More than once and you’re somewhere else, and the people
who went there sort it two ways: by how many turns are allowed, and by how long
the game runs. The philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark Gold,
212   10 Records over any base: the latch


               a computer scientist at a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in
               1965, looked at questions a machine answers by guessing and revising, where the
               answer is whatever the guesses finally settle on. Putnam’s paper says outright that
               you’re never sure you have the correct answer. That stopped me the first time. What
               kind of answer can’t you ever be sure you have? The way I came to read it: the
               cup’s position at any moment is the current guess, the answer is where it ends up,
               and nobody watching can tell when it’s done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in
               Novosibirsk, sorted those in 1968 by how many revisions they’re allowed (that’s
               how his hierarchy is described; I haven’t read his paper). Allow one, from no to yes,
               and you get exactly the sets a program can list. That level is in a modern account of
               the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl Jockusch, Timothy McNicholl and Paul Schupp,
               four computability theorists, and you don’t need their word for it. If a program
               lists the set, guess no for every number and flip the guess to yes when the number
               shows up on the list. Going back, if every guess flips at most once, from no to yes,
               run all the guessing side by side and write a number down the moment its guess
               flips. That’s what a permanent record raised by a search catches. Allow two, three,
               and so on, and every extra change buys new sets: the rungs of the ladder are all
               different. A record that can come back down lives on that ladder. Now put Putnam’s
               worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a yes is final the moment it
               appears, and a no never is. Down means not yet. A single cup of mine can certify
               that something happened and can never certify that it didn’t; a final no would take
               a second cup, turned by finding a reason, and that’s the pair of latches again. That’s
               what the bottom rung costs, and I’d rather name it. This book stays on the bottom
               rung. I’m pointing at the ladder. I’m not climbing it.
                    The ladder doesn’t stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity
               have names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever
               adds, stage after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an inductive
               definition (the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel,
               two recursion theorists). That’s the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes
               up at some stage and is still up at every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep
               what stays put from some stage on, and you have what John Burgess, a philosopher
               and logician at Princeton, called in 1986 quasi-inductive definitions, which he met
               in the revision theories of truth that grew up beside the logician Saul Kripke’s
               1975 theory of truth, which builds up the true sentences in stages. Burgess’s paper
               measures how complicated the truths of those theories get. I’ve read its abstract. The
               place where he names them I haven’t. What took me a few reads is that Burgess’s
               rule at a limit is Putnam and Gold’s rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on,
               applied at every limit stage along the way. That’s my reading of how the two fit. If
               it’s right, the split between a cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same
               split at finite time and past it. A permanent record is the first kind. A toggle that’s
                                               10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp   213


allowed to settle is the second. Joel Hamkins and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a
Turing machine keep running through the ordinals in 2000. At a limit a cell keeps its
value if it settled, and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth forever, and the trick
they use again and again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a guess
changes, and at the limit the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely
often. A flag that can come back down is how that machine learns what no finite
run could tell it. A permanent one can’t do that trick, because at a limit a cell that
only ever goes up just stays up. So past infinity the toggle is the clever one. A latch
tells you a thing happened at least once. Their flashing flag tells you it happened
infinitely often. I threw the toggle out a few paragraphs back anyway, and I’d do it
again, because before the limit its reading can’t be relied on, and nobody using a
machine of mine gets to wait for a limit. One finite-time fact belongs beside it, so
nobody concludes too much from permanence. Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford,
described in 1957 a machine whose only write is to mark a square and which can
never erase one, and it computes everything a Turing machine does. Permanence
of a machine’s own memory costs it no computing power, given an endless tape:
each mark goes on a square nobody marked before, which is the room column
again. What the book prices is a permanent reading raised by a step that has to
work whether or not the reading is already up, which is a different thing. So the
cost I named a paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim. Computing
power doesn’t pay it.
    Drop “driven by the computation.” Take a base that counts, and a record that
switches on at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, whatever the base is doing. It’s
permanent. The computation doesn’t drive it. This is a timestamp. A timestamp is
not evidence. It says when. It doesn’t say what happened, and a record switched by an
outside party or a clock records that party or that clock and leaves the computation
out. Try it with the recorded die list. Keep a second tally hidden beside it, and turn
the cup when that tally reads five before a move; then advance both the tally and
the finger on the list. Run two trials from the same list entry with the cup down, but
start the hidden tally at five in one trial and zero in the other. The next cup values
disagree although everything the base shows agrees. That is the failure of being
driven by the base. If the tally always starts synchronized with the list position, the
position can predict the cup; the distinction matters below.
    The two examples do exactly what I said they do: the toggle is driven, isn’t
permanent and isn’t a latch; the timestamp is permanent and isn’t driven. That each
also keeps the other rules (the ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one,
a run reaches it) is true by inspection.
    Permanent but undriven is a timestamp, driven but impermanent is a toggle,
and a record is the thing that’s both. Undriven, for the timestamp, means that
along the runs that actually happen the base state doesn’t fix when the record turns;
214   10 Records over any base: the latch


               Lemma 10.7 below says why that’s the condition, and what (R1) as written adds to
               it. That’s the whole discrimination, and I think it’s the most useful single sentence
               in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is why it’s here.
                   The pair lemma and the two counterexamples, exactly. The base for both coun-
               terexamples is the counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state
               is a starting state, and nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: ¬r is r flipped,
               and a statement in square brackets, like [k = 5], reads on when it’s true and off
               when it isn’t.


               Lemma 10.4 (Two records are two latches). Let c1 , c2 be two records on
               M, with cover π onto a base B, such that: there is one function F with
               (c1 (next M (m)), c2 (next M (m))) = F (π (m), c1 (m), c2 (m)); the ledger never goes
               down; a step that turns either record on costs at least one; and each record is
               permanent. Then there are h1 , h2 with c1 (next M (m)) = c1 (m) ∨ h1 (π (m), c2 (m))
               and c2 (next M (m)) = c2 (m) ∨ h2 (π (m), c1 (m)) for every m.

               Proof. Take h1 (b, r2 ) to be the first part of F (b, off, r2 ) and h2 (b, r1 ) the second part
               of F (b, r1 , off), then split on each record as in Observation 10.1.



               Lemma 10.5 (The toggle). Let the toggle have states (n, r ), step (n, r ) 7→ (n +
               1, ¬r ), every state starting, record r, ledger n, cover (n, r ) 7→ n onto the counter. It
               is driven by the computation, with f (b, r ) = ¬r; it is not permanent; and it factors
               as the latch of no event.

               Proof. At (0, on) the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch
               gives on ∨ h(0) = on there.



               Lemma 10.6 (The timestamp). Let the timestamp have states (b, k, r ), step
               (b, k, r ) 7→ (b + 1, k + 1, r ∨ [k = 5]), every state starting, record r, ledger b, cover
               (b, k, r ) 7→ b onto the counter. It is permanent and not driven by the computation.

               Proof. Permanence: on ∨ x is on. Not driven: the states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off)
               have the same base state and the same record, and their next records are on and off,
               so no f of the base state and the record can give both.
                               10.4 Is there only one such machine? No. One structure, two free choices.   215


    “Driven” is a condition on every state. The timestamp makes every state a starting
state, so the two states the proof compares are both ones a run can begin at, even
though a timestamp started at (0, 0, off) would never reach (0, 5, off).
    That last sentence does more work than it looks, so here it is as a lemma. Start
the same timestamp in sync, at (b, b, off) only. On every state its runs reach, the
hidden count equals the base, and the timestamp is exactly the latch of [b = 5].
(R1) still rejects it, because (R1) asks about every state, and (0, 5, off) is a state,
though no run from a synchronised start reaches it. So (R1) as written separates the
timestamp from a latch partly by how the cover is drawn and through states nobody
visits. The separation I mean is the one on reachable states: the timestamp with
every state a start fails (R1) even when only states some run reaches are counted,
since two starting states sit over the same base state with the same record and
disagree about the next one. And the latch theorem holds in that reachable form
too.


Lemma 10.7 (The timestamp, on the states runs reach). Say M’s record is driven on
reachable states when (R1) holds for every state reached from a starting state in some
number of steps. (1) If M’s record is driven on reachable states and permanent, then
on every reachable state M steps as the latch of some event. (2) The timestamp of
Lemma 10.6 isn’t driven on reachable states. (3) The timestamp started in sync, with
starting states (b, b, off) and the same step, record, ledger and cover, is permanent,
isn’t driven by the computation, is driven on reachable states, and on every reachable
state steps as the latch of [b = 5].

Proof. (1) is the proof of Observation 10.1, run on reachable states only. (2) The
states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off) are starting states, reached in no steps, and the proof
of Lemma 10.6 applies to them. (3) From (b, b, off) every step adds one to both
counts, so a reachable state has k = b and its next record is r ∨ [b = 5]. Over every
state, (R1) fails at the same pair as in Lemma 10.6.
    So “permanent but undriven is a timestamp” is a sentence about the timestamp
with every state a start, over the cover that hides its count, and it holds there in the
strong form: undriven on the very states its runs pass through. A timestamp started
in step with its base is a latch on the runs it has, and (R1) throws it out only because
(R1) also looks at states those runs never reach.


10.4 Is there only one such machine? No. One structure, two free choices.

Here’s a sentence I have to take apart: “there’s only one way to carry a record.”
Three different things get squeezed into that breath.
216   10 Records over any base: the latch


                   First claim: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the
               books, starting at zero and adding each move’s price? Yes, on every state reachable
               from the start; that’s Section 6’s initiality, and it assumes the price list.
                   Second claim: is every base-driven record over a base the same machine, charges
               and all? No, and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any
               base-driven record and add one more coin to the bill on every step, whatever the
               step is. Now walk the five rules. The record still answers only to the base and its
               own value (R1); the bill never touches it. The ledger still never goes down (R2); it
               climbs faster, if anything. The step that turns the record on still costs at least one
               (R3), because the toll is a floor and a surcharge only raises the price. Once on, the
               record stays on (R4), and the same run still reaches the write (R5). So the billed
               machine is base-driven, and it isn’t the machine you started with: wherever the
               original sat still at no charge, the billed one pays a coin a tick for sitting still. Do it
               with the cup and the die. Charge a coin for every roll, six or not. The cup turns over
               on the same roll as before. You’ve changed the bill and nothing about the record. A
               machine that charges for CPU time is base-driven and isn’t the one that doesn’t.
                   But the billed machine isn’t a different structure. It’s the same record, steps and
               halting with a different price list. So the claim worth keeping is sameness up to the
               price schedule: compare two machines by their record, their halting and their steps,
               through their maps down to the base, and don’t compare charges. Fix which event
               the record is, and the bill stops mattering; a flat surcharge, or any surcharge that
               depends on the current state, sits on the same structure. That’s the first free choice.
               The walk above is the whole argument, and it works over an arbitrary base, with
               any surcharge that depends on the current state: the billed machine is base-driven,
               has the same latch event, steps along with the original on record, halting and base,
               and pays each step’s cost plus the surcharge.
                   And then the second free choice, and this one still surprises me. Which event is
               the record? Nothing in the five rules picks it. The converse above already says so, if
               you read it twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at
               one unit per write, is a base-driven record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on
               the first six. Another turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire;
               both are base-driven. Roll a one first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree
               about whether anything has been recorded. So which permanent reading counts as
               the record is a second thing nobody forces on you. The price list is one free choice.
               The event is the other. That second choice is the question Section 18 is about: what,
               if anything, makes certification the event worth recording. “The ledger passed one”
               is an event only if the chosen base includes enough information to decide it. An
               extension-only ledger is hidden from a base event, just as the hidden clock was. The
               free choice is among functions of the chosen base.
                                     10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about   217


Corollary 10.8 (The event is a free choice). Let B be any base and h1 , h2 two events,
each meeting the supposition of Theorem 10.2. Then Latchh1 and Latchh2 are both
base-driven records over B. If some base state b has h1 (b) on and h2 (b) off, then
one step from (b, off, 0) leaves the first record on and the second off.

Proof. That both are base-driven is Theorem 10.2 applied twice. The step is the
latch’s own rule: off ∨ h1 (b) is on and off ∨ h2 (b) is off.
    Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and some-
times doesn’t, with odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix
the odds? No, and the counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and
differently loaded coins. Here’s the setup, said carefully. Let a record be a single bit
that moves at random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight
positive, never empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on
charged at least one. Call such a record a permanent probabilistic record. Call two
such records the same schedule when the same moves are possible and every move is
charged the same, and the same in probability when the weighted lists give every
move the same odds.


Theorem 10.9 (The schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities). (1) There are two
permanent probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in
probability. (2) There is a permanent probabilistic record that no deterministic latch
on its current value describes.

Proof. (1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights 1 and 1, the other
with weights 1 and 2; from on, both stay on with weight 1; both charge 1 for the
write. Same possible moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record
moves from off both to off and to on, while a latch r ∨ h(r ) gives one value.
   These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath; they say
nothing about any particular machine.
   Third claim: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every base-driven
record-carrier has to have? No. The extension may carry any hidden field it likes,
so two carriers over one base can have state spaces of different sizes, and nothing
needs them to match.


10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about
The theorem is stated for any base, so let me put it on three models of computation
that other people built: a small Turing machine (any program); a register machine
218   10 Records over any base: the latch


               of the kind the computer scientists Stephen Cook (of the certificates) and Robert
               Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost indirect addressing (any program); and
               a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an argument is worked out before it’s
               plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a term with no step left to take step
               to itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one generic theorem applied to that
               base (the bases are defined below). So a register machine with a base-driven record
               is a register machine plus a cup. So is a lambda calculus. (There’s one more instance,
               the machine I build later, where a particular flag is shown to be a base-driven record
               and the same theorem makes it a latch, in Section 15.)
                   Here are the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function, a
               set of starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing else
               about its instruction vocabulary.

               Definition 10.3 (Three concrete bases). The tape base has a finite Boolean list t, a
               head index h, a program counter q and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond
               the list returns false. Writing at h extends the list with false cells if needed, then
               changes that cell. Moving right increments h and extends the list through the new
               head position. Moving left decrements a positive h; at h = 0, it prepends a false cell
               and keeps the head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:

                Instruction                                Next state
                Write a bit                                Perform the write and advance q by one.
                Move left or right                         Perform the move and advance q by one.
                Branch to j                                Set q := j if the current cell is true;
                                                           otherwise advance q by one.
                Halt                                       Leave the entire state unchanged.
                ClaimTapeIsZero with a label ℓ             Advance q by one and do nothing else.


                  An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state,
               and halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by
               every instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction neither
               erases the tape nor charges the cost field; neither the name nor the label supplies
               any semantics.
                  The random-access base has a register function X : N → N and a program
               counter q. For a fixed finite program its instructions are:

                Instruction                                Next state
                Constant (i, c)                            Set X (i ) := c.
                Add (i, j, k)                              Set X (i ) := X ( j) + X (k).
                                    10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about   219


Instruction                                Next state
Subtract (i, j, k)                         Set X (i ) := max(0, X ( j) − X (k)).
Indirect load (i, j)                       Set X (i ) := X ( X ( j)).
Indirect store (i, j)                      Set X ( X (i )) := X ( j).
Positive branch ( j, a)                    Set q := a if X ( j) > 0; otherwise advance q
                                           by one.
Jump to a                                  Set q := a.
Halt                                       Leave the entire state unchanged.


    Each register-writing instruction advances q by one; its operands are evaluated
in the old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program
also leaves the state unchanged. Starting states have q = 0 and arbitrary register
contents. A state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program. Unit cost
here counts instructions. It has nothing to do with the record’s ledger.
    For the indirect instructions, draw boxes 1, 2 and 3 and put 2, 7 and 0 in them.
Indirect load (3, 1) first reads the 2 in box 1, uses it as an address, and copies box
2’s 7 into box 3. Now put 9 in box 3 and execute indirect store (1, 3): the 2 in box 1
tells it where to put the 9, so box 2 changes and box 1 stays 2. An address is being
read from a box; it is not necessarily the box’s own number.
    The lambda base uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in Defi-
nition 13.3. To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function part of an
application. If that part cannot step and is an abstraction, either substitute an
argument that is already an abstraction or take a step in the argument. If neither
applies, the term cannot step. Variables and abstractions cannot step by themselves,
and there is no reduction under an abstraction. The base leaves a term unchanged
when it cannot step and calls precisely those terms halted. Every term is allowed as
a starting state, including open terms.

    So all three are bases in the sense of Definition 10.1, and the latch theorem
applies to each. That’s all it says about them: nothing about what they can compute
or how fast.
    There’s also a relation defined between bases, weak base equivalence: two bases
are equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related
states agree on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched
by some number of steps, possibly zero, on the other. That “some number of steps”
is the stuttering idea Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section 6’s message
counters) put forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn’t
count as different because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one.
The relation carries no cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step
and a Turing machine differ in price. The relation never looks at price, so on what it
220   10 Records over any base: the latch


               does look at they can match. It’s proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch
               form is preserved across it.
                   Draw a coarse machine 0 → 1, with 1 halted, and a finer one a → b → c, with
               c halted. Let a and b both show 0 and c show 1; halted states stay where they are.
               Relate 0 to both a and b, and 1 to c. The fine move a → b changes nothing visible,
               so the coarse machine matches it by taking no step. Its move b → c matches 0 → 1.
               Starting from a, the coarse move is matched by two fine steps. This is what “possibly
               zero” allows; the relation is about matching observations and halting, not matching
               the number of ticks or their bill.
                   There is a limit to that statement. The “preserved across it” proof throws away its
               equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds on every base regardless, so the preservation
               is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in this book are two of the bases actually
               related by this relation. The relation is defined, it’s an equivalence, and it is not
               used to connect the Turing machine to the register machine to the lambda calculus,
               or any of them to the machine of Section 15. It would be easy to read that list as if
               it did. What’s proved is that each base, separately, carries a latch. That’s the honest
               sentence.

               Definition 10.4 (Weak base equivalence). Bases B1 and B2 , with observations o1
               and o2 into one common set, are weakly equivalent when some relation R relates
               every starting state of each to some starting state of the other, and any related x,
               y have o1 ( x ) = o2 (y), the same halting, some n ≥ 0 with R(nextB1 ( x ), nextnB2 (y)),
               and some n ≥ 0 with R(nextnB1 ( x ), nextB2 (y)).



               Theorem 10.10 (Outside bases, and the relation). (1) Weak base equivalence is
               reflexive, symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly equivalent, Observa-
               tion 10.1 holds over one exactly when it holds over the other. (3) Observation 10.1
               holds over each of the three bases in Definition 10.3, for every fixed program where
               the base has one.

               Proof. (1) Reflexive with equality as R and one step against one. Symmetric by
               reversing R. Transitive by composing the two relations; a step on the first base
               is matched by n steps on the second, and those n steps by some number on the
               third, by induction on n. (2) and (3) apply Observation 10.1 directly. In (2) the
               equivalence hypothesis is discarded.
                                                               10.6 Records with more than two values   221


10.6 Records with more than two values
A cup has two positions. Some records have more: a counter of how many checks
passed, a level that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a
time. For each value a, “the record has reached a” is a yes/no reading, and each of
those readings is a latch. What doesn’t go through is squeezing the whole record
into one cup. “Rises” needs one word: the values come with an order ≤, “is at or
below,” which needn’t compare every pair (that’s what makes it a partial order), and
[ a ≤ x ] is the yes/no reading “x has reached a.”

Definition 10.5 (A growing record). Let the record take values in a set A with
a partial order ≤ decided by a Boolean test. A record ρ on M, with cover π
onto a base B, is a base-driven growing record when: there is one function f with
ρ(next M (m)) = f (π (m), ρ(m)); it grows, ρ(m) ≤ ρ(next M (m)); the ledger never
goes down and every step that changes ρ costs at least one; and some run from a
starting state reaches a step that changes it.



Theorem 10.11 (Growing records are families of latches). (1) For every base-driven
growing record there is an h with

                 [ a ≤ ρ(next M (m))] = [ a ≤ ρ(m)] ∨ h( a, π (m), ρ(m))
for every value a and state m: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read
the current value. (2) The thresholds determine the value: if [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y]
for every a, then x = y. (3) For a growing record, charging every change is the
same as charging every threshold that switches on. (4) One latch is not enough:
a three-valued record that climbs 0 → 1 → 2 over a one-state base, each climb
charged one, is base-driven, and no single Boolean latch with a decoding from the
base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct k-bit words, each
word’s set bits contained in the next one’s, has at most k + 1 members.

Proof. (1) Take h( a, b, x ) = [ a ̸≤ x ] ∧ [ a ≤ f (b, x )]. If a ≤ ρ(m) already, growth and
transitivity give a ≤ ρ(next M (m)); otherwise the equation is the definition of h. (2)
Antisymmetry, with a = x and a = y. (3) Growth plus antisymmetry turn “the value
changed” into “some threshold switched on,” and back. (4) Over one base state, a
latch and a decoding can produce at most two values, and the record takes three.
(5) Each strict step up the chain adds at least one set bit, and there are only k bits.
   Two cautions about that. In (1) each threshold’s event may read the record’s
current value, so the events aren’t all functions of the base alone. And (3) charges a
222   10 Records over any base: the latch


               step when it switches some threshold on: a step that switches on three thresholds at
               once owes at least one, and nothing here makes the charges add up per threshold.
                  The order need not be finite; (5) is the finite-memory bound.


               10.7 What the base being free buys you
               The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record
               isn’t special pleading for one machine. Over any base that steps deterministically,
               under rules you can read, a record that answers to the computation and never comes
               down is a latch on an event, and the proof doesn’t care what the base is. What
               a particular machine adds on top of the latch is a choice of price list and a choice
               of event, and both are choices. That is why the chairs theorem in Section 3 never
               needed the word certify: it forces a merge in whatever stays. The surcharged cup
               shows the first: the bill can change and the record not notice. The two cups on one
               die show the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine I build
               will have to make both choices, and whether its choice of event is the right one is
               a question I’ll get to (Section 18), and won’t claim to have settled. Before that, a
               record can have more than two positions. Earlier in this section a record that rises
               got cut into one cup per threshold; the next section asks how much of the rest of the
               book survives once a record has more places to be than up and down.


               10.8 What it takes to be complete

               The latch left two choices open, the price list and the event. A machine I can hold up
               against everything else has to make both, and a name for “this machine computes,
               and its record keeps something” has to ask for more than the toll does. The toll
               alone is a low bar. A machine that charges one mark for every step it takes obeys
               the toll for any record at all: every raise costs at least one because every move does.
               That’s a clock bolted to a computer. And a machine whose record never goes up
               obeys it too, because a toll on a raise that never happens is never broken. Neither
               one keeps anything a computation made, and a name both of them get without
               trying isn’t saying much.
                   So here are the names, all of them, once, and the reason for each. They work
               the way Turing’s do. The Thiele Machine, with capitals, is the model: a computer
               with a reading that can go from no to yes, a ledger, and the toll. A Thiele machine,
               lower case, is any particular system that fits the model, the way one rule table is a
               Turing machine. That bar is low on purpose, and a clock clears it. Thiele-complete,
               defined next, is the bar worth meeting, the way Turing-complete is: a machine
               that computes anything, with its record kept apart from its computing and able to
               tell starts apart. Part III adds one stricter bar, certified Thiele-complete, for a record
                                                                10.8 What it takes to be complete   223


that, from a clean start, goes up only on a claim that was checked, committed and
certified. And Appendix D names a universal Thiele machine: one machine that runs
the others, the way Turing’s universal machine runs every Turing machine. The
model, the systems that obey it, the ones that compute and keep, the ones whose
keeping is earned, and the one that runs them. That’s all of them.
   So here’s the bar, in four clauses, and nothing in it mentions what the record is
about.

Definition 10.6 (Thiele-complete). A Thiele machine is Thiele-complete when it
can be read through an interface that hands over three things: a universal base, a
split of its moves into computing moves and marks, and a ledger, a whole number
for each state. A universal base is a way of reading each state as a configuration
of a machine that runs every program (I use Minsky’s two counters, Section 15.2),
with a computing move for each of that machine’s instructions that does to the
configuration exactly what the instruction does, from every state it’s live at, and a
loaded state for each start. The interface has to meet four clauses. (A) Computing
can’t reach the record, and the record stays. No computing move changes the record,
and a record that’s up stays up under every move. (B) Starts are blank. Every loaded
state has the record down. (C) Computing costs no marks, marks cost one. Computing
moves cost 0, every other move costs exactly 1, and each move adds its cost to the
ledger. (D) The record tells starts apart. Some run, the same list of moves, ends with
the record up from one loaded state and down from another.
   Read the clauses as four plain sentences, with the universal base underneath
them: the machine computes anything a Turing machine can. (A) The computing
never touches what’s kept, and what’s kept stays. (B) Nothing is kept before the
run starts. (C) The ledger counts the marks, and only the marks. (D) What’s kept
depends on where you started: there’s a run whose record says something about its
start.
   (D) is where distinction lives. It’s a low bar: a mark that reads one bit of the
input meets it. What it excludes is a record that ignores the start. A record that goes
up on every run from every start keeps a before and an after, and nothing about
where the run began. (D) doesn’t ask that every raise tell starts apart. It asks that
the machine can. A machine may have a mark that raises the record from any state
at all; it pays one for it, like every raise, and (D) is still met by some other run.
Which runs a machine wants its record to tell apart is its own choice, and Part III
makes one.
   The name echoes Turing-complete, but this is a specification a machine meets,
not a class closed under simulation: a machine is held up against it through an
interface, and changing the unit of price drops a machine out.
224   10 Records over any base: the latch




               Theorem 10.12 (What every Thiele-complete machine has). Let a machine be
               Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) It obeys the toll, and the move that raises
               its record is a mark, never a computing move, and costs exactly one. (2) Along any
               run, the ledger rises by exactly the number of marks in it. (3) From any state with
               the record down, every run that ends with the record up raises the ledger by at least
               1. (4) Some run from some loaded state raises the record. (5) Every move costs 0
               or 1, and some move costs 0. (6) Its base runs every two-counter program step for
               step from every live state, and halting from a loaded state matches halting from the
               configuration it shows.

               Proof. (1) If a computing move raised the record it would change it, against (A); so
               the raising move is a mark, and a mark costs one by (C). (2) is (C) added up along
               the run. (3) Somewhere along the run the record goes from down to up, and that
               move is a mark, by (1), so it adds one. (4) is (D), and by (B) the record started
               down. (5) Every move is a computing move or a mark, and (A) supplies computing
               moves. (6) is (A), one instruction at a time.
                   The floor is one, and one is reached: the lift below gives a machine whose record
               goes up after a single mark.
               Observation 10.13 (A clock is a Thiele machine and isn’t Thiele-complete). Take the
               two-counter machine, let every move cost 1, and take as the record any yes/no question
               about its configuration; or a flag that switches on, and stays on, the first time a chosen
               test of the configuration says yes. It obeys the toll and has a two-counter machine inside
               it, and it isn’t Thiele-complete. No machine whose every move costs at least 1 is.
               Proof. A Thiele-complete machine has a move priced 0, by Theorem 10.12(5), and
               this one has none.
                 A machine whose record is down at every state obeys the toll and meets (A), (B)
               and (C), and isn’t Thiele-complete either: (D) asks for a run that raises the record.


               Theorem 10.14 (Each of the four clauses is needed). For each clause there’s a
               machine that meets the other three through some interface and is Thiele-complete
               through none. Each is built on the two counters with two marks, one that raises the
               record when A is 0 and one that always raises it. (A) fails: that machine, and one
               more move, priced 0, that puts the record back down. (B) fails: the two counters
               with a record that no move ever changes, up at the starts where A is 0 and down
               elsewhere. (C) fails: that machine with every move priced 1. (D) fails: the two
               counters with a record that’s always down.
                                                                 10.8 What it takes to be complete   225


Proof. Each machine meets the three by construction. The first fails (A) through
every interface, because a move lowers the record, so the record doesn’t stay. The
second: every one of its moves costs 0, so (C) makes every move a computing move
under any interface; then by (A) no run changes the record, and with every start
blank by (B) no run raises it, so (D) fails. The third has no move priced 0, so it fails
by Observation 10.13. The fourth never raises its record.



Theorem 10.15 (The record can’t be read off the window). Let a machine be
Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) Every configuration is shown, at no cost,
with the record down, by one computing move from some loaded state. (2) Some
loaded state has two runs that end on the same window, one with the record up and
one with it down, and their ledgers differ by at least 1. (3) So no rule that reads
only the window says, at the end of every run from every loaded state, whether the
record is up, and none says what the ledger reads.

Proof. (1) From the loaded state (1, x + 1, y), the computing move “DEC A to line
p” shows ( p, x, y), costs nothing by (C), and leaves the record down by (A) and (B).
(2) Take the run (D) gives, from the loaded state where it raises the record. Its end
shows some configuration. From the same loaded state, computing moves alone
reach any configuration at all: count each counter down to zero, count it up to the
value wanted, and jump to the line wanted. That run ends on the same window,
and it’s all computing, so by (A) and (B) its record is still down and by (C) its ledger
hasn’t moved, while the first run’s ledger went up by at least one, at its raise. (3)
A rule that reads the window gives one answer for one window, and (2) has one
window with two answers.
   Part III proves the same blindness for its certified machines (Observation 15.27),
with a gap of three marks, because a certified raise costs three. Here the gap is one,
and one is reached.


Theorem 10.16 (Every universal base becomes Thiele-complete). Take any machine
with a universal base and any events on its states, and add, for each event, a mark
that costs one and raises a record exactly when the event holds; computing moves
cost nothing and leave the record alone. If some run of computing moves makes
some event hold from one loaded state and not from another, the result is Thiele-
complete, its computing is the original machine’s step for step, and its record goes
up after a single mark from any state where the event already holds.
226   10 Records over any base: the latch


               Proof. (A): computing moves are the original’s and don’t touch the record, and a
               mark only adds to it. (B): the record starts down. (C): by construction. (D): run the
               moves that make the event hold from one loaded state and not the other, then the
               event’s mark. Step for step: a computing move acts on the original part and nothing
               else. And a mark from a state where its event holds puts the record up.
                   One mark on “A is at least 1” always works: the starts with A at 0 and at
               1 already differ on it, so that mark alone, run from each, tells them apart. So
               Thiele-complete isn’t a property only a special machine has. Any model with a
               universal base becomes Thiele-complete by adding marks, and needs no claims and
               no checker to do it; a model that simulates the two counters some other way does
               so once its moves are grouped into ones that carry out a counter instruction each
               (Theorem E.4). Two kinds of base don’t lift, whatever the events: one whose moves
               don’t depend on the state it’s in, and one whose moves lead from each state to only
               finitely many next states. A universal base needs, from one state, a move at no
               marks to every line of a program, and that’s infinitely many places to go.
                   Some Thiele-complete machine runs every Thiele machine a program can de-
               scribe. Appendix D defines a universal Thiele machine and builds hosts that run any
               machine a program can describe, in order, matching its record and its ledger up to a
               fixed surcharge, with every computing step done by counter moves on the host and
               every rise of the host’s record placed by its program. None of that needs certification:
               the presented host’s own program, read on a host with no claims, no checker and
               no table of facts, meets the definition too.
                   This is the bar the rest of the book holds machines to. Part III builds one machine
               that clears it, and asks for more: that from a clean start its record go up only on a
               claim that was checked, by a checker proved to mean it, and then committed, and
               that some claim’s check can come out either way. That’s a choice of what the record
               answers to, the second free choice of the latch, made one way, with clean starts and
               three priced acts added (Theorem 15.18).
CHAPTER 11




The whole direction

I have a hunch I can’t fully back up, and Part III tells where it came from (Section 14):
established doesn’t feel like a switch to me. It feels like a direction with lines drawn
across it, and the switch is just the first line. The one piece of that I can settle is that
a single switch isn’t enough once there are three or more stages. So here’s where I
settle it, and where I find out how much of the rest survives being pushed on.
    A row of cells that only ever go from blank to written is a direction: you can tell
how far along it a state is, and nothing walks it back. The cup of Section 10 has two
positions. Everything the book has proved about the toll so far (the universal floor,
the merges, the squeeze, the windows) was proved for a cup. The question for this
section is blunt: if the record has more places to be than up and down, how many
of those results come along, and which ones break?


11.1 A row of cups
Get four cups and a pencil. Write five stages of an experiment on a strip of paper,
left to right: proposed, set up, run, read, recorded. Agree to do them in that order.
Put an upside-down cup between each pair of neighbours. The first means “the
setup happened,” the second “the run happened,” the third “the result was read,”
the fourth “the result was recorded.” As you complete a stage, turn over its cup.
Cups only ever get turned right side up; none has a reset wire. These are records
of completed acts. A fourth cup up does not make a false conclusion true, and a
different experiment may need a different order.
    Two things to notice with the cups in front of you. Each cup by itself is exactly
the cup of Section 10: it reads yes or no, and once yes it stays yes. And four cups
were enough for five stages. Try it with three. You can’t: three cups that only ever
turn up, in order, give you at most four different arrangements along the way. I’ll
prove both of those in a minute, and the proof is about as short as the experiment.
    Now a harder strip. Some checks don’t line up. One person repeats the experi-
ment; another independently works through the calculation. Neither act includes
the other. Draw a diamond: neither at the bottom, experiment repeated on the left,
calculation checked on the right, both at the top. There are two ways up, and the
middle points don’t compare. That’s what a partial order allows. Put a cup on each
point except the bottom, one for the repeat, one for the calculation, one for both.

                                                    227
228   11 The whole direction


               Each cup is still a latch. The three cups tell you which acts have happened. They
               do not decide whether the experimental model or the calculation’s premises were
               appropriate.
                  Whatever the shape of the strip, a straight line of stages or a diamond or some-
               thing with a hundred points, I’ll call the set of places the record can be the direction,
               and each question “has the record reached at least this place?” a line across it. One
               line is one cup.


               11.2 The order, said exactly

              The strip and the diamond each come with an order you can see by looking: whether
              one place is at or below another. Said exactly, the order is a test. For any two places
              x and y it answers “is x at or below y?” with yes or no, and I write a yes as x ≤ y.
              The test has to obey two rules: every place is at or below itself, and if x ≤ y and
              y ≤ z then x ≤ z. An order that obeys just those two is called a preorder. If it also
              obeys a third rule, that x ≤ y and y ≤ x together force x = y, it’s a partial order,
              and that third rule is called antisymmetry. The two-point order, no below yes, is the
              cup. The whole numbers in their usual order are a straight strip that never ends.
                  The cups say the same thing in their own terms. For a place a, the cup for a asks
              “has the record reached at least a?”, so with the record at x it’s up exactly when
              a ≤ x, and I write its answer as [ a ≤ x ]. In the row of cups I said the cups together
              tell you which place the record is at. On the strip and the diamond you can check
              that with your eyes, and part (2) of Theorem 10.11 already proved it whenever the
              order is partial, though I hadn’t asked what in that proof was doing the work. My
              first guess was that it held for every order.
                  Why bother with the bare preorder at all, when every strip on the table is a
              partial order? Because I wanted to see what the third rule was doing, and the way
              to see what a rule does is to take it away. Take a preorder with two places, call them
              left and right, where each is at or below the other. There are two cups, one asking
              “at least left?” and one asking “at least right?”, and both are up at left and both are
              up at right. Look at the table and you can’t say where the record is. Now build a
              record that swaps between left and right on every single step and charges nothing.
              Every rule I’m about to state is satisfied. The record never drops below anywhere
              it was, because each place is at or below the other. No cup ever moves, so the toll
              in the next subsection has nothing to charge. The record moved on every step and
              nothing on the table noticed.
                                                              11.3 The toll, over the whole direction   229




Theorem 11.1 (The cups fix the place, and only with antisymmetry). (1) In a
partial order, if two places x and y leave the same cups up, [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y] for
every a, then x = y. (2) In a preorder that isn’t a partial order this can fail: there’s a
preorder with two different places that leave the same cups up, and a record over it,
driven by the computation and growing in that preorder, that changes on every step
while no cup moves.

Proof. (1) Look at the cup for x. It’s up when the record is at x, since x is at or below
itself, so it’s up at y too, and that says x ≤ y. The cup for y gives y ≤ x the same
way. Antisymmetry gives x = y. (2) Left and right above, with the record swapping
every step.
    So in a partial order the cups are the place, and in the preorder I built they aren’t.
That second half holds in every preorder that isn’t partial, by one line: if x ≤ y and
y ≤ x with x ̸= y, then a cup that’s up at either one is up at the other, by transitivity.
So the cups fix the place if and only if the order is partial. My first guess was right
on every strip I could draw, and it was right because of a rule I hadn’t noticed I was
leaning on. On a bare preorder, putting two places on the same rung tells the toll
not to care about moves between them, and it doesn’t. I don’t think that’s a defect.
It’s the order telling you what you agreed to count.


11.3 The toll, over the whole direction

One cup had one rule: the step that turns it right side up pays. Now there’s a row of
cups, or a diamond of them, and a single step can turn over several at once. Here’s
the rule I’d guess first, and it turns out to be the right one: a step that turns over any
cup pays at least one. A step that turns over three cups at once still only has to pay
one. The rule asks whether a step turned something over. It doesn’t ask how many.
   What does that rule buy? The same thing one cup bought. Take any run, and
suppose some cup is up at the end that was down at the start. Somewhere along
the run a step turned that cup over, and that step paid. So the run paid at least one.
Count the same way and you get more: the run paid at least once for every step that
turned anything over.
   Now look at what that argument didn’t use. It didn’t care whether the cups sat in
a row or a diamond or something with a hundred points. It didn’t care how many
there were. It didn’t even use the fact that cups never get turned back down. If
something could knock a cup back over, the argument still works, because all it
needs is the one step where that cup went up.
230   11 The whole direction


                 To say it exactly I want to put it in terms of places, so here’s the translation. The
              cup at a place a is up exactly when the record is at or above a. Say a step takes the
              record from x to y. The cup at y is up afterwards, since y is at or above itself, and
              it was down before exactly when y isn’t at or below x. And if y is at or below x,
              any cup that’s up at y was already up at x. So a step turns over some cup exactly
              when it lands somewhere that isn’t at or below where it started. The same reasoning
              says a run ends with some cup up that was down at the start exactly when it ends
              somewhere that isn’t at or below where it started.


              Theorem 11.2 (The toll over any direction). Take a machine whose record is a
              place in any preorder, and say a step turns a cup over when it takes the record from x
              to a place that isn’t at or below x. (1) Every step that turns a cup over costs at least
              one exactly when every run, from whatever state it starts, that ends somewhere not
              at or below its start costs at least one. (2) When that holds, a run costs at least the
              number of its steps that turn a cup over. (3) It holds exactly when every cup, on its
              own, pays the toll of Section 10: for every place a, a step that turns the cup at a from
              down to up costs at least one. The universal floor of Section 2 (Observation 2.1) is
              (1) with one cup.

               Proof. (1) and (2) are the walk above. For the other half of (1), a run of one step
               that turns a cup over ends somewhere not at or below its start. (3) is the translation
               above.
                   When the cups only ever go up, as on the strip and the diamond, a step that turns
               a cup over is just a step up.
                   That surprised me a little. I’d filed the floor away as a fact about one bit. Nothing
               in it was about one bit. It was about one cup going up, and anything you build out
               of cups has that.


               11.4 One line isn’t enough

               Now the payoff I promised at the start of this section. Could a cleverer single cup do
               the job of all four? One latch, and some decoding that reads the record’s place off
               the latch and whatever the machine shows? Section 10 already shut that door in the
               smallest case: over a machine with one visible state, a record that climbs through
               three places can’t be produced by one latch and a decoding, because one latch and
               one visible state make two outcomes and the record has three.
                   So try a second guess, closer to the cup’s own rule. The cup’s rule was “new value
               is old value or the event.” The obvious rule for a whole row is “new place is old
               place joined with the event’s place,” where joining two places means going to the
                                                                       11.4 One line isn’t enough   231


lowest place at or above both. On the row: the event names a place, and you turn
up every cup as far as that place. Here’s where it breaks. Take the strip 0 < 1 < 2, a
cup at 1 and a cup at 2, over a machine with one visible state, so the event has to be
one fixed place. Let the record jump from 0 straight to 2, turning up both cups in
one step, and stay put at 1 and at 2. From 0 the event has to turn up both cups, so
the fixed place is 2. From 1 the same event would turn up the second cup as well,
and the record stays at 1.
   What works is giving every cup its own event, and letting the event for a cup
look at where the record already is. That’s exactly what Theorem 10.11 said, and
this is why it had to say it. That leaves how many cups. In the row of cups I
asked you to try five stages with three and said you couldn’t. Theorem 10.11 (5)
already bounded the chain from above. Here’s the count behind that again, with the
matching example added, and with an arrangement of k cups read as a k-bit word, a
one for every cup that’s up.


Theorem 11.3 (Lines a direction needs). (1) A list of different arrangements of k
cups, each keeping up every cup the one before had up (a chain of different k-bit
words in which each word’s set bits are among the next word’s), has at most k + 1
members, and for every k there’s such a chain with exactly k + 1. So a straight strip
of n + 1 stages needs exactly n cups. (2) Over a machine with one visible state, take
the record on the strip 0 < 1 < 2 that jumps from 0 to 2 and stays put at 1 and at 2.
It grows and is driven by the computation, and no rule of the form “join the record
with a fixed place” reproduces its steps.

Proof. (1) Going from one arrangement to the next, which is a different one, turns
up at least one more cup, and there are k cups, so there are at most k steps and k + 1
arrangements. For the matching chain, take no cups up, then the first, then the first
two, and so on, packed to the left: that’s the row of cups. (2) Joining 0 with a fixed
place g gives g, and from 0 the step has to give 2, so g is 2. Joining 1 with 2 gives 2,
and from 1 the step has to stay at 1.
   So five stages need four cups. One won’t do it, and three won’t either. Cups that
only turn up, that is. An ordinary binary counter holds a thousand stages in ten bits,
because its bits go down as well as up, and the theorem says nothing against that.
The switch isn’t wrong. It’s the first line, and a straight strip with more than two
places needs more of them, exactly one fewer than it has stages. A direction that
branches needs at least as many cups as the steps in its longest strict climb, and it
can need more. Put three places above a bottom, none of them above another. The
longest climb is one step, and one cup can’t tell four places apart.
232   11 The whole direction


                  People got here before me, and from a direction I didn’t expect, which was
              programming for many processors at once. Lindsey Kuper and Ryan Newton’s LVars
              (2013), “lattice-based data structures for deterministic parallelism” in their own
              title, are memory cells whose value only climbs in an order, where a read can’t ask
              for the value and can only ask whether it has climbed past a threshold. That’s a
              cup. Writers running side by side can push the value up in different orders, and
              a threshold once passed stays passed. Their deterministic behaviour also depends
              on which reads and updates the language permits. Permanence alone would not
              do it: a program allowed to ask whether the cup is up yet could still see another
              writer’s timing. Amin Timany and Lars Birkedal (2021), coming at it from proofs
              about programs, show, as I read their paper, that any preorder at all can be carried
              as monotone ghost state in a program logic. That’s the closest thing I’ve found to
              somebody else arriving at the decomposition into lines.
                  The two rest on the same thing, a value that only climbs and a question that
              only asks whether it’s past a point, and they use it for opposite jobs. In an LVar the
              threshold read steers the program. Ghost state, as far as I understand the term,
              lives in the proof, and the running program never reads it. Here the record is never
              allowed to steer the base computation, so that particular restriction sits closer to the
              ghost state. Push on that and it gives a little: Section 5’s glance, the whole reason to
              keep a record, is a read. What keeps me on that side is that a glance worth trusting
              gives the answer the long way would have given. Their purposes aren’t mine. But
              the shape is theirs first. What I can’t find in either is a price on crossing a line.


               11.5 Why crossing a line has to cost
               Part I showed that the cup’s toll isn’t an arbitrary rule. It’s forced by three premises,
               and the argument that ties them together was the chairs: on a machine with finitely
               many states, the move that raises a record that goes up and stays up has to seat two
               possible states in one chair (Theorem 3.1), and a step that seats two in one chair
               is a step that forgets which one it came from. Does that survive the whole row of
               cups? Mostly, and the parts that don’t survive are the interesting ones.
                   The room needs a flag, and now there are many cups, so the first job is to pick
               one. My first guess was the cup for the place where the record starts. That goes
               nowhere: the starting state already has that cup up, so it’s already inside the room,
               and there’s nobody at the door. The cup that works is the one the step turns over,
               the cup for the place where the record lands. It’s up after the step, since a place is at
               or above itself, and it was down before, which is what turning a cup over means. So
               the room is every state with that landing cup up, and the state the step starts from
               is the one at the door. If the move keeps everybody in the room inside it and seats
               nobody twice, the insiders fill the inside chairs between them and there’s no chair
                                                                11.5 Why crossing a line has to cost   233


left for the newcomer. So one of two things happened. Either two states shared a
chair, or somebody who was in the room got moved out, which means their landing
cup went back down. I’ll call that second thing a revocation.


Theorem 11.4 (Turning a cup over merges). On a machine with finitely many states
and a record in any preorder: (1) if a move turns a cup over at some state and lands
the record at a place a, then either the move merges two states, or there’s a state
with the cup at a up that the same move takes to a state with the cup at a down,
which is a revocation; (2) if the record only grows, so that no cup ever goes back
down, the move merges; (3) if the record only grows, the toll holds exactly when
every move that turns a cup over at some state, and merges, costs at least one, so
merge pricing gives the toll.

Proof. (1) Gather every state with the cup at a up. There are finitely many. If the
move keeps each of them there and is injective, it maps that collection into itself
