without two landing on one, so it hits all of them, including the state it sends the
starting state to; injectivity then says the starting state was in the collection already,
and it wasn’t, because its cup at a was down. So either some state in the collection
has its cup at a knocked down, or the move isn’t injective. (2) Growth rules out the
knocking down. (3) If the toll holds, every move that turns a cup over somewhere
pays, merging or not. The other way, a move that turns a cup over merges by (2), so
the hypothesis charges it.
    It’s the room again, once for every cup.
    Each premise there can be knocked out, and I wanted to see each one go, because
a premise you’ve never seen fail is one you don’t understand yet.
    Knock out finiteness. Take the whole numbers as the states, which gives a row of
cups that never ends, and let the record be the state itself, one more on every step,
at no charge. Every step turns up one more cup. The step never merges anything:
different numbers go to different numbers. Merge pricing holds, because there are
no merges to price, and the toll fails on every single step. The room broke at the
one place it needed to be finite. Everybody moved one chair along, and there was
always another chair. That’s Charles Bennett’s 1973 construction in miniature: a
machine that keeps its whole history never has to forget, so it never has to merge. It
hasn’t got out of paying. Every step lands it in a chair nobody has sat in, and that’s
the room column. The toll fails here because merge pricing only charges merges
and this machine pays in room, which that price list doesn’t charge. Take the infinity
away and the room goes with it.
    Knock out growth. Take a two-state machine whose record flips back and forth
between two places, so a cup goes up on one step and gets knocked back down
234   11 The whole direction


              on the next. The two states just trade chairs, so nothing merges, and the price list
              is honest about merges. The step that turns the cup up pays nothing. It takes the
              other branch of (1): the state that had the cup up gets moved to where it’s down. It
              revokes.
                  Knock out the price on merges. A two-state machine that stamps every state
              with yes turns the cup up wherever it was down, merges at the stamp, and charges
              nothing. Of course the toll fails; nobody asked the merge to pay.


              Theorem 11.5 (Each premise does work). (1) There’s a machine with infinitely
              many states, a growing record and an honest merge price on which every step
              turns a cup over and the toll fails. (2) There’s a two-state machine with an honest
              merge price whose record doesn’t grow, which turns a cup over and fails the toll.
              (3) There’s a two-state machine with a growing record whose merges aren’t priced,
              which fails the toll.

               Proof. The three machines above, in order.
                  So the toll over a whole direction rests on exactly the three things the cup’s toll
               rested on: finitely many states, a record that doesn’t come down, and merges that
               pay. Nothing extra got smuggled in when one cup became a row, and nothing the
               one cup needed got left behind.
                  I’d half expected the diamond to need something new, some extra rule for the
               two middle cups that don’t compare. It didn’t. Every cup gets its own room, and
               every room is the old one.
CHAPTER 12




The shadow, exactly

Section 7 put the machine behind a window and asked what an outsider could tell.
It found that two states can look the same through the window and differ in what
matters, and that a price computed from the window can’t be exact if the window
has a collision (Observation 7.2). That was for one cup. With a whole row of cups
in hand I can ask the sharper version of the same question, which is also the one I
actually care about. Take the ordinary machine, the one with no cups and no ledger,
and let it look at itself. What’s the shape of everything it can’t see, and what does
the toll cost in terms of that shape?


12.1 The ordinary machine is a shadow
Take any machine with a record and a ledger, and sweep both off the table, the
cups and the counter. What’s left is a machine that steps the same way and knows
nothing about either, provided the step’s effect on everything else never depends on
the cups or the counter: sweeping them off has to commute with the step. A system
whose control reads its record or its ledger has no shadow in this sense. Where the
premise holds, call what’s left the shadow. Over any one state of the shadow there’s
a pile of full states, one for each place the record could be, with its own cups up, and
each value the ledger could hold, all of them casting that same shadow. Section 7
already called the pile over a point the fibre over it. The shadow is one particular
window, the one that shows everything except the cups and the ledger.
   The shadow has its own fibres, and every move has piles of its own too: the states
a move sends to one landing spot. I’ll call those the move’s landing piles. A fibre is
everything that looks the same before anybody moves. A landing pile is everything
that ends up in the same spot after one move. Keep the two kinds apart, because
the whole section turns on how they meet.


12.2 Pricing from the shadow

First the window question, over a whole row. A window price charges each step from
what the window shows before and after it. It meets the floor if it charges at least
one for every step that turns a cup over, and it’s exact if it also charges nothing for


                                                  235
236   12 The shadow, exactly


              any step that turns no cup over. A collision is two steps that look the same through
              the window, where one turns a cup over and the other doesn’t.
                 With one cup, the fix in Section 7 was to put the cup in the window. So my first
              guess for a row was that the window has to show some of the cups. Try the smallest
              version: a record in the whole numbers, and a window that shows only the first cup,
              the one that asks “at least one?” Let the record rise on some steps and hold still on
              others. Once it’s past one, that cup is up before and after both kinds of step, so a
              step that turned over a cup further along looks exactly like a step that turned over
              nothing. That’s a collision. So then, I thought, the window has to show every cup.
              That’s wrong too, from the other side. Take a record in the whole numbers with two
              moves, one that adds one and one that leaves it alone, and a window that shows
              only whether the record is even, which on the row is whether an even number of
              cups are up. You can’t read the record off that window, and no flat charge is exact,
              since some steps turn a cup over and some don’t. But the evenness changes on
              exactly the steps that turn a cup over, so charging one exactly when the evenness
              changed is exact.


              Theorem 12.1 (Window prices over a direction). (1) If the window has a collision,
              every window price that meets the floor charges at least one for some step that turns
              no cup over, so no window price is exact. (2) On a machine with finitely many states
              and moves, whose views can be told apart by a yes-or-no test, an exact window
              price exists exactly when the window has no collision. (3) Along any run, a window
              price that meets the floor charges at least the number of steps that turn no cup over
              but look, through the window, like a step that does. When it can be decided, for
              each pair of views, whether some step showing them turns a cup over, some window
              price meets the floor and, among the steps that turn no cup over, charges one on
              exactly those, so that number is the least overcharge. (4) A window can price exactly
              without showing where the record is: there’s a record in the whole numbers with a
              move that raises it and a move that leaves it alone, and a window that shows only
              whether the record is even; the evenness changes exactly on the rises, no charge
              that is the same for every step is exact, and charging one exactly when the evenness
              changes is exact, although no rule reads the record off the window. (5) There’s a
              record in the whole numbers and a window that shows only the one cup “at least
              one,” and that window has a collision.

              Proof. (1) The two colliding steps get the same bill. The floor makes it at least one
              because of the step that turns a cup over, and the other step pays it too. (2) Without
              a collision, “does some step that looks like this turn a cup over?” is a question
              about what the window shows, and on a finite machine you can answer it for every
                                                                12.3 What a priced move destroys   237


pair of views; charge one exactly when the answer is yes. (3) A step that turns no
cup over but looks like one that does gets that step’s bill, which is at least one by
(1)’s argument; add along the run. For the other half, charge one exactly when the
answer to (2)’s question is yes, which needs that question to be decidable, and count
the overcharge. (4) A rise changes the evenness and the other move doesn’t, so the
window sees exactly the steps that turn a cup over; a flat charge either bills nothing
for a rise or bills something for a step that turns nothing over; and 0 and 2 look the
same through the window. (5) The first cup, as above.
   Item (4) changed how I think about this. I’d assumed a window had to see the
cups to price them. It doesn’t. It has to see them move. A window that cannot tell
you your exact place, but detects every rise and every pause, can send the right bill
every time.


12.3 What a priced move destroys

Now the fibres. Part I showed that the move raising a permanent flag on a finite
machine seats two possible states in one chair, and Theorem 11.4 showed the same
for a step that turns any cup over, once the cups only go up. Which two? It matters
a great deal. If they’re in different shadow fibres, then the ordinary machine lost
a distinction too; the record may also differ between them. If they’re in the same
fibre, the ordinary machine lost nothing, and what got destroyed was only ever off
the table: two states that cast one shadow, told apart by their cups or their ledger,
crushed into one.
    My first guess was that it’s always the second kind, because the cups are where
everything happens. It isn’t always. It depends on whether the ordinary machine
forgets anything on its own.


Theorem 12.2 (The toll prices a collapse inside a fibre). On a machine with finitely
many states and a growing record: (1) a move that turns a cup over somewhere
sends two different states to one landing spot; (2) if the shadow exists, so that
sweeping commutes with the step, and the shadow’s step for that move forgets
nothing, sending different shadow states to different shadow states, then those two
states are in the same shadow fibre, and every landing pile of the move lies inside
one fibre; (3) without that premise it can fail: there’s a two-state machine whose
two states sit in different fibres and whose shadow step forgets, so the merge at the
step that turns the cup over lands two states from different fibres and no fibre loses
a point. (4) The halving price, which says a move of cost c shrinks any collection of
states by at most a factor of 2c , holds exactly when every landing pile has at most 2c
states, on a machine of any size.
238   12 The shadow, exactly


              Proof. (1) is the room of Theorem 11.4, with growth. (2) If two states land on one
              spot, their shadows land on one shadow spot, and the shadow’s step tells shadows
              apart, so the two states cast the same shadow to begin with. (3) The stamp of
              Theorem 11.5, with the record’s value also shown in the visible part, so each state is
              its own shadow: both states land on yes, and so do their shadows. (4) is the worst
              pile-up of Premise 3.4: one landing pile is a collection that lands on a single spot,
              and any collection is at most the number of spots it lands on times the biggest pile.
              Neither half needs the machine to be finite.
                 So on a machine with finitely many states and a record that only grows, when the
              ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll is a price on crushing a fibre: on taking
              two states that cast one shadow, which only what’s off the table told apart, and
              making them one. The last of those premises is the one I just showed you failing.


              12.4 How much gets destroyed, on average

              The halving price is a worst case. It prices the largest landing pile a move can have.
              The next question is the average one: if I don’t know which state the machine was
              in, cups and all, but I have some spread of chances over the states, how much do
              I lose, on average, about which state it was, once I know where it landed? That’s
              what Shannon’s conditional entropy measures (Section 3 built the entropy from
              scratch, so I won’t do it again here). Write it in bits.



              Theorem 12.3 (The halving price in bits bounds the average loss). Take any spread
              of non-negative weights over the states, uniform or not. (1) If every landing pile has
              at most N states, with N ≥ 1, the weighted conditional entropy of the state given its
              landing spot is at most the total weight times log2 N bits. (2) So on a machine with
              finitely many states and the halving price, that weighted information loss is at most
              its cost in bits times the total weight. For a probability distribution, the total weight
              is one and the average loss is at most the cost. (3) If a landing pile has 2c states, the
              uniform probability distribution on it loses exactly c bits and attains that bound. (4)
              On a machine of any size and for any spread, even one whose entropy is infinite,
              the same bound holds for every finite family of landing piles of a priced move.

              Proof. Inside one pile, Gibbs’s inequality: the entropy of a spread over n states is at
              most log2 n, with equality for the even spread. Add over the piles, weighting each
              by its share. The halving price makes n at most 2cost , and log2 2c = c.
                Where does it stop? My first guess was one place, a landing pile with infinitely
              many states, and that the average would blow up there right along with the worst
                                                            12.4 How much gets destroyed, on average   239


case. That’s half right, and the half that’s wrong surprised me. No finite charge
satisfying the halving price can price a move that sends infinitely many states to one
spot. The weaker merge price could still charge one; it does not measure the pile’s
size. But the average depends on the spread. Put weight 12 on the first state, 14 on
the next, 18 on the next, and so on, and the information lost by crushing the pile
never reaches 2 bits, however many of its states you count. Under that spread, a
two-bit information budget covers the average, though no finite budget covers the
worst case. So I went looking for a spread that does blow up, and it took a nastier
                                           k                          1
one: blocks of states, block k holding 22 states and a share (k+1)(     k +2)
                                                                              of the weight,
which adds up to one. Under that spread the loss grows past every bound. No finite
information budget covers that average loss.
     You can generate the first spread by tossing a fair coin until the first head. Zero
tails names state 0, one tail names state 1, and so on. State j has chance 2−( j+1) ,
and identifying that outcome takes j + 1 toss-results. Its entropy term is then
( j + 1)/2 j+1 . Add these by counting each possible toss position: the first is reached
with chance 1, the second with chance 1/2, the third with chance 1/4, and so on.
The total is 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + · · · = 2; every finite partial sum of the state terms is
smaller. Resetting all those outcomes to one box can lose only those two bits on
average, despite having infinitely many possible starts.
     For the block spread, split each block’s weight equally among its states. The
block weights sum to one because 1/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = 1/(k + 1) − 1/(k + 2).
                              k
Within block k, there are 22 equally likely choices, so just identifying a state within
that block contributes 2k /((k + 1)(k + 2)) to the average bits. Those contributions
grow without bound as k grows. Forgetting which block it was only adds to the loss.
And no finite worst-case price can handle an infinite pile: for any proposed cost c,
select 2c + 1 different states in it. They all land together, violating the halving rule’s
maximum of 2c .


Theorem 12.4 (An infinite pile). (1) A move that sends infinitely many states to
one spot isn’t priced by the halving price at any finite cost. (2) Under the halving
spread 2−( j+1) , the information lost by crushing the pile, counted over its first n
states, is less than 2 bits for every n. (3) Under the block spread, the information
lost grows past every bound, so no finite bit budget covers it.

Proof. The three computations above.
   And heat? Part I already said where the line is, and it’s the same line here.
Landauer’s principle, that crushing c bits’ worth of possibilities costs at least c kT ln 2
of heat on average, is a premise from physics, and a contested one (Section 3).
240   12 The shadow, exactly


              Nothing in this section proves anything about heat. What the counting does give
              is this: under that premise, on a machine with the halving price, a move’s cost
              priced at kT ln 2 per unit, times the weight of the piles, is always enough to cover
              the minimum the premise would demand, for every spread and every finite family
              of landing piles. If the premise falls, that sentence falls with it, and every theorem
              above it stands, because none of them used it.


              12.5 What the shadow is
              Put the two sections together and here’s the shape I’ve been circling since the
              Flatland night (the night a video about Flatland gave me the hunch behind this book;
              Section 24 tells it). The ordinary machine is the shadow of a machine with a row of
              cups beside it. Over every shadow state there’s a whole fibre, a pile of states that
              differ only in their cups and their ledger, and the ordinary machine can’t tell them
              apart, on a machine whose step never looks at the cups. On a machine that pays
              the toll, a step that turns a cup over costs, whichever cup it is and however many it
              turns, and on a machine with finitely many states whose record only grows, when
              the ordinary machine forgets nothing, what that cost pays for is exactly crushing
              two states of one fibre into one. A window can send the right bill without seeing the
              cups, if it sees them move. And on a machine with the halving price, where each
              unit of cost pays for at most one halving, the bill in bits, times the weight of the
              spread, is never less than what got crushed on average.
                  What I haven’t shown is that any of this is out there in the world, that nature
              keeps a direction like this over its own shadows. That’s a belief of mine, and nothing
              in this book proves it. What I’ve shown, and you can check, comes with its premises
              showing. A machine whose record is driven by the computation and climbs a partial
              order is a row of cups, one latch for every line. If it also has finitely many states,
              never lets the record come down, and prices its merges, it has to pay this way. And
              when its ordinary machine forgets nothing, what it pays for is exactly this. It’s less
              than the Flatland night promised me. It’s also the part of it that held when I pushed.


              12.6 Shortcuts

              Here’s the question every machine with a record has to face, and no amount of
              good design makes it go away. A cup is worth turning over because something later
              glances at it and doesn’t have to work the thing out again: that’s Section 5’s glance,
              reading a block’s bucket off the table without applying the rule from scratch. Call
              any move like that a shortcut, and call it sound when it gives the answer the long
              way would have given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning on what was done so
              nothing is redone, and the wall I’m about to show you doesn’t look at cost at all;
                                                                              12.6 Shortcuts   241


the next section says exactly what it does look at.) So: can a machine decide, from
inside, whether its own shortcuts are sound? That’s a wall, and it’s the same wall
Kurt Gödel and Alan Turing hit, and I have to show you that it’s there before I show
you anything that pretends to be on the other side of it.
CHAPTER 13




The diagonal

In Section 5 I said you’d watch the same move get made again and again as the
book went on: somebody says “everything is X,” it’s true enough to do real work
with, and then somebody draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now,
because Sections 10 to 12 just handed a record, and a whole direction of them, to
any system that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record
is for it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything
claim that, I have to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show
you exactly where a system with a record stands relative to the wall. Not on the far
side. Nobody’s on the far side. A record keeps a distinction and pays for it. What
it can’t do is the judging: no machine that can hand a program its own code, and
can run the flip of a verdict as one of its own programs, can sort all its programs,
from inside, by a question about what they do that some pass and some fail. So the
record carries a commitment, and somebody still has to make it.


13.1 Five names and a table

Do this first, with a pencil, because the whole family of arguments is this one trick
and you should own it. Write five friends’ names down the left of a page. Next
to each name, write a five-digit string of zeros and ones, anything you like. Now
build a new string: its first digit is the opposite of the first digit of the first row; its
second digit is the opposite of the second digit of the second row; and so on down
the diagonal. Look at what you’ve made. It differs from row one in position one,
from row two in position two, from every row at that row’s own position. So it’s
nobody’s string. Your table of five missed something.
    With five rows and five digits that’s a cute fact. Georg Cantor, a mathematician
working out how to compare infinite sets, made the point in 1891 that it works for
any list, however long, even infinite: hand me a complete list of all infinite strings
of two symbols, I’ll walk the diagonal flipping as I go, and I’ll hand you back a string
that’s on no row. So there is no complete list. There are more such strings than
there are places on any list, and that’s where “some infinities are bigger than others”
comes from. (He wrote the two symbols as m and w, where I’d write 0 and 1, and
that paper wasn’t even his first proof of the fact. The first was in 1874, by a harder


                                   242
                                                               13.2 The same move, again and again   243


road through the real numbers, and in 1891 he called the new one much simpler.
The diagonal was him finding the easy way.)
   Now look at what the argument did, because it’s going to do the same thing
again and again, in new clothes, and I want you to recognise it each time. (Not
every name below is a flipped diagonal in the table sense. Kleene’s theorem is the
tool that makes the diagonal buildable, Rice’s is the general form, the one from Ken
Thompson, who built the original Unix operating system at Bell Labs, is an attack
that uses the same trick, and the last, Lawvere’s, is the theorem that makes them all
one.) There was a table: rows are the things being listed, columns are questions,
each cell says “does row i do column j.” There was the diagonal: the cells where
a thing is asked about itself. There was a flip: something with no fixed point, like
turning yes into no, applied along the diagonal. And the thing that got refuted was
the assumed object, the complete list. Nothing outside the assumption was touched.
Table, diagonal, flip, and the assumption eats itself. Hold those four.


13.2 The same move, again and again

Russell, 1902, from Section 5: the collection of all collections that don’t contain
themselves. That’s Cantor’s flipped diagonal with “contains” as the table, and Russell
said as much, in The Principles of Mathematics in 1903. He got there, he wrote, by
running Cantor’s argument on a supposed collection of everything, which ought to
be the biggest collection there is. What got refuted was the assumed object, the
collection of everything, and Zermelo’s fix was to stop assuming it. This is the place
I promised in Section 5. Every reading in this book is a yes or no question on the
states of one machine, a collection cut out of a collection I was already given, and
never a sort of everything. When Part I asked for one state that codes every question
about the states (Section 1), the same flip refuted it.
     Jules Richard, a French mathematician who taught at the lycées of Tours, Dijon
and Châteauroux, took his doctorate in Paris in 1901 and wrote mostly on geometry.
In 1905, in a short note, a letter to the editor of a French science review, he
observed: some phrases (his were in French) define real numbers (“the ratio of a
circle’s circumference to its diameter”); there are only countably many phrases, so
list the numbers they define in order; run Cantor’s diagonal down their decimal
expansions and you get a real number no phrase defines, except that you just defined
it, in the phrase that describes the diagonal. The lesson I take from that one is the
lesson this whole section turns on: keep apart the language a system talks in and
the language you use to talk about it. Mix them and the diagonal bites you.
     Richard’s paradox has a cousin small enough to do at the table, and it comes
with a footnote I can’t resist. Russell, the first to put it in print, in 1906, credited it
to G. G. Berry, a junior librarian at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. A paradox that
244   13 The diagonal


              has outlived empires, and it came from the library desk. In the version in Principia
              Mathematica it’s about syllables. Take the phrase “the least integer not nameable
              in fewer than nineteen syllables.” There are only so many phrases shorter than
              nineteen syllables, so they name only so many numbers, so some least number is
              left over, and the phrase picks it out. Now count the phrase: the, least, in-te-ger, not,
              name-a-ble, in, few-er, than, nine-teen, syl-la-bles. Eighteen. In eighteen syllables it
              has named the number that can’t be named in fewer than nineteen. Same lesson as
              Richard’s, in a smaller coat: “nameable” is a word about the language, used inside
              the language, and that’s where the bite is.
                  Kurt Gödel, 1931, with an improvement in 1936 by Barkley Rosser, a logician
              who had studied under Alonzo Church at Princeton and whose trick lets the theorem
              assume only that the system is consistent: the big one, and I’ll say exactly what it
              says, because every word of it is carrying weight. Take any consistent formal system
              with a mechanically checkable list of axioms that can do a bit of arithmetic. Then
              there are sentences it can neither prove nor refute. The engine is a lemma that lets
              you build, for any property you can write down, a sentence that the system proves
              equivalent to that property holding of the sentence’s own code number. Apply it
              to “not provable” and you get a sentence equivalent, inside the system, to its own
              unprovability. Table: sentences by code. Diagonal: a sentence about its own code.
              Flip: provable to not-provable. Two cautions the Stanford Encyclopedia stresses,
              and I’ll repeat them. The sentence doesn’t literally “say” anything about itself. It’s
              provably equivalent to a claim about its code, which is less mystical and more exact.
              And the theorem doesn’t say the sentence is unknowable. It says this one system
              can’t settle it.
                  And how did the world take it? Mostly, at first, it didn’t. Gödel, twenty-four years
              old, announced the first theorem during a round-table discussion on the last day
              of a conference in Königsberg in September 1930, and by the account of Solomon
              Feferman, one of the editors of Gödel’s collected works, the room met it with general
              incomprehension. Except for one man. John von Neumann pulled Gödel aside
              to talk about it, kept thinking about it, and a couple of months later saw that the
              argument gave something more: a consistent system of this kind can’t prove its own
              consistency. He wrote to Gödel with it in a letter dated 20 November 1930. Gödel
              had already got there. His paper had reached the journal three days earlier, with
              that second theorem announced in it, and von Neumann left the credit with Gödel.
              It’s the “somebody got there first” shape from Section 4, with one difference: here
              the man who got there second was von Neumann.
                  Alan Turing, 1936. I’d always taken it that Turing proved the halting problem
              undecidable, and here I had to go and look. The set theorist Joel David Hamkins and
              his coauthor Theodor Nenu went back to the 1936 paper and report that the word
              “halting,” the modern statement, and the self-referential proof everyone teaches are
                                                              13.2 The same move, again and again   245


all, strictly speaking, absent from it. What Turing proved undecidable were two
other questions about his machines (whether a machine prints infinitely many digits;
whether it ever prints a given symbol). The second is equivalent to halting and the
first is strictly harder. So their answer cuts both ways, and they say so: Turing never
stated the halting problem, and he essentially proved it, because his second question
is a short translation away from it. The name came later. Martin Davis seems to
have been the first to write “halting problem,” in a book of 1958, and Stephen
Kleene had already stated the problem, without that name, in his 1952 textbook
Introduction to Metamathematics. The textbook version is still right as mathematics,
and here it is, on two index cards. Card A is the Checker: hand it any program
card and it announces “halts” or “runs forever.” Card B is the Contrarian: “Hand
me to the Checker. If it says I halt, run forever. If it says I run forever, stop.” Hand
B to A. Either answer is wrong. There’s no Checker. Table: programs by programs.
Diagonal: a program run on itself. Flip: halt to loop.
    Stephen Kleene, 1938, the logician whose textbook I just mentioned, and this is
the one that turns the paradox into a tool, so slow down. Everything above needs the
self-referring object to exist: Gödel’s sentence has to be buildable, the Contrarian has
to be able to “hand me to the Checker.” Kleene’s second recursion theorem says: for
any transformation of programs you can compute, there’s a program that behaves
exactly as if it had been handed its own source code. Any program may be written
as though it already had a copy of itself in hand. He stated it almost in passing, in a
paper on something else, and proved it in the last two lines of one of its sections.
I have that count from Yiannis Moschovakis, a logician at UCLA and Athens who
wrote a 2009 paper on it, expanded in the Bulletin of Symbolic Logic in 2010, called
“Kleene’s Amazing Second Recursion Theorem,” and he calls it a little gem. It’s the
reason “programs that print their own source” exist in every programming language
that can compute whatever a Turing machine can (they’re called quines, after a
philosopher I’ll come to in a moment; try “Print the following twice, the second
time in quotes: ‘Print the following twice, the second time in quotes:’ ” and obey it).
Self-reference in computation isn’t a paradox. It’s a construction. The paradoxes
happened only when someone assumed an unrestricted collection or language; the
theorem happens when you build the self-referrer honestly.
    And where does the word quine come from? Not from the philosopher himself.
Douglas Hofstadter coined it in 1979, in Gödel, Escher, Bach, in honour of Willard
Van Orman Quine, who had made a long study of self-reference that works indirectly.
Quine left a sentence you can take apart at the table, from a 1962 essay on paradox.
Here it is, all of it: “yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation” yields falsehood
when preceded by its quotation. Do what it says. Take the part in quotation marks,
put a quoted copy of it in front of itself, and look at what you’ve built: it’s the whole
sentence, word for word. So the sentence says that it itself is false. That’s the liar
246   13 The diagonal


              paradox, but look at how it got there: no “this sentence” anywhere, no pointing
              at itself, just an instruction to quote and copy, the same move as the print-twice
              instruction above. That’s Kleene’s trick in plain English, and it’s why the paradox
              and the tool look so alike. The paradox is what you get when the copy asserts
              something about its own truth. The tool is what you get when the copy just does
              something.
                  Henry Rice, 1953, whom you met briefly in Section 7: the general form. Any
              property that depends only on what a program does, whatever its text, and that’s
              true of some programs and false of others, has no algorithm that decides it for all
              programs. “Does this program halt” is one such property. “Does this program ever
              output 7” is another. “Does this program contain an if-statement” isn’t, because
              that’s about the text. One standard proof goes straight through Kleene.
                  And the one that’s actually an attack: Ken Thompson, in his Turing Award lecture,
              published in 1984. Build a compiler that, when it compiles the login program, plants
              a back door, and when it compiles a compiler, plants both habits into that one too.
              Then delete the trick from the source. The compiled compiler still carries it, and
              recompiling a clean source with the poisoned binary re-plants it, forever. Reading
              the source never reveals it. A locksmith teaches an apprentice to cut a spare for
              every town-hall key and to teach that to every apprentice they train, and never to
              write it in the manual; years later the manual is spotless and every locksmith in
              town cuts the spare. That’s the recursion theorem with a knife in it, and his moral
              was that you can’t trust code you didn’t write entirely yourself.
                  And Thompson wasn’t first either, and he said so. Pull on the lecture’s acknowl-
              edgment the way Section 14 pulls on Bitcoin’s footnotes: he writes that he first read
              of the possibility in an Air Force critique of the security of an early implementation
              of Multics, a time-sharing system from the 1960s, and that he couldn’t find a more
              specific reference to it, and he asks anyone who can to send him one. The critique is
              Paul Karger and Roger Schell’s 1974 security evaluation of Multics, which already
              described a trap door planted in a compiler that, because the compiler is written
              in its own language, keeps itself alive. So the knife was in the drawer ten years
              before the lecture was printed. Then the obvious next question: is there any way
              out, or is “trust no binary you didn’t build” the bottom? There’s a partial answer,
              and it took a while. David A. Wheeler, in a 2005 paper and a 2009 dissertation at
              George Mason University, worked out diverse double-compiling: compile the suspect
              compiler’s source with a second, independently made compiler, use the result to
              compile that source again, and compare the output bit for bit with the suspect binary.
              If they match, the binary really is what its source says, unless both compilers were
              poisoned in the same way. The trust doesn’t vanish. It moves, from one compiler to
              the claim that two unrelated ones weren’t rigged together. That’s the shape of every
                                                              13.3 Four things it doesn’t give you   247


stopping point in this book. You don’t reach the bottom. You reach a place where
you can say exactly what you’re trusting.
    Bill Lawvere, in 1969, proved a fixed-point theorem that, as I read it, makes all
of these one theorem in disguise: if a set can be mapped onto all the functions from
itself to some target, then every function on the target has a fixed point; so if the
target has a function with no fixed point (a flip), no such covering exists. Cantor,
Russell, Gödel, halting, as instances of one shape. Noson Yanofsky retold it in 2003
without the category theory. I mention it because “it’s the same wall” is a claim I
make below, and I want you to know it’s fair at the level of proof shape, and that
every instance has its own boundary of who counts as a decider, and that boundary
is exactly where most overclaims live.


13.3 Four things it doesn’t give you

Before I point this at a system with a record, here are four conclusions the theorem
doesn’t reach. Each one looks as if it follows, and I wanted to see exactly where
each one stops.
    “Gödel shows minds aren’t machines.” John Lucas, a philosopher who spent
thirty-six years as a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, argued it in 1961, in a paper
called “Minds, Machines and Gödel.” Roger Penrose, the Oxford mathematical
physicist who later shared a Nobel prize for his work on how black holes form,
revived it twice, in two books, The Emperor’s New Mind in 1989 and Shadows of
the Mind in 1994. I’m sure of who argued it and when. Whether they’re right is
the question, and the standard replies, as far as I can tell, have held up: the Gödel
sentence is true only if the system is consistent, so a human who “sees” its truth has
to know the system is consistent, which is the hard part; and nobody can build the
Gödel sentence of a system they can’t specify, so humans might be machines too
complicated to diagonalise. The theorem has a conditional in it and the argument
drops the conditional.
    And here’s the part that’s easy to miss: Gödel himself didn’t go as far as Lucas.
In a lecture on the day after Christmas in 1951, at a meeting of the American
Mathematical Society at Brown University, he drew from his own theorems only an
either-or. Either the human mind, even inside pure mathematics, infinitely surpasses
the powers of any finite machine, or there are problems about whole numbers, of
a certain simple kind, that no proof the human mind can conceive will ever settle.
Feferman, writing about that lecture, says Gödel privately believed the first half and
still stated only the disjunction, because he didn’t have a knock-down argument
against the machine side. Gödel wrote soon afterward that he meant to publish the
lecture, and never did; the text sat among his papers until after his death. So the
man whose theorem gets quoted for “minds aren’t machines” stated an either-or and
248   13 The diagonal


              left the deciding to whoever came next. That’s the conditional again, kept, by the
              person with the most right to drop it.
                  “Undecidable means unknowable.” Two senses share the word: a problem with
              no single algorithm correct on every instance, and a sentence independent of one
              particular system. Neither means nobody can know a given answer. Any single
              instance is decidable, trivially: for any one program, one of “say yes” and “say no” is
              right. What’s ruled out is one inside procedure that’s right on every case.
                  “Everything interesting is undecidable.” Rice is about behavioural properties over
              all programs. It says nothing against checking the text, nothing against deciding for
              specific programs, nothing against analyses allowed to say “I don’t know,” nothing
              against finite-state model checking or type checking. Real compilers and analysers
              live with Rice by being sound but incomplete, and what limits them in practice is
              mostly cost. The diagonal shapes them; it doesn’t stop them.
                  “Self-reference is a paradox.” It’s a theorem with a construction. Kleene, quines,
              Thompson.


              13.4 Now point it at the record
              Here’s the question Section 12 left open, with nothing in it but what Parts I and II
              have built. A system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event (Section 10);
              when the event is a certification, Section 8 said the reading, with its object and its
              paid event behind it, is what lets an auditor treat a claim as established, and for a
              claim that a shortcut is sound, that’s what makes the shortcut admissible. So: can a
              system like that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that correctly decides,
              for every program, “does this program admit a sound shortcut”? That would be
              autopilot. Hand it any program and it says yes or no, and it’s always right.
                   That’s the question in plain words, and the exact statement is narrower, so here it
              is before the proof. In the theorem, “admits a shortcut” is any property of programs
              with two features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there’s one
              program that has it and one that doesn’t. That’s all the argument gets to look at.
              The diagonal doesn’t see soundness. Each system that wants the wall picks its own
              property, and whether that property lines up with being entitled to soundness in
              Section 8’s sense is a separate fact about that system, checked one system at a time
              if it’s checked at all. A procedure that returns soundness records for some programs,
              or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not what the wall rules out.
                   So in the theorem “shortcut” is a label. The plain-words gloss at the end of
              Section 12, leaning on a record so the thing isn’t worked out again, is about how a
              program gets its answer, and how is exactly what extensionality throws away: the
              theorem only gets to see what programs do, and it treats any two that do the same
              as one. A question like “is there a cheaper program that gives the same answers?”
                                                                   13.4 Now point it at the record   249


isn’t the theorem’s question, and a wall for it would need a different theorem. The
nearest thing I know of is Manuel Blum’s speedup theorem, from 1967, and it goes
somewhere stranger: there are computable functions with no fastest program at all,
where every program for the function has another that’s faster on all but finitely
many inputs. That’s a fact about cost. It isn’t a wall about deciding, and nothing
in this book proves anything in that territory. Each use of the wall also names its
sameness. In the substrate theorem it’s the substrate’s own ≃; on L it’s what a term
computes; on the host of the small machine Part III builds, in Appendix D.4, it’s
the partial function a program computes (Theorem D.20). A particular notion of
shortcut gets the wall only after someone proves it behaves alike on programs that
are the same in the sense in use, and holds of one program and fails of another.
    The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I’ll give
you the premises because they’re the whole content. Suppose there were such a
decider, one that says yes exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the flip:
“if the decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut;
if it says no, behave like one that does.” If the system has a recursion theorem (a
program can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations
the system can carry out, and if “admits a shortcut” depends only on behaviour (two
programs that behave the same agree on it), and if there’s at least one program each
way, then there’s a program that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever
the decider says about it is wrong. Both cases close in a line each. This rules out a
decider that says yes if and only if a program admits a shortcut, for any substrate
with those parts. (A substrate here is the mathematical structure just described:
programs, a run that may fail to give back a state, a counter with a step relation it
never goes down along, an encoding of programs as data, a notion of “representable”
transformation, and the recursion theorem for those. Nothing about what the states
are made of. The smallest instance is the nat family below.) It’s Rice’s trick one floor
over, and I should be careful with that. Rice’s theorem is stated for the functions
Turing machines compute. This wall is the same diagonal with different premises: it
carries its own recursion theorem and its own list of representable transformations,
and it picks the property. So it isn’t a corollary of Rice as Rice stated it, and it
doesn’t show that any property is harder or easier to decide than classical halting.
And here’s something about its proof that I want you to have: it never touches the
counter, the toll, or the step relation. It uses the recursion theorem, representability
of the flip, the two witnesses, and extensionality, and nothing else.
    Here’s the setting and the wall, with every word pinned down so you can poke at
it.
250   13 The diagonal


              Definition 13.1 (Substrate). A substrate has a type of states, a type Prog of pro-
              grams, and a run map that takes a program and a state and either gives back a state
              or gives nothing. It has a counter µ on states and a step relation along which µ
              never decreases; an encoding enc of programs as states with a decoder dec such
              that dec(enc( p)) = p; and a predicate Rep on maps f : Prog → Prog, the transfor-
              mations the substrate counts as its own. Two programs are equivalent, p ≃ q, when
              run( p, s) = run(q, s) for every state s. The last condition is the recursion theorem:
              for every f with Rep( f ) there is a program p with p ≃ f ( p).


              Definition 13.2 (Shortcut predicate). A shortcut predicate on a substrate is a prop-
              erty A of programs with two programs y and n such that A(y) holds, A(n) fails,
              and A is extensional: p ≃ q implies A( p) ⇐⇒ A(q). For a Boolean function d on
              programs, its flip is f d ( p) = n if d( p) is true and f d ( p) = y if d( p) is false.



              Theorem 13.1 (No inside decider). Let a substrate carry a shortcut predicate A
              with witnesses y and n. Then there is no Boolean function d on programs such that
              Rep( f d ) holds and, for every program p, d( p) = true ⇐⇒ A( p).

              Proof. Suppose d is such a function. Since Rep( f d ), the recursion theorem gives
              a program p with p ≃ f d ( p). Split on d( p). If d( p) is true, then A( p) holds by
              correctness, and f d ( p) = n, so p ≃ n, and extensionality turns A( p) into A(n),
              which fails. If d( p) is false, then A( p) fails by correctness, and f d ( p) = y, so
              p ≃ y, and extensionality turns A(y) into A( p). Both cases are contradictions. The
              argument uses the recursion theorem once, the two witnesses, extensionality, and
              nothing about µ, the step relation, or the encoding.
                 So what’s ruled out is a d that says true exactly when A holds, and whose flip the
              substrate can represent. Every part I named is a premise, and the theorem covers
              every substrate that supplies them all.
                 So the wall is there. Now the honest part: who counts as a decider. The theorem
              rules out a decider whose flip the substrate can itself represent. It says nothing
              about a decider standing outside, and an outside decider can exist for the very same
              property, correct on every program. That’s the boundary of the sentence, and the
              boundary is Richard’s lesson: the language you talk about a system in is a different
              language from the one it talks in. You’ll see it in miniature in a minute, on the nat
              family, with a pencil.
                 Two forms of the wall live in this section, and they’re honest in different ways.
                 The nat family: a tiny substrate built so that program two is the Contrarian for a
              given candidate decider d, and for every d, d is wrong about program two. It’s a
                                                                   13.4 Now point it at the record   251


family, one instance per d, and its recursion theorem holds by construction. It’s the
index cards made formal and nothing more.


Theorem 13.2 (The nat family). Fix any Boolean function d on N. Let the substrate
Nd have programs and states N; program 0 returns 1, program 1 returns 0, program
2 returns 0 if d(2) is true and 1 if it is false, whatever the input state, and every
other program gives nothing; each program is encoded as itself; µ is constantly 0, so
any step relation will do; Rep( f ) holds when f ( p) = 1 for every p with d( p) true
and f ( p) = 0 for every other p; and A( p) holds when program p returns 1 on input
0. Then it is not the case that d( p) = true ⇐⇒ A( p) for every p.

Proof. The recursion theorem of Nd holds with the fixed witness 2: for a repre-
sentable f , f (2) is 1 or 0 according to d(2), and program 2 returns exactly what
that program returns. The witnesses for A are 0 and 1, and A is extensional because
it reads only what a program returns. The flip of d is representable by the definition
of Rep, so Theorem 13.1 applies to d itself. Directly: A(2) holds exactly when d(2)
is false.
    Now push on it once more, because the nat family shows the outside decider
in three lines, and you can do them yourself. Stand outside Nd , knowing d. Write
down a new decider e: say yes on program 0, say “not d(2)” on program 2, and
say no on everything else. Check it against A. Program 0 returns 1, so A(0) holds
and e says yes. Program 1 returns 0, so A(1) fails and e says no. Program 2 returns
1 exactly when d(2) is false, and that’s what e says. Every other program gives
nothing, so A fails and e says no. So e is right about every program. Does that break
the wall? No, and here’s the bit that matters: in Nd a flip is representable only if it
says 1 exactly where d says yes, so the flip of e is representable only if e and d agree
everywhere, and they disagree at program 2. The correct decider exists; its flip just
isn’t one of the substrate’s own moves. (It’s three lines and a pencil, and you just
did it.) Undecidable from inside and decided cleanly from outside, at the same time,
about the same property. That’s not a paradox. It’s two different people asking.
    And the one where the recursion theorem is proved from the reduction rules
rather than assumed: L, the weak call-by-value lambda calculus that Yannick Forster
and Gert Smolka presented in 2017 as a model of computation, and which a group
at Saarland has since used as the seed of a whole library of undecidable problems.
Here L is built from its reduction rules. The recursion theorem is proved, Rice’s
theorem follows, halting follows, and the diagonal is reproved in the shape of the
substrate theorem, for any property of programs that depends only on what they
compute and that holds of one program and fails of another. The statement mentions
no shortcut. That’s the diagonal for one fixed model, and I don’t plug L into the
252   13 The diagonal


              substrate theorem. I don’t, and here’s why: a substrate’s run map has to answer,
              with a state or with nothing, and to read L’s evaluation that way you’d have to settle,
              for every term, whether it ever reaches a value. That’s a decision made from outside
              L, and L is in this book as the model where nothing is taken from outside. So on L I
              run the argument again from scratch instead of applying the general one. Both are
              true; they’re different sentences.
                  Here’s what that string of words means, because L is the strangest thing in this
              book that computes, and the smallest. The lambda calculus is Alonzo Church’s,
              from the 1930s, and it’s a programming language with one idea in it: functions. A
              term is one of three things. A variable. A function, written λ followed by its body,
              the body saying what to do with whatever you hand it. Or one term applied to
              another, written side by side. Running a program is one move, over and over: when
              a function meets an argument, put the argument into the body where the variable
              was. No numbers, no memory, no instructions, and in 1937 Turing published a
              proof that it computes exactly what his machines compute. “Weak call-by-value” is
              two house rules about the order of moves: an argument is run down to a finished
              function (a value) before it’s put in, and nothing runs inside a function that hasn’t
              been handed anything yet. Variables are written as numbers counting how many
              λs back they were bound (a trick of Nicolaas de Bruijn; it means two variables can
              never get mixed up by sharing a name), and a term is closed when every variable in
              it is bound inside it, so it leans on nothing outside. Last piece: to hand a program to
              a program, L needs a way to write any term as data, the way a program’s source is
              a string you can pass around. The one used here is the Scott encoding, named for
              Dana Scott, a student of Church’s who went on to build mathematical models of the
              lambda calculus itself. As far as I can trace it, the encoding first appeared in lecture
              notes of his from Berkeley in 1962 that he never published, as a way to write data;
              Torben Mogensen carried it over to lambda terms themselves in 1992, and that’s the
              form used here. All you need about it is that every term t gets one code, written ⌜t⌝,
              and the code is itself a closed value. Two tools get built on top of that in the proof:
              a quoting term Q that takes the code of a term to the code of that code (a program
              that prints its own source needs exactly this move), and a fixed-point combinator, a
              term that lets a function call itself, which is how Q works its way through a code of
              any size.
                  Do two of these on paper before I give you the general rule. Write I = λx.x: its
              instruction is “return whatever you were handed.” Hand I its own card and you
              get I I → I, and it stops. Now write D = λx.x x: “make two copies of what you
              were handed and apply the first to the second.” Hand it its own card. Putting D in
              for both copies of x gives D D → D D. You’re back at exactly the same instruction
              and argument, so the rule never finishes. Both arguments were already functions,
                                                                   13.4 Now point it at the record   253


so neither example sneaks any work under a function that hasn’t been handed
anything.
    The variable numbers are what keep the copying from getting confused. In
λx.λy.x, the last x points past the nearest λ (the one for y) to the one before it, so
its number is 1; in λx.λy.y the last variable has number 0. Rename x and y however
you like and neither recipe changes. The codes below are a way of putting a whole
recipe on a card that another recipe can read.

Definition 13.3 (L, as built here). A term of L is a variable (a de Bruijn number),
an application s t, or an abstraction λs; the values are the abstractions. One step
is weak call-by-value, left to right: (λb) v steps to b with v substituted when v is a
value, a step inside the left part of an application is a step of the application, and
so is a step inside the right part once the left part is a value. A term s evaluates to
v when s reaches v in some number of steps and v is a value; p ≡ q when p and q
evaluate to the same values. Every term t has a code ⌜t⌝, its Scott encoding, which
is a closed value. A map f on terms is L-computable when some closed value s has
s ⌜ p⌝ ≡ f ( p) for every p. A term D decides a property P of terms when, for every p,
D ⌜ p⌝ reaches λλ.1 (true) if P( p) holds and λλ.0 (false) if it fails. P is extensional
when p ≡ q and P( p) give P(q).



Theorem 13.3 (Recursion, Rice and halting for L). (1) For every closed value s
there is a closed term t that reaches s ⌜t⌝; so every L-computable f has a term p
with p ≡ f ( p). (2) Let P be extensional, with P(y) and not P(n) for closed terms
y and n. Then no closed term decides P. (3) No closed term decides halting, the
property of evaluating to some value.

Proof. (1) A closed quoting term Q takes ⌜t⌝ to the code of ⌜t⌝; its construc-
tors, recursive program and terminating induction are given in Appendix J. A
closed term mkapp takes two codes to the code of their application. Let A =
λx. s (mkapp x ( Q x )) and t = A ⌜ A⌝. One step gives s (mkapp ⌜ A⌝ ( Q ⌜ A⌝)),
and the argument reduces to ⌜ A ⌜ A⌝⌝ = ⌜t⌝. For the second half, take s
computing f ; then t ≡ s ⌜t⌝ ≡ f (t). (2) Given a closed decider D, the flip
λx. D x (λ_. n) (λ_. y) (λz.z) is a closed value; on the code of p it reaches n when D
answers true and y when D answers false. Take its t from (1). If P(t), then t ≡ n
and P(n); if not, t ≡ y and P(t). Both are contradictions. (3) Halting is extensional;
apply (2) with y = λz.z and n = (λx. x x )(λx. x x ), which steps only to itself and so
never reaches a value.
254   13 The diagonal


                  The construction in that proof isn’t mine, and the credit belongs right here.
              Forster and Smolka’s L development of 2017 has the Scott encoding of terms,
              a closed quoting term with exactly this specification, the code of a term to the
              code of its code, and a fixed point built the same way: their t is C ⌜C⌝ with
              C = λx. s ( A x ( Q x )), so their C is my A, and their A, which builds the code of an
              application, is my mkapp. They say they follow the proof in the Dutch logician Henk
              Barendregt’s textbook on the lambda calculus (1984), where statement (1) is the
              full lambda calculus’s second fixed-point theorem, and part (2) is what they call
              Scott’s theorem. The term construction is given in Appendix J; the route is theirs,
              and Barendregt’s before them.
                  That’s the wall on paper, on a family built to fit it, and on one outside model. The
              machine built in Part III (Section 15) fills in this same shape: on its host machine, the
              one the universal program of Appendix D.1 runs on, which has a counter for every
              whole number, programs are numbers, Kleene’s recursion theorem is a theorem, and
              so is Rice’s, and the fixed point can be taken to agree on what the program computes
              and also on the ledger and the flag (Appendix D.4).
                  Here’s the picture all of that fills in, lined up against Turing’s, one column per
              axis.

               Time axis                                   Structural axis
               counts: steps                               counts: µ
               asks: does it halt?                         asks: does it admit the shortcut?
               the wall: no Turing machine decides halting the wall: no decider whose flip is
                                                           representable, under a recursion theorem


                  Read the table as two uses of one diagonal, each under its own premises. That’s
              all it says. The structural wall never uses µ; the µ entry only says what that axis
              counts. The nat result is a family indexed by the candidate decider, and L’s results
              are about one fixed model and properties that mention no shortcut. Neither hands
              you a second fixed undecidable problem, and neither separates Turing degrees: a
              property can sit behind the wall from inside and be decided cleanly from outside,
              as the pencil argument on Nd showed. And “admits the shortcut” in the right-hand
              column is the theorem’s sense, any behavioural property with a yes and a no. “Has
              a cheaper way to the same answer” is a second question, and the column has no
              wall for it.


              13.5 How to kill it
              Three ways, and I mean them as instructions.
                                                                  13.6 What this does to the book   255


   One: produce, for some substrate with a shortcut predicate, a decider whose flip
the substrate can represent and that’s correct on every program. That breaks the
generic proof at a named step, and I’ve named the steps.
   Two: for the nat family, produce a d that correctly decides the predicate of the
substrate built from d.
   Three: for L, produce a closed term that decides some extensional property
holding of one closed term and failing of another. That breaks Rice’s theorem for L,
whose proof rests on the reduction rules.
   An outside decider alone doesn’t count against any of the three; the pencil
argument on Nd is why.


13.6 What this does to the book

It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system
with a record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that’s a wall, the
same wall, and I showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record can do,
which is the thing Part II has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut
with its receipt, so that the question “was this earned” is answered by an event you
can point at. No decider has to exist for that, which is lucky, because on a system
with a recursion theorem no inside one can. The diagonal says such a system can’t
automate the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a
no. The latch says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a
record does the second.
    The diagonal has a famous cousin that seems like it ought to bite a record too, so
let me walk right up to it. Gödel’s second theorem says a consistent system strong
enough for arithmetic can’t prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician
answering another logician’s question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system
proves “if this is provable, it’s true,” it already proves the thing itself. So can a
record vouch for itself, and does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops
it, since a record looked like a system talking about itself. Here’s where I landed
instead, and mostly it’s a relief. Hold two things side by side: “there’s a receipt for
this somewhere,” and the receipt in your hand. Löb’s theorem is about provability,
the bare claim that some proof exists, the receipt somewhere. A record of the kind
this book keeps is a different animal: an event, a check of some claim that passed,
a commitment to it, and a certificate, at a definite step of the run. The receipt in
your hand. It doesn’t say which claim or which step, as the two runs near the end
of Section 15, under what the small machine doesn’t do, show; it says the event
happened. Sergei Artemov, a logician who comes back in Section 14, drew exactly
that line in 2001, between implicit provability (“there is a proof”) and explicit
evidence (“this is a proof”). As I read him, for explicit evidence the reflection step
256   13 The diagonal


              “if this is a proof of F, then F” is harmless, while for the bare “there is a proof” it’s
              what Gödel and Löb forbid. Why, in my words: a receipt in your hand you can look
              at, and a receipt somewhere you take on the system’s own word. A record sits on
              the explicit side.
                   Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it.
              Its trust rests on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from
              outside the machine. That’s where I chose to stop this machine’s chain of reasons.
              Gödel’s second theorem does not forbid a machine from checking a proof about a
              checker. What it limits is a system’s ability to prove its own consistency, when the
              system is strong enough to do arithmetic and its axioms can be listed by a machine.
              Eliezer Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff’s 2013 draft on agents that trust their
              own rewrites describes a related problem, the Löbian obstacle: how an agent can
              justify trust in a successor’s proofs. That’s a cousin of this question, and it doesn’t
              settle it, and it doesn’t make my design the only one possible. So I didn’t get rid of
              the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the machine and handed it to whoever
              reads the record.
                   One more thing follows from the same picture, by a short argument. Can a record
              rest on itself, the way the sentence “this sentence is certified” would like to? Not if
              it’s earned and permanent. The check that a certificate stands on happened while
              the record was still down, because the record goes up only after that check passes,
              and once up it never comes back down. So no claim whose truth needs the record
              already up can be the claim a certificate stands on. Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory of
              truth calls a sentence like that, one that only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and
              earned records are grounded in his sense: every one bottoms out in a check that
              didn’t lean on it. Caspar Oesterheld’s 2019 work on programs that cooperate by
              simulating each other needed a grounding step of the same kind to stop an infinite
              regress. I haven’t written this argument out anywhere else; the claim is exactly what
              this paragraph says, and it’s short enough to check by hand.
                   One last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and conflating them
              is the easiest way to misread this book. There’s a second wall, nothing to do with
              the diagonal. It’s Section 7’s kind of wall, a window with a colliding pair in it.
              Two states that differ in their certification reading can look identical through a
              window that doesn’t show that reading, the stamp inside the closed drawer and
              the drawer opened and shut, and then no function of the window recovers the
              reading (Theorem 7.1: a decoder has to give one answer on everything the window
              lumps together). That’s missing information. Nothing about it is undecidable; it
              holds for finite things with nothing to compute; and it sits beside Rice. None of
              Rice is underneath it. The property the diagonal uses (any behavioural property
              of programs with a yes and a no) is a different kind of thing from the reading the
              window hides, and nothing here says the two are the same. Two walls, two axes.
                                                                13.6 What this does to the book   257


The diagonal is about what no inside procedure can decide. The window is about
what no outside observer can see. I’ll need both, and I’ll try not to call one by the
other’s name again. The machine I build later has a colliding pair of exactly that
kind (Theorem 15.14).

          Part III is step four, the sharpest case. A record that a claim was checked and
      closed is a distinction that stays, so it pays the bill of Part I, and it’s the case where
      you can point at the kept 0 and at what it cost. It starts with what established means,
      and why two computers with the same bits can differ in it. Then it builds a machine
      for it: an ordinary computer of two counters, with a record layer on top whose flag
      is the blank cell, six kinds of instruction in all. The step that raises the flag is the
      write of a 0, a merge in the record layer, and that’s why it’s charged; the order the
      step enforces, check, then commit, then certify, is what makes this record’s raise
      mean a claim held. That’s certification, and it’s the layer this part adds to the bar
      Part II set. Then how far the machine reaches, the real systems that already put a
      price on a write, the thesis about which kept distinction is worth paying for, and
      what the machine’s counter has to do with heat. The ordinary computer’s own steps
      merge too (counting a counter down lands two states on one), and like every step
      that changes something they dissipate when they happen; the ledger leaves them
      alone.
CHAPTER 14




What established means

Parts I and II were about any kept distinction at all. This chapter picks one: the
distinction between an answer that was checked and the same answer that wasn’t.
It’s the case the first pages of the book called the sharpest, and here’s why it’s sharp.
The two answers are the same bits. Everything that differs is in what was kept.


14.1 Two computers that end up the same

You met these two computers in one paragraph at the start of the book. Here they
are slowly: what an ordinary computer does with the bill of Part I, and why that
matters to anybody who isn’t a physicist.
    Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand
numbers.
    The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until
nothing is out of order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to
back and checks that every number is no bigger than the one after it. That check
could have failed. It passes. Then it tidies up after itself, wipes its scratch work,
and leaves the sorted list in memory. (That check compares neighbours, so what it
settles is that the output is in order. That the output holds your thousand numbers
and no others is a second claim, and it would take a second check comparing the
output with the input. When I say sorted below, I mean in order.)
    The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into
it earlier, same thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.
    Now wait until both are done and look inside. Same bits in memory. Same bits on
the screen. Set it up right, which you can, and it’s the same everything, down to the
last bit. The first compared the entries and checked their order. The second loaded
the same answer without doing either. The list is in order in both; the difference is
what each run did with it. Wheel them out on a cart, swap them, wheel them back,
and ask me which is which. I can’t tell you. You can’t tell me. And the part that bugs
me most: built the ordinary way, neither machine can tell you either.
    Sure, while they ran they were different. One did thousands of comparisons, the
other did a copy. But the runs are over and the runs are gone, and nobody was being
sloppy. Ordinary computers are built to forget how their bits got there, on purpose.


                                                  261
262   14 What established means


              That’s Landauer’s sentence about standardizing signals, from the start of the book,
              and why he said it costs heat.
                   Who cares? Anybody who’s been handed a sheet that says “all tests passed.”
              Anybody who’s looked at an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the
              same whether somebody checked the brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit,
              a proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of itself: every one of them is a pile
              of bits that could have come out of either computer, and the question that matters
              is the one the bits can’t answer. Did something establish this, or did it just print it?
              I’ll come back to every one of those later in this chapter and say which of them this
              book actually helps with. Fair warning: fewer than you’d hope.
                   I’m going to call the first run’s relation to that answer established: it checked the
              order of this list. The second run has the answer without that relation. The list’s
              order is there either way. What can a machine keep of the difference between the
              runs? The rest of this chapter takes that question apart.
                   Here’s why it belongs in a book about a 0. A record that the check ran would be
              a distinction that stays, a 0 in some cell that says “checked,” and it would pay the
              same bill the 0 pays. Ordinary computers don’t write that one.


              14.2 Look harder

              The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don’t look at the end, look at everything.
              So make the computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of
              a warehouse, every wire a lamp that’s lit or dark, every switch something you can
              walk up to and touch. Nothing hidden in a chip too small to see. Put both of them
              side by side and walk the floor.
                  While they run, sure, you’d see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting up,
              comparing and swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish. The comparing
              wing goes dark. Now walk the floor and look at every single lamp. The sorted list is
              spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both, the same pattern, and everything else is
              dark in both, because both cleaned up.
                  There is no lamp anywhere that says “a check ran here and passed.” Not hidden.
              Not encrypted. Just not there. You can see everything there is, and the thing I’m
              after isn’t one of the things there is. Looking harder doesn’t help, because the
              problem isn’t that you can’t see enough. It’s that nothing was kept.
                  That’s the shape I want you to carry through the rest: the problem was never
              visibility. It’s keeping.
                                                                            14.3 So keep the trace   263


14.3 So keep the trace
Then the fix is obvious, isn’t it? Don’t let the run go. Keep the trace: every
comparison, every swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens.
Wheel the computers out on the cart and back, read the traces, and you’ll know
which one sorted. Problem solved?
    It’s the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart,
because “just keep the trace” has three things wrong with it, and each one is a piece
of what comes later.
    First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into
the second machine can type a trace in too: “compared, swapped, checked, passed,”
a few thousand lines of it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program
is something the program produced, and the machine running the program doesn’t
care whether it’s true. So keeping the trace doesn’t answer the question. It moves it.
Did something establish this trace, or did it just print it?
    Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don’t let
the program write its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace, one
step at a time, as the steps actually happen, so nothing a program does can add a
line that didn’t happen or erase one that did. Airplanes do a version of this. Flight
recorders go back to a prototype David Warren built in Melbourne in the 1950s.
He was an Australian scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories, working
on jet fuel, and after a string of unexplained airliner crashes he wanted a box that
would hold the instrument readings and the voices in the cockpit for whoever came
looking afterwards; I know his story from museum and encyclopedia accounts, and I
haven’t read his own report. The recorders that came out of that idea are fed by the
aircraft’s own instruments. Nobody’s account of events goes into them. And they’re
built to survive the crash, so the investigators don’t have to depend on anyone’s
memory of what happened. That’s the right shape, and it isn’t mine. Later in this
