chapter it gets its name from computer security, a reference monitor, and I’ll say
outright that a machine built that way would be doing what this book describes.
What the book adds is narrower than a rulebook for everything underneath. It’s
about the records that go up and never come back down: what that something has
to keep for good, and what keeping it costs.
    Third, you can’t keep all of it. A full trace grows with every step and never
stops growing, and a machine with finite memory runs out. Even the flight recorder
doesn’t keep everything. The cockpit voice recorder is a loop. I went looking for how
long the loop is, and it has kept growing: for decades it held the last thirty minutes,
an American rule in 2008 raised that to at least two hours, and the international
rules ask big airliners built since 2021 to carry twenty-five hours. Whatever the
264   14 What established means


              length, everything older gets recorded over. Every real machine that keeps a trace
              keeps a window of it, or a fingerprint of it, and forgets the content.
                  The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of
              the trace into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you’ve got a hash
              chain. The timestamps of Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, two cryptographers at
              Bellcore whose story comes later in this chapter, work that way; so do the audit logs
              the cryptographers Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do
              the measurement registers in the security chip a lot of computers carry, the TPM. A
              running program can only extend those registers, folding a new measurement in. It
              can’t write a value of its own into them, and the ones that matter here start over only
              at the next reboot. That really does keep something about the whole trace in a few
              dozen bytes. But look at what it keeps. It keeps a binding. The content isn’t in it: to
              read the history you still need the trace stored somewhere, and the fingerprint only
              tells you whether a copy somebody hands you is the one that went in. The binding
              holds only because nobody knows how to find two traces with the same fingerprint,
              which is a bet on how hard a search is. No law of nature backs it. That part isn’t only
              my opinion. The computer scientists Moni Naor and Guy Rothblum proved a sharp
              version of it in 2005, and they even call the thing a fingerprint: keep a small private
              fingerprint of a big file somebody else stores, check the file by reading only a little
              of it, and against an opponent with unlimited computing the size of the fingerprint
              times the amount you read has to be on the order of the whole file. Do even slightly
              better than that against an opponent with limited computing, and you’ve shown
              that one-way functions exist, which is the hardness bet in its barest form. Their
              setting is a stored file. A growing trace is a different setting, but it’s the same bet,
              with its terms written down. And squeezing traces that keep growing into a fixed
              number of bits has to land many traces on one fingerprint. That’s a merge, hidden
              behind how hard it is to find which traces share a seat. It’s the same merge as the
              people and chairs of Part I (Section 3), where four people have to sit in three chairs.
              Fingerprints are great. They’re not a way out of forgetting. They’re a very clever
              way of forgetting.
                  So the real question was never “save everything.” It’s this: what’s the smallest
              thing worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it cost? The answer this book
              ends up with is the commitment, in the database’s sense, a question closed, and
              the trace drops away. (The cryptographer’s sealed envelope also goes by the name
              commitment. It’s a different thing, and both come up later.) Not every comparison
              the sort made. Just the one fact that a check of this very claim passed and the
              question got closed. And here’s the part that matters most: keeping even that one
              fact for good isn’t free on any machine. It’s paid by forgetting something somewhere
              else or by taking room the machine never gets back, and on a finite machine the
                                                                 14.4 Computed, stored, established   265


room runs out, so it’s the forgetting. That’s the chairs again, and Part I counted the
room.
    So the premise was never that computers can’t keep records. They keep records
all day. It’s that nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid
for, permanent, or earned, and those three come in at different places, so here’s
where. Paid for is the model’s one rule: in the Thiele Machine, the step that raises
the record has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the one the chairs need,
and one of the conditions Part II puts on a record. Earned, meaning a check of this
very claim passed first, isn’t in the model’s core at all. It’s what the step of the small
machine in the next chapter enforces, proved for that machine and every program
on it run from a clean start. One more word rides along with permanent, and it’ll
come up when I line my record up against other people’s: dated. A record that goes
up and stays up went up at one particular step of the run and not another, even
though the record doesn’t write down which step. So dated, in this book, means
it has a place in the run’s history. Carrying a timestamp is something else, and my
record doesn’t do it. A machine that charges one mark for every step it takes meets
the first rule, and the charging does nothing toward the others, and I’ll keep pointing
that out.


14.4 Computed, stored, established

Three words that get used like they’re one.
    Computed is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The
second didn’t.
    Stored is about the bits. Both machines stored it.
    Established is neither, and that’s the whole problem. It isn’t the steps, because
they’re gone. It isn’t the bits, because they’re identical. It’s something like this: the
first machine has a right to lean on “this list is sorted,” because it ran a test that
could have failed, the test passed, the test was about this very list, and then the
question got closed. The second machine has the same sentence and no right to it.
That’s a true fact about the two of them, and it’s written down nowhere, in either
one. (Whose right, strictly? A machine doesn’t lean on anything, any more than a
filing cabinet does. It’s the right of whoever reads the first machine to lean on what
it says, and the machine is where the grounds for that right would have to be kept.
“The machine has a right” is shorter, so I’ll keep saying it, and now you know what
it’s short for.)
    Four words I’ll hold still from here on. A check is the test, the thing that could
say no. A commit is the closing, the question shut for good, about that edition of
that thing. The record is whatever stays behind to say so. And established is all three,
about one thing. That’s the working sense. The book cashes it at three depths: a
266   14 What established means


              paid closing in the bare model; an object with a checked relation and a paid event,
              in Part II (Section 8); and the whole chain on the small machine, in the next chapter.
              Each place says which one it means.
                  Which raises a fair question. What if the second machine, handed the typed-in
              list, runs the check on it? Then it has established that the list is sorted. Full stop. It
              didn’t do the sorting and it doesn’t need to. The line I’m drawing is between checked
              and unchecked. Whether the list was computed or copied doesn’t enter into it, and
              “without doing either” up there was about the copier that never looked. So whatever
              this book ends up counting, it isn’t how hard anybody worked.
                  People say “a right to lean on it” about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so
              I had to find out whether this one was anything. I went looking. Here’s what I ran
              into.


              14.5 The clerk who forgets everything
              The picture of a computer I used in Section 5 is a person with a pencil, a strip of
              paper and a short list of rules. So I went back to the source, Alan Turing’s 1936
              paper, to see how far he actually takes it.
                  He takes it a long way. Back then a “computer” was a job, a human doing sums
              by hand, and Turing modelled that person. He’s careful with the person’s mind:
              whatever the clerk knows, beyond a handful of states, has to go down on the paper.
              Then he goes all the way. He imagines the clerk getting up, walking off, forgetting
              everything, and coming back later. To pick up where he left off, the clerk leaves
              himself “a note of instructions,” and Turing says that note is the clerk’s state of mind,
              as far as the computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note. That’s the whole
              state.
                  My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn’t write
              the note. Somebody slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right
              instructions. He comes back, reads it, carries on, and every mark he makes from
              then on is exactly what he’d have made if he’d written it himself. Turing’s model
              can’t tell the clerk who did the work from the clerk who was handed a note saying
              he did. It was never asked to. Turing wanted something you could check without
              crawling into anybody’s head, and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets.
              That’s why the paper still works ninety years later. It’s also why there’s no place in it
              for the thing I’m after.
                  So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets
              everything he was doing, and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.
                  And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is
              exactly the kind I can’t leave alone: who were those clerks? Real people. In the late
              1800s the Harvard Observatory hired rooms full of women to do the arithmetic of
                                                            14.6 Information doesn’t have it either   267


the sky, cataloguing stars by hand for a fraction of a man’s wage, and some of them
made discoveries of their own, Henrietta Leavitt’s way of telling how far away a star
is among them. (I took the wages and the discoveries from Dava Sobel’s history
of those women, and from the historians at the American Institute of Physics, who
put the men’s hourly pay at nearly five times the women’s.) Rooms like that ran
artillery tables in both world wars; that part I took from David Alan Grier’s history
of human computers. So when Turing modelled “the computer,” he was modelling
somebody’s actual afternoon. Does that change the argument? Not a bit. But it
changes the picture, for me anyway: the sticky note was always a person trusting
another person’s work, and the question of whether the work behind it was really
done is older than any machine.


14.6 Information doesn’t have it either

My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn’t. That one
died fast. Claude Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says
on his first page that the meaning of a message is “irrelevant to the engineering
problem.” His number measures how many messages you could have sent. What the
one you sent did is outside it, which is exactly right for building telephone lines and
exactly no help to me. Same message out of the same set, same number, for both
computers. He’d give them the same number if one of them got hit by lightning and
came out right by luck.
    Fine, forget the set and look at the one message. In the 1960s three people, sepa-
rately, worked out how to measure the information in one string: Ray Solomonoff,
an American who was after a theory of guessing what comes next from what came
before; Andrei Kolmogorov, the great Soviet mathematician; and Gregory Chaitin,
an Argentine-American mathematician who later worked at IBM. Their measure is
the length of the shortest program that prints the string. Same two computers, same
string, same number. And then there’s the thing in that theory I keep going back
to and standing on, to see if it creaks. Running a program can’t add this kind of
information. What comes out can’t hold more than what went in plus the program,
give or take a little. Leonid Levin, who studied under Kolmogorov in Moscow and
later left the Soviet Union to teach at Boston University, proved a general version of
this, and he has a one-liner for it that’s too good not to repeat: you can torture an
uninformed witness all you want, you won’t get information about the crime.
    Which means, as far as information goes, sorting your list told you nothing. The
sorted list holds nothing that “your list, plus the word sort” didn’t already hold.
    Logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of knowing, the
one the Finnish philosopher Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property
people call logical omniscience: if you know some facts, you automatically know
268   14 What established means


              everything that follows from them. So by that logic, once you knew every number
              on your list, you already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem
              himself, in the same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fixes read
              like a pile until I asked each one the same thing: when it lets you write known next
              to “sorted,” what does it make you write in the margin? Hintikka’s margin is empty.
              Each fix writes one thing there.
                  The fix that comes closest to me is from 1995, by Sergei Artemov, a logician
              at the City University of New York who studied under that same Kolmogorov (the
              1995 report came out of Cornell). He wanted a logic that could name the proof
              itself. What I think he’s saying: you only get to know a thing if you’ve built an
              actual justification for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That’s a
              reason traveling with the claim, which is almost a record. Only almost, because
              it’s a way of writing things down and reasoning about them, and nothing in his
              margin says the reason was ever run, or when. People have taught it to count, too:
              Ho Ngoc Duc, a logician at Leipzig, in 1997, made knowing take reasoning steps,
              and Artemov and Roman Kuznets, a logician then at Bern, in 2014, asked how big
              a justification can get before knowing by it stops being feasible (Part II weighed
              both properly, in Section 8). I took those for rivals at first. As I read them now, Duc
              counts the steps the knower takes and Artemov and Kuznets weigh what you’d hand
              somebody to check it, one distance from two ends. It has a computational side, too:
              Francisco Bavera and Eduardo Bonelli, two Argentine computer scientists who work
              on what programming languages mean, in 2018 turned justification logic into a
              lambda calculus whose terms carry, and can inspect, the history of the computation
              that made them, and Samuel Bucheli, Meghdad Ghari and Thomas Studer, three
              logicians, Studer the head of the logic group at Bern, put justifications on a time
              line in 2017, where they persist and change.
                  Line that up against the margin this book wants: earned, paid for, permanent,
              dated. Artemov’s reason is nearly earned, the steps and the sizes are prices, the time
              line is a date. Their time line keeps its dates. Mine is dated only in the execution
              history: the raise happened at a definite step, and the record doesn’t keep the step
              number. What none of it has is the closing of a question as a step with a price. Their
              prices are on reasoning, and the Bern justifications change, the one thing a closed
              question doesn’t do. Push on mine, though, and it gives twice. Artemov’s margin
              holds the reason itself, and mine only says a check passed. And their prices grow
              with how hard the thing was to know. This book charges the step that raises the
              record, and how long the checking took never enters it, so for a measure of effort,
              read theirs.
                  So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about
              knowing, say the same thing: the sort added nothing.
                                                                        14.7 The guy who got closest   269


   And yet you know something after the sort that you didn’t before. You can read
the smallest number off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened.
That’s the clue, and it’s the first solid thing I’ve got: whatever established is, it isn’t
new bits. It’s the same bits, settled: a question sorted into yes and no, with yes made
to stay. The 0 again, about a claim.


14.7 The guy who got closest
Somebody had that clue before me, and on that clue he’s the closest neighbour I’ve
found, so he gets the most room and the hardest push.
    Bennett again, the one from the chairs and the demon, wrote a paper in 1988
that starts where I just ended up: information isn’t the same as value. His example
is an almanac of where the moon and planets will be every day for a hundred years.
It has no more information than the equations it was calculated from, but it saves
you doing the calculating. So the value is the work. He called the amount of work a
thing carries its depth.
    Was this my idea, already done, by a guy at IBM? The only way to find out was
to find where it parts from mine, because if I couldn’t find that place I’d just be
renaming his idea. And it’s one word: plausibly. Depth is the amount of work a
thing was plausibly made with. Bennett says straight out that you can’t know how a
message actually came to be; for all you know it came from flipping coins. Depth is
read off the finished thing, the way a fossil’s age is read off the fossil.
    Bring the two computers back. The sorted list in the first one has some depth.
The identical list in the second has exactly the same depth, because depth looks at
the list and nothing else. A photocopy of a deep thing is just as deep. Depth tells
you what work a plausible way of making the thing would take. It’s not a record
that this machine did it, and it’s not a receipt for what doing it cost.
    So Bennett’s standing right next to the line, on the other side of it, and as far as I
can tell he got his own question right. He asked how much work a thing embodies.
I’m asking who has the right to lean on it and what they paid to get there. His
answer lives in the object. Mine, if I’ve got one, has to live in the machine.


14.8 Statues that walk off

If it isn’t in the information, maybe it’s in the knowing, so I went and read the
philosophers. And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference
between having the right answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.
    Plato’s version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor
Daedalus made statues so lifelike they’d walk off if you didn’t tie them down. Plato
says true opinions are like that: they wander off, and they’re not worth much until
270   14 What established means


              you tie them down with the reason why. Once they’re tied down, they’re knowledge,
              and they stay put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge that stays. Of
              everybody I’d have bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn’t on the list.
                  Then in 1963 Edmund Gettier, whose trap Part II played with cups (Section 8),
              broke the tidy version in three pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job.
              Smith has good reason to think Jones will get it, and he’s counted the coins in
              Jones’s pocket: ten. So Smith figures, with good reason, that the man who’ll get
              the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then Smith gets the job, and, unknown to him,
              Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. True, believed, backed by a reason. Not
              knowledge. He was right by luck, because his reason was about the wrong pocket.
                  That’s the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and committing
              to a claim about another is right by luck. So whatever a machine commits to, the
              check underneath has to be about this very claim, and I’d better say exactly what
              that means, because it carries a lot of weight later.
                  A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property
              the commit names. A cousin of that property won’t do. It tests that property on the
              same thing the commit names, and the thing next to it won’t do either. Nothing has
              written to that thing between the check and the commit, so it’s still the same edition
              the check looked at. And the check is honest: it says yes when the property is true
              and no when it isn’t, on every value it could ever be handed, this one and all the
              others. Break the first three and you’re Smith with his ten coins. Break the fourth
              and the check is just a rubber stamp. The next chapter builds a machine whose step
              won’t let a commit through unless the first three hold, and whose checks come with
              a proof of the fourth.
                  Two notes on those four, because they matter later. The fourth asks for more
              than it needs. To rule out luck, a check only has to never say yes when the property
              is false; saying yes every time it’s true is a bonus. And the third is a very old bug in
              computing wearing Gettier’s coat. Security people call it time-of-check-to-time-of-
              use: check a file, use it, and something swaps the file in between (Matt Bishop and
              Michael Dilger, two computer security researchers at the University of California,
              Davis, wrote up how to hunt for it in 1996). Databases guard against the same thing
              by making sure, just before a commit, that nothing they read has been written since;
              H. T. Kung and John Robinson, two computer scientists at Carnegie-Mellon, called
              that optimistic concurrency control in 1981. A philosopher’s pocket and a sysadmin’s
              race condition, same bug. One limit, said now: a machine can only promise “nothing
              has written to that thing” about its own memory; for brake pads or a voter roll the
              third condition becomes a premise about whoever measured (Section 17).
                  And here’s where I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious
              next question is: does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch
              is “no false steps in the reasoning”: Smith’s mistake was believing Jones would get
                                                              14.9 What “could have failed” means   271


the job, so rule that out. Then a philosopher named Alvin Goldman came back with
barns, and he credits the barns to Carl Ginet, another philosopher working on what
it takes to know something. You’re driving through a county that, unknown to you,
is full of fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look like the real thing. You
look at the one real barn in the county and think “that’s a barn.” True. Believed.
Good reason, your own eyes, and no false step anywhere. And still you were lucky:
if you’d glanced at the next one over you’d have believed the same thing and been
wrong. Every patch gets a new barn, and as far as I can tell the arguing hasn’t
stopped. Which tells me something I’ll keep: whether a check was good isn’t only
about this one case. It’s about what the check would have done on the cases next
door. Hold on to that, because it’s the next section.


14.9 What “could have failed” means

I keep saying the first machine’s test could have failed. Take that apart, because it’s
the piece everything else hangs off.
    The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass.
So in what sense could it have failed? By “could have failed” I mean this: hand
the checking stage an out-of-order candidate output and it says no. I do not mean
hand the whole sorter an unsorted input; putting that input in order is its job. The
relevant counterfactual is a defective candidate reaching the checker. An ordinary
unsorted input reaching the sorter isn’t it. Chance has nothing to do with it. The
copier that never checks has no corresponding rejection.
    Here’s the shape. A check is a question asked of every possible input, and it splits
them into two piles: the ones it says yes to and the ones it says no to. “Could have
failed” just means the no pile isn’t empty. A check that says yes to everything has
an empty no pile, and it distinguishes no inputs, however long it runs and however
official it looks. It can still be sound, when its property holds of everything, and
then it’s sound and tells you nothing you didn’t have. A philosopher, Robert Nozick,
made a version of this a condition for knowing, in 1981: you know a thing only if,
had it been false, you wouldn’t believe it.
    Push on it once more, because this is where it really gives. “Could have failed” is
a fact about the procedure, about what the check would have done on other lists.
It isn’t a fact about the end state at all. Look at the first machine’s memory when
it’s done: a sorted list. Nothing in those bits says “and whatever made me would
have caught a mistake.” That’s the warehouse again, every lamp visible and none of
them saying it. The one thing that makes the first machine’s answer worth more
is exactly the kind of thing those bits can’t hold: the copier ends with the same
bits, and neither machine kept anything else. An end state can hold more than the
answer, and the only way a machine can own this is to write something down at
272   14 What established means


              the moment the check passes, and to have that something mean what it says. More
              than anything else in this chapter, that’s why I ended up needing a record. A better
              answer wouldn’t have done it. Even then the record only carries half of it. It can say
              a check ran on an edition and passed. That the check would have said no on a bad
              list is a fact about the checker, and that half rides on a proof about the checker; on
              this machine that proof sits outside, and whoever reads the record reads and accepts
              it. Where that kind of chain of reasons stops is the swamp of the philosopher Karl
              Popper, a little further down.
                  One more thing that tripped me up and then didn’t. Rig a check to pass only on
              your one list. Is that cheating? No. It’s a perfectly honest check of a different claim,
              “this is that exact list,” and it has a big no pile: every other list. It establishes exactly
              that and nothing more. What a check establishes is whatever it’s honest about.
                  Put that next to the empty no pile and the two fit together: a check establishes
              what it’s honest about, and a check with an empty no pile is honest only about what
              you already had. One thing I’ll say plainly now, so it doesn’t ambush you in the next
              chapter: the small machine I build there doesn’t police this. Its step makes sure
              a commit was checked first, about the same thing, by a checker proved honest. It
              doesn’t stop you asking a question that can’t come out no, like “is this number at
              least zero.” Ask one and the whole chain runs, three marks paid, and nothing is
              established but the chain. The certificate I show off there asks one that can fail.


              14.10 Settled, whether it’s true or not

              Then I ran into Charles Sanders Peirce again, the one from Section 5, in an 1877
              essay called “The Fixation of Belief.” He was asking what inquiry is for, and his
              answer named the thing I’d been running together without noticing. The point of
              inquiry, he says, is to get out of doubt and settle on a belief. And when someone
              objects that surely what people want is a true belief, he answers like a guy who’s
              watched a lot of arguments end: “as soon as a firm belief is reached we are entirely
              satisfied, whether the belief be true or false.”
                  That’s funny, and then it isn’t, because he’s right. Settling and being right are two
              different events. A question can be closed on a wrong answer, and once it’s closed it
              acts closed. Peirce cares a lot about which ways of settling hold up (science wins,
              for him, because it has to answer to something outside any one person), but the
              settling itself, the question snapping shut, is there every time, and it never comes
              with a guarantee.
                  Karl Popper came at it from the other side. He was a philosopher from Vienna
              asking what separates science from everything else, and in his 1934 book, the one
              that came into English as The Logic of Scientific Discovery, he says every test has to
              stop somewhere, at some statement somebody decides to accept, and nothing in
                                                              14.10 Settled, whether it’s true or not   273


the evidence forces you to stop there instead of one step further. You stop when
you’re satisfied. His picture is a jury: the verdict is a decision about what happened,
and the jury deciding it doesn’t make it true. Science, for him, is a building on piles
driven into a swamp, and the piles stop where somebody’s satisfied they’ll hold.
They never reach firm ground.
    A real jury has a problem Popper doesn’t mention, because a real jury is twelve
people. Lewis Kornhauser and Lawrence Sager, two law professors writing in the
Yale Law Journal, noticed in 1986 that a court that votes by majority on each premise
of a case and also on the verdict can end up contradicting itself: every judge is
consistent, and the court isn’t. Christian List and Philip Pettit, two philosophers
writing in Economics and Philosophy, turned that in 2002 into a theorem. No way of
combining people’s yes-or-no judgments on connected questions meets a short list of
conditions that each look harmless on their own and always hands back a consistent,
complete group judgment. A group’s settling is a rule’s settling, and which rule you
pick decides which of the honest settlings sticks. Try the problem with three ballots
and a rule that a payment is due only if a contract was signed and a deadline was
missed. One voter says yes to both, one says signed but not missed, and one says
missed but not signed. Each voter applies the rule consistently. Count separately: a
majority says signed, a majority says missed, and a majority says no payment. You
can point to the disagreement on the paper without blaming any one voter’s logic.
I haven’t tried to put a group on the machine, and that’s where I’d expect the first
wall to be.
    Popper’s swamp sent me further down, because it’s the oldest problem in the
book and it doesn’t have a bottom. Ask why you believe something and you get a
reason. Ask why you believe the reason and you get another one. Sextus Empiricus,
a skeptic and doctor who lived probably in the second or third century and whose
whole method was holding off judgment, wrote down the ancient version, credited
to someone called Agrippa, and in 1968 the German philosopher Hans Albert, who
with Popper led the school called critical rationalism, gave it a name with a joke in
it: the Münchhausen trilemma, after the baron who claimed he pulled himself out of
a swamp by his own hair. Every chain of reasons does one of three things. It goes on
forever. It loops back on itself. Or it stops somewhere, because somebody decided it
stops. People have argued for a very long time about which of the three to live with.
So “when do I actually know, and when am I done checking?” doesn’t get a clean
answer from anybody. What you can do is be honest about where you stopped and
why. That’s a lot of what the rest of this book is: every place it stops is written down,
with its name on it, so you can decide whether you’d have stopped there too.
    Lay Peirce and Popper on top of each other and here’s what shows through. The
check is one act. The stopping is another. The check can run as long as you like and
it never makes you stop; at some point something decides, and the deciding is its
274   14 What established means


              own event. That’s the second machine’s whole trick: it skipped the check and kept
              the answer.
                 And a logician said the part I didn’t expect a logician to say. Per Martin-Löf, a
              Swedish logician, says a proof is an act, and once it’s done it’s done. His words,
              from lectures he gave in Siena in 1983: “a proof is, not an object, but an act . . .
              Only secondarily, and irrevocably, does it become the act that has been performed.”
              That took me a few reads, and the tenses unlocked it: first the act being done, then,
              for good, the act that has been done. You could say that’s true of everything that
              ever happened. Fine. But it’s the two computers again: the first machine’s check
              happened, irrevocably, and the machine right now carries no trace of it. The past
              can’t be undone. The record of it can be lost, unless something keeps one. That gap
              is where this book lives.
                 Then the intuitionists got there first, which by now I should’ve expected. The
              Dutch mathematician L. E. J. Brouwer, who held that a mathematical truth is some-
              thing a mind makes evident, argued from 1948 on about an idealised mathematician
              working in stages, the creating subject. The people after him only came clear to me
              once I sorted them by three words: the act, the object, and the trace the act leaves
              behind, which Martin-Löf’s sentence has no room for. The logician Georg Kreisel
              (1967), Austrian-born and then at Stanford, wrote it down as a formula: the subject
              has evidence for A at stage n. That’s a trace, something you can come back and
              ask about after the act is over. Anne Troelstra (1969), a Dutch logician who studied
              under Brouwer’s student Arend Heyting and became one of the leading authorities
              on intuitionism, added that the subject never forgets what it has made evident, so
              the trace never fades. That’s how Mark van Atten (2018), a philosopher in Paris
              who has spent years on Brouwer, credits it; the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on
              intuitionism lists the never-forgets axiom among Kreisel’s own, and I haven’t settled
              which is right. Van Atten, going through the whole history, reads the formula as “by
              stage n the Creating Subject has made A evident.” Look at the tense. Has made is
              Martin-Löf’s “the act that has been performed,” reached from the other end. And
              look at what that carries. It’s tied to a stage; at any stage you can ask whether it’s
              happened yet; it never goes away; and it’s never wrong. Van Atten even says the
              subject can’t just accept a proof handed to it from outside: it has to go through the
              steps and rebuild the evidence itself. That’s the copier who runs the check. And then
              there’s Göran Sundholm, a philosopher of logic at Leiden. He has long kept a proof
              as an act apart from a proof as an object (1998), and, as I understand his work,
              apart from its trace as well. In a 2014 paper he worked through how Brouwer’s
              theory of the creating subject sits beside the thesis that every effective procedure is
              a program, which is the side this book’s machines live on. I know that second paper
              only by what it sets out to do, so I lean on it lightly.
                                                                               14.11 Not a switch   275


    Set their trace beside my record and the columns nearly all fill: their stage is my
dated, their never forgetting my permanent, their never wrong my earned. Their
stage is written into the trace, though, and my dated is only a step in the run that
the record doesn’t keep. The empty one is the price, and I think I see why. A mind
with unlimited memory pays for never forgetting in room, and an idealised mind
has room to burn, so nobody sends it a bill. On a finite machine the room runs
out, and writing a record that stays up forces the instruction to merge some states.
Charging for that merge is a further premise. Those are the chairs of Part I, and the
price rule Part I sets. So it’s the closest thing to my established that I’ve found. The
formula is around sixty years old, and the idea under it, Brouwer’s creating subject,
is older than that. Push on my side from theirs, though, and it gives twice. Van
Atten’s subject won’t take a proof from outside, and my machine takes exactly one:
its checker is trusted on a proof about the checker that somebody did outside every
run. And their evidence is never wrong because, for Brouwer, made evident is what
true means. Mine is right only as far as that checker is honest. Where they differ,
the difference is honest: their subject is an idealised mind with unlimited time and
memory, and mine is a machine with a finite table that establishes only the claims
its program checks.


14.11 Not a switch

So far I’ve been talking about established as if it were a light switch: on or off, the
first computer on and the second one off. That bothered me the whole time I was
writing it, and for a while I couldn’t say why. It felt too small, the way a word can be
technically right and still not cover what you’re pointing at. I don’t trust that feeling
on its own, because I’ve had it plenty of times about things that turned out to be
nothing. So I went looking for something outside my own head that would either
give the feeling something to stand on or show me I was imagining it.
    I didn’t know what I was looking for, at first, beyond a rough shape: two things
that look exactly the same and differ in how far something about them has been
settled. So I started collecting anything that seemed to have that shape, and most
of what I collected fell apart as soon as I looked at it closely. How each one fell
apart taught me more than the thing itself did, so I’ll go through them in the order it
happened. Every story below is the version I could piece together from the records I
could reach, and where I couldn’t reach a record I’ll say so. Check me.
    The first batch was all hidden things. A pea under one of three cups. A tree, whose
age you can’t see from the outside. A forged painting that looks right until somebody
tests the paint. A glass of gas, where the thermometer shows one temperature and
underneath there are uncountably many arrangements of molecules that would all
show the same reading. Plato’s prisoners in the cave, who see shadows on a wall.
276   14 What established means


              The things casting them stay behind their backs (Section 7 tells their story). Every
              one of these looked promising for about a minute. Then I noticed they all fail the
              same way: look harder and the hidden thing shows up. Lift the cup. Cut the trunk
              and count the rings. Run the paint test. Look at the molecules, at least in principle.
              Turn around in the cave. In each case the hidden part is a fact about the object that
              better eyes could find. That isn’t what the two computers have. You can see every
              lamp in the warehouse and not find the check.
                  That failure gave me the first real tool I had, and it’s a crude one. Give an
              observer perfect vision of the visible thing, as much detail as they want, and ask
              whether they could read the difference off it. If they could, it’s something hidden,
              and that’s not what I’m after. If they couldn’t, it might be. I should say how much
              weight that test holds. It’s a judgment, and I’m the one making it, so it’s a way of
              sorting my own examples, not a verdict. If you find a case it sorts wrongly, that tells
              me something about the test and about me.
                  The second batch got past that test and failed a different way. A clock face reads
              three o’clock and doesn’t show how many days have gone by; no amount of staring
              at the face tells you. And a computer can keep a complete history of what it did. It’s
              Bennett’s 1973 machine from the chairs, and the story is better than I let on there.
              Landauer had argued in 1961 that real computers throw information away all the
              time, and Bennett, his younger colleague, asked whether they had to. His answer, in
              a 1973 paper, was no. A machine can write down every step it takes, copy out its
              answer, and then run itself backward, retracing its steps and wiping the history as it
              goes, until it holds only the input and the answer and has never thrown anything
              away. It takes a forward run, a copy of the answer and a backward run, with scratch
              space for the history. Bennett thanks Landauer at the end for raising the question in
              the first place, which I like: the man whose principle says forgetting costs is the one
              who asked whether you could get out of it. The history it keeps along the way is
              real extra information, sitting out where anyone could read it, so it isn’t a hidden
              fact of the first batch’s kind. Keeping it and unwinding it throws nothing away, so
              by Landauer’s own reckoning there’s no floor under its heat: run it slowly and the
              heat comes down as near nothing as you like, though never to nothing for a run
              that finishes, which Part I proved for Bennett’s own model (Theorem 1.8). What it
              spends besides is room, the scratch space the history sits in. And it can be run back
              down. Neither of those two, the keeping that merges nothing and the running back
              down, fits what happened to the first computer, which did something that can’t be
              undone and paid for it. If the standing I’m after could be put up and taken back
              down with nothing kept and no floor either way, it would just be bookkeeping. So
              that batch taught me what else I needed: something that only moves one way, and
              costs something to move.
                                                                              14.11 Not a switch   277


   The third batch came closer and still didn’t quite fit. In 1782 James Six, a
Canterbury man from a family of silk weavers who had taken up watching the
weather, described a thermometer for the Royal Society. He wanted the coldest
moment of every night, and he’d found that with an ordinary thermometer you had
to be looking at it when it happened, because, in his words, “if it be not immediately
noticed, it can never after be known.” His fix was two little steel markers in the
tube that the column pushes up and that stay where they’re left. That’s a record
that only moves one way. Then he spoils it, for my purposes, in the same paper:
every evening he wrote the numbers down and slid the markers back with a magnet,
“without a touch.” A record anybody can reset with a magnet is not the thing I’m
after, and Six would have been the first to say he wasn’t the first to build one; his
paper lists the thermometers that came before his.
   Since 1996, starting with oral polio vaccine, vials of vaccine bought through
UNICEF have carried a small sticker, a square inside a circle. The square darkens as
the vial takes on heat, and the darkening doesn’t undo when the vial cools. When
the square matches the circle, the vaccine shouldn’t be used. One way, and it can’t
be reset. But it’s chemistry. The reaction in the square is chosen to run about as
fast as the vaccine itself spoils, so the sticker is really reading the vaccine’s own
condition by a proxy. Nobody ran a check; the heat did.
   Closer still: the International Vocabulary of Metrology, the reference book that
measurement laboratories work from, says a result is traceable only if it “can be
related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each
contributing to the measurement uncertainty.” That’s a lot like what I want, a
standing earned by checks, step by step. The same document adds that traceability
“does not ensure . . . that there is an absence of mistakes,” which is the true-versus-
established split written into an international standard. And the top of the chain
wasn’t fixed either. When the official copies of the kilogram were compared with
the prototype in 1889, 1946 and around 1991, they had drifted apart by tens
of micrograms over the century, and nobody can say which one moved, because
the prototype was the kilogram. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined by fixing a
constant of nature, Planck’s constant, instead. A chain like that can also lapse: if the
calibrations stop, new results stop being traceable. The standing has to be kept up,
which my record doesn’t.
   The rules of chess have the shape too. The current Laws of Chess of FIDE, the
international chess federation, say in Article 9.2.3 that two positions are the same
only if “the same player has the move, pieces of the same kind and colour occupy
the same squares and the possible moves of all the pieces of both players are the
same,” and they spell out that a king that could still castle and one that can’t are in
different positions, even on an identical board. That passes the perfect-vision test.
And the official text says why it passes: the castling right changes which moves are
278   14 What established means


              legal. So the hidden part steers the game: it decides what can happen next. In the
              machine I’m building, the flag never steers. It never touches the ordinary computing
              at all. The table and the trap that give the flag its meaning do steer, and Section 15
              says where that line falls. Each of these got something right and missed something
              else.
                  The one that fit best, and I want to say clearly that it only fit best among the ones
              I found, was the standing of a mathematical statement. Here’s how it went for one
              statement, as far as I could follow it.
                  In 1611 Johannes Kepler, the emperor’s mathematician in Prague, owed his
              friend and patron Johann Matthäus Wackher von Wackenfels a New Year’s present
              and, he said, had nothing to give. Wackher, Kepler wrote, loved nothing, for the
              games you can play with the word, so Kepler wrote him a little pamphlet about the
              nearest thing to nothing he could find, a snowflake, which had landed on his coat
              as he crossed a bridge. Why six corners? Kepler couldn’t say in the end. But along
              the way he stacked equal balls in his head and asserted that one way of stacking
              them, the way grocers stack oranges, packs them so tightly that, in the 1966 English
              translation, “in no other arrangement could more pellets be stuffed into the same
              container.” He didn’t prove it. He said it.
                  Then the sentence sat. In 1831 Carl Friedrich Gauss, reviewing somebody else’s
              book on a piece of number theory, proved what amounts to the special case of
              stackings laid out on a regular grid. In 1900 David Hilbert put the general question
              of packing equal spheres on his famous list of problems for the new century, without
              mentioning Kepler. In 1953 the Hungarian geometer László Fejes Tóth showed how
              the whole thing might be cut down to a problem with finitely many numbers in
              it, and a decade later he guessed that computers might one day finish it. Thomas
              Hales, a mathematician then at the University of Michigan, started on it in earnest
              in 1994, and in August 1998 he and his student Samuel Ferguson announced a
              proof that leaned on a great deal of computer work. The Annals of Mathematics
              gave the paper to a panel of twelve referees, led by Gábor Fejes Tóth, László’s son.
              They ran seminars on it for years. A journalist, George Szpiro, later reported that by
              July 2002 they were 99 percent certain it was right; I couldn’t find those words in
              anything the referees wrote themselves. What Szpiro printed in Nature in 2003 was
              the editor’s letter as Hales reported it: the referees had “not been able to certify the
              correctness of the proof, and will not be able to certify it in the future, because they
              have run out of energy . . . ” The Annals printed the human part in 2005, and the
              whole proof appeared in 2006. Hales started the Flyspeck project in 2003 to have
              the entire proof checked by proof assistants. It was finished on 10 August 2014.
                  Lay those dates out on the table and look at what moved. The sentence never
              changed. Hilbert’s version of the question didn’t even name the man who first said
              it. Whether it’s true never changed, as far as anyone can tell. What changed was
                                                                               14.11 Not a switch   279


how far it had been established, and it changed in stages, each one paid for by
somebody’s work: a guess, a special case, a place on a list, a plan, an announcement,
a panel’s reported ninety-nine percent and their exhaustion, a printing, a machine
check. A perfect reader of the sentence can’t see which stage it’s at. And it only ever
moved one way.
    Then I tried to break that one too, because by this point I’d watched a lot of
good-looking examples fall over, and there’s an obvious place to push. Standing can
fall. In 1852 a student named Francis Guthrie, colouring a map of the counties of
England, noticed that four colours always seemed to be enough to keep neighbouring
counties different. The question passed to his old teacher Augustus De Morgan,
who wrote to the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton that a student had
asked him for “a reason for a fact which I did not know was a fact,” and that he
didn’t know it yet either. In 1879 Alfred Kempe, a barrister who did mathematics on
the side and sang counter-tenor, published a proof, and his description of finding
it is wonderful: “After a somewhat arduous search, I have succeeded, suddenly, as
might be expected, in hitting upon the weak point . . . ” The journal’s associate editor,
William Story, added a note saying Kempe had “substantially proved” the theorem,
and tightened the counting part of the argument. Eleven years later Percy Heawood,
a lecturer at Durham who by one account brought his dog to his lectures, showed
that one step of what he called “the now apparently recognised proof” doesn’t work.
Kempe swaps colours along two chains at once, and swapping the first can spoil the
second.
    So standing can fall, and I went back and forth on what that does to my picture.
Where I’ve landed for now: the check that got Kempe’s proof accepted, Story’s note,
went through the counting and never examined the double swap. A check that
never looked at a step can’t have said no to that step. In the sense of the previous
few pages, the part that fell was never earned in the first place. I’m aware that’s a
convenient reading for me, and I’m wary of convenient readings, especially my own.
Take it as where I ended up. It isn’t a settled answer. It is, though, the reason the
machine in the next chapter only lets its record go up after a passing, sound check
and a matching commitment.
    And then the part I didn’t expect. The four-colour statement was true all along.
Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken, two mathematicians at the University of Illinois,
proved it in 1976 with a computer, and the proof was met with suspicion for years;
a cleaner version came in the 1990s; and in 2005 Georges Gonthier, a computer
scientist at Microsoft Research in Cambridge, finished a proof of the whole thing
checked by a small proof-checking program. So here’s a statement that stayed true
the entire time while its standing went up in 1879, came down in 1890, went up
again in 1976 against a lot of doubt, and went up further in 2005. The fall wasn’t
a fall of the truth. It was a fall of how far the truth had been established, and it
280   14 What established means


              was the right fall to have, because what had been established was less than anyone
              thought.
                  Laying all of that out together is what changed my picture. If there are stages,
              then at each one there’s a line, and the line has two sides: not this far yet, and
              at least this far. Each line amounts to its own yes-or-no question. But choose the
              question carefully. “Do we still trust this proof?” can turn back to no, as Kempe’s did.
              “Did we carry out this particular check?” asks about a completed act. Cross out the
              acceptance and the act still happened. To keep that answer, the machine has to keep
              a record of it and have no move that knocks the record down. A check that could
              have failed doesn’t give you that by itself. Maybe the switch wasn’t wrong. Maybe it
              was just incomplete, the first of many lines, and the real shape is a direction with
              lines drawn across it. I’ve gone around many times on whether the lines create the
              direction or the direction comes first and the lines are just places where you cut
              it, and on whether yes and no are even different from each other until something
              draws the line between them. I don’t have an answer to that. The one part I could
              actually settle is that a single switch isn’t enough once there are three or more stages,
              and Part II proved it (Section 11). Everything else in this paragraph is me thinking
              out loud.
                  Flatland, where this hunch started (Section 24), turned out to belong in the first
              batch. It’s a novel Edwin Abbott published in 1884, narrated by a square who lives
              in a flat, two-dimensional world (Section 7 says more about him and it). When a
              sphere passes through the flat world, the narrator sees a line whose ends fade wrong
              and whose length keeps changing, and only when he feels it does he find a circle, a
              perfect one. Then the sphere tells him it will rise, and he watches it dwindle to a
              point and vanish, and come back larger and larger. The hidden direction leaks into
              his view, faintly, and a sharp enough flat observer could in principle work out where
              the sphere is. In this machine, as far as I can make out, you could move a state all
              the way along the established direction without changing a single bit of the ordinary
              machine. That may be exactly why the ordinary machine can’t see it. It may also
              be why, if the direction is worth having, someone has to build it in on purpose and
              keep it on purpose. Keeping it costs; the chairs of Part I say so. What’s still open is
              what has to be kept, and that’s what the rest of this chapter is for.
                  None of these people were writing about what I’m writing about, and none of
              them is the reason any of this is true or false. Reading them didn’t make anything
              truer. It raised how far I’d established a few things for myself, and I could still be
              wrong about every one, the way the people who read Kempe in 1880 were. I went
              through them because I needed something to test the feeling against, and most of
              what I tested failed. The failures told me what the thing isn’t: not hidden, not free,
              not reversible, not steering. What’s left after all that is a list of what it isn’t. What
              it is was on the book’s first page: a distinction made to stay, the 0, about a claim
                                                       14.12 Computing already had a word for it   281


this time, and so on the same bill. The next few sections put it in computing’s own
words, and the next chapter builds the machine for it.


14.12 Computing already had a word for it
Computing already has a word for this and uses it every day. Anyone who’s used a
database has seen it: COMMIT.
    A database does a pile of tentative work, and then there’s one moment, the
commit, written to a log, after which the change counts. Jim Gray, who more or less
built the theory behind that, opens his 1981 paper on it by saying the idea comes
from contract law, and his example is a wedding. People negotiate, somebody asks,
two people say “I do,” and from then on it’s binding. If it was a mistake, you don’t
erase it. You do another transaction to fix it, the way a bad contract gets a second
contract. Nobody reaches for a time machine.
    The wedding was a philosopher’s example first. The Oxford philosopher J. L.
Austin, lecturing in 1955, said “I do” makes a marriage. It doesn’t describe one, and
sayings like that aren’t true or false. They can misfire (the wrong person says it, a
step gets skipped). They can’t be false. That’s a commit exactly. Writing the commit
record doesn’t report that a question got closed. Writing it is the closing. And a
commit can’t be false. It can misfire: committed without the check, committed about
the wrong pocket. Gettier and Peirce again, from a third direction. Then somebody
else reads the record, and for them it stops being a performance and turns into a
report: “this was checked and closed.” A report can be false. On the small machine
of the next chapter it can’t be, about the machine’s own history: if its flag is up
from a clean start, some claim was checked and closed, and that claim held of that
edition when it was checked. That’s how this book ties a commit to the truth, on
that machine and the ones built on it, and it took a proof to do it.
    Robin Milner, building a proof checker in the 1970s, ran out of memory, so he
decided to keep only the finished theorems and throw the proofs away, like a teacher
rubbing out the blackboard to make room. The obvious worry is forgery: if the
proofs are gone, what stops someone just writing a theorem down? His answer was
beautiful. Theorems got their own type in the programming language, and the only
way to make one was through the rules of logic. You couldn’t forge one because the
language wouldn’t let you build it any other way. He named that language ML, for
Meta Language. I wanted to call my machine the meta machine. I’m choosing to
treat that as a coincidence. Calling it a sign would be more my style, so this is more
restraint than I usually manage.
    Bitcoin is the loud modern version. Its records can’t be changed without redoing
all the work that came after them, and a computer that drops off the network and
comes back trusts the longest chain as the story of what happened while it was gone.
282   14 What established means


              That’s Turing’s clerk again, coming back to a note. The difference is that the clerk’s
              note costs next to nothing to forge and Bitcoin’s costs a mountain of work. It’s the
              clearest case I know of somebody making a settled fact expensive to fake, and they
              got there by paying for a search. The settling itself carries no price.
                  That’s a different job from the one this book’s price does, the mark it charges
              for raising a record. Bitcoin makes it tempting to read the toll of Section 2 as a
              deterrent, so I’d rather say this here. One mark deters nobody. Bitcoin’s work is tied
              to something scarce, electricity and hardware; a mark in this book is tied to nothing.
              Eric Budish, an economist at the University of Chicago, built a model in 2025 of
              what that tie has to cost. As I read him, for Bitcoin’s kind of trust to hold, the honest
              work has to stay expensive at every moment compared with what an attacker could
              win, and the bill grows in step with the value being protected. A flat mark can’t do
              that job, and it isn’t trying to. It’s a count, not a lock, as the start of the book put it:
              the lock is the order rule, check, then commit, then certify, and it would work at a
              price of zero. The price is there because nothing is kept for free: the chairs of Part I
              show that a machine with finite room that prices its merges can’t avoid it. Scaring
              anybody off has nothing to do with it. The machines I actually build have counters
              with no top, endless room, so the chairs alone don’t force the mark on them. There
              it comes from pricing the merges in the record’s own part of the state, a premise I
              choose (Theorem 3.17), and the size of the mark is my choice too (Section 15 says
              why).
                  And Bitcoin wasn’t first. Pull on its footnotes: three of the eight references in the
              paper that started it point to Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, who in 1991 worked
              out how to stamp a document with a time nobody could fake later, by chaining each
              stamp to the ones before it. A company built on their idea, Surety, printed a short
              fingerprint of its chain in the classified ads of the New York Times once a week from
              1995, and it was still doing it in 2018. I found that in a piece the journalist Daniel
              Oberhaus wrote that year, which says the ad runs under “Notices & Lost and Found.”
              Think about that for a second. To make a record nobody could quietly rewrite, they
              put it somewhere a million people would keep a copy of without even meaning to.
              A physicist named Wojciech Zurek has spent decades arguing that the world does
              the same thing with a measurement, copying the result into so many places that
              nobody can take it back. I’ll get to him properly later in this part (Section 18).
                  There are more fences like these: logs that can’t quietly change, certificates you
              can check. Later in this part, Section 17 takes five of them apart. I lean on all of
              them. They work. I want that said plainly, because the next thing isn’t “they’re
              broken.”
                  The next thing is where they sit. The database’s commit is bits in a log, kept by
              a database program, on a machine whose own step will overwrite those bits the
              moment some instruction says to. Milner’s guarantee is a type checker; it holds
                                                                    14.13 What settling looks like   283


inside programs written in his language and nowhere else. Bitcoin is a protocol
on ordinary computers that will do whatever they’re told. Every one of them is a
program or a rule, on top of a machine that can’t tell my two computers apart. The
machine underneath keeps nothing and charges nothing for what got settled.
    The obvious comeback: so put the rule one level lower, in the operating system, or
what security people call a reference monitor, the small always-on piece everything
has to pass through. Yes. Exactly that. A monitor that wouldn’t let any program raise
its record without paying would be doing the thing I’m talking about. In this book’s
words it would be implementing the model, and I’d count that as agreement. What I
care about isn’t who builds the fence. It’s what the fence has to obey, wherever it’s
built, and whether that’s forced or just a good idea.
    That comeback has a history, and it’s older than me by a lot. In 1972 James
P. Anderson’s planning study for the US Air Force described a reference monitor:
a piece every access has to pass through, that can’t be tampered with, and small
enough to check. In 2000 Fred Schneider, a computer scientist at Cornell, argued
that a monitor that only watches a run as it goes can enforce only rules whose
breaking shows up at some finite point, the kind computer scientists call safety rules.
“No certificate without an earlier passing check and a commit” is one of those. And
in 2015 Arthur Azevedo de Amorim, a computer scientist then at the University
of Pennsylvania, and six coauthors built monitors that check a rule at every single
instruction, and proved them correct. So putting a rule under every program, so
nothing can get around it, is their move. I didn’t invent it. What I’m putting under
that move is narrower: a record that has to be paid for, on the small machine one
that has to be earned, and a reason, from counting, why a finite machine that prices
its merges can’t make the price of a record that never comes down zero.


14.13 What settling looks like
The chapter on what structure is (Section 5) ends with a pile of things sorted into
buckets. Settling a question is that, plus one more thing, and it’s the 0 from the start
of the book at a bigger size.
    Picture every state the machine could be in as a field of dots. A yes-or-no question
about the state splits the field into two rooms: yes and no. That’s a sorting, the
smallest one there is. And remember the no pile: if one of the rooms is empty,
there’s no sorting at all, just a field. Now the extra thing that makes it a settlement:
once the machine is in the yes room, no step it can take leads back out. The door
opens one way. A settled question is a sorting plus a door that only swings in.
    At its best, what goes through the door is a relation: these numbers are in this
order, these two things belong together. Sultan, the chimpanzee of Section 9, fitted
284   14 What established means


              two short sticks into one long one and reached the food. Nothing new got added to
              the cage. Two sticks became one tool. That’s what I’d want the door to be for.
                  But the door doesn’t care, and this is the honest edge of the whole picture. Hook
              the door to a check that says yes to everything and the machine walks through even
              when the claim is false. Settled whether true or false, like Peirce said. A door that
              only swings one way tells you a question was closed. It doesn’t tell you it was closed
              right. Price and correctness are two different books, and I keep both, separately.
                  One more edge, the one Gray’s wedding already hinted at. What stays shut for
              good is that the question got closed, about that edition of that thing. Whether the
              claim is still true is another matter. Change the list after the commit and the record
              still says, truthfully, that the old edition was checked and closed. And if the claim
              turns out bad, the fix is another act on top, a second record that says “withdrawn.”
              The first one never quietly comes back down. So “entitled to lean on it right now” is
              three things at once: closed, not withdrawn since, and the thing unchanged.


              14.14 What the Thiele Machine is

              So here’s what I built, and which parts I was pushed into and which parts I chose,
              because you should know which is which.
                  You’ve had the model since the start of the book: five parts (states, moves, a
              step, a price on each move in whole marks, and a yes-or-no reading), one rule, the
              toll, and a counter and a window when a result needs them. You can’t buy it in a
              box. It isn’t a device, a CPU or an instruction set; those are things you build to carry
              it, and the next chapter builds one, as small as I could make it. It counts what a
              computation makes the case, and this chapter’s case is the sharpest one: the reading
              is a record that says whether something’s been established, and the toll is what the
              first page of the book said about records, nothing becomes something for free. The
              event it accounts for happens on any computer, whether anybody keeps track of it
              or not, and the record exists only if something keeps it. The window earns its place
              here too, because the two computers already showed you the problem: the usual
              window, the bits, can’t see the record.
                  The mark isn’t a joule or a dollar; whether it’s worth anything physical is
              Landauer’s assumption, named, and nowhere else. And one mark is just the floor:
              Part I shows that if you charge one mark per halving, a step that squeezes a lot
              together pays at least the logarithm of the squeeze, roughly how many times it
              halves the number of states it can tell apart. Don’t read that backwards, though.
              One mark isn’t one halving. A single state flipping into a big room of states that
              already read yes, with every state in play equally likely, squeezes things together
              only a little, much less than a halving, and the whole-number count rounds that up
                                                                14.14 What the Thiele Machine is   285


to one. Read in the worst case over what the machine might be holding, the same
flip can remove a full bit; Section 3 has both readings.
    What “new model of computation” means here. The Thiele Machine takes distinc-
tions I choose and writes them into the state, the step and the price. In the case
on the table that means which thing a check was about, which edition of it the
check saw, and which later act gets to lean on it. A record keeps some of that. A
window decides how much of it somebody looking in can get back. Change what’s
kept, or what the window shows, and you change which questions the end state can
answer. The machine underneath does the computing. The record adds no function
it couldn’t already compute.
    Which leaves a fair question hanging: if it computes nothing new, does it even
get to call itself a model of computation? It does, for the reason the start of the
book gave: the random-access, cell-probe and input-output models compute exactly
what Turing’s does and differ only in what they count, and so do the energy-aware
random-access machines of Demaine and his coauthors (2016), which count the
bits destroyed. Add one more to that family, the bulk-synchronous parallel model of
Leslie Valiant, a computer scientist at Harvard (1990), which charges for rounds of
communication between processors. Closest in kind are Blum’s axioms, also from
the start of the book, which constrain every cost the way the toll constrains every
price list on the model. The Thiele Machine’s own axis is what a run made the
case, and what that cost. Part II laid the toll over a register machine of Cook and
Reckhow’s kind, and over a Turing machine and a lambda calculus, and none of
them computes one function more afterward (Section 10). What each of them gains
is a record and a bill.
    The opening split what I found from what I assumed and what I chose, and the
choice that matters most here is the first on its last list: the count goes inside the
step.
    About the name. I named it after myself, on purpose. Half of that is a joke and
half of it is a stake in the ground. Turing got a machine, so here’s mine. The longer
story, meta machines and all, is in the afterword, “How I got here” (Section 24).
    The names are the ones Section 10.8 set out, and they work the way Turing’s
do. A clock is enough to make something a Thiele machine. It isn’t Thiele-complete,
because it charges for computing, and neither is a machine whose record never
goes up. The small machine of the next chapter is held to a higher bar, certified
Thiele-complete: on top of all that, from a clean start the record goes up only after a
passing check of a claim, by a checker proved to mean what the claim says, then a
commitment to that same claim, then a certificate, one mark each; and some claim’s
check can come out either way. A universal Thiele machine runs any machine of a
stated class as a guest, with every computing step done by its own counter moves
286   14 What established means


              and every rise placed by its program; a certified one also earns each guest’s record
              again. The end of this chapter pins every one of these words down (Section 14.18).

              and the counter written out, so you can watch it happen. You don’t have to take
              my word. The prices are the ones on the smallest machine, which the next chapter
              builds: one mark each to check, to commit, and to certify (raise the record), and
              nothing for ordinary work like moving numbers around.
