down, and it’s paid 2 for two refusals, because on that machine a refused attempt
still costs what it costs. (Read those as two separate attempts. Written as one stored
program, the copier would stop at its first refusal and pay 1.) Nothing the copier can
do raises its record without first running a passing check of the claim it then commits
to. And no outside window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the
difference is all in the part the window doesn’t show. Walk that warehouse now and
there’s finally a lamp that’s lit in one and dark in the other.
    Now how literally to take that table. It’s a picture of the chain, and the chain
is what’s proved. The small machine’s own checks are three questions about one
counter: is it zero, is it even, is it at least some number. What its proofs need from
the questions is a checker proved to say yes exactly when the answer is yes, and an
exact test for telling two questions apart. That’s enough for “sorted”: a version of
the machine that takes any questions with checkers like that proves the same chain
once for all of them, and with a list packed into one counter it certifies a sorted
list for three marks and refuses an unsorted one forever (Section 15). Without a
proved checker for “sorted,” the chain would be honest about a counter and only by
convention about your list, which is Gettier’s pocket again, one level down.
    And a lamp for whom? The record is bits too. It’s a lamp on the machine, for
anybody walking that warehouse. Hand somebody a printout of it across a desk and
you’re back at the sticker on the windshield: they have to trust whoever hands it
over, or have some way to check the box that says it ran. That crossing is a different
problem with its own tools, signatures, attestation and proofs a stranger can check,
and this book doesn’t solve it. Section 7 says what those tools rest on, and the
small machine’s record, like any record kept in a machine’s state, carries nobody’s
signature. What the step changes is the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust
the box that says it ran?” That’s a smaller question. It isn’t no question.
    So, the list from the start of this chapter: the test sheet, the sticker, the audit, the
ledger, the proof, the confident AI. Here’s the straight answer on which of those this
helps. The sticker is a question of whether a piece of paper is genuine, and nothing
here touches it. The “all tests passed” sheet fits only if the test is a checker proved to
mean what it says, in the machine’s own language; a set of tests that can miss a bug
certifies “this procedure said yes,” which is true and smaller. An audit and a ledger
get the test sheet’s answer: kept by a program on an ordinary computer, they’re bits
the program wrote, and they fit only where the step underneath keeps the record
and refuses to raise it without the check. A proof is one example: checking its steps
is a procedure that can reject them. Whether its statement says what you meant
is still yours to read. The AI that talks as if it’s sure of itself isn’t addressed at all.
Section 22, under “Outward consequences,” says how little of the outside world I’ve
reached.
288   14 What established means


                  Now the honest half. Take away the small machine’s rules and keep only the bare
              toll, and the copier has an easier move: pay one mark, flip the record to yes, done.
              The toll is satisfied. The receipt is real. It’s a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices
              the closing of the door. The check behind it goes unpriced.


              14.16 What putting it in the step buys

              So here’s the hardest objection, and I’d rather make it myself. You defined a flag
              and a charge, then proved the charge gets paid when the flag goes up. That’s your
              definitions agreeing with each other.
                  On the bare model, that’s fair, and the copier’s receipt for nothing is the proof.
              What makes the record mean established is the small machine’s step, which won’t let
              a commit through unless a check of that very claim passed, meeting the first three of
              the four conditions from Gettier’s pocket, with the fourth, an honest checker, proved
              about the checker separately. And what it proves isn’t about one program. It’s this:
              on every list of instructions anybody can write, starting clean, if the record is up,
              then somewhere earlier a check of some claim, about some edition, passed; then
              a commit of that same claim; then the certificate; with nothing touching the thing
              between the check and the commit.
                  So a raised flag, from a clean start, tells you some claim went through a passing
              check, a commitment to it about the same edition, and a certificate. That piece
              of history is what the flag keeps, and only that. The channel names the latest
              commitment that got through, which needn’t be the one the flag first went up on,
              and in general you can’t read off the end state which claim was certified at that first
              rise, or when. And the flag doesn’t say the claim still holds, at the certificate or at
              the end, because the counter can change after the commitment.
                  That “every” is the whole answer to what the step buys. A log kept by a program
              gives you a fact about that program: if the program’s right, the log’s right. The
              database’s guarantee holds for work that goes through the database. A rule in the
              step gives you a fact about every program the machine can run, the buggy ones and
              the hostile ones too, because there’s no way to run anything on it that isn’t a string
              of its steps. That’s what moving the rule down a level changes. Not what can be
              computed. Which programs the guarantee covers: this one becomes every one. And
              the tie between a check and the thing it checked gets a job: the step reads it, and
              refuses a commitment when it no longer fits. That’s structure doing something in
              the machine, not sitting in a note beside it.
                  Two limits on that “every,” said now so you don’t have to find them later. First,
              it’s every program. It isn’t every everything. The guarantee covers any list of
              instructions, run from a clean start, one step at a time, on a step that does what
              its definition says. Hostile programs, yes. A hostile start (a table of facts nobody
                                                                              14.17 What it isn’t   289


checked, a reset), hostile hardware (a soldering iron on the flag’s bit, a second writer
the step can’t see) or a hostile reader, no; Section 22 lists the whole fence. That’s
the same shape as the database’s guarantee, true if the layer underneath is faithful,
with a much bigger class of programs inside it.
    Second, the flag and the counter on their own are what people who verify
programs call ghost state: erase them and every program computes exactly what
it did before (Section 6 has where that idea comes from). What isn’t ghost on the
small machine is the table of checked facts, which the step reads and refuses on, at
run time, for every program. And the move of putting a rule under every program
isn’t mine either. It’s the reference monitor’s, and its history is a few sections back.


14.17 What it isn’t

It isn’t more computing power. Anything a Thiele machine computes, the machine
under its record computes without it. The book proves that over any machine at
all, a base-driven record is a switch the machine’s own events flip once and nothing
flips back (Section 10); it watches the computing and adds nothing to it. That’s
a sentence about the record. The checker belongs to the machine under it, and
the definition of certified Thiele-complete doesn’t ask the checker to be a program.
Hand it a checker that knows which programs halt, and whether a CHECK of “this
program halts” passes tells you whether it does, so that machine decides halting
(Section 15 has the details). With a checker that is a program, as every checker in
this book is, nothing in the machine goes past what a program can do. The record
makes nothing faster either: erase the flag and the counter, and every run takes the
same steps to the same places. CHECK is another matter. It’s a test at unit cost, and
one CHECK of “A ≥ m” settles whether A ≥ m in one step, where the two counters
alone would count A down. It isn’t quantum. It says nothing about which problems
are hard.
    And an ordinary computer can keep a record like this. Give a Turing machine
a spot for the record and a track for the counter, write its rules so it never sets the
spot without bumping the counter, prove that, and it is a Thiele machine. It’s no
counterexample (Section 15.13). What an ordinary programmable computer, as
built, doesn’t do is make its own step enforce a record for the programs it runs. When
it runs another program, that program’s record is just data in memory the program
can write, and a buggy program can flip it without paying a mark, because the host’s
step has no opinion about it. Could it be built otherwise? Sure. A universal machine
with one fixed table, the kind Turing built, could have that table written so it mirrors
each guest’s record and charges for the raise, and it would qualify. Nothing about
ordinary computers stops that. They just aren’t built that way. That gap, between
the machine doing the stepping and the program it runs, is where the databases and
290   14 What established means


              the proof checkers and Bitcoin built their fences, and it’s the gap the universal Thiele
              machine of Appendix D.1 closes, first for the programs of the small machine it’s built
              on, and then for every Thiele machine whose workings a program can compute.
                  There’s a cheap version of a universal machine, so here’s which one this is. A
              host with a move that means “run one guest step” runs any guest because I wrote
              it that way, and the book has one of those, as the simple picture (Appendix D.3).
              The universal Thiele machine doesn’t get that move. It’s one fixed program, written
              in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters,
              and it fetches, decodes and carries out each guest instruction itself, the way Turing’s
              universal machine does. The theorems are about that program: it halts exactly
              when its guest halts, with the guest’s answer in its counters; its flag goes up at some
              step of its run exactly when the guest’s goes up at some step of the guest’s, by its
              own check, its own commit and its own certificate; its ledger equals the guest’s
              at every point where the two runs match; and the machine it runs on is certified
              Thiele-complete (Appendix D.1). Its guests are the small machine’s programs, from
              every clean start, and those programs compute everything a Turing machine can,
              under Minsky’s encoding. Add one move that pays a mark and does nothing else,
              and the same kind of program runs every Thiele machine whose next move, step,
              prices and reading are computed by programs, the reading answering yes or no on
              every state: it halts when the guest’s run stops, its flag goes up at some point exactly
              when the guest’s reading is yes at some state of its run, on a chain whose check is
              the guest’s own reading, and its ledger is the guest’s prices plus at most two marks at
              the raise when the guest’s reading starts at no (when it starts at yes, the host has to
              raise its flag at once and pays three on a ledger of nothing), a surcharge no program
              on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest’s whole ledger at the
              raise is below three (Appendix D.2). A Thiele machine whose reading no program
              decides isn’t covered, and I say exactly where the edges are.


              14.18 Two layers, and the names

              The layers, once. The core definition (Definition 2.1) is a Thiele machine: states,
              moves, a step, a cost for each move, a yes-or-no reading, and the toll. Everything
              else is added on top, and each theorem names what it adds. First come extra
              structures and requirements: a ledger that sums the costs, a window, permanence of
              the reading, a price on merges. Then an earned implementation, the small machine
              of the next chapter, with a checker proved sound and a provenance theorem. Then
              two interfaces any machine can be read through: Thiele-complete, about computing
              and a record that tells starts apart, and certified Thiele-complete, which adds the
              earned chain. Then a universal interpreter for a stated class of guests. The bare
                                                                   14.18 Two layers, and the names   291


definition doesn’t ask the step to be computable, so when I say the record adds no
computing power, I mean relative to a fixed base.
    Substrate versus scaffolding. Two layers run through the book, and confusing
them makes the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The substrate is the
shape: a kind of state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape
for different extra pieces, and the pieces aren’t the same. The universal floor (the
“pays something” result of Section 2) asks for a yes-or-no reading and the toll on it.
The counter’s uniqueness (only one count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a
starting value and a schedule of increments; Section 6 gives the argument, a short
induction that works for any system with those two pieces, and on the small machine
of the next chapter the ledger is the sum of the charges by theorem (Section 15). The
diagonal asks for a way to write programs as states and a recursion theorem for the
transformations the substrate can express, and needs no toll at all. “Substrate-level”
doesn’t mean one fixed plug that every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use
the parts it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it’ll tell you, and whatever else is lying
around the workshop isn’t the theorem’s. So each result is stated over exactly the
extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a theorem names is what I mean
by the model, and the name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. The scaffolding is
everything that holds the shape up so you can touch it, and when I say my machine,
the small machine, the machine I build or the build, this is what I mean: the machine
of the next chapter, with its two counters and their versions, its table of checked
facts, its channel, trap, ledger and flag, its six instruction kinds and their prices, the
host with a register for every whole number, and the universal programs that run on
that host (Appendix D.1). The build fills in several extensions at once and borrows,
for any one theorem, only the extension that theorem names. Let that line blur and
a theorem stated over one extension starts reading as if it carried premises it never
uses. “Substrate” never means the build, and it never means the side of a simulation
doing the stepping; for that I say “the machine doing the stepping,” as against “the
program it runs.”
    So here’s how the book keeps the two apart. Parts I and II were about any system
with the pieces each result names, and their pictures were toys you could hold (two
boxes on a sheet of paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots). My machine wasn’t
one of them; where they said something about it, they pointed ahead, and the next
chapter builds it. Every Part II claim that has a machine instance gets that instance
there (Section 15.14) or in Appendix D.1, with its own theorem, and Part II said so
in one sentence at most. When the origin story (the afterword, Section 24) says the
shape “was the substrate the entire time,” it means this layer, the model’s shape. It
doesn’t mean any piece of the build. Same story with two more of its words. When
it says “the machine” about the thing it named the Thiele Machine, or calls that
thing a meta machine, it means the model; “my machine” is the build of the next
292   14 What established means


              chapter. And when it lists what the model asks for (a state, a step, a record, a ledger,
              a window), read the ledger and the window as two of the extra pieces: a result asks
              for them only if it uses them.
                  The build is one piece of scaffolding, and I’d rather you know up front how
              small it is. Section 15 builds the smallest honest machine I could: two counters, six
              instructions, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are
              proved there (a flag raised from a clean start was checked, then committed, then
              certified, on the same edition, with nothing touching that thing between the check
              and the commit), and so is universality, through Minsky’s two-counter machines and
              a halting result due to Minsky, using the construction of Forster, Larchey-Wendling
              and coauthors. Then one fixed program, on a host made of the same kinds of
              instruction with more counters, runs every program of it, and with one paid move
              added, every computably presented Thiele machine (Appendix D.1). None of that is
              the model. It shows the model fits in six instruction kinds.
                  The names again, with every part of the certified one pinned down, because I’ll
              hold to them for the rest of the book. A Thiele machine is any particular system that
              fits the model’s core definition, its five parts and its toll (Definition 2.1); the toys on
              paper in Part I count, and so does the small machine, with its toll proved. Thiele-
              complete (Definition 10.6) says nothing about what the record is about. Certified
              Thiele-complete asks for four things of its own (Definition 15.7), and it is exactly
              Thiele-complete with clean loads, the earned record and a claim that can fail added
              (Theorem 15.18). A universal base whose moves can’t touch the record, and a
              record that stays up once it’s up. A record that, from a clean start, rises only after
              a passing check of a claim, then a commitment to that same claim with nothing
              it’s about changed in between, then a certificate, with the checker proved to mean
              what it says: the claims and what they mean come from a language fixed first, and
              the proof is that the checker’s yes makes the claim true in that language’s sense.
              Exact prices: one mark for each of those three acts and nothing for anything else.
              And a claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record from a loaded
              start exactly when the claim holds there, with the claim holding at some loaded
              starts and failing at others. Every clock-style machine fails the definition, because
              it charges for computing, whatever its record, and every machine that meets the
              definition hides its record and its ledger from its own window, both by theorem.
              That’s about an observer who sees only where a run ended; one who also has the
              program and the start can work both out. None of the four clauses is there for
              decoration: for each one there’s a machine that meets the other three and fails it,
              each of them a Thiele machine with a two-counter machine inside that no interface
              makes certified Thiele-complete (Theorem 15.24). The small machine meets it, and
              so does the same machine over any properties with an exact test for telling two of
              them apart and a proved checker, as long as one of them can come out both ways,
                                                                  14.18 Two layers, and the names   293


sorted lists included. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine running one
fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with every step of
the guest’s computing done by the host’s own counter moves and every rise of its
record put where its program put it; a certified one also earns each guest’s record
again by its own check, commit and certificate. Nothing is left to the guest’s good
manners. Appendix D.1 builds one, U: a fixed program in the small machine’s own
six kinds of instruction, on a host with more counters, with no step of any guest
built in. Its guests are the small machine’s programs, so every computation runs
on it under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine, and it matches each
guest’s halting, answer, flag and ledger exactly, raising its own flag by its own check,
commit and certificate. Then UP , the same program with one more handler for a
paid move that does nothing else, takes as its guests every computably presented
Thiele machine, one whose next move (picked by a driver), step, prices and reading
are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. It matches the
guest’s halting, raises its own flag on its own earned chain exactly when the guest’s
reading has said yes, and keeps the guest’s prices to within a surcharge of at most
two when the guest’s reading starts at no, which no program on that host, run from
a clean start, can avoid in general. And a computer that runs the small machine,
your laptop say, isn’t a Thiele machine. It implements one, inside bounds, the way a
laptop implements a Turing machine. Push on that comparison, because it’s loose,
and the looseness is the point. Does a laptop implement a Turing machine? Not
exactly. Turing’s tape never runs out, and a laptop’s memory does; strictly, a laptop is
a very large machine with finitely many states, and it behaves like a Turing machine
only on computations that fit. Nobody minds, because the bound is known and most
computations people care about fit inside it. That’s the same deal any device running
the small machine gets: its counters stop somewhere, and the theorems speak only
for runs that fit. The bounds aren’t fine print. They’re the whole difference between
implementing a model and being one.
    How much can a difference in width matter? There’s a famous answer, and
it’s worth the detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and
broke apart about forty seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by
the mathematician Jacques-Louis Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial
reference software: a sixty-four-bit floating-point number, an alignment value called
BH that’s tied to horizontal speed, squeezed into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On
Ariane 4, where the software came from, that value could never get big enough to
overflow, because of how that rocket flew in its first forty seconds. Ariane 5 flew
differently. The value got too big, the backup unit failed on it, the main unit failed
the same way one cycle of its software later, seventy-two thousandths of a second,
and the function doing the converting didn’t even serve a purpose once the rocket
had lifted off; it was kept for commonality with the old rocket. The board’s report
294   14 What established means


              says the assumption that made the conversion safe had been agreed on and then,
              not on purpose, kept out of sight of any outside review. A width premise that holds
              on one machine is a fact about how that machine gets used. The code doesn’t carry
              it, and yet it travels with the code without anybody noticing. The only defence I
              know is the dull one: write the premise into every statement that needs it, where
              the next person will trip over it.
CHAPTER 15




The smallest honest machine

The chapters before this one never built a machine you could program. They said
“any states, any steps,” and whenever a picture was needed, a board or some chairs
or a cup stood in. Now I have to build a machine, and the first question is about
the one I built before it. I built a big one first, on the way here (the Afterword,
Section 24, tells that story), with dozens of instructions, some picked for reasons
and some picked because I had to pick something, and theorems held of it. What
does that show? That the model works, or that I’m good at stacking instructions
until the proofs go through? A big machine is a wonderful place to hide a mistake.
It’s a garage so full of stuff that you could lose a car in it.
    So the machine in this book is a small one. I want the state and every way of
changing it where you can inspect them. Six instruction kinds, and you can follow
how a check stays tied to an object, how a change makes it stale, and how the
next move uses that relation. Each kind takes operands, a counter or a property
or a line to jump to, so there are unboundedly many instructions. It’s one way of
building the model, not the only one, and the theorems will say which facts hang on
these particular choices. “Smallest,” in the title, is me telling you how I built it: by
throwing things out until nothing more would go. I haven’t got a proof that nothing
smaller works, and I’m not claiming one.


15.1 What the model actually asks for
Here’s the machine in three sentences, before any of its parts. It’s an ordinary
computer, two counters and a jump, with a record layer on top. The flag in the
record layer is the blank cell, and raising it is the write of a 0, a merge in the record
layer (flag down and flag up land on the same state), which is why the step that
raises it is charged once merges in that layer are priced (Theorem 3.17, in Part I).
And the order rule, check, then commit, then certify, is what makes a raised flag
mean something.
   Here’s what Parts I and II say the model adds to a machine. A record: a flag that
reads no or yes and, once yes, stays: the blank cell’s 0, on a machine. Here yes
means “certified,” because that’s the event I picked (Section 18, later in this part,
asks whether the pick was free). A toll: the step that raises the flag costs something
(Section 2). A ledger: the running total of those costs, a whole number that only

                                                  295
296   15 The smallest honest machine


              climbs (Section 6). And Section 10 proved the thing this whole chapter stands on:
              over any base at all, a base-driven record is a latch, a bit that switches on at an event
              the base decides and never switches off (Observation 10.1). The record watches the
              base. It doesn’t compute anything the base couldn’t compute without it.
                  Push on that for a second, because it cuts the job in half. If the record adds
              no computing power, then all the computing power comes from the base, and the
              question “how small can the machine be” splits into two questions that don’t touch
              each other. For the base: what’s the smallest thing that can compute everything
              there is to compute? For the record: what’s the smallest set of pieces that makes the
              flag mean something?
                  One honest asterisk on “don’t touch,” because the machine below makes it matter.
              What’s blind is the flag and the ledger: the base never reads either of them. But
              the pieces that make the flag mean something (a table of checked facts, a slot for a
              commitment, a trap that stops a refused run) have to sit where the step can read
              them, which is in the base, and they do steer the run: a failed check stops a program
              dead. The latch theorem holds wherever you draw the line between base and record,
              which is exactly why it can’t tell you where the meaning lives. On this machine the
              meaning lives on the base side of the line, in the bookkeeping, and the flag on top
              reports it.
                  The record question, the second of those two, is the one Part II left to the machine,
              on purpose. Section 9 said that testing a claim and committing to it are two different
              acts, and that nothing in the five parts of the model makes the second wait for the
              first. Read Section 2’s definition again with that in mind: a machine where you pay
              one unit and raise the flag over nothing in particular obeys every rule in it. That
              machine is honest about the price and silent about what was bought. A receipt for
              nothing. The toll alone can’t fix that, because the toll is a rule about cost, and “was
              this earned” is a question about order: did a check happen, of this claim, before the
              commitment, with nothing changing underneath in between?
                  This machine is my attempt to make the order part of the machine, in the smallest
              place I could find to do it. I’ll show you the pieces, then the proofs, then the places
              it falls short, which there are, and which I’d rather you hear from me.


               15.2 Where the counters come from

              The base first, and the base isn’t mine. It’s Marvin Minsky’s. In a 1961 paper in the
              Annals of Mathematics, and then in his 1967 book Computation: Finite and Infinite
              Machines, Minsky studied a machine so bare it’s almost a joke. Picture a few bins of
              pebbles and a numbered list of instructions. There are only two kinds of instruction:
              put a pebble in bin c and go to the next line; or take a pebble out of bin c if there’s
              one to take, and go one way if there was and another way if the bin was empty.
                                                               15.2 Where the counters come from   297


That’s it. No memory but the bins, no tape, no arithmetic beyond plus one and
minus one. When the line you’re on has no instruction, the machine stops.
    What Minsky proved is that two bins are enough to compute anything a Turing
machine can compute, as long as you’re willing to pack the input in a strange way.
The trick is to keep many numbers inside one number, as the powers of different
primes (2x 3y 5z holds three numbers in one), and to do arithmetic on the exponents
by multiplying and dividing with the second bin as scratch space. Packing numbers
that way can turn a modest input into an enormous pile of pebbles, handled one at
a time, so it’s no way to build a fast machine. It’s a way to settle a question: with
that packing, the two bins can do every Turing computation. What the bins give me
here is a base whose ordinary moves you can see all of. Each of the earlier results
says which properties of a base it needs, and Appendix E carries the earned layer
over to other bases once you’ve named what they have to supply.
    Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of
computation sits and how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means
the base of this chapter’s machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with
plus one, minus one and a jump, then nothing about the record can be smuggling
computing power in through some instruction I made fancy. For this construction I
use the two-counter result of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors. The halting
reduction is their work, and Appendix K sets it out; the step-for-step connection to
this machine is the part I have to establish.
    And the pebbles aren’t only my picture. They were somebody’s actual machine,
the same year. In one issue of the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, September 1961,
Z. A. Melzak, a mathematician at the University of British Columbia, described a
computer made of distinguishable holes and an unlimited supply of pebbles, with
one three-place operation, and a few pages later Joachim Lambek, a mathematician
at McGill University, trimmed it to two moves: put a pebble in hole X; take one
out of hole X if there’s one to take. He called it an infinite abacus, and early on
he writes “Our method is probably not new,” which is a hard sentence to beat. He
also tells anybody who distrusts infinity not to worry about all those holes, since
any one computation only ever uses finitely many of them. Is that two inventions or
one? Lambek says his was a modification of Melzak’s, so call it one and a half, with
Minsky’s as a separate find the same year. And then Lambek went somewhere you
wouldn’t guess: in 1986, with Philip Scott, a logician who had come to McGill to
work with him and later taught at the University of Ottawa, he wrote a book whose
first part, as the publisher describes it, shows that typed lambda calculi and a certain
kind of category are essentially the same thing. Pebbles to category theory in one
career, twenty-five years end to end. Does any of it change the argument? No. The
machine uses Minsky’s version and Minsky’s name. But a bare machine that several
298   15 The smallest honest machine


              people reach for in the same year looks like a shape that was sitting there. It doesn’t
              look much like anybody’s invention.
                  The title of Minsky’s 1961 paper is the clue I can’t leave alone. It’s about “Post’s
              problem of tag.” Who’s Post, and what’s tag? Emil Post was a logician, a fresh PhD
              from Columbia, who in 1921, on a fellowship at Princeton, was playing with about
              the simplest rewriting game there is. Take a word of 0s and 1s. Look at its first
              letter, chop the first three letters off the front, and stick something on the end: 00
              if the letter you looked at was 0, 1101 if it was 1. Repeat, and stop when fewer
              than three letters are left. Try it at the table. Start from 1000: you get 01101, then
              0100, then 000, then 00, and it stops. Start from 100: you get 1101, 11101, 011101,
              10100, 001101, and then 10100 again, and it goes round forever. Post wanted a rule
              that tells you, for every starting word, which of those happens. He worked at it for
              months and later called it hopeless, and as far as I can tell it still is: a hundred years
              on, nobody knows whether that one little game, with that one rule, can be decided.
              Stephen Wolfram, the physicist who built Mathematica, wrote a 2021 article on
              it that tells the Princeton story, and it’s where I’d start. In his 1961 paper Minsky
              proved that tag games in general can compute anything, which is why Post’s name is
              on it. It didn’t settle Post’s own game. And the chase goes one step further. In 2008
              Liesbeth De Mol, a historian and philosopher of computing who wrote her doctoral
              work on tag systems, turned the famous 3n + 1 problem (halve an even number,
              triple an odd one and add one, and ask whether you always get down to 1) into a
              small tag game of the same kind. So is Post’s game secretly as hard as everything, or
              just stubborn? I can’t tell you, and as far as the published work goes, nobody can
              yet.
                  None of that changes the machine below. It changes the picture. The two-counter
              machine came out of a hunt for the smallest thing that can’t be predicted, and the
              smallest things are exactly where the open questions are still sitting.
                  One word clash, before it bites. Minsky’s machine is usually called a counter
              machine, and its bins are counters. Section 6 also had a counter: the ledger µ, the
              number that only climbs. Same word, two completely different things, and I’d love
              to say I set that up on purpose. In this chapter, counter means one of Minsky’s two
              bins, called A and B, and the climbing total is always the ledger µ.


               15.3 The machine
               Here’s the whole state. I’ll say each piece in words first.
               • Two counters, A and B. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
                                                                                15.3 The machine   299


• A version for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and
  goes up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter’s
  edition number: a new value is a new edition.
• A line number, which instruction comes next, counting from 1 (more on that
  choice just below).
• A fact table: a list of facts. A fact is three things stuck together: a property, a
  counter, and a version. “A is even, as of edition 3” is a fact. The table has room
  for sixteen. Why sixteen? It’s a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the
  pick costs is in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the machine
  doesn’t do.
• A channel: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
• A trap: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused
  something, and it stays up.
    Counting lines from 1 looks like the least interesting choice in the chapter, and
it’s one of the oldest arguments in programming, with a famous referee. Edsger
Dijkstra was a Dutch computer scientist, one of the generation that founded the
field, and for over forty years he mailed numbered notes to a few dozen colleagues.
In 1982 he wrote one of them, EWD 831, titled “Why numbering should start at
zero.” His case goes through ranges first. Of the four ways to write “2 up to 12” with
less-than signs, he picks the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top out,
2 ≤ i < 13: two ranges that meet end to end then share one number written once,
and the length is just the top minus the bottom. Start a sequence of N things at zero
and it’s 0 ≤ i < N, and each thing’s number is how many things came before it. He
reports that programmers on the language Mesa, which allowed all four conventions,
found the other three a steady source of clumsiness and mistakes, and he points
out that FORTRAN starts at one. Does that settle it? It settles which convention is
tidier, by an argument you can check. It doesn’t settle which convention somebody
else’s work used, and that’s the trap: the two-counter machine used by Forster,
Larchey-Wendling and coauthors numbers its lines from 1, and so does this machine,
because matching it line for line is worth more here than tidiness. Is zero the right
place to start counting? Dijkstra’s title says it is, and I can’t tell you more than that.
What his note carries is an argument about which way makes fewer mistakes. That
part you can check for yourself, and it’s the more useful thing to have.
    Everything in that list is the core, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit
the two pieces from the model: the ledger µ and the flag. The machine never reads
either of them to decide what to do next. I’m not asking you to take that on trust.
It’s how the step is written, and it shows up as a theorem below.
    The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words:
is zero; is even; and is at least n, for any whole number n you like. Each one comes
300   15 The smallest honest machine


              in two forms. There’s the checker, a little program that computes yes or no: compare
              with 0, look at the last bit, compare with n. And there’s the meaning, the plain
              arithmetic statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the
              number is two times something; n is less than or equal to the number. Why both?
              Because a checker is code, and code can be wrong in ways that look right, and
              “the checker says yes” is only worth anything once somebody has proved it says yes
              exactly when the meaning is true. That proof is one line per property, and it’s the
              first block below.
                  Why can a machine check a claim at all? Because a claim with a precise meaning
              is something you evaluate: plug in the values and turn the crank. George Boole
              worked out in 1847 that you can do arithmetic on claims this way, treating “and”
              like multiplication and “or” like a kind of addition. Why multiplication? Try it at
              the table. Write 1 for true and 0 for false, and multiply: one times one is one, and
              anything times zero is zero. That’s “and” to the letter. Then the stranger thing Boole
              noticed. Say “x and x” and you’ve said nothing new; it’s just x. In numbers that’s
              x × x = x, and he made it a law of his system, and it’s a law ordinary numbers
              mostly break. Which numbers equal their own square? Two times two is four, no. A
              half times a half is a quarter, no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That’s the whole list. So when
              Boole wrote his bigger book in 1854, The Laws of Thought, he asked you to imagine
              an algebra whose letters take the values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every checker on
              this machine answers in that algebra.
                  And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour, which I found in the Stanford
              Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on Boole. Boole was largely self-taught and spent
              about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early in
              1847, was a loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish
              philosopher Sir William Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical
              idea in the old logic of syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a
              schoolmaster watching from the side picks up the subject and writes the little book
              this paragraph is about. Few people remember what the quarrel was over. Every
              checker in this chapter runs on what the bystander wrote.
                  Then push on it, because Boole’s “or” isn’t quite the one a checker uses. His plus
              only made sense for things that can’t both hold at once, so “x or y” with both of them
              true had no meaning in his system. William Stanley Jevons, an English economist
              who also worked on logic, read “or” as “either or both,” which gives “x or x is x,”
              the same trick as before. He wrote to Boole in 1863 saying plus ought to work that
              way, and in 1864 he put it in a book called Pure Logic. Boole wouldn’t have it, since
              it broke the tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The “or” in every
              programming language I know is the inclusive one Jevons argued for. Does that
              change anything about the checker? No; the crank turns the same way. It changes
                                                                             15.3 The machine   301


the picture: the “or” a checker uses is the one the man who invented the algebra
turned down.
    Hanging a checked claim on a point in a computation is an old move too. Tony
Hoare, in 1969, built a whole way of reasoning about programs out of it: attach a
claim to a point in a program (“whenever execution reaches here, this is true”), and
reason forward from claim to claim. Robert Floyd had done it two years earlier on
flowcharts. Their claims were checked on paper by the person writing the proof.
This machine’s version is a property of one counter at one edition, checked by a step
while it runs.
    And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a
paper this book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held
for the new EDSAC computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, “Checking
a large routine,” the same note the counter chapter used for stopping (Section 6).
Stopping was the second half of it. The first half is this move, twenty years before
Hoare: the programmer should make “definite assertions which can be checked
individually,” and the correctness of the whole should follow from them. His example
program computes a factorial using nothing but addition, and his picture for why
you’d bother is one you can do on the back of an envelope. Add up a long column
of four-digit numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to redo the
whole sum at one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before
it. Hand them the total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small
checks they can do one at a time. That’s a claim hung on a point in the middle
of the work, so the person checking never has to hold all of it at once. The paper
got its due mostly later: in 1984 two computer scientists, F. L. Morris of Syracuse
University and C. B. Jones of Manchester University, who had worked on it together
at Oxford, republished it, with its misprints corrected, as an early program proof by
Alan Turing. Theirs is the text I read, and the column of numbers is Turing’s own
example in it. Does any of that change the machine? No. It changes the date on
the idea, and it tells you something I like: the first person to ask how you’d check a
program put the claims in the middle of it. He didn’t save them for the end.
    Now the six instruction kinds.

                 The first two are Minsky’s machine, and HALT lets a program say it’s done. The
              last three are the record’s. Read them as a chain: you can only certify with a
              commitment in the channel, you can only commit to a fact in the table, and the only
              way into the table is a check that passed. Three links, and each one costs.
                 One of what? One unit of µ, the same unit as Section 2’s toll. Why one? Why
              would ten be worse? Because one is the smallest positive whole number, which is
              honestly the whole defence, and Section 3 is the section where I tried to do better
              than that for the flag. The argument for a whole finite machine doesn’t reach this
              one: these counters have no top, and some of the base moves merge states at a
              price of zero. What does reach it is the record-layer merge named at the start of this
              chapter (Theorem 3.17, in Part I), which gives the toll once you’ve agreed to price a
              merge in the record’s own part of the state. Agreeing to that, and picking one unit
              for each of these three acts, are still my choices.
                 The whole numbers have a history of their own. In 1888 the German mathe-
              matician Richard Dedekind published a little book whose title asks what numbers
              are and what they’re for, and in 1889 the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano
                                                                               15.3 The machine   303


published a booklet, written in Latin, that set out the axioms for the whole numbers
in the form people still teach: there’s a first number, and every number has a next
one, and a few rules about how “next” behaves. I had the two of them down as
working independently. I went looking, and the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on
Dedekind says Peano acknowledged Dedekind’s priority, which is why the axioms
often go by both names. (Peano’s booklet is also where the sign ∈ that you met in
Section 5 comes from: he wrote it as a Greek epsilon, for the Latin est, “is.”) Start
from zero and take “the next one” three times, and you have three. Once prices are
whole numbers, one is the smallest price that isn’t nothing.
    The zeros matter just as much: computing costs no marks on this ledger. Plus
one, minus one and jumping around cost zero marks, though in a real device each
of them still dissipates when it happens. Only the three acts that make a claim cost,
and each of them costs whether it passes or traps. Failing is not a discount.
    The version rule. Here’s why versions exist, with numbers. Start with A = 4,
version 0. CHECK is even A passes, and the table gets the fact (even, A, 0). Now
INC A: A becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT is even A. The
machine looks for (even, A, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only
has (even, A, 0). No match. Trap. The old fact is still sitting in the table, still true
about edition 0, and completely useless for committing to anything about edition 1.
A fact is about one edition of one counter, and an edition never comes back, because
versions only go up and never wrap. That’s the whole trick against stale evidence:
you can’t check a number, change it, and then commit to the check.
    That’s the time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug from Section 14, the file checked and
then swapped, and the database answer to it is Kung and Robinson’s: at commit
time, check that nothing you read was written in the meantime, and back out if
something was. The version rule is that check, done by the step, on one counter. It
also shows where the guarantee ends. It works because one step does every write
and every write bumps a version. A second writer that changed a counter without
bumping its version, a second processor or a device writing memory on its own,
would walk right around it, and none of the theorems below are about a machine
with one of those.
    Processor designers put a cousin of this check in silicon. Jensen, Hagensen and
Broughton, at Lawrence Livermore in 1987, described a pair of instructions now
called load-linked and store-conditional: the load reads a word and the processor
starts watching it, and the store goes through only if nothing has written that word
since; otherwise it fails and the program tries again. It’s tempting to say CHECK
is the load and COMMIT is the conditional store, and it’s wrong in two places.
COMMIT doesn’t write the counter it checked, and the thing doing the watching,
the fact, sits in a table the step keeps. No single processor holds it. The hardware
304   15 The smallest honest machine


              version does cover the second writer, because the watching happens on the memory
              everyone shares, which is exactly the case the version rule leaves out.
                  The real kinship is older, and it’s somewhere else. Picture the table and the
              counters shared by many processors, with CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY each
              done as one indivisible step. Maurice Herlihy (1991), a computer scientist who has
              spent his career on how many processors can share memory safely, ranked shared
              objects by how many processors each one can bring to agree on a single value with
              nobody ever waiting on anybody. Test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and
              reports what was there, brings exactly two. A sticky bit, the idea of Serge Plotkin
              (1989), a Stanford computer scientist working on distributed algorithms, is a cell
              the first writer jams for good, with the first writer’s value, and everyone after can
              read it; it brings any number. I guessed that the shared object would sit at the top
              with the sticky bit, because a write that kills every fact about a counter, together
              with a commitment other processors can see, looks like a way to build one. Ranking
              the object takes its operations, what each one returns, which steps are indivisible,
              how it starts and which processes run it, and then a proof that every processor
              decides, they all decide the same value, the value is one somebody proposed, and
              nobody waits. Here it is, with every instruction one indivisible step and the whole
              state readable, and the object is at the top. The reason is the order of the fact table.
              Start it clean, with counter A at zero and the trap down. Each processor CHECKs
              a property that holds of A at zero, Zero to propose 0 and Even to propose 1, then
              reads the table and decides the bit of its oldest fact. Nobody touches A, so the first
              CHECK of the run passes. The table never loses an entry or reorders the ones it has,
              and a CHECK that finds it full trips the trap, after which nothing moves, so the first
              CHECK of the run fixes the oldest fact for good. Every processor that decides decides
              that bit, the bit is somebody’s proposal, and each one decides after two of its own
              steps whatever the others do. The version rule and the commitment play no part.
              The trap alone doesn’t do it: it records that something trapped, and it doesn’t hand
              everyone the first writer’s value.
                  Now take the version rule away, let failures change nothing, keep only the
              properties “at least n” so that a checked property only ever turns true, drop the
              decrement, and make the fact table (with no room limit), the commitments and
              the flag sets and latches that only grow. I guessed that then the object drops to the
              bottom rung, the level of plain memory, which is the shared-memory face of what the
              database researchers Joseph Hellerstein and Peter Alvaro (2020), at Berkeley and
              Santa Cruz, call CALM, where monotone means nobody has to coordinate. That’s
              proved too, by Herlihy’s own kind of argument. Let the updates return nothing and
              let the whole state be readable. If at every state, of any two updates, one leaves
              the state alone, or the two commute, or one overwrites the other, then no protocol
              brings two processors to agreement with nobody waiting. Here’s why. Give one
                                                                              15.3 The machine   305


processor 0 and the other 1. At the start the answer isn’t settled, since either one
running alone has to decide its own bit. Nobody waits, so it can’t stay unsettled
forever, and there’s a last unsettled state: whichever processor moves next settles
it, one way if it’s the first and the other way if it’s the second. Look at those two
moves. If one is a read, or an update that leaves the state alone, the other processor
can’t tell whether it happened, and running alone it decides the same bit either
way. If the two commute, both orders end on the same state with both processors
in the same place. If one overwrites the other, the overwriter running alone can’t
tell whether the other move happened first. Each case contradicts the two ways the
answer was settled. The monotone object, with registers beside it, has that property.
An update that fails changes nothing. Two updates that both succeed still succeed in
either order, because an instruction that would succeed still succeeds after anything
else has run, and adding to sets and to counters gives the same result in either order.
Two of the conditions do real work there. The table needs no room limit: a full table
that turns away the latecomer is a first-writer-wins cell again, and that’s back at the
top. And the ledger: it changes neither result as long as a failed act in the variant
isn’t charged, or nobody reads the ledger. Charge a failed CHECK where everyone
can read the total, and one processor INCs while the other CHECKs at least 1; the
total and the table then tell each of them which act came first, and that’s enough
for two to agree. Neither idea is mine: the top is Plotkin’s and the bottom is the
monotone fact that field already knows.
    Process-calculus people have a statement of the same split. Johannes Åman
Pohjola and Joachim Parrow, computer scientists at Uppsala University (Parrow
is one of the inventors of the pi-calculus, a mathematical model of processes that
talk over channels), in 2016 proved that no model whose parallel composition is
monotonic, where a neighbouring process can never stop a step, has a consensus
process. One of their examples of a model that does is test-and-set. Test-and-set isn’t
a sticky bit: in Herlihy’s ranking it brings two processors to agree, and a sticky bit
brings any number.
    Their setting is small enough to go through here whole. A model is any set of
processes with a step relation and a way to compose two processes that doesn’t care
about order or grouping. Composition is monotonic when whatever a process can
reach alone, it can still reach with anything set beside it. A consensus process is one
where any number of copies, run together, can end up agreeing on either of two
outcomes; once a run has one outcome it can never show the other; and an outcome,
once reached, survives having more copies, run any way you like, set beside it. Their
theorem goes through in a few lines: run half the copies to one outcome and the
other half to the other. If neither half can block the other, the whole crowd can
reach the pair of end states set side by side, and since each outcome survives the
company, both outcomes hold there, which is forbidden. Then the machine goes
306   15 The smallest honest machine


              into it. A process is a shared machine state with a crowd of threads, each proposing
              a bit. Composing two processes pools their threads, each thread keeping whatever it
              has already decided, and settles the shared state like this: if one side is still at the
              fresh start, the composite takes the other side’s state; if both have already moved,
              the composite is jammed, a state where no thread can take a step. That composition
              doesn’t care about order or grouping: a fresh start is neutral, and any two moved
              states jam whichever way round you put them. One thread proposing each bit is
              a consensus process in exactly their sense, for the outcomes “some thread decided
              0” and “some thread decided 1”: copies started fresh can reach either outcome and
              never both, because the first passing check fixes the oldest fact and every later thread
              reads the same one; and an outcome survives company, because pooled threads
              keep their decisions. So by their theorem the composition isn’t monotonic, and
              the small machine sits on their non-monotonic side. That verdict is cheap, though:
              a composition that jams any two moved states makes every shared-state machine
              non-monotonic, so the encoding puts it there, not the fact table. What does the
              work in the run, making every thread read the same outcome, is the order of the
              fact table, the same as above; a store that refuses a stale commit for good, as the
              version rule does, refuses in the same spirit. The shared-memory version of their
              split is the pair of results above: the small machine’s object reaches agreement for
              any number of processors, and the monotone variant, with its table unbounded and
              no charge for failing that anyone can see, doesn’t reach it even for two.
                  Security people know the pattern by a third name. A check that blesses a value,
              and a write that takes the blessing away, is close kin to dynamic taint tracking,
              where a label rides along with the data and a sanitizing step changes it; the labels go
              back to the computer-security researcher Dorothy Denning’s 1976 lattice model of
              how information is allowed to flow. How much a monitor like that has to remember
              is a studied question too: Chamseddine Talhi, Nadia Tawbi and Mourad Debbabi
              (2008), three security researchers at universities in Quebec, worked out which rules
              a monitor can still enforce when its memory is bounded. The version rule is one
              small, specific member of that family, done by the step.
                  Notice what isn’t a write. DEC on a counter that’s already 0 doesn’t change the
              counter, so it doesn’t change the version. It’s a test that happens to move the line
              number.
                  The fact table. Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
              overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK traps. It doesn’t push
              an old fact out to make room. That’s a choice with a bill attached, and I’ll put the
              bill in the subsection on what this machine doesn’t do.
                  Traps. Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else in the core; the
              ledger still takes the instruction’s cost. Once it’s up, every instruction leaves the
              core alone. A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove things about any list
                                                                                   15.3 The machine   307


of instructions, programs or otherwise, because an adversary doesn’t have to run
my programs; they can feed the machine whatever they want. For those lists, an
instruction after a trap is still charged its cost, and still changes nothing.
    Now the exact version.

Definition 15.1 (Properties, checker, meaning). A property is one of: Zero, Even,
or Ge(n) for a whole number n. The checker eval( p, v) computes yes or no: v = 0
by equality, evenness by the parity function, n ≤ v by comparison. The meaning
holds( p, v) is the arithmetic statement: v = 0; there is an m with v = 2m; n ≤ v.



Lemma 15.1 (The checker says what it means). For every property p and every
whole number v, eval( p, v) = yes if and only if holds( p, v).

Proof. Split on the three properties. Equality with zero returns yes exactly at zero;
comparison with n returns yes exactly when n ≤ v. For evenness, the parity checker
returns yes at 0, no at 1, and the same answer at v + 2 as at v. Induction in steps of
two gives yes exactly at 0, 2, 4, . . ., the numbers 2m. Those are precisely the three
meanings.


Definition 15.2 (Core, state, claim, start). A core k holds two counters A, B and
their versions (whole numbers), a line number, a fact table (a list of facts, a fact
being a triple of a property, a counter and a version), a channel (empty or one fact),
and a trap bit. Write val(k, c) and ver(k, c) for counter c’s value and version. A state
s is a core, written core(s), with a ledger µ(s) and a flag cert(s). The claim p of c in
k is the fact ( p, c, ver(k, c)). The table’s room is 16. The start start( a, b) has counters
a and b, versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an empty channel, the trap down, µ = 0
and the flag down. A state is clean when its table and channel are empty and its flag
is down.


Definition 15.3 (Instructions, costs, the step). The instructions are INC c, DEC c j,
HALT, CHECK p c, COMMIT p c and CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap
down as in the table above. Passing any check, commitment or certification requires
the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK passes when eval( p, val(k, c)) =
yes and the table holds fewer than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim p of
c is in the table, and CERTIFY passes when the channel holds a fact; a failing one
sets the trap and changes nothing else. On a core with the trap up, every instruction
308   15 The smallest honest machine


               changes nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost 1, the rest 0. One step
               on a state is
                                                                                                  
                   exec(s, i ) = cexec(core(s), i ), µ(s) + cost(i ), cert(s) ∨ fires(core(s), i ) ,

              where cexec is the core’s step and fires(k, i ) is yes exactly when i is CERTIFY and
              passes at k. For any list t of instructions (a trace), run(t, s) applies them in order
              and cost(t) adds their costs. A program is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a
              program run fetches the instruction at the line number and executes it, and stops
              when the trap is up, the line holds HALT, or the line holds nothing.

                  Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The
              core moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag
              becomes “it was up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.” The core’s move doesn’t
              mention µ or the flag anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.
                  A worked run, the shortest one there is. The program: CHECK is zero A; COMMIT
              is zero A; CERTIFY. Start at start(0, b), for any b. Line 1: A is 0, the checker says
              yes, the table is empty so there’s room, and the fact (zero, A, 0) goes in. µ = 1. Line
              2: the claim about A’s current edition is (zero, A, 0), and it’s right there. Into the
              channel. µ = 2. Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up. µ = 3. Line 4 has
              no instruction, so the program stops. Three paid acts, in order, a flag that’s up, and
              a channel that names the last earned commitment, which here is (zero, A, 0).
                  Now start the same program at start(5, b). Line 1: A is 5, the checker says no,
              the trap goes up, µ = 1, and the program stops right there. The flag is down, and
              you can run it as long as you like: it stays down. That second run is the point of the
              first. The same three instructions certify from some starts and refuse from others,
              because the check could have failed, and from most starts it does. A check like that
              has a no pile, which is the only kind Section 14 counts as establishing anything.
                  Could I have picked an even dumber claim? Sure. CHECK at least 0 A passes
              on every number there is, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for
              3 from every start. The step doesn’t ask whether the question was worth asking,
              and it shouldn’t. Worth is a count over the rivals a run narrows (Section 8), and
              a step that sees one state has no list of rivals to count. What the step checks is
              order, aboutness and that the checker tells the truth. What a check that can’t fail
              is worth, the entitlement count says exactly: zero bits, for three marks. The price
              is for standing behind the claim. What the claim bought is a separate number, one
              the step doesn’t compute, and I keep the two apart. It’s on the list at the end of the
              chapter.
                  Others walked into the same line from communication. Three theoretical com-
              puter scientists, Oded Goldreich, Brendan Juba and Madhu Sudan (2012), built a
              theory of communication with a partner you may not understand, in which getting
                                                       15.4 It computes everything two counters can   309


a message across counts only as a way to reach a goal, and the central notion is
sensing: being able to tell, from what you see, whether you’re making progress. The
sensing they ask for is safe: when there’s no progress it says so, and so it never
reports a success that didn’t happen. Their main result, as I read it, is that safe
sensing, with a partner who could help if you spoke its language, is enough for one
strategy that reaches the goal with every such partner. A check that can fail and
never lies, standing in front of a verdict you can’t take back. That’s their theorem, in
their setting, and it’s the same shape.


15.4 It computes everything two counters can

First the base, because if the base can’t compute, nothing else here matters.

Definition 15.4 (Two-counter program, compile, window). A two-counter program
M is a list of instructions, each either MINC c or MDEC c j. A configuration is a
triple (line, a, b). One step of M: if the line holds no instruction, M has stopped;
MINC adds one to c and goes to the next line; MDEC subtracts one from c and goes
to line j if c is above 0, and goes to the next line if c is 0. mrun(n, M, x ) is n steps
from x, staying put once stopped. The compile of M replaces each MINC c by INC c
and each MDEC c j by DEC c j. The window of a core k is the triple (line number,
val(k, A), val(k, B)).



Theorem 15.2 (Step for step). For every two-counter program M and every core
k with the trap down: M has stopped at window(k) if and only if the program
compile( M ) has halted at k; and if M steps from window(k ) to y, then one program
step of compile( M ) from k lands on a core with window y and the trap still down.
So for every n, n program steps of compile( M ) from k land on a core whose window
is mrun(n, M, window(k )), with the trap down.

Proof. Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If it’s
MINC c, the compiled INC c adds one to c and goes to the next line, which is exactly
the window’s move (the version also moves, but the window doesn’t show versions).
If it’s MDEC c j, split on whether c is 0, and both sides do the same thing in each
case. Neither instruction can trap. The run statement is induction on n, one step at
a time.
310   15 The smallest honest machine




              Theorem 15.3 (Halting matches). For every two-counter program M and whole
              numbers a, b: M stops after some number of steps from (1, a, b) if and only if the
              program compile( M ) halts after some number of program steps from start( a, b).

              Proof. The start has window (1, a, b) and its trap is down. Apply Theorem 15.2
              after any number n of steps: the two configurations still have the same window, the
              trap is still down, and one is stopped exactly when the other is halted. The same n
              witnesses termination in either direction.
                    Now the part that isn’t mine. Two-counter universality is Minsky’s, and the
               constructions of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors connect it to several
               other models. The counter convention matters: DEC at zero goes on to the next
               instruction; otherwise it takes one off and jumps, the convention used in Andrej
               Dudenhefner’s certified decision procedures for two-counter machines (2022). Ap-
               pendix K builds the route from a tape to counters, packs finitely many counters
               into two, and gives the halting diagonal. The remaining step here is to match
               that two-counter machine to this machine’s INC/DEC fragment, instruction for
               instruction.
                    I want to be exact about what “undecidable” means in the theorem below, because
               it’s stated as a connection between two problems. Suppose you had a procedure that
               answered the halting question for this machine. Then you could write a program
               that lists, one by one, every single-tape Turing machine that doesn’t halt. No such
               list can exist: the ones that do halt can already be listed (just run them all, a step at
               a time, and call out each one as it stops), and with both lists running side by side
               you’d have a halting decider. So the theorem says: a decider here would give you
               that impossible list.


              Theorem 15.4 (Halting is undecidable for this machine). The two-counter machine
              with the instruction convention just stated agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its
              step, its stop, and its termination match those of the compiled program, so its
              halting problem at ( M, a, b) has a positive answer if and only if compile( M) halts
              from start( a, b). Consequently, the question “does program P halt from start( a, b)?”
              is undecidable in the following reduction sense: a decider for it would make the
              complement of single-tape binary Turing machine halting enumerable.

               Proof. The agreement is a case split on the counter-machine instruction at the
               current line, and then induction along the run, ending in Theorem 15.3. Composing
               a proposed decider for the compiled program with the compile map would decide
                                                    15.5 It’s a Thiele machine, and the flag is a latch   311


two-counter halting. The tape-to-counter reduction in Appendix K would then
decide single-tape binary halting and so list its complement, as claimed.
     What that buys, and what it doesn’t. It buys: the base of this machine is a
universal machine in Minsky’s sense, and no algorithm can predict in general what
it’ll do. What it doesn’t buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives
conveniently. The counters start holding a and b, given directly; there’s no encoding
layer in this construction. Minsky’s prime-power packing is how you’d get from
“any Turing machine” to “two counters,” and I use that construction as it stands
(Appendix K.3 sets it out).
     Is “given directly” just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody
found exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, then at the MIT AI Lab, wrote a
ten-page memo titled “A Two Counter Machine Cannot Calculate 2 N .” He spells out
the convention first: a counter machine computing a function starts with n in one
counter and zero in the others. Then he gives a proof that a two-counter machine
started that way can’t compute 2n . That’s his theorem, and I don’t reprove it. What
I prove is a cousin, in Appendix D.4 (Theorem D.23): no program multiplies every
input by one large constant fixed by the program’s length. So the packing Minsky
needs is precisely the thing two plain counters can’t do for themselves. Hand the
small machine its inputs straight and there are functions of them it can’t compute;
hand it the inputs already packed and it computes anything a Turing machine can.
That’s no contradiction with the undecidability above, which ranges over every
program and every starting pair, packed ones included. The base hides nothing. It
just needs its input pre-chewed, and the chewing is somebody else’s.


15.5 It’s a Thiele machine, and the flag is a latch

Now the record. Three facts first, all of them read straight off the step line.


Theorem 15.5 (Ledger, toll, permanence). For every state s and instruction i,
µ(exec(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ), and for every trace t, µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + cost(t).
If cert(s) is down and cert(exec(s, i )) is up, then i is CERTIFY, it passes at core(s),
and cost(i ) ≥ 1. If cert(s) is up, so is cert(exec(s, i )).

Proof. Read the ledger component of Definition 15.3: it adds exactly cost(i ). Re-
peated substitution along a trace gives the sum of its costs, or, equivalently, in-
duction on the length of the trace does. The flag’s new value is its old value or
fires(core(s), i ). So a change from down to up needs that event, and the event needs
a passing CERTIFY. CERTIFY costs 1. An already true flag stays true under the same
disjunction.
312   15 The smallest honest machine


                  The middle clause of those three is Section 2’s toll, for this machine. Which means
               this machine is one of the things Section 2 was about, and Section 2’s universal floor
               applies to it without my lifting a finger.


              Theorem 15.6 (The small machine is a Thiele machine). The states, the instructions,
              the step exec, the cost and the flag, with the toll of Theorem 15.5, form a Thiele
              machine (Definition 2.1). So the universal floor (Observation 2.1) holds here: if
              cert(s0 ) is down and cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

              Proof. Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions 15.2 and 15.3, their step and
              cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the five components of Definition 2.1.
              Theorem 15.5 supplies its one required rule. Applying Observation 2.1 gives the
              claimed bound.
                  Then Section 10. Section 10 said: take any base, and any record that answers
               only to the base and never comes back down, and the record is a latch. This machine
               has a base: a program together with a core, stepping by the program step. And it
               has a record, the flag, with the ledger riding along. So the question is whether it’s a
               base-driven extension in Section 10’s five-rule sense (Definition 10.2), and if it is,
               Section 10 does the rest.



              Theorem 15.7 (The flag is a latch of the base). Let the base have states (program,
              core), stepping by the program step, starting at start( a, b)’s core for any a, b, and
              halting when the program has halted. Map each (program, state) to (program, core).
              Then the machine, run as a closed machine on (program, state), is a base-driven
              record over that base, and so its flag factors as the latch (Observation 10.1) of the
              event “the next instruction is a CERTIFY that passes.”

              Proof. First the cover (Definition 10.1): the map sends starts onto starts, it commutes
              with the step because the core’s move never reads µ or the flag, and whether the
              program has halted is read off the core. Then the rules of Definition 10.2 one at a
              time. Driven by the computation: the next flag is the old flag or “the next instruction
              is a passing CERTIFY,” which is a function of the base state and the old flag (that’s
              the step line). Ledger: µ only adds. Toll: Theorem 15.5. Permanence: Theorem 15.5.
              A reachable write: the three-line program of the worked run raises the flag from a
              start. Section 10’s theorem then gives the factorization.
                                                                    15.6 Commitments are earned   313


   So far, nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Parts I and II
already promised about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part
neither of them could give.


15.6 Commitments are earned
Here’s the shape before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of
instructions at all, chosen by somebody who’d love to cheat. Look at the moment
a COMMIT would pass. Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there’s a CHECK of
exactly the same claim that passed and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and
between that CHECK and now, nothing touched the counter. Not “probably.” Not
“on the programs I wrote.” On every list of instructions anybody can write.
   To say “nothing touched it” exactly, one word.
