Definition 15.5 (Untouched). A list of instructions mid, run from a state s, leaves
counter c untouched when, for every way of splitting mid as t1 , then i, then t2 ,
executing i at the core reached by running t1 from s leaves both ver(·, c) and val(·, c)
as they were.



Theorem 15.8 (A commitment was checked first). Let s0 be clean and pre any trace
after which COMMIT p c would pass. Then pre splits as pre1 , then CHECK p c, then
mid, where: the CHECK passes at the core reached by pre1 ; CHECK p c and COMMIT
p c each cost at least 1; c’s version after pre1 equals its version after pre; and mid,
run from just after the CHECK, leaves c untouched.

Proof. COMMIT passes, so the claim ( p, c, ver(c)) for the current version is in the
table. By the no-forging invariant (Theorem 15.12 below), that fact was written by
a passing CHECK p c at some point pre1 , with the version c had then; since it’s the
current version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go down, and any
instruction that changes a counter’s value also raises its version, so an instruction in
mid that touched c would have left c’s version higher at the end than at the CHECK.
It isn’t. So nothing in mid touched c.



Theorem 15.9 (A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified). Let s0
be clean and t any trace with cert(run(t, s0 )) up. Then for some p and c, t is

         pre1 , CHECK p c, mid1 , COMMIT p c, mid2 , CERTIFY, post,
314   15 The smallest honest machine


              where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY
              passes at its state, c has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and
              mid1 leaves c untouched. And when the CERTIFY runs, the channel holds exactly
              the claim that COMMIT made: the fact (p, c, c’s version at the CHECK). CERTIFY
              takes no operand; this is what ties it to the claim.

              Proof. The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by Theorem 15.5
              it’s a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the channel, the channel
              starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some earlier COMMIT
              p c passed. Take the last one before the CERTIFY: the fact in the channel is the one
              it wrote. Theorem 15.8 at that COMMIT gives the CHECK, the equal version, and
              the untouched stretch, and the equal version makes the committed fact (p, c, c’s
              version at the CHECK).
                  And the failure side, so you can see the refusals are clean, with nothing left
               half-done:


              Theorem 15.10 (Unearned steps trap and change no claim). If COMMIT p c would
              not pass at a core k, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the channel and the
              table as they were. If CERTIFY would not pass at a state s, executing it puts the trap
              up and leaves the flag as it was.

              Proof. If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up.
              Otherwise, the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set
              the trap, leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch,
              and its fires value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false, which leaves
              it unchanged. The instruction’s charge still applies to the ledger.
                 If that rings a bell, it should. It’s Milner’s move from Section 14: in LCF a
              theorem is a value that only the rules of the logic can build, so nobody can just
              print one (Milner and two colleagues on his Edinburgh project, Michael Gordon and
              Christopher Wadsworth, wrote the system up in 1979, and Gordon, who went on to
              build the HOL prover at Cambridge, told its history in 2000). Here the thing nobody
              can print is one bit, and what guards it is one step rule. Milner’s guard was a type
              checker. Same architecture, much lower down.
                 A provenance theorem is also an itemised receipt, and the itemised receipt has
              a history that’s exactly this gap. James Ritty ran a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and
              believed some of his staff were pocketing money. On a steamboat trip to Europe in
              1878 he watched a mechanism that counted the turns of the ship’s propeller, and
              wondered whether something like it could count the money instead. In 1879 he and
                                                                 15.7 What a passing check means   315


his brother John patented a “Cash Register and Indicator,” and they sold a version
under the wonderful name Ritty’s Incorruptible Cashier. The first model was this
book’s counter (Section 6) with brass on it: press a key, the amount goes onto a dial
showing the day’s running total. No drawer, no paper. At closing time you hold the
dial up against the cash. And that’s all a total can do. It tells you that the money is
short. It can’t tell you which sale went missing or who rang it up. The paper came
later. The patents passed to other owners, first a Cincinnati salesman named Jacob
Eckert, and in 1884 to John H. Patterson, who renamed the business the National
Cash Register Company, and the story told about that company is that it added a
paper roll: one copy kept for the shop’s own books, one handed to the customer.
That last part I only have from histories of the company and of the machine, so hold
it the way you’d hold any company’s story about itself. The order is right either way:
first a total that can tell you something’s wrong, then a list that tells you where. The
ledger µ is the dial. Theorem 15.9 is the list: which CHECK, of which claim, about
which edition, before which COMMIT. The theorem supplies that list about the run.
The machine doesn’t keep it as data anyone can read back from the end state, and
nothing in the theorem gives a procedure for rebuilding it from there. A fact in the
table holds a property, a counter and a version number. That’s neither the counter’s
value back then nor a log of what happened in between.
    Read Theorem 15.9 once more for what it doesn’t say. Between the CHECK and
the COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY,
it isn’t promised anything. You can check A is even, commit to it, add one to A,
and then certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about
the edition that was current when you committed. The certificate is historical: it
says “this was checked and committed about this edition,” and it says nothing about
whether that’s still true. I think that’s the right meaning for a certificate (a birth
certificate doesn’t expire when the baby grows), but it’s a meaning, and you should
know which one you’re getting. So a certificate doesn’t say the claim holds at the
CERTIFY, and it doesn’t say the claim holds at the end of the run. A CERTIFY that
rechecked the version would give a different guarantee. That’s a possible extension,
and the historical theorem doesn’t need it.


15.7 What a passing check means

Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn’t yet say the CHECK was right, and
that’s a separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly
ordered chain of check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to
everything. So: what does a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?
316   15 The smallest honest machine




              Theorem 15.11 (Checker soundness). Let s0 be clean and t any trace, and let k
              be the core of run(t, s0 ). For every fact ( p, c, v) in k’s table with v = ver(k, c), the
              property holds of the counter’s current value: holds( p, val(k, c)). In particular, if
              COMMIT p c would pass at k, then holds( p, val(k, c)).

              Proof. Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a
              version no higher than its counter’s, and if its version equals its counter’s, its property
              holds of its counter’s value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds
              there. A passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said
              yes, so by Lemma 15.1 the property holds. A write raises one counter’s version, so
              every old fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer
              applies to it. Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after
              every instruction, so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where
              the claim is in the table at the current version.
                  So, on a run from a clean start, a live fact means exactly this: one of three
              arithmetic properties holds of one counter’s current value. Not “the program is
              correct.” Not “the number is interesting.” The property, of the value, now. That’s
              all “checked” means on this machine, and it’s enough to be true. Three events stay
              separate here. The property holding of the value is one. A CHECK passing is another:
              a CHECK of a property that holds still doesn’t pass when the table is full or the trap
              is already up. A certification is a third, and it needs a COMMIT and a CERTIFY after
              the CHECK. So a CHECK that didn’t pass says nothing about whether its property is
              false.
                  So who checked the checker? Nothing on the record did. From a clean start, the
              record carries the run’s half of the story: a CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same
              claim about the same edition, then a CERTIFY. The other half, that the checker says
              yes exactly when the property holds, isn’t in any run. It’s Lemma 15.1, a proof
              about the little program the step calls, priced by nothing on the ledger. So a claim
              established here stands on two legs: a fact about this run, carried by the record, and
              a fact about the checker, carried by a proof that whoever reads the record has to
              accept. That’s the Münchhausen trilemma from Section 14 taking its third horn on
              purpose: the chain of reasons stops at a proof, named and on the page, where you
              can decide whether you’d have stopped there too. And the entitlement it gives is the
              reader’s. The machine doesn’t know anything. It keeps the order.
                  The question in that paragraph is older than any checker, and its most famous
              wording isn’t about what you’d guess. “Who will guard the guardians?” gets quoted
              about governments and police and, lately, proof assistants. Where’s it from? Plato’s
              Republic has the worry, sort of: in Book III (at 403e), Glaucon, Plato’s older brother
                                                                  15.7 What a passing check means   317


and one of the people Socrates is talking with, says it would be absurd for a guardian
to need a guardian, which is close in words and opposite in mood, a man calling
the question silly. The Latin, quis custodiet ipsos custodes, is from the Roman satirist
Juvenal’s sixth satire, and it’s a joke about a husband. His friends tell him to bolt his
wife in and set guards on her; the line asks who’ll watch the guards, since she’ll start
with them. And it gets better. In 1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt,
found extra lines of that satire in a medieval manuscript in the Bodleian Library,
lines the other copies lack, partly overlapping the familiar ones, and the famous
question sits in that tangle. Scholars have argued ever since about whether those
lines are Juvenal’s at all. So the most quoted sentence about trusting the checker
comes with a doubtful source of its own. Does that change anything here? No. The
answer used here is simple: you never get rid of the last guard, you make the last
guard small enough to watch yourself. Lemma 15.1 is one line per property. Euclid
had the instinct: five postulates you can hold in your head, and everything else
meant to follow from them.
    That split, a fixed checker proved sound from outside and a process that only
gets to act when the checker says yes, has a name in the writing on self-improving
programs. The AI researcher Jürgen Schmidhuber, at the IDSIA lab in Lugano,
described a Gödel machine (2003) that rewrites its own code only after its built-in
proof searcher has proved the rewrite useful, and Benja Fallenstein and Nate Soares
(2015), researchers at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, survey
agents that reason about their successors through formal proofs a fixed checker
accepts. Same architecture, aimed at a different question: they want to know when
a machine may trust a smarter version of itself, and this machine only wants to know
whether a flag was earned. Keeping the checker’s proof outside the machine is my
design choice. The nearest theorem, in Section 13, is narrower: no procedure the
substrate can represent decides, for every program, a property that depends only on
behaviour and holds of one program and fails of another. It doesn’t say a machine
can’t check a proof about a checker, or verify a restricted part of itself.
    Soundness rules out a lying checker. It doesn’t rule out a pointless question:
at least 0 has a perfectly sound checker and an empty no pile, as the worked run
showed.
    Program checking has a theory of its own, and its founding paper asks for a
checker that could have said no. The computer scientists Manuel Blum and Sampath
Kannan (1989; journal version 1995) defined a checker for a computational problem:
given a program and an input, it may run the program as it likes, and it must say
“correct” with high probability when the program is right everywhere and “buggy”
with high probability when its answer on that input is wrong. A checker that always
says “correct” isn’t one. Here the checker is fixed, deterministic and proved sound
318   15 The smallest honest machine


              once, and the part of their demand that survives is the fourth clause of certified
              Thiele-complete (Definition 15.7 below): some claim whose check can fail.


               15.8 Nothing gets forged
              The proof of Theorem 15.8 leaned on an invariant I promised to show you. Here it
              is. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions get a fact into
              the table without a CHECK writing it? A DEC with a funny jump target, a COMMIT
              after a trap, something I didn’t think of? I answer it one instruction at a time, which
              is the only way I trust myself to answer it.

              Definition 15.6 (Earned fact; no forgery). After a trace t from s0 , a fact f = ( p, c, v)
              is earned when t is pre, then CHECK p c, then mid, where the CHECK passes at the
              core reached by pre, f is exactly the claim p of c at that core, and, if f is live at the
              end (v equals c’s version after t), mid leaves c untouched. The trace has no forgery
              when every fact in the table after it is earned.



              Theorem 15.12 (No forging). For every core k, instruction i and fact f in the table
              after executing i at k: either f was already in k’s table, or i is CHECK of f ’s property
              and counter, it passes at k, and f is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has
              no forgery, so does that trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean
              start, every trace has no forgery.

              Proof. The first part is a case for each of the six instruction kinds: only a passing
              CHECK adds anything, and it adds exactly its claim. For the second, a new fact is
              earned by the CHECK that just wrote it; an old fact stays earned, and if it’s still live
              after the new instruction, its counter’s version didn’t move, so the new instruction
              didn’t touch the counter and the untouched stretch grows by one. A clean start has
              an empty table, which has no forgery, and the step carries it along any trace.
                 The closest earlier result is in capability hardware, and it’s much bigger. The
              computer scientists Jack Dennis and Earl Van Horn, at MIT, introduced capabilities in
              1966: tokens a process has to hold to touch an object, which it can pass on and can’t
              forge. CHERI, a capability extension of real instruction sets built at the University
              of Cambridge and SRI International, rests on that idea, and in 2020 Kyndylan
              Nienhuis and twelve coauthors proved, for the whole CHERI-MIPS instruction set,
              that arbitrary code given some capabilities can’t increase them as it runs (up to any
              change of protection domain). That’s nothing gets forged across a full instruction
                                                                            15.9 A full table traps   319


set. Theorem 15.12 is the same shape, one instruction at a time, for six instruction
kinds and a table of checked facts.


15.9 A full table traps
Sixteen facts of room, and no eviction. Two halves to prove: nothing ever leaves,
and nothing ever overflows.


Theorem 15.13 (Bounded table, no eviction). Every instruction keeps every fact
already in the table. If the table holds 16 or more facts, CHECK p c puts the trap
up and leaves the table as it was. If the table holds at most 16 facts, it still holds at
most 16 after any instruction.

Proof. With a raised trap no instruction changes the table. With the trap down, only
CHECK can change it, and a successful CHECK adds one fact without removing an
entry. Success requires a previous length strictly below 16, so the new length is at
most 16. At length 16 or greater that branch is unavailable: CHECK raises the trap
and preserves the table. Every other instruction preserves it as well.
    Why trap? Why not make room? Because “making room” means deciding which
fact dies, and a fact that can die is a fact whose absence you have to explain later.
A table that only grows keeps the checked facts available to read back, and the
provenance proofs above lean on exactly that. The bill for it is real, though, and it’s
in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the machine doesn’t do.


15.10 The window can’t see the record

Section 7 was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the
theorem that a window which shows the same before-and-after pair for a raise and
a non-raise cannot price both exactly (Observation 7.2). Here’s the smallest pair I
could build where the window is Minsky’s view of the machine (line number and
the two counters) and the record is everything else.
    Run two traces from start(0, 0). The earned run is CHECK is zero A; COMMIT
is zero A; CERTIFY. The idle run is DEC A 0, three times. In the idle run, A is 0
every time, so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs end
on line 4, with A = 0 and B = 0, both versions 0. Through the window, identical.
One of them has paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag up. The
other has paid nothing, holds nothing, can’t commit, and its flag is down. Two
photographs, same picture, different people.
320   15 The smallest honest machine




              Theorem 15.14 (Same window, different record). The earned run and the idle run
              from start(0, 0) end at cores with the same window and the same versions of A and
              B, and with different ledgers, different flags, different tables, and different answers
              to “would COMMIT is zero A pass.”

              Proof. In the earned run, CHECK adds (Zero, A, 0), COMMIT puts that fact in the
              channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. No counter
              is written. In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without
              writing a counter or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or
              commitment. So both final windows are (4, 0, 0) with versions (0, 0). The earned
              table contains the current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated
              difference in whether another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and
              flag.



              Theorem 15.15 (No window oracle). There is no function g from windows to whole
              numbers with g(window) = µ at the end of every trace from start(0, 0). Likewise
              there is no function from windows to yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every
              such trace, and none that gives whether COMMIT is zero A would pass.

               Proof. Such a g would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs
               of Theorem 15.14 share. The same for the flag and the commit right.
                 This is Section 7’s shape, made of pebbles: the record lives off the window.
              Anybody who only watches the counters and the line number, which is everything
              Minsky’s machine is, can’t tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether
              the flag is up. Not because they looked carelessly. Because it isn’t there to see.
                 Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy
              has an old fight about exactly that, and it’s worth a detour, because it tells you which
              side of the fight these theorems stand on. Leibniz said that for real things it can’t
              happen. There are no two individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote in
              1716 to Samuel Clarke, the English philosopher and theologian who was taking
              Newton’s side against him in an exchange of letters, and he told a story to go with it.
              A clever gentleman of his acquaintance, talking with him in front of the Electress
              Sophia of Hanover, Leibniz’s friend and patron, in the garden at Herrenhausen she
              had helped lay out, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. She dared him
              to. He “ran all over the Garden a long time” looking, and it was “to no purpose.”
              You can run his search tonight with a handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains
                                                                      15.11 The exact price is three   321


of rice: look hard enough and every pair differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max
Black, a Russian-born philosopher teaching at Cornell, pushed back with a universe
you can’t build at the table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same size, the
same colour, the same everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between
them. There isn’t one, and there are still two of them. People have argued about
Black’s spheres ever since, and I’m not going to settle it.
    Here’s why I don’t have to. Leibniz’s claim is about every property a thing has.
The theorems above are about three: the line and the two counters. The two runs
aren’t indiscernible in his sense at all: one has a fact in its table and its flag up, and
the other doesn’t. They’re indiscernible to a window, which is a much cheaper thing,
and it’s the thing that matters for a machine, because an observer of a machine only
ever gets a window. Leibniz’s gentleman would always find his difference if he could
look at everything. It doesn’t help him if all he’s allowed to look at is three things
about each leaf.
    There’s a horse in this, too, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a
mathematics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever
Hans, who answered arithmetic questions by tapping a hoof, and got them right,
in front of crowds. Same answers out as a horse that could count: that’s the idle
run’s matching window. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst stopped looking at the
answers and started changing the conditions, and published what he found in 1907.
Put blinders on Hans, or have him asked by someone who didn’t know the answer,
and the arithmetic fell apart. Hans was reading the questioner: tiny, unintended
movements of the head and body as the hoof reached the right number. That’s the
probe. Pfungst didn’t argue with the answers. He asked a question the answers
couldn’t fake, one that needed the real thing to be there, the way a COMMIT needs
a checked fact to be in the table: run COMMIT is zero A after each of the two runs,
and one passes and the other traps (Theorem 15.14). And the part of the story I
like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten was never persuaded by Pfungst and kept
showing his horse. A matching window doesn’t need a cheat behind it, which is why
you want a probe. An accusation is the wrong tool for it.


15.11 The exact price is three

Section 2 said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that’s true and too
modest. A raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT
needs a CHECK, and each of those is its own instruction costing one. So at least
three. One of what: three units of µ, one per paid act, each one the “one” I picked
back in the table. And three is the number of links in the chain. It isn’t a guess that
happens to hold.
322   15 The smallest honest machine


              Observation 15.16 (The minimum price of a certificate). If s0 is clean and
              cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 3 and µ(run(t, s0 )) ≥ µ(s0 ) + 3. For programs:
              if the flag is up after n program steps from start( a, b), then µ ≥ 3 there.
               Proof. Theorem 15.9 finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
               places in t, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
               statement is Theorem 15.5. A program run is the run of the instructions it actually
               executes, so the program form follows.
                   The three is three independent units, one for each part of a clean start. A flag
               that is down buys the first: a run that raises it costs at least one. An empty channel
               buys the second: with the flag down and the channel empty, a run that raises the
               flag costs at least two. An empty table buys the third, and that is the theorem above.
               Leave out any one part and its floor fails, and a cheaper certificate is there: with the
               flag already up it costs 0, with a commitment already in the channel 1, and with a
               live fact already in the table 2. The exact condition is this: every run from a state
               that ends with the flag up costs at least three exactly when the flag is down and one
               of two things holds: the trap is up, or the channel is empty and every fact in the
               table is about an older version of its counter. And three is paid exactly from every
               clean start whose trap is down.


              Theorem 15.17 (Three is tight). For all whole numbers a and b, run the program
              CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero A; CERTIFY for 4 program steps from start( a, b).
              If a = 0, it ends with the flag up and µ = 3 exactly. If a ̸= 0, it ends with the flag
              down and the trap up, and for every n, n program steps from start( a, b) leave the
              flag down.

              Proof. If a = 0, the checker for Zero says yes at 0, so the first instruction adds
              (Zero, A, 0) to the empty table and charges 1. No counter changes, so the second
              instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges 1. The third finds
              the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges 1. The line is now 4, beyond the
              three-instruction program, and the fourth program step adds no charge. The final
              ledger is exactly 3. If a ̸= 0, the checker says no, so the first instruction sets the trap
              and leaves the flag down. A program run takes no step once the trap is up, so every
              later program step leaves the state, flag included, exactly where it is.
                 The version whose check can’t fail, CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A;
              CERTIFY, certifies from every start for exactly 3. So the floor of three is reachable
              from every loaded start, and that’s the machine declining to police trivial checks.
              On that program the check distinguishes no inputs.
                                                                 15.12 What it takes to be certified   323


   That’s the worked run from early in this chapter, now as a theorem. The floor is
3, and a run whose check could have failed pays exactly 3, so 3 is the price. The
bound has no slack in it.
   Don’t mistake that 3 for a measure of how hard a claim is to certify. It’s the
same 3 for every claim, easy or hard, because only the three acts that make a
claim are priced and the counters work out whatever the check needs at no charge
on the ledger. A cost of certifying that grows with the claim would have to price
the checking itself, and that’s a different question with its own literature. Four
theoretical computer scientists, Guy Blanc, Caleb Koch, Jane Lange and Li-Yang
Tan (2022), studied one version of it under the name the query complexity of
certification: how many questions an algorithm has to ask a black-box function to
hand back a small certificate for its answer. Their count moves with the function.
Mine doesn’t move at all.
   And that’s every piece of the machine, standing on six instruction kinds: a base
that computes everything two counters can, a ledger that’s exact, a toll the universal
floor applies to, a flag that’s a latch of the base, a window that can’t see the record,
and, from a clean start, a commitment that can’t happen unless a check of the same
claim, on the same edition, came first and was right.


15.12 What it takes to be certified

Section 10.8 set the bar worth meeting, Thiele-complete, and it says nothing about
what the record is about. A clock fails it, and so does a machine whose record
never goes up. The small machine clears it (Theorems 15.26 and 15.18(2) below),
and it does more: its flag goes up only on top of a check of a claim, by a checker
proved to mean what the claim says, then a commitment to the same claim with
nothing changed underneath, then a certificate. A Thiele-complete machine can
raise its record with one mark that goes up from any state at all, a receipt for nothing
(Section 14). A certified one can’t. So here’s the second definition, the first one with
three things added, written so that any machine can be held up against it. You name
a language of claims first, then hand over a reading of the machine in that language,
a list of things, and then the reading has to pass four clauses.

Definition 15.7 (Certified Thiele-complete). A machine has states, moves, a step, a
cost for each move and a yes/no reading of each state, the record. A claim language
for it is fixed first: a type of claims with an exact equality test; a meaning for
each claim, a statement about a state; for each claim, a relation “the thing this
claim is about is unchanged” between two states; and a proof that a meaning that
holds keeps holding while the thing it’s about is unchanged. An interface over that
language hands over the rest: a universal base, meaning a two-counter configuration
324   15 The smallest honest machine


              shown by each state (its window), a class of live states, a move for each two-counter
              instruction, and a loaded state for each start (1, a, b); a checker that says yes or no
              to a claim at a state, with a proof that a yes means the claim’s meaning, as the
              language gives it, holds of that state; a set of clean states; a ledger, a whole number
              for each state; and a kind for each move: a base move, CHECK of a claim, COMMIT
              of a claim, or CERTIFY. The machine is certified Thiele-complete over the language
              when some interface over it meets four clauses, and certified Thiele-complete when
              some interface, with claims, meanings and “unchanged” of its own, meets them. (a)
              Universal base. Each two-counter instruction’s move is a base move; from every live
              state it acts on the window exactly as the instruction acts on a configuration, and the
              state stays live; each loaded state shows (1, a, b), is live and is clean; no base move
              changes the record; and a record that’s up stays up under every move. (b) Earned
              record. Clean states have the record down. Every run from a clean state that ends
              with the record up contains a CHECK of some claim c that passes, then a COMMIT
              of c with the thing c is about unchanged at every state in between, then a CERTIFY,
              with the record down just before that CERTIFY and up just after it. A passing check
              means its claim’s meaning holds of the state it checked, and a meaning that holds
              keeps holding while the thing it’s about is unchanged. (c) Exact prices. Base moves
              cost 0, each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY costs exactly 1, and each move adds its
              cost to the ledger. (d) Non-vacuity. Some claim c has a CHECK, a COMMIT and a
              CERTIFY such that those three moves alone, from a loaded state, raise the record
              exactly when c’s meaning holds there; and c holds at some loaded state and fails
              at another. A Thiele machine has a universal base when some interface gives it one
              and nothing more is asked: each two-counter instruction’s move acts on the window
              exactly as the instruction does from every live state and keeps it live, and each start
              (1, a, b) has a live loaded state showing it. Nothing is asked about the record, the
              prices or the checker.

                  An interface over a language becomes an interface of the plain kind by taking
               the language’s claims, meanings and “unchanged” as its own, and the four clauses
               are asked of that.


              Theorem 15.18 (Certified is Thiele-complete plus certification). (1) A machine is
              certified Thiele-complete through an interface exactly when it is Thiele-complete
              through the same interface read without its claims (its base moves as the computing
              moves, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY as the marks, the same universal base and
              ledger), and three more things hold: its loaded states are clean; clause (b) holds, so
              clean states have the record down, every run from a clean state that ends with the
              record up contains the earned chain, a passing check means its claim holds, and a
                                                                  15.12 What it takes to be certified   325


claim that holds keeps holding while what it’s about is unchanged; and clause (d)
holds, a claim whose three moves raise the record from a loaded state exactly when
it holds there, true at one loaded state and false at another. (2) Every certified Thiele-
complete machine is Thiele-complete. (3) Not the other way: the two counters with
two marks, one that raises the record when A is 0 and one that always raises it, is
Thiele-complete, and certified Thiele-complete through no interface.

Proof. (1) Clause (a) is (A) together with “loaded states are clean”. Clause (c) is
(C), with the three record kinds as the marks. Clause (b) says clean states have the
record down, which with clean loads gives (B), and it gives the earned chain. Clause
(d) gives (D): the claim’s three moves end with the record up from the loaded state
where it holds and down from the one where it fails. Going back, the same pieces
put the four clauses together again. (2) is (1) read left to right. (3) From any state
with the record down, counting A to zero costs no marks and the first mark then
raises the record: a raise for one mark from every clean state, where a certified raise
from a clean state takes three (Theorem 15.20(3)).
    So certification is exactly three things on top of the bar: clean starts, an earned
record (the chain, a checker proved sound, claims that stay true while what they’re
about is unchanged), and a claim that could have come out either way. Everything
Section 10.8 proved holds of every certified machine. What this section adds is what
those three things buy: a floor of three instead of one, from a clean start a raise that
is always a CERTIFY, a check that can fail, and no receipt without a check.
    Why the language comes first. If the interface could name the meanings, it could
take “the checker says yes” as the meaning of every claim, and checker soundness
would hold for nothing. In the language-first form the meanings are written down
before any checker is handed over, so “a checker proved to mean what it says” has
the content it has on the small machine: what the claim says is the language’s, and
the proof is that a yes from the checker makes it true. The theorems that build
certified Thiele-complete machines ask the checker for one thing more, that it say
yes exactly when the claim holds, because clause (d) needs a check that can come
out yes. The plain form stays because the theorems that follow hold for any interface
at all, so they hold over every language too.
    Read the four clauses as four plain sentences. (a) It computes anything a Turing
machine can, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine, and the
computing can’t reach the record: the base moves are the two-counter machine, they
leave the record exactly where it was, and a record that goes up stays up. (b) From
a clean start, the record goes up only on top of the small machine’s chain: a check
that passed, a commitment to the same claim with nothing changed underneath,
then a certificate. (c) Computing costs no marks on the ledger and each of the three
acts costs one mark, so the ledger counts the acts. The steps in between add nothing
326   15 The smallest honest machine


              to it. (A mark is a unit of the ledger, not of heat.) (d) Somewhere there’s a claim
              whose check could have said no. A machine whose every claim is “at least 0” doesn’t
              qualify, and neither does one with nothing to certify.
                  And look where the checker’s honesty sits. In (b), “a passing check means its
              claim holds” is a condition on the interface, proved once, outside every run, exactly
              where it sat for the small machine (Lemma 15.1), and over a claim language it’s
              proved against meanings the interface didn’t write. The definition doesn’t ask the
              machine to vouch for its own checker. The nearest reasons not to ask are Gödel’s
              second theorem, about a system proving its own consistency, and the diagonal of
              Section 13, about deciding a property of every program. Neither forbids a machine
              checking a proof about a checker, so keeping that proof outside is a choice. Nor does
              it ask the checker to be something a machine could run. Clause (b) wants a yes or no
              for every claim at every state, sound for the claim’s meaning, and nothing in it says
              that answer has to be computable. Every instance in this book has a checker that’s
              an actual program, so anything those machines certify could be listed by a program
              that runs them. For example, take a function that answers whether an arbitrary
              program runs forever. No program computes it (that’s Turing’s halting theorem).
              Hand the definition a checker built on it and it’s still met, and the machine certifies
              claims no program could ever confirm. Nothing in this book builds one. So “a
              certified Thiele-complete machine certifies exactly the claims a program could list”
              is true only with “and its checker is computable” added, and the definition doesn’t
              require that.
                  The same scope goes on Section 14’s “it isn’t more computing power.” The record
              (the flag and the ledger) is never read by the step that computes the next core,
              so erasing it changes no run, and it makes nothing faster. The checker is part of
              the machine under the record. With an oracle checker that machine decides what
              the oracle decides, since whether a CHECK traps is there for anyone to see; with a
              checker that’s a program, it does what programs do. And a checker that’s a program
              still makes CHECK a test at unit cost.


              Theorem 15.19 (CHECK is a unit-cost test). From any start ( a, b), the single move
              CHECK Ge(m) A costs 1, and the trap latch is down after it exactly when a ≥ m.

              Proof. At a start the latch is down and the table is empty, so the check passes exactly
              when eval(Ge(m), a) says yes, that is when m ≤ a; a failing check sets the latch.
              The price table charges a CHECK 1.
                  The two counters alone look at A only through the zero test of DEC, and started
               one pebble below a threshold or right at it, that test can’t come out differently until
               the pile has been counted down to zero, so they need about as many steps as the
                                                                 15.12 What it takes to be certified   327


threshold for what CHECK does in one. Theorem 15.38 gives the precise lower
bound and the matching ladder. So the record makes nothing faster, and CHECK, a
primitive test, can.
    Three kinds of exact. The word exact does three jobs in this book, and each job
keeps one name. Rise-only pricing charges at least one mark on every step that raises
the reading and nothing on any other step; its tightest bill, one mark per raise and
nothing else, is the exact schedule. Instruction-exact pricing charges every instruction
a fixed listed price. On this machine that’s one mark each for CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY and nothing for the rest, and the definition of certified Thiele-complete
calls it exact prices, not a toll, because it charges acts that raise nothing. CHECK
and COMMIT raise no flag, so the small machine is instruction-exact without being
rise-only, and no rule is broken by that. What the three marks pay for isn’t one thing
three times. A passing CHECK adds a fact to a table that holds sixteen, so its mark is
a price on room, one slot of a bounded store; COMMIT overwrites the channel and
CERTIFY raises the flag, each sending two states with the same base to one, so their
marks are prices on merges (Theorem 3.17). Room or merge, the two columns of
Part I: one mark of the first kind and two of the second. Simulation-exact accounting
is a host whose ledger equals its guest’s ledger at every point where the two runs
match, as the universal program U’s does (Appendix D.1). A machine can meet any
one of the three and fail the others.
    One word needs pinning before the theorems, using those three names. In clause
(c), exact prices means instruction-exact pricing: each of the three acts, CHECK and
COMMIT included, costs exactly one, so the ledger counts the moves filed as record
moves. That’s the acts that make a claim, and also a check that fails, a COMMIT of a
fact already committed, and a CERTIFY with the flag already up: each is filed as a
record move and costs one. Back in Section 6, one result is about rise-only pricing
in its tightest bill, the exact schedule: one mark on the step that raises the flag and
nothing on any other step. Measured against the flag alone, the small machine isn’t
rise-only, since CHECK and COMMIT raise no flag and cost one each; measured
the way (c) asks, it is instruction-exact. Neither is wrong. They answer different
questions: does the ledger count the acts, or does it charge the flag and only the
flag? Simulation-exact accounting, the third name, comes up with the universal
program U in Appendix D.1.


Theorem 15.20 (What every certified Thiele-complete machine has). Let a machine
be certified Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) It obeys the toll and has a
universal base; its base runs every two-counter program step for step from every
live state, and halting from a loaded state matches halting from the configuration
it shows. (2) Along any run, the ledger rises by exactly the number of CHECK,
328   15 The smallest honest machine


              COMMIT and CERTIFY moves in it. (3) A run from a clean state that ends with the
              record up contains at least three of those moves and raises the ledger by at least 3.
              (4) Some CHECK fails at some loaded state, on a claim that is false there, and some
              run from some loaded state raises the record. (5) On a run from a clean state, the
              move that raises the record is a CERTIFY. (6) Every move costs 0 or 1, and some
              move costs 0.

              Proof. (1) A raise of the record isn’t made by a base move, by (a), so it’s a record
              move, which costs one by (c). Running a program on the base is induction on its
              steps, each matched by (a). (2) is (c), added up along the run. (3) Clause (b) finds
              a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different places, and (2) counts them.
              (4) is (d): the three moves certify exactly where the claim holds, the claim fails at
              some loaded state, and the check can’t pass there because (b) says a passing check
              means the claim holds; at the loaded state where it holds, the three moves raise the
              record. (5) Cut the run just after the move where the record rises. That shorter run
              starts clean and ends with the record up, so clause (b) puts the record down right
              before a CERTIFY in it and up right after. The record never comes down, so it rises
              only once, and that CERTIFY is the move. (6) Every move is a base move or a record
              move, and (a) supplies base moves.



              Theorem 15.21 (The language first, and what a certificate then means). (1) A
              machine that is certified Thiele-complete over some claim language is certified
              Thiele-complete, so every part of Theorem 15.20 holds of it. (2) If a machine is
              certified Thiele-complete through an interface whose claims have an exact equality
              test, it is certified Thiele-complete over the language made of that interface’s claims,
              meanings and “unchanged,” with clause (b)’s proof that a meaning keeps holding
              as the language’s own. (3) If a machine is certified Thiele-complete over a claim
              language L, some interface over L meets the four clauses and has this property:
              every run from one of its clean states that ends with the record up contains a CHECK
              of a claim c of L that passed, then a COMMIT of c, and L’s meaning of c holds at the
              state the CHECK saw and at the state the COMMIT saw.

              Proof. (1) Take the plain interface the language-first one becomes. (2) The checker’s
              soundness and the keeping proof are the ones clause (b) already supplies. (3) Clause
              (b) gives the chain; the checker’s soundness proof against L gives c’s meaning at the
              state checked; L’s keeping proof carries it, through states where the thing c is about
              is unchanged, to the state committed.
                                                                 15.12 What it takes to be certified   329


   Part (2) says where the strength of the language-first form lives: in the naming.
Any reading can be turned into a language when its claims come with an exact
equality test, so for those “certified Thiele-complete over some language” asks no
more than certified Thiele-complete does. “Certified Thiele-complete over L,” for an
L written down without looking at the checker, says that what the machine certifies
is what L says. Every instance below is stated that way.
   Each item in the proof names the clause it comes from, and that’s all the definition
gives. A certified Thiele-complete machine needn’t have a fact table, a CHECK that
traps when it fails, a COMMIT that looks anything up, or claims about counters.
The definition asks for an earned chain on the runs that raise the record and leaves
the rest to the machine. So the small machine’s table provenance, its trap, and its
channel are facts about that machine, and they don’t carry over to every machine
that meets the definition. Through a plain interface its claims can be any labels
the interface names; over a claim language they are the language’s. Either way its
checker can be an oracle, as the halting-function checker above shows.
   The second half of (6) in Theorem 15.20, that some move costs 0, is the one
that rules out the clock: a machine that charges every move. It doesn’t rule out a
program that makes the ledger tick. On the host of Appendix D.1, a program that
checks one fact once and then commits it again before every instruction runs any
two-counter program with the flag down and pays one mark a step, plus one for the
check: the checked fact is about a counter the program never writes, so its edition
never changes, and every COMMIT finds it.
Observation 15.22 (A clock is a Thiele machine and isn’t certified Thiele-complete).
Take the two-counter machine, let every move cost 1, and take as the record any yes/no
question about its configuration whatsoever; or take a flag that switches on, and stays
on, the first time any chosen test of the configuration says yes. Either way the machine
obeys the toll and has a two-counter machine running inside it, and it is not certified
Thiele-complete. More generally, no machine whose every move costs at least 1 is
certified Thiele-complete.
Proof. Every move costs one, so any raise costs at least one: the toll holds for any
record. The machine’s own moves are the two-counter instructions, which gives the
universal base. But a certified Thiele-complete machine has a move priced 0, by
Theorem 15.20(6), and this one has none.
   (It also follows from Observation 10.13 and Theorem 15.18(2).) That’s short,
and it’s short because clause (c) does exactly the job it was written for: it says
computing costs no marks, and a clock charges marks for computing. The other
clauses earn their keep too, and that’s worth checking, because a definition with a
clause nothing needs is a definition hiding something.
330   15 The smallest honest machine




              Theorem 15.23 (Each clause does work). (1) Take a two-counter base priced 0
              with a ledger beside it, and one extra move TICK that costs 1 and raises a flag. It
              obeys the toll, and read with TICK as CERTIFY it meets the universal base clause
              and the exact prices clause; it is not certified Thiele-complete, and more generally
              no machine with a move that puts the record up from every state is. (2) Take a
              two-counter base priced 0 and a record that is down at every state, so it never rises.
              It obeys the toll and meets clauses (a), (b) and (c); it is not certified Thiele-complete,
              and more generally no machine whose record never rises is.

              Proof. (1) The base moves leave the flag alone, TICK never lowers it, the base costs
              0 and TICK costs 1, which gives (a) and (c). Through any interface, (a) gives a
              loaded state, which is clean, so its record is down by (b), and a move that puts
              the record up from every state raises it alone. Clause (b) would need a CHECK, a
              COMMIT and a CERTIFY inside that one-move run, and one move can’t be three.
              (2) The base gives (a) and costs 0, which with no record moves is (c). No run ends
              with the record up, so (b) asks nothing of a run, and a checker that always says no
              is sound for any meaning. Clause (d) needs a run from some loaded state that raises
              the record, and none does.
                  The paid latch, the TICK machine of (1), is the receipt for nothing from Section 14,
              wearing a universal base: honest about the price, silent about what was bought. The
              definition throws it out.
                  The silent machine of (2) meets three clauses and fails only (d). The paid latch
              fails (d) as well as (b), so it doesn’t show (b) doing work alone, and nothing above
              says whether a clock meets (a), (b) and (d). So here’s the sharper check, the usual
              evidence that a definition isn’t written around one machine: for each clause, a
              machine that meets the other three and fails it.


              Theorem 15.24 (The four clauses are independent). For each clause of Defini-
              tion 15.7 there is a machine with an interface that meets the other three clauses
              and fails that one. Each of the four machines obeys the toll and has a two-counter
              machine running inside it, and none of them is certified Thiele-complete through
              any interface at all. (a) fails for this chapter’s machine with one more move, DROP,
              priced 0 and read as a base move, which lowers the flag and trips the trap latch.
              (b) fails for this chapter’s machine with one more move, FORGE, costing one and
              read as a CERTIFY, which raises the flag on any state whose trap is down, with no
              commitment behind it. (c) fails for this chapter’s machine with every move costing
              one. (d) fails for the silent machine of Theorem 15.23(2).
                                                                15.12 What it takes to be certified   331


Proof. (a) Nothing moves a trapped state’s flag, so a run that uses DROP ends with
the flag down. A run from a clean state that ends with the flag up never used DROP;
it’s a run of this chapter’s machine, and Theorem 15.9 gives its chain. DROP is
priced 0 and read as a base move, so (c) holds, and (d) holds as it does for the
plain machine. A state with the flag up has it down after DROP. That breaks the
permanence in (a), and permanence is about the machine alone, so no interface
meets (a). (b) FORGE never lowers the flag, costs one and is read as a record
move, so (a), (c) and (d) hold as before. From a clean start FORGE alone raises the
flag, and a run of one move has no room for a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY.
Through any interface: (d) gives a loaded state from which the record rises, so its
trap is down; (a) makes that state clean, so its record is down by (b); and FORGE
alone raises it, which (b) forbids. (c) Clauses (a), (b) and (d) never mention a price,
and they hold as for the plain machine. Base moves cost one, so (c) fails, and every
certified Thiele-complete machine has a move priced 0 (Theorem 15.20(6)). (d) is
Theorem 15.23(2).
   Three of the four are this chapter’s machine with one thing changed, and in each
case the one clause it fails is the only thing keeping it out. Clause (c) also fixes
something it has no business fixing: the size of a mark. Double every price on the
small machine and it leaves the class, because its CHECK now costs two and (c) asks
for one. A definition that a change of currency breaks would be a strange one, so
here is (c) with the unit left open.



Theorem 15.25 (Any unit). Call a machine certified Thiele-complete at unit c, for
a whole number c ≥ 1, when some interface meets clauses (a), (b) and (d) and
this form of (c): base moves cost 0, each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY costs
exactly c, and each move adds its cost to the ledger. (1) At unit 1 that is certified
Thiele-complete. (2) Multiply every price of a certified Thiele-complete machine by
c ≥ 1 and the machine is certified Thiele-complete at unit c; divide every price of
a machine certified Thiele-complete at unit c by c and the machine, with the same
states, moves, step and record, is certified Thiele-complete, with the ledger read
as ⌊ℓ/c⌋. (3) At every unit some move costs 0, so the clock of Observation 15.22,
with any reading or any latch as its record, is certified Thiele-complete at no unit,
and neither is any machine whose every move costs at least 1. (4) At unit c, a run
from a clean state that ends with the record up contains a CHECK, a COMMIT and
a CERTIFY and raises the ledger by at least 3c; the claim it stands on held when it
was checked and still held when it was committed; and the move that raises the
record is a CERTIFY. (5) The small machine with every price doubled is certified
Thiele-complete at unit 2 and isn’t certified Thiele-complete.
332   15 The smallest honest machine


              Proof. (1) 1 · r = r. (2) Clauses (a), (b) and (d) never mention a price, and the two
              machines have the same runs. The ledger is multiplied along with the prices, or,
              going the other way, replaced by ⌊ℓ/c⌋, and ⌊(ℓ + c r )/c⌋ = ⌊ℓ/c⌋ + r for whole
              numbers, so the new ledger is a whole number and still adds each divided price.
              (3) Clause (a) makes the move for each two-counter instruction a base move, and
              base moves cost 0 at every unit. (4) Clause (b) finds the three acts in the run as
              before, and each costs c. The other two parts are the unit-1 results on the divided
              machine, which runs exactly as this one does. (5) is (2) with c = 2, and the doubled
              machine has a CHECK that costs 2, which no certified Thiele-complete machine has
              (Theorem 15.20(6)).
                  So the class doesn’t care what a mark is worth. It cares that computing costs no
               marks and that the three acts cost the same. The clock fails at every unit for the
               reason it failed at one: it charges marks for computing. I keep unit 1 in the definition
               because the small machine is built that way and every count in this chapter is in its
               marks.
                  Now the other direction. A definition nobody meets is as useless as one everybody
               meets.


              Theorem 15.26 (The small machine, the generic one and the sorted one are certified
              Thiele-complete). (1) This chapter’s machine is certified Thiele-complete, read with
              INC, DEC and HALT as base moves, CHECK p c and COMMIT p c as record moves
              on the claim “p holds of c,” CERTIFY as CERTIFY, the window as (line, A, B),
              live states as those with the trap down, start( a, b) as the loaded state for (1, a, b),
              “unchanged” as “same value and same version of c,” clean states as in Definition 15.2
              and the ledger as µ. (2) So is the same machine over any property language with
              an exact equality test and a checker proved to say yes exactly when the claim
              holds, as long as some property is true of one number and false of another. (3) In
              particular the machine whose property is “this counter, read as a list, is sorted” is
              certified Thiele-complete. (4) Every certified Thiele-complete machine is a Thiele
              machine (Definition 2.1) and obeys the universal floor; for this chapter’s machine,
              that system agrees step for step and cost for cost with the one of Theorem 15.6, and
              for the generic machine with the generic machine’s own. (5) Each of the three is
              certified Thiele-complete over its own claim language, fixed before the checker. For
              this chapter’s machine the language’s claims are pairs of a property and a counter,
              equal when both parts are, the meaning of “p holds of c” is the meaning holds of
              Definition 15.1 applied to c’s value, written without the checker, and “unchanged” is
              “same value and same version of c.” For the generic machine the language is built
              from the properties, their equality test and what they mean, and the checker isn’t
              part of it; the sorted machine is that case.
                                                                  15.12 What it takes to be certified   333


Proof. (1) Clause (a) is Theorem 15.2 together with the step line: INC, DEC and
HALT never touch the flag, the flag never comes down, and a start is clean with its
trap down. Clause (b) is Theorem 15.9 with checker soundness (Lemma 15.1), and
a meaning about c keeps holding while c’s value doesn’t move. Clause (c) is the
price table. Clause (d) is Theorem 15.17 with the claim “A is zero,” which holds
at (0, b) and fails at (5, b). (2) and (3) are the same argument with the property
language left open. For (3), read a number as a list in the list code: 0 is the empty
list, and 2x (2y + 1) is x followed by the list numbered y (every positive number
splits that way in exactly one way, and y is smaller than the number, so the reading
ends). The meaning of sorted is that each entry is at most the one after it. The
checker reads the list from the front: yes on the empty list and on a list of one entry,
and on x followed by a list that starts with y, yes exactly when x ≤ y and it says yes
on that rest. Induction on the length of the list shows it says yes exactly when the
meaning holds, and a language with one property has an exact equality test. The
sorted claim holds of the list numbered 18, which is [1, 2], and fails of 20, which
is [2, 1]. (4) is (1) of Theorem 15.20 and Section 2’s floor. (5) The interface over
the language is the one of (1), (2) and (3) with the meanings handed over by the
language, and the checker’s soundness is Lemma 15.1 and its generic form.
    Appendix E carries the same fixed-language form to other bases. The claims keep
their stated meanings; the new interfaces supply the checkers.
    And here’s the thing every machine that meets the definition can’t help doing.
It’s Section 7’s shape again, only this time it isn’t about one machine. It’s about all
of them.
Observation 15.27 (Every certified Thiele-complete machine hides its record and
its ledger from its window). Let a machine be certified Thiele-complete through an
interface, and let its window be the two-counter configuration its universal base shows.
(1) For every state s there’s a loaded state and one base move priced 0 from it that lands
on a state with s’s window, with the record down and the ledger unchanged. (2) There’s
a loaded state and two runs from it that end with the same window, one with the record
up and one with it down; and likewise two runs from one loaded state that end with the
same window and ledgers at least 3 apart. (3) So no function of the window gives the
record at the end of every run from every loaded state, and no function of the window
gives the ledger. (4) The same holds of the Thiele machine built from the machine.
Proof. Theorem 15.20(4) gives a loaded state and a run from it that raises the
record, and (3) says that run paid at least 3. Say it ends with window (line ℓ, x, y).
Two-counter instructions can steer any configuration to any other: empty A, fill it
to x + 1, empty B, fill it to y, then one DEC of A that jumps to line ℓ. Those are
base moves, so from the same loaded state they reach the same window, cost no
marks, and leave the record down, by (a) and (c). That’s two runs, one window, two
334   15 The smallest honest machine


               records and two ledgers, which is (2). A function of the window would have to give
               both answers on that one window, which is (3). For (1), load ( x + 1, y) and take just
               the last DEC. (4) is (3) read as a Thiele machine, whose runs are the machine’s.
                  The observer in that theorem sees one thing, the final window. An observer who
              sees the window before and after each step, or the whole trace of windows, or who
              is also handed the program and the start, is a different observer, and the collision
              says nothing about them; given the program and the start, the run is fixed and so is
              its record. The theorem’s two runs also start from the same loaded state, so they’re
              reachable witnesses, which is stronger than two arbitrary states that happen to look
              alike. And “no function of the window gives the record” is all it says. It doesn’t say
              the window tells you nothing about it.
                  Notice how little that took, and say it out loud so nobody mistakes it for more.
              It’s the fibre fact from Section 7 plus one observation: a universal base can print
              any window for no marks. Which is the point. The window here is everything a
              Turing machine would call the machine, the line and the counters. On a certified
              Thiele-complete machine, that’s never enough to tell you what was established or
              what it cost, and it can’t be, because computing costs no marks and can’t touch the
              record. A richer window, one that shows the flag, is a different window, and nothing
              above says it fails.


               15.13 The machine versus the program it runs
              The three hosts of Appendix D (the simpler host, U and UP ) all come down to one
              distinction, and it’s worth saying on its own, because the two halves are easy to run
              together: the machine doing the stepping (what the machine is) and the program it
              runs (what runs on it). The toll of Section 2 is a property of the machine doing the
              stepping. A rule a program keeps holds as long as the program keeps it.
                  Here’s the picture I keep for it. Play Monopoly on the counter of a real bank. The
              game has a bank of its own, with its own rules, and one of them is printed in the
              rules sheet: the Bank never goes broke, and if it runs out of money the Banker may
              issue more by writing on any ordinary paper. Inside the game that’s fine; the players
              agreed to it. The real bank’s teller, standing right there, has no opinion about any of
              it. Push a thousand in Monopoly money across her counter and her ledger doesn’t
              move, because her rules are about her own money. The game’s money is nothing
              to them. The real bank is the machine doing the stepping. The game is a program
              it happens to be hosting. A rule that lives in the game holds as long as the players
              keep to it. A rule that lives in the bank holds whatever the players do.
                  (And since the game is on the table: its box told an origin story for decades, that
              an out-of-work salesman named Charles Darrow invented it during the Depression.
              The board is older. Elizabeth Magie, an American writer and game designer with an
                                                     15.13 The machine versus the program it runs   335


economic argument about land to make, patented The Landlord’s Game in 1904,
with a square track, railroads and a square that sends you to jail, and in 1902, in The
Single Tax Review, described it as “a practical demonstration of the present system
of land-grabbing with all its usual outcomes and consequences.” Darrow sold his
version to Parker Brothers in 1935, and the company bought Magie’s patent for
a few hundred dollars, five hundred by the accounts I found. A story told by the
company selling the product is a lead to check, every time. It changes nothing about
banks. It’s a good reminder of who writes the story on the box.)
    A fixed machine can enforce an invariant in its own transition table, and that
includes a Turing machine. Give its tape a ledger track and a certification cell, and
write a table that never sets the cell without bumping the ledger: that machine
obeys the toll in its step relation. It’s a Thiele machine itself, so it can’t be a
counterexample to the model. What it doesn’t do, built the ordinary way, is enforce
the toll on the programs it runs. A universal machine whose table was written only
to interpret carries the simulated certification bit as plain data on its tape. If the
host is programmable, so that other code shares that tape with the guest, any of
that code can flip the bit without paying, because the host’s step has no opinion
about it. So an ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn’t enforce the toll
for its programs. That’s how it’s built. It could. The simpler host of Appendix D.3
enforces it by having its own step mirror the guest’s bit and charge for its crossing
(Observation D.10 and Theorem D.12), and the universal programs U and UP are
fixed tables that go one better: they earn their own flag, by their own check, commit
and certificate, exactly when the guest’s would rise, and pay on their own ledger
what the guest pays, U exactly and UP to within a surcharge of at most two when
the guest’s reading starts at no (Theorems D.5, D.4, D.7 and D.8). That’s a statement
about which reading a step rule prices. It isn’t a claim that Turing machines can’t
price one.
    Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the
detour. In 1974 two computer scientists, Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, asked
when a machine can run guests, a whole operating system inside another, efficiently
and safely. Their answer is one sentence you could check against any instruction
set. Call an instruction sensitive if it reads or changes the machine’s own settings,
the things the host has to keep for itself, and privileged if running it outside the
host’s own mode makes the machine stop and hand control to the host, which is
called a trap. For the kind of machine they modelled: if every sensitive instruction is
privileged, a host can be built. The guest runs at full speed, and whenever it touches
something that matters, the machine itself stops it and lets the host decide. That’s a
host whose step has an opinion.
    Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass
the test? The most common one didn’t. In 2000 John Scott Robin, an Air Force
336   15 The smallest honest machine


              officer, and Cynthia Irvine, a computer-security researcher at the Naval Postgraduate
              School, went through every instruction of Intel’s Pentium and found seventeen that
              are sensitive and not privileged; POPF, which loads the processor’s flags, is the one
              usually pointed at. A guest could run them and the host would never hear about
              it. The fixes came two ways: VMware rewrote the guest’s code on the fly so the
              troublesome instructions never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel
              and AMD added hardware support so they’d trap. Does that change anything here?
              Not the theorems. Popek and Goldberg were after speed and isolation. A record
              and a price weren’t their question, so their result isn’t mine and mine isn’t theirs. It
              changes the picture, though. The universal programs sit where they’d want a host to
              sit: the host’s own steps collect each guest’s toll and earn each guest’s record again.
              And an industry learned the same lesson the expensive way: a rule binds the guest
              only if it lives in the step underneath.
                  The smallest version of “a ledger beside an ordinary machine” is a Turing machine
              configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one more if
              it writes a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn’t disturb the machine.


              Theorem 15.28 (A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing). Let a Turing
              machine with transition table δ step a configuration c to tmn (δ, c) after at most n
              steps (stopping when δ has no entry). Pair each configuration with a counter, and
              step the pair by stepping the configuration and adding the step’s charge. Then for
              every n, δ and pair (c, m), the configuration part after at most n steps of the pair is
              tmn (δ, c). In particular this holds from (c, 0).

               Proof. By induction on n. For n = 0 both sides are c. For n + 1, if δ has no entry at
               c, both runs stop and both sides are c. Otherwise the pair steps to (c′ , m′ ) where c′
               is exactly the Turing machine’s next configuration, whatever m′ is, and the induction
               hypothesis at (c′ , m′ ) finishes it.
                  That’s a Turing configuration with a number riding beside it, and nothing more.
              It isn’t a Thiele machine in this book’s sense, so don’t read it as a Thiele machine
              running Turing machines; it isn’t one. A counter beside a machine is the scorekeeper’s
              tally from Section 2: honest about the machine, and kept by whoever holds the
              pencil.
                  One limit on all of this, so it isn’t read as more. Certification is one event. If you
              wanted a machine to carry some other kind of reading, you’d need an event for it,
              evidence for it and a price law for it, and nothing here supplies any of those.
                                                          15.14 Parts I and II, run on this machine   337


15.14 Parts I and II, run on this machine
Parts I and II proved their counts and their collisions for any system with the named
pieces, and they left a promise: that the machine of this part would be put through
them. Here it is. The eight-state machine of Section 3 gets run by the small machine,
price for price. Structural entitlement, the count of what narrowing a list of rivals
costs, is proved for every certified Thiele-complete machine, with the small machine
as a worked member, a larger search on the host that has a counter for every number,
and a run that shows the count’s one awkward hypothesis, the covering, can’t be
dropped. And the time a check saves gets an exact exchange rate, for the part of the
machine that has no record. (The no-bare-verifier result is in Section 7, next to the
collision it comes from.)
     The eight-state machine, run by the small machine. Look at the small machine
through a window that shows two things: its line number read modulo four, which
I’ll call its slot (the eight-state machine’s word from Section 3, unrelated to the slot
registers of the universal program U in Appendix D.1), and its flag. Call a state live
here, a narrower use of the word than in the definition of certified Thiele-complete,
when its trap latch is down, the fact “A ≥ 0” about A’s current version is in its table,
and its channel holds a commitment, which is what CERTIFY needs in order to run.

Definition 15.8 (The eight-state machine, compiled). Stamp is the single instruction
CERTIFY. Next-slot is the single instruction INC B. Jump to slot a, for a one of
0, 1, 2, 3, is the four instructions COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A; INC B;
DEC B a. The setup is the two instructions CHECK (A ≥ 0) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A.

   The two COMMITs in a jump change nothing but the line and the channel, and
each costs one, which is where the jump’s price of two comes from. The INC makes
B positive, so the DEC takes one off and jumps to line a for no marks, and B is back
where it was.


Theorem 15.29 (The small machine runs the eight-state machine). (1) For every
live state s and every move m of the eight-state machine, running m’s instructions
from s ends in a live state whose window is the eight-state machine’s step of s’s
window by m, and the ledger has risen by exactly m’s charge: one for stamp, two
for jump, zero for next-slot. (2) The same holds for any list of moves: the window
after the compiled list is the eight-state machine’s run of the list, the state is live,
and the ledger has risen by the sum of the charges. (3) So a run of compiled moves
from a live state that takes the flag from down to up has raised the ledger by at least
one. (4) From any start ( a, b), the setup ends in a live state with window (slot 3,
flag down) and the ledger at 2; after it, any compiled list runs as on the eight-state
338   15 The smallest honest machine


               machine from (slot 3, flag down), with the ledger at 2 plus the sum of the charges;
               and if the flag is up at the end, the whole run, setup included, contains the earned
               chain of Theorem 15.9.

               Proof. (1) By cases on the move. On a live state CERTIFY runs, because a committed
               claim is on the channel; it raises the flag, moves the line on by one and charges one.
               INC B moves the line on by one and charges no marks, and it touches only B and
               B’s version, so the fact about A and the commitment stand and the state stays live.
               In a jump, each COMMIT finds its fact in the table and succeeds, charging one, and
               the INC and the DEC charge no marks and end at line a, whose slot is a; the flag
               isn’t touched. (2) is (1) over the list, by induction. (3) The eight-state machine’s
               own toll (Section 3) says a run of its moves that takes the flag from down to up is
               charged at least one, and (2) carries that charge across. (4) CHECK (A ≥ 0) passes
               at every value of A and the COMMIT after it passes, which takes line 1 to line 3,
               slot 3, with two marks paid; then (2) applies. A raised flag was raised by a CERTIFY,
               and Theorem 15.9 gives the chain.
                 Three reservations, said now. The setup’s claim is true of every value, so its
              CHECK can’t fail; it’s there because the small machine won’t CERTIFY without a
              checked, committed claim. It isn’t there as a test. And the jump’s price of two is
              two paid COMMITs, a choice a program makes that the machine allows and doesn’t
              force. The window is a projection, too: the small machine’s full state keeps far more
              than eight states’ worth.
                 And the whole small machine isn’t the eight-state piece it runs. It merges some
              states without putting a mark on the ledger.


              Theorem 15.30 (The small machine’s merges). (1) A move of the small machine
              that takes the flag from down to up is CERTIFY; CERTIFY merges two different full
              states into one (a state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up land
              on the same state), and it costs at least one. (2) DEC A 2 also merges two different
