              full states, and it costs no marks. So it is false of the small machine that every move
              that merges is priced.

              Proof. (1) Only CERTIFY changes the flag, and it costs one. The two states with
              the flag down and up, and a committed claim, are the same state after CERTIFY.
              (2) Take a core at line 1 with A at 1 at version 0, and the same core with A at 0 at
              version 1. DEC A 2 takes the first to A = 0 at version 1, line 2, a write; it takes the
              second to line 2 with A still 0 at version 1, because DEC on zero is no write. Same
              state, zero marks.
                                                           15.14 Parts I and II, run on this machine   339


   That’s the last item on the list of what this machine doesn’t do, near the end of
this chapter, now with names. The chairs argument wants a finite machine that
puts a price on every merge. This machine has counters with no top, and it prices
the three record acts and leaves its counting merges at zero marks, so the chairs
don’t reach it whole, and that’s why the eight-state piece is a piece. The record
layer closes the rest: asked only of merges between states with the same line and
counters, the merge premise holds for this machine’s own prices and forces the toll
on it with no finiteness premise (Theorem 3.17).
   Structural entitlement, for every certified Thiele-complete machine. Theo-
rem 8.3 was about any Thiele machine and handed the run’s payments in as a bill.
For a certified Thiele-complete machine (Definition 15.7) the bill is known. Call the
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY moves of a run its record moves; each costs exactly
one, so the ledger rises by the number of record moves, and clause (b) says what a
raised record must contain.


Theorem 15.31 (Structural entitlement represented). Let a machine be certified
Thiele-complete through an interface. Take a clean start s0 and a run t from it; a type
of rivals and a type of observations with an exact equality test; an observation obs of
each rival; a decoder d from runs to observations; lists Ω, Ω′ of rivals and a decision
tree T. Suppose (M1) Ω′ strictly narrows Ω, as in Theorem 8.3, and (M2) some
dropped rival shows an observation different from every survivor’s; (M3) the run
ends with the record up and the decoded run d(t) is shown by some survivor; (M4)
depth( T ) is at most the number of record moves in t; (M5) |Ω′ | > 0; and (M6) the
covering: |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |. Then (1) the membership test of Ω′ is strictly stronger
than that of Ω; (2) t contains the earned chain of clause (b), with the meaning of
the claim true at the CHECK and at the COMMIT; (3) ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is
at most the number of record moves of t; (4) the number of record moves of t is
exactly the ledger’s rise; and (5) the ledger rose by at least 3.

Proof. (1) is Theorem 8.3(1). (2) Clause (b) applied to a run from a clean state
that ends with the record up gives the chain, and a passing check means the claim’s
meaning holds, which keeps holding while the thing it’s about is unchanged. (3)
The covering (M6) and Theorem 8.3’s count finish it, with the record moves, which
are the paid steps, in place of the charged steps. (4) is clause (c) added up. (5) is
Theorem 15.20(3).
   It’s a checklist, as I said in Section 8, and the small print is the same kind. (M3)’s
second half feeds no conclusion: only the record’s being up is used. (M1) is used only
for the inclusion; its gap feeds nothing, since (M2) already hands over a dropped
rival. What the machine adds to Theorem 8.3 is conclusions (2), (4) and (5): the
340   15 The smallest honest machine


              payment is the machine’s own three acts, each at exactly one, and a raised record
              carries the earned chain.
                 Two more, one where the tree comes from the run’s own questions and one about
              what the record adds.


              Theorem 15.32 (A floor with no supplied tree). Take a machine and an interface
              that meets the exact-prices clause (c) of Definition 15.7, so each record act costs
              exactly one. Call the questions of a run the claims of its CHECK moves, and say
              two rival states answer alike when every one of those claims gets the same verdict
              at both (each verdict taken at the rival itself, as it starts; the states the run passed
              through don’t enter). If, for a list Ω of rival states and a number m > 0, the rivals of
              Ω that answer alike with any one rival, itself included, are never more than m, then
              ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 m⌉ is at most the number of CHECK moves of the run, which is
              at most its number of record moves, which is the ledger’s rise.

               Proof. A run’s questions give each rival an answer list, and answer lists are lists of
               Booleans of length equal to the number of CHECK moves, so there are at most 2c
               answer classes among the rivals, c the number of CHECK moves. The classes have at
               most m members each, so |Ω| ≤ 2c · m, and the rounded logarithms follow. The rest
               is clause (c).
                  The tree has gone: it is the run’s own questions. There are limits, and they’re the
               ones in the statement. The verdicts are taken at the rivals as they start. The states
               the run had reached when it asked don’t come into it, and a branch that costs no
               marks, DEC on zero, can still narrow a list without a mark on the ledger. So this
               prices a narrowing that the paid checks explain, and no more.
                  The next statement takes the verdicts where the run took them. A rival is a state
               the run could have started from; a CHECK the run passed is asked of a rival by
               running the moves before it from the rival and checking the same claim at the state
               that reaches. Nothing is supplied but the prior.



              Theorem 15.33 (Structural entitlement, with the narrowing made by the run). Let
              a machine be certified Thiele-complete through an interface. Take a clean start s0 , a
              run t from it that ends with the record up, and a list Ω of rival starts that contains
              s0 . Let the posterior Ω′ be the rivals that pass every CHECK t passed, each asked as
              above, in the order t made them, and let bi and ai be the numbers of rivals standing
              just before and just after the ith. Then (1) Ω′ sits inside Ω and contains s0 ; (2)
              every rival of Ω that isn’t in Ω′ fails, asked that way, a CHECK that t made and
              passed; (3) |Ω| · ∏i ai = |Ω′ | · ∏i bi ; (4) if every CHECK t passed keeps at least a
                                                             15.14 Parts I and II, run on this machine   341


2−k share of the rivals standing before it, bi ≤ 2k ai , then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is
at most k times the number of CHECKs t passed, that number is at most the record
moves of t, the record moves are the ledger’s rise, and so the index bits are at most
k times the ledger’s rise; (5) t contains the earned chain and the ledger rose by at
least 3; and (6) with no share assumed, the index bits are at most the sum over the
CHECKs t passed of ⌈log2 ⌈bi /ai ⌉⌉.

Proof. (1) The run passes its own checks from s0 , and a rival is kept only if it passes
them all. (2) A rival dropped failed one of the tests, and each test is a CHECK of
t at the prefix where it passed. (3) Each test turns a standing list of bi into one of
ai , and the products telescope. (4) Each test keeps at least bi /2k , so |Ω| ≤ 2kn |Ω′ |
with n the number of tests, and the rounded logarithms follow. The tests are among
the run’s CHECK moves, which are record moves, and clause (c) makes the record
moves the ledger’s rise. (5) is clause (b) and Theorem 15.20(3). (6) is (4) with
2k replaced at the ith test by the smallest power of two at least ⌈bi /ai ⌉; every ai is
positive because s0 is never dropped.
   Part (3) is the exact form of “index bits are the sum of what each test took”: take
base-two logarithms and log2 |Ω| − log2 |Ω′ | is the sum of log2 (bi /ai ). Parts (4)
and (6) are what survives rounding to whole bits. Here the run does the narrowing,
every candidate dropped was dropped by a check the run paid for, and what stays a
premise is the prior and the share. The share can’t go.


Proposition 15.34 (One CHECK can take four bits). Take the sixteen starts ( a, 0)
with a = 0, . . . , 15, and the run CHECK (A ≥ 15) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 15) A;
CERTIFY from (15, 0). It raises the record. Its one passing CHECK keeps one rival
of sixteen, so the posterior is (15, 0) alone and the index bits are 4, while the
run has 3 record moves. So index bits at most the record moves, the bound of
Theorem 15.33(4) read with k = 1, fails here.

Proof. A ≥ 15 holds at exactly one of the sixteen starts. From (15, 0) the CHECK
passes and files the claim, the COMMIT finds it with A’s version unchanged, and
the CERTIFY raises the record. The posterior is the one rival that passes the run’s
only CHECK, so the index bits are ⌈log2 16⌉ − ⌈log2 1⌉ = 4, and the run has three
record moves.
   The share here is 2−4 , and with k = 4 part (4) reads 4 ≤ 4. It’s the example of
Section 8 that showed the covering can’t be dropped, seen from the run’s side: one
test can take many bits, and the bill covers the bits per test times the tests.
342   15 The smallest honest machine




              Theorem 15.35 (What the record adds). Let a machine be certified Thiele-complete
              through an interface. (1) From a clean start, the record is up at the end of a run
              exactly when the run contains the earned chain, and a run with the record up raised
              the ledger by at least 3. (2) Conclusions (1), (3) and (4) of Theorem 15.31 hold
              without a clean start and without the record being up, for a machine that only meets
              the exact-prices clause (c): the hypotheses (M1), (M2), (M4), (M5) and (M6), and
              the decoded run being shown by some survivor, are all it needs.

              Proof. (1) One direction is clause (b): a run from a clean start that ends with the
              record up contains the chain. For the other, the chain’s CERTIFY leaves the record
              up, which is part of what the chain is, and by the last words of clause (a) a record
              that’s up stays up under every move, so whatever the run does after that CERTIFY it
              ends with the record up. The floor of 3 is Theorem 15.20(3). (2) Read the proof
              of Theorem 15.31 again and mark what each conclusion used. Its (1) used (M1)
              and (M2), through Theorem 8.3(1), and nothing about the machine. Its (3) used
              (M5) and the count |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ | of (M6), and (M4) to put the record moves
              in place of the tree’s depth; the clean start and the raised record never entered. Its
              (4) is clause (c) added up along the run, from whatever state the run starts at. The
              decoded run being shown by some survivor is in the hypotheses and, like the second
              half of (M3) above, feeds none of the three. The conclusions dropped, (2) and (5),
              are exactly the two that used the clean start and the record.
                   So the record doesn’t make narrowing cost more. It adds the earned chain and
               a floor of 3, and that’s all it adds: a run meeting the same counting and payment
               hypotheses is still bound by that index-bit floor even if it never raises the record,
               and the floor of 3 no longer applies to it.
                   Weights, fibres and partitions. Three more pieces of the same count. First, suppose
               the rivals aren’t equally many: give each a whole-number weight, a multiplicity, and
               call the sum of the weights of a list its mass. The count survives with masses in place
               of lengths. If the prior’s mass is at most L( T ) times the posterior’s, the rounded
               index bits of the two masses differ by at most depth( T ); so for any Thiele machine a
               run that paid at least that many charged steps has a bill at least the drop, and for a
               certified Thiele-complete machine the representation theorem goes through with
               masses and the same five conclusions. On such a machine the ledger rises by the
               same number from every start, the number of record moves, so the weighted sum of
               ledger rises is the prior’s mass times the record moves, and the drop in rounded bits
               times that mass is at most the weighted sum. Divide by the total mass and you’d
               have an average rise; I leave the weights as whole numbers, cross-multiplied, so no
               probability comes into it. Second, a way to meet the covering (M6) that you can see.
                                                            15.14 Parts I and II, run on this machine   343


Give each survivor a little crowd of rivals, its fibre, no bigger than the tree has leaves,
and let the fibres’ sizes add up to at least the prior. Then |Ω| is at most the sum of
the fibres, which is at most L( T ) times the number of survivors, and that’s (M6).
Third, a plainer way to get fibres. Pick a representative observation of each rival, and
say the rivals are partitioned by it when every rival looks like some survivor under it
and no observation class, counted inside the prior, has more than L( T ) members.
Take each survivor’s class as its fibre: every rival is in the class of some survivor, so
the fibres add up to at least the prior, and (M6) holds. The converse is false: take
four rivals that all look alike, two survivors and a tree with two leaves, and give
each survivor two of the four as its fibre. That covers, but the one class has four
members, more than two.
   A worked member on the small machine. Eight rivals: the starts ( a, b) with
a ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3} and b ∈ {0, 1}, counter A at a and counter B at b. The run is
CHECK (Even) A; CHECK (A ≥ 2) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 2) A; CERTIFY, from (2, 0).
The program raises the flag from a rival exactly when a is even and at least 2, so
exactly from (2, 0) and (2, 1), and the posterior is those two. The decoder reads
one “passed” for each CHECK in the run’s receipts; the tree is the complete tree of
depth 2; and the covering comes from fibres by a representative observation, “B is
0,” which isn’t constant: each survivor’s fibre is the four rivals that share its B.



Proposition 15.36 (The eight-start member). For every a and b, the run raises
the flag from ( a, b) exactly when a is even and at least 2. All hypotheses of Theo-
rem 15.31 hold, with eight rivals narrowed to two: the test of the posterior is strictly
stronger; the index bits are 3 − 1 = 2; the run has 4 record moves and the ledger
rises by exactly 4; and the earned chain is in the run. The run’s own questions
(Theorem 15.32) are its 2 CHECKs, so the floor is met with equality. With the two
CHECKs alone, the record stays down, the ledger rises by 2, and the bound 2 ≤ 2
still holds.

Proof. CHECK (Even) A passes at ( a, b) exactly when a is even, and CHECK (A ≥ 2)
A exactly when a ≥ 2, so both pass exactly when a = 2, whatever b. From (2, 0)
and (2, 1) the COMMIT then finds its fact with A’s version unchanged, nothing
having written A, and the CERTIFY raises the flag; from every other start the first
failing CHECK traps the machine, and a trapped machine raises nothing. So the
posterior is those two. The hypotheses: the posterior narrows the eight strictly (M1);
a dropped rival whose run fails a CHECK shows receipts no survivor shows (M2);
the run ends with the record up and its receipts, two passes, are the survivors’ (M3);
the tree has depth 2 and the run 4 record moves (M4); two survivors (M5); and the
fibres, the four rivals with B at 0 for the survivor (2, 0) and the four with B at 1 for
344   15 The smallest honest machine


              (2, 1), cover all eight, add up to eight, and have four members each, the leaves of
              the tree, so 8 ≤ 4 · 2 (M6). Then ⌈log2 8⌉ − ⌈log2 2⌉ = 3 − 1 = 2; the four record
              moves are two CHECKs, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and the ledger rises by exactly
              those four by clause (c); and the chain is in the run. For Theorem 15.32, the run’s
              questions are its two CHECKs, and two rivals answer them alike exactly when their
              a’s agree on being even and on reaching 2, which puts the eight starts in four classes
              of two, so m = 2 and ⌈log2 8⌉ − ⌈log2 2⌉ = 2 is the number of CHECKs. With the
              two CHECKs alone there’s no CERTIFY, so the record stays down, the ledger rises by
              2, and the index bits are still 2.
                   It’s a real narrowing. The cups of Section 8 aren’t sitting under it in a costume,
               and the posterior is exactly the set of rivals the run certifies, so here a proof ties the
               lists to the run. Nobody supplies them. Read with Theorem 15.33, the run’s two
               passing CHECKs, replayed from the eight rivals, leave four and then two, the same
               two, so the posterior is the one the run makes; each keeps half, so k = 1, and the
               index bits, 2, are at most 1 · 2 and at most the ledger’s rise of 4.
                   A search through n bits. The same shape at a size you can’t enumerate, on
               the machine of Definition D.2, the host in Appendix D.1 with a counter for every
               number, with the small machine’s property language of Zero, Even and At-least-n,
               read at registers, in place of Slot. That machine is certified Thiele-complete too,
               by the argument of Theorem D.6 with these three properties in place of Slot. Hide
               n = k + m bits, one in each of registers 0 to n − 1. The program asks k questions,
               one per bit of the first k: CHECK “at least 1” of register i for a 1, CHECK “is 0” for a
               0. Then it COMMITs the first claim and CERTIFYs. The prior is every n-bit value;
               the posterior is the 2m values that begin with the answers; the tree is the complete
               tree of depth k; and a survivor’s fibre is the 2k values that agree with it on the m bits
               nobody asked about.


              Theorem 15.37 (A search through n bits). For 1 ≤ k ≤ 16 and any m: from a
              world holding a value v of at least k bits, the program certifies exactly when v begins
              with its answers, so the posterior is exactly the set of rivals it certifies from; the test
              of the posterior is strictly stronger than the prior’s; the earned chain is in the run;
              the prior has 2k+m members and the posterior 2m , so the index bits are exactly k;
              the run has exactly k + 2 record moves and the ledger rises by exactly k + 2; and the
              run’s own questions are k CHECKs, so Theorem 15.32 is met with equality. With the
              COMMIT and the CERTIFY left off, the questions alone narrow 2k+m values to 2m ,
              the record stays down, and the ledger rises by exactly k. And no run from a clean
              start that raises the record contains more than 16 CHECKs before its CERTIFY, so
              with 17 questions no start certifies.
                                                          15.14 Parts I and II, run on this machine   345


Proof. Each question is a CHECK of whether one register holds a given bit, which
passes exactly when it does; a failing CHECK traps. So the program certifies exactly
when every answer is right, which is when v begins with the answers. The counting
is the count of bit strings: the 2m fibres of 2k values each add up to the 2k+m of
the prior, and none is longer than the 2k leaves of the tree, so the representation
theorem applies with every hypothesis a theorem. The cap is the fact table: it holds
sixteen facts, never evicts, and a CHECK on a full table traps (Theorem 15.13), so a
seventeenth CHECK before the CERTIFY ends the run in a trap.
    The sixteen belongs to the machine. The program has no say in it: it’s the same
ceiling as the item “Sixteen checks per run, ever” in the list of what the machine
doesn’t do, near the end of this chapter, and it’s why this search never asks more
than sixteen questions however many bits are hidden. Unasked bits can be any
number. The lists, the tree and the fibres are supplied here, as in the representation
theorem, and tied to the run only for this member. The covering still prices only the
size of the drop. Its reason goes unpriced.
    The covering can’t be dropped. It’s a hypothesis, and one might hope it’s a nuisance
one could remove. It isn’t, and the small machine shows it. Fix n ≥ 4, take the 2n
starts ( a, 0) with a below 2n as the rivals, and run the three-move chain on the claim
“A ≥ 2n − 1”: CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY. It certifies exactly from A = 2n − 1, so
the posterior is one start, n index bits are gone, and the ledger rose by 3. So for
n ≥ 4 the claim “the index-bit drop is at most the ledger’s rise” is false for this run,
and no tree of depth at most 3 covers the narrowing: (M6) would need 2n ≤ 8 · 1.
One property with a big constant in it carries n bits in a single yes-or-no question;
what the bound prices is a narrowing whose classes are balanced, a tree with enough
leaves. A narrowing of any other shape is outside it.
    The time a check saves. The question is whether counter A is at least m. There
are two ways to find out. The unpaid way uses base moves only, INC and DEC,
which put no marks on the ledger. But a base move reads A one pebble at a time: a
DEC takes a pebble off A or finds it empty. After n moves, a run that started with A
at least n has never seen A empty, so it can’t have behaved differently for different
such A except by a constant shift in A itself. The paid way is one CHECK (A ≥ m):
one move, a ledger of one, and the line it ends on says which way it went. Certifying
the answer takes the whole chain, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY.


Theorem 15.38 (The time tax). (1) For every program of two-counter instructions
and every n < m, the line number and B after n moves (or where the run stopped,
if it stopped sooner) are the same from A = m − 1 as from A = m, with the same
B. So no such program, read off its line number and B after fewer than m moves,
tells whether A ≥ m at every start; in particular none that stops within fewer than
346   15 The smallest honest machine


              m moves does. (2) A program of m DEC/INC pairs (a ladder: pair i is DEC A on
              line 2i − 1, jumping on success to the next pair at line 2i + 1, and INC B on line 2i,
              where a DEC that finds A empty falls through) decides it in exactly m moves: after
              m moves its line is 2m + 1 exactly when A ≥ m; and it costs 0 marks. (3) Executed
              as a three-move trace from start( a, b), the paid chain raises the flag exactly when
              a ≥ m and has a ledger of exactly 3, whatever m is. As a stored program it pays 3 on
              success and stops after its first failed CHECK with a ledger of 1. (4) A single CHECK
              (A ≥ m) decides it in one move from the line number, with a ledger of exactly 1,
              whatever m is. (5) So if a ledger mark is worth λ moves, the paid route to deciding
              costs 1 + λ and the unpaid route costs at least m, and the paid route is cheaper
              exactly when 1 + λ < m; the paid route to certifying costs 3 + 3λ.

              Proof. (1) Take the starts (m − 1, b) and (m, b). At the jth move, j ≤ n < m, at
              most j − 1 pebbles have left A, so A is at least m − j ≥ 1 in both runs, and no DEC
              finds A empty in either. The two runs take the same branches and differ only by
              the one pebble in A. They are at the same line with the same B, and they stop at
              the same moment if they stop at all, though A ≥ m holds of one start and not the
              other. (2) Run the ladder from A = a. Each of the first min( a, m) moves takes a
              pebble off A and jumps two lines on. If a ≥ m that’s all m moves, ending on line
              2m + 1. If a < m, the run reaches line 2a + 1 after a moves and from there goes on
              one line per move (a DEC falling through, then an INC), so after m moves it’s on
              line a + m + 1, below 2m + 1. It’s all DEC and INC, so it costs 0 marks. (3) is the
              price table: CHECK (A ≥ m) passes exactly when A ≥ m, a failing CHECK traps
              and the flag stays down, and the three moves cost three. (4) is the same price table
              with one instruction: a passing CHECK goes on to line 2 and a failing one traps and
              leaves the line at 1. (5) is arithmetic on (1) to (4).
                  Try m = 3 with A = 2. The ladder takes a pebble on line 1 and jumps to line
              3, takes the second and jumps to line 5, then finds A empty and falls through to
              line 6, the INC: after three moves it sits on line 6, not 7. With A = 3 the third DEC
              succeeds and the run is on line 7. Two moves in, both runs are on line 5 with B
              untouched, which is (1).
                  So the paid route to a certificate wins when 3 + 3λ < m, and the paid route to a
              bare answer wins when 1 + λ < m. That’s a sharper exchange rate than comparing
              two programs I happened to write: the unpaid side is a floor under every program
              of INC and DEC there is, so no choice of program comes into it, and the paid side
              doesn’t move with m at all. The limits: the bound is for programs that make no
              record move, INC and DEC with HALT or falling off the end as stopping. It doesn’t
              cover every certified Thiele-complete machine, because the definition doesn’t forbid
              a base move that changes a counter by more than one pebble, and such a machine is
              a different machine, one the bound doesn’t speak for. And the two routes put their
                                                                       15.15 What it doesn’t do   347


answers in different places, the unpaid one in the line number and the paid one in
the flag; this compares two ways to answer one question. It doesn’t compare two
certifications. Zero marks isn’t zero heat, either: every move on either route is an
event, and the moves are what λ prices.


15.15 What it doesn’t do

Here’s where it falls short, in plain words, because a small machine is only honest if
its edges are as visible as its middle.
• The check price is flat. CHECK costs 1 whether it’s asking “is this 0” or “is
  this at least a billion.” The property language is fixed and each property is one
  evaluation, so “pays for its work” here means that flat price, the same however
  hard the question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty of the check
  would be a different machine, and I haven’t built it.
• DEC on zero isn’t a write. It doesn’t change the counter, so it doesn’t change
  the version. That’s the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means
  DEC on zero is a way to move the line number that puts no mark on the ledger
  and leaves no trace in the record. The idle run in the subsection on the window,
  earlier in this chapter, uses exactly that.
• After a trap, a trace still pays. On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
  traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them
  changes the core. I chose to keep charging so that the ledger stays the plain sum
  of what was issued (Theorem 15.5 has no exceptions); the price of that choice is
  that a trapped machine can still be billed for instructions that change nothing.
• “Checked” means what the property language can say. On this machine that’s
  is zero, is even and is at least n, and a live fact means one of those holds of
  one counter’s current value. It doesn’t mean the program is correct, or that
  anything follows from the property, or that the property was worth checking.
  So can a proved machine of this kind check “sorted,” the claim the sorter-and-
  copier table of Section 14 runs on? Yes, through an encoding. A copy of this
  machine, instruction for instruction, with its property language left open, has
  provenance, checker soundness, no forging and the floor of three proved once
  for every property language that comes with an exact equality test and a checker
  proved equal to its meaning. Give it “the list this counter encodes is sorted” as
  a property and it certifies a sorted list for three and refuses an unsorted one
  forever. The instruction rules are those already given, with the chosen property
  language in place of the three original properties. For sorted lists, decode 0 as
  the empty list and 2h (2t + 1) as the list with head h and tail decoded from t,
  the list code of Theorem 15.26. Every positive code has t smaller than itself,
348   15 The smallest honest machine


                 so decoding terminates. The checker returns yes on an empty list or singleton,
                 and on a, b, . . . exactly when a ≤ b and it returns yes on b, . . .. Induction on the
                 list proves that this is exactly adjacent nondecreasing order. The provenance
                 proof uses only equality of properties and agreement of checker and meaning, so
                 the same instruction-by-instruction argument applies. What makes that a check
                 of the list is the proof that the checker means sortedness. Without that proof,
                 “sorted” would be a number some unconstrained code wrote into a counter, and
                 the record would be honest about the counter and silent about the list.
               • The certificate is historical. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter
                 can change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and
                 committed about an edition. It says nothing about whether the claim is still true.
               • One latch, and a channel that moves on. The flag records that an earned chain
                 happened, once. After that it stays up, and later CERTIFYs change nothing. The
                 channel is the part that names a fact: with the flag up from a clean start, it names
                 a fact that some earlier passing COMMIT committed. But a later commitment
                 replaces it, so at the end it names the last earned commitment, which needn’t
                 be the one the flag rose on. Two runs from start(0, 0) show it, worked from the
                 instruction table. First run: CHECK is zero A; CHECK is zero B; COMMIT is zero
                 A; CERTIFY; COMMIT is zero B. Second run: the same five instructions with
                 the last two swapped, so COMMIT is zero B comes before CERTIFY. Both end in
                 the same state: both counters 0 at version 0, both facts in the table, the channel
                 holding (zero, B, 0), the trap down, a ledger of five and the flag up. In the first
                 run the flag rose at step four, on the commitment about A. In the second it rose
                 at step five, on the commitment about B. So the flag is an ever-certified latch: it
                 says an earned chain happened at some step, and the end state doesn’t say which
                 claim or which step. A receipt naming the claim the flag first rose on would need
                 that claim kept where nothing can overwrite it; a receipt with a time on it would
                 also need the step number kept; and several certifications that each last would
                 need a record richer than one flag. None of those is built or proved here. They’re
                 extensions. Several claims need a latch each.
               • Sixteen checks per run, ever. Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a
                 run gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth
                 traps. A certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but
                 it’s a hard wall for any program that wants to keep checking forever, and it’s this
                 machine’s small version of “you can’t keep all of it” from Section 14. A CHECK
                 that repeats a claim already in the table, same property, same counter, same
                 edition, passes again and takes another entry. So the wall is sixteen passing
                 CHECKs, and sixteen different claims is a different count. Removing duplicates,
                                                                       15.15 What it doesn’t do   349


  evicting old facts or collecting dead ones would each be a different design, and
  each would need its own invariants proved.
• The clean start matters. Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of
  three are all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded with
  facts nobody checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems are about
  what the machine produces. What you smuggle in at the door is outside them.
  Spell the door out once: the theorems cover any list of instructions anybody can
  issue, from a clean start, on a step that runs as written, with nothing else writing
  to the machine. They say nothing about whoever sets or restores the start, about
  a reset, about a device that misbehaves, or about whoever carries the flag’s value
  to you.
• The universal programs have stated guests. U (Appendix D.1) runs every
  one of this machine’s programs from every clean start start( x, y), with halting,
  answers, flag and ledger matched (the flag over the whole run, the ledger at
  matching points). UP (Appendix D.2) runs every computably presented Thiele
  machine, with its reading decided by a program, its record carried as a latch, and
  its ledger matched to within a surcharge of at most two when its reading starts
  at no, and of three when it starts at yes. When the guest certifies with a ledger
  below three, no program on that host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger
  exactly. A machine outside that class, with a reading no program decides, isn’t
  covered by either. The simpler host with the built-in guest step (Appendix D.3)
  pays one per guest step whatever the step was, so its ledger is at least the guest’s
  and usually more; U’s is exact, and UP ’s is exact up to the surcharge.
• Encoding and running time. The universality result takes its inputs already
  packed into the counters. Getting there from an arbitrary Turing machine goes
  through Minsky’s exponential packing (Appendix K), and that packing is the price
  of reaching the two-counter base this way. Carrying the record to another base
  has its own conditions, in Appendix E, and anyone who wanted this to run fast
  would have to start the analysis over.
• The step charges for the act, not for what the claim is worth. CHECK at
  least 0 passes on every value, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag
  for three from any fresh loaded start (the note after Theorem 15.17). That’s by
  design. The step checks order, aboutness and an honest checker. What a claim is
  worth is the entitlement count of Section 8, a number computed over the rivals a
  run narrows. A step sees one state, so it cannot compute that count. A check that
  cannot fail narrows nothing and costs three, and the book keeps both numbers,
  apart.
• The toll on this machine comes from the record layer, with no finiteness
  premise on the whole machine. Section 3’s chairs argument forces a toll on a
350   15 The smallest honest machine


                  finite machine that prices every merge. This machine is neither, by design. Its
                  counters have no ceiling, so it’s infinite. And its unpriced instructions merge
                  states: take a core at line ℓ with c at 1 and version w, and a core at line j − 1 with c
                  at 0 and version w + 1, everything else alike, and DEC c j sends both to line j with
                  c at 0 and version w + 1, for zero marks. Zero marks is not zero cost. Every one of
                  those moves is an event, and whatever it costs the hardware, heat for happening
                  and, under Landauer’s premise, a floor for each merge of states that were really
                  possible, is off the ledger. The ledger leaves those merges out on purpose. It
                  counts the keeping in the record, not what computing spends. Computing doesn’t
                  have to merge; a reversible base computes by paying room. On this machine
                  full merge pricing would charge DEC, an ordinary step, and clause (c) asks for
                  computing to cost no marks. Pricing the dissipation of happening would be worse.
                  Every step that changes something on a real device dissipates, so that ledger
                  charges every step, and that’s the clock of Observation 15.22: its marks say how
                  long it ran and nothing about what it kept. So merge pricing on this machine
                  applies to the record layer only: a move that sends two different states with the
                  same line and counters to one state costs at least one. This machine’s own prices
                  meet it. The endless counters would leave room for a raise that merges nothing,
                  and the flag doesn’t take it: CERTIFY lands a state with the flag down and the
                  same state with the flag up on one state, a merge of exactly that kind, in plain
                  view. So every price list that meets the premise charges the flag-raising step at
                  least one, with no finiteness premise (Theorem 3.17). That’s a price I assume for
                  losing distinctions in the record, and assuming it is all it is. Turning it into heat
                  takes the physical conditions of Section 3; a mark on a ledger isn’t heat on its
                  own. The exact price of one, where the premise asks for at least one, is still a
                  design choice.


               15.16 What this chapter adds up to
              So this chapter has one machine, and it isn’t the model. It’s a Thiele machine in
              the opening’s sense, a Thiele machine with the toll proved (Theorem 15.6), and
              its toll charges the blank cell’s 0: raising its flag is a merge in its record layer
              (Theorem 3.17). It’s Thiele-complete, the sense no clock meets (Section 10.8),
              and certified Thiele-complete, in the sense of Definition 15.7 (Theorem 15.26): it
              computes whatever a Turing machine can, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside
              the machine, its computing puts no marks on the ledger and can’t touch the record,
              and, from a clean start, its record is earned.
                  If you ever find yourself wondering whether a property of this machine is the
              model’s or just the machine’s, hold it up against Section 2’s definition of a Thiele
              machine, the latch of Section 10, the four clauses of Thiele-complete, and the four
                                                                15.16 What this chapter adds up to   351


of certified Thiele-complete. What follows from those holds of every machine that
meets them; the rest (a table of sixteen facts, three properties, a flat price of one) is
this machine’s choice. Six instruction kinds, and a seventh, PAY, for a host that has
to bill somebody else’s prices (Appendix D.2). If the machine needs more than that,
this is where it’ll show.
CHAPTER 16




How far it reaches

The small machine earns its flag, and pays for it, on its own programs. Everything
in this chapter asks how far that carries. Every statement in it is proved, and the
runs are reported as runs. I give each statement here and leave the constructions to
the appendices, because they’re about the reach of the case, not the case.
    Other machines as guests. One fixed program, U, written in the small machine’s
own six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters, runs every program of
the small machine as a guest, from every clean start. It fetches, decodes and carries
out each guest instruction itself, the way Turing’s universal machine does; nothing
in the host means “run one guest step.” It halts exactly when its guest halts, with
the guest’s answer in its counters; its flag goes up during its run exactly when the
guest’s goes up during the guest’s, by its own check, its own commitment and its
own certificate; and its ledger equals the guest’s at every point where the two runs
match. The host is certified Thiele-complete, and whether U halts is undecidable.
Add one move, PAY, that costs a mark and does nothing else, and the same kind of
program, UP , runs every Thiele machine whose next move, step, prices and reading
are computed by programs that always answer: it halts when the guest’s run stops,
its flag goes up exactly when the guest’s reading is yes at some state of its run, on
a chain whose check is the guest’s own reading, and its ledger is the guest’s prices
plus a surcharge of at most two at the raise when the guest’s reading starts at no,
and exactly three when it starts at yes, a surcharge no program on that host can
always avoid. Appendix D has both, with their proofs.
    Other models of computation. Lay the toll over a register machine, a Turing
machine (with one move for each whole program, not one for each row of one fixed
table, which provably can’t serve as a base) or the lambda calculus and none of
them computes one function more; what each gains is a record and a bill. What
carries over from any base, what never does, and why the small machine uses two
counters, are in Appendix E.
    Machines from parts. Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a
Thiele machine stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What
breaks, breaks for reasons you could name in advance: a single flag for two claims
costs two claims’ worth, a clock is still a clock, a shared value without a version can’t




                                  352
                                                                                         353


be trusted, and a hand-off that costs no marks can’t be allowed to carry a certificate
(Appendix F).
    Running it. The machine is built twice, once from the definitions and once by
hand, and the two are compared after every step; U and UP have run on guests
small enough to finish; a compiler from a small programming language to the host
is proved correct stage by stage, and Ackermann’s function at (3, 5) comes out of
nothing but INC and DEC (Appendix G).
    A check worth earning. A flag is only as interesting as the claim under it. The
CHSH game, the two-player game behind Bell’s theorem, gives a claim whose check
is a piece of real mathematics: an integer test on the game’s tally whose passing
implies Tsirelson’s bound, earned on the host by the same check, commit and certify
(Appendix H). It’s there to show the toll charges the same however deep the check
behind it is.
CHAPTER 17




Five small models

A toll, a counter, two kinds of wall and a latch, every one of them shown on paper,
on cups and cards and dice I made up, and then a small machine to run them on.
I’ve been building a toy and claiming it’s the smallest version of something people
actually do. Time to go and look at what people actually do. I picked five systems
that keep records other people rely on, with real money or real security behind
them, and asked each the pricing question from the paper models: is there a price
on the moment the record is written? Not on the work around it. On the write, the
moment the 0 goes on the page and stays. I’ll tell you the answer first, because it’s
a single sentence and it surprised me: of the five specifications, read through the
transcriptions I made of them, only one takes a fee at the moment of the write, and
that one has a leak at exactly the place Section 6 said a counter leaks, where it goes
down.
    “Price” needs one meaning for all five, or the answer is whatever I want it to
be, so here it is, and every system below gets classified by it. A specification prices
an event when it attaches one of three costs to it. A fee: something taken at the
event itself, whatever happens afterward. A bond: value put at risk by the event
and lost only if some later event happens, a contradiction, say. A budget: a finite
allowance the event draws down, so that only so many such events can ever happen.
A wall isn’t a price under this definition. Nobody pays a hash; reversing one is just
infeasible. Neither is work a protocol needs and never charges for. The table at the
end of the section has a column for each of the three kinds, and what it shows is a
finding about the five, because the definition came first.
    Three things are easy to blur in a section like this, so I’ll name them now and
keep them apart all the way through. There’s the real specification: the document
real money and real security run on. There’s my transcription: one mechanism
copied out of that document into a mathematical model, small enough to examine.
And for some of the five there’s a wrapper: a tiny abstract model that takes one
premise as given and says what follows from it. A claim proved at one level isn’t a
claim at the level above it. Near the end I’ll walk one system, gas, through all three,
so you can see exactly where each claim stops.
    What I built for each is a fragment: a small mathematical model of the one
mechanism I’m asking about, transcribed from the system’s own specification where


                                 354
                                                17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back   355


there was one, and nothing more. Not the system. I’ll say for each one what the
fragment is and what it isn’t, because “Ethereum has been formalised” is the kind of
sentence that gets a book thrown across a room, and rightly.


17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back
Ethereum and chains like it decide which blocks are final by having validators,
people who’ve locked up money (their stake), vote on checkpoints: blocks picked out
at regular numbered rounds called epochs. A vote isn’t for one checkpoint. It’s a link
from a checkpoint the validator already trusts, the source, to a later one, the target,
and every chain starts from one first block, its genesis, which counts as trusted from
the start. In the design Vitalik Buterin and Virgil Griffith published in 2017, called
Casper, a checkpoint is justified when validators holding two thirds of the stake vote
a link to it from a justified source, and finalized when it is justified and a two-thirds
link runs from it to its direct child. The record is “this checkpoint is final.”
    What’s priced? Two rules: don’t vote for two different targets in the same
epoch, and don’t cast a vote whose span, source to target, surrounds the span of
another of your votes. Break either and your deposit can be destroyed, which is
called slashing. The theorem they prove, called accountable safety, says that if two
conflicting checkpoints are ever both finalized, at least a third of the stake broke a
rule and can be slashed. So the price is on reversal, on making the record contradict
itself. The write itself, finalizing, takes no fee: honest validators finalize all day and
nobody loses anything. In the terms from the start of the section, Casper’s price is a
bond. The deposit stands behind every vote, the finalizing votes included, and it’s
taken only if the record is later made to contradict itself.
    Do it with three validators of equal stake. Draw genesis at epoch 0, two competing
children at epoch 1, and one child of each at epoch 2. Let A and B vote both links on
the left branch, from genesis to its first child and from that child to the next. Let B
and C do the same on the right. Each link has two of the three votes. Both epoch-1
blocks are justified and have the required link to their child, so both finalize. B voted
for different targets at the same epoch. B is the third that gets slashed; A and C are
clean. That’s what a fork costs and who pays, and Theorem 17.2 below has exactly
this instance, so the theorem’s premise isn’t vacuous: forks of that kind can be built,
and the theorem fires on them.
    The fragment: a reconstruction of the published casper-proofs argument from
Runtime Verification and the University of Texas at Austin, based on Yoichi Hirai’s
proof, with validator sets and quorum intersection as a premise. A quorum is a set
of validators big enough to act, here two thirds of the stake, and quorum intersection
is the arithmetic of the three-validator example: two thirds plus two thirds is four
thirds, so any two quorums share at least a third. The fragment takes the overlap as
356   17 Five small models


              given. It doesn’t do that arithmetic. No deposits, no rewards, no fork choice (the
              rule for picking a branch to build on), no connection to anything else in this book.
              A finalization fork implies that a set of validators the size of that overlap, at least
              a third of the stake, is slashed. And a one-validator chain finalizes and nobody’s
              slashed, which is the “write costs no stake” sentence in a degenerate setting, and
              only there.
                 Here’s the fragment, small enough to read in one sitting. Every name below is
              from the transcription.

              Definition 17.1 (Casper setting and votes). A setting has a type of validators, a
              type of block hashes with a parent relation and a genesis hash, and two classes of
              validator sets, the “two-thirds” sets Q1 and the “one-third” sets Q2 . It carries two
              premises: quorum intersection, for any two sets in Q1 some set in Q2 lies inside
              both; and at most one parent per hash. A state says, for each validator, target hash h,
              target epoch t and source epoch u, whether that validator voted the link (h, t, u). A
              link from p at epoch u to h at epoch t is justified by q when q ∈ Q1 , every member of
              q voted (h, t, u), h is the (t − u)-th descendant of p, and t > u. Genesis is justified
              at epoch 0, and a block reached from a justified block by a justified link landing
              at epoch t is justified at t. Block h is finalized at epoch v with child c when c is a
              child of h, h is justified at v, and the link from h at v to c at v + 1 is justified. A
              finalization fork is two finalized blocks h1 ̸= h2 , neither an ancestor of the other. A
              validator is slashed when it voted two different targets with the same target epoch (a
              double vote), or voted links (h1 , t1 , u1 ) and (h2 , t2 , u2 ) with t1 > t2 and u2 > u1 (a
              surround vote). The state is quorum-slashed when some set in Q2 consists of slashed
              validators.



              Theorem 17.1 (Accountable safety). In every setting (so under quorum intersection
              and at most one parent), every state with a finalization fork is quorum-slashed.

              Proof. Let the fork be h1 finalized at v1 and h2 at v2 . If v1 = v2 , the two links
              into epoch v1 + 1 are each voted by a set in Q1 ; quorum intersection gives a set in
              Q2 that voted both; their targets differ, since equal children would give h1 and h2
              the same child and so, by at most one parent, h1 = h2 . That set double-voted. If
              v1 ̸= v2 , say v1 < v2 , walk down the chain of justified links that justifies h2 . Every
              block on that chain is an ancestor of h2 , so none descends from h1 . (So v1 > 0: the
              only block justified at epoch 0 is genesis, an ancestor of every justified block.) Some
              link in the chain starts at or below v1 and lands above v1 . If it lands at v1 + 1, it and
              the finalization link of h1 have distinct targets at that epoch, and the intersection set
              double-voted. If it starts at v1 , its source is a justified block at v1 other than h1 , and
                                                  17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back   357


the links that justified those two blocks give a double vote the same way. Otherwise
it starts below v1 and lands above v1 + 1, so it surrounds the finalization link of h1 ,
and the intersection set made a surround vote.
   Everything the fragment promises stands on those two premises, the overlap and
the one parent. Take either away and it promises nothing.


Theorem 17.2 (The premise can hold, and the write costs no stake). (1) In the
three-validator setting where each validator has stake 1, Q1 is the sets of stake at
least two thirds and Q2 the sets of at least one third, the state where A and B vote
one branch and B and C the other has a finalization fork; B is slashed, A and C
are not, and { B} is in Q2 . (2) In the one-validator chain setting, one vote finalizes
genesis and no validator is slashed.

Proof. Both are computations on fixed finite data. In (1) every link carries two of
the three votes, so stake two thirds, so both epoch-1 blocks are justified and each has
a justified link to its child at epoch 2: both are finalized, and as siblings neither is an
ancestor of the other. B voted two different targets at epoch 1, which is the double
vote; A’s and C’s votes are one link at epoch 1 from source 0 and one at epoch 2
from source 1, which neither double-vote nor surround. In (2) the one validator’s
vote from genesis at 0 to its child at 1 is a justified link, so genesis is finalized, and a
single vote can neither double-vote nor surround.
    One thing that means for the record itself: finality is revocable at a price, the
price is named, and a final block can hold a false statement.
    And the obvious next question: is the 2017 design what Ethereum actually runs?
Partly, and the paper’s own title is the clue. It’s called Casper the Friendly Finality
Gadget, and its first sentence says it’s a finality system that overlays a chain still
choosing its blocks by proof of work. A gadget, bolted on top. In 2020 a larger group,
Buterin among them, wrote up Gasper, which joins Casper’s finality to a fork-choice
rule called LMD GHOST, and on 15 September 2022, in the switch people called
the Merge, Ethereum stopped choosing blocks by proof of work at all and went
over to proof of stake. So the checkpoints and the two slashing rules above are
one part of a system that holds real money today, and the transcription is of that
part’s safety proof as the 2017 design states it. Everything between the two, the fork
choice and the rest of the running protocol, is the gap between my transcription
and the running system, which I walk through near the end of this section with a
photocopied recipe and a kitchen. Does any of that move the price? No. Finalizing
still costs an honest validator no stake. What costs is contradicting yourself.
358   17 Five small models


              17.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write
              Every operation on Ethereum costs gas, paid in ether by whoever sent the transaction.
              The yellow paper, Ethereum’s formal specification, gives the reason in one line: every
              computation is fee-bearing so the network can’t be abused and halting questions are
              sidestepped. The record I care about is a nonzero slot in the shared storage, which
              every full node in the world (every computer keeping its own complete copy of the
              chain) has to keep until it’s cleared. Clearing a slot is allowed, and the refund rules
              below exist to reward it.
                  And here it is: writing a fresh storage slot from zero to nonzero costs twenty
              thousand gas, by the table in the paper’s appendix, plus twenty-one hundred for
              touching a cold slot, one the transaction hasn’t touched yet (after the first touch it’s
              warm). As I read it, the point is to discourage storage growth, since storage grows
              every node’s database. That’s a fee on the write, at the moment of the write, and
              it’s the only fee in the five. Gas has a budget too, in the sense from the start of the
              section: every block has a gas limit, and the gas its transactions use can’t exceed it,
              so only so many writes fit in a block.
                  Where does a number like twenty-one hundred come from? Somebody picked
              it, so the obvious next question is who, and why, and the answer has a date on it.
              In September 2016, just as Ethereum’s developers were gathering in Shanghai for
              Devcon 2, their developer conference (the third one, since they started counting
              at zero), attackers started filling blocks with an operation that was cheap in gas
              and expensive in fact: it sent every node off to read data from its disk, and nodes
              fell behind the chain. The first repair, a fork that October called Tangerine Whistle,
              raised the prices of the operations the attack had leaned on. The cold-slot charge
              came later, in a proposal by Vitalik Buterin and Martin Swende called EIP-2929,
              switched on in the Berlin upgrade of April 2021, and the motivation it gives is still
              those 2016 attacks. So twenty-one hundred isn’t a law of nature or a measurement
              of anything deep. It’s a scar: a price set after somebody found the place where the
              old price was wrong. That doesn’t change the argument; the write is still priced at
              the moment of the write. It does change how I read the rest of that table: some of
              its numbers, at least, are somebody’s answer to “what did this cost last time,” which
              is a record of a different kind.
                  Now the leak, and it’s Section 6’s leak. Set a slot and then clear it in the same
              transaction and you get a refund. Count it through: first write twenty-two thousand
              one hundred; clearing it costs a hundred and credits a refund of nineteen thousand
              nine hundred; net, twenty-three hundred. The other half is this: leave it set and you
              pay at least twenty thousand. The write is priced. The revoked write nearly isn’t.
              But I have to add what the fragment leaves out, because twenty-three hundred on
              its own misleads: the realized refund is capped at one fifth of the gas the whole
                                                    17.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write   359


transaction used (that’s the 2021 change from Section 6, the one that ended the
refund-hoarding token’s advantage). So a real set-then-clear pays a lot more than
twenty-three hundred. How much more? The cap is a fifth of everything the
transaction used, and that includes the twenty-one thousand every transaction pays
just for existing. Take a transaction that does nothing but set and clear the slot, and
count only that base and the two stores (the instructions that load their arguments
add about a dozen more): it uses 43,200 gas, so the cap is 8,640, so it pays 34,560,
which is 13,560 on top of the base. (Look at the slot alone and forget the base, which
the rule doesn’t do, and you’d get 17,760.) Either way it’s far above twenty-three
hundred. The counter-level net is twenty-three hundred. The bill is not.
   Here’s the arithmetic the way the specification has it, so you can redo it with a
pencil.

Definition 17.2 (One slot in one transaction). A slot run records the slot’s value at
the start of the transaction (original), its current value, whether it has been touched
(warm), the gas charged so far, and the refund counter. A store of a new value
charges 2100 if the slot is cold, plus 20000 if the slot still holds its original value,
the new value differs, and the original is 0 (2900 if the original is nonzero), and
otherwise 100. If the value is unchanged, the refund does not change. Otherwise
add together these applicable adjustments: add 4800 when the original and current
values are nonzero and the new value is zero; subtract 4800 when the original is
nonzero and the current value is zero; and, when the new value restores the original,
add 19900 if that original is zero, or 2800 if it is nonzero. Store the new current
value, mark the slot warm, and keep the original value unchanged. The run starts
fresh: original and current 0, cold, gas and refund 0. The net charge is gas minus
refund.



Theorem 17.3 (Pricing the persistent write and the revoked one). (1) For every list
of stores from a fresh slot, if the slot ends nonzero then the net charge is at least
20000. (2) Storing 1 then 0 leaves the slot at 0 with net charge 2300; storing 1
alone has net charge 22100.

Proof. (1) By induction on the list, with the invariant: while the original value is
0, the net charge is at least 0 when the current value is 0 and at least 20000 when
it is not. For the fresh original value 0, the four cases are short. Zero to zero adds
100 to net; zero to nonzero adds 20000; nonzero to nonzero adds 100; and nonzero
to zero adds 100 − 19900 = −19800. The last case starts with net at least 20000
and so ends at least 200, still nonnegative. A cold access adds another 2100 in any
case. These updates preserve the invariant, and a fresh slot satisfies it. (2) Direct
360   17 Five small models


              computation: 2100 + 20000 = 22100 for the first store, 100 for the second, refund
              19900, and 22200 − 19900 = 2300.
                  The fragment: one slot, one transaction, the gas and refund arithmetic copied
              out of the Ethereum execution specification’s storage instruction and gas table, at
              a named commit. No stack, no call context, no other slots, and no refund cap, the
              one-fifth rule applied at the end of a transaction.
                  Then the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near the end
              is about exactly that difference. It’s a gas schedule in the abstract: any states, any
              steps, a cost per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying
              which steps get billed. It formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at
              all. It is Section 7’s result with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount
              as well as which steps pay, under a new name. Its two halves are worth reading
              separately. Leave one committing step unbilled, and a one-step run commits at no
              charge, so the floor fails outright; one missed commit is enough. Bill one step that
              doesn’t commit, and the schedule charges more than the number of commits on
              that one-step run, so the ceiling fails. And the class isn’t empty: in any system, the
              bill that charges one exactly on a step that raises the flag and nothing on any other
              meets both halves (Section 7’s step price).
                  And the wrapper itself, which is the cleanest thing in this section and has the
              least Ethereum in it.

              Definition 17.3 (A gas schedule). A gas schedule has states, instructions, a step,
              a cost c(s, i ) ∈ N that may depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on
              states, and a Boolean charge predicate χ(s, i ), with two premises: a charged step
              costs at least 1, and an uncharged step costs 0. A step commits when it takes the flag
              from false to true. For a run t from s, let c(t) be its total cost and n(t) its number of
              committing steps. The schedule has the floor when c(t) ≥ n(t) for every run, and
              no overcharge when c(t) ≤ n(t) for every run. It has unit pricing when c(s, i ) = 1 if
              χ(s, i ) and 0 otherwise.



              Theorem 17.4 (Gas schedule exactness). For every gas schedule: it has the floor
              and no overcharge if and only if χ(s, i ) holds exactly when the step from s by i
              commits, and it has unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some committing step from an
              uncommitted state is uncharged, that one-step run costs 0 and the schedule fails the
              floor; (2) if some charged step does not commit, the schedule overcharges.
                                              17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past   361


Proof. The equivalence is Section 7’s characterization with the whole-run ceiling,
under another name. From right to left, each step’s cost is 1 on a committing step
and 0 otherwise, so a run’s cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply
the floor and no overcharge to one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1,
so it is charged; a charged step costs at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment
count, so it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts (1) and (2) are those one-step runs
read the other way.
   Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says nothing about whether what’s
stored is true.


17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past
A trusted platform module, the small chip on most laptop motherboards, keeps a
handful of registers that can only be extended: the new value is a hash of the old
value together with a digest (a short hash) of whatever software just loaded. You
can’t set them; you can only fold more in. A quote is the chip signing those register
values together with a number the asker chose, a nonce, so the asker knows the
quote is fresh. Intel’s SGX does the equivalent for an enclave, a walled-off region a
program runs in. The record is the extended register.
    What’s priced? On the registers, nothing in the specification: no fee, no bond,
no budget. Reversal isn’t expensive. It’s infeasible: you’d have to invert a hash or
steal a key. That’s the difference between a price and a wall, and it’s easy to blur,
which is why the definition at the start of the section leaves walls out. What stands
behind a cost can come in three currencies. It can be economic, a fee or a deposit
the protocol takes (Casper and gas are here). It can be cryptographic, a reversal
made infeasible by a hardness assumption, which makes it a wall with no exact price
on it (attestation and transparency are here). Or it can be physical, energy spent or
hardware worn, which none of these five specifications charges as a fee or a bond;
the nearest thing is the chip’s write budget, below. And the record’s permanence is
only as long as the register lives: a platform’s registers are cleared when it resets, so
the permanence is per boot.
    Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record?
Because the quote is what a remote asker reads, and the registers are what it signs.
The same chip has longer-lived records, and they’re closer to the cup than anything
else in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has storage slots of a kind it calls a
bit field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the old value: a bit can
be set and never cleared, which is r ∨ h from Section 10, on a laptop motherboard.
It has counters that can only be incremented, and a counter’s first increment starts
it at the largest value any counter on that chip has ever held, so deleting one and
making a new one can’t wind it back. And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and
362   17 Five small models


              his coauthors, building a system called Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification
              of the day only required a counter to be able to tick once every five seconds, and that
              the chip’s storage was expected to survive about a hundred thousand writes in its
              whole life, so writing once a second would wear it out in under twenty-eight hours.
              Memoir writes to it twice per boot. Permanent, finite and rationed: the permanent
              record has a budget, in exactly the sense from the start of the section, and it sits on
              these slots and counters; the registers the quote signs have none. It’s the budget of
              Theorem 10.11’s chain of k-bit words, which can only climb k times. Phones and
              small controllers go one floor further down, to fuses like the PROMs in Section 10: a
              version number kept as a row of fuses, one more blown at each security update, and
              boot code that refuses anything older. An industry guide on it, Rob Smart’s 2021
              explainer for PSA Certified, a security certification scheme for chips and devices,
              tells designers to make sure there are enough fuse bits to last the number of updates
              expected over the device’s lifetime, which is part (5) of that same theorem, written
              as a design rule.
                  What all of this is for is rollback. Memoir’s example is a password checker restored
              to an old saved state to undo a user’s password change, and in 2017 a system called
              ROTE did the same job for Intel’s enclaves by having several machines vouch for
              each other’s counters, with the stated result that the only way left to break it is to
              reset every one of them to its start. In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens’s
              Ariadne got the cost of that job down to flipping a single bit of non-volatile memory
              per state update, which they call the theoretical lower limit. Notice who the attacker
              is in every one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad program
              doesn’t come into it. A record kept by the step can’t see that attacker, which is why
              every guarantee the small machine gives about a record’s earned history (Section 15)
              is stated from a clean start, and a restored start is outside all of them. The per-step
              toll still holds after a restore. It just can’t tell you what happened before it.
                  Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each
              replica, where a replica that’s been taken over still can’t make it say two different
              things. Byung-Gon Chun and coauthors’ attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007)
              is a log a replica can only add to; Dave Levin and coauthors’ TrInc (2009) shrinks
              that to a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and coauthors, 2013) uses
              a trusted counter to reach agreement with 2 f + 1 replicas when f of them can lie,
              where the usual count is 3 f + 1; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya,
              Vincent Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker,
              that keeps a monotonic counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio
              Junqueira, Aniket Kate and Rodrigo Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what
              such a record buys, and as I read their result it’s a good warning for this book. On
              its own, stopping a replica from saying two different things doesn’t lower the 3 f + 1
              bound in an asynchronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can
                                             17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past   363


check, and it turns any protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars,
with no extra replicas. The way I read it, a record helps the others only as far as
they can check what it says, which is Section 7’s point from the other side.
   There’s a fourth currency under those three, and it’s the one every permanent
record on a finite chip pays in. It’s the logical kind: Section 3’s room of chairs applies
to any of these records. On a finite state space, a step that switches a record on
somewhere, and never switches it off anywhere, forgets something. Forgetting alone
doesn’t single out a record write: any step that overwrites a field able to hold two
values forgets something too. What singles it out is where the forgetting lands. Take
the states the record already reads yes on, together with the one the step switches
on. The step sends every one of them to a yes state, and it can’t keep them apart, so
what it destroys is a distinction on the record’s own yes side: two states it already
vouched for, or the state it just raised and one that was up already. Any overwrite
merges states somewhere; a permanent write is forced to merge them on that side.
That needs no premise about money, keys or heat. The economic, cryptographic
and physical payments each need a premise of their own about their kind (a fee
rule, a hardness assumption, Landauer’s principle), and they hold exactly where
that premise holds.


Theorem 17.5 (A permanent write forgets on its own yes side). For any states S,
instructions I, step and Boolean reading: suppose a duplicate-free list names every
state, the instruction i never turns the reading from on to off, and i turns it on at
some state s. Then the step by i is not injective. More: the step by i sends every
state that reads on, and s, to a state that reads on, and it is not injective even on
those states.

    The proof is Theorem 3.1 with permanence required only of the one instruction i.
For the second half: if the step were one-to-one on the states that read on together
with s, it would map the states that read on onto themselves, and then s would land
where some state that reads on already lands.
    What the quote can do is say what was measured. It can’t say the measured
code is correct, and it can’t say anything about runtime state that was never folded
in. A correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The fragment proves
that exact limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a
pair, and no function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores, which
is Section 7’s cube again. And a second small result shows that a sign-and-verify
interface alone gives no authenticity (a scheme where verify always says yes passes
the interface), so a cryptographic premise has to be added; the fragment doesn’t
364   17 Five small models


              model signatures, formats, or a freshness check (the nonce is just a field the verifier
              fixes).
                  The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the four conditions of
              Section 14. Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property,
              same thing, same edition, honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is
              hot, the parcel arrived) there’s no edition the machine controls. Whatever reads
              the world is a window onto it, and “nothing changed between the check and the
              commit” stops being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about the
              sensor. So a record can establish claims about the machine’s own state, and claims
              about the world only through named premises about whatever measured them. A
              correctly recorded sensor reading certifies the sensor.

              Definition 17.4 (Platform and quote). Fix any functions H : N × N → N (the
              extend hash) and δ : N → N (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A
              platform is a measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag.
              Its register is the log folded from 0 by H. The quote with nonce n is the pair
              (δ(register), n).



              Theorem 17.6 (The quote cannot attest unmeasured state). For every nonce n
              there is no function D from quotes to Booleans with D (quoten ( P)) = flag( P) for
              every platform P.

              Proof. Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their
              quotes are equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so D would have to return
              both values on one input.
                  Anything that depends only on δ(register), the quote can answer; that’s what it’s
              for. And the second result is the one I mentioned: a “signature” scheme whose check
              always says yes fits the sign-and-verify interface perfectly and accepts a signature
              no key ever made, so the interface on its own promises nothing.


              17.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced

              The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds
              of authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain
              it shouldn’t. Certificate Transparency makes authorities submit every certificate
              to public append-only logs built as Merkle trees, so that anyone can check that a
              certificate was logged and that the log never rewrote its past. It was specified in
              RFC 6962 in 2013 and revised as RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one
                                                     17.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced   365


the running logs follow, and it’s still 6962: Mozilla’s reference for web developers
says browser implementations are based on 6962, and as late as November 2025
Chrome’s team was only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a
timestamp from at least one 6962 log. The fragment I transcribe is 9162’s. A Merkle
tree is Section 2’s hash chain folded into a tree: hash each certificate (those are
the leaves), hash the leaf hashes in pairs, hash those in pairs, and so on up to one
root hash. To prove one leaf is in, the log hands you only the few hashes sitting
beside the climb from that leaf to the root, the path, and you redo the climb yourself.
A second check, consistency, shows that a bigger tree is a smaller one with leaves
added on the end and nothing rewritten. The record is a leaf in the tree.
    The data structure has a history of its own in security. The computer scientists
Scott Crosby and Dan Wallach, at Rice University, built tamper-evident logs on the
same kind of tree in 2009, with a proof that an entry is in the log and a proof that a
later version of the log extends an earlier one, each a logarithmic number of hashes;
a logger that rewrites its past gets caught by the second.
    Priced? Nothing. The RFC says it in its first section: logs let interested parties
detect misissuance afterward. They don’t prevent it. And a log that shows different
views to different people (a split view) can defeat the auditing, so logs are still
trusted parties. What it buys is visibility.
    Which raises the obvious question: if nothing’s priced, why does any authority
