bother logging? Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser. Chrome’s
team set the rule, enforced from Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every certificate
issued after 30 April 2018 had to meet its transparency policy, and a publicly trusted
certificate that doesn’t is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor gets a full-page
warning in front of the site. So there is a price after all. It isn’t anywhere in the
specification. It lives in one vendor’s browser, and it’s the price of being shown to
that browser’s users at all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because it means the
strongest lever on this record is a policy one company can change, which is a fact
about who holds the stamp. The tree has nothing to do with it. That policy changes
nothing in the table at the end of this section, which asks what each specification
prices. But it’s worth keeping two sentences apart: “the specification prices nothing”
and “nothing is priced.”
    Do the inclusion proof by hand. Lay out seven cards d0 through d6 . Join
neighbours with paper brackets: a = ν(d0 , d1 ), b = ν(d2 , d3 ) and c = ν(d4 , d5 ).
The last card stands alone. Next join a to b, giving L = ν( a, b), and c to d6 , giving
R = ν(c, d6 ). The root is ν( L, R). Here ν means “put these two expressions, in this
order, inside one labelled bracket.” Equal symbolic hashes must have exactly the
same bracket structure.
    To check d3 , keep only that card and the three siblings d2 , a, R. Combine d2 on
its left to recover b, then a on the left to recover L, then R on the right to recover
366   17 Five small models


              the root. You never needed to open the cards inside a or R. That’s the inclusion
              path. The hashes here are brackets, not numbers, so what you just checked is how
              the tree is put together; a real log uses short hashes, and “two different trees can’t
              give the same root” is then a separate promise from the cryptography. Nothing in
              this fragment signs anything, no auditors talk to each other, and no log misbehaves.

              Definition 17.5 (Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2). Given a leaf index
              m, a tree size N, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check rejects unless
              m < N. Otherwise start counters f = m, s = N − 1 and an accumulated hash r
              equal to the leaf hash. For each path element p, reject if s = 0. If f is odd or f = s,
              replace r by ν( p, r ); in this branch, while f is positive and even, halve both counters
              with rounding down. In the other branch replace r by ν(r, p). After either branch
              halve both counters once more. At the end accept exactly when s = 0 and r is
              the claimed root. A symbolic hash makes a leaf hash ℓ( x ) and a node hash ν( a, b)
              distinct constructors: two hashes are equal only when their entire constructions
              agree.
                  The consistency check used here takes old and new sizes M, N, roots u, v and a
              path, and rejects unless 0 < M < N. If M is a power of two, prepend u to the path.
              Reject an empty resulting path; otherwise its first element seeds two accumulated
              hashes rold , rnew . Start f = M − 1, s = N − 1, and halve both while f is odd.
              Process each remaining path element p: reject if s = 0; when f is odd or f = s, put
              p on the left of both accumulated hashes and halve both counters while f is positive
              and even; otherwise leave rold alone and put p on the right of rnew . After either
              branch halve both counters once. Accept exactly when s = 0, rold = u and rnew = v.
              All halvings round down.



              Theorem 17.7 (The RFC’s own examples pass). With the symbolic hash, in the
              RFC’s seven-leaf tree with leaves d0 , . . . , d6 (writing dk also for its leaf hash ℓ(dk )),
              the inclusion check accepts leaf 3 with path [d2 , ν(d0 , d1 ), ν(ν(d4 , d5 ), d6 )], and
              likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6 with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size
              7 accepts. For every input with m = N, the inclusion check rejects.

              Proof. Use the brackets a, b, c, L, R built above. For leaf 3, the counters start at
              (3, 6): put d2 on the left, leaving (1, 3); put a on the left, leaving (0, 1); put R on
              the right, leaving (0, 0) and root ν( L, R). Leaf 0 has path [d1 , b, R] and three right
              combinations. Leaf 4 has path [d5 , d6 , L]: right, right, left. Leaf 6 has path [c, L]: left,
              then left; its first branch shifts (6, 6) to (3, 3) before the ordinary halving, which
              accounts for the unpaired last leaf. Each reconstructs the same root. For consistency
              from 4 to 7, the old root is L and the supplied path is [ R]. Prepending L seeds both
                                                    17.5 Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence   367


hashes with L; shifting the initial (3, 6) gives (0, 1), so the sole remaining element
leaves the old root alone and makes the new root ν( L, R), with final counters (0, 0).
The boundary case m = N fails the first test m < N.
    And the append-only part of the fragment is as plain as it sounds: the history is a
list, and adding to the end of a list leaves every old entry where it was.


17.5 Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence

Necula’s idea from Section 8: ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys the
host’s policy; the host computes what would need to be true and checks the proof
with a small checker. The record is the checked proof, and it’s held only for the
moment of loading. Priced? No. Checking is cheap by design, which is the whole
point, and the producer paid to build the proof off the host. Permanent? No;
nothing’s written. The fragment is a three-instruction memory-bounds language
with the policy “every address is below the limit”: the checker accepts exactly when
the condition holds, and a certificate implies the condition. One example sits on top
of that, a computation you can do in your head: a program that reads address two
under a limit of two is rejected. Not the paper’s real case study, and no bridge to
anything else in this book. And its limit: a program that writes garbage to address
zero passes if zero is below the limit. The proof is of the stated policy and nothing
else.
    And what was the paper’s real case study, the one my fragment isn’t? Network
packet filters: the little programs an operating system runs on incoming network
traffic to decide which program gets to see which packet. They run inside the kernel,
the most trusted part of the system, and they have to be fast, so they’re exactly the
code you’d most like to take from a stranger and least like to trust. In the 1996
paper that first set out the idea, Necula and Peter Lee wrote several filters by hand
in the assembly language of a DEC Alpha, shipped each with its proof, and reported
a one-time cost of 1 to 3 milliseconds to check the proof, after which the filter ran
with no checks at all. That’s “checking is cheap by design” with a number on it. It
changes nothing about my fragment, which still isn’t that case study, and it doesn’t
add a price: the milliseconds are the checker’s work, and nothing is being written
down for them to be a toll on.

Definition 17.6 (The bounds fragment). Instructions are READ a, WRITE a v, and
HALT. For a memory limit L, the policy allows READ a and WRITE a v when a < L,
and always allows HALT. The verification condition of a program is that the policy
allows every instruction in it. A certificate is a list of per-instruction policy facts, one
for each instruction in order. The checker tests the policy on each instruction and
returns the conjunction.
368   17 Five small models




              Theorem 17.8 (The checker is the verification condition). For every limit L and
              program P: the checker accepts P exactly when the verification condition holds; any
              certificate for P gives the verification condition; and with L = 2 the checker rejects
              READ 2 followed by HALT.

              Proof. The first two are induction on the program and on the certificate, one instruc-
              tion at a time. The third is a computation: 2 < 2 fails.


              17.6 One example, three levels

              Before I lay all five side by side, let me walk one of them up and down the three
              levels from the start of the section, because every claim in here lives at exactly one
              level and it’s easy to let a claim slide up a floor without noticing. Gas, since it’s the
              one place all three line up. Think of a restaurant’s real recipe, my photocopy of one
              page of it, and a cookbook chapter on what any recipe has to contain. I can check
              my photocopy line by line. That tells you nothing about what the kitchen cooks
              tonight.
                  The real specification. Ethereum’s execution specification says, in a document
              that runs real money, what a storage write costs, what clearing it refunds, and how
              the refund is capped at the end of the transaction. None of what I proved is at this
              level. What the network actually charges is whatever the clients people run actually
              compute, and the evidence for that is the clients and the chain. This book has none
              of it.
                  The transcription. I copied one mechanism out of that document, one slot in one
              transaction, gas and refund arithmetic only, at a named commit (Definition 17.2,
              Theorem 17.3). What the result tells you: if the storage rule is what I copied,
              then leaving a fresh slot set costs at least twenty thousand, and set-then-clear nets
              twenty-three hundred at the counter. What it can’t tell you: anything about the
              refund cap (not copied, which is why the bill came out so different from the counter
              earlier), the stack, calls, other slots, or whether any client implements the rule as
              written. The boundary of the claim is the edge of the copy.
                  The wrapper. The gas schedule of Definition 17.3 isn’t Ethereum. It’s any system
              with steps, a cost per step and a yes/no commitment flag, plus one thing stipulated:
              a charge predicate, with the premise that a charged step costs at least one and an
              uncharged one costs zero. That premise is the whole of what the wrapper adds, and
              it’s added by hand; no specification supplies it. Given it, the theorem says the bill is
              exact, never letting a commit go unbilled and never billing a non-commit, exactly
              when the charge predicate is the commit predicate at unit price. What that tells you
                                                                    17.7 The same table, five ways   369


is what exact pricing would have to look like, in any system. It doesn’t say Ethereum
meets it, and Ethereum doesn’t: real gas bills computation that commits nothing,
which the transcription shows in numbers. So the wrapper prices a definition, the
transcription prices a copied rule, and neither prices the chain.
    The other four sit on the same three levels, and only one more wrapper is spelled
out in this section. Casper’s transcription is the accountable-safety proof above; its
wrapper is a small gadget with the stake at risk handed in. A finalize step that risks
nothing turns the record on at no charge, which breaks Section 2’s toll, and one
that risks at least one unit has a floor. It records exposure to loss (no collateral is
destroyed in it), has no Casper checkpoints in it at all, and is priced by stipulation,
the same way the gas wrapper is. Attestation, transparency and proof-carrying code
have transcriptions that prove what their verifiers do and no price theorem, because
their specifications carry no price. Their wrappers, which I don’t spell out here, are
Section 7’s verifier argument told in each system’s vocabulary, with a colliding pair
behind each one, and that argument is all they carry here.
    How to knock down the four claims with the most weight on them, since the
book’s rule is that every claim gets a way to break it. For the gas transcription: a list
of stores from a fresh slot that ends nonzero with net charge under twenty thousand.
For the gas wrapper: a schedule that never lets a commit go unbilled and never bills
a non-commit, whose charge predicate still differs from the commit predicate at
some step. For the finality gadget: a finalizing trace from unfinalized to finalized
whose charged stake is zero while the gadget claims a floor. For the attestation
fragment: a verifier reading only the quote’s fields that decides a runtime flag the
quote ignores.


17.7 The same table, five ways

Lay them out by the one definition of price from the start of the section. Casper puts
a bond behind the write and takes it on reversal (slashing). Gas takes a fee at the
write (and refunds the revocation, capped), and rations writes with a gas limit per
block. Attestation prices nothing on the registers the quote signs, and puts a budget
on its longer-lived slots and counters. Transparency prices nothing. Attestation and
transparency make reversal infeasible or visible. Proof-carrying code prices nothing
and keeps nothing.

                 Each row proves what its own transcription says, and no more. To read a row
