                 So the thing my toy charges for, the moment the record is written, is charged
              a fee in one of the five specifications I read, and in that one the designers had
              to patch the place where the charge could be clawed back. I find that neither a
              vindication nor a refutation. It’s a fact about what people built, and what they built
              was mostly walls (hash chains, signatures) and penalties for contradiction. Tolls
              on commitment were rare. Whether a toll on commitment is a better design than a
              wall is not something I can prove, and I won’t pretend the five say so. What I read
              in them, and it’s a reading of five fragments I chose, is that each has a condition
              treated as a record, though the conditions differ in durability, and that the price axis
              is mostly empty. With one definition of price fixed before the survey, that last part is
              a count: of fifteen cells in the table, four are filled (one fee, one bond, two budgets),
              and only gas takes a payment at the moment of the write.
                                                                     17.7 The same table, five ways   371


   That leaves the question Section 10 raised and Section 18 has to face. Five
systems, five different events chosen as “the record”: finalized, committed, attested,
logged, checked. Is there anything that picks out one event as the one worth
recording, or is it a free choice every time? I have a guess. It’s a thesis, and I’ll show
you how to kill it.
CHAPTER 18




The pointer thesis

Everything so far leaves one choice open. A permanent record driven by the machine
is a latch on an event, and the event is yours to pick (Section 10, the two cups on one
die). Five real systems each picked a different one (Section 17). For the machine in
this book I picked certification. So I owe you an answer to the obvious question: is
that just my choice, or is there something about how people and machines lean on
records that picks this event out?
    What I have is a thesis, in the sense the Church-Turing thesis is one (Section 5):
a claim tying defined things to the world, which no proof can settle. Whether it
stands or falls is what decides whether the choice of event was free. Nothing before
it depends on it; the latch, the windows and the counting arguments hold whichever
event a system records. Here’s the claim, where I got it, what can be checked, and
how to kill it.


18.1 The claim
Of all the events a machine could put on its ledger, the ones its price list charges
for and its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records get copied and
relied on by parties who didn’t produce them: checked, stored, and acted on across
independent places that share no other state. Copying alone can’t be the test. A
replicated system copies everything it holds to every node, the gas used in a block
header as faithfully as the word final, so rival events get copied too. Nobody who
didn’t produce them acts on them. If that’s true, choosing certification has a reason
behind it, given a premise about incentives. It’s the one event the world around the
machine keeps redundant copies of and leans on, and that’s a reason to price it and
leave the others unpriced. So the thesis has two halves, and the ways to kill it at the
end aim at both: certification is that event, and where a deployed discipline puts a
price on writing a record, the record it prices is one that’s copied and relied on in
that sense.
    There’s a second handle on the same question, and it comes from Section 3.
The permanent-certificate theorem (Theorem 3.1) never uses the word certification
for anything special: given Section 3’s rule that forgetting is charged, it prices any
yes-or-no reading that, once on, stays on, on a machine with finite memory. So it
points at a narrower candidate: the events to price are the ones that write a record

                                 372
                                       18.2 Where the shape comes from, and how much of it survived   373


no later step can take back. Certification is one of them. As an exact answer that
candidate is false, because a merging step can also revoke (Section 3’s three cards).
Whether the records that are copied and relied on are the permanent ones, and
whether being copied and relied on picks out anything the merge criterion doesn’t,
is what the two handles have to settle between them.
   Two holes in that, which I can see from here, so you don’t have to find them for
me. The first is a missing premise. Even if the world copies certification records
more than any other kind, “copied” doesn’t give you “priced” on its own. Something
has to connect them, and the best candidate I have is a premise about incentives: a
record that many independent parties copy and lean on is exactly the record worth
forging, so it’s the one where a price buys the most protection. That’s a reasonable
premise. It’s also a premise. The thesis’s second half states the connection as a claim
to be tested; it doesn’t explain it, and nothing in this book supplies the explanation.
The second hole is a circle. If “certification” just means “the record other people rely
on,” then of course it’s the one that gets relied on and copied, and the claim says
nothing. So the event has to be picked out without mentioning reliance: here it’s a
reading going up for good right after a check of the same claim passed, which you
can find in a run without asking who reads it. Whether the world copies that event
more than its rivals is then a real question, and it could come out no.
   That’s the whole thesis. Now the rest of what a thesis owes you.


18.2 Where the shape comes from, and how much of it survived

The shape is from physics, and I want to tell you where exactly, because I borrowed
a word and I didn’t get to keep the whole thing.
   Quantum mechanics has a famous problem: a system can be in a blend of states,
and when you measure it you find one definite state, and nobody agrees on what
“measuring” did. In 1981 Wojciech Zurek asked a sharper question: of all the ways a
measuring device could end up, why does it end up recording one particular kind
of quantity (the position of a pointer on a dial, say)? Why never some blend?
His answer, developed over twenty years and summarised in a 2009 paper called
“Quantum Darwinism,” is that the environment decides. The air, the light, the table,
everything the device touches, is constantly interacting with it, and only certain
states of the device survive that interaction; those are the pointer states. And more:
the environment selects them, and then it copies them. The light bouncing off a
dial carries the dial’s reading to every corner of the room, redundantly, so that
a thousand observers can each read a different scrap of the environment and all
agree on where the pointer is, without touching the dial. Objectivity, on this view, is
redundancy: a property is objective when many independent fragments of the world
each carry it.
374   18 The pointer thesis


                   Zurek isn’t the only one behind it. Fernando Brandão, Marco Piani and Paweł
               Horodecki (2015) published a proof that, as I read it, makes something like it
               generic: under any quantum dynamics at all, observers who learn about a system
               only through its environment get at most classical information, about one and the
               same measurement of the system. That’s their theorem behind the word “objective,”
               and it’s a statement about separate fragments, which is exactly the part I didn’t keep.
               Xiao-Liang Qi and Daniel Ranard (2021), as I read their paper, sharpened it into a
               statement about every possible evolution of system and environment: everywhere
               in the environment outside a region of fixed size, whatever an observer can learn
               about the system is classical, read off one fixed measurement. A statement about
               every evolution and every input is the quantum cousin of what the definitions below
               ask of an observer, that it record the event in every state, including ones that never
               happen to turn up.
                   That’s the shape I borrowed. Certification is to a machine’s ecosystem (the
               machine plus everything around it that reads, stores and relies on its records) what
               the pointer reading is to the room: the thing that gets copied everywhere. It’s a good
               shape and I think it’s the right intuition. Here’s what survived into the definitions
               below, and I’m going to be exact because the word “redundant” is doing less than it
               does for Zurek.
                   Zurek’s redundancy is graded (each fragment carries almost all the information,
               with some small loss) and it requires the fragments to be disjoint: different observers
               reading different parts of the environment. The definition below is the zero-loss case
               with no disjointness at all. An ecosystem is a state type, some number of observers,
               and one bit per observer; an observer records an event when its bit is true exactly
               when the event holds; an event proliferates when every observer records it. Nothing
               in that says two observers draw on separate parts of the state. They could all be
               reading the same bit. The definition permits it. So I kept the word and dropped the
               independence that makes Zurek’s version mean “objective.” That’s a gap between
               the thesis’s prose and that first formal object, and the prose is where the thesis lives.
               The definitions under the thesis below close part of the gap: they define independent
               carriers, and the definition turns out to force something (Theorem 18.1).
                   The independence I dropped is exactly what the thesis’s closest published neigh-
               bour keeps. Jess Riedel, Zurek and Michael Zwolak (2016) took histories of a closed
               quantum system, the story a whole sequence of events tells, and asked which of
               them the world keeps records of in many separate pieces of the environment. As I
               read their paper, redundant records in separate pieces make a history consistent, so
               ordinary yes-or-no reasoning about it works, and they pick out a small set of histories
               from the huge number that are merely consistent: in their words, an objective past.
               That’s “what proliferates is what counts” in quantum form, with the disjointness in it,
               and it came before this book. Halliwell, in a second 1999 paper, “Somewhere in the
                                      18.2 Where the shape comes from, and how much of it survived   375


universe,” had already carried the link between records and consistent histories from
pure starting states to mixed ones, where the records still exist but are necessarily
imperfect.
    There’s a deeper mismatch in the borrowing, and it runs against the book, so it
goes here. In Zurek’s picture the whole thing, system and device and environment
together, evolves by quantum mechanics’ rule for closed systems, and that rule never
sends two states to one; every step can be run backwards. So, seen from the whole,
the environment’s copying is just that, copying: the dial’s reading gets written onto
fresh light, and no two states anywhere are merged. That doesn’t make it free. Every
copy lands on light that hadn’t carried anything yet, so it spends room, and the rest
of the universe is the page it spends. It’s Door one of Section 3, the room column,
with the universe as the endless strip, and it’s Bennett’s demon copying onto a blank
page (Section 4): no merge, so no floor owed under Landauer’s premise, and a page
used up. The forgetting shows up only when you look at the dial alone and ignore
what the light carried off. Then a blend of pointer readings decays into a plain
either-or, and two different blends can decay into the same either-or: two states,
one result, a merge in the coarse picture. So the opening’s “every keeping pays”
comes out right from both sides: from the dial’s own view it pays by forgetting, and
from the whole nothing merges and it’s paid in room instead, the light that carried
the copies away. And the thing the thesis leans on, copying, is the half of the story
that borrows room and owes no floor. What that does to the thesis: if there’s a floor
under Landauer’s premise, it isn’t on the copying. It’s on whatever makes the copy
final from the dial’s side, or wipes a page for reuse, and the claim above, as written,
points at the copy.
    A published no-go cuts closer still. Philippe Allard Guérin, Veronika Baumann,
Flavio Del Santo and Časlav Brukner (2021) gave an argument that, under assump-
tions that look natural in quantum mechanics, an observer’s own perceptions of her
outcome at two different times can’t share one reality: no joint chance for the two,
depending linearly on the starting state, reproduces what unitary quantum theory
predicts for each. A record that persists, for the one holding it, is exactly what gets
into trouble once the whole is treated as one-to-one. It isn’t a theorem about my
machine, which isn’t quantum. It’s still the strongest published reason I know to
hold the word “permanent” loosely when a physicist is in the room.
    Which leaves the question to ask of any borrowed shape: has anybody checked
the original? For a long time quantum Darwinism was a theory without a lab. Then,
in 2018 and 2019, three groups working separately, in Italy, China and Germany,
went looking for its fingerprint, as Philip Ball’s 2019 report in Quanta Magazine
tells it. The German one, at Ulm, with Zurek among the authors, watched the
spin of a single defect inside a diamond and the carbon atoms around it, and
saw the redundancy the theory predicts: the defect’s state turned up copied in its
376   18 The pointer thesis


               surroundings, and it didn’t take much of the surroundings before more of them told
               you nothing new. The other two did it with photons. Is that the bottom? Not by a
               long way, and the people involved said so. Zurek himself pointed out that the photon
               experiments make their copies artificially and that the diamond’s environment is
               small, and others noted that all three are schematic versions of a real environment
               and don’t rule out rival accounts. So the shape I borrowed has passed some first tests
               in a lab, at the scale of a handful of atoms or photons, with the caveats written on
               it. None of that touches the thesis here, which is about machines and never rested
               on quantum physics. It changes the picture: what I borrowed is a lead somebody is
               checking. It isn’t settled, and I don’t get to lean on it as if it were.


               18.3 What’s proved

               Definitions, two toys, a theorem about independence, a survey, and two refutations
               of things that would have been stronger.
                   The definitions above, plus “unique pointer among rivals”: the event proliferates
               and none of a listed set of rival events does. Uniqueness is relative to the list,
               necessarily, since any event that holds on exactly the same states as a proliferating
               event proliferates whenever it does: the same fact under another name, so someone
               has to say which names count as rivals. And the first criterion, as a schema: for
               every ecosystem in some class, its metered event is the unique pointer among its
               rivals. The class and the rivals are inputs. Nothing about them is proved. A second
               set of definitions, after this one, tightens “proliferates” to “copied and relied on” and
               drops the rival list.
                   Here’s the formal object, small enough to hold in one hand.

               Definition 18.1 (Ecosystem, records, proliferates, pointer). An ecosystem is a type
               of states, a number N of observers, and for each observer i a Boolean fragment Fi
               on states. Observer i records an event E (a property of states) when, for every state
               s, E(s) holds exactly when Fi (s) is true. E proliferates when every observer i < N
               records it. E is the unique pointer among a list of rival events when E proliferates
               and no rival in the list does. Given a class C of ecosystems, and for each member a
               designated metered event and a list of rivals, the pointer criterion holds for C when
               every member’s metered event is the unique pointer among its rivals.
                   Nothing in the definition makes two fragments read different parts of the state,
               and “metered” is only a label: the definition has no metering in it.
                   One bit per observer can’t even state the objection a replicated system raises.
               Every full node of a blockchain holds the whole shared state, so every fact about
               it, “gas used is at least one” as much as “final,” sits on every node. The tightened
                                                                              18.3 What’s proved   377


definitions give each observer whatever it holds, an action it takes on what it holds,
and a flag for whether it produced the record.

Definition 18.2 (Copied and relied on, independent carriers, the pointer). An
ecosystem with reliance is a type of states, a number N of observers, and for each
observer i a view Vi (a function from states to some type of things an observer can
hold), an action ai (a Boolean function of the view) and a producer flag. Fix a
set R of reachable states. An event E is copied on R when for each i < N some
Boolean function d of the view has E(s) exactly when d(Vi (s)) is true, for every s
in R. Observer i relies on E when ai (Vi (s)) true gives E(s) for every s in R, and
ai (Vi (s)) is true for some s in R. E is relied on by parties who didn’t produce it when
some observer i < N is not a producer and every such observer relies on E; it is
copied and relied on when it is both. E is the pointer on R when it is copied and
relied on, and every event that is copied and relied on holds at every state of R
where E holds. An event a step rule could meter is one decided by a Boolean function
of the state, so a price list can charge exactly the steps that turn it on. The carriers
are independent under a family of relations Pi (states that agree on observer i’s own
part of the world) when each view gives equal values on states related by its Pi ,
and for any two observers i ̸= j below N and any states s, t there is a state u with
Pi (u, s) and Pj (u, t): the two parts can be set separately.

    Two pointers on the same R agree on every state of R, so the pointer is unique
with no list of rivals. And the definition of independence has a consequence I didn’t
put in on purpose.
    Put one yes/no card in front of each of two readers. If the cards can be set
separately, all four arrangements are allowed: no/no, no/yes, yes/no and yes/yes.
Ask each reader to recover one shared event using only their own card. Suppose
that event is false at no/no and true at yes/yes. At no/yes, the first reader sees
exactly what they saw in the false case, while the second sees exactly what they saw
in the true case. Their answers conflict. That mixed arrangement is exactly what the
independence condition hands the proof.
    Now impose a copying procedure that only leaves no/no or yes/yes. On those
reachable arrangements each reader can report the shared bit correctly. Separate
cards are things that could carry a copy; what makes them copies is that the
arrangements you actually reach have the two agreeing. The theorem below is
about recovering the event exactly on all arrangements, the mixed ones included,
which the copying never leaves behind.
378   18 The pointer thesis




               Theorem 18.1 (Independent copies on every state: the event is equivalent at any
               two states). In any ecosystem with reliance whose carriers are independent and
               which has at least two observers, an event copied on the set of all states holds at
               one state exactly when it holds at any other, so it holds at every state or at none.

               Proof. Let observers 0 and 1 decide the event by d0 and d1 . Given states s and t,
               take u with observer 0’s part from s and observer 1’s from t. Then the event at s is
               d0 of observer 0’s view, which is the same at u, so it equals the event at u; and the
               event at u equals the event at t the same way through observer 1.
                  So separate parts of the world can each carry an exact copy of a real record only
               on the states the world actually reaches, where the copying made them agree, and
               that’s why the definition asks for copies on a set R of reachable states. Zurek’s copies
               are the same: the light carries the dial’s reading because the dial put it there.


               Theorem 18.2 (A replicated header: copying doesn’t separate, reliance does). Let
               the states be a block header (a finalized bit, a gas-used count) and three nodes’
               copies of it, with R the states where every copy equals the header; node i’s view is
               its own copy, its part of the world is that copy, node 0 is the producer, and every
               node acts exactly when its copy says finalized. Then the carriers are independent;
               “finalized” and “gas used is at least one” are both copied on R; “finalized” is the
               pointer on R; and “gas used is at least one” is not relied on by parties who didn’t
               produce it.

               Proof. Independence: to give node i the copy from s and node j the copy from t,
               overwrite node j’s copy in s. On R every copy is the header, so each node reads
               either fact off its copy. Node 1 acts only where its copy, and so the header, says
               finalized, and acts at the finalized header with no gas used; that state shows gas
               used fails node 1’s reliance. Any event relied on by node 1 holds wherever node 1
               acts, which on R is wherever the header is finalized, so “finalized” is the strongest.
                  It’s a sanity check with maps I wrote, and it shows only that the tightened
               definition can tell the two apart where plain copying can’t.


               Thesis 18.3 (The pointer thesis). Let C be the class of ecosystems with reliance
               that faithfully model deployed record-keeping disciplines, each with its reachable
               states, its observers reading independent carriers in the sense of Definition 18.2, its
                                                                              18.3 What’s proved   379


certification event, and the records its discipline prices. Then for every member of
C: (1) the certification event is the pointer on the reachable states, so it is copied
and relied on by parties who didn’t produce it, and every event copied and relied
on in that sense, every event a step rule could meter among them, holds wherever
certification does; and (2) every record the discipline prices is copied and relied on
by parties who didn’t produce it.

    The thesis leans on two notions with no precise mathematical definition: what
it is to “faithfully model” a system, and which systems count as “deployed.” Those
two tie the definitions to the world, the way “computable in the plain-English sense”
does in the Church-Turing thesis, and no definition can do that job, so the claim is
a thesis. The other two terms it needs, independent carriers and the events a step
rule could meter, are defined in Definition 18.2. The schema takes the class, the
reachable states, the certification event and the priced records as inputs; it proves
nothing about which real systems satisfy them.
    A toy: three observers on a replicated ledger, where certification proliferates and
“work done” doesn’t. It’s an illustration, and that’s all it is. It isn’t evidence.


Theorem 18.4 (The toy). Let the toy have states (a certified bit, a work count),
three observers, and every fragment equal to the certified bit. Then “certified” is the
unique pointer among the one rival “work at least 1”.

Proof. Every fragment is the certified bit, so every observer records “certified” by
definition. For the rival, take the state with the bit false and work 1: the event holds
and observer 0’s fragment is false, so observer 0 does not record it.
    A survey of twelve events, one theorem: for each of the five systems in Section 17,
the designated event (finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked) proliferates
in the observer map I wrote for that system, and a rival (proposer work, a scratch
counter, measurement noise, submission latency, prover steps) doesn’t. The five
together are one statement, an instance of the schema above. Plus a symmetric
message-authentication code, which does not proliferate, and a digital signature,
which does. Twelve rows. The five maps all use the same construction: a state has a
designated Boolean event and a separate nonnegative rival count, three observers
each return the event bit, and the rival asks whether its count is at least one. The
bit and count can vary independently. The signature map likewise gives all three
observers the authentic-signature bit. In the MAC map, observers 0 and 1 receive
the authentic-tag bit and observer 2 always returns false. These maps, not a protocol
running on a network, are the entire tests here. And a thirteenth that I think is the
most important one: swap which bit every observer copies, and the criterion picks
380   18 The pointer thesis


               the other event. The criterion selects whatever the observer map copies. The map
               is where the argument lives, and I wrote the maps. So the five “confirmations” are
               five instances of one construction with the fields renamed. I’m saying that twice on
               purpose, so it can’t slip past once.


               Theorem 18.5 (The survey, and the swap). (1) In each of the five observer models
               (proof-of-stake, gas, attestation, transparency, proof-carrying), the designated event
               proliferates and the designated rival does not; in the symmetric-MAC model the
               authentic-tag event does not proliferate; in the signature model the authentic-
               signature event does. (2) Let the states be pairs of bits (first, second), with three
               observers whose fragments all equal the second bit. Then “second is true” is the
               unique pointer among the one rival “first is true”.

               Proof. Each confirmation holds by definition: each observer’s fragment is true
               exactly when the event holds. Each refutation exhibits one state where the event
               holds and some observer’s bit is down. In (2) that state is (true, false).
                  Two stronger claims, both refuted, and I’d ask you not to merge them because
               they fail for different reasons.
                  The first stronger claim: every forgery-resistant commitment proliferates. If that
               were true, certification would be the pointer because it’s the commitment. It’s
               refuted in three observer models (deniable authentication, where only the designated
               verifier’s bit tracks the event; a symmetric MAC, where the key holders share a secret
               and nobody else can check; an object capability, an unforgeable token that grants
               access to whoever holds it) and confirmed in two (a public log; a digital signature).
               Build the first with three observers: give one a copy of the event’s bit and the other
               two a constant false. The one records it; it doesn’t proliferate. The proved half is the
               map computation. Whether my maps are fair to the real designs is argued in prose,
               and you should argue back.


               Theorem 18.6 (One blind observer is enough). (1) In any ecosystem, if some
               observer i < N has Fi (s0 ) false at a state s0 where E holds, then E does not
               proliferate. (2) Let the deniable model have states (authentic, verifier-accepts),
               three observers, observer 0’s fragment the authentic bit and observers 1 and 2
               constantly false. Then observer 0 records “authentic”, and “authentic” does not
               proliferate. The symmetric-MAC and object-capability models also fail to proliferate
               their events; the public-log and signature models proliferate theirs.
                                                                              18.3 What’s proved   381


Proof. (1) Recording would require E(s0 ) ⇐⇒ Fi (s0 ), and the left side is true
while the right is false. (2) Observer 0’s fragment is true exactly when the event
holds. Apply (1) with observer 1 and the state (true, true). The other two refutations
apply (1) to a blind observer of their own model (the symmetric-MAC map gives
observer 2 a constant false; the object-capability map gives the token holder the bit
and the other two constant false). The two confirmations hold by definition: the
public-log map gives all three observers the logged bit, and the signature map gives
all three the authentic-signature bit.
    The theorem is about the observer maps, and only them. That a third party in
deniable authentication really cannot be convinced is the modelling claim, and the
model has no transcript, key or verifier in it to check that against.
    The second stronger claim: agreement plus accuracy plus locality imply permanence.
That is, if all observers agree, each sees the event exactly, and each updates by the
same local rule with no coordinator, then the recorded event can’t be undone.
Refuted by the smallest thing imaginable: one bit, two observers who both see it,
and the rule “flip.” All three conditions hold and true becomes false in one step.
Do it on paper; it takes a minute and it’s humbling. What does give permanence
is durability, “an observer’s true view stays true,” added as a premise, and then it
follows in a few lines. So durability is the premise doing the work, and durability
is Section 3’s permanence wearing a different coat. Agreement doesn’t buy it. Do
the paper version again with one change, the rule “stay true once true” in place of
“flip,” and the bit can’t fall, because the rule won’t let it. The observers agreeing has
nothing to do with it. (The small machine of Section 15 has a reading that’s durable
in exactly this sense: its flag never comes down, by its step rule (Theorem 15.5).)
None of this rules out a narrower theorem with real assumptions about the network,
the adversary or durability; it rules out these two strong forms.

Definition 18.3 (Observation game). A game has states, a number N of observers, a
Boolean event e, a Boolean view Vi for each observer, and a step map. For i, j < N it
has consensus when Vi = Vj on every state; authenticity when Vi (s) = e(s) for every
state and every i < N; coordinator-free update when one function ℓ on Booleans has
Vi (step(s)) = ℓ(Vi (s)) for every state and every i < N; durable views when Vi (s)
true gives Vi (step(s)) true for every i < N; and a permanent event when e(s) true
gives e(step(s)) true.



Theorem 18.7 (What buys permanence). (1) It is false that every game with N > 0,
consensus, authenticity and coordinator-free update has a permanent event. (2)
Every game with N > 0, authenticity and durable views has a permanent event.
382   18 The pointer thesis


               Proof. (1) The toggle game: states are Booleans, two observers, event and both
               views the identity, step “flip”. Consensus and authenticity hold trivially, the local
               rule is “flip”, and the state true steps to false. (2) If e(s) is true, observer 0’s view
               is true by authenticity, stays true by durability, and authenticity turns it back into
               e(step(s)).


               18.4 What isn’t proved, and must stay that way on the page
               That certification in deployed systems is singled out by being copied and relied on
               across independent carriers. The criterion defines independence; it has no precise
               definition of “deployed” or “faithfully model,” and no cost law connecting being
               copied and relied on to price. Every correspondence between a mathematical
               observer map and a real system is a sentence I wrote. The thesis is a thesis, and
               anyone who says the formal object proves it is reading more than is there.


               18.5 How to kill it

               Three ways, in the order I’d try them.
                   One: find a deployed discipline that puts a price on writing a record that parties
               who didn’t produce it don’t copy and rely on. A real system with a toll on something
               nobody else leans on. That breaks the second half, “the priced record is the copied
               and relied-on one.”
                   Two: find a rival event, one certification doesn’t imply, that is copied and relied
               on as well as certification in a real ecosystem. Then certification isn’t the pointer and
               the first half’s “the one” is wrong. Or do it in a model: show that something like a
               multiplication count, or the number of times a Turing machine’s head turns around,
               is copied and relied on by the same standard, so the criterion picks out more than
               one event and decides nothing.
                   Three: formalise an ecosystem honestly, with independence as Definition 18.2
               defines it, where certification fails the test. The symmetric-MAC row is already most
               of the way there for a different claim; push it.
                   The theorems above have already refuted two stronger forms of the thesis’s claim,
               which I take as a sign the method works and as a warning about the main claim.


               18.6 The end of the logic

               That’s the end of the logic that started in Part I. Part I found the bill: anything kept
               is paid in a merge or in room, on top of the dissipation of every change a real device
               makes (Section 1), and a toll on raising a flag is forced by three premises (Section 3).
               Learning doesn’t have to merge anything, so it owes no floor; it borrows a blank
                                                                          18.6 The end of the logic   383


page, which is room, and can hand it back. Committing on finite room has to merge
(Section 4). Part II earned the rest. The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is
fixed (Section 6). A window with a colliding pair in it can’t price the flag exactly
(Section 7). Entitlement is an object, a check, and a paid event, and, given lists, a
tree and a covering that someone supplies, and a run that paid for the tree’s depth,
it costs at least the index bits it commits to (Section 8). Insight is a distinction made
to stay, and a committed relation is that at its best (Section 9). A feeling doesn’t
qualify. Over any base a record that is driven by the computation and never comes
down is a latch, with two free choices, the price list and the event (Section 10).
With more than two places, a record that is driven by the computation and climbs a
partial order is a row of cups, each one a latch; the toll over the whole row charges
at least one on any step that turns up some cup, and a straight strip needs exactly
one cup fewer than it has stages, cups that only turn up (Section 11). When the
machine has finitely many states, its record only grows, and the ordinary machine
forgets nothing, the toll prices crushing two states of one fibre, and a window can
price exactly by seeing the cups move (Section 12). No inside procedure whose flip
a substrate can represent decides a shortcut property, given a recursion theorem,
which the nat family has by construction. L is handled on its own terms rather
than as a substrate, and on L the same diagonal is proved again from a recursion
theorem it has by proof. What a record can do is carry the commitment (Section 13).
This part made “established” a record that a check of the claim passed (Section 14),
and the small machine earns one by a check, a commitment and a certificate, a
mark each (Section 15). Of five specifications, read through my transcriptions, one
charges a fee at the write (Section 17). For the choice of event, the pointer thesis
proposes certification and lists how that proposal could fail (Section 18).
    One question about the bill itself is still open: do the requirements I’ve put on a
price pick out the toll and nothing else? If a short list of them left only one price
standing, that would settle it. The lists I tried don’t, and the no is small enough
to check on three states. Call them blank, once and twice, with once and twice
reading yes. The flip takes blank to once and leaves the other two where they are.
The smooth takes both once and twice to twice and leaves blank alone. The smooth
forgets something, so the price on merging from Section 3 charges it a mark. (The
flip forgets too, blank and once both land on once, so the price on merging charges
it as well, as the list requires.) It raises nothing, so the toll charges it nothing. Now
try requirements that name no reading: no charge on a move that changes nothing,
none on a move that forgets nothing, the same bill when you rename the states,
a total that adds up along a run, a bill that looks only at the step, and one mark
on the flip from blank. The toll, read as the bill that charges the flip from blank
and nothing else, meets every one of them on this machine. So does the price on
merging. They disagree on the smooth, so that list doesn’t pick between them. What
384   18 The pointer thesis


               picks the toll is a requirement that names the record: over any run the total is never
               more than the number of times the reading went up. With the floor, that leaves
               exactly one bill, one mark per raise and nothing else (Section 7), and it rules the
               price on merging out, because the smooth costs that price a mark and raises nothing.
               The only renaming of the three states that respects the moves is the identity, so the
               renaming requirement asks nothing there. So the uniqueness is real and it’s small.
               It holds once you’ve said which reading you’re charging for, and which reading
               deserves the charge is the pointer thesis, which is still a thesis.
                   The uniqueness theorems that do exist are about pricing information loss, and
               they’re worth a look because they say what kind of bill the price on merging is. John
               Baez, Tobias Fritz and Tom Leinster (2011), mathematicians who work in category
               theory, the mathematics Lawvere’s diagonal theorem came from, asked what a
               measure of information loss has to look like. As I read their paper, they proved
               that, for maps that preserve a probability measure, Shannon entropy is up to a
               constant factor the only measure of information loss that is functorial, convex-linear
               and continuous. János Aczél and Bruno Forte, mathematicians at the University
               of Waterloo who worked on functional equations, and C. T. Ng, who had taken
               his doctorate there under Aczél in 1971, asked in a paper of 1974 which entropies
               deserve to be called natural, and proved, by their account, that the entropies with
               a short list of natural properties are exactly the linear combinations of Shannon’s
               and Hartley’s, where Hartley’s is the log of the count, so even for merges the choice
               between the average and the worst case is a real choice. Both price merges. Neither
               prices raises, so neither picks out the toll, and that’s the three-state example in
               a bigger room. On the other side of the fence, Luciano Pomatto, Philipp Strack
               and Omer Tamuz (2023), economists at Caltech and Yale who asked what learning
               something should cost, proved, by their account, a uniqueness result for what it costs
               to acquire information, with constant marginal costs. That’s a price on producing a
               signal, a different bill from the one Section 4 reads off a copy onto a blank page,
               which owes no floor and borrows room.
                   Most of that isn’t a machine. The theorems of Parts I and II quantify over “any
               states, any steps,” and the five models are small copies of somebody else’s systems.
               The one machine is the small one of Section 15, the least I could make that still
               shows the whole model, with every part named and every price written down, and
               the program that runs every program of it and, with one paid move added, every
               Thiele machine whose workings a program can compute, is in Appendix D. That’s
               where everything above has something to bump into. If a statement up there doesn’t
               mean what I think it means, that’s where it shows, and Part IV is how you’d go
               looking.
CHAPTER 19




The counter against physics

Section 3 did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag
merges states, a price list that charges merges (a named premise, with Landauer’s
principle, another named premise, as the physics behind it) charges the flag, and
the toll follows. I’m not going to do it again. This section is about what a machine’s
counter, the small machine’s µ included, has to do with any of that, and the answer
is: less than naming Landauer might suggest, and I want you to hear the exact
amount from me.


19.1 The calibration is a unit conversion

Multiply the counter by an energy per mark that you choose, and you get a theorem:
a state with one mark, at the scale kT ln 2 per mark, carries kT ln 2 of energy, for
every k and T. Read that for exactly what it is: a unit conversion, true by definition,
with the scale as a free input. Nothing in it picks the scale. The theorem would be
just as true with the scale set to a dollar a mark. What would connect marks to joules
is the premise in Section 3, Landauer’s principle, which is a physical premise. And
even as a scale, k B T ln 2 a mark is the floor for one particular squeeze, a halving.
Corollary 3.11’s floor for a flip that brings k states into a room already holding
m, starting from the even spread on those m + k states, is k B T ln mm+k , and for one
newcomer into a big room that’s far below a halving, roughly k B T/m. Price every
mark at k B T ln 2 and you can overstate the floor of a single narrow flip by a factor
that grows with m.
    Remember the constant from Boltzmann’s grave in Section 3, the exchange rate
between a count and heat? It has a newer chapter, and it makes the point sharper
than I can. The k B in k B T ln 2 turns a temperature into an energy, and for most
of its history it was a measured number, with error bars, pinned down by careful
experiments. Since 20 May 2019 it isn’t. That day the international system of units
was redefined so that Boltzmann’s constant is exactly 1.380649 × 10−23 joules per
kelvin, by definition, and the kelvin is whatever makes that true. So the conversion
from temperature to energy has been a convention since then, in the strictest sense:
its numerical value in those units is fixed. Realising the kelvin in a laboratory still
requires measurements, with uncertainty. What’s still physics is everything around
it, whether wiping a bit at a temperature really sheds that much heat, which is what

                                                 385
386   19 The counter against physics


               the Lyon bead was measuring. The calibration theorem is the same kind of move as
               that redefinition. It fixes a conversion, and the physics, if there is any, is somewhere
               else.

               Definition 19.1 (Energy at a scale). For a real number c (joules per mark) and a
               state s, the energy of s at scale c is µ(s) · c. The Landauer calibration at k B and T is
               the statement that every state with µ(s) = 1 has energy k B T ln 2 at scale k B T ln 2.



               Theorem 19.1 (The calibration is a unit conversion). (1) For all real k B and T,
               the Landauer calibration at k B and T holds. (2) For any counter, there are two
               real-valued functions of the state that give 1 and 2 on every state with one mark, so
               the counter alone fixes no energy value.

               Proof. (1) Substitute µ(s) = 1: 1 · k B T ln 2 = k B T ln 2, by ring arithmetic, for any
               k B and T, positive or not. (2) Take the two functions to be the energy at scales 1
               and 2. At µ(s) = 1 they give 1 and 2.
                  The physics is the premise of Section 3, restated here once in the form the next
               theorems test. In words first: a dissipation hands each instruction a whole number
               of heat units, each unit worth kT ln 2. The floor premise says an instruction that
               takes at least one state where some yes-or-no property is false to a state where it’s
               true, never sends a true one back to false, and sends two different states to one,
               dissipates at least one unit. That’s a different statement from Landauer’s principle as
               Premise 3.5 has it. That one depends on the spread over states, Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H,
               and gives no floor for a known state (there the distinction was already kept by
               whoever knows the state, and the bill went with that knowing). This one gives every
               such instruction a floor of one whole unit, whatever the spread. To get the second
               from the first you’d need more, at the least a spread with a full bit of uncertainty
               removed at every such step, and the known-state theorem and the narrow squeeze of
               Section 3 show that isn’t automatic. So I give it its own name, structural dissipation
               pricing. The calibration says no instruction dissipates more units than the counter
               charges it. One word about that word: “dissipation” here means heat handed to
               the surroundings, the quantity Section 3 read off Sagawa as owed even when no
               entropy is produced: a bill for where the forgotten bit goes. It is not what Section 1
               calls dissipating, which is entropy produced, and it has nothing to do with waste, or
               with doing the job badly. Two premises, nothing proved about either, and the only
               question is whether they can sit in the same room:
                                                    19.2 The premises have to be able to hold together   387


Premise 19.2 (Structural dissipation pricing). A dissipation is a function δ from
instructions to naturals, counted in units of k B T ln 2. The floor, a hypothesis separate
from Premise 3.5 of Section 3: every instruction that collapses a yes-or-no property
has δ(i ) ≥ 1, where i collapses P when some state with P false is sent to a state with
P true, every state with P true is sent to one with P true, and some two different
states are sent to the same state. The calibration: δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) for every instruction.
Neither is proved anywhere; the theorems below ask whether they can hold together.

    The last clause of the floor is there because the first two don’t make a step forget
anything on a machine with infinitely many states. INC A sends a state with A = 0
to one with A = 1 and keeps every positive A positive, so it raises “A ≥ 1” one way,
and it is one-to-one. Any one-to-one map that misses some state does the same to
the property “is in my image”. Its input can be read back off its output, so it loses no
entropy, and Landauer’s premise as this book takes it then puts no heat floor under
it at all. It pays in room instead: INC moves every value of A up one, Hilbert’s front
desk, and only a counter with no top can keep doing it. A real implementation of
it still dissipates when it runs, as every real step that changes something does; the
premise only sets no floor under it. A floor read without the last clause would charge
a whole unit. On a finite machine the clause asks nothing extra. A step that sends
one false state into the true ones and keeps every true state true puts one more state
into the true set than the set holds, so two of them land on the same state.


19.2 The premises have to be able to hold together

Here’s the one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline, and it’s
a consistency test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You
need two premises: that every step you’ve chosen to count dissipates at least one
unit, and an upper calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those
two hold at once? There’s a theorem saying exactly when: a model satisfying both
exists precisely when every operation you’ve chosen to count (the statement below
calls those eligible) costs at least one. I should say how cheap that is. The model
the proof builds takes the dissipation to be the cost itself, so the theorem shows the
two premises don’t contradict each other. It doesn’t show that the counter tracks
any dissipation. Still, it does bite on a schedule: if you count a zero-cost step, no
such model can exist. One example where the premises hold is a one-bit restore,
where restoring the bit to one costs one and idling costs nothing; the small machine’s
flag-raising steps, below, are another.
   Now point the test at the small machine of Section 15, counting every step that
collapses some yes-or-no property, and it fails. Read without the last clause of the
floor, it would fail at a step that forgets nothing: INC A raises “A ≥ 1” one way, is
388   19 The counter against physics


               one-to-one, and costs zero. With the clause in place the failure sits at a merge. Its
               unpriced instructions merge states (the last item of the list at the end of that chapter
               has the pair: two cores that one DEC sends to the same core, at zero marks), so DEC
               A 2, which collapses the property “A is zero or the line number is 2” by sending a
               state where it’s false and a state where it’s true to the same state, costs zero there,
               and (1) below says no dissipation can charge it one and stay under its cost. The
               machine prices the certifying chain and leaves its other merges unpriced, so the
               premise pair holds for the steps the toll is about and fails for the whole instruction
               set. That’s by design. The hardware pays for those unpriced merges in heat, off the
               ledger. The ledger counts the record only. A mark is not a joule.


               Theorem 19.2 (When the premises can hold together). (1) For any set of operations,
               any predicate “eligible” on them, and any cost, a dissipation with δ(i ) ≥ 1 on every
               eligible i and δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) on every i exists if and only if every eligible operation
               costs at least one. (2) On a one-bit machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost
               0, taking “eligible” to mean “sends two different states to one”, such a dissipation
               exists.

               Proof. (1) If such a δ exists, 1 ≤ δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ). Conversely, take δ = cost. (2) The
               reset is the only operation that sends two states to one, and it costs 1; apply (1).
                   Three statements are in play, and each points its own way. Energy at a scale, µ · c,
               is a conversion and points nowhere. The calibration, δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ), puts the charge
               above the dissipation: an upper bound. Landauer’s principle puts the heat above
               an entropy loss: a lower bound. The theorem above says the assumptions can hold
               together. That’s compatibility, and it isn’t evidence. It doesn’t make the ledger the
               least energy anything needs, and it doesn’t make it the heat anything gives off.
                   But now Door one of Section 3, keep everything and pay in room, pointed at a
               machine. Keep the previous state in a history list (push it onto the front each step;
               below, s :: h is the list h with s put on the front) and every fixed-instruction step
               becomes injective, while the step you can see stays the same; the line number can
               collapse to one place while the bigger state keeps its past. The unpriced merge,
               lifted to a machine with history, isn’t a merge. It isn’t free either: the list gets one
               state longer every step, so the run never comes back to a state it has been in, and
               that’s the room column of the bill. On any memory you can build the list runs out
               of room, and then the merge is back. So “this step merged, so it dissipated” can’t
               be said of the visible step alone. It’s a sentence about the whole state including
               whatever history is retained, and a physical model has to say what’s retained. The
               permanent-certificate theorem in Section 3 supplies that for the certifying step on
               finite memory. For the rest of a machine’s steps it’s unsaid.
                                                        19.3 The calorimeter protocol, as a specification   389




Theorem 19.3 (Keeping history makes every step injective). Let the history step
send a pair (s, h), a state and a list of past states, to (apply(s, i ), s :: h). For any step
function, the history step with a fixed instruction is injective, and its first component
is the original step. Each step makes the list one longer, so a run of history steps
never visits the same pair twice.

Proof. Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two
pairs with the same image are equal. The list after n steps has n more entries than
at the start, so two pairs at different times of one run differ in the length of their
lists.


19.3 The calorimeter protocol, as a specification
Here is how one would measure this, and it’s here because it makes the boundary
exact. Take a two-state register with energies zero and a gap, a population p in the
excited state, and the simplest possible rate equation for how p changes in one time
step (a rate for climbing into the excited state, a rate for falling out of it, and the
length of the step). For the canonical reset (population one half to zero, with the
rates chosen so the equation closes), the heat delivered to the bath is exactly half
the gap. Choose the gap to be twice kT ln 2 and that heat is exactly kT ln 2.
   Read that twice, because the temptation is to read it as a derivation of Landauer’s
number and it’s the opposite. The gap was chosen to make the heat come out as
Landauer’s number. The same populations and rates with half that gap give half
the Landauer value, and there’s a theorem exhibiting identical population dynamics
with different heat. The rate equation fixes the shape; the energy scale is a selected
Hamiltonian (the physicist’s name for the rule that says what energy each state has),
and selecting it is not deriving it.
   The canonical reset is a bookkeeping toy, and its rates show it. A register that
trades heat with a bath at temperature T has rates in detailed balance: the rate up
over the rate down is e−∆/k B T , which at the gap 2k B T ln 2 is 1/4. The canonical
rates are 0 and 1, and the factor e−∆/k B T is never 0, so no gap and no temperature
put them in that ratio. With rates that are in it, a relaxation at a fixed gap moves
toward the equilibrium population 1/(1 + e∆/k B T ) and, with steps short enough
not to overshoot, never goes below it. At the gap 2k B T ln 2 that population is 1/5.
The toy has no work term either; nothing in it pays for the squeeze. Part (4) of the
theorem below says what that costs: at the gap k B T ln 2 the toy books less heat than
Landauer’s bound asks for the same squeeze from one half to zero, so the toy has no
second law.
390   19 The counter against physics


               Definition 19.3 (The two-state protocol). For a gap ∆, the register’s mean energy
               at excited population p is ∆ · p. One step of the rate equation is
                                         p′ = p + δt k01 (1 − p) − k10 p ,
                                                                         

               and the heat to the bath over a step from p to p′ is defined as ∆p − ∆p′ . The
               canonical reset takes p = 12 , δt = 1, k01 = 0, k10 = 1, ending at p′ = 0, and counts
               one logical event.



               Theorem 19.4 (The heat is fixed by the chosen gap). (1) The canonical numbers
               satisfy the rate equation. (2) For every ∆, the canonical reset’s heat is ∆/2. (3) For
               all k B , T, the gap ∆ = 2k B T ln 2 gives heat k B T ln 2. (4) If k B > 0 and T > 0, the
               gap k B T ln 2 gives heat strictly below k B T ln 2. (5) There are two different gaps for
               which the same canonical populations satisfy the rate equation and the heats differ.

               Proof. All five are field arithmetic on the definitions: 12 + 1 · (0 − 12 ) = 0; ∆ · 12 −
               ∆ · 0 = ∆/2; and ln 2 > 0 for (4). For (5) take gaps 1 and 2.
                  A reset that pays its way is driven. Raise the gap a little, let the register settle
               with rates in detailed balance, raise it again, and so on, starting from a gap of zero,
               where the two states are alike and the population is one half. Raising the gap while
               the population holds is work done on the register; settling at the new gap is heat
               to the bath. That’s the textbook way to wipe a bit slowly, and here it is with its
               numbers worked out.

               Definition 19.4 (The driven reset). Write kT for k B T. At gap ∆ the equilibrium
               excited population is π (∆) = 1/(1 + e∆/kT ) and the register’s free energy is F (∆) =
               −kT ln(1 + e−∆/kT ). Rates satisfy detailed balance at gap ∆ when k01 = k10 e−∆/kT .
               A driven reset along a schedule of gaps g0 , g1 , . . . , gn takes, at step m, the gap from
               gm to gm+1 with the population held at π ( gm ), which is work π ( gm )( gm+1 − gm ),
                                                                                                         
               and then lets the register settle to π ( gm+1 ), which is heat gm+1 π ( gm ) − π ( gm+1 )
               to the bath. The reset’s work and heat are the sums over its steps. The uniform
               schedule from 0 to D in N steps has gm = Dm/N.



               Theorem 19.5 (A driven reset pays kT ln 2 in work). (1) With rates in detailed
               balance at gap ∆, one step of the rate equation takes p to π (∆) + 1 − δt (k01 +
               k10 ) p − π (∆) ; when δt (k01 + k10 ) = 1 it lands on π (∆) from any p. (2) For any
                               

               schedule, work minus heat is gn π ( gn ) − g0 π ( g0 ), the change in the register’s mean
               energy. (3) If kT > 0 and the schedule never falls, the work is at least F ( gn ) − F ( g0 );
                                                     19.3 The calorimeter protocol, as a specification   391


if also every step raises the gap by at most h, the work is at most F ( gn ) − F ( g0 ) +
                     
h π ( g0 ) − π ( gn ) . (4) If kT > 0, D ≥ 0 and N ≥ 1, the uniform reset from 0 to
D in N steps does work between kT ln 2 − kTe− D/kT and kT ln 2 + D/(2N ), and
leaves an excited population of at most e− D/kT .

Proof. (1) Under detailed balance k01 = (k01 + k10 ) π (∆), so the step is linear in
p − π (∆) with that factor. (2) The terms telescope. (3) The slope of F is π, which
falls as the gap rises, so the mean value theorem gives π (b)(b − a) ≤ F (b) − F ( a) ≤
π ( a)(b − a) for a ≤ b; add over the steps. (4) F (0) = −kT ln 2, π (0) = 12 ,
ln(1 + x ) ≤ x for x ≥ 0, and π ( D ) ≤ e− D/kT ; put these into (3) with h = D/N.
    Try one finite step in units where kT = 1: start with gap zero and half the
registers excited, then raise the gap to ln 2. The work is 12 ln 2. After settling, the
excited share is 1/3, so the bath receives ( 12 − 13 ) ln 2 = 16 ln 2 and the registers
retain 13 ln 2 more energy. Work equals those two amounts added together. A third
are still excited: one such step has not wiped the bit.
    Here nobody picked the gap to make the number come out. Take D large and
N much larger than D: the work closes in on kT ln 2 from both sides, and the
population left in the excited state goes to zero. The bit is wiped, and Landauer’s
number is the work it took. The temperature gets in through detailed balance, which
is the thermal premise the toy didn’t have. It’s still a model. The settling step is the
one part (1) describes, and the work and heat are the standard bookkeeping for a
slowly driven two-state system.
    What ties it to a machine: the protocol counts one logical event, by definition,
and one is what the small machine’s CERTIFY charges, the last of the three paid acts
behind a raised flag (Section 15). That’s two numbers that happen to match, both
one by choice, and nothing more. No theorem maps the protocol’s two register states
onto any state of the machine. And “heat to the bath” here means the register’s mean
energy before minus after, which quietly assumes the bath gets exactly what the
register loses; nothing here establishes that. So a device test would have to measure
the gap, the populations, the rates, and the bath heat independently; separately
establish that the device’s rates are in detailed balance (that the up and down rates
stand in the ratio the temperature dictates), which the driven reset assumes and the
canonical one breaks; and separately establish that the device’s physical reset is the
machine’s certify event. The driven reset is an executable experimental specification.
The canonical reset is a bookkeeping toy. Neither is a measured device, and neither is
an unconditional conversion of marks to joules, and anyone who tells you otherwise
has skipped the conditions.
392   19 The counter against physics


               19.4 What permanence adds to Landauer, and what it doesn’t
               Is there a heat prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make that Landauer’s
               principle alone doesn’t? No. The reason is short. The smallest case, one certified
               state and one flipping in, is “set a bit to one whatever it held,” which is the reset
               Landauer described and Bérut measured; Landauer’s own name for it is “restore to
               one,” and Section 2 put it beside the toll. The general bound, kT ln((m plus k) over
               m) for squeezing m plus k equally likely states into m, is what Landauer’s principle
               gives for that squeeze, at kT ln 2 for each bit removed. What the permanence
               theorems add is the structural half: finiteness and a permanent reading force any
               flag-raising instruction to merge some full states. They don’t say the newly certified
               state is one of the states that collide, and they don’t supply the spread over inputs or
               the physical conditions a heat bound needs. Supply those and Landauer’s premise
               prices the uncertainty that was actually removed. The machine result and the
               physical premise do different jobs, and neither does the other’s.


               19.5 What this section is
               A calibration that’s a unit conversion; a pair of premises, consistent on the steps the
               toll is about and inconsistent on the whole instruction set; a history that makes any
               step injective by paying in room; and a measurement protocol that’s a specification
               with a selected scale. The physics in this book is in Section 3, as a named premise
               with its critics named. Here there’s accounting, and I’ve tried to call every line by its
               right name. That’s the end of the machine. What’s left, after one suspicion I can’t
               prove, is how you’d break any of this, and where it stops.


               19.6 At the bottom: what I suspect and can’t prove

               This is underneath the proofs, so read it with the lights on. None of it is a theorem,
               and I’m not going to dress it up as one. It’s why I care, and I’m putting it here, after
               the main text’s proofs and apart from them, so you can check that none of it got into
               them.
                  Physics has a word for the moment a question closes: measurement. And the
               people who thought hardest about it keep describing it in this book’s shape. They
               ran together for me until I put them on one picture. Flip a coin in a crowded room.
               Before it lands, it could go either way. After, it’s settled, somebody chalks it on a
               board, and the result gets copied out into the world, the light and the air, so many
               times that it can’t be taken back and everybody who looks agrees. Five pieces: the
               question, the landing, the chalk mark, the copies, the agreeing. Each person leans
               on a different one. Zurek, in Section 18, leans on the copies. Rovelli’s coin has to hit
               the ground, so his piece is the landing.
                                                   19.6 At the bottom: what I suspect and can’t prove   393


     Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist whose institute in Copenhagen was where
quantum mechanics got argued into shape, leans on the mark. In a 1954 talk he
said seeing anything at that scale depends on an apparatus that works irreversibly,
like permanent marks on a photographic plate: a door that swings one way. I found
that line quoted in a recent paper and haven’t seen the page in Bohr’s book myself.
John Wheeler, the Princeton physicist who made the name “black hole” stick, went
further in a 1989 talk in Tokyo and leaned on the question: every physical thing
gets its existence from yes-or-no questions answered and registered, boiled down to
“it from bit.” As I read him, the coin has no face until something asks and something
writes the answer down. How literally he meant that, I can’t tell. And Peirce, way
before any of them, leans on the agreeing: the kind of settling worth trusting is the
kind that has to answer to everybody. Laid out like that, they pair up. Bohr and
Rovelli lean on a step that only goes one way, in the plate and in the coin. Zurek
and Peirce lean on many onlookers who agree, one with light and one with people.
     Lay that next to everything in this book and the parts line up: a check that could
have come out either way, a result that’s now settled, a price paid in forgetting or in
room, a record that stays. I suspect that isn’t a coincidence. I suspect the event this
book prices on a machine is the same kind of event physics calls a measurement,
showing up in a different place. The forgetting is my step. Bohr only says irreversible,
and getting from a record that stays to a merge or to room is the chairs. Push on
it and it gives at Zurek, for the reason Section 18 gave: copying onto fresh light
merges nothing and spends room, which is Bennett’s measurement that owes no
floor. So physics’ own word lands on both sides of Bennett and Rovelli’s door: the
chalk on the paying side, the copies on the borrowing side. The landing I’d put
with the chalk, and when Section 4 pushes on Rovelli’s paper it slides toward the
borrowing side, the side of finding out. So two pieces already stick out, and I’ll
leave them sticking out. Which picture a settling on a machine matches is part of
the suspicion, and the suspicion doesn’t settle it. That’s as far as I’ll take it here: a
suspicion.
     Now let me point the biggest gun I can find at it, and that’s John Bell, the
Northern Irish physicist at CERN whose 1964 theorem is behind the CHSH check
of Appendix H. In 1990 Bell wrote a short, furious essay against the word “mea-
surement,” with a list of words he said have no place in a physics that wants to be
precise. On the list: system, apparatus, environment, irreversible, information, and
measurement, which he called the worst of all. I used half of them in the last few
paragraphs without even trying. Bell would have taken my suspicion apart in an
afternoon, and he’d have been right to, because every piece of it leans on words
physics hasn’t pinned down. Nothing in this book proves any of it. The proofs are
about models and machines, and whenever physics shows up in them it shows up as
394   19 The counter against physics


               an assumption with a name on it. The suspicion is why I went looking. It isn’t what
               I found.

         Part IV is where you aim at all of it: how to break each claim, the ledger of what’s
      proved and what isn’t, the fence around what I’ve shown, and the conclusion. The
      thing to aim at first is the bottom: find a 0 kept with no merge and no fresh room,
      and the bill falls, and the derivation of the toll with it.
CHAPTER 20




How to break this

Every main claim in this book comes with the exact shape of the thing that would
kill it. I went to the trouble on purpose. A claim you can’t break is a claim that
wasn’t saying anything. So I’m handing you a loaded gun pointed at my own work,
with every sentence sharp enough to aim at. These are written as instructions: here
is the trace to find, the object to build, the theorem to exhibit. Build one and the
proof tree falls, and I mean that as an invitation.
    The invitation is an old one, and people have put prices on it. Donald Knuth
gives the first person to find each error in his books one hexadecimal dollar, 0x$1.00,
which is $2.56, deposited these days at the Bank of San Serriffe, a bank that doesn’t
exist, since real checks turned out to be an open door for fraud. Why pay strangers
to find your mistakes? His own page says it plainly enough: whoever finds a mistake
makes the book better for everyone who reads it next. This chapter doesn’t come
with a bank, real or made up. What it comes with is, for every claim, a description
of the exact object that would make it fall, so you know before you start what counts
as winning.
    Before the list, three places to aim at me. A sentence of mine that says more
than the mathematical statement and argument it refers to. A definition that doesn’t
capture the English word it’s named for: on the small machine, “is at least 0” is
a check that can’t fail, and the step certifies it anyway, so “certified” there doesn’t
mean “found something out” (Section 15 says so, and that’s the kind of gap to hunt).
And a list of premises that only its own example satisfies.


20.1 Where I already looked
Before you aim, here’s where I aimed first. A result nobody has tried to break has
only been believed, so I wrote a search whose whole job is to make the results
of Part I fail. It takes every machine small enough to list: every way of sending
each of up to six states to a next state (the table says how many states each result
got), every yes-or-no reading on them, every set of starts and every run length
the statement talks about, and for the statements about chances or amplitudes,
hundreds of random tables of chances, done in exact fractions, and hundreds of
random unitaries. For each machine where a result’s premises hold, it checks the


                                                 397
398   20 How to break this


              conclusion. A false statement would turn up a machine where it fails, and the search
              would print it.
                 That alone proves nothing about a search that’s broken. So every result with a
              premise to drop also gets a control: the same search with one premise taken away.
              The control has to find a machine where the conclusion fails, and every one of them
              did. That shows two things at once: the premise is doing work in the statement, and
              the search is able to catch a failure when there is one. A table of zeros from a search
              that couldn’t have found anything would be worth nothing. These zeros sit next to
              controls that found something every time there was a premise to drop.
                 None of this is why the results are true. The arguments on the page are. A search
              over small machines can’t reach a machine with a million states, and the results
              are about every machine. What it does is give each statement a fair chance to be
              wrong, in the place where wrong statements usually get caught, the small cases.
              The search is the file scripts/break_it.py in the repository, standard Python, no
              other library; run it and you get this table, or a counterexample.

    Three rows deserve a word. For the quantum chairs, a unitary keeps right angles
by definition, so the search can only catch an arithmetic slip; its control, an invertible
map that isn’t unitary, shows what goes wrong without it. Time’s bill is a sweep over
a formula, a check of the algebra and nothing more. And the floor-and-ceiling row
is the one to read twice: with a price per move name the two don’t leave exactly
one bill, they leave none, because the raising move, played again from yes, raises
nothing and still costs one. Section 2 says so; the one bill, a mark per raise and
nothing else, needs a price that can depend on where the step starts (Section 6).
Where a statement was about the infinite, the finiteness control is the endless strip
of Door one, checked on as long a stretch as you like; no search reaches the end of
it, and the argument on the page is what covers it.
