              20.2 The abstract claims (Parts I to III)
              What a chair is (Section 1). For the step law, a deterministic step whose next state is
              neither new to the run, nor a revisit from a different state than the one that first got
              there, nor a return that puts the run on a loop. For the write, a finite set of states
              extending blank, zero and one on which writing a 0 takes blank to a definite state, is
              one-to-one, and never brings “definite” down; the count in the write theorem forbids
              it. For reversible keeps nothing, a one-to-one step on finitely many states and a start
              whose run never returns to it. For the noisy chairs, a table of chances with every
              row and every column adding to one and a positive chance of entering a closed set
              from outside; or a table that can enter a closed set from outside and leaves the even
              spread’s collision weight unchanged. For the quantum chairs, a finite-dimensional
              unitary and a projector with (1 − P)UP = 0 and PU (1 − P) ̸= 0. For time’s bill, a
              biased walk at a speed other than zero that gives off no heat, or one whose heat
              times time comes under the square of the distance. For the measurements, a record
              that stays, in a closed finite system whose step is one-to-one, with no heat out and
              no fresh degrees of freedom taken; recurrence says it can’t be built, and the law dies
              if it is. For the same bill at every scale, a finite set of fine states that a one-to-one
              fine step keeps inside itself, with a coarse description exact on it whose rule merges.
                  The universal floor (Section 2). Build a Thiele machine, which obeys the one-step
              toll by definition, and give a run from a state reading no to one reading yes with
              total cost zero. The universal floor falls. A run of such a system that costs less than
              its number of steps from no to yes; one mark per crossing falls. A price per move
              name, a system whose flag rises, and every run costing at least its crossings and at
              most its raises; the claim that no such price meets both falls. If you instead drop the
              toll, you’ve built a system that certifies for zero marks. That’s a different system, not
              a Thiele machine, and it counts for nothing against the theorem.
                  The toll from premises (Section 3). Exhibit a finite, duplicate-free list of every
              state, a certificate no step revokes, and an injective step that switches it on. The
              permanent-flip theorem falls, and the derivation of the toll with it. An infinite state
              space, a revocable certificate, or an unpriced merge is not a counterexample; that
              chapter already builds one of each, and the infinite one, the endless strip, pays
              in room. For the raise with no merge, on any machine at all: a move that keeps
              a reading permanent, raises it somewhere, merges no two states, on a machine
              with only finitely many yes-states; Hilbert’s hotel falls, and Dedekind’s definition
              of infinite with it. For the squeeze bound, a finite permanent machine with a cost
              meeting the halving premise where one step switches k states on beside m certified
              ones and two to the cost times m is less than m plus k; the squeeze bound falls.
              For merge-or-revoke, a finite machine and an injective instruction that switches
              a reading on without switching it off anywhere; the merge-or-revoke claim falls.
                                                            20.2 The abstract claims (Parts I to III)   401


A move that merges and also revokes counts against nothing. It’s the three cards.
For the eight-state machine, a move of it that merges two states and costs nothing;
merge pricing on that machine falls. For the small machine, with no finiteness in
play: an INC, DEC or HALT that sends two different states with the same line and
counters to one state, or a CERTIFY, or a COMMIT of some claim, that never joins
two such states; the toll on the machine I built falls. For heat or room, a run of
one rule (every state has one next state) on a machine with a permanent reading,
in which the reading goes from no to yes, that repeats a state, and in which no
two of its states merge; the run form falls. A machine run by one rule, N different
starts, exactly one already reading the fixed value, every state in the next T steps
reading it, no two states among steps 0 to T − 1 sharing a next state, and fewer than
1 + ( T + 1)( N − 1) states; the retention bound falls, and the exactness claim falls if
the path construction merges within T repetitions or needs more chairs than it says.
    The bill in bits (Section 3). Exhibit a finite machine with a permanent certificate,
a move that switches k states on beside m certified ones (k at least one), and a
spread of probability over those m plus k states whose image under the move has
entropy above log base two of m. The entropy ceiling falls. For the general form,
a step and a spread on a finite list of every state under which two different states,
each with some probability, land on the same state while the entropy doesn’t drop;
the strict entropy-drop claim falls. A heat measurement on a real device below what
the bound asks doesn’t touch either theorem. It refutes Landauer’s premise for that
device, and that’s a fight with physics. The counting stays where it was. And a
certifying step from a state already known that gives off less heat than the bound
isn’t a counterexample: the known-state argument says the premise sets no positive
floor there. The distinction was already kept by whoever knows the state, and the
bill sits with that knowing.
    Learning borrows, committing pays (Section 4). A cost meeting the halving price, a
run, and a list of starts with no repeats, where the rounded-up logarithm of the list’s
length is more than the run’s cost plus the rounded-up logarithm of the number of
places the run can end; the machine’s own narrowing falls. Show that the four-state
demon’s MEASURE merges two states, or that its observer’s candidate list doesn’t
shrink; the claim that learning needn’t merge falls. Show that a second MEASURE
doesn’t put the display back to blank; the claim that the copy can be handed back
falls. Show that WIPE merges nothing; the claim that freeing the page is where the
bill lands falls. A price list that charges MEASURE anyway is allowed and isn’t a
counterexample. The claim is that learning owes no merge, so it isn’t forced to pay
one. It never says learning costs nothing: it uses up a blank page, which is room. A
zero-mark teacher on two states; the three-state minimum falls. A finite machine
with an entropy-priced cost, a spread and a run after which the end state leaves
more bits about the start unknown than the run cost in marks, or a run of zero
402   20 How to break this


              marks after which two starts that both had a chance and showed different things at
              the window end in the same state; the certainty bill falls.
                  The counter (Section 6; on the small machine, Section 15). Find a state of the
              small machine and an instruction such that the ledger after is anything other than
              the ledger before plus that instruction’s cost; the loud version is a ledger that goes
              down. Conservation falls. The uniqueness half, that only one bookkeeping starts

              run on a machine meeting only the exact-prices clause, from any start, with the

    The latch (Section 10). Exhibit an extension of a base whose record is driven by
the computation and never switches off, and which is not a latch on any event. The
latch theorem falls. A record that switches off, like the toggle, or the timestamp,
switched on by a hidden clock, isn’t a new one: those are the two counterexamples
already given.
    The whole direction (Sections 11 and 12). Two different places of a partial order
that leave the same cups up; the cup reading falls. A chain of different arrangements
of k cups, each keeping up every cup the one before had up, with more than k + 1
members; the cup count falls. A machine with finitely many states, a record that
only grows in some preorder, and an injective move that turns a cup over; the claim
that turning a cup over merges falls, and the toll over a direction from merge pricing
with it. On a machine where every step that turns a cup over costs at least one, a
run that costs less than its number of such steps; the count falls. A window with a
collision and a window price that meets the floor and charges nothing for any step
that turns no cup over; the window obstruction over a direction falls.
    The diagonal (Section 13). Two routes. A decider for some substrate with
a shortcut predicate whose flip the substrate can represent and which answers
correctly on every program; the generic proof fails at a named step. For the nat
family, a d that correctly decides the predicate of the substrate built from d. L
has its recursion theorem by proof, so it gets a target of its own: a map on L’s
terms, computable by an L term, with no term that behaves like its own image;
L’s recursion theorem falls. On the host machine: a host program that decides an
extensional property of host programs that some program has and some lacks, or
a map of host programs that a host program carries out, with no host program
that computes the same function as its image; Rice’s theorem for the host or its
recursion theorem falls. On the small machine: a decider for a property of what two-
counter programs do from the clean start that some program has and some lacks;
the fixed-input Rice theorem falls. A decider for such a property over every input of
two-counter programs; the all-input Rice theorem falls. A two-counter program of n
lines that multiplies every plain input by the number Theorem D.23 names for n; the
multiplication obstruction falls. A map of two-counter programs that a two-counter
program carries out on program numbers, with inputs and outputs written as powers
of two, and no program that computes the same packed function as its image; the
packed recursion theorem falls. A program number e and an input x on which U2 ,
started on 2x · 3e , and the program numbered e, started on 2x , stop with different
packed outputs, or one stops and the other doesn’t; the packed universal program
falls. A map of host programs that a host program carries out, with no host program
that stops when its image stops and agrees with it on register 0, the trap latch,
the ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether the channel is empty, is a
counterexample to the fixed-point theorem for the record. A map whose fixed point
404   20 How to break this


              disagrees with its image on some other register is not one: some computable map
              has no fixed point that agrees with its image on every register.
                  The five models (Section 17). Each fragment has a theorem with a named falsifier:
              a finality fork with nobody slashable; a gas schedule meeting floor and no-overcharge
              whose charging predicate differs from the commit predicate on some step; a nonce n
              and a function from quotes to Booleans that returns flag( P) on quoten ( P) for every
              platform P; one of the RFC’s own example proofs that the transcribed inclusion check
              rejects, or an input with leaf index equal to tree size that it accepts; a program the
              bounds checker accepts whose verification condition fails. Each kills one fragment.
              None of them, and I want this clear, says anything about the real system beyond the
              fragment.
                  The pointer thesis (Section 18). It’s a thesis, so the three routes are its own: a
              deployed discipline pricing a record that parties who didn’t produce it don’t copy
              and rely on; a rival event copied and relied on that fails at a reachable state where
              certification holds in a real ecosystem; an honest formalisation, with independence
              as defined there, where certification fails the test.
                  One line gets drawn with it, and I draw it in full. The window results, the
              separation of the two runs, and the counter’s uniqueness don’t single out certification.
              Their proofs use only that the step carries something the classical picture doesn’t
              determine, so the same shape of result holds for any such field. Nothing in Parts I to
              III or the appendices proves that certification is the one event a model is forced to
              price; the merge pricing of Section 3, a premise, charges every merge, certifying or
              not. That’s the thesis, and Section 18 is the case I make for it.


              20.3 The machine claims (Part III and the appendices)

              The small machine (Section 15). Four targets. From a clean start, a run that raises
              the flag without an earlier passing CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY of the same
              claim, with the counter’s version unchanged between the CHECK and the COMMIT;
              certification provenance falls, and commitment provenance for a COMMIT alone.
              From a clean start, a trace that leaves a fact in the table nobody checked; the
              no-forging claim falls. From a clean start, a run that ends certified for a total charge
              under three; the minimum-price theorem falls, and a run at exactly three is not a
              counterexample: CHECK “A is 0”, COMMIT, CERTIFY from a start where A is 0 is
              one, and the same program from any other start is refused forever. A check that
              can’t fail certifying for three isn’t a counterexample either; the step doesn’t police
              trivial checks, and the book says so. A two-counter machine and a program whose
              run on the small machine disagrees with it step for step, or halts when it doesn’t;
              the step correspondence or the halting correspondence falls.

    Thiele-complete (Section 10.8). A machine that charges at least one for every

    Certified Thiele-complete (Section 15). A machine that charges at least one for

finitely branching box, or a box whose step ignores its state, with a universal base,
406   20 How to break this


              or with a choice of claims and fact table whose lift is certified Thiele-complete; or a

              a clean start that ends with each side at a point not at or below its floor, with fewer
              than six record moves or a ledger rise under six; the floor of six falls. A machine
              mapping into both sides, preserving records, with two different maps into the pair
              that do both jobs, or none; the product’s universal property falls. For nesting: a
              host that pays the toll, a guest it simulates faithfully with a record map that reflects
              the order, and a guest run with no host run that follows it, or a following host run
              that doesn’t end on the image of the guest’s end state, or one that costs less than
              the number of guest steps that turned a cup over; the nesting bound falls. A tower
              of presented machines on UP , each level presented by the next, where some level
              above the first adds other than exactly 2; the tower count falls.
                  The classical CHSH bound (Appendix H). Exhibit four fixed bits and a tally consis-
              tent with that one plan, every pair sampled, scoring above two. The classical bound
              falls, and so does known mathematics. A randomised plan landing past two by
              luck doesn’t count; the theorem is about one fixed plan, and Appendix H’s coin-flip
              example shows the luck.
                  The integer check (Appendix H). The game check has two walls, and here’s how
              to knock each one over. A correlator that passes the three contraction inequalities
              whose five-by-five is not PSD (forward), or a PSD five-by-five of that shape whose
              correlators aren’t contractive (reverse); the matrix equivalence falls. A correlator
              whose pinned five-by-five is PSD (contractive, by the equivalence) with S squared
              above eight; the bound on the score falls. The PR box and the classical mixture
              (1, 0, 1, 0) are not counterexamples to any of these. Both fail contraction by plain
              arithmetic (the table in Appendix I.4), which is exactly what the theorems need
              them to do. On the machine: a raised flag from a clean start with no passing CHECK
              of the packed-counts property before it, or whose counts give S2 > 8; the earned
              game-check guarantee falls. A tally that passes the seven facts while its pinned
              matrix isn’t PSD, or one with every pair sampled and a PSD pinned matrix that fails
                                                                 20.4 What’s mine and what isn’t   407


them; the exact integer-check equivalence falls. The all-ones tally and the PR box
being refused are not counterexamples; those refusals are the point.
    The nine-by-nine (Appendix H). A point and five extra numbers where the
contraction-like condition holds and the nine-by-nine isn’t PSD, or the other way
round; the nine-by-nine equivalence falls. A point where the condition holds with
all five extras at zero and S is above two; the zero-extras bound falls.
    The elliptope completion (Appendix H). This one’s a shape, so you’re trying to
push a point in or out of it. Three targets, one per theorem, plus the decider beside
it. Signs a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 , each squaring to one, and a vector on which the completed
matrix of that plan goes negative; the inclusion of deterministic plans falls. A
correlator with some positive semidefinite completion and S squared above eight;
the completion bound falls. Real numbers x and y that make the PR box’s completed
matrix positive semidefinite; the exclusion of the PR box falls. And for the decider
that sits beside it: inputs on which it says yes while the correlators have no PSD
completion at all (S squared above eight is one way to show that); the decider’s
soundness falls. The all-ones plan and (1, 0, 1, 0) aren’t counterexamples here
either, from the other side: the completion admits them, which is what the theorems
require.


20.4 What’s mine and what isn’t

This is not a claim to have been first. Appendix C does the sorting item by item,
with sources: what was known, what’s added, and what kind of addition it is. Here’s
the short form. A boundary that’s wrong gets moved, and the appendix is where to
point.
    Borrowed, with names. As The point warned, I usually had the hunch first and
found these names after, and that order doesn’t make any of it mine. Everything
in Section 5 and the Afterword (every source is cited where it’s used), the category
theory (Eilenberg, Mac Lane) included. Minsky’s two-counter machines and the
constructions that prove their halting undecidable and compile computable functions
into them (Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors). Turing, Church, Kleene, Rice,
Cantor, Gödel, the diagonal pattern, Lawvere’s unification, and the mechanized
versions of them: Michael Norrish’s, Mario Carneiro’s, and Yannick Forster, Fabian
Kunze and Gert Smolka’s. Bell, CHSH, Tsirelson, Stephanie Wehner’s semidefinite
proof of Tsirelson’s bound (2006), NPA, Landau, Masanes, Fine, the elliptope,
and the machine-checked proofs of Tsirelson’s bound (Echenim and Mhalla in
Isabelle, and Lean’s mathlib). Landauer, Bennett, Szilard, Maxwell, and their
critics. The potential method (Tarjan) and its mechanizations (Nipkow, Charguéraud
and Pottier), Lamport’s clocks, Floyd and Hoare. Gettier, Necula, Cook, Hartley,
Shannon, Rissanen. Zurek. The guarantee about every program: the reference
408   20 How to break this


              monitor (Anderson), execution monitors (Schneider), and monitors checked at every
              instruction and proved correct (Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors). The counting
              under the permanence results: Poincaré’s recurrence, as Zermelo used it. The seL4
              and CompCert discipline. The facts under the permanence results are Landauer’s
              own example and Shannon’s bounds, and “set a bit to one whatever it held” is my
              way of saying his RESTORE TO ONE.
                  What I proved, each inside its stated interfaces. First the bill, with no price list,
              no reading and no finiteness: the step law, that every run of a machine with one
              next state for every state takes fresh states until its first return, which lands on
              its start or is a merge, and after it only repeats steps it already took; the write of
              a 0 as a merge, with every finite extension of the cell still merging and only the
              endless tape, paying room, avoiding it; recurrence for reversible finite machines;
              the noisy and the quantum forms of the chairs; time’s bill on the biased walk; and
              the same bill at every scale. Beside them, the lab’s measurements of each, cited
              and not reproved, and, as a simulation and not a proof, the bead’s erasure law.
              Then the toll: the abstract floor, which is the potential method with one particular
              potential, and its count of one mark per crossing. The derivation of the toll from
              finiteness, permanence, and a named price, in counted states and in bits, with each
              premise’s counterexample built. The eight-state machine on which every one of
              those premises is a theorem. The dichotomy under the derivation, on any state
              space, that a run which keeps a record either merges two of its own states or never
              repeats a state, so time cannot replace room; its one-move form, that a raise which
              merges nothing needs endlessly many yes-states, which is Hilbert’s hotel; its exact
              bound on how long a bounded memory can put the merge off; and the reading
              of it as heat or room with time setting how much heat the happening costs, with
              Bennett’s trade of room for time cited rather than reproved. The four-state demon
              that learns with no merge and pays when it wipes, and the certainty bill. The
              window that can’t price the flag exactly, and the small machine’s own colliding
              pair. The latch form over any base, with its two counterexamples and converse.
              The definition of Thiele-complete over any base and any event, with the clock and
              the silent machine failing it, each clause needed, the window blindness with a
              gap of one, every universal base lifted by marks, and the theorem that certified
              Thiele-complete is exactly it with certification added. The small machine’s earned
              record from a clean start (checked, then committed, then certified, about the same
              edition, nothing forged, three at least), its exact ledger, its universality through
              Minsky, the definition of certified Thiele-complete that every clock fails and the
              window blindness of every machine meeting it, the universal program U with its
              guest’s halting and flag matched exactly, its ledger equal to the guest’s at every
              matching point, and its own flag earned, the priced program UP that runs every
              computably presented Thiele machine with its reading latched, its flag earned on
                                                                    20.4 What’s mine and what isn’t   409


the guest’s own reading and its ledger within two of the guest’s when the reading
starts at no, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid
when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three, and the simpler host’s
mirror, its isolation and its refusal to certify for no marks. The substrate diagonal
and the L results, with Rice’s and Kleene’s theorems on the machine’s host and Rice’s
from the clean start on the two-counter machine. The integer check, exact for every
pair being sampled and the pinned matrix being PSD (and so a sufficient test for
the bound, which tells you nothing about quantum behaviour), the equivalence
with contraction, Tsirelson’s bound from PSD, which is known mathematics proved
again here, and the check earned on the host, a raised flag standing on it. Structural
entitlement for every certified Thiele-complete machine, with its worked members,
its floor that takes no supplied tree and its proof that the covering can’t be dropped;
the eight-state machine run by the small machine; the time a check saves; and the
collision of every bare-transcript verifier on every certified Thiele-complete machine.
All of it with premises printed. Of that list, the toll derivation on a reading that stays,
from a price on merging moves (Ouldridge and Wolpert priced the same merge
in entropy first, and Li and Vitányi had assumed a unit price per erased bit), the
pricing form of the window fact, and the latch form are the only pieces I’d call
new statements, and only in the sense that I didn’t find them stated where I looked.
The mathematics under Section 1 is old: the step law is the first-return argument
every textbook on dynamics makes, recurrence is Poincaré’s and Zermelo’s, the
noisy chairs are the fact that a doubly stochastic chain has no closed class reachable
from outside, the quantum chairs are that a unitary preserving a finite-dimensional
subspace preserves its complement, the entropy gap is Gibbs’s inequality, and the
entropy the walker hands its surroundings is Schnakenberg’s. What’s mine there is
the reading, that the write of a 0 is the merge and the toll is the price of something
being the case, the assembly of those facts as instances of one law, a merge or room
for anything kept, beside the cited physics that every change a real device makes in
a finite time dissipates, and a short proof of each, on the page. The fourth thing I’d
name is something built, and its idea isn’t new: a record that’s priced, and on the
small machine earned, under the reference monitor’s every-program move, which is
old and isn’t mine. Appendix C names the same four the same way, with the prior
work beside each.
    Interpretation, which is mine and not proved. That structure is what a computation
establishes and the toll is the right thing to price. That certification is the pointer
event. That the record axis “belongs in the step.” Those are proposals, with the
arguments I’ve given, and the proposals are where I’d aim first if I were you.
CHAPTER 21




The claim ledger

Here’s everything this book claims, one line each: what kind of claim it is, and where
it lives. “Proved” means proved under the premises printed in that section, and
nothing more. If a line here ever says more than its section does, the section is right
and the line is wrong. “By unfolding” after it means the proof does little more than
read the answer off the definitions, a case split whose every branch is a line: true,
and carrying almost nothing the definitions didn’t already say. If you’re counting
results, count those differently. I mark them so they don’t pad the list, and where
they’re stated in the book they carry the label observation, with two exceptions:
Theorem 15.5, and part (3) of Theorem D.8.
    Ledger is a good word for it, and it’s older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a
ledger was a book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from
the old verb leggen, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. A book
that stays put. That’s the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander,
and this is the one place where every claim lies still, so you can come back and find
it where you left it.


21.1 Claims about the model
First the model. Every line in this table is about any system that has the pieces the
line names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading and the
toll, a counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about my
machine, except the lines that run these results on it, which say so. The table runs
over several pages, in reading order, except that a line running a result on the small
machine sits beside the result it runs.
    Here’s one way to use it, and it takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book
you trust least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to
the home section and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it
says more, you’ve found my mistake, and the end of this section says what I’d like
done about it.

               21.2 Claims about the machine
              Part III built one small machine, with the hosts that run it in an appendix, and
              the ledger keeps them apart from the model. The machine is the small one of
              Section 15, two counters and six instruction kinds, where commitments are earned
              and universality is proved, with the definition of certified Thiele-complete that every
              machine can be held against, the universal program U on a host made of the same
              instruction kinds, and the priced program UP that runs every computably presented
              Thiele machine. Every line in the next tables is about those machines, or about every
              machine meeting that definition, or about the physics section that closes Part III and
              the game check in Appendix H, or about the hosts, bases, models, parts and tools
              the appendices build around them, and nothing else, under the premises printed in
              its section.

               21.3 What I propose

              What ties all of those results together is a proposal, and it’s mine: put the relations a
              computation carries, and the bill for them, into the state and the step. The items
              below spell that out, along with one narrower bet inside it, the pointer thesis about
              certification. Every one of them reaches past the theorems, and none of them adds
              to the physics, which stays in the premises the book names and the results it cites.
               • That the axis belongs in the step (Section 22, Section 23).
               • That the usual account of a computation is a shadow of the step, for machines
                 whose control never reads their record (Section 12). The small machine’s control
                 does read its own record layer: a commitment that finds no fact traps. So for it
                 the claim is about its ordinary computer, not the whole machine.
               • Within the record construction, that certification is the event selected by the
                 reliance criterion of the pointer thesis (Section 18).
                                                                              21.3 What I propose   447


• That this is a structural account of computation, with a cost model as one part of
  it (Section 22).
• That the toll is the right thing to price. The alternatives are a wall or a penalty
  for contradiction (Section 17, Section 23).
   And three things this book doesn’t settle, with what would settle each. Whether
Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every theorem standing and one
premise unowned by the world: that takes measurements of real devices (Section 3).
Whether certification really is the pointer event: that takes a way to tie the definitions
to the systems the thesis is about, and Section 18 gives three ways to kill it. And
whether there’s a smaller start than a partition: that takes a ruler someone can state
and a smaller structure measured by it (Section 5).
   That’s the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn’t on it, or a line
that says more than its home does, that’s my mistake, and I’d want to hear about it.
CHAPTER 22




Scope

This is the line around what I’ve proved. Inside it: the count that says anything kept
is paid for in a merge or in room, beside the cited physics that says every change
a real device makes in a finite time dissipates; an accounting law that writes that
bill into the step for one event, and a derivation of that law from premises each
with its own counterexample, the exact bound on how long a bounded memory can
postpone the merge, a set of windows that provably lose it, a record axis that’s a
latch over any base, a diagonal that holds by proof on L, a machine of six instruction
kinds on which commitments are earned and which computes what two counters
can, one fixed program in its instruction kinds, run on a host with more counters
and one paid move, that runs every computably presented Thiele machine, and an
integer check that implies a bound by algebra. Outside it: everything that follows.
This is the fence. I built it myself, so lean on it before you trust it.
    G. K. Chesterton, the English writer who has been called the prince of paradox,
has a famous fence, in a 1929 book called The Thing. A reformer finds a fence across
a road, can’t see what it’s for, and wants it cleared away; the wiser one tells him to
go off and find out why it was put there, and only then come back and argue for
tearing it down. This section runs the other way round. Every post below comes
labelled with what it’s there for, the overclaim it stops, so you don’t have to go off
and find out first. Pull up any post you like. Just look at what walks through the
gap when you do.
    Physical interpretation of the counter. The ledger is unique once the start and
schedule are chosen. That doesn’t make it entropy, and it doesn’t make it energy. A
physical bridge needs a model of which states carry information, premises that can
all hold at once, and a real argument tying the formal charge to dissipation. The
permanent-certificate theorems supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a
permanent reading. The two premises are shown able to hold together whenever
every counted step costs at least one, and for a one-bit reset. The small machine’s
unpriced steps merge states and are charged nothing, so its ledger is not a heat
meter for computing: whatever those merges cost the hardware is off the ledger,
and the two premises hold together for the record steps only (Section 19); and the
calorimeter protocol shows that population dynamics don’t fix the energy scale. No
joule value attaches to one mark without thermal and device premises (Section 3,


                                 448
                                                                                           449


Section 19). Once you pick the start and the price list, the number is forced by
arithmetic, and it isn’t energy. What I’d need before it could be is the list at the top
of this paragraph.
    Class separation. The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They
don’t stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No
separation of standard complexity classes follows from the collisions (Section 7,
Section 15). I’ll be blunt about why I’m careful here. Whether P equals NP is
one of the seven problems the Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on,
at a meeting in Paris in May 2000. One of the seven has been solved since, the
Poincaré conjecture, by the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who posted the proof
as preprints in 2002 and 2003. P versus NP hasn’t. If a two-state collision on my
machine settled it, I’d be owed a million dollars. Nobody owes me anything. A
window that loses a field is a fact about that window. A complexity class is a fact
about what every possible program can do within a budget, and nothing in these
collisions reaches that far.
    Trace initiality, and what it doesn’t settle. The universal property of the trace
fold is about evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there’s
exactly one way to fold a list into it (Section 6). The counter’s uniqueness assumes a
schedule. Rise-only pricing assumes an event, and a reference count that says what
charging too much means (Section 7). Those results make the construction precise.
None of them shows that the schedule I chose, or the event I chose, is physically
necessary.
    Other observables. Certification is one worked example. A family of other
observations might turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own
events, its own evidence, and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The
window and oracle results are about what specific maps keep, and nothing more.
    Program predicates versus state observations. The state-level collision (Section 7’s
wall) and the program-level diagonal (Section 13’s wall) live in different domains.
Linking them would take a theorem of its own. The nat family and L (Section 13)
keep their explicit quantifiers and representability premises.
    Entitlement bounds. The count is handed its tree and its covering, along with
the payment condition. It doesn’t dig the tree out of an arbitrary run, and it isn’t
a Shannon bound on every trace (Section 8). On every certified Thiele-complete
machine the payment is the record moves, each exactly one mark, and a floor
that takes no tree exists when the questions are the run’s own CHECKs; but its
answers are taken at the rivals as they start, a branch that costs no marks can still
narrow, the lists, tree and fibres are supplied except in the worked members, and
the covering can’t be dropped. The search through n bits is capped at 16 questions
by the machine’s fact table, and the time tax is a lower bound for programs of INC
450   22 Scope


             and DEC only. Nothing here extends it to every certified Thiele-complete machine
             (Section 15.14).
                 Quantum behaviour. The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with
             zero marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party
             moments move, at the level of correlators. A completion of the correlators is realised
             by actual measurements, by the construction in Appendix I. A full behaviour, with
             each room’s own odds prescribed as well, asks for more, and the construction doesn’t
             deliver those extra probabilities. A sound check isn’t complete for those bigger sets,
             and the elliptope decider is mathematics on the page, not a part of the small machine
             (Appendix H).
                 The record axis. The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a
             base computation is a latch on an event; on a finite machine its write merges states;
             and the named windows don’t recover it. Certification is one instance. No theorem
             selects it as the unique event every system must record (Section 10, Section 18).
             A finite monotone multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches. One
             Boolean latch can’t hold it. Revocation, including revocation priced from the other
             side as in Casper, lies outside the permanent-record axis; a price on revocation
             doesn’t transfer to a price on the write (Section 17). Probabilistic records don’t
             inherit the uniqueness result either. Two honest random records can have the same
             branches and the same charges and still give those branches different weights, one
             choosing evenly and one two to one, so the schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities.
             And no single deterministic latch explains a record that can branch both ways from
             the same observation. Weak base equivalence is defined and is an equivalence; no
             two of the three bases of Definition 10.3, and none of them and the small machine,
             are related by it in this book, and the latch form holds on each separately, so it
             doesn’t tell them apart (Section 10). Records that can come back down lie outside
             all of this: they’re limit computability’s, and Section 10 points at Ershov’s ladder.
                 Who it’s safe against. Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any
             list of instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says,
             one writer stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It
             doesn’t cover whoever sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts
             nobody checked), a reset or a power cycle, whoever picks the program, the wire
             that carries the report, someone who flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built
             the step, or a second writer that changes a counter without bumping its edition.
             Those are the operator, the device and the tool chain, and they’re outside this fence.
             A record read by someone who didn’t watch it being made is only as good as their
             reason to believe the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote over
             measured state and a proof that travels on its own, are in Section 7 and Section 17,
             and this book builds neither. What the guarantee gives inside the fence is safety: no
             program forges the chain. Availability is a different promise, and it isn’t given. A
                                                                                          451


hostile program can put the trap up or fill the table, and after that nothing useful
gets done. The mathematical machine uses whole numbers, which never overflow,
so versions and the ledger grow without bound. A build with fixed-width counters,
versions or ledger has to stop before any of them wraps, failing safe with the trap up,
because a wrapped version could make an old fact look live again and a wrapped
ledger would fall. Starting, restoring, resetting and that overflow stop belong to the
implementation, and none of them is proved here.
    The diagonal on the machine. What’s proved for the small machine’s programs is
that halting is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.4, for them and for
the universal program (Section 15; for the universal program, Appendix D.1). L has
its recursion theorem, Rice and halting by proof (Section 13). On the host machine,
the one with a counter for every number, Rice’s theorem holds for properties that
depend on everything a program ends with (every register, the table, the channel,
the trap, the ledger and the flag; the line number and the versions are left out), for
programs run on an input in register 1; s-m-n holds with no premise on register
2; and Kleene’s recursion theorem holds for the transformations a host program
carries out on numbers, with a fixed point that agrees with its image on stopping,
register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether the
channel is empty; for some of these transformations no fixed point agrees on every
register. On the two-counter machine itself Rice’s theorem is proved on every input,
with facts compared by what they’re about, their versions left out of the comparison;
Kleene’s is proved with inputs written as powers of two and refuted with plain inputs
(Appendix D.4).
    The five models. Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice;
the gas fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures;
the transparency verifier covers control flow and leaves collision resistance out; the
proof-carrying checker is a three-instruction memory-bounds language. None is a
claim about the real system beyond its fragment (Section 17).
    The machine. Part III has one small machine, with the hosts that run it in an
appendix, and here’s its fence. The small machine of Section 15 (two counters, six
instruction kinds) is where commitments are earned: from a clean start, a raised flag
went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the same claim,
nothing is forged, and the cheapest such run adds exactly three to the ledger, a price
reached by a check that could have failed (the step doesn’t police trivial checks: a
check that can’t fail certifies for three too). It’s also where universality is proved,
by matching Minsky’s two-counter machines step for step and using the halting
reduction of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors. It’s certified Thiele-complete
under a definition every clock-style machine fails, and every machine meeting that
definition hides its record and ledger from its own window. The universal Thiele
452   22 Scope


             machine for the small machine’s programs (Definition D.1) is a host with the small
             machine’s instruction kinds and more counters, running one fixed program, U, with
             no guest step built in: it runs every program of the small machine from every clean
             start start( x, y), halts when the guest halts, raises its own flag by its own check,
             commit and certificate if and only if the guest’s flag rises somewhere in the guest’s
             run, and keeps a ledger equal to the guest’s at every matching point. With one
             paid move added, one fixed program, UP , runs every computably presented Thiele
             machine: its step, prices and reading computed by programs, the reading decided
             on every state, the run fixed by a driver. The host halts when the guest stops, its
             flag is the latch of the guest’s reading, raised on its own earned chain whose claim
             is that reading, and its ledger is the guest’s plus a surcharge of at most two when
             the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start,
             can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three. A machine
             whose reading no program decides is outside. A simpler host with a guest step built
             in runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest’s flag; its ledger only
             covers the guest’s. The small machine’s check price is flat, its fact table holds sixteen,
             and its certificate is historical (Section 15 lists the rest).
                 The comparison machines. The bases I put the latch on are fragments too. The
             register machine of Section 10 is the one with indirect addressing in Definition 10.3,
             and Theorem 10.10 is about it. The reversible result (Theorem 10.3) covers any
             base whose step is injective, and on a finite state space says only that no injective
             step raises a permanent reading. None is a theorem about real memories or full
             reversible languages. The cost-semantics results are local correspondences, short of
             full cost-framework embeddings: the trace’s cost is a writer cost and a grade, and
             the toll is the potential method with one potential (Section 6). Nobody’s whole type
             system gets embedded either.
                 Outward consequences. I looked for results about real systems that would need the
             record axis. What’s proved are the five fragments of Section 17, each a transcription
             with its own named limit, and none is a theorem about the deployed system. Stronger
             candidates would need protocol or hardware semantics I haven’t formalised, and
             I’ve proved nothing about them. So none of this yields a new outside result that
             both needs the record axis and is ready to use.
                 Where each result lives. Every deterministic machine, finite or endless: the step
             law, heat or room for a kept reading, and the endless room a raise with no merge
             needs. Every system that follows the toll, whatever its states: the floor, at most as
             many certifications as cost, and the potential-method reading. Every machine with
             finitely many yes-states whose price covers merges: the toll for permanent records.
             Every machine whose move names can be decided equal or different, finite or not:
             which instructions every price that covers merges must charge, namely the merging
             ones. Every finite machine paying per halving: the machine’s own narrowing bound.
                                                                                            453


Every machine extending a base with a driven, permanent record: the latch. Every
window through which a certifying and a non-certifying step look alike: no exact
price from the window. Every machine meeting the definition of Thiele-complete: a
move that costs no marks, at least one mark on any run from a state with the record
down that ends with it up, and a final window that doesn’t determine the record
or the ledger. Every machine meeting the definition of certified Thiele-complete: a
move that costs no marks, at least three marks on any run from a clean state that
ends certified, and a final window that doesn’t determine the record or the ledger.
Any eight counts: the integer check and its PSD bridge, which are mathematics.
This machine only: its six instruction kinds and their prices, its sixteen slots, its own
colliding pair, and the encodings its universal programs use.
    What I’m proposing beyond that. A way of describing computation in which the
relations a computation carries live in the state, what each move does to them lives
in the step, and a price list is one part of the description, not an afterthought. The
permanent record is the one case I took apart all the way. The pointer thesis asks
whether certifying is the thing that deserves that record in the systems it talks about,
and it can be wrong without touching the latch or the window arguments, which
never use it.
    Underneath that is a question about which distinctions a description of a compu-
tation ought to keep. The constructions show particular ways of keeping some, and
what follows once you do, under premises I’ve printed. What that’s worth depends
on what you need the description to answer. If a program’s log, plus a proof about
the program, recovers every distinction you care about, that’s a point against putting
the account in the step. If a system out in the world has good reasons to use a wall
or a penalty instead of a toll, that’s a point against the toll there. Those are the ways
to push on the proposal, alongside the counterexamples that push on the theorems
one at a time.
CHAPTER 23




Conclusion

Put the blank cell, the triangle, the cups and the two computers back on the table.
The cell went from nothing to a 0 and stayed, and that was an event with a bill.
Turning the triangle preserves relations you can check with your fingers. Turning a
cup records an act; a row of cups can distinguish stages that one cup cannot. The
two computers can leave the same answer while differing in what they did to reach
it. In each case I had to say what the things were, which moves were allowed, which
relations survived, and what my way of looking could tell apart.
    Part I started at the bottom, with the cell. On any machine run by one rule,
every step lands on a fresh state, merges two into one, or goes round a loop, and
a run that raises a reading that stays either merges somewhere or never repeats a
state, so it’s paid in a merge or in room, on top of the dissipation of every change
a real device makes, more the faster it goes. The counting needs no premise. A
single 0 written on a blank cell is already a merge, and the same bill holds at every
zoom. Then the model got an exact form: five parts, one rule, one theorem you
proved at the table, the bill written into a step. Then the rule stopped being only my
preference. With finitely many yes-states the room runs out, every move that raises
the flag merges, and under the merge-pricing rule the toll follows. The collision
belongs to the instruction, over the states it’s allowed to act on; the state that just
came in needn’t be one of the two that collide. Turning that into heat takes a spread
over inputs and Landauer’s premise on top, its critics named; from a start somebody
already knows, the premise puts no floor under it, because the distinction was kept,
and paid for, in the knowing; the step still dissipates when it happens. The toll is a
derivation under three premises you can refuse one at a time, each with the machine
that walks past it built; the bill underneath it isn’t. Learning borrows: copying onto
a blank page merges nothing, the copy can be handed back, and the page is paid for
when it’s wiped. Committing makes a record that can’t be handed back, so it pays.
That’s as far as physics goes in this book, and I’ve tried to keep it exactly that far.
    Part II gave the triangle and the cups their words: structure is relations among
things, kept under the changes you choose, carried by whatever stuff happens to
be there, relative to a frame. A partition turned out to be the smallest sorting by
the ruler I picked, and a cell that goes from blank to 0 and stays is the smallest
sorting there is. And making a grouping, keeping it, checking it and standing behind


                                 454
                                                                                              455


it came apart into four different acts. So the question became how an account of
computation could carry the cell’s bill, and the difference between those acts, in its
step.
    The rest of Part II was the logic, and here’s what it earned, in the order it was
earned. The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window in which a
raising step and a quiet one look the same can’t price the raise exactly, by a fact about
functions far older than the machine. Entitlement is defined as an object, a checked
relation, and a paid event; given lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, a
run that paid a charged step for every level of the tree has paid for the index bits it
commits to (that count doesn’t show a run has to pay them, the run doesn’t recover
the tree, the lists count repeats, and the index bits aren’t the questions anybody
asked); when the run makes the narrowing itself, every candidate dropped was
dropped by a test the run paid for, and the index bits are at most k times the bill
when each test keeps a 2−k share; on every certified Thiele-complete machine the
same count, for a run from a clean start, is a theorem about its record moves, with
the earned chain inside the run, and the count can’t do without the covering; and it
is a license to lean on a claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true. Insight, in the sense
the toll prices, is a distinction made to stay. A feeling doesn’t count. Its floor is flat:
at least one, however deep. The claim behind the flag is something a check could
have refused, and in the bare model nothing makes the commit wait for the check.
Over any base, a base-driven record is a latch, with two free choices, the event and
the price list; “only one substrate” is false and “one structure, many price lists” is
true once the event is fixed. No procedure the substrate itself can represent decides
the shortcut predicate, given a recursion theorem, by the same diagonal that broke
Frege’s floor, and the machine’s answer is to record the commitment. It leaves the
judgement unautomated.
    Part III built it. The small machine’s state ties a checked claim to an edition
of a counter, and its step uses the tie: change the counter and the old check no
longer lets you commit. So from a clean start a raised flag needs a passing check, a
commitment about the same edition and a certificate, in that order. Three marks
are enough, and no such run pays less. Those are facts about the thing I built, the
check that can’t fail included, and its two-counter base is universal under Minsky’s
packing.
    The universal programs ask whether those relations survive somebody else’s
machine doing the work. On the host with more counters, U runs the small
machine’s programs from clean starts, halts when they halt with their answers, earns
its own flag exactly when the guest raises one, and matches the ledger wherever the
two line up. With PAY added, UP runs every computably presented Thiele machine,
latches the guest’s reading through its own earned chain, and carries the guest’s
ledger to within the stated surcharge: at most two at the raise when the reading
456   23 Conclusion


              starts at no. The theorems say which states match; the appendix on running it
              (Appendix G) says how long this particular build takes to get there, which is a long
              time.
                  Then I changed the base and joined machines up, to see what carried over. The
              panel bolts onto any box with a universal base, with the boxes it won’t fit named
              (Appendix E). Two machines side by side need both records kept; one total loses
              which side did the work. Hand-offs and nested runs each come with conditions
              of their own (Appendix F). Every one of those constructions makes you say which
              relation survives the change and which is lost, and that saying is the work.
                  Then a check worth earning, the two-player game with an integer test whose
              pass forces Tsirelson’s bound for the tally it’s handed. Of five record disciplines I
              modelled in fragments, one charges a fee at the write, and which event to record
              is a thesis, with its refutations listed. And what the counter has to do with physics,
              which is less than the name Landauer might suggest. Two facts about the machine
              sit where they belong. Its unpriced steps merge states, because that’s what forgetting
              scratch work is; whatever those merges cost the hardware is off the ledger, so the
              toll on this machine comes from the record layer’s merge premise, with no finiteness
              premise on the whole machine; the only finiteness in it is the flag’s two readings.
              And a check that cannot fail still certifies for three, because the step charges for the
              act, and the entitlement count says what the claim bought.
                  This last part is where to challenge it and what would break it. Every result
              carries the shape of the thing that would kill it, gathered in one place (Section 20).
              The bottom one comes first: a finite set of states extending blank, zero and one
              on which writing a 0 is one-to-one and never brings “definite” down, which is a 0
              kept with no merge and no fresh room. Then a state of the small machine and an
              instruction after which the ledger goes down; a contractive correlator whose pinned
              matrix isn’t positive semidefinite; a Thiele machine, toll and all, whose reading goes
              from no to yes at total cost zero; a function on numbers that correctly decides the
              shortcut predicate of the substrate built from it. Any one of them brings down the
              theorem it matches. I hunted. I came up empty. That leaves the arguments here
              for you to examine. Even where a theorem holds, my sentence can say more than
              it establishes, or a definition can fail to catch the word it’s named for. Section 20
              starts with those.
                  If you asked what’s new here, I wouldn’t give you one thing, because there isn’t
              one. There are four, and each comes with its fence and its neighbours. First, the toll
              isn’t only my preference: on a finite machine a reading nothing turns off can only
              be turned on by a step that merges states, so if merges are priced, raising it costs
              (Theorem 3.1, Observation 3.2); and on any machine a raise that merges nothing
              needs endlessly many yes-states, so it pays in room instead (Proposition 3.3). The
              counting under it is the finite cousin of the recurrence argument Zermelo threw at
                                                                                         457


Boltzmann in 1896, and the abstract merge price is motivated by Landauer’s reset
example. Identifying that price with heat needs the further premises stated in Part I.
Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had already put a physical price on that merge for
finite automata, and Li and Vitányi (1996) had already assumed a unit price on each
irreversibly erased bit in a model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors
(2016) a price on instructions that destroy bits, so what’s here is the toll such a
price forces on a reading that stays. Second, a window that shows a raising step
and a quiet one the same can’t price the raise exactly (Observation 7.2); that a price
computed from what a window shows can’t tell apart two steps the window shows
the same is elementary, and what’s here is the pricing form. Third, a record driven
by the computation that never switches off is a latch on one event, over any base
(Observation 10.1); latches and history variables are old, and the theorem covers
only records that never come down; and the definition of Thiele-complete, which
any universal base meets once marks are added (Section 10.8). Fourth, a record
that’s priced, and on the small machine earned (Theorem 15.9), under the move of
guaranteeing something about every program. That move isn’t mine at all. It’s the
reference monitor’s (Anderson, 1972), made precise for monitors that watch a run
(Schneider, 2000), and proved for monitors checked at every instruction (Azevedo
de Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What I put together under it is built, and its
idea isn’t new: the check bound to the edition it looked at, the toll paid on top,
and universal programs that carry both to every program of the small machine and
to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go.
Appendix C sorts all four with sources.
    And two things I’d point at if you asked how far the proofs reach. Neither is a
fifth new thing.
    In the game: an integer check on eight counts forces a five-by-five matrix to be
positive semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows, and the chain
never once reaches for physics. No Hilbert space, no operators, no observables. The
route through the matrix is the first rung of a ladder Navascués, Pironio and Acín
built in 2007. None of that route is mine, and the semidefinite road to Tsirelson’s
bound is older than that. What’s here is the check that runs in whole numbers, and
the proved link from “the check passed” to the bound. It’s algebra you can follow
line by line. It’s algebra and nothing more, because nothing in the definitions or
the argument ties the counts or the matrix to any physical device. And on the small
machine’s host a raised flag can stand on that check: from a clean start a raised flag
contains a passing CHECK of the packed counts, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and the
check passes exactly when every pair was sampled and the five-by-five is positive
semidefinite (Appendix H).
    In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be
expressed inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the
458   23 Conclusion


              fixed point is proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice’s theorem.
              On the small machine’s host, Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem are
              proved for its own programs, so the wall stands there by proof, with its premise
              a theorem: no host program decides a property of what a program computes that
              some program has and some lacks; such a property is undecidable in the reduction
              sense of Theorem 15.4 (Appendix D.4).
                  What this book doesn’t settle, by my count. Whether the toll is the right thing
              to price. The five real systems mostly built a wall or a penalty for contradiction.
              Whether certification is the pointer event. Whether Landauer’s critics are right,
              which would leave every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world.
              And the question I’d most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start
              than a partition, by a ruler they can state? I said in Section 5 it would change this
              book. It would.
                  And the two computers of Section 14, the sorter and the copier, holding the same
              list. Walk the warehouse again. The list is in order on both. On the machine with
              the earned layer, a different part of the state tells you whether a check happened
              and a matching commitment followed it, and the rules keep that tied to the edition
              that was checked. Put your hand over that part of the machine and the difference
              between the two computers vanishes from where you’re standing. Change the
              counter and you can watch the old check go stale. Those are different operations
              with different consequences, and you can follow each one with your finger.
                  Carry a report out of the warehouse and you’ve got another question: what
              connects the report to the machine? The flag on its own doesn’t answer it. A
              window, a copy, a second machine and a reader each bring relations of their own,
              and the constructions in this book ask, one at a time, which of those relations hold.
              That’s how the example gets past the lamp: by what survives a change of view, a
              change of state, or a change of machine.
                  So that’s the Thiele Machine. At the bottom of it is one cell going from blank
              to 0, and the claim that nothing gets to be the case for free. Built on that cell, it’s
              structure held as state, acted on by a step, with an account of the changes and a view
              that may keep or lose their distinctions. What I’m arguing is that those relations are
              part of computation itself, and not something you bolt on afterwards. The record
              and its toll are the part of that I’ve worked all the way through. The small machine
              and its interpreters are things you can take apart. Each theorem answers a stated
              question under stated premises. Which questions an account of computation ought
              to keep is the part that’s still open, and it’s yours to push on.
CHAPTER 24




Afterword: how I got here

What I am is curious, past the point of good sense.
   I pick a thing up and cannot set it down until I have turned it over enough times
to see how it holds together, and this time it did not let go.
   I am not a programmer and I was never formally taught any of this.
   I was not trying to build a new model of computation.
   I would not have known what one was if it bit me.
   I was trying to build a 3D renderer.
   There was no plan behind it.
   Just a pull to make something real with my own hands, and the kind of stubborn-
ness that will not let a thing go until it stands up on its own.
   I have worked on it in off hours every day since.
   Once I started digging in, two things came clear fast. I knew nothing about
computers, and the field was already saturated, every obvious road paved and
crowded. So I needed an angle nobody else was standing on, and the angle I had
wasn’t a strategy. It was just the only way my head works. I did not know what
compositional meant. I had never heard of category theory. I called the thing I was
building digital DNA, because that is what it felt like in my hands, and I thought
about it in the only language I had: gravity pipes and directions and vectors, things
that were linear and somehow not linear at the same time, structure that flowed
and joined and came apart without my owning one proper word for any of it. I built
a custom rendering pipeline out of those intuitions, by feel, throwing out pieces that
did not sit right even when I could not have told you the rule they were breaking.
And then, the way I always do, I went looking for what I was actually doing, and
found out it already had a name. An old one. A deep one. What I had been reaching
for in the dark was composition. It was category theory, a whole field I had never
once heard of, sitting there describing the exact shapes I had been shoving around.
The moment that landed, the rendering pipeline stopped being a rendering pipeline
and started turning into a categorical engine, and I started swallowing the real
theory as fast as I could find the words for things I had already built.
   I took it one concept at a time, and I would not move to the next until I could
watch the current one actually run. Category. Object. Morphism. Functor. Monoidal
product. It came together in pieces and never in chapters, the way a picture resolves


                                                 459
460   24 Afterword: how I got here


               out of static. The Yoneda lemma (a result buried deep in category theory) was the
               piece that made the rest snap into place.
                   Then within weeks I found out the engine I had built to draw pictures was
               general enough to run a physics simulation on the exact same primitives, without my
               rewriting any of it. I wrote Newton’s laws as a program in it, half expecting nothing,
               and it ran. I want to be careful about what that was and what it was not, because
               this is exactly the kind of thing that gets misread. It was not me deriving physics, and
               I am not claiming the machine explains gravity. It was the compositional structure
               being general enough to express a physics simulation the same way it had expressed
               a renderer, and that generality is what told me the structure was the point and the
               pixels never were. Somewhere in those weeks I crossed from debugging why one
               pixel would not show up to understanding that I had quietly built a categorical
               computing engine, and that the rendering had only ever been the first thing I aimed
               it at. The pixel did eventually show up, for what it is worth.
                   I kept going, because by then I could not not keep going. The night the engine
               first ran a program declaratively, meaning I told it what should happen and let it
               work out the how without my spelling out each step, I told my wife, Julie, I thought
               I was onto something. She said okay.
                   Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about. Every tool I
               had for settling questions about what I’d built could settle the small ones and fell
               over on the exact ones I needed answered, which left me staring down an infinite
               hallway of guess-and-test with no proof waiting at the end of it, ever. One night, not
               even working, I was watching a video about Flatland, the old story about a creature
               living in two dimensions who cannot so much as picture a third. And it landed on
               me sideways, all at once, the way the real ones always do. I said it out loud: I get it
               now. There is another axis. Classical computation only ever sees what it can read
               and write off its own surface, and there is a whole direction it is blind to. It isn’t
               broken. It was just never built with an eye that points that way. That’s how it landed
               that night, and it didn’t survive in that form: the direction turned out to be one
               an ordinary computer can reach, and what the usual rules leave out is the price
               (Section 2.6 says where the axis ended up). The two computers in Section 14 are my
               attempt to show you that blindness with something you can hold. That same night
               I gave the idea a name: the Thiele Machine. The name began as a working title
               and became the name of the model. It carries the larger claim plainly: the machine
               treats structural state as part of computation.
                   What survived the whole trip from there to here is not the renderer. Not one
               piece of it, and good riddance. What survived was a single commitment I made
               early and never once let anyone talk me out of: structure is the state itself, the
               actual thing the machine runs on. It is no metaphor laid over some realer state
               underneath. Category theory was the first language I found for that structure. It is
                                                                                           461


not what the model is. The model asks for a state, a step, a record, a ledger, and a
window, and category theory appears nowhere in that list. The morphisms in that
first engine, the night they first composed correctly at two in the morning, were
objects that remembered where they came from; the records in the small machine I
ended up with remember where they came from too, and you can walk up to one
and challenge it. The receipt grew teeth. But the shape itself never moved. The
shape was the substrate the entire time, and everything else, every renderer and
every proof, was me slowly learning to see what I had already built. By the shape I
mean structure held as state. Not category theory. Category theory was just the first
language I had for it.
    Every step pulled back to show another layer underneath that I had not known
was there, and I mean that plainly: I did not know what a Turing machine was when
I started, I did not know most of the words in this document existed. I learned each
one the same way, by walking face-first into a wall that needed it and not being let
past until I had it. The needing always came first. The learning came after, dragged
along behind the needing because it had no say in the matter.
    Large language models were my hands the whole way through, and I want
the division of labor exact, because it is the thing people most want to get wrong
about work like this. The hands had nothing like this to draw on: no reference
implementation, no prior project to point at. The ideas, the architecture, the
direction, the demand that the thing be true: those are mine, all of them, no asterisk.
The symbol-pushing, the code and the formal derivations, the models produced. So I
read every statement. A derivation can settle an empty question, and I had to refuse
that too. However the symbols got onto the page, the argument on it is checkable
by reading, and it would be exactly as right or as wrong if a million monkeys had
typed it. The monkeys could not have refused.
    A word on what I actually do, because it runs under everything after it. I do
not write code or math by hand. I do not pick constants. I do not grind through
derivations. I have never written a line of code on paper or in a notepad in my life.
What I do is see, and direct, and refuse. When I take hold of an idea it does not stay
a point. It opens up. It becomes a shape I can blow up and turn over and take apart,
lay across another shape to find where the two of them touch, run forward and then
back to where it started, zoom into until it is the only thing in the world and pull
back until it is one dot in a field of other dots, and the whole time it stays wired to
everything I have ever connected it to, the right connections and the wrong ones
both, all of them live at once. I am not reading that field neutrally, the way a search
would. The thing doing the looking is me, the whole of me, my gut and my mood
and my stubbornness picking what lights up and which way I move through it, and
that is the part you cannot lift out without turning me back into a search engine. So
I see where a thing has to fit, the shape it is obligated to have, usually well before I
462   24 Afterword: how I got here


               could write it down in a single symbol. Then the model gives me the symbols, and I
               refuse anything whose argument does not hold or does not match the shape I am
               holding. That refusal is the one thing in this entire document that is mine and only
               mine: the demand that it be true, and the throwing-out of everything that wasn’t.
                   I am telling you all of this because it’s the engine. I did not come up through
               anywhere that hands you a foundation and says trust us, this part is settled. No
               professors, no colleagues, no field full of authority to lean back on when a claim got
               heavy. From the outside that is a deficit. From the inside it is the whole reason any
               of this is solid: when I meet a claim I either find the proof or I do not believe it, and
               that goes double for my own, because my own are the ones I most want to wave
               through. It is how I am built. It is the only way I know to hold a thing and actually
               trust that I am holding it.
                   So everything in here gets built from the ground up. It isn’t a courtesy to you. I
               build it because I do not believe I understand a thing until I have built it with my
               own hands, watched it stand up on its own, and tried to knock it over. I built this
               document the exact way I built the machine, brick by brick, refusing each brick until
               it held weight. That includes the parts you already knew cold before you opened
               this. I did not skip them for you, and I could not skip them for me.
                   The vocabulary I had to go look up to do any of this sits at the back of the book,
               so the argument comes first. If a word stops you, it is there. If you already know this
               material, you never have to open it. But if you catch something in the basics that is
               wrong, I want to know, and I mean that as a real ask. It isn’t politeness. Nothing in
               here is correct just because I wrote it. Especially the parts I wrote.
                   On the name. I wanted to call it the meta machine. Then, in October 2021,
               Facebook renamed its company Meta: a company taking a term for self-reference as
               its name and draining the word of meaning in the same motion. So I went one level
               up, where this machine already lives. The most meta move available, for a machine
               that runs on meta-level reasoning, was to put my own name on the cover and take
