               the word back. That’s the whole of it, a meta move on a meta machine. It happens
               to be my dad’s name too, and my wife’s now. So I asked them before I did it. They
               said go ahead.
APPENDIX A




Things I had to learn first

I came in with none of the formal fields this work turned out to need. By the time
the argument had taken shape I’d needed enough of half a dozen of them that I had
to put down somewhere what those fields had words for. This appendix is that place.
None of it is the argument. It’s what I needed to be able to make it. Everything
below is what I understood after I went and read about it; I’m not claiming to teach
you these subjects, and if you already know a part, skip it.


A.1 Bits, bytes, and what a CPU sees

A bit is one digit that’s either zero or one, the smallest fact a machine can hold.
Everything else is bits stacked up. Eight of them make a byte, which lands you any
number from 0 to 255, and the first thing that genuinely surprised me is that the
same byte is also a letter: a convention called ASCII simply agrees to call 65 the
letter A, 48 the digit 0, 32 a space. Nothing in the byte knows which it is. The
meaning is a convention laid on top.
    You can see the convention’s seams with a pencil. Write 65 in binary: 1000001.
Knock off the first two digits and what’s left, 00001, is 1, and A is the first letter. B
is 66, which ends in 00010, two. Now lower case: a is 97, which is 1100001, the
same pattern with one more bit switched on, the one worth 32. Every capital and its
small letter differ in exactly that bit. That’s on purpose. The first version of the code,
in 1963, had no lower case at all; when lower case arrived, in the 1967 revision,
it was placed so the two cases differ by one bit, which made matching them, and
building keyboards and printers, simpler. Nothing in the byte knows it’s a letter, but
somebody made the letters easy for a circuit to tell apart.
    Everything in this subsection is about real CPUs. None of it belongs to the abstract
model, which has a kind of state and a step rule and nothing about widths or slots,
and the small machine of Section 15 needs very little of it: its two counters have no
width at all, and hold any whole number.
    A word is a chunk of bits the CPU treats as one unit, in 2026 usually 64 bits (0 to
about 18 quintillion) on a desktop or server and 32 (0 to about 4 billion) on many
small devices. The abstract model doesn’t care which width.
    A register is a named storage slot inside the CPU that holds one word, the fastest
place to read or write. Memory is a longer list of word-sized slots accessed by index,

                                                   463
464   A Things I had to learn first


               the address. The program counter is one specific register that tracks where in the
               program the machine is; after every instruction it moves on to the next instruction
               unless the instruction says jump. On the small machine it’s called the line number.
               A stack pointer is a register pointing at the top of a region used for nested calls. A
               port is a named channel for talking to the outside world.
                  Modular arithmetic means counting wraps around: counting modulo 16, the
               numbers run 0 to 15, and 17 wraps to 1. Bitwise operations work on the bits of a
               value one position at a time: AND is 1 only when both bits are, OR when either is,
               XOR (exclusive or) exactly when they differ. A logical shift moves bits left or right:
               for unsigned values it multiplies or divides by a power of two, discarding overflow
               on a fixed-width left shift and rounding down on a right shift. Popcount is the count
               of one-bits in a value. Hexadecimal is base 16, digits 0 to 9 then A to F, written with
               a 0x prefix: 0xFF is 255.
                  A trap, on a CPU, transfers control to a handler; the interrupted program may
               later resume. It can report an error or request a service. On the small machine a
               trap is one bit that goes up when an instruction refuses, and then the core stops
               moving. An ISA, instruction set architecture, is the list of every instruction a CPU
               recognises, each identified by an opcode, a numeric tag the CPU decodes. The small
               machine’s has six. The abstract model has none; it has a step rule.


                A.2 The notation the formal parts use
               I don’t think in these symbols, and I had to learn to read them. The natural numbers
               are 0, 1, 2, and so on, written with a double-struck N; the integers add the negatives;
               the reals are the whole number line. A function from a set A to a set B is written
               with an arrow. For a finite set, vertical bars around it mean its size; for a number, its
               absolute value. A big sigma is a sum over every member of a set. A delta before a
               quantity means the change in it. An upside-down A means “for every”; a backwards
               E means “there exists.” A double arrow is implication; a double-headed one is “if
               and only if.” A small circle between two functions is composition, apply the right one
               first. Angle brackets mean one of three things, and the sentence around them says
               which: a pair of numbers packed into one, ⟨m, n⟩ (Appendix D.1); a dot product of
               two vectors; or, around a random quantity, its long-run average, which I picked up
               from the Bell-test papers. The circled times ⊗ in the quantum derivation combines
               two systems: A ⊗ B acts as A on the first and B on the second; Appendix I gives
               its entries. The integer check itself uses neither it nor any quantum system. A
               superscript T on a matrix is its transpose, rows and columns swapped, and I with a
               subscript n is the identity matrix.
                                                               A.3 Category theory beyond the sketch   465


A.3 Category theory beyond the sketch
Section 5 sketches objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, and the
identity laws. Beyond that: a functor is a structure-preserving map from one
category to another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows while respecting
composition and identities; think of it as a translation rule between two worlds of
structure. An embedding is a functor that throws nothing away, and faithful is the
precise version for arrows: two distinct arrows never land on one. Conservative
is the version for inverses: if the image of an arrow has an inverse, the arrow
already had one, so the functor can’t manufacture an isomorphism (an arrow with
an inverse) that wasn’t there. The two properties are different, and neither gives
the other. Read the natural numbers under addition as a category with one object
and an arrow for each number, and the same for the integers. The inclusion of the
first into the second is faithful, since distinct naturals stay distinct integers. It isn’t
conservative: 1 has no inverse among the naturals, and its image has one, minus
1. The other way round, the functor from the integers onto the trivial one-arrow
group is conservative, since every arrow of the integers already has an inverse.
It isn’t faithful: it sends every integer to the same arrow. An embedding needs
faithfulness specifically. A monoidal product combines two objects or two arrows
into one, with a unit and laws that make the combining behave. An initial object
has exactly one arrow into every object; the counter’s uniqueness in this book is
a uniqueness-on-reachable-states fact, and no category-theoretic initial object is
involved. Yoneda’s lemma was the piece that made the categorical engine snap into
place for me (Section 24), and nothing in the formal development uses it.


A.4 Bell-test vocabulary

A correlation between two outcomes is the average of their product; with outcomes
plus or minus one it lies between minus one and one, plus one meaning always
match, minus one always differ. A correlator is one such average in a labelled setting,
E00 for Alice’s setting 0 and Bob’s 0. The marginal of a joint distribution is the
distribution of one side alone with the other averaged out; zero-marginal means
each side’s outcome is plus or minus one equally often on average. A local hidden-
variable model is one where both outcomes are fixed by a shared random variable
agreed before the game plus each side’s own setting; Bell’s theorem says no such
model produces certain correlations quantum mechanics does. No-signalling means
neither side’s marginal depends on the other’s setting. Quantum-realisable means
compatible with some quantum state and measurements; the NPA hierarchy gives a
ladder of necessary tests, each a positive-semidefiniteness condition on a moment
matrix. For the four correlators of this game alone, the first rung is already exact;
466   A Things I had to learn first


               for the full table, each side’s own odds included, Chaturvedi’s 2026 preprint argues
               that no finite rung is, even in this simplest case. The PR box is the no-signalling
               correlation that wins the game every time, stronger than quantum mechanics allows.
               Cauchy-Schwarz is the inequality that a dot product is bounded by the product of
               the lengths. The Tsirelson bound is two root two, the largest game score quantum
               mechanics allows; the classical bound is two and the PR bound is four. (If you
               go looking for Boris Tsirelson’s 1980 paper, look under Cirel’son, the spelling the
               journal printed, or you may not find it.) The elliptope is the set of correlators that
               can be filled out into a positive-semidefinite matrix with ones down the diagonal.


                A.5 Other terms I use without rebuilding
               Provenance is the recorded chain of where an object came from; on the small
               machine, a commitment’s provenance is the passing check that came before it
               (Section 15). Simulation, in computer science, is one system imitating another’s
               input-output behaviour; a Turing machine can simulate a system with effective finite
               encodings of its states and moves and a computable step on those encodings, my
               small machine included, by representing its state on tape, and the difference this
               book is about is what a window on that tape shows. That’s real, and it raises a fair
               question: if a tape can stand in for the state, what was the difference? The tape
               carries a picture of the state, the way a photograph carries a fire, and a photograph
               of a fire keeps you exactly as warm as any other photograph. The counter and the
               toll live in the step rule. An encoding copies the bytes, and the step rule isn’t in
               them. A Turing machine built with the toll in its own transition table is a different
               case: it directly satisfies the model’s rule. Whether it also simulates another machine
               is a separate question. What no machine can do is make a simulated rule binding
               just by writing it down on tape.
                   Projection is a function that drops information on purpose. The window on the
               small machine keeps three things, the line number and the two counters, which are
               what Minsky’s machine already has, and that’s why projecting lands you back in
               ordinary computation. It drops everything else, including the parts doing the new
               work: the versions, the table of checked facts, the channel, the trap, the ledger and
               the flag. Nothing is wrong with it. It’s a perfectly good function. It just costs you
               what made the state more than a pair of counters. A quotient is the operation of
               declaring two things the same when they agree on what you chose to look at and
               working with the classes instead. A projection does exactly that. Dropping fields one
               at a time also glues together states that the dropped fields kept apart. The fibre of a
               function over a value is everything the function sends to that value. An injection
               sends no two inputs to the same output; a surjection covers every output. Decidable
               means an algorithm always halts with a yes-or-no answer; keep the claim and the
                                                                                  A.6 Matrices   467


algorithm apart, since the algorithm decides the claim only once there’s a proof that
its answer matches. Polynomial time means running time bounded by a power of the
input size; P is the problems solvable that way, NP the problems where a candidate
solution can be checked that way, and whether the two are the same is open.
    “Kernel” has two uses here. In mathematics, the kernel of a map is what it sends
to the identity; for a projection the useful version is the relation “these two states
project to the same thing.” An operating-system kernel is the core of an operating
system, as in the packet-filter example in Section 17.


A.6 Matrices

A matrix is positive semidefinite (PSD) when vT Mv ≥ 0 for every vector v; the game
check is all about one matrix being PSD. The determinant of a square matrix is a
single number that is zero exactly when the matrix squashes some direction flat.
For a two-by-two matrix with rows ( a, b) and (c, d) it’s ad − bc. For a bigger one,
expand along a row: for each entry, delete its row and column, take the determinant
of what’s left, multiply by the entry, alternate the signs, and add up; the recursion
bottoms out at two by two. A principal submatrix is what you get by choosing some
of the indices and keeping only those rows and the same columns; its determinant
is a principal minor. A symmetric matrix is PSD exactly when every principal minor
is at least zero, every one of them, and the step from the game check to Tsirelson’s
bound uses two of the three-by-three ones (Appendix I.4). The Schur complement
turns a question about a block matrix into a question about a smaller one. For a
symmetric block matrix with corner block P, off-diagonal block Q and other corner
R, it’s R − QT P−1 Q, and when P is positive definite the whole matrix is PSD exactly
when that complement is (Lemma I.8). Positive definite matters; invertible isn’t
enough. Take P = −1 and every other entry zero: the complement is zero, which is
PSD, and the whole matrix isn’t.


A.7 Borrowed ideas the book pushes on
These get their full story in the chapter that uses them; here’s the one-line version
for when you’ve forgotten which one Landauer was.
    The pigeonhole principle: put more pigeons than holes and some hole holds two.
Section 3’s room with too few chairs is that, and so is the proof that, when only
finitely many states read yes, a permanent flag can only be raised by a move that
forgets something, two states landing on one. Landauer’s principle (Rolf Landauer,
1961): a step that wipes information, lowering the entropy of what a machine holds
by some number of bits, gives off mean heat at least Boltzmann’s constant times the
temperature times the natural log of two per bit, under a physical model relating
468   A Things I had to learn first


               that logical entropy to the memory’s thermodynamic entropy. That’s a floor, and
               going slowly doesn’t lower it. It isn’t the whole bill: any step that actually happens in
               a finite time and changes something dissipates, merge or no merge, and going slower
               shrinks that part toward zero without ever reaching it. In this book Landauer’s
               floor is always a premise with its name on it. Nothing here derives it (Section 3,
               Section 19). Entropy, in Claude Shannon’s sense: for a spread of chances over states,
               roughly the average number of yes-or-no questions you’d need to pin the state down,
               so an even spread over n states has log2 n bits. A spread, in this book, is just a list
               of chances that add up to one. Maxwell’s demon (Section 4): a little creature that
               watches molecules and sorts fast from slow, seemingly for nothing; Charles Bennett’s
               answer was that the looking can be done without merging anything, so Landauer’s
               premise sets it no floor (it still dissipates as it happens, less the slower it goes), and
               the floor lands when the demon wipes its notes to look again. The potential method
               (Robert Tarjan, 1985): pay for a run with a quantity stored in the state, so a step’s
               bill plus the change in the stored quantity is what you count; Section 6 reads the
               toll as that method with one particular potential.
                   The halting problem (Alan Turing, 1936, who essentially proved it without
               stating it in this form; Stephen Kleene stated it in 1952, and Martin Davis seems
               to have been the first to name it, in 1958, Section 13): no program decides, for
               every program and input, whether it stops. Kleene’s recursion theorem (Stephen
               Kleene, 1938): for any transformation of programs that can itself be computed, some
               program computes the same partial function as its own transform. Its timing, storage
               and records need not agree. Rice’s theorem (Henry Rice, 1953): any property that
               depends only on what a program does, and isn’t true of all programs or of none,
               can’t be decided by a program. The diagonal is the move under all three: build the
               thing that does the opposite of what the table says about it (Section 13). L is a small
               lambda calculus, a language made of nothing but functions applied to functions,
               which Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka presented and which Section 13 uses as a
               tool. A cryptographic hash is a short fingerprint of a longer piece of data, made so
               that finding two inputs with the same fingerprint is supposed to be hard; a hash
               chain folds each new record into the fingerprint of the last, and a Merkle tree folds
               them pairwise into one root (Section 2, Section 17).


                A.8 Words this book builds
               These are mine, or mine in the sense that I pinned them down for this book. Each is
               built properly in the chapter named; this is only a reminder.
                  A few words first, because everything else hangs off them and each has exactly
               one meaning. The model (or the abstract model) is the definition of a Thiele machine,
               Definition 2.1, five parts and the toll, plus exactly the extra pieces a given theorem
                                                                        A.8 Words this book builds   469


asks for: a counter in the state, or a window, or programs written as states and
a recursion theorem. A few theorems, the step law among them, use only the
states and the step. The name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. Parts I and II
develop those general arguments, and Part III applies them to the machine it builds.
A substrate is the model’s shape with whatever extension a theorem names, and
nothing else; the word never means my machine, and never the side of a simulation
that does the stepping (Section 14.18). My machine (also the machine I build, the
build, the small machine, the smallest honest machine, Section 15) is the concrete
machine of Part III that fills in those pieces at once: two counters with their versions,
a table of checked facts, a channel, a trap, a ledger and a flag, six instruction kinds
and their prices, with its hosts and universal programs. The scaffolding is that
machine and everything built on it, and it lives in Section 15 and in the appendices
that carry the machine on, from the universal machines (Appendix D.1) to the CHSH
check (Appendix H). A Thiele machine, lower case, is any system proved to fit that
definition (Definition 2.1), five parts and the toll; the paper toys are, and so is the
small machine. That bar is nearly empty, since a clock that charges one for every
move pays the toll for any record. Thiele-complete means more (Definition 10.6):
computing that runs every program, costs no marks and can’t touch the record, a
record that stays up once it’s up, blank starts, and some run whose record ends up
from one start and down from another; a clock fails it, every universal base becomes
one by adding marks, and every machine that meets it hides its record and ledger
from its own window. Certified Thiele-complete means more again (Definition 15.7):
a universal base whose moves cost no marks and can’t touch the record, a record
that stays up once it’s up and is raised from a clean state only after a passing check,
a commitment to the same claim with the thing it’s about unchanged in between,
and a certificate, one mark for each of those three acts, and a claim whose check,
commit and certificate raise the record from a loaded start exactly when the claim
holds there, true at some loaded starts and false at others. Every clock-style machine
fails it; the small machine meets it; and every machine that meets it hides its record
and ledger from its own window. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine
running one fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with
every step of the guest’s computing done by the host’s counter moves and every rise
of its record put where its program put it, and, in the certified case, each guest’s
record earned again by the host’s own check, commit and certificate (Definition D.1).
The ones in this book are U (Appendix D.1), a fixed program in the small machine’s
instruction kinds, with no guest step built in, that runs every small-machine program
with halting and flag exact and its ledger equal to the guest’s at every matching
point, and UP (Appendix D.2), the same program with one paid move added, that
runs every computably presented Thiele machine, one whose driver, step, prices and
reading are computed by programs with the reading decided on every state, keeping
470   A Things I had to learn first


               its reading as a latch and, when the reading starts at no, its ledger to within two of
               the guest’s, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid
               when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three. The simpler host with a
               built-in guest step runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest’s flag.
               A computer running the small machine isn’t a Thiele machine; it implements one,
               inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a Turing machine. When a word below
               belongs to only one of the two layers, the entry says which.
                   A partition is a sorting of a pile into groups, nothing in two groups and nothing
               left over (Section 5). A Thiele machine is a state type, moves, a step, a cost per move,
               and a yes-or-no reading, plus one rule, the toll: a move that turns the reading from
               no to yes costs at least one (Section 2). The rule is called A2 in the conditions table
               (Appendix B). A move merges when two different starting states land on the same
               end; one that never does is injective, it forgets nothing. A reading is permanent when
               no move turns it from yes back to no (Section 3).
                   A chair is a distinction that stays: a cell that reads 0 and not 1 and not blank, a
               bead in the left well and not the right, a flag that’s up (Section 1). The step law says
               what any step of any machine with one next state for each state does to its chairs,
               with no finiteness anywhere (Theorem 1.1). It lands on a chair the run hasn’t used
               yet, which is room. Or, the first time it comes back to a used chair other than the
               start, it comes from a different chair than the one that first got there, which is a
               merge, two states sharing a next state, and under Landauer’s premise a merge carries
               a heat floor. Or it comes back to the start, or retakes a step it already took, which is
               all a run does after its first return: it’s going round a loop and makes nothing new.
               Heat or room is that law aimed at a reading that stays up: a run that raises one either
               merges two of its states somewhere or never repeats a state (Proposition 3.4). That’s
               the bill for keeping. On top of it there’s always the dissipation of happening: in any
               real device, every step that changes something in a finite time dissipates, merge or
               not, reversible or not, and time sets how much. Slower means less, never none, and
               slowness does nothing to the floor a merge adds. The book proves that for Bennett’s
               walker (Theorem 1.8); the general finite-time bounds are physics (Schmiedl and
               Seifert, 2007; Shiraishi, Funo and Saito, 2018). A reversible machine never merges,
               so it owes no floor, but it isn’t free: each step still dissipates as it happens, and it
               pays in room; on finitely many states it comes back to its start and keeps nothing
               (Theorem 1.5). Finiteness is what takes the room column away: when only finitely
               many states read yes, the raising move has to merge (Proposition 3.3).
                   The counter, which I also call the ledger: in the model, a number carried in
               the state that starts at zero and that every step raises by exactly that step’s charge
               (Section 6). My machine has exactly one, the ledger µ (Section 15). Two other
               things get called counters, and each chapter says which: Minsky’s two bins on the
               small machine, and the eight counts that tally the game’s rounds (Appendix H).
                                                                       A.8 Words this book builds   471


Neither is the ledger. A price list says what each move costs; the model takes it as
given, and my machine’s table of what each instruction costs is in Section 15. A
receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges
on every path including the failures, and is the only such total, on the states a run
reaches, for its price list (Section 6 proves it for any system with a counter and a
price list; on my machine the sum is a theorem too, Section 15). In the model there
is just a reading, yes or no (Section 2); on the small machine it’s the flag, set by a
CERTIFY that passes and never cleared.
    These belong to the small machine only (Section 15). A two-counter machine
is Minsky’s: two counters holding whole numbers with no upper limit, and two
instructions: add one, and subtract one and jump if the counter is above zero,
or else go on to the next line; already enough that nobody can decide in general
whether one halts. The small machine is a two-counter machine plus HALT and
three instructions for the record, six in all: INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY. A counter’s version is its edition number: it starts at 0 and goes up by
one every time the counter is written, so an edition never comes back. A fact is
a property, a counter and a version together, such as “A is even, as of edition 3”;
the properties come from a fixed language with three forms, is zero, is even and is
at least n. The same theorems also hold for any property language with an exact
equality test whose checker is proved to say yes exactly when the claim holds, and
one such language reads a counter as a list and asks whether it’s sorted. The fact
table holds up to sixteen facts, and the only way in is a CHECK that passed; nothing
ever leaves it. The small machine’s channel holds one committed fact or nothing,
and COMMIT puts a fact there only if the table has it about the counter’s current
edition. With the flag up from a clean start it names a commitment earned that way,
and a later COMMIT replaces it, as a two-commit run shows. The trap is a bit that
goes up when an instruction refuses, and then nothing in the core moves again. A
commitment is earned when a passing check put its fact in the table first, about the
same edition, with no write to that counter in between; on the small machine every
flag raised from a clean start is earned, and that’s a theorem. CHECK, COMMIT
and CERTIFY cost one mark each and everything else costs no marks, so from a
clean start a run ending with the flag up adds at least three to the ledger, and a run
whose check could have failed adds exactly three: CHECK is zero on A, COMMIT,
CERTIFY, from a start where A is 0. The step doesn’t police trivial checks; is at
least 0 passes every value and certifies for three too. The host machine is the small
machine with a counter, called a register, for every whole number, and one property,
Slot, true of a number that packs a property of the small machine together with a
value it holds of. A slot is a register of the host used for nothing but holding one
checked fact about the guest, and its mirror is a register beside it, safe to read, that
says which claim the slot holds while its fact is live. U is the fixed program of host
472   A Things I had to learn first


               instructions that runs every small-machine program; it reads guest instructions out
               of one register, keeps the guest’s counters in two others, and puts every checked fact
               in a slot, because on this machine reading a counter into a program’s control flow
               writes it. The universal program’s guest is a program of the small machine, held as
               one number in a register of the host and run one instruction at a time by U’s fetch
               and decode. UP is U with one more handler, for PAY, an instruction that costs one
               and does nothing else; its guests are programs compiled from computably presented
               Thiele machines (Appendix D.2).
                  A window is any function that shows you part of a state (Section 7); a shadow,
               said loosely, is what a window leaves you with. A collision is two steps that look
               the same through a window, before and after, where one raises the flag and the
               other doesn’t (Section 7). Entitlement is what a run has when it carries an object,
               a checked relation between that object and a claim, and a paid event that put the
               object in place: a license to lean on the claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true
               (Section 8). A latch is a record that switches on the first time some event holds and
               never switches off (Section 10). The diagonal’s substrate (Section 13) is the model’s
               shape extended with programs, a run that may give nothing back, a counter that
               never falls, a way to write programs as states, the transformations the substrate
               counts as its own, and its own recursion theorem for those; the proof of the diagonal
               uses neither the counter nor the toll.
APPENDIX B




Every assumption in one place

Everything in this book is a system built out of stated conditions, or a theorem with
stated premises, and I’ve named each condition where it’s used. Here they are side
by side, because a reader who wants to break this book should be able to see every
place where it says “suppose,” in one list, with what each “suppose” buys.
   The labels A2 to A6 in this appendix are shorthand for the conditions listed below.
They are not additional claims: each label names the rule written beside it.


B.1 Systems and their conditions

Definition B.1 (Thiele machine). A Thiele machine consists of a set of states S, a
set of moves I, a step function step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a reading
cert : S → {no, yes}, satisfying the toll: every move that turns the reading from no
to yes costs at least one. This is the condition of Section 2, called A2 in the table
below. Every result stated “for any Thiele machine” assumes it.


Definition B.2 (Quantitative Thiele machine). A quantitative Thiele machine is
a Thiele machine with a witness, a function W from states to N, and a threshold
N ∈ N, satisfying: (A3) W (s) + cost(i ) ≥ W (step(s, i )), the witness grows by at
most what the move cost; and (A5) a state that reads yes has W (s) ≥ N. An optional
additional condition is (A4) W (s) ≤ W (step(s, i )).



Theorem B.1 (The floor raised to a threshold). In a quantitative Thiele machine,
every run from a state with witness 0 (this starting condition is called A6) to a state
that reads yes has total cost at least N.

Proof. Adding A3 along the run telescopes: the witness at the end is at most the
witness at the start plus the total cost, so, the start witness being 0 by A6, at most the
total cost. A5 says the end witness is at least N. Neither A4 nor the toll is used.
   A3 and A4 bound opposite directions, and neither implies the other: witness 1,
cost 0, witness 0 satisfies A3 and breaks A4, and witness 0, cost 0, witness 1 does


                                                   473
474   B Every assumption in one place


               the reverse. These conditions describe a general setting. The small machine’s own
               floor of three is proved directly (Observation 15.16) and never goes through it.
                  Here are the labels side by side, so none of them is left without a meaning.

476   B Every assumption in one place


                   Four remarks on the table. First, the recursion premise holds by construction for
               the nat family and by proof for L (Section 13) and for the programs of the small
               machine’s host (Appendix D.4). Second, the substrate used for the diagonal also
               carries a different rule from the toll: the counter never goes down on a step. Neither
               implies the other, and the diagonal uses neither. Third, merge pricing is an abstract
               lower bound on every merging instruction. It is the pairwise restriction of worst-case
               entropy pricing, which is equivalent to the halving price. Landauer’s premise instead
               bounds heat from the uncertainty actually removed under its thermal conditions. A
               known starting state supplies no positive floor from that premise (Theorem 3.15).
               That isn’t a hole in the bill. The distinction was already kept by whoever knows the
               start, and the bill was paid in that knowing, or will be paid when that record is wiped.
               And a write from a known start that changes the cell still dissipates when it happens
               in a finite time. It lacks a floor that survives going slowly only when the device doing
               it was chosen knowing the start; a fixed device that merges K inputs produces at
               least k B ln K of entropy on its worst one (Section 3.7). Riechers, Boyd, Wimsatt and
               Crutchfield (2020) derive additional work bounds under time-symmetric control
               of metastable memories. Their low-error bound depends on the initial distribution
               and the memory’s time-reversal behaviour; it is not a universal heat charge on each
               logical move.
                   Fourth, finiteness, because it’s the premise people most often think the book leans
               on, and it leans on it less than it looks. The step law and the first half of heat or
               room need none: on any machine, finite or endless, a run that raises a reading that
               stays up either merges two of its states somewhere or takes a fresh state at every
               step. Finiteness is what takes the second option away. With infinitely many states
               reading yes, a price list that charges only merges lets a machine certify for zero
               marks, the endless strip of Door one (Section 3), by taking a fresh state at every
               step. That isn’t a way around the bill. It’s a price list that doesn’t charge the room
               column. Every memory anyone can build is finite; that’s a fact about devices, and
               nothing here proves it.
APPENDIX C




What’s mine, and what isn’t

Every chapter of this book leans on somebody, and I’ve named them where I lean.
This appendix does a different job, and it’s the one where I’d most like to be caught
out, and caught out early. For each thing the book could be accused of claiming as
its own, it says what was already known, what this work actually defines, builds,
proves, or connects, and what kind of contribution that is. Five kinds, and they aren’t
the same claim: a new result (a statement nobody had); a new proof of something
known; an implementation (something built that runs); a synthesis (known pieces
put together under one question); and a conjecture or thesis (a claim stated and not
proved; a thesis ties defined notions to the world, so no proof can settle it). Every
kind can be worth doing. None of them is the others. And if you read down the list
and notice that “new result” hardly shows up, good. You’re reading it right.
    Two warnings about my own evidence before the list. First, “I didn’t find it” is a
fact about my searches. The literature is bigger than my searches. I searched with
every tool I had, and some tools will cheerfully invent a citation if you let them, so
where it matters I say where I looked, and you should assume it may well be sitting
in a paper I’d need a few more lifetimes of homework to read. Second, nothing
below is inferred from how many theorems there are or from a good story about
who came before. A proof, if it’s right, tells you the statement is true. It doesn’t
tell you it’s new. A thousand correct proofs could be a thousand careful ways of
agreeing with Tarjan.
    After the prior-work map come the items themselves, fifteen of them, numbered
as their subsections are, in the order the book reaches them: the bill first, certification
last.


The prior-work map

What I do and don’t know about prior work. I came to this with no formal training in
the fields it turned out to need, and I’ve read what I could reach, with every tool I
had. The prior-work map below is orientation. It doesn’t pretend to be scholarship.
For each piece of this book it says who did the thing it leans on, and what, if anything,
this development adds. A row that’s wrong gets fixed, and, as the end of Section 21
says, I’d want to hear of one.


                                                   477
478   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


                   There’s a law about rows like these, and it’s a joke that keeps turning out true. In
               1980 the statistician Stephen Stigler proposed that no scientific discovery is named
               after the person who first found it, and then credited the idea to the sociologist
               Robert K. Merton, who had been writing about fights over scientific priority since
               1957. So Stigler’s law is an example of itself, which is either the best joke in the
               history of science or a very tidy accident. Is it a law? No. It’s a pattern. Nobody
               proved it. But this book has already tripped over it twice, in The point at the front
               and in Section 3: the pigeonhole principle wears Dirichlet’s name, and Leurechon
               had it two centuries earlier. And I put my own name on a machine. By Stigler’s law,
               that makes it somebody else’s. The table below is my best attempt at finding out
               whose.
                   What I compare each time is what a result is about. Landauer’s bound is about
               heat, a physical cost under a thermodynamic model. No Free Lunch (an optimisation
               result, in the list below the table) is about averages over a whole spread of problems.
               The toll is a floor on one kind of step, the step that turns the reading on. Rise-only
               pricing adds a second rule on top: charge nothing on a step that doesn’t turn it on.
               So the comparisons are about the shape of each result. They aren’t claims about
               who got somewhere first, and they don’t show that certification is the only event
               worth pricing.
                   The right-hand column uses words built in the body of the book (the latch, the
               fibre, the universal program, the integer check, the matrix test); the subsections
               after the table say where each one is built.

                   Everything in the right column is stated with its premises in the body of the book,
               and everything in the middle column is cited where it’s used. The table is the short
               form. The long form is the rest of this appendix, which takes each row, says what
               was already known with sources, and says what kind of addition each one is. Very
               little of the right column is a new result. Most of it is things built, new proofs of
               known things, and known pieces put together under one question.
                   A few more labels I went and looked up are neighbours. Some of them also sit in
               the table above, and one, the reference monitor, is the move the small machine’s
               step makes. I list them so you can see why I don’t think the toll is one of them under
               a new name. Each is a claim inviting correction.
               • Linear logic (Girard 1987) treats an assumption as a resource that gets used up.
                 It constrains what a program, or a proof, may consume. The toll constrains the
                 model’s step function instead. Same instinct, different layer.
               • Foundational proof-carrying code (Appel 2001) checks safety proofs against the
                 smallest trusted base it can: a logic plus the machine’s semantics. Here no proof
                 rides along with the program. The step rule writes the receipts as the run goes.
               • Session types (Honda 1993) constrain how programs talk to each other so the
                 conversation can’t go off script. The toll is about what one computation has paid
                 to establish. Different problem.
               • No Free Lunch (Wolpert and Macready 1997): averaged over every problem,
                 whatever an optimiser gains on some problems it gives back on others. That’s an
                                                                                           483


  average over a whole problem space, and the edge is paid for elsewhere. The toll
  charges one step in one run, with no refund anywhere.
• Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965): the description complexity of a
  string is the length of the shortest program that prints it, relative to a fixed
  description language. That’s a property of a finished string, with no steps and no
  moment of paying. The toll is a law about a step.
• Irreversibility cost and information distance (Zurek 1989; Bennett, Gács, Li,
  Vitányi and Zurek 1998; Li and Vitányi 1996): the fewest bits a reversible
  machine must take in and erase irreversibly to turn a string x into a string y,
  about C ( x | y) + C (y | x ), where C ( x | y) is the length of the shortest program
  that prints x given y; and Kolchinsky and Wolpert’s thermodynamic complexity
  of a Turing machine’s outputs (2020). These tie algorithmic information to steps
  and erasures, and they price a transformation between strings, or an output, in
  erased bits. The toll prices the rise of a chosen reading.
• Cook and Levin (Cook 1971; Levin 1973): checking can be cheap while finding
  looks expensive, and whether finding is really harder is the open P-versus-NP
  question, a gap in how difficulty grows with size. The toll puts a fixed floor under
  the one step that commits, however easy or hard the finding was.
• The thermodynamic cost of choosing (Rovelli 2024): settling a binary choice at
  temperature T dissipates at least kT ln 2, with no outside heat bath. That’s the
  closest thing to the toll itself I’ve found, because it charges a commitment. An
  object or an average isn’t what it prices. But it’s physics, indexed to a temperature,
  and its choice is unpredictable, a branching, and stable only for a while, where
  the toll prices a deterministic no-to-yes transition. On my side, finitely many
  yes-states and permanence are what force the raising move to merge states. The
  toll charges the commitment in a model of computation, with no temperature in
  it. Closest neighbour. A different chair.
• Persistent copies (Ouldridge and ten Wolde 2017; Ouldridge, Govern and ten
  Wolde 2017): making a copy that stays correlated with its original after the two
  come apart has a thermodynamic bill. The nearest physics I’ve found to “learning
  borrows, committing pays.” It’s heat for a correlation, in chemistry; the toll is a
  count in a model of computation.
• Thermodynamics of finite automata (Ouldridge and Wolpert 2023): if the smallest
  automaton for a language has a letter that sends two states to one, recognising
  that language on a device that repeats one local step produces entropy, and if the
  smallest automaton only reshuffles, recognition carries no such floor. That’s the
  chairs with a physical price on them, and one of their worked examples is the
  latch’s language turned inside out. It’s the closest neighbour of all to the road
  the toll is derived on; Section 3 says exactly what’s left over for me.
484   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               • CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a verified
                 C compiler that carries the object code’s execution cost back up to annotations
                 on the source. There the cost decorates the program and survives compilation.
                 Here it lives in the model’s step rule.
               • Reference monitors and execution monitors (Anderson 1972; Schneider 2000;
                 Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors 2015). A small piece every action passes
                 through, enforcing a rule on every program. Schneider argued that a monitor
                 watching a run can enforce only rules whose breaking shows up at a finite point,
                 and “no certificate without an earlier passing check and commit” is one of those;
                 the micro-policies check a tag rule at every instruction, proved correct. That’s
                 the move the small machine’s step makes, so this one is the house itself. What’s
                 added is the edition-bound check-then-commit with a paid, permanent record
                 on top, and the derivation of why the payment can’t be zero. Kevin Hamlen,
                 Greg Morrisett and Fred Schneider (2006) went on to sort which rules monitors,
                 program rewriters and static checkers can each enforce, and they differ, which is
                 one reason this book doesn’t claim that every enforcement mechanism is a Thiele
                 machine underneath.
               • Trusted components in replicated services (Chun and coauthors 2007; Levin and
                 coauthors 2009; Veronese and coauthors 2013; Decouchant and coauthors 2022;
                 Clement, Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues 2012): a small record inside each replica
                 that a replica taken over still can’t make say two things, with a proof of exactly
                 what that buys. The record is theirs. The toll isn’t in their picture.
               • Ghost state (Owicki and Gries 1976; Filliâtre, Gondelman and Paskevich 2014):
                 variables added for a proof that can be erased without changing what the program
                 computes. The flag and the counter are ghost in that sense. The small machine’s
                 table of checked facts isn’t, because the step reads it and refuses on it, for every
                 program.
               • Verifiable computation and proof-carrying data (Parno, Howell, Gentry and
                 Raykova 2013; Chiesa and Tromer 2010): a short proof, checkable by a stranger,
                 that a computation’s output is right. That establishes the claim for the stranger,
                 and anyone with the inputs can make one, the copier included. The record here
                 is about one machine’s own history. A proof like that is one way to carry the local
                 record out of the box.
               • Commitments and entitlements (Brandom 1994): talk as score-keeping, tracking
                 who is committed to what and who is entitled to it. Brandom’s entitlements can
                 be defeated and can be passed on by testimony. Here entitlement is priced, step
                 by step, and a copy carries it only as far as the copy is genuine. Same words,
                 different machinery.
                                                                                         485


• Correspondence assertions (Woo and Lam 1993; Gordon and Jeffrey 2003). In
  protocol verification, “this end event must be preceded by a begin event for the
  same thing” is a correspondence assertion, and a type system can prove a protocol
  keeps it against any opponent. “No certificate without an earlier commit, and
  no commit without an earlier check of the same claim” has that shape. Theirs is
  proved about programs by typing. Mine is enforced by the step, which is the LCF
  comparison again, at the level of single instructions.
• Monotonic parallel composition (Åman Pohjola and Parrow 2016) and persistence
  in the pi-calculus (Palamidessi, Saraswat, Valencia and Victor 2006). Åman
  Pohjola and Parrow separate models where a neighbouring process can never
  stop a step from models that can solve consensus, and test-and-set, an instruction
  that writes a cell and reports what was there, is on the consensus side. Palamidessi
  and coauthors compare messages that are used up with messages that stay, and
  the end of their study is a reduction from Minsky machines. The small machine,
  put into Åman Pohjola and Parrow’s setting with threads pooled on one shared
  state (two states that have both moved jam), has a consensus process in their
  sense, so it lands on their non-monotonic side; their theorem and that placing
  are argued in a few lines in Section 15. The comparison with Palamidessi and
  coauthors’ persistence stays a comparison.
• Constructor theory (Deutsch and Marletto 2015; Marletto 2016; Marletto, Vedral
  and coauthors 2022; Violaris and Marletto 2022): physics as which tasks a device
  that runs in a cycle can do, with irreversible meaning possible while the inverse
  isn’t. It’s the nearest physics I know to “committing costs” stated for a cycling
  device. It’s quantum and approximate, and the chairs are classical, finite and
  exact (Section 3).
• Accountability and fault detection (Haeberlen and Kuznetsov 2009; Küsters,
  Truderung and Vogt 2010; Treitz and Künnemann 2026): when an outside party
  can tell who misbehaved. Their windows are this book’s windows, and the trust
  they leave over, an honest log or a trusted step, is left over here too (Section 7).
• Transferability (Easwaran 2009): a deductive proof lets you learn from someone
  you don’t trust because you can check every step, and a probabilistic proof doesn’t.
  That’s the argument for carrying the object and re-running the check (Section 7).
    And then the silly question that list raises, which I’m going to chase anyway: why
is an optimisation theorem named after lunch? Wolpert and Macready borrowed
an old saying, “there ain’t no such thing as a free lunch,” and the saying is older
than almost everyone who gets credit for it. American saloons in the 1800s put out
a free lunch for anyone who bought a drink, and the drink paid for the lunch. A
Washington newspaper was already saying in 1909 that somebody has to pay for a
free lunch; a newspaper fable by Walter Morrow had the whole line in 1938; a book
486   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               by Pierre Dos Utt already had the squeezed form, TANSTAAFL, as its title in 1949;
               Robert Heinlein’s 1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress made that squeezed
               form famous; and the economist Milton Friedman put the saying on the cover of
               his 1975 book of essays on public policy. I’d have credited Heinlein or Friedman.
               As far as anything I could find goes, neither coined it. Stigler’s law again, at lunch.
               Here’s what it changes. No Free Insight is named like a cousin of the saying, and the
               family resemblance misleads in one way. The saloon’s lunch was paid for somewhere
               else, in the price of the beer, and that’s Wolpert and Macready’s shape: a gain
               here, handed back over there. The toll isn’t that. On the ledger nothing gets paid
               somewhere else: the step that raises the flag pays, on the spot. A blank tape is the
               saloon’s shape, paid for before the run by whoever wiped it; the toll is the step that
               won’t hide its share that way.


               C.1 Every step is room, a merge, or a loop
               Known: the step law is the first-return argument every textbook on dynamics makes,
               and under it sits the pigeonhole. A one-to-one move that raises a reading and keeps
               it is Hilbert’s hotel, everybody moving up a room so that a room comes free (Hilbert’s
               lecture course of 1924–25, made famous by Gamow in 1947), and a collection that
               can be matched one-to-one with a part of itself that leaves something out is exactly
               what Dedekind (1888) called infinite. Recurrence for reversible finite machines is
               Poincaré’s (1890) and Zermelo’s (1896) in its finite form. The noisy chairs are the
               fact that a doubly stochastic chain has no closed class it can enter from outside,
               with Gibbs’s inequality for the entropy gap; the quantum chairs are that a unitary
               preserving a finite-dimensional subspace preserves its complement; the bilateral shift
               is the standard example of what goes wrong without finite dimension. Time’s bill is
               Bennett’s Brownian computer (1982) with Schnakenberg’s formula for the entropy a
               biased walk hands its surroundings; that any change of a device’s states finished in a
               finite time dissipates, shrinking toward zero only as the time grows without bound,
               is finite-time stochastic thermodynamics (Schmiedl and Seifert, 2007; Shiraishi,
               Funo and Saito, 2018); and the trade of room for time by recomputing is Bennett’s
               (1989). The measurements are Bérut and coauthors’ (2012), Jun, Gavrilov and
               Bechhoefer’s (2014), Hong and coauthors’ (2016) and Gaudenzi and coauthors’
               (2018). Mine: the reading, that the write of a 0 on a cell is a merge and the toll
               is the price of something being the case; putting those old facts side by side as
               one law with three columns (fresh room, a merge, a loop that makes nothing new)
               and no fourth, for deterministic, noisy and quantum steps alike; the heat-or-room
               dichotomy for a reading that stays up, with no finiteness in it; and the exact chair
               count for a bounded memory, M ≥ 1 + ( T + 1)( N − 1), with a building that reaches
               it (Section 3, Section 1); and that a merge seen in a coarse description forces, in
                                                  C.2 The universal floor and the potential method   487


any finer description it’s exact about, a fine merge, a fine step out of the set, or
infinitely many fine states (Theorem 1.9). Kind: synthesis and a reading, with the
chair count and the every-scale theorem as small exact lemmas. The mathematics
is old. What I’d defend is the arrangement: endless memory, history-keeping and
reversible machines aren’t a way out of the bill, they’re the room column, which
dodges only the floor a merge adds and never the dissipation of a step happening;
and finiteness is what takes that column away.


C.2 The universal floor and the potential method

Known: the potential method of amortized analysis, a function on states whose
drop bounds the cost of a run, is Tarjan’s (1985), and it has been mechanized more
than once (Nipkow in Isabelle/HOL, 2015 and 2019; Charguéraud and Pottier’s
time credits, 2019), built into type systems for automatic resource analysis (from
Hofmann and Jost, 2003, and Hoffmann and coauthors, 2011, onward), and recast
in cost-aware type theories (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022). Mine: choosing
the potential that is one when a designated reading says no and zero when it says
yes, so that “the crossing costs” (the toll) and “every run that crosses paid” (the
floor) are the potential method’s two halves (Section 6), and its count, one mark per
crossing (Observation 2.2), the same sum read crossing by crossing. Kind: a known
technique, used with one particular potential. The choice is the point: it makes “was
certified” something the account must carry. The theorem is not new mathematics.
If it looks clever, that’s Tarjan’s cleverness; my part was picking which number to
plug in.
    Go back to Tarjan’s paper and there’s a sentence that sits right on the line this
book draws. He opens with the dictionary (to amortize is to put money aside at
intervals, as in a sinking fund) and then gives two views of the method. In the
banker’s view the computer is coin-operated, and each operation is handed credits
to spend or save; in the physicist’s view, which he credits to Daniel Sleator, every
state has a potential and you count its changes. Then he stops to say that the credits
are only an accounting device: the programs that actually run contain no mention
of credits or debits. That’s exactly right for what he wanted, a bound proved about
a program from outside. It’s also exactly the gap. In his method the coins live in the
proof. The one move I chose was to put them in the step, where no program takes a
step without it being counted. Same arithmetic, different place.


C.3 The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges
Known: that steps which merge states (no single-valued inverse) are what Landauer’s
principle charges for is Landauer’s (1961), sharpened by Bennett (1973, 1982, 2003;
488   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               the words “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths” are from
               the 2003 abstract); generalizations and the dependence on the input distribution
               are Maroney’s (2009), Sagawa’s (2014), Wolpert’s; the critique is Earman and
               Norton’s and Norton’s. Write-once memory is an old topic in coding theory (Rivest
               and Shamir, 1982), where the question is reuse and price never comes up, and
               Chris Heegard (1985) worked out the capacity of permanent memory with noise,
               again a question of how much fits. What it costs doesn’t come into it. Statisticians
               priced permanence on finite memory in their own currency: in Hellman and Cover’s
               analysis of hypothesis testing with finite memory (1970), a machine that settles its
               answer by falling into states it never leaves does worse than one that doesn’t, so a
               decision held for good costs memory states. Heat never enters their analysis. And
               the counting under the theorem is older than any of that, twice over. Theorem 3.1
               is the finite, discrete cousin of the recurrence argument Zermelo, using Poincaré’s
               theorem of 1890, turned on Boltzmann in 1896, here aimed at a reading. Zermelo
               aimed it at entropy, and Bocchieri and Loinger gave the quantum recurrence in 1957.
               In automata form it is classical: a finite machine whose moves are all one-to-one
               reshuffles recognises only group languages, and the inputs that raise a permanent
               reading form a language that is never one of those unless it is empty (Pin’s 1992
               paper on reversible automata is the reference I’d check; automata theorists treat the
               step as folklore), and going quantum doesn’t change it (Brodsky and Pippenger, 2002:
               quantum finite automata that measure once, at the end, accept with bounded error
               exactly the group languages). The closest of all is recent. Ouldridge and Wolpert
               (2023) give a proof that if the smallest automaton for a language has a step that
               merges states, every automaton for it does, and argue that recognising it on a device
               that repeats one local step carries an entropy floor, while a language whose smallest
               automaton only reshuffles carries no such floor; one of their worked examples is
               the strings with no b, the complement of the latch’s language. That’s the core with
               a physical price already on it. And the logarithm in the heat floor matches the
               absolute-irreversibility bound of Murashita, Funo and Ueda (2014), which Manzano,
               Kardeş, Roldán and Wolpert (2024) carried over to computation. The logarithms
               coincide for the stated counts. This does not supply a physical reverse process:
               absolute irreversibility needs forward and reverse path probabilities that the logical
               map alone does not specify. Constructor theory states a cousin of the same core
               for devices that run in a cycle: Marletto, Vedral and coauthors (2022) and Violaris
               and Marletto (2022) built an irreversible task out of the quantum homogeniser and
               argued that erasure may cost more than Landauer’s bound. Section 3 tells all of it.
               The price isn’t mine: Li and Vitányi priced each erased bit (1996), and Demaine
               and his coauthors priced named instructions that destroy bits (2016). Mine is what
               a flat price of at least a mark on every merging move does to a reading that stays:
               it turns “the flip merges” into “the flip costs” on any machine with finitely many
                                                            C.4 Learning borrows, committing pays   489


states reading yes, whether or not anybody’s physics is right, and gives the toll
(Observation 3.2); what comes with that form, namely the characterisation of the
moves every merge-pricing schedule must charge, when move names can be decided
equal or different (the merging moves, so the core again in pricing words), the
merge-or-revoke dichotomy for a single move, the squeeze and entropy forms for
a permanent flip, and a built counterexample for each premise (Section 3). The
counterexample for finiteness is the endless strip, and it says what the premise is
for: the strip raises its reading with no merge by taking new room at every step,
so a price list that charges merges and nothing else lets it certify for zero marks.
That’s a price list that doesn’t charge the room column, not a machine that got out
of paying, and its steps still dissipate as they happen. Kind: the core is classical,
and somebody else’s: Zermelo’s in physics, folklore in automata theory, with Pin’s
paper as the place to check it. The pricing form isn’t wholly mine either: priced in
entropy, for automata, it’s Ouldridge and Wolpert’s. They derive the price from the
physics. An assumed price is older than mine too: Li and Vitányi (1996) took a unit
charge per irreversibly erased bit, with reversible steps priced at zero, as axioms of
a model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) put that charge on
named instructions of the random-access machine. What’s mine is the toll derived
from a price on merging moves for a reading that stays, its single-move and counted
forms, and the counterexamples. The physics is a named premise and is Landauer’s.
Searches: the core turned up in the places just named, and its physical price in
Ouldridge and Wolpert; I didn’t find the derived toll stated anywhere I looked, and
nobody’s search covers a whole field, mine least of all.


C.4 Learning borrows, committing pays

Known: that a measurement can be made without merging anything, so that
Landauer’s premise sets it no floor, and that the floor lands when the demon wipes
its notes to look again, is Bennett’s resolution of Maxwell’s demon (1982), with the
quantitative trade-off by Sagawa and Ueda (2009); that the bill can be split between
measuring and erasing in more than one way is Fahn’s (1996), and that what an
erasure costs depends on what the eraser already knows is del Rio and colleagues’
(2011). The closest physics I found to the line between learning and committing
is Ouldridge and ten Wolde’s fundamental costs of persistent copies (2017; with
Govern, 2017), copies that stay correlated with their originals after the two come
apart; theirs is heat for a correlation in chemistry, and Section 4 says how it differs.
The sharp chemical form, that a persistent copy grown at equilibrium carries no
information about its template, is Poulton, ten Wolde and Ouldridge’s (2019). Mine:
the four-state demon, where copying a hidden bit onto a display known to be blank
merges nothing and wiping the display merges two pairs of states; the second copy
490   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               that hands the display back blank while the original is still there; the three-state ring
               and the two-state impossibility (Section 4); and the certainty bill (Theorem 4.4),
               which splits the uncertainty about the start into the part a run destroyed, paid for
               in marks, and the part the end state still holds. That split is Shannon’s chain rule
               (1948), and bounds of this kind on the actual spread are Maroney’s (2009) and
               Sagawa’s (2014); mine is reading it on the ledger, about what an observer saw.
               Kind: finite models and one bookkeeping identity illustrating a known physical
               point inside my ledger. Not a new physical claim. Bennett did the hard part in
               1982. My four dots put the line where you can work it through yourself: the copy
               owes no floor and can cost no marks, but it isn’t free. Like any step that happens, it
               dissipates as it happens, less the slower it goes. And it uses up a blank page, which is
               room; while the original is still there it can hand the page back, so learning borrows.
               The page’s floor gets paid when it’s wiped for reuse, and a blank page was itself
               a distinction somebody paid to set. Committing makes the record permanent, so
               there’s nothing to hand back, and on finite room it has to merge.


               C.5 The counter as a receipt
               Known: one-way counters that give order and termination are old: Turing’s 1949
               note on checking a large routine, Floyd’s ranking functions (1967), Lamport’s clocks
               (1978). Carrying a run’s cost beside its result is the writer cost of Danner, Licata and
               Ramyaa (2015) and of Danner and Licata (2022), and the graded effect semantics of
               Katsumata (2014), with a working-language version in Orchard, Liepelt and Eades
               (2019). The receipt side of time credits is Mével, Jourdan and Pottier’s (2019): in
               their extension of the Iris logic every step uses up a credit and produces a receipt,
               receipts prove lower bounds, and enough of them prove that a counter can’t overflow
               in any feasible time, which is the closest published neighbour of a total that only
               climbs. Mine: putting three properties side by side (the total only climbs, it equals
               the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and it is the only such
               total, on the states a run reaches, for a given price list), the argument for any system
               with a counter and a price list, and the sum proved from the small machine’s own
               step (Section 6, Section 15). Kind: synthesis; the abstract statements are proved
               for any system with a counter and a price list, and on the small machine the sum
               is proved too. Against the graded frameworks the answer is split: the counter is
               their writer exactly, and their type systems, bounding relations and before-the-run
               checking of grades are not embedded, because the grade here is written by the
               step during the run (Section 6). For the well-graded, loop-free programs defined in
               Section 6, on runs that do not trap, the counter’s rise equals the fixed grade. The
               loop built there costs its input value, so no fixed whole number is its exact grade
                                                        C.6 Windows that can’t price what they hide   491


on every input; an input-dependent grade is exact. The arguments are given there.
Cost-aware type theories such as calf allow grades that depend on the inputs.


C.6 Windows that can’t price what they hide
Known: a function of an observation is constant on the observation’s fibres; that’s
elementary, and the systems version of it is Moore’s distinguishing experiments
(1956), Kalman’s observability (1960), and the completeness question of abstract
interpretation (Cousot and Cousot, 1977; Giacobazzi, Ranzato and Scozzari, 2000);
in control theory it is diagnosability and opacity of discrete-event systems (Sampath
and coauthors, 1995; Saboori and Hadjicostis, 2007), where a collision is a hidden
event no observer can diagnose without delay; in economics it is the hard-evidence
view of mechanism design (Green and Laffont, 1986; Bull and Watson, 2007), where
what a mechanism can tell apart is limited by the evidence on offer; and its sharp
form for fingerprints is Naor and Rothblum’s lower bound for checking a stored file
(2005); in distributed systems it is Haeberlen and Kuznetsov’s (2009), that only
omission and commission faults can be detected from outside, and in philosophy it
is Easwaran’s transferability (2009). Mine: stating the pricing version (no window
price is exact across a collision), exhibiting a colliding pair for the small machine’s
window, and the theorem that every certified Thiele-complete machine has two runs
from one clean start that end looking the same through the window its base shows,
one certified and one not (Section 7, Section 15). Kind: an elementary observation
about what a window hides, plus specific facts about the machine and the definition.


C.7 Structural entitlement and its bound

Known: decision-tree counting bounds (a tree that tells N cases apart has depth at
least log2 N); certifying algorithms that hand over checkable certificates (McConnell,
Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011); proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997); the
gap between justified true belief and knowledge (Gettier, 1963). Mine: the definition
of entitlement as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event on the record, and
the count that, given lists, a tree and a covering, a run that paid for the tree’s depth
pays at least the index bits it commits to (Section 8). Kind: synthesis; the counting
idea is standard, the assembly and its vocabulary are this work’s, the pricing policy is
assumed (nothing derives it), and the count is proved in its bill form over any Thiele
machine, and for the record moves of every certified Thiele-complete machine on a
run from a clean start, with the earned chain in the run, a floor that takes the run’s
own checks in place of a tree, and a counterexample showing the covering can’t be
dropped (Section 15.14); and in a form where the run makes the posterior from a
prior, every drop is made by a check the run passed, and the index bits are at most k
492   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               times the bill when each passing check keeps a 2−k share, a hypothesis the same
               counterexample shows is needed (Theorems 8.4 and 15.33).


               C.8 The record axis is a latch
               Known: monotone, write-once state is old: the latch (Eccles and Jordan, patent
               filed 1918, paper 1919), sticky bits (Plotkin, 1989), grow-only state in replicated
               data types (Shapiro and coauthors), history variables and stuttering in refinement
               (Abadi and Lamport, 1991), append-only authenticated sets for transparency logs,
               which fit revocation as a once-only event (Tomescu and coauthors, 2019), and, in
               program logic, monotonic state, where a property witnessed once on state that only
               moves forward can be recalled at any later point, with a soundness proof and a
               working home in F⋆ (Ahman, Fournet, Hriţcu, Maillard, Rastogi and Swamy, 2018):
               the type-theory name for a record that stays up. Past the finite case, inductive and
               quasi-inductive definitions (Richter and Aczel, 1974; Burgess, 1986) and the flag
               trick of infinite time Turing machines (Hamkins and Lewis, 2000) are the transfinite
               versions of a record that only grows and a toggle, and Danos and Krivine’s (2004)
               reversible calculus needs an action declared irreversible in order to commit. Mine:
               the exact statement that a record driven by the computation that never switches
               off is, over any base, a latch on one event, with its converse and a counterexample
               for each of the two conditions, and the argument that base-driven records agree
               up to the price list while the stronger uniqueness fails (Section 10). Kind: a small
               structural lemma, I think not stated before in this form (I found no prior statement
               in the searches I ran), built from old notions. The proofs show why the record must
               latch and why its price list remains a separate choice.


               C.9 The diagonal and L
               Known: Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem; Lawvere’s fixed-point form
               (1969) and Yanofsky’s retelling (2003); mechanized recursion theorems and Rice
               (Norrish in HOL4, 2011; Carneiro in Lean; Forster, Kunze, Smolka and coauthors,
               including L itself, 2017, and their library of undecidability results). Mine: the
               diagonal stated once over any substrate that supplies a recursion theorem; and Rice
               and halting proved again for L from its reduction rules (Section 13); and Rice’s and
               Kleene’s theorems proved for the small machine’s host, with Rice’s on every input
               of the two-counter machine itself, Kleene’s there with inputs written as powers of
               two, and Kleene’s refuted for plain inputs (Appendix D.4). Kind: new proofs of
               known theorems of computability, for particular machines. The theorems hold for
               any model with universality and s-m-n, and the work is in building those for each
                                                                        C.10 The small machine   493


machine; the refutation on plain inputs is a small fact about two counters, resting
on Schroeppel’s.


C.10 The small machine
Known: two-counter machines and the undecidability of their halting are Minsky’s
(1961, 1967), mechanized by Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors (2019, 2020).
The guarantee about every program is older than any of this, and it isn’t mine either.
It’s the reference monitor (Anderson, 1972): a check that sits in the path of every
operation, so no program gets around it. Schneider (2000) worked out what a
monitor that watches a run can enforce: only safety properties, the kind a bad run
breaks at some finite moment, and “no CERTIFY without an earlier earned COMMIT”
is one of those. Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors (2015) verified monitors that
check tags at every instruction. The shape of “earned,” a certificate nothing can
make except through the rules, is Milner’s LCF, where a theorem is a value only
the logic’s rules can build (Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth, 1979; Gordon, 2000);
the small machine is that architecture at the level of single instructions. “No certify
without an earlier commit” is also a correspondence assertion in the sense of Woo
and Lam (1993), which Gordon and Jeffrey (2003) check with a type system, and a
store of commitments that the rules of a dialogue keep, each speaker’s updated by
the rules as the moves are made, is Hamblin’s (1970, chapter 8, on formal dialectic);
the difference from all three is again that here the step enforces it. A check that
blesses a value and a write that takes the blessing away is close kin to dynamic
taint tracking, whose labels go back to Denning’s lattice model of information flow
(1976), with the blessing itself, controlled endorsement, given a type system and a
security theorem by Cecchetti, Myers and Arden (2017), and what a monitor can
enforce with bounded memory is Talhi, Tawbi and Debbabi’s question (2008). A
small monotone record inside each replica of a replicated service is A2M (Chun
and coauthors, 2007), TrInc (Levin and coauthors, 2009), MinBFT (Veronese and
coauthors, 2013) and Damysus (Decouchant and coauthors, 2022), and Clement,
Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record
buys and what it doesn’t. The signature route to the same goal, which needs no
trusted step, is IA-CCF (Shamis and coauthors, 2021): replicas sign and log their
protocol messages in the ledger, so blame lands on individual members however
many of them misbehave. And “check once, issue a capability the system trusts, rely
on it later” is built and deployed in Garg and Pfenning’s proof-carrying file system
(2010), whose logic lets a policy’s consequences change with time and state, and
in Sirer and coauthors’ logical attestation for the Nexus operating system (2011),
unforgeable statements about programs used as credentials; those are the closest
systems I’ve found to check, commit, certify. Mine: a machine of six instruction kinds
494   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               on two counters, with a version for each counter, a bounded fact table and a channel;
