               its theorems that, from a clean start, a committed fact was checked first about the
               same edition, that nothing is forged, that nothing is evicted, that with the flag up
               from a clean start the channel names a fact an earlier passing COMMIT committed,
               and a later commit can replace it, as a two-commit run shows, and that a run from
               a clean start to a raised flag adds at least three to the ledger, with three reached by
               a run whose check could have failed (the step doesn’t police trivial checks, so one
               that can’t fail costs three too); the same theorems for any property language with an
               exact equality test whose checker is proved to say yes exactly when the claim holds,
               a sorted list read out of a counter included; and the step-for-step match with the
               two-counter machine, so halting is undecidable for it (Section 15). Kind: an instance
               of monitor enforcement with two things on top that I didn’t find put together where
               I looked: the check is bound to the edition of the thing it checked, and a toll is paid
               for the commitment. The first of those alone is old: checking at commit time that
               nothing you read has changed since is optimistic concurrency control (Kung and
               Robinson, 1981), and each counter’s version here is that scheme’s version number.
               What I didn’t find is that check put together with a toll. The universality and the
               undecidability are borrowed, and the other properties are short consequences of the
               step rule. Whether the design is new I can’t say, and I make no claim beyond the
               proofs.


               C.11 Thiele-complete and certified Thiele-complete, defined so a clock fails

               Known: Turing completeness, and the observation every theorist makes in four
               seconds, that a toll alone is cheap: a machine that charges for every step pays
               any toll. Enforcement mechanisms have been compared and sorted before, and
               they aren’t one notion seen several ways: James Morris (1973) separated access
               limitation from authentication in programming languages, and Kevin Hamlen, Greg
               Morrisett and Fred Schneider (2006) classified which policies execution monitors,
               program rewriters and static analysis can each enforce, and they differ; Wai Wong
               (1995), on a neighbouring track, recorded and checked HOL proofs so a theorem
               could carry its derivation. Mine: a definition of Thiele-complete with four clauses
               that say nothing about what the record is about (computing that runs every program,
               costs no marks and can’t touch the record; a record that stays; blank starts; and
               some run whose record tells two starts apart), with the proofs that a clock and a
               silent machine fail it, that each clause is needed, that every universal base becomes
               one by adding marks, and that every machine meeting it hides its record and ledger
               from its own window (Section 10.8); and a definition of certified Thiele-complete
               with four clauses (a universal base that can’t touch the record and a record that stays
               up once it’s up, an earned record, exact prices with no marks for the base and one
                                                         C.12 Five record disciplines, one question   495


for each of the three record acts, and some claim whose check can fail), the proofs
that every clock-style machine and a paid latch and a silent machine fail it while the
small machine, the same machine over any property language with an exact equality
test, a proved checker and a property that holds of one number and fails of another,
and the universal program’s host meet it, that the four clauses are independent, each
failed by some machine with a two-counter machine inside that meets the other
three (Theorem 15.24), and the theorem that every machine meeting it hides its
record and ledger from its own window (Section 15), with the theorem that it is
exactly Thiele-complete with clean starts, the earned chain and a claim that could
have failed added (Theorem 15.18). Kind: definitions with short consequences. The
window theorem is the fibre fact of item 6 plus one observation, that a universal
base prints any window at no cost on the ledger. I’m not claiming the definition is
the only reasonable one, or that LCF kernels, reference monitors and proof-carrying
code are all certified Thiele-complete machines in disguise; Hamlen, Morrisett and
Schneider’s sorting says such mechanisms genuinely differ, and the book doesn’t
have a theorem showing the definition holds up across such differences.


C.12 Five record disciplines, one question
Known: each system and its guarantee belongs to its designers: Casper (Buterin and
Griffith, 2017), Ethereum’s storage gas and refunds (EIP-2200, EIP-3529), extend-
only TPM registers, Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162), proof-carrying code. Mine:
asking all five whether the write is priced, with a small worked fragment of each
(Section 17). Kind: synthesis and an organizing reading; the fragments are not
verifications of those systems.


C.13 The pointer thesis
Known: Zurek’s quantum Darwinism (2009), with Ollivier, Poulin and Zurek (2004)
and Blume-Kohout and Zurek (2006): preferred states are the ones whose records
proliferate redundantly in the environment. Mine: borrowing that shape for the
question of which event deserves a record, with definitions (copied and relied on by
parties who didn’t produce it, independent carriers), two toys, and refutations of
two stronger forms (Section 18). Kind: thesis. No claim about quantum physics.


C.14 The universal host

Known: Turing’s universal machine (1936), which runs any machine given as data,
and the universal register machines that run two-counter programs. Keeping a guest
and the code running beside it out of each other’s state is what a virtual machine
496   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               monitor promises (Popek and Goldberg, 1974). Compiling computable functions
               into counter machines is Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors’ work. Mine: one
               fixed program, U, written in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction on a
               host with a register for every whole number, with no guest step built in, that runs
               every program of the small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts exactly
               when its guest does, raises its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if
               and only if the guest’s rises somewhere in its run, and keeps a ledger equal to the
               guest’s at every matching point; its host machine is certified Thiele-complete, and
               whether U halts on a loaded guest is undecidable (Appendix D.1). Two small facts
               force its shape, and they’re stated there: reading a counter into the program’s control
               flow on this machine writes it, and a finite program can’t keep the guest’s facts on
               a copy of the guest’s counter, by the pigeonhole. Beside it, a simpler host with a
               built-in guest step runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest’s flag,
               with the mirror, isolation and earned-chain theorems. Code that shares unprotected
               memory with a record can overwrite it, and ordinary computers isolate memory and
               enforce rules with monitors too, so what I claim is narrower: the simulation and the
               record guarantee proved for this one fixed program U. Kind: an implementation,
               with its proofs, of a design whose shape is Turing’s universal machine, with the
               record and the toll carried through. The universality is borrowed from the small
               machine and from Minsky. And the same program with one paid move added,
               UP , runs every computably presented Thiele machine, with its halting matched, its
               reading carried as a latch on the host’s own earned flag whose claim is that reading,
               and its ledger to within a surcharge of at most two when the reading starts at no
               (exactly three when it starts at yes), which no program on the host, run from a
               clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three
               (Appendix D.2); the counter-compilation construction is given in Appendix K. Kind
               for that part: an implementation with its proofs again. That a universal machine
               runs any computable machine is Turing’s; what’s carried through here is the record,
               earned again, and the prices, exact up to the surcharge, and I didn’t find that put
               together where I looked. In the words of Definition D.1, U is a universal Thiele
               machine for the small machine’s programs with no surcharge, and UP is one for
               every computably presented Thiele machine with a surcharge of at most two when
               the guest’s reading starts at no and three when it starts at yes.


               C.15 The game check

               Known: that positive semidefiniteness of a correlation matrix gives the Tsirelson
               bound is Tsirelson’s (1980) and Stephanie Wehner’s semidefinite proof (2006), from
               a paper on Tsirelson bounds for generalized CHSH inequalities; the moment-matrix
               hierarchy, the Schur-complement analysis of the level-one matrix of this scenario
                                                                       C.16 What that adds up to   497


and the level 1 + AB are Navascués, Pironio and Acín’s (2007, 2008), with both four-
body cells free where my matrix ties them; that every point with a PSD completion is
the correlator table of a quantum strategy, built from anticommuting observables in
a maximally entangled state, is Tsirelson’s too (1980); the arcsine characterization
is Landau’s (1988) and Masanes’s (2003); and Tsirelson’s bound has already been
checked by machine, in Isabelle/HOL (Echenim and Mhalla, 2023) and in Lean’s
mathlib. Rational sum-of-squares certificates are Helfried Peyrl and Pablo A. Parrilo’s
(2008), from a paper on computing sum-of-squares decompositions with rational
coefficients. Mine: a decision procedure in integer arithmetic on outcome counts;
a proved chain from “the counts pass” to “the pinned level-one matrix is positive
semidefinite” to “S2 ≤ 8”; explicit constructions of the representation in finite
dimension, real or complex, on two eight-level systems, and a proof of the arcsine
characterization; proofs of the contraction equivalence by explicit test vectors; and
the level-1 + AB cascade (on the slice ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0) and an elliptope
gate in whole numbers, with a soundness proof (Appendix H and its derivation,
Appendix I). Kind: an integer procedure connecting counts to these known bounds,
with known theorems (Tsirelson’s representation, the arcsine characterization, the
equivalence of contraction and PSD) proved again. I found no earlier chain that
takes counts as input where I looked. The same check earned on the small machine’s
host, a raised flag standing on it, is built and proved (Theorems H.4 and H.5); the
idea isn’t new.


C.16 What that adds up to

Read straight down the list. The mathematics underneath this book is mostly known,
and some of it is very old. The question organizing this book is what it costs
for a distinction to come into being and stay, written into the step of a model of
computation, with certification, a record that a claim was checked, as its sharpest
case, and what’s mine in the answer isn’t one result. It’s four, and I name them the
same way wherever they come up. The toll derived from finiteness, permanence and
a price on merges (item 3; the counting is classical, the finite cousin of Zermelo’s
recurrence objection and folklore about permutation automata, and Ouldridge and
Wolpert already priced it in entropy for automata, so what’s mine is the toll a price on
merging moves gives for a reading that stays, after Li and Vitányi’s price per erased
bit and Demaine and his coauthors’ price on instructions, and the price is an abstract
premise motivated by Landauer’s reset). The pricing form of the window fact (item
6; the fact itself is elementary). The latch form of a record that never comes down
(item 8; latches and history variables are old). And a record that’s priced, and on the
small machine earned, under the reference monitor’s every-program move (items
10, 11 and 14; the move is Anderson’s, Schneider’s and the micro-policy authors’,
498   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               and what’s added is the check bound to its edition, the toll on top, a definition of
               Thiele-complete that a clock fails, over any base and any event, a certified refinement
               the small machine meets, and universal programs that carry the check and the toll
               to every small-machine program and to every computably presented Thiele machine,
               earning their own flag). Under all four sits item 1, which is old mathematics read
               one way: every step of every machine takes new room, merges, or goes round a loop,
               a merge in a coarse description is, in every finer description it is exact about, a fine
               merge, a fine step out of the set, or endless room, any step that changes something
               in a real device dissipates besides, and finiteness is what takes the room away. The
               first is a ledger form of a core that’s classical and already priced in physics; the
               second and third are small exact statements I didn’t find stated where I looked; the
               fourth is built, with its proofs on the page, and its idea isn’t new. The proofs connect
               those statements to one small machine and the programs that run on it. Around
               it is my best attempt at saying which is which, which you should check as hard as
               anything else in here. If someone shows me item 3’s ledger form, the pricing form
               in item 6, or item 8 stated earlier, I’ll move it up the list.
APPENDIX D




The universal machines

This appendix carries the two universal programs of Section 16 in full: U, which
runs every program of the small machine, and UP , which runs every computably
presented Thiele machine, with the simpler host that has the guest step built in, the
diagonal on the small machine’s programs, and exactly what the universal machines
cover.


D.1 One machine that runs them all
The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and
it pays for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for a
whole class of machines, the way Turing’s universal machine stands in for every
Turing machine. Here’s what I mean by that. A universal Thiele machine is one
fixed machine running one fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as
a guest, with every step of the guest’s computing done by the host’s own counter
moves and every rise of the host’s record put where the host’s program put it. No
program running on the host has to keep a convention for it. In full:

Definition D.1 (Universal Thiele machine). Fix a class C of Thiele machines, each
with its runs from given start states. A universal Thiele machine for C is a Thiele
machine H, the host, with one program P fixed for the whole class, a way to load
any guest M in C with any start s0 into a start state of H, and a way to read a guest’s
state off the host’s registers, such that: (1) H is Thiele-complete (Definition 10.6),
and its computing moves are its counter moves; (2) the run of P from the loaded
state halts exactly when M’s run from s0 stops, and then shows the observable part
of M’s last state, as the class names it, its reading, and its ledger up to the surcharge;
(3) the run passes, in order, through host states that show the observable part of
M’s states along its run, at which the host’s record equals M’s reading kept as a
latch and the host’s ledger equals M’s ledger plus a surcharge bounded by a number
fixed for the class; (4) the rise is the program’s: each record move either traps or
raises the record exactly when the line it sits on is one P marks as raising, from
every untrapped state, so nothing the move reads decides it; (5) H is a register
host: its counter moves are INC, DEC and HALT on registers, its record moves leave
the registers alone and go to the next line or trap, and which move comes next

                                                   499
500   D The universal machines


              depends only on the line and whether the trap is up; (6) each guest is loaded with
              the record down, no trap, a fixed line and the guest written into the registers, and
              the guest’s state is read off the registers in a coding fixed with the class, before
              any guest is named. A certified universal Thiele machine also has its host certified
              Thiele-complete with clean loads, and its record, whenever it’s up, standing on the
              host’s own check of the guest’s own justification, as the class supplies it.

                  For U the guest’s justification is its chain claim; for UP , the guest’s reading at a
              state of the run. For U the observable part I’ve proved it matches with all six clauses
              is the guest’s two counters, and in order it matches everything but the guest’s version
              numbers, which no run of the guest can show; for UP it’s the whole state.
                  The guest lives only in the loaded state; the machine and the program are fixed
              before any guest is named. For U the surcharge is zero; for UP it is at most two
              when the guest’s reading starts at no, and exactly three when it starts at yes, so
              three bounds it over the whole class. Both are certified universal Thiele machines,
              by the theorems of this appendix put together: each meets the six clauses, each host
              is certified Thiele-complete with clean loads, and each one’s flag stands on its own
              check of the guest’s justification.
                  The two that UP adds once a guest’s record is up is the price of certification,
              not of universality. A certified host raises its record from a clean load only after
              three marks, so on a guest that raises its reading for one mark it falls two behind
              at least. A host without certification can keep up exactly: on a host with registers,
              INC, DEC, HALT, a paid move TICK that always raises the record and a paid move
              PAY that never does, the program “count register 0 down to zero; TICK; HALT” runs
              the guests that count a pile down to zero and then raise their reading for one mark,
              each from its own pile, with surcharge zero. A guest whose reading is already yes at
              its start costs any host loaded with its record down at least one, and one is reached.
              Whether one host gets surcharge zero on every guest whose reading starts at no,
              across a universal class, is open; the best I’ve proved is two. (And PAY is needed on
              such a host: a guest that pays while its reading is down makes the host run a record
              move that doesn’t raise, which is what PAY is.)
                  Each clause stops something. For clauses (1), (4) and (5) there’s a host that
              meets the others and fails it; (2) and (3) together stop a host that ignores its guest;
              (6) I state in words below. Clause (1) stops a host that raises its record early and
              lowers it again before anyone looks. Clause (4) stops a mark that reads the registers,
              or a copy of the guest kept outside them, and raises when the guest would: the same
              move on the same line would raise from one state and not from another. Clause (5)
              stops a host with a move that takes one step of the guest. In the one I built that
              move costs no marks on the guest’s unpriced instructions and traps on its paid ones;
              costing no marks, it would have to be a counter move, and a counter move never
                                                                D.1 One machine that runs them all   501


traps. Charge such a move a mark instead and it’s a record move, which has to
leave the registers alone, so it can’t move the guest’s counters, which (6) puts there.
Clause (5) also stops a move at no marks that fetches, decodes and carries out a
guest instruction on the registers, because that move adds one to one register from
one state and to another register from another, which no single INC or DEC does.
Clause (6) makes the guest come in through the registers. It’s the one clause I’ve
stated in words without a theorem that it discriminates: a reading of the registers
that adds part of the guest back in isn’t excluded by anything I’ve proved. What
stops a host that ignores its guest is (2) and (3), on any class whose guests differ in
when they halt or what they record, which a universal class does. What the clauses
allow is exact too. By (1), (4) and (5), the line, the registers, the record and the
ledger of a run before any trap depend only on the line, registers and record it was
loaded with: each counter move acts on those alone, each record move leaves the
registers and moves the line, and its effect on the record is fixed by its line. So a
host may carry anything else along, even a copy of the guest that its counter moves
step, and that passenger can’t touch anything the host shows. One channel I haven’t
closed: a move that traps may read anything, and stopping the run is all it can do.
UP never traps on its class, so for it the channel is shut; for U it isn’t proved.
    None of this needs certification. UP ’s own program, read on a host with no
claims, no checker, no table and no channel, with CHECK, COMMIT and PAY read
as PAY and CERTIFY as TICK, meets (1) to (6) with the same surcharge: UP never
traps on its class, and while nothing traps the two hosts agree, step for step, on the
line, the registers, the record and the ledger. Certification adds the tie to the guest’s
own justification, and it needs (4) as much as anything: a host that carries out a
hidden copy’s own check, commit and certificate meets the tie and fails only (4) and
(5).
    And I want it the hard way. The easy way is to give the host a move that means
“take one step of the guest,” and then “it runs any guest” is true because I wrote it
that way. There’s a host like that two subsections on, after the two programs, and
it’s useful as a picture. It isn’t Turing’s kind of universal. Turing’s universal machine
has no instruction for “do what the machine on the tape would do.” It has the same
kind of instructions every other Turing machine has, and one fixed table, and the
table does the reading and the deciding and the carrying out. That’s the bar here,
and clauses (4) and (5) make it exact: one fixed program, every computing step
a counter move, every rise where the program put it, and anything else the host
carries unable to touch what it shows.
    Turing’s own explanation is worth having in your head, because the program
below copies its shape. In the 1936 paper the universal machine’s tape starts with
the machine to imitate, written out as a string of letters, its standard description, and
after it the imitated machine’s complete configurations, one after another: where its
502   D The universal machines


              head is, what state it’s in, what’s on its tape. To take one step, the universal machine
              finds the last configuration, looks through the description line by line, comparing,
              until it finds the line for that state and that symbol, and then writes out the next
              configuration the way that line says. Then it goes back and does it again. It leaves
              marks on squares so it doesn’t lose its place. Every bit of that is ordinary instructions
              on an ordinary tape, and nothing in its table knows any particular machine.
                 Turing’s universal program came first on paper, and one that people actually
              came to use arrived through the side door. John McCarthy, who had started the
              artificial intelligence project at MIT with Minsky, was writing up his new language
              Lisp around 1960 and wanted to show it was neater than Turing machines, so he
              wrote a universal function for it, eval, the language describing how to evaluate itself,
              and argued it was shorter and easier to follow than a universal Turing machine. In
              his own history of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing to read; the notation for
              writing programs as data was made up for the paper with no thought of using it in
              practice. Then Steve Russell (S. R. Russell in McCarthy’s account), a programmer
              on that MIT project, noticed that eval could serve as an interpreter and coded it
              by hand, and there was a running language with an interpreter that nobody had
              planned. McCarthy adds that the surprise froze some decisions he’d made “rather
              lightheartedly” for the paper. So the trick has a habit: written to be read, it ends up
              being run. The program below goes the other way round, on purpose. It’s written to
              run, and the proofs show that what runs is what the page says.
                 The host. The program runs on a machine with the small machine’s instructions
              and the small machine’s prices: INC, DEC, HALT at no marks, and CHECK, COMMIT,
              CERTIFY at one each, with the same table of sixteen facts, the same channel, trap,
              ledger and flag. One change: it has a counter for every whole number, each with its
              own version, where the small machine had two. No new kind of instruction, no new
              price. Take away the table, the channel and the flag and what’s left is old: a machine
              with as many registers as it needs, adding one, taking one away and jumping on
              zero, is the unlimited register machine of John Shepherdson and H. E. Sturgis, two
              logicians who proved in 1963 that such machines compute every partial recursive
              function.

              Definition D.2 (The host machine). The host machine is the machine of Defini-
              tion 15.3 with one change: it has a counter, with its version, for every whole number
              r (a register), and INC r, DEC r j, CHECK p r and COMMIT p r name one register
              each. Its property language has one property, Slot. Write ⟨m, n⟩ for the number
              (2n + 1) · 2m ; every positive number is ⟨m, n⟩ for exactly one pair, and 0 is no pair.
              Number the small machine’s properties Zero 7→ 0, Even 7→ 1, Ge(n) 7→ n + 2.
              The checker of Slot says yes at a value x exactly when x = ⟨m, v⟩ and the small
                                                             D.1 One machine that runs them all   503


machine’s checker says yes to the property numbered m at v; its meaning is the
same with holds in place of the checker.
    There’s one place the guest’s machine shows up in the host. The host’s single
property knows how to read the small machine’s three-word property language: “this
number is the pair (property, value) and the property holds of the value.” It doesn’t
know the small machine’s step. That’s the counter version of Turing’s universal
machine knowing the alphabet its guests write in.
    Two facts that force the design. Why more counters? Because of two facts, and
the program looks the way it does because of them.
    The first is about reading. On this machine a program that wants a counter’s
value in its own control flow has to take pebbles out (DEC) and put them back (INC),
and every INC, and every DEC on a counter above 0, is a write, so the counter’s
version goes up. A fact is about one version, so a read done that way kills every
live fact about the counter. Not every look is a write: CHECK reads a value without
writing it, a DEC on 0 changes no version, and a fresh CHECK after such a read can
make a new live fact. But the guest’s counters are exactly the ones the host has to
read by taking pebbles out, again and again, to decide which way a DEC jumps and
to work out a property’s answer, and each of those reads kills whatever fact was kept
there. So the host can’t keep the guest’s facts on its copies of the guest’s counters.
    The second says that even if reading wrote nothing, a fixed program couldn’t keep
them by sending each guest property to one of a fixed, finite list of host properties
and checking it on the same register the guest’s fact is about. That’s all the theorem
below rules out, and it’s the pigeonhole.


Theorem D.1 (No host fact on an exact copy of the guest’s counter). Take any host
property language with an exact equality test and any checker, a finite list Q of host
properties, and any translation of the small machine’s properties into members of
Q whose host check passes whenever the guest’s check passes on the same number.
Then there are n ̸= m, with Ge(n) and Ge(m) translated to the same host property,
such that the guest program CHECK Ge(n) A; COMMIT Ge(m) A traps within two
steps from every start, while on every host state with the trap down and room in
its table, and some register holding a number at least n, the translated CHECK and
COMMIT on that register both pass and put the committed claim in the channel.

Proof. A fixed program mentions finitely many properties, so Q is finite, and the
translation sends the infinitely many Ge(0), Ge(1), . . . into it: two of them land on
the same member. The guest’s COMMIT asks for Ge(m), and its table can only hold
Ge(n), so it traps (or its CHECK already trapped). The host sees one property twice:
504   D The universal machines


              its CHECK passes, since the guest’s would, and its COMMIT finds exactly what that
              CHECK wrote.
                  So the host keeps the guest’s facts somewhere else: in slots, extra registers
              used for nothing but holding facts, one per checked fact, each holding the pair
              (property number, value) that the guest checked. The pigeonhole doesn’t bite a slot,
              because the property lives in the slot’s number. The instruction doesn’t have to carry
              it: CHECK Slot on a slot asks about whatever pair is sitting there, and there are
              infinitely many pairs. A slot’s number changes only when the program is moving a
              fact into it. And when the guest writes the counter a fact was about, the program
              gives every slot about that counter a nudge, one INC and one DEC, which leaves the
              number alone and pushes the version up, so the host’s facts go stale at exactly the
              moment the guest’s do.
                  Do one slot by hand. The property “even” has number 1. Checking it on value 4
              puts ⟨1, 4⟩ = (2 · 4 + 1)21 = 18 in a separate slot. To read that pair, halve 18 until
              what’s left is odd: one halving gives 9, so the property number is 1; subtract one
              from 9 and halve to recover value 4. The host checks that property of that value. A
              second card, the mirror, says 2: the property number plus one. COMMIT can read
              this second card while leaving the checked slot untouched.
                  When the guest changes the counter that fact concerned, nudge the slot 18 →
              19 → 18 and set the mirror to zero. The number is back where it was, but the
              version went up twice, so the host’s old fact about that slot is stale. Putting a number
              back doesn’t put an old check back. The mirror is what tells the search to leave that
              slot alone, and if the search tried it anyway, the version rule would refuse it.
                  The program. Here’s U the way Turing would describe it, one register at a time
              and then one job at a time. Registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and B. Register 2
              holds the guest’s whole program as one number: each instruction gets a number
              (an opcode paired with its operands, INC as 0, DEC as 1, HALT as 2, CHECK as 3,
              COMMIT as 4, CERTIFY as 5), and the list of them is packed with ⟨·, ·⟩, the empty
              list as 0. Register 3 is the guest’s line. Registers 4 to 13 are scratch. Registers 14 and
              15 count how many CHECKs on A and on B have passed. Registers 16 to 47 are
              mirrors, sixteen for each guest counter, and registers 48 to 79 are the slots, sixteen
              for each guest counter. The guest’s table holds sixteen facts in total, across both
              counters, and all sixteen can be about one counter, so the host gives each counter
              room for all of them. That’s a host reservation, and the guest’s own capacity stays
              sixteen in all. Register 80 is a dead end that’s never written.
                  Each guest step goes like this. At line 1 the program copies the program number
              and the guest’s line into scratch, putting the originals back as it goes, because
              copying a counter on this machine means emptying it into two others and refilling
              it. If the guest’s line is 0, or past the end of the program, it stops. Otherwise it peels
                                                                 D.1 One machine that runs them all   505


instructions off the front of the copy, one per line, until it holds the one at the guest’s
line, and splits that into opcode and operands. Then a chain of DECs on the opcode
sends it to one of six handlers.
• INC c: INC the guest’s counter c, nudge every slot about c and zero its mirrors,
  add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.
• DEC c j: DEC the guest’s counter c. If it was 0, add one to the guest’s line. If it
  wasn’t, nudge every slot about c, zero its mirrors, and set the guest’s line to j.
  Back to line 1.
• HALT: stop.
• CHECK p c: let k be the count of passed CHECKs on c. If k is below 16, build
  ⟨number of p, value of c⟩ in slot k of c, run CHECK Slot on that slot, set its mirror
  to the number of p plus one, add one to the count and to the guest’s line, and go
  back to line 1. If k is 16, run CHECK Slot on the dead end, which holds 0, which
  is no pair, so it traps, just as the guest’s seventeenth CHECK does.
• COMMIT p c: look through the sixteen mirrors of c for one equal to the number
  of p plus one. At the first match, run COMMIT Slot on that slot. With no match,
  run COMMIT Slot on the dead end, which traps.
• CERTIFY: run CERTIFY, add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.
    Why the mirrors? COMMIT has to find the slot holding the claim, and it can’t
read the slot to find out, because reading would make the fact stale. So beside
every slot sits a mirror the program is allowed to read: the property’s number plus
one while the slot’s fact is live, 0 once the guest has written the counter. If a guest
CHECK fails its property, the host’s CHECK on the slot fails too, since the slot holds
exactly the pair the guest checked. If the guest table is full across both counters, the
host’s own sixteen-entry table is full as well, even when this counter’s slot count is
below sixteen; its CHECK then traps for lack of room. So both kinds of refusal come
through.
    Count what costs anything. Fetching, unpacking, copying, nudging, branching:
all INC and DEC, all at zero marks, the way computing is on the small machine.
The only paid instructions are the CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY sites, and each
guest CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY makes the program run exactly one of them.
So the host’s ledger lands on the guest’s, mark for mark. And when the guest’s flag
goes up, the host’s goes up by the host’s own CERTIFY, standing on the host’s own
COMMIT and CHECK on a slot. It isn’t copying a bit. It runs the same chain on its
own registers.
506   D The universal machines


              Definition D.3 (The program U, and loading a guest). U is the fixed list of 3728
              host instructions specified by the block expansions in Appendix L, starting at line
              1 and mentioning registers 0 to 80; exactly 69 of them cost anything. For a guest
              program P and a start ( x, y), the loaded host hload( P, x, y) has register 0 at x,
              register 1 at y, register 2 at the number of P, register 3 at 1 and every other register
              at 0, every version 0, line 1, an empty table and channel, the trap down, ledger
              0 and flag down. Write grun(m) for m program steps of P from start( x, y), and
              hrun(n) for n program steps of U from hload( P, x, y).



              Theorem D.2 (U keeps pace with its guest). For every guest program P, start ( x, y)
              and number of guest steps m, there’s a number of host steps n such that one of
              two things holds. Either the host is back at line 1 with m ≤ n and related to the
              guest: registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and B, register 3 holds the guest’s line,
              the guest’s trap is down, the two ledgers are equal, the two flags are equal, and the
              host’s table and channel hold, fact for fact, slot facts matching the guest’s facts and
              channel. Or both have stopped, with the same counters, the same trap, the same
              ledger, the same flag, and matching tables and channels. And from any related pair
              where the guest hasn’t stopped, one guest step is matched by at least one host step
              that lands related again, or with both stopped.

              Proof. The one-step part is a case for each thing the guest can do at its line: stop;
              INC; DEC, taken or not; CHECK, passing, failing, or with a full table; COMMIT,
              found or not; CERTIFY, passing or not. The block invariants and the case analysis
              in Appendix L show where each matching stretch lands. The relation carries the
              bookkeeping that makes the next case go through: each count register equals the
              number of slots in use for its counter, each slot in use holds (property number,
              checked value), a slot’s fact is current exactly when the matching guest fact is, a live
              slot’s mirror is the property’s number plus one and a stale one’s is 0, and unused
              slots, unused mirrors and the dead end are 0. A freshly loaded host is related to the
              guest’s start. The run statement is induction on m.



              Theorem D.3 (Halting and answers match). For every P, x and y, the guest’s run
              of P from start( x, y) halts if and only if U’s run from hload( P, x, y) halts. And
              whenever the guest has halted at step m and U at step n, the host’s registers 0 and 1
              hold the guest’s A and B, and the two traps, the two ledgers and the two flags are
              equal.
                                                                D.1 One machine that runs them all   507


Proof. Theorem D.2: a halted guest is matched by a stopped host, and a host that
has stopped can’t be back at line 1 with the guest still running, because line 1 isn’t
a stop. A halted machine stays halted, so the two halting points carry the same
values.



Theorem D.4 (The host’s flag is the guest’s, and its ledger is exact). (1) The guest’s
flag is up at some step of its run if and only if the host’s flag is up at some step of
U’s run. (2) For every m there’s an n at which the two are related, with m ≤ n, or
both stopped, with µ(hrun(n)) = µ(grun(m)). And for every n there’s an m with
µ(grun(m)) ≤ µ(hrun(n)) ≤ µ(grun(m + 1)): in between matching points, the
host’s ledger never gets ahead of the guest’s next step.

Proof. (1) Flags are equal at matching points and never come down. (2) Ledgers
are equal at matching points; inside the stretch of U that runs one guest instruction,
at most the one paid site of that instruction runs, so the host’s ledger sits between
the guest’s before and after it.
    That’s a third sense of “exact,” and it’s the plainest of the three (Section 15 names
all three): two ledgers, one number.


Theorem D.5 (The host earns its own flag). If the host’s flag is up after n steps of
U from hload( P, x, y), then the instructions U executed contain, in order, a passing
CHECK Slot on a slot, then a passing COMMIT Slot on the same slot, with the slot
untouched and its version unchanged in between, then a passing CERTIFY; the slot
held ⟨number of p, v⟩ at the CHECK, with holds( p, v). And the guest’s own run from
start( x, y) contains a passing CHECK p c, then, with c untouched and its version
unchanged, a passing COMMIT p c, then a passing CERTIFY, with c holding v at its
CHECK.

Proof. By Theorem D.4 the guest’s flag rises too; find the guest step where it rises, a
passing CERTIFY, and the related host point just before it. The guest’s channel there
names a fact, and the relation says the host’s channel names the matching slot fact.
The host’s own flag rises at its own first passing CERTIFY, and nothing paid runs
between the related point and that CERTIFY, so the host’s channel hasn’t moved: it
names that slot fact. The host machine’s version of Theorem 15.9 gives the host’s
CHECK and COMMIT on that slot. The record kept with the slot says what pair it
held and when, and the checker’s meaning gives holds( p, v). The same theorem
508   D The universal machines


              on the guest’s run, up to the step where its flag rose, gives the guest’s chain on the
              same p and c, and the record says c held v at its CHECK.



              Theorem D.6 (The host is certified Thiele-complete, and U’s halting is undecidable).
              (1) The host machine, with Slot as its property and one move per instruction, is
              certified Thiele-complete (Definition 15.7), and certified Thiele-complete over its
              own claim language, whose claims are “Slot holds of register r,” whose meanings
              are written without the host’s checker, and whose “unchanged” is “same value and
              same version of register r”; and U’s run from hload( P, x, y) is a run of it. (2) Read
              as a Thiele machine it obeys the universal floor; a run of U that raises the host’s flag
              costs at least 3 there. The system built from its certified Thiele-completeness agrees
              with it step for step and cost for cost, so the same run costs at least 3 on that one
              too, and the universal floor of 1 holds there directly. (3) U halts from hload( P, x, y)
              exactly when P halts from start( x, y), so the question “does U halt from this loaded
              host?” is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.4.

              Proof. (1) The base is registers 0 and 1, run by INC and DEC; the claims are “Slot
              holds of register r”; the rest is the host machine’s own versions of the small machine’s
              theorems, and for non-vacuity, register 0 loaded with 1, which is ⟨0, 0⟩, the pair
              of Zero and 0, against register 0 loaded with 0, which is no pair. Over the claim
              language the interface is the same one, with the meanings handed over by the
              language. (2) is Theorem 15.26(4) and Theorem D.5. (3) is Theorem D.3, and
              the loading map reduces the small machine’s halting question, undecidable by
              Theorem 15.4, to this one.
                  Put it together, plainly. One fixed program, 3728 instructions of the small
              machine’s six kinds, with no guest step built into anything, runs every program of
              the small machine from every clean start start( x, y). It halts exactly when its guest
              halts, with the guest’s answer in its first two registers. Its flag goes up at some step
              of its run exactly when the guest’s goes up at some step of the guest’s run, by its own
              check, its own commit and its own certificate. Its ledger is the guest’s, mark for mark,
              wherever the two line up. And the machine it runs on is certified Thiele-complete.
              Since the small machine runs every two-counter program, through those guests U
              runs every computation, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine.
              That’s the universal Thiele machine of this book, for the small machine’s programs;
              the next subsection carries it to every computably presented Thiele machine whose
              reading a program decides on every state.
                  The fine print, before you take that anywhere. The guests start clean, from
              start( x, y); the whole-run theorems are about loaded hosts, and only the one-step
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  509

theorem is about any related pair. The host’s property reads the small machine’s
three-word language, so a guest with a different property language needs a different
host property; the host of the next subsection has one, a single property that reads a
universal claim language. Sixteen slots per counter is the guest’s whole table size,
reserved for each counter in case every fact is about that one. And it’s slow: for
every guest step it unpacks the program number from the front again, and it copies
a number one pebble at a time. That’s where the running time in Appendix G comes
from. The theorems above say nothing about time; they match states and ledgers at
the points where the two line up.
    Enforcement in the step is the reference monitor’s move from Section 14, An-
derson’s 1972 move: one mechanism everything has to pass through. What’s put
together here is a priced, earned record under that move, carried to every guest by
one fixed program. The move itself is Anderson’s. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett
and Fred Schneider (2006) worked out, in their model, which policies mechanisms
like that can enforce at all, and their paper is where I’d go to see why enforcing a
property of every run escapes the Rice-style walls that deciding one runs into.
    Why make such a fuss about proofs that walk every case? Because the first
universal machine had bugs. It’s the machine in Turing’s 1936 paper, and nobody
gets to call Turing careless. In 1947 Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a
problem of Thue, pointed out that the construction leaned on a convention it hadn’t
earned, and he patched a small defect in how the universal machine writes out
each complete configuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined
the National Physical Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer,
worked through the universal machine’s tables and found more mistakes, much to
Turing’s annoyance, as the accounts of Davies’s life have it. (It’s the same Davies who
later named the packet in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed
in a collection edited by Jack Copeland, a philosopher and historian of computing
who runs an archive of Turing’s papers, The Essential Turing, in 2004. They may be
some of the first bugs ever written, in a program for a computer that didn’t exist
yet. That’s a lovely claim, and I haven’t been able to confirm it, so take it as a lead.
What it changes here: a universal machine is exactly the kind of construction where
a careful person leaves a hole, U has 3728 lines for a hole to hide in, and each case
of its simulation argument has to hold. The definitions are on the page so you can
examine what those cases establish.


D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided,
    priced in whole units, carried as a latch
U runs the small machine’s programs, and through them every computation, under
Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine. But a Thiele machine from
510   D The universal machines


              somewhere else has its own states, its own moves, its own prices and its own
              reading, and running it through the two-counter encoding keeps its computation
              and nothing else. So the question Turing’s machine raises for this book is the bigger
              one. Take any Thiele machine whose workings can be computed. Is there one fixed
              program that runs every such machine as a guest, keeping its halting, raising its own
              flag exactly when the guest’s reading would rise, on an earned chain of its own, and
              keeping a ledger equal to the guest’s own prices, with the host’s flat ones nowhere
              in it? There is, within limits I’ll list, and here it is.
                  First the class, said plainly. A computably presented Thiele machine is a Thiele
              machine in Section 2’s sense (states, moves, a step, a price for each move, a yes/no
              reading, and the toll: a move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one)
              together with a driver that picks the next move from the current state or says stop,
              and a way of writing states and moves as whole numbers. “Computably” means four
              little programs, written in the plainest language of computable functions there is,
              the one built from zero, plus one, picking an argument, composing, recursion and
              search: one computes the driver, one the step, one the price, and one the reading,
              and each of the four halts on every input: the driver with a move or stop, the step
              with a state, the price with a whole number, and the reading with yes or no. Run
              from a start s0 , the driver’s moves give one run. Its ledger after n moves is the sum
              of their prices, and its latch after n moves says whether the reading has been yes at
              any state so far.
                  The host gets one thing the small machine doesn’t have: a paid move that certifies
              nothing. On the small machine every charge comes from a CHECK, a COMMIT or a
              CERTIFY, and those can bill without raising the flag: one passing CHECK and six
              COMMITs of the same claim cost seven. But every passing CHECK takes one of the
              table’s sixteen entries for good, every COMMIT rewrites the channel, and a failing
              CHECK traps. So the host machine gets a seventh instruction kind, PAY: it costs one,
              goes to the next line, and changes nothing else; it never raises the flag, takes no
              table entry and leaves the channel alone. That’s why the compiler uses it.
                  How far the small machine gets without it is proved, and the count is short. Take
              a run that never traps and ends with the flag down. No CERTIFY ran in it, since a
              passing one raises the flag and a failing one traps. Every CHECK in it passed, since a
              failing one traps, and each passing CHECK filled one of the table’s sixteen entries, so
              there were at most sixteen. Every COMMIT in it committed a claim the table holds,
              and the table holds at most sixteen, so at most sixteen COMMITs can be of claims
              the run hadn’t committed before. That’s 32, and the only way past it is a COMMIT
              of a claim already committed earlier in the run. A claim names its counter’s version,
              and the version changes at every write, so a repeat needs its counter left alone
              since the earlier COMMIT. A guest that writes both counters between any two of its
              payments can’t do that, so it runs out of ways to pay after 32. And 32 is reached:
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  511

sixteen rounds of CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A; INC A pay 32 with
no trap and the flag down. A guest that writes both counters at every move of the
machine it simulates needs a fresh CHECK for each move it pays for, so it can pay
for at most sixteen of them. A simulated machine that bills more often than that
has to bill somewhere, and PAY is where. The 32 is a fact about the small machine,
with its two counters. The host has a counter for every whole number, and on it the
count doesn’t hold: a program that checks one fact about a counter it never writes
can commit that fact again and again, a mark each, for as long as it likes, with the
flag down and no trap, because the counter’s version never changes. So on the host
the 32 isn’t a ceiling. Whether UP can run its class without PAY I haven’t settled:
those repeated commits overwrite the channel, and UP ’s certificates read it. On a
host without certification PAY is a necessity: a guest that pays while its reading is
down makes the host run a paid move that doesn’t raise its record.
    Read as a Thiele-complete machine, the host needs no filing at all: PAY is a mark
that never raises the record. The definition of certified Thiele-complete sorts every
paid move into CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY, so PAY has to be filed under one of
them, and it’s filed as a CHECK of the empty claim, a claim that never holds. That’s
a filing for the interface. It isn’t what PAY does on the machine: a CHECK that fails
on this machine traps, and PAY goes on to the next line. With PAY filed that way
the host stays certified Thiele-complete, and certified Thiele-complete over its own
claim language, in which the empty claim holds of no state. PAY costs exactly one,
as clause (c) asks of a CHECK; its check never passes, so it can’t stand in a chain;
and it leaves the table, the channel and the flag alone, so it can’t add to a chain or
raise the flag either. For the same reason the floor of three for a flag raised from a
clean start still holds with PAY present: the flag still needs a CHECK, a COMMIT and
a CERTIFY.
    The program is U with one more handler: a seventh branch on the guest’s opcode,
for PAY, that runs the host’s own PAY once. Call it UP ; it’s 3735 instructions, with
70 paid sites, the 69 of U plus the PAY. The guest it runs is a program of the small
machine with PAY added, and that guest is where the presented machine goes. Its
four programs are compiled into two counters, by the packing Minsky used, using
the translations of Appendix K from computable functions to counter programs; the
guest keeps the presented machine’s state coded in its counter B, takes one of its
moves by running the compiled driver and step, runs the compiled reading on the
new state, and pays the move’s price in PAYs; the first time the reading says yes, it
checks, commits and certifies, and those three marks count toward that move’s price.
The host’s one property is fixed too: a claim is either one of the small machine’s
three words about a number, or “run reading program r on the coded state v,” and
the host’s checker evaluates that with one fixed routine for every presented machine
512   D The universal machines


              there is. So nothing in UP knows any particular presented machine. The machine
              arrives as data, the way Turing’s guests arrived on the tape.
                  A fixed checker that runs whatever program it’s handed and always answers
              needs saying how, so here is the routine. A claim of the second kind carries a number
              r. The checker decodes r as a counter-machine routine: its instructions, where they
              sit, which register holds the answer, which register holds the fuel, and how many
              registers to load. If r doesn’t decode to a routine, the answer is no. Otherwise the
              checker loads the routine’s registers from v, reads a fuel number f out of v too (the
              fuel register’s entry in v’s prime factorisation), runs the routine for at most f steps,
              and says yes exactly when by then the routine has left its code with 1 in its answer
              register. Every input gets an answer within f steps, so the checker is total, and what
              it means is that bounded run: yes if and only if the routine halts within the fuel
              the value carries, with answer 1. That’s how it stays clear of the diagonal. A total
              evaluator E that agreed with every total yes-or-no program on that program’s code
              alone would let g(n) = ¬ E(n, n) contradict itself at its own code, as long as E is
              itself computable. This checker never evaluates a program on its code alone: the
              fuel comes with the claim’s value. The guest compiled from M runs M’s reading
              routine itself and puts at least the step count it took into the fuel register, and at
              such a value the checker says yes if and only if the reading says yes.
                  For the fuel rule, take a routine containing just one instruction: increment an
              answer register initially holding 0, then leave its one-line code. Give it fuel 0 and
              the check says no: it has not completed. Give it fuel 1 and the check says yes: it
              has left the code with answer 1. The first no did not mean the routine would never
              answer yes. It meant “not within this allowance.” You can run that distinction with
              a pebble and one instruction card. The real checker does the same job for any list of
              instructions, with the allowance handed in alongside the claim.


              Theorem D.7 (One host runs every computably presented Thiele machine). Let
              M be a computably presented Thiele machine, so that a driver picks its next move
              (one run per start), a program decides its reading on every state, and its prices are
              whole numbers; and let s0 be a start state. Load UP with the guest compiled from
              M’s presentation and s0 coded in. What the host carries of M’s reading is its latch.
              Then: (1) UP halts exactly when M’s run stops. (2) For every n such that M hasn’t
              stopped before move n, there’s a host time t at which the host’s register for the
              guest’s counter B decodes to M’s state after n moves, the host’s ledger is M’s ledger
              after n moves plus a surcharge, and the host’s flag is M’s latch after n moves; and
              if M stops at n, such a t has UP halted as well. (3) The host’s flag is up at some
              time exactly when M’s reading is yes at some state of its run. (4) If the host’s flag is
              up at time t, the host’s own instructions up to t contain a passing CHECK on a slot,
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  513

then a passing COMMIT on the same slot with the slot untouched in between, then
a passing CERTIFY; and the slot held the claim “reading program r says yes of v” for
M’s own reading program r, that claim holds, and v decodes to a state of M’s run
where the reading is yes.

Proof. Two layers, each proved on its own. The bottom layer is the compiler: for
every presented machine, its guest program’s run passes through points that code
M’s states in order, with the guest’s ledger equal to M’s ledger plus the surcharge
and the guest’s flag equal to M’s latch, and the guest’s own flag stands on an earned
chain whose claim is M’s reading program applied to the coded state where the
reading first said yes. Here is why. The guest keeps a few registers packed into its
counters the way Minsky packed them: the coded state, a latch bit, the price still
owed, and a register that counts the reading’s steps. It starts at the reading with
nothing owed, and goes round one loop. Run the compiled reading on the coded
state, counting its steps. If it says yes and the latch bit is 0, run CHECK, COMMIT
and CERTIFY on the claim “reading program r says yes of v,” v being the packed
registers with the step count as fuel, set the latch bit, and take three off what’s owed,
stopping at zero. Pay what’s owed in PAYs. Run the compiled driver, and halt if it
says stop. Otherwise run the compiled step and price for the move it picked, put
the new coded state and that price in place, and go round again. Everything but
the PAYs and the one chain is INC and DEC, at no marks. So at the point just after
the PAYs and before the driver runs, once n moves have been made, the coded state
is M’s state after n moves, the latch bit is M’s latch, and the ledger is M’s ledger,
except that the move where the latch bit was set was paid with the chain’s three
and the larger of c − 3 and 0 in PAYs instead of its price c (or, if the reading is yes at
s0 , the start was charged the chain’s three). The CHECK passes, because the fuel is
the reading’s own step count, and at such a value the fixed checker says what the
reading says; the COMMIT finds that fact, since nothing wrote B in between; and
the latch bit lets the chain run once. The top layer is UP , proved the way U was in
the previous theorems, with the PAY case added: it keeps pace with any guest of
this kind, halting and flag matched, ledger equal at matching points, and its flag
earned on a slot. Compose the two. The earned part takes one more step: the host’s
chain gives a guest CHECK that passed, and a guest run that ends with its flag up
has exactly one passing CHECK, the compiler’s CHECK of the reading on counter
B. So the guest CHECK the host’s chain points to is that one, and its claim is M’s
reading at the first state where it said yes.
   Two things the theorem doesn’t say. First, the host’s flag is M’s latch. If M’s
reading says yes at some state and no at a later one, the host’s flag stays up, so it
says the reading was yes somewhere in the run, and it doesn’t say the reading is
yes now. Second, what the host re-establishes is the reading: the claim it checked
514   D The universal machines


              is “M’s reading program says yes of this coded state,” and that’s all. A bare Thiele
              machine needn’t tie its reading to anything true about sorting, proofs or the world
              outside. If M’s reading is meant to say a list is sorted, that it does is a separate
              correctness theorem about the reading, and the host doesn’t supply it. The two
              universal programs also keep their own guests: U runs the small machine’s programs
              over its three words about numbers, and UP runs computably presented machines
              over the universal claim language.
                  Now the surcharge, because that’s where the ledger stops being exact, and below
              three marks it can’t be helped. The host raises its flag the only way the host machine
              allows, by a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and those cost three. If M’s first
              move that turns its reading to yes costs at least three, the host pays the difference in
              PAYs and nothing more is owed. If it costs less, the host pays three there anyway,
              which is the larger of three and the move’s price. The surcharge starts at that move:
              while M’s latch is down it’s zero, so a run that never certifies is matched exactly.
              Whether anything could do better depends on what M paid before. When M’s whole
              ledger at the raise is below three, no program on the host machine can match it,
              since a raised host flag costs three from a clean start. When M’s ledger at the raise
              is three or more, nothing here says this compiler’s surcharge is the least possible:
              part (1) of the theorem below bounds this compiler, and part (3) is the only lower
              bound proved.
                  Keep two tally lines for a guest whose first three moves each cost one and whose
              reading first says yes after the third. The guest’s totals are 1, 2, 3. This compiler
              pays one PAY on each of the first two moves, then its three-act chain: the host totals
              are 1, 2, 5. The excess is two, added once. If the third move instead costs four, the
              host runs the chain and one PAY there; both totals then read 6. These are counts of
              charged instructions, not counts of all the work needed to decode the guest.


              Theorem D.8 (Exact, within two, and no better). Let M, s0 and the loaded host
              be as in Theorem D.7, and let M’s reading be no at s0 . (1) For every n before M
              stops there’s a host time at which the host’s ledger lies between M’s ledger after n
              moves and that plus two, with the state decoded and the flag matched as before.
              (2) If moreover every move that first turns M’s reading to yes costs at least three,
              the surcharge is zero and the host’s ledger equals M’s exactly at those times. (3)
              If M’s latch is up after n moves while its ledger is below three, then no run of the
              host machine from a clean start, under any program at all, ends with its flag equal
              to that latch and its ledger raised by exactly M’s ledger. (4) If instead M’s reading
              is yes at s0 , then at the host time matching each move n before M stops, the host’s
              ledger is M’s ledger after n moves plus exactly three.
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  515

Proof. (1) and (2): the guest pays M’s prices in PAYs, a unit at a time, except at the
move where M’s reading first says yes. There it has to run its CHECK, COMMIT
and CERTIFY, three units, and it makes up the rest of the move’s price in PAYs, so it
pays the larger of the price c and three. The price is at least one, because the move
raised a reading (the toll), so the excess is at most two, and none when c ≥ 3. (3):
a raised flag on the host machine costs at least three from a clean start, whatever
the program, and M’s ledger is less. (4): the guest finds the reading yes before M
has made a move, runs its CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY there, three units on top
of a ledger of nothing, and from then on its flag is up, so the reading never first says
yes again and every move’s price is paid in PAYs, exactly.
   Part (3) is an observation in the sense of Section 2: it reads off Observation 15.16,
which holds on the host machine with PAY for the reason given above. Part (4) is
the same three paid at once: if the reading is already yes at the start, the host has to
raise its flag before M has paid anything, and no program can do better, since M’s
ledger at that point is nothing.
   And one machine carried all the way, by proof, so the class isn’t empty. Its states
are whole numbers, its one move adds one and costs three, its driver always picks
that move, and its reading is “at least three.” The driver returns the fixed move;
the step adds one; the price returns three; and the reading compares the state with
three. The counter constructions in Appendix K implement all four. Loaded into UP
from 0, the host never halts, its flag goes up, at the host time matching move n its
ledger is exactly 3n and its flag is up exactly when n ≥ 3, and the raised flag stands
on a host chain whose slot claims the machine’s own reading of a state at least three.
That follows from the two theorems above: the reading is no at 0, and the one move
that turns it to yes, from 2 to 3, costs three, so part (2) of the surcharge theorem
makes the ledger exact.
   Now the limits, each of which is in the statement, said plainly.
• Readings that are decided. The reading’s program has to answer yes or no on
  every state. A reading a program could only confirm, waiting forever on the no
  cases, isn’t covered, and neither is a reading no program computes at all.
• One run per start. The driver picks the move, so the guest is deterministic. A
  machine whose next move is somebody’s free choice gets in only with that choice
  written into its driver.
• The record is the latch. The host’s flag is up once M’s reading has been yes at
  any state of the run, which is exactly the latch of Section 10. A reading that goes
  yes and then back to no is carried as “it was yes once.”
• The ledger is exact up to the surcharge. When the reading starts at no, at most
  two, and zero when the first raising move costs three or more; when it starts at
516   D The universal machines


                 yes, three. And no program on this host, run from a clean start, can do better
                 when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three.
               • Prices in whole units, paid one at a time. A move that costs a million is a
                 million PAYs. The compiler also uses Minsky’s packing. Between them, those two
                 choices set how long the host takes to pay the guest’s bill.
               • Proved; never run on a presented machine. The demonstration machine’s
                 numbers come from the two theorems above. UP itself has run on guests small
                 enough to finish; a presented machine’s compiled guest is far too large for that,
                 and nobody has run UP on one. Appendix G says what was run.


              D.3 A simpler host, with the guest step built in

              There’s a much simpler host than U, and I keep it in the book because it’s easy to
              read and it shows the copy rule in one line. Its universality is by construction: it has
              a move that runs one guest step by calling the small machine’s own step. It isn’t a
              universal Thiele machine in the sense of Definition D.1, and the reasons are exact. It
              never halts, since it has no HALT and its guest step never traps; its surcharge grows
              without bound, since it charges a mark even for a guest step that costs nothing; and
              it isn’t a register host, since its guest step does the computing. A host that fixed the
              first two and kept the built-in step would still fail the last (the argument after the
              definition). U is the universal Thiele machine of this book. Read it as a picture of
              what U does the long way, and as a host that starts from any guest state at all, clean
              or not.
                  It carries a guest inside its own state: the guest’s program as data, the guest’s
              counters, its table, its ledger, its flag. The host has one extra move, run one guest
              step. In that one move it looks at the guest’s flag, takes the step, looks again, and if
              the flag went from down to up, the host’s own copy of that flag goes up in the same
              move, and the host pays for it.

              Definition D.4 (The host). A guest is a program P of the small machine together
              with a state g of it (Definition 15.2). A host state h has six parts: its own core
              core(h), its ledger µ(h), its own flag own(h), the guest program P(h) held as a
              list of instructions, the guest state g(h), and the mirror m(h), a yes/no copy of
              the guest’s flag. The host has two kinds of move. OWN i runs the instruction i
              on the host’s own core, costs what the small machine charges for i, and raises
              own exactly when that machine’s flag would rise. GSTEP b costs b. If the host’s
              core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to its next line
              and, if the guest’s next instruction costs at most b, runs that instruction on g(h);
              in the same move the mirror becomes m(h) ∨ (¬cert( g(h)) ∧ cert( g′ )), where g′ is
              the new guest state. The host’s reading is own(h) ∨ m(h). Its stored program is
                                                      D.3 A simpler host, with the guest step built in   517


U0 = [GSTEP 1; OWN (INC A); OWN (DEC A 1)]: one guest step, then two moves
that bring the host back to its first line.
    Every instruction of the small machine costs at most one, so GSTEP 1 runs every
guest instruction there is. Why charge the budget b? Why not the cost of whatever
instruction got fetched? Because charging the budget keeps the price a function of
the move alone, which is what the definition of Section 2 asks for: you read the
price of a host move off the move, the way you read the small machine’s prices off
its table, without peeking inside the guest. The bill for that is easy to see. A host
that steps a guest instruction priced 0, an INC say, still pays one mark for the move.
    So the host’s ledger is closer to a clock than to a receipt for its guests: one unit
per guest step, whatever the step was. It never falls behind the guest’s own bill
(part (3) of Theorem D.11 below), and it matches that bill only when every guest
step happens to cost one. Could a cleverer host have simulation-exact accounting,
a ledger equal to its guest’s? Not with this one fixed-price move: GSTEP 1 is the
same move whether the guest’s next instruction is an INC priced 0 or a paid CHECK,
so one price can’t match both. Some other built-in step, with more moves or a
price that looks at the state, might; I haven’t ruled that out. U gets the match with
ordinary instructions: it pays only on the record moves it runs itself, so its ledger
equals its guest’s (Theorem D.4).
    And one thing about the definition before the theorems, so you know which of
them carry weight. GSTEP runs the guest’s instruction by calling the small machine’s
own step on the guest’s state: the guest’s step is a primitive of the host. So “the
host runs any guest” (Theorem D.9) is true by construction. The host was built to
do exactly that, and the proof is mostly unfolding. The theorems with something
in them come after it. From a loaded host, or any state where the two agree,
the mirror always equals the guest’s flag (Observation D.10). Nothing raises the
mirror unless the guest itself passes a CERTIFY inside a guest step the host paid for
(Theorem D.12). No OWN move, in any host program at all, touches the guest’s
state or the mirror (the second sentence of that same theorem), and no host move
of either kind rewrites the guest’s program. And the mirror is tied to the guest’s
earned chain: after any host run from a loaded host, if the mirror is up, the guest’s
own run from its start contains a passing CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same
claim, then a CERTIFY, since the mirror is the guest’s flag and the guest started clean
(Theorem 15.9). So this host runs any small-machine program by construction and
keeps the guest’s record by theorem, as a copy of the guest’s flag. The mirroring
program U0 does not earn the host’s own flag; a different program could do so with
the host’s OWN CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. U does both the long way: it runs
the guest with its own instructions, and it earns its own flag.
518   D The universal machines




              Theorem D.9 (The host runs any guest). (1) If the host’s core is not trapped, then
              after n moves GSTEP 1 the guest state is the guest program’s own run of n steps
              from g(h), the guest program is unchanged, and the host is still not trapped. (2) If
              the host’s core is at line 1 and not trapped, then 3n steps of the program U0 leave
              the guest exactly where n steps of its own program put it. (3) For every two-counter
              program M and inputs a, b: M halts from (1, a, b) exactly when the host program
              made of OWN moves of the compiled M halts, from a host whose core starts at
              ( a, b), whatever guest that host carries.

              Proof. (1) Induction on n: a host that isn’t trapped stays untrapped through a guest
              step, and with budget 1 the guest step is the guest’s own step. (2) One pass of U0 is
              a guest step, then INC A and DEC A back to line 1, so it is (1) once per pass. (3)
              A host program made only of OWN moves is the small machine, core for core, and
              Theorem 15.3 does the rest.
              Observation D.10 (The copy is the record). Say a host state h agrees when m(h) =
              cert( g(h)). Every host move takes an agreeing state to an agreeing state, so every host
              trace and every stored host program does too, and a freshly loaded host agrees. In
              particular, if h agrees and is not trapped, the mirror after n moves GSTEP 1 is the
              guest’s flag after n steps of its own program.
              Proof. One move at a time. An OWN move touches neither the mirror nor the guest.
              A trapped GSTEP touches neither. An untrapped one sets the mirror to the old
              mirror or the crossing, and the guest’s flag is a latch (Theorem 15.5), so if the old
              mirror equalled the old flag, the new mirror equals the new flag. The last sentence
              is this together with Theorem D.9.



              Theorem D.11 (The host’s step collects the guest’s toll). (1) If h agrees, is not
              trapped, and the guest step that budget b allows takes the guest’s flag from down to
              up, then the mirror is down before GSTEP b and up after it, the host’s ledger rose
              by exactly b, and b ≥ 1. (2) In the run of (1) of Theorem D.9, from a host that
              agrees, if the guest’s flag goes up between its steps n and n + 1, the mirror goes up
              between the host’s moves n and n + 1, and that move costs 1. (3) For every host
              trace t, µ( g(run(t, h))) + µ(h) ≤ µ(run(t, h)) + µ( g(h)): the host’s ledger grows at
              least as fast as the guest’s.
                                                       D.3 A simpler host, with the guest step built in   519


Proof. (1) The guest’s flag rises only on a passing CERTIFY (Theorem 15.5), which
costs 1, and the budget let it run, so b ≥ 1; the mirror was the guest’s flag, so it was
down, and the move sets it to the crossing. (2) is (1) at the matching move. (3)
Induction on t: a guest step that runs costs the guest at most the budget the host
paid, and every other move leaves the guest’s ledger alone.
