Theorem D.12 (No unpaid host certification). If the mirror is down at h and up
after a host move i, then i is GSTEP b with b ≥ 1, the host was not trapped, the
guest’s next instruction was CERTIFY, and the guest’s flag went from down to up in
that move. A trace made only of OWN moves leaves the mirror and the guest state
exactly where they were. And the host’s own flag rises only by an OWN CERTIFY
that passes on the host’s core.

Proof. An OWN move copies the mirror unchanged, and a trapped GSTEP does too,
so the rise is an untrapped GSTEP b whose guest step crossed; a crossing is a passing
CERTIFY, which costs 1 and needed the budget. The own flag moves by the small
machine’s step line.



Theorem D.13 (The host is a Thiele machine). For every host state and move, if
the host’s reading goes from no to yes, the move costs at least 1; the same holds for
the mirror alone and for the own flag alone. So the host read through own ∨ m, the
host read through m alone, and the guest class are Thiele machines (Definition 2.1),
and any host trace that raises the host’s reading costs at least 1.

Proof. The mirror’s half is Theorem D.12; the own flag’s half is the small machine’s
toll on the host’s core. The trace form is Section 2’s universal floor.

Remark D.1 (Two guests, run). Load the guest CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
A; CERTIFY; HALT with both counters at 0. After two moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is
down; after three it is up, the guest’s flag is up, the host’s own flag is still down, and
the host has paid 3. Under the program U0 the mirror is down at host step 6 and up
at step 7, with 3 paid. The guest CERTIFY; CERTIFY traps on its first step: after five
moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is down, the guest is trapped, and the host has paid 5 for
nothing.
   That copy can’t be faked. The proof walks every host move there is, and the
copy only rises in a guest step where the guest itself ran CERTIFY and passed. A
host program that never touches the guest leaves the copy exactly where it was.
520   D The universal machines


              From a loaded host the copy always equals the guest’s flag, and the host’s ledger
              always grows at least as fast as the guest’s, and a three-instruction loop runs any
              small-machine program one guest step per pass. Here the mirror, the crossing test
              and the charge sit in the host’s step rule, so Theorems D.11 and D.12 hold for every
              sequence of host moves, including ones that never run a guest. That’s the simple
              version. Everything it gets from its built-in move, U gets from ordinary instructions,
              plus an exact ledger and a flag of its own.


              D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs

              Section 13 left the diagonal standing on any substrate, on a little family built to fit
              it, and on L, handled on its own terms rather than as a substrate. It also said what a
              machine has to supply to fill in the same shape, two things: programs that can be
              handed to programs as numbers, and a recursion theorem for the transformations it
              can carry out. This machine’s universal program reads a whole guest program out of
              one register, with a numbering of programs that goes there and back (Definition D.3),
              and halting is undecidable here in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.4. What’s left
              are the two classical results that turn a universal machine into a place where the
              diagonal bites: Rice’s theorem and Kleene’s recursion theorem. They come with a
              wrinkle I should put first, because it decides which machine they’re about.
                   The wrinkle is the one from Section 15, at the end of the subsection on what two
              counters compute. The small machine takes its inputs straight into two counters,
              and Schroeppel’s memo gives a proof that two plain counters can’t even compute
              2n from n. Rice’s reduction has to keep a program’s input safe while a copy of a
              halting instance runs. Kleene’s construction has to run an evaluator while keeping
              its input. Two counters have nowhere to keep it. So the two theorems land where
              they’re true and where I could prove them. The host machine of Definition D.2, the
              one with a counter for every number that U runs on, is a fine programming system:
              its programs are numbers, an input sits in register 1, and there’s room to spare. On
              it both theorems hold in full. On the two-counter machine itself the story splits, and
              I’ll tell it at the end of the subsection: Rice’s theorem holds on every input, by a trick
              for keeping the input that I’ll show you; Kleene’s holds when inputs are written as
              powers of two, the way Minsky packed them; and on plain inputs Kleene’s is false,
              and that’s a theorem too.
                   The host machine’s programs are numbered in the same style as U numbers a
              guest’s. Write ⟨m, n⟩ for (2n + 1) · 2m . INC r is ⟨0, r ⟩, DEC r j is ⟨1, ⟨r, j⟩⟩, HALT is
              ⟨2, 0⟩, CHECK r is ⟨3, r ⟩, COMMIT r is ⟨4, r ⟩, CERTIFY is ⟨5, 0⟩, and a program is the
              list code: the empty program is 0, and an instruction x followed by a program t is
              ⟨ x, code(t)⟩. An instruction number that is none of these codes reads as HALT. Then
              every number decodes to some program, since a positive number is ⟨ x, n⟩ with n
                                                      D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   521


smaller than it, and decoding a program’s code gives the program back. When I put
one program after another, the later one’s jumps move down by the length of what
comes before it, and a jump to a line where it has no instruction, line 0 included,
goes to the line just after it, so a stop inside it hands on to whatever follows. Say
a host program outputs y on input x when, started with x in register 1 and every
other register 0, with a clean table, it halts with y in register 0.
     Rice first, because it’s the shorter road. Henry Rice, whom you met in Section 7,
proved in his 1951 doctoral thesis, and published in 1953, that no program de-
cides any property of what programs do unless every program has it or none does.
Properties of how a program is written aren’t covered. The road from halting is a
single detour. Take a property of what programs do, a program y that has it, and a
program n that doesn’t. Given an instance of two-counter halting, a Minsky program
H with starting counters a and b, build a host program that first loads a and b into
two fresh registers (not register 1, and named by neither y nor n), then runs a copy
of H moved onto those registers, then empties both, then runs y. If H halts on
( a, b) the built program behaves like y and has the property. If H runs forever the
built program never stops on any input, and it behaves like the program that loops,
which lacks the property (if the looping program has it instead, swap the roles of y
and n). Everything the built program does before y is INC and DEC, which put no
marks on the ledger and touch no fact, channel, trap latch or flag. So a decider for
the property would be a decider for halting, and by Theorem 15.4 that would let a
program list every single-tape Turing machine that doesn’t halt. Two words carry
the weight, and they’re the ones to check in the statement: what “behaves the same”
sees, and where the program starts.

Definition D.5 (Behaving the same, on the host). A host program ends in a state
when it halts there, from the start with x in register 1 and the rest clean; a trap
counts as stopping. Two host programs behave the same when for every input x, any
state one ends in has a state the other ends in that agrees with it on every register’s
value, the fact table, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag, and the
same the other way round. The line number and the versions aren’t compared. A
property of host programs is extensional when behaving the same carries it from one
program to the other.



Theorem D.14 (Rice’s theorem on the host machine). Let Π be an extensional
property of host programs that some program has and some program lacks. Then Π
is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.4.
522   D The universal machines


              Proof. The reduction above. The prefix before y leaves every register but the two
              fresh ones as it found them, and empties those, so when H halts the built program
              ends in whatever state y ends in from the same input, with the same ledger, table,
              channel, trap and flag. When H doesn’t halt, the built program stops on no input.
              You don’t even need to know whether the looping program has Π: ask the decider
              about it, and its answer says which of y and n to put at the end.
                 A property that depends only on the partial function a program computes,
              whether it stops and what it leaves in register 0, is extensional, so it is covered. That
              case also follows from the recursion theorem below.
                 On the small machine itself the same road works from the clean start, and only
              from there. Say two two-counter programs behave the same from the clean start
              when, whatever state one halts in from counters (0, 0), the other halts in a state
              with the same counters, trap latch, ledger and flag, and the same the other way
              round. The fact table and the channel aren’t compared, because the prefix moves
              the versions of A and B by fixed amounts and the facts, the channel’s included,
              carry versions. There is no input to keep, since the program starts at (0, 0), and H’s
              instance is loaded straight into A and B.


              Theorem D.15 (Rice’s theorem for the small machine, from the clean start). Let Π
              be a property of two-counter programs that’s carried from a program to any program
              that behaves the same from the clean start, held by some program and lacked by
              some other. Then Π is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.4. In
              particular “halts from the clean start” is undecidable.

              Proof. The road of Theorem D.14, with the input dropped. Take a two-counter
              program H with a start ( a, b), and let y have Π and n lack it; as before, if the
              program that loops has Π, swap the roles of y and n. Build the program that does
              INC A a times and INC B b times, runs a copy of H with its jumps moved down
              (a jump to a line where H has no instruction, line 0 or past its end, goes to the
              line just after the copy), empties A and then B with a one-line DEC loop each, and
              then runs y with its jumps moved down. From the clean start the copy of H begins
              at ( a, b), which is H’s own start, so it stops exactly when H does. If it does, both
              counters are emptied and y runs from (0, 0). Every instruction before y is an INC
              or a DEC: it puts no mark on the ledger and touches no fact, channel, trap latch or
              flag. It does move the versions of A and B up, each by the number of writes that
              counter took before y started, and the facts y records carry versions. But a CHECK
              or a COMMIT reads versions only to ask whether two versions of the same counter
              are equal, and adding one fixed amount to both keeps the answer. So y takes the
              same steps inside the built program as it takes from the clean start, with the same
                                                       D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   523


counters, trap latch, ledger and flag at every point, and with facts that differ only
by that fixed shift in their versions. That shift is why the fact table and the channel
are left out of “behaves the same from the clean start.” If H doesn’t stop, neither
does the built program: the copy of H never reaches a HALT, and nothing before
y can trap. So the built program behaves the same as y when H stops from ( a, b),
and the same as the two-line program that loops, INC A then DEC A back to line
1, when it doesn’t. A decider for Π would then decide whether H stops from ( a, b),
with the consequence stated in Theorem 15.4; which of y and n goes at the end is
the decider’s own answer about the looping program. “Halts from the clean start” is
carried by behaving the same from the clean start, held by the empty program and
lacked by the looping one, so it’s covered.
    That’s the clean start only. Every input is harder, because the standard reduction
has to keep the input safe while the halting instance runs, and two counters have
nowhere obvious to keep it. The way through is at the end of the subsection.
    Kleene’s recursion theorem is the deeper one, and it’s a construction, which is
Section 13’s point about Kleene’s little gem (Moschovakis’s phrase): the content is
the building, and the contradiction in Section 13 was just the last line. It says: for
every transformation F of programs that some program can carry out on numbers,
there’s a program p that computes the same thing as F ( p). The shape of the building
is the old one. From the program that carries out F, build an evaluator that reads a
number, treats it as a program’s code, specialises that program to its own code, runs
F’s program on the result, and runs whatever program comes back. The specialising
step is what logicians call s-m-n: fix one input of a program and get a new program
that needs one input fewer. Then the witness is the evaluator specialised to its own
code. Run on any input, it builds its own code, hands it to F’s program, gets the
code of F ( p), and runs that.
    Here’s each piece on the host machine, with its exact premise.


Theorem D.16 (s-m-n, and a universal program for host programs). (1) For a
number c and a host program V, let spec(c, V ) be c copies of INC 2 followed by V
with its jumps moved to follow them. Then for all x, y, spec(c, V ) outputs y on input
x if and only if V, started with x in register 1 and c in register 2, halts with y in
register 0. (2) There is a host program W made only of INC, DEC and HALT such
that, for all c, x, y, W started with x in register 1 and c in register 2 halts with y in
register 0 exactly when the host program numbered c outputs y on input x.

Proof. (1) The prefix writes register 2 c times and nothing else, so it moves that
register’s version from 0 to c. A fact records a version, so after the prefix every later
version of register 2, and the version in every fact the run records about register 2,
524   D The universal machines


              is c more than in a clean run. A CHECK or a COMMIT reads versions only to ask
              whether two versions of the same register are equal, and adding c to both keeps the
              answer, so the two runs take the same steps. The run is V’s run from the stated start,
              moved down by c lines. (2) is the evaluator. A finite algorithm decodes a number
              into a program, runs it step by step on given registers, record layer included, and,
              searching over the number of steps, returns the output of the first halting run. It
              is a finite tape algorithm, and the translation of Appendix K turns any finite tape
              algorithm into a finite program of INC and DEC on finitely many counters. The host
              runs those instructions on registers of its own, with HALT marking the returned
              output. That’s W.
                 One thing to be exact about: U is not that universal program. U runs two-counter
              guests, and a two-counter guest given its input plainly can’t run the evaluator. With
              inputs written as powers of two one can, as Theorem D.22 near the end of this
              subsection shows. W runs host programs, and it can, because it’s a host program on
              a machine with registers.


              Theorem D.17 (Kleene’s recursion theorem on the host machine). (1) For every
              host program T there is a host program e such that for all x, y: e outputs y on
              input x if and only if, for some d, T outputs d on the number of e, and the program
              numbered d outputs y on x. (2) So for every transformation F of host programs
              that some host program carries out on numbers (on the number of p it outputs
              the number of F ( p), for every p), there is a host program e such that for all x, y, e
              outputs y on x if and only if F (e) does. (3) The same on numbers: for every function
               f on numbers, defined everywhere, that some host program computes, some number
              e has the program numbered e and the program numbered f (e) output the same on
              every input.

              Proof. (1) Let E be the following program of INC and DEC, built the same way as
              W from one finite evaluator, with T’s number t written in. On inputs x and c it
              computes the number of spec(c, Pc ), where Pc is the program numbered c, runs T
              on that number to get d, and then runs the program numbered d on x. Let c0 be the
              number of E, and let e = spec(c0 , E). By (1) of Theorem D.16, e on input x does
              what E does on x and c0 . And E on c0 builds the number of spec(c0 , Pc0 ), which is
              the number of e, since Pc0 is E. So e hands its own number to T, gets d, and runs d
              on x. (2) and (3) are (1) with T carrying out F or f .
                  That fixed point is of the function: e and F (e) stop on the same inputs and leave
              the same number in register 0. Their ledgers, flags and fact tables can differ: e is
              all INC and DEC, so whatever F (e) pays, e only simulates. I’d like a fixed point that
                                                        D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   525


agrees on the record too, and the next two theorems say how much of that can be
had. The ledger and the flag can be had. Every register can’t.


Theorem D.18 (The recursion theorem, up to the record). Let F be a transformation
of host programs that some host program T carries out on numbers. Then there is a
host program e such that, for every input x, any state e ends in has a state F (e) ends
in that agrees with it on register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of
facts in the table, and whether the channel is empty, and the same the other way
round. So e stops on x exactly when F (e) does, and the ledgers are equal exactly,
with no surcharge. T may itself check, commit and certify.

Proof. The construction is Theorem D.17’s, with a different evaluator. The first step
is to see that a record is small. From a clean start, a host program that stops has a
record I can read off five numbers, in this order: what it left in register 0; how many
facts the table holds; what is left of the ledger once the facts, the trap and the flag are
paid for, which I’ll call the replay allowance; 1 if the flag is up and 0 if not; and 1 if
the trap latch is up and 0 if not. The record obeys a short rulebook, and you can read
each rule off the price table. A run stops at its first trap, so its ledger is its passing
CHECKs, plus its passing COMMITs, plus its passing CERTIFYs, plus one if it trapped
(only those three can fail, and the failing one is charged). Its passing CHECKs are
its facts, at most sixteen. Its flag is up exactly when some CERTIFY passed. So the
allowance is the passing COMMITs plus the passing CERTIFYs less one for the flag,
which is never negative, and the ledger is the facts, plus that allowance, plus the
flag, plus the trap. A COMMIT needs a fact behind it, so a positive allowance means
at least one fact. A CERTIFY needs a commitment, so a raised flag means a passing
COMMIT, and so a positive allowance. And the channel is empty exactly when no
COMMIT passed, which is exactly when the allowance is zero, since a CERTIFY can’t
pass before a COMMIT has. The allowance counts repeated CERTIFYs as well as
COMMITs; it counts marks the replay can spend on commitments, not the original
commitment events. Those are the only properties of a record the replay will use.
    The second step is five blocks, one for each number. Each block reads the code of
T, runs T on the number of the specialised program, runs the program that comes
out on x, and returns its number. All of that happens on plain data: the blocks are
programs of INC and DEC, built the way W was, from a finite evaluator translated
into INC and DEC. So if T has marks of its own, they are simulated and never paid.
    The third step is the payment. The evaluator puts 1 in a fresh register, which is
⟨0, 0⟩, the pair of Zero and 0, so it satisfies the host’s one property, and CHECKs it
once for every fact; there are at most sixteen, so the table has room. It COMMITs to
that claim once for every mark in the replay allowance. It CERTIFYs once if the flag
526   D The universal machines


              is up. It copies the first number into register 0. And if the trap latch is up, it CHECKs
              a register that holds 0, which fails, since 0 is no pair, and the host traps. Everything
              before the payments is INC and DEC and costs no marks, and the payments cost
              what the record costs, so the ledger is exact. Specialise the evaluator to its own
              number, as before.
                 Try CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY, CERTIFY on a true claim. The ledger is four, the
              table holds one fact, the flag is up and the trap is down, so the replay allowance is
              two. The replay pays CHECK, COMMIT, COMMIT, CERTIFY: the same four marks
              and the same summary, in a different order. That’s the agreement the theorem
              claims, and all of it.
                 In the replay, the trap latch is up exactly when the fifth number is 1, and the
              flag exactly when the fourth is positive. Look only at the function computed and
              you get the usual fixed-point statement back. Two limits, and the second one is a
              theorem. First, e pays after it has computed everything. It is not the way U runs
              a guest, mirroring every move: e pays the counts, CHECKs, then COMMITs, then
              the CERTIFY, whatever order F (e) used, so the order of the record’s events isn’t
              preserved, and for a program F (e) that never stops, e never stops and pays nothing,
              though F (e) may pay without bound. The relation says nothing about states in the
              middle of a run. Second, no fixed point agrees on every register, or on what the
              facts name.


              Theorem D.19 (No fixed point of full behaviour). There is a transformation F of
              host programs, carried out by a host program, such that no host program e behaves
              the same as F (e) in the sense of Definition D.5.

              Proof. Let F ( p) be the one-line program INC r, with r one above the number of
              p. To carry this out on numbers, add one to the input code, encode INC with that
              register, and encode the one-element instruction list. These are finite arithmetic
              operations of the counter construction in Appendix K. A program’s number is at
              least every register it names: the number of an instruction is above its register, and
              the code of a list is above every instruction in it. So e can’t name r, the register F (e)
              writes. On input 0 the run of F (e) ends with 1 in register r, and if e stops at all, it
              ends with 0 there. If e doesn’t stop, then it already differs from F (e), which does.
              Either way they don’t behave the same.
                 A variant of F that also CHECKs register r and commits to it gives F (e) a fact and
              a commitment about r that e can’t have, so no fixed point agrees on the fact table
              alone, or on the channel alone, or on the versions of the registers. What survives is
              what Theorem D.18 states, plus any register named in advance, or any finite set of
                                                      D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   527


them: before it pays, the evaluator reads that register’s final value off the simulated
run of F (e) and writes it into its own copy of the register, keeping its scratch work
and its two payment registers elsewhere. The register F above writes is chosen by
looking at e, and that’s the one no fixed point can follow.
   And with the recursion theorem proved, the wall of Section 13 goes up on this
machine without assuming that theorem as an extra premise. Call a property of
host programs functional when it depends only on the partial function a program
computes.


Theorem D.20 (The diagonal on the host machine). Let Π be a functional property
of host programs that some program has and some program lacks. (1) Read “ f is
representable” as “some host program carries f out on numbers.” Then no function
d from programs to Booleans whose flip is representable is right about Π on every
program: this is the argument of Theorem 13.1, reproved for host programs, with its
recursion premise a theorem here. (2) No host program decides Π outright: there
is no program D that, on the number of every program, halts with a number in
register 0 that’s 1 exactly when the program has Π.

Proof. (1) The flip, send programs that d calls good to the program lacking Π and
the others to the one having it, is carried out by a host program by hypothesis.
Theorem D.17(2) gives a program e that computes what its image computes; Π
holds of e exactly when it holds of the image, and the image lacks it exactly when d
calls e good, so d is wrong at e. (2) From a deciding program D build a host program
that computes D’s flip on numbers, by the finite-simulation search of Appendix K,
reading the Boolean from the first halting run of D; then (1) applies. This one is a
plain no; the “representable” reading of (1) doesn’t come into it.
   Rice and Kleene are the ingredients the diagonal of Section 13 asks a substrate for,
and the wall they put up doesn’t care about the record: the base does the computing
and the flag watches. A program’s ledger and flag are among what “behaves the
same” sees on the host, so a nontrivial property of those is undecidable too, in the
reduction sense of Theorem D.14, and the fixed point is up to the record, as far as
the theorems above say and no further.
   Now the two-counter machine itself, which I promised at the start of the subsec-
tion: Minsky’s two bins of pebbles and nothing else. Rice, first. Say a two-counter
program behaves the same as another on a set X of inputs when, on every input n in
X, started with n pebbles in bin A and none in bin B, one stops exactly when the
other does, and then they agree on both bins, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, and
on which property and which counter each recorded fact and the channel are about.
528   D The universal machines


              The versions are left out: they say which write a fact is about, and the trick below
              moves them.
                  The trick is the whole problem. Rice’s reduction has to keep the program’s input
              safe while a copy of a halting instance H runs, and there’s no third bin to keep it
              in. My first guess was bin B, and that dies at once, because H needs both bins. The
              second guess is Minsky’s own packing: keep several numbers in one bin as powers
              of different primes, H’s two counters as the exponents of 2 and 3, and the input
              as the exponent of 5. That dies more quietly. To put the input there, the program
              would have to turn n pebbles into 5n , an exponential, and Schroeppel’s memo, from
              Section 15, gives a proof that two plain counters can’t even build 2n from n. I had
              no way to build 5n .
                  What works is to stop keeping the input beside the work. Turn n pebbles into
              6n + 5, which is only adding, and then multiply in H’s counters as powers of 2 and 3.
              H runs by halving the pile and splitting it in thirds and building it back up, and the
              6n + 5 rides along in the middle of every one of those piles. It’s odd, and counted
              off in threes it leaves two over, so no halving or thirding ever reaches into it.


              Theorem D.21 (Rice’s theorem for the two-counter machine, on any inputs). For
              any set X of inputs, a property of two-counter programs that’s carried from a
              program to any program that behaves the same on X is undecidable in the reduction
              sense of Theorem 15.4, unless every program has it or none does, and then it’s
              decidable. X can be every input, the powers of two, or {0}.

              Proof. For every input: given a two-counter instance H starting from counters a and
              b, build a program that turns the input of n pebbles in bin A into (6n + 5) · 2a · 3b ,
              runs H inside the exponents of 2 and 3, divides out every 2 and every 3 when H
              stops, takes away 5, divides by 6, and then runs the program that has the property.
              Because 6n + 5 shares no factor with 2 or 3, the coding never mistakes it for an
              exponent, and the input comes back whole. If H halts, the built program behaves
              the same as the one with the property on every input; if not, it never stops on
              any input, like the program that loops. As before, if the looping program has the
              property, put a program that lacks it at the end instead, and the decider’s own
              answer about the looping program says which. So a decider for the property would
              decide two-counter halting.
                  Try input 2 while the simulated counters hold 1 and 2. The pile is 17 · 2 · 9 = 306.
              Raising the first simulated counter doubles it to 612; lowering the second divides it
              by three, to 204. Strip off every factor of two and three and 17 remains; subtract
              five and divide by six, and the original input 2 is back.
                                                       D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   529


   So 6n + 5 is the place to keep the input that two counters seemed not to have. It
isn’t beside the work. It’s inside it, in a factor the work never touches. I like that
one more than I can justify: the input hides in the leftover that every halving and
thirding walks straight past.
   Kleene needs more than keeping an input. It needs a program that runs a
program. So write a number x as 2x pebbles and read a result as the exponent of 2,
the way Minsky did. With inputs written that way, there’s one two-counter program,
call it U2 , that, started on 2x · 3e , stops with 2y exactly when the program numbered
e gives y on x; specialising a program to a number is exact; and the recursion
theorem holds. (U2 is a different program from the universal host program U, which
runs on the machine with a register for every number.)


Theorem D.22 (Kleene for the two-counter machine, inputs written as powers of
two). (1) For every transformation F of programs that some program carries out
on program numbers, there’s a program e that computes the same function as F (e),
with inputs and outputs written as powers of two. (2) The fixed point is of the
function only: there’s such an F for which no e behaves the same as F (e) once the
properties and counters of the recorded facts count.

Proof. (1) The host’s three pieces, with two counters in place of registers. First, the
universal program. Load a program’s number e and its input x together as 2x · 3e in
bin A, with bin B empty. The evaluator of Appendix K, the one that searches budgets
and runs the program numbered e on x, is a finite counter program on finitely many
counters, and packing those counters into two by the prime-exponent construction
of Appendix K.3 gives U2 : started on 2x · 3e it stops with 2y in bin A exactly when
the program numbered e, started on 2x , stops with 2y . Second, specialising. For a
number c and a program V, let spec(c, V ) be c copies of a block that multiplies bin
A by three, followed by V with its jumps moved down. The block is INC and DEC
only, so it puts no marks on the ledger and records nothing, and started on 2x the c
copies leave 2x · 3c ; so spec(c, V ) on 2x does what V does on 2x · 3c . Third, the fixed
point. Let T be a program that carries out F: on 2n , n the number of a program
p, it stops with 2m , m the number of F ( p). Build E from the same finite evaluator,
with T’s number written in, and pack it into two counters as before: on 2x · 3c it
computes the number of spec(c, Pc ), where Pc is the program numbered c, runs T
on that number to get d, and runs the program numbered d on 2x . Let c0 be the
number of E and e = spec(c0 , E). On 2x , e does what E does on 2x · 3c0 : it builds
the number of spec(c0 , Pc0 ), which is the number of e itself since Pc0 is E, hands it
to T, gets the number of F (e), and runs F (e) on 2x . The machine is deterministic,
530   D The universal machines


              so a packed output is unique, and for every x and y, e started on 2x stops with 2y
              exactly when F (e) does. (2) is the counterexample that follows.
                  The counterexample in (2) is short. Number the programs the way U numbers
              its guests (Appendix L), so a program’s number is above the code of every property
              it names. Let F ( p) be the one-line program that checks that bin A holds at least the
              number of p plus one. A program can only record facts about properties it names,
              so no e can record the fact F (e) records, and from a large enough input F (e) does
              record it.
                  Even with Schroeppel in hand, my first guess about Kleene was that the powers
              of two were a convenience, and that plain inputs would only take more work. They
              don’t take more work. With plain inputs, Kleene’s theorem is false. A transformation
              is carried out if some program, started on 2n where n is the number of a program p,
              stops with 2m where m is the number of F ( p).


              Theorem D.23 (No plain recursion on two counters). (1) No program of n lines
              stops with c · x pebbles in bin A, started on x pebbles in bin A and none in bin
              B, for every x, where c = N! + 1 and N = 16(n + 1)(4n + 1)16 . (2) So there’s
              a carried-out transformation F such that no program e computes the same plain
              function as F (e).

              Proof. (2) from (1): let F ( p) be a program that multiplies bin A by the constant c
              determined by the length of p. Multiplication by a fixed constant is the transfer loop
              of Appendix K. Decoding a finite program, counting its lines, forming the factorial
              and writing that loop are computable operations, so a program carries out F on
              encoded program numbers. A fixed point would multiply every plain input by the
              constant forbidden by (1).
                 For (1), suppose an n-line program did it. Split each state into the two bin counts
              and a finite control: the line (one of the n lines, or “stopped” for any line with no
              instruction), the trap, whether the channel is empty, and the table read entry by
              entry as a fact’s property, its counter, and whether it is current (its version is its
              counter’s version now) or stale. Only properties the program names can enter the
              table, at most n of them, so an entry is one of at most 4n kinds, and a table of at
              most sixteen entries is one of at most ∑k≤16 (4n)k ≤ (4n + 1)16 lists. So there are at
              most Q = 4(n + 1)(4n + 1)16 controls. The control and the two counts decide the
              next control and counts: a CHECK writes a current fact, a write to a counter makes
              that counter’s facts stale, a COMMIT passes exactly when a current fact with its
              property and counter is in the table, a CERTIFY passes exactly when the channel isn’t
              empty, and the ledger, the flag, the channel’s contents and the versions themselves
              never decide a branch. Call the control with the two counts a configuration.
                                                       D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   531


    Pick a threshold h ≥ 1 above every number k in a property Ge(k) the program
names. At h or above, a count answers every question the program can put to it (is
it zero, is it even, is it at least k, can a DEC take one off) the same way as any other
count of the same parity at h or above. Call a control together with the parities of
both counts a pattern; there are at most 4Q = N of them.
    The forced run. A stage start is a configuration with one count below h, in the
exact bin, and the other at h or above, in the large bin, which holds v. From it, run
the program while pretending the large bin can never fall below h: follow the exact
bin exactly, the large bin only by its parity, and keep a tally of the large bin’s net
change. This forced run depends on the control, the exact count and the parity of v,
and not on v itself. The real run does exactly what the forced run does, with the
large bin at v plus the tally, up to the first step where v plus the tally drops below h,
the crossing. A move changes a count by at most one, so at the crossing the large
bin holds exactly h − 1.
    What a forced run does. One of three things, fixed by the stage start. (a) It stops.
(b) It comes back to a step with the same control, the same exact count below h and
the same parity of the large bin as an earlier step; it’s deterministic in those, so it
repeats that stretch forever, and the exact count stays bounded. (c) Neither. Then
it has at most 2Qh steps with the exact count below h, one per combination, so
from some step on the exact count stays at h or above for good. Among any N + 1
consecutive steps of that tail, two have the same pattern, at steps t1 < t2 ≤ t1 + N,
and between them the exact count changes by some δ, even because the parities
match. If δ < 0, the run from t2 repeats the run from t1 with the exact count
lowered by |δ| each time round, so after finitely many rounds it goes below h, which
the tail never does. So δ ≥ 0, and the stretch repeats forever, lifted by δ each time
round, never dipping below h. In every case but (a), then, the forced run from some
step on repeats one stretch forever, and each time round the exact bin changes by a
fixed g and the large bin by a fixed amount; in (b) g = 0, and in (c) the stretch is at
most N moves long.
    What the real run does, once v is large enough for that stage start, meaning the
large bin can’t reach the crossing before the forced run stops or its repeating stretch
has gone round once in full. If the forced run stops, the real run stops the same
way, with the exact bin at a count fixed by the stage start and the large one at v
plus a fixed amount. If the large bin doesn’t lose each time round, the real run
never crosses and never stops. If it loses and g = 0, the real run crosses with both
bins below a bound fixed by the stage start. The remaining case is a transfer: each
time round the large bin loses m > 0 and the exact one gains g > 0. That’s case
(c), so the stretch has at most N moves, each moving one bin by at most one, and
m, g ≤ N; both are even. Now the stage rule. Start the same stage with v + m
in place of v. The parity is the same, so the forced run is the same, and since the
532   D The universal machines


              crossing comes after the stretch has gone round once, the bin needs exactly one
              more time round to get down to h − 1. So the real run crosses one time round later,
              with the same control, the formerly large bin at h − 1, and the other bin larger by g.
              With v + km it crosses k times round later, the other bin larger by kg. After a transfer,
              the crossing is a new stage start with the bins’ jobs swapped. For example, a loop
              that takes two pebbles from the full bin and puts four in the other has m = 2 and
              g = 4: two more pebbles going in buy one more trip round the loop, and four more
              coming out.
                  Choosing the input. Apart from v, a stage start is one of finitely many things:
              a control, an exact count below h, a parity, and which bin is which. Take one
              bound V ≥ h that’s large enough, in the sense above, for every one of them, and
              above every count that was called fixed or bounded above: the exact bin of a stage
              that stops, and both bins at a crossing with g = 0. The configurations with one
              count below h and the other below V are finitely many. If the program multiplied
              every input by c, no two different inputs could pass through the same configuration,
              because everything after it, the output included, would be the same, while cx ̸= cx ′ .
              So only finitely many inputs pass through that finite set. Pick an input x that passes
              through none of it and has cx above V. Since ( x, 0) is itself a configuration, x ≥ V.
                  Following that input. The run from ( x, 0) starts a stage: bin B exact at 0, bin A
              large at x. Every later stage start along the run has its large bin at V or above, or the
              run would pass through the finite set. The run stops, since the program multiplies,
              so no stage runs forever. No stage crosses with g = 0, since that crossing is in the
              finite set. So each stage before the last is a transfer, with its own pair (mi , gi ), and
              the last one stops. It stops with its exact bin below V and its large bin at its v plus
              a fixed amount, and the output cx is above V, so the output bin A is the large one.
              There are finitely many stages, because each takes at least one step of a run that
              stops.
                  The comparison. Put D = 2 ∏i mi and run the input x + D. It is x plus a multiple
              of m1 , so by the stage rule the first stage crosses at the same configuration except
              that the other bin is larger by ( D/m1 ) g1 = 2g1 ∏i≥2 mi , which is a multiple of m2 .
              So the second stage crosses the same way, with the next bin larger by 2g1 g2 ∏i≥3 mi ,
              and so on through every stage. The last stage starts with its large bin larger by
              2 ∏i gi , an even amount, so it stops the same way with bin A larger by exactly that.
              So the outputs from x + D and from x differ by 2 ∏i gi . But multiplication by c
              makes them differ by cD = 2c ∏i mi . Cancel two:
                                                  c ∏ m i = ∏ gi .
                                                    i         i

              Empty products are 1. Every factor on the right is between 1 and N, and c = N! + 1
              is coprime to every such factor: any common divisor divides both N! and N! + 1,
                                          D.5 What the universal machine covers, and what it doesn’t   533


so it divides 1. So c can’t divide the right side unless c = 1, and c ≥ 2. That’s the
contradiction.
    Nothing in that proof used more than this: two bins that move one pebble at
a time, finitely many controls, and bins that, above some threshold, are read only
through their parity. Any machine like that has the same obstruction, and the same
computable transformation F with no program e equivalent to F (e) on plain inputs.
    I went looking for Schroeppel’s own memo and found a scan of it. As I read it, his
route is close in spirit: he trades a two-counter machine that starts with one counter
empty for a machine with one register that can only add, multiply and divide by
fixed numbers and take one away, each of those built out of one of the program’s
loops, and that’s the stages here under another name. I haven’t followed his proof
line by line, so I compare the two at that level and no further; the argument this
book stands on is the one above. The c it uses is astronomically bigger than anything
a real multiplier needs, and finding the best bound is a question I leave alone.
    So on two bins: Rice holds on every input. Kleene holds with inputs written as
powers of two, for the function. It fails for the facts. And with plain inputs Kleene
fails outright. The last one is the answer I didn’t see coming. The powers of two
weren’t a convenience. On two bins they’re the difference between a recursion
theorem and none.
    That failure has a setting computability theorists know. The mathematician
Hartley Rogers, in his 1967 textbook, calls a numbering of the computable functions
acceptable when every other computable numbering of them can be translated into
it by a computable map, and in every acceptable numbering Kleene’s theorem holds.
Read on plain inputs, the two-bin programs number something smaller than all
the computable functions, since none of them computes 2n from n (Schroeppel’s
theorem; compare Theorem D.23), so they fall outside Rogers’s class, and his route
to the theorem isn’t open there. The computer scientists James Royer and John
Case (1994) studied that territory: programming systems for classes of functions
smaller than all the computable ones, which can’t be acceptable, and what can still
be programmed and proved in them. And the logician and puzzle writer Raymond
Smullyan’s two books on recursion theory and self-reference (1993, 1994) take
the fixed-point theorems apart axiomatically, so you can see which property of a
numbering each one leans on. The plain-input failure is a small instance on the map
they drew.


D.5 What the universal machine covers, and what it doesn’t

Here’s what the two universal programs cover, said plainly, a sentence at a time.
The guests of U are the small machine’s programs, every one of them, from every
clean start start( x, y). That’s the stated class. The whole-run theorems don’t cover a
534   D The universal machines


              guest handed facts in its table, a commitment in its channel or a raised flag at the
              start; the one-step simulation, by itself, works from any related pair. It’s the same
              kind of class Turing’s universal machine has: a fixed instruction set, and a finite
              program held as data, here packed into one number the way Turing packed his into
              a description number. Each guest keeps its computation, its halting, its answer, its
              record and its prices, exactly: the host halts when it halts, its flag goes up when the
              guest’s would, on a chain of its own, and its ledger is the guest’s.
                  The guests of UP are every Thiele machine whose driver, step, prices and reading
              are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. Each keeps its
              computation and its halting; its reading becomes the host’s flag as a latch, raised on
              an earned chain whose claim is the guest’s own reading; and its prices become the
              host’s ledger, exactly, except for a surcharge at the move where the reading first says
              yes: at most two when the reading starts at no, exactly three when it starts at yes.
              The surcharge is zero when that move costs three or more, and it can’t always be
              avoided: when the guest certifies with a ledger below three, no program on that
              host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger exactly (Theorems D.7 and D.8).
              Picture a clerk who’ll stamp anybody’s receipt. He copies it onto his own forms,
              bills at your rates to within two, and the stamp at the bottom is one he earned by
              checking your own reading. He didn’t copy it.
                  What’s outside the class is outside the theorems. A machine whose reading no
              program decides (an oracle checker, say, which the definition of certified Thiele-
              complete doesn’t rule out) doesn’t come in. Nor does a machine whose next move is
              nobody’s computation. The two universal programs have different start conditions:
              U’s whole-run result starts its guest clean; UP starts its guest where the presentation
              says, even if that state already has a yes reading. The host starts clean and earns a
              claim about that reading. It does not reconstruct or authenticate the guest’s earlier
              history.
                  And here’s why insisting on no built-in step is the point. A plain interpreter
              on an ordinary computer runs guests too, but then the guest’s record is data the
              interpreter’s program updates by convention, which is exactly the position of the
              ordinary programmable computer from Section 14 and Section 15.13. That’s a fact
              about how such interpreters are built. It says nothing about what they can do: U
              and UP are fixed interpreters, and their record isn’t kept by convention. Nothing in
              them raises the host’s flag except the host’s own CERTIFY, and the host’s step won’t
              let that pass without a COMMIT, or the COMMIT without a CHECK on a slot nobody
              has touched. The guest’s record isn’t data the host updates. It’s a record the host
              earns again, under the same rule, on its own registers.
APPENDIX E




Every model

Here’s the worry I couldn’t put down after the smallest honest machine (Section 15)
and the universal programs of the previous appendix. Everything in them was
built on Minsky’s two counters. The definition of certified Thiele-complete names a
two-counter window in clause (a). The universal program runs two-counter guests.
So is all of this a fact about counters? Pick a different machine to start from, a
Turing machine with its tape, a register machine, Alonzo Church’s lambda calculus,
and does the record still go on the same way, or did I just find a trick that happens
to work for one toy?
   I chased it with a picture: a box with a panel bolted to its front. The box
computes, with levers for moves and a window showing what clause (a) asks to
see, two numbers and a line number. The panel is the small machine’s earned layer:
version tallies that click when the box writes, a rack for facts, the flag, and the three
buttons CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY at one mark each. The worry is whether
that panel only bolts onto the one box I built.
   So this appendix goes both ways. First the panel goes onto boxes I didn’t build,
and I say exactly what a box has to supply for it to fit. Then other boxes, panel
and all, get run inside mine. If the record is really about the record and not about
pebbles, both trips should work, and the conditions on the way should say what has
to survive the move.


E.1 From any base up

Start with the direction I care about most: the panel onto a box I didn’t build. The
box can be any machine at all that has a universal base in the sense of clause (a),
and in the picture that’s two things. It shows a two-counter window. And for each
two-counter instruction it has a lever that acts on the window as that instruction
does. What else is inside, what its states look like, I don’t get to know.
   My first guess was to keep whatever the box came with. Plenty of machines have
a meter of their own, or a light on the front that means something’s done, so leave
those where they are, bolt the panel on beside them, and see what happens. It can’t
work, and the definition says why. If a lever can cost a mark, computing puts marks
on the ledger, and certified Thiele-complete asks that it put none, which is a rule of
the price list, not a claim about heat. If a lever can switch on the box’s own light, a

                                                  535
536   E Every model


              record went up with no CHECK behind it. Certified Thiele-complete rules out both.
              So the meter and the light come off, along with everything else the box already had:
              its costs, its record, all of it, except the states, the levers and what each lever does to
              the state.
                  Then bolt on a panel cut down from the small machine’s, and nothing else:
              one version number for the whole box that every lever raises, which is the tally, a
              table with room for at least one fact, and three new moves, CHECK, COMMIT and
              CERTIFY, at one mark each, with every lever at zero marks. Call that the lift of the
              machine.



              Theorem E.1 (Every universal base lifts). (1) The lift of any box with a universal
              base, over a language of claims about the box’s state (“unchanged” meaning the
              box’s state is the same), with an exact equality test and a checker proved to say
              yes exactly when the claim holds, is certified Thiele-complete, as long as the claims
              its CHECK can ask include one that’s true at one loaded state and false at another,
              and the fact table has room for at least one fact. (2) The claims “this register is at
              least n” and “the program is at line n,” read off the window, always include such a
              claim, so with those claims every universal base lifts. (3) Conversely, every certified
              Thiele-complete machine has an interface meeting the four clauses under which
              its base moves, taken alone, form a machine with a universal base. (4) The panel
              leaves the box alone: from a state whose trap is down, a run of lever pulls in the lift
              moves the box exactly as the box’s own run does, and the trap stays down.

              Proof. (1) The four clauses, one at a time. (a) The lift keeps the box’s states, levers
              and step and adds the tally, the table, the channel, the flag and the trap. A lever
              moves the box’s part of the state as the box’s step does, raises the tally by one, and
              touches nothing else. So from a live state, which is a state whose box part is live, the
              window moves as the instruction does and the state stays live; no lever changes the
              flag; the loaded states are the box’s loaded states with an empty panel, so they’re
              clean; and the flag, once up, is lowered by nothing. (b) Start with the panel empty.
              The only move that raises the flag is CERTIFY, and CERTIFY traps unless the channel
              holds a fact; the channel is filled only by a COMMIT, which traps unless the table
              holds its claim at the current tally; and the table is filled only by a CHECK that
              passed, which files the claim with the tally it was checked at. So in front of the raise
              there’s a passing CHECK of some claim c, then a COMMIT of c at the same tally, then
              the CERTIFY. The tally rises with every lever pull, so an unchanged tally means no
              lever was pulled in between, so the box’s state is unchanged, and that’s what “the
              thing c is about is unchanged” says in the lift’s language, whose claims are about
              the box’s state. A passing CHECK means the checker said yes, and the checker was
                                                                             E.2 What never lifts   537


proved to mean what it says. (c) is the price list: levers at zero marks, the three
buttons at one each, the ledger the running sum. (d) Take the claim that’s true at
one loaded state and false at another. From the first, CHECK passes and files it, the
table having room, COMMIT finds it at the same tally, and CERTIFY raises the flag.
From the second the CHECK traps, and a trapped machine raises nothing. (2) “A is
at least 1” is true at the loaded state showing (1, 1, 0) and false at the one showing
(1, 0, 0). A window claim is a register and a number, or a line number, so two claims
can be tested equal, and its checker reads the window, which is its meaning, so
the checker is sound by definition. (3) Take an interface the machine is certified
Thiele-complete with and throw away every move whose kind isn’t base. What’s left
has the same states, the base moves as levers, and the interface’s window, live states
and loaded states, and clause (a) says of exactly these that the window follows every
instruction from every live state, that the state stays live, and that each loaded state
shows (1, a, b) and is live. That’s a universal base. (4) A lever pull with the trap
down changes the box’s part by the box’s step and the tally by one, and nothing
else; the trap goes up only on a CHECK that fails, a COMMIT without its fact, or a
CERTIFY with the channel empty, never on a lever. So along a run of lever pulls the
box’s part follows the box’s own run, pull for pull, and the trap stays down.
   Clause (b) is the small machine’s proof with the bins swapped out for whatever
the box has. That’s the part I’d braced for, and it turned out to be nothing. The chain
CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY never looked at anything but the tally and the claim.
The levers changed only the tally on the panel, making old facts stale; they never
inserted a fact, made a commitment or raised the flag. Neither side of the proof ever
needed to know it was looking at pebbles.
   So the earned layer isn’t something two counters do. It sits on top of any box
with a universal base, and it never needed to know which one. I’d half expected to
be rewriting the proof once per model.


E.2 What never lifts
A theorem that says the panel fits every box is one I don’t trust until I’ve watched
it fail to fit something. So I went looking for boxes it won’t turn into a certified
Thiele-complete machine, and the first one I tried was the one I was surest would
work.
    A Turing machine, with one fixed table. Each lever does one row of the table.
That looked like the obvious base to me, and it isn’t one at all. Clause (a) asks for a
lever for every two-counter instruction, and there are infinitely many two-counter
instructions, since a jump can go to any line. A fixed table has finitely many rows,
so it has finitely many levers, and it runs out of levers long before it runs out of
538   E Every model


              instructions. The first two items below are that failure in two forms, and the others
              fail for other reasons. Each is proved.


              Theorem E.2 (What doesn’t lift). (1) A box with only finitely many levers has no
              universal base, and no box with a universal base is finitely branching, meaning
              that from every state all its levers together lead to only finitely many different
              states. (2) The lift of a finitely branching box is never certified Thiele-complete,
              whatever claims and fact table it gets. (3) Neither is the lift of a box whose step
              ignores the state it’s in, where each lever sends every state to the same place. (4)
              On a record axis where every place is at or below every other, there is no certified
              Thiele-complete machine at all. (5) The lift’s own non-vacuity clause holds exactly
              when the fact table has room and some claim is true at one loaded state and false at
              another.

              Proof. (1) Take a universal base and its loaded state showing (1, 1, 0). For each j
              the lever for DEC A j must take it, in one pull, to a state showing ( j, 0, 0): A was
              above 0, so one comes off and the line jumps to j. Different j, different window,
              different state. So one state has infinitely many different successors, which is what
              not finitely branching means; and since one lever lands in one place from one state,
              the levers for the DEC A j are all different, so there are infinitely many of them.
              (2) In the lift the moves that cost no marks are the levers, since each button costs
              one, and from any state the levers together lead to finitely many states: the box’s
              finitely many successors, each with the tally raised by one. (The buttons can lead
              to infinitely many, one CHECK for each claim, but each costs a mark.) If the lift
              were certified Thiele-complete through some interface, that interface’s base moves
              would cost no marks by clause (c), so they’d all be levers, and by Theorem E.1(3)
              they’d form a universal base on their own. By (1) a universal base has a state from
              which its moves reach infinitely many states, and levers of a finitely branching box
              can’t. (3) Suppose each lever lands in one place whatever the state. The move an
              interface gives an instruction is a base move, at zero marks by clause (c), while each
              button costs one, so it’s a lever. Pull the lever for INC A twice from a loaded state
              showing (1, 0, 0), and pull the lever for INC B and then the lever for INC A from
              the same state. Both runs end with the lever for INC A, so both end with the box in
              the one place that lever lands, with the tally two higher and the panel untouched:
              the same state of the lift. But the window would have to show (3, 2, 0) after the
              first run and (3, 1, 1) after the second, and a window is a function of the state. The
              same two runs refute the box on its own. (4) On a record axis, raising the record
              means leaving the down-set of where it stood. If every place is at or below every
              other, every down-set is the whole axis and no move ever leaves one; but clause
                                                                              E.2 What never lifts   539


(d) asks for three moves that raise the record from some loaded state. (5) If the
table has no room, every CHECK traps and no CERTIFY ever fires, so (d) fails. If
no claim is true at one loaded state and false at another, (d)’s second half has no
witness. And when both hold, (d) was proved in (1).
    So my first test case failed, and at first I read item (1) as saying a Turing machine
can’t be a base at all. It says something narrower. A Turing machine with one fixed
table can’t be one. A classic model comes in the other way round, with one lever for
each whole program, run to the end. Pull it and the box runs that program from
start to stop in a single move. That’s how the register machine below comes in,
and it’s the honest reading of “a Turing machine is a base” too. The levers are the
programs. They aren’t the rows.
    That still leaves a worry about clause (a) itself. It asks for one lever per two-
counter instruction, which is a fact about how the two-counter machine is presented,
and a box that does each instruction in several pulls looks shut out for a reason
that has nothing to do with computing. It isn’t shut out, and the fix is to let the
pulls be grouped. Call a box a base by simulation when it has a window reading
a two-counter configuration off each state, through any encoding at all, a class of
live states, a finite list of its own levers for each two-counter instruction, and a live
loaded state showing (1, a, b) for each start, such that from every live state the list
acts on the window exactly as the instruction acts on a configuration and the state
stays live. The grouped box has the same states, and its levers are finite lists of the
box’s levers, a list pulled in order.


Theorem E.3 (The one-lever presentation loses nothing). (1) Every box with a
universal base is a base by simulation. (2) Every base by simulation is a universal
base of its grouped box, and a run of the grouped box is the box’s run along the
joined lists. (3) So for every base by simulation, the lift of its grouped box, with
the window claims and a fact table with room for at least one fact, is certified
Thiele-complete. (4) The box with five levers, add one to A and go to the next line,
the same for B, add one to a jump target (leaving the window alone), and for each
of A and B “if it’s above 0, take one off and jump to the target, otherwise go to the
next line, and put the target back to 0 either way,” is a base by simulation, has no
universal base, and its grouped box lifts to a certified Thiele-complete machine.

Proof. (1) Each list has one lever. (2) The grouped box’s step is the box’s run along
the list, so the simulation clause of a base by simulation is clause (a) for the grouped
box. (3) is (2) with Theorem E.1. (4) INC r is one pull; DEC r j is j pulls of the
target lever, then the decrement lever for r, from a live state, where live means the
540   E Every model


              target is 0; the decrement lever puts the target back to 0, so the state stays live. The
              box has five levers, so item (1) of Theorem E.2 says it has no universal base.
                  So clause (a) can be read by simulation, and nothing is lost: a box that simulates
              two counters in finite runs of its own moves, through any window, is a universal
              base the moment its moves are grouped, and it lifts. Item (1) of Theorem E.2 is
              about the presentation, and the five-lever box is the proof that a finite lever set is
              not what fails. What this doesn’t give is a Turing machine’s rule table running a
              tape: the five-lever box is a register box, and the next subsection is still how Turing
              machines come in.
                  Item (3) is a box with no memory. Pull a lever and it lands wherever that
              lever always lands, whatever happened before. So a window on it can’t tell INC A
              followed by INC A from INC B followed by INC A, and a box that can’t tell those
              apart can’t keep two counters in its window.
                  Item (4) is the trouble with bare preorders from Section 11, where the cups
              stopped telling you the place, showing up one level higher. If every place on the axis
              is at or below every other, the flag has no up to go to. No step ever turns a cup over,
              nothing ever owes a mark, and the earned chain has nothing to earn.


              E.3 The same thing, in seven models
              Now the other direction, the one the worry was really about. Put boxes with different
              insides in a row: one with a tape, one rewriting lambda terms, one with bins. Is a
              panel riding on one of them the same as a panel riding on another? The honest way
              to ask is whether the boxes agree on what they compute.
                  My first idea was to wire the boxes to each other myself, two at a time, with a
              relation that says one box’s run keeps pace with another’s. That’s the wrong tool.
              Section 10’s weak base equivalence is about runs keeping pace, and what I need
              here is coarser: do the boxes compute the same relations on numbers? For that the
              work is already done, and it isn’t mine. The seven models are the weak call-by-value
              lambda calculus L, Turing machines, two Minsky instruction conventions, binary
              stack machines, Conway’s FRACTRAN, and the µ-recursive functions, and that they
              all compute the same things is Minsky’s, Shepherdson and Sturgis’s, and Forster,
              Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors’ work. The translations, with how each one
              writes its inputs and reads its outputs, are in Appendix K.


              Theorem E.4 (The base doesn’t matter). (1) A relation on numbers that’s com-
              putable in any one of those seven models is computable in all seven. (2) The box
              that keeps a whole two-counter configuration in one number, with one lever for
              each instruction, has a universal base, its step is computable in all seven models,
                                                                E.3 The same thing, in seven models   541


and its lift, with a table of sixteen facts, is certified Thiele-complete. (3) A register
machine of the kind Cook and Reckhow described, where each two-counter instruc-
tion compiles to at most six of its own instructions, has a universal base too, and its
lift is certified Thiele-complete. (4) Any box on numbers with a universal base lifts
to a certified Thiele-complete machine, and its step, computable in one model, is
computable in all seven.

Proof. (1) Compose the translations of Appendix K. (2) Encode a configuration as
⟨ℓ, ⟨ a, b⟩⟩. Decoding, performing one INC or DEC, and encoding the result are the
total finite arithmetic operations constructed there. So the window follows each
instruction exactly; loading is the encoding of (1, a, b). (3) Let RAM registers 0, 1
and 2 hold the simulated line, A and B, and keep register 3 equal to 1. To increment
counter register r, add register 3 to r and then to register 0. To decrement it with
target j, use these six lines, numbered 0 to 5: if r > 0 jump to 3; add register 3 to
register 0; jump to 6; subtract register 3 from r; set register 0 to j; jump to 6. At
line 6 the finite block has ended. A base move restarts a block at its first line, runs it
for its length, and keeps the resulting registers; an ended block stays put. The zero
and positive cases give exactly the required window, and neither changes register
3. Loading puts (1, a, b, 1) in registers 0 to 3. (4) Apply the lift theorem to that
universal base and apply (1) to its step function.
    So the answer to the worry is that the record doesn’t care. A box with a universal
base, described in any of the models people have used to say what computing is,
takes the same panel, becomes the same kind of machine, and pays the same three
marks for the same three acts.
    And the trip goes back down. So far the panel went onto other boxes. Now
put another box, panel and all, inside mine. Appendix D.2 proved that the fixed
program UP on the small machine’s host runs every computably presented Thiele
machine. In terms of the seven models, that reads: if the four relations that describe
a machine (its driver, which picks the next move or says stop, its step, its cost and its
reading, on codes) are computed in any one of the seven by programs that answer
on every input, then the machine is computably presented, and UP runs it, halting
when it halts, with its flag, and with a surcharge of at most two when its reading
starts at no.
    So a Thiele machine described in lambda calculus runs, under one fixed program,
on the small machine’s host. That’s model independence in both directions: up, by
lifting any universal base, and down, by running anything presentable on one fixed
program. When I saw both arrows close I stopped worrying that I’d built a trick for
one toy. A trick for one toy wouldn’t survive being carried both ways.
542   E Every model


              E.4 Why two counters
              If the box doesn’t matter, why did I build on two bins? Because I wanted the smallest
              box that holds up, and the obvious smaller one has a single bin. Nothing earlier in
              this book says one bin is too few. So before I’d let myself say two is the fewest, I
              tried one.
                  Watch what a program on one bin can see. While the bin isn’t empty, it can’t
              tell how full it is: a stretch of lines that never finds the bin empty does exactly the
              same thing from a fuller bin, with the extra pebbles riding along. So the only news a
              one-bin program ever gets is the bin running dry. Between two of those moments it’s
              just walking its own lines, and among more moments than there are lines, two are
              on the same line, which is the pigeonhole again. Put those together and a one-bin
              program either stops within a count you can write down in advance, or never stops
              at all.


              Theorem E.5 (One counter is too few). (1) A program P of INC, DEC and HALT
              instructions on one bin, started with n pebbles in it, halts exactly when it has stopped
              within k (n + k + 1) steps, where k is the number of lines in P. So whether it halts is
              decidable. (2) Halting for the book’s two-counter machine is undecidable. (3) So no
              computable translation takes each two-counter program and start to a one-counter
              program and start that halts exactly when the original does.

              Proof. (1) If k = 0, the program has already stopped. Otherwise suppose it is
              still running after T = k (n + k + 1) steps, so the T + 1 configurations at times
              0, 1, . . . , T are all live. If the counter has stayed at most n + k up to time T, those
              live configurations have only k (n + k + 1) = T possibilities: k lines and n + k + 1
              counter values. There are T + 1 of them, so one repeats, and the deterministic run
              loops forever.
                  If instead the counter reached n + k + 1 by time T, take the first time it did, and
              look back to the last time before that when it was at most n. In between it stayed
              above n, so above 0. It moves at most one per step, so on the way up it arrived at
              each of the k + 1 levels n + 1, . . . , n + k + 1; mark the first arrival at each. There
              are k + 1 arrivals and k lines, so two arrivals have the same line ℓ, at levels a < b.
              Every DEC in the stretch between them found the counter positive. Start that same
              stretch at level b: every counter value is larger by b − a, so still positive, every DEC
              goes the same way, and the run comes back to line ℓ at level 2b − a. Repeat forever.
              Either way a run still live at time T never stops, so a run that stops does so within T
              steps, and running P for T steps decides it. (2) The tape simulation, prime packing
              and halting diagonal of Appendix K, carried over to the book’s instruction set line by
                                                                 E.5 What this appendix doesn’t say   543


line. (3) Such a translation, followed by the test in (1), would decide two-counter
halting, against (2).
   So two counters are the fewest in exactly this sense: one counter can’t compute
everything, because its halting can be decided, and two, handed their inputs packed,
can. I like where the answer came from. The pigeonhole that left no spare chair in
the closed room is the same one that says why the box has two bins.


E.5 What this appendix doesn’t say

A panel that bolts onto anything is an easy picture to hear too much in, so here are
four things the appendix might be heard to say, and doesn’t. First, it doesn’t prove “a
lift is certified Thiele-complete exactly when its base is universal” as one equivalence.
It proves the upward direction, the converse for every certified Thiele-complete
machine’s own base moves, and the two kinds of base that never lift. Second, the lift
does not itself give each Turing transition a record operation. The tape-to-counter
construction of Appendix K connects the bases through what they compute; the lift
supplies the record operations. Third, the lift’s tally is one version number for the
whole machine. It doesn’t keep one per register, the way the small machine keeps
one per counter. That’s coarser, and it’s enough for every theorem above. Fourth,
it doesn’t show that a lifted machine is computably presented in general. The trip
down needs the four relations, and for a particular machine somebody has to supply
them.
     If you want the whole appendix in one sentence: any box with a universal base
takes the panel, and any box written down by programs that always answer runs
inside mine.
     I went into this appendix looking for the place where the bins were doing secret
work for the panel. I didn’t find one, and the four items above are where I’d send
anybody who wants to look harder.
APPENDIX F




Built from parts

Back in Section 2 I asked a question and only got halfway: bolt two Thiele machines
together, and do you get one? Everything real is built out of parts. A computer is
a processor and memory and a disk, a bank is branches, a proof is lemmas. If the
record and its toll only held for one machine at a time and fell apart the moment
you put two together, they’d be a property of toys.
    So put two Thiele machines on a bench, each box with its own panel, and wire
them up the three ways anybody wires machines. Side by side, with no wire between
them at all, so that every move is a lever pulled on one box or the other. End to
end, with the first box’s bins tipped into the second’s when the first is done. And
one inside the other, with the inner box running as a guest on the outer one. Some
of it holds. Some of it provably doesn’t, and the places where it doesn’t were where
I learned the most.


F.1 Side by side
Two boxes on the bench, no wire between them. A move of the pair is a lever pulled
on one box or the other. The question is what the pair’s record should be, and my
first answer was the wrong one: a single count of how many certifications the bench
has made. One number, easy to read. I’ll come back to why it fails, because it’s in
the list of things that break. What works is to keep both panels showing. The pair’s
record is the pair of records, a place for the left machine and a place for the right
one, compared one side at a time.
    Since that record has more than two places, “certified Thiele-complete” in this
appendix means the definition of Section 15 with the record allowed to be a place
along a direction, the way Section 11 set it up. The old definition had a single bit
there, and at two places this one is exactly the old one.


Theorem F.1 (Side by side). (1) The cost of any run of the pair is the left machine’s
cost of its moves plus the right machine’s cost of its moves, and the order in which
levers on the two boxes were interleaved doesn’t change where the pair ends up or
what it paid. (2) The pair pays the toll exactly when both machines do. (3) Read
through “either flag is up,” two Thiele machines side by side are a Thiele machine

                                544
                                                                                   F.1 Side by side   545
