with floor one; read through “both flags are up,” a run that starts with both flags
down and ends with both up costs at least two, and two is reached when each part
can certify for one. (4) Two certified Thiele-complete machines side by side are a
certified Thiele-complete machine. (5) In that pair, call a side’s floor the place on
its record axis where its clean states sit. A run from a clean start that ends with
each side at or above a point that isn’t at or below that side’s floor makes at least
six record moves and raises the ledger by at least six. Six is reached, from suitable
loaded starts, by a three-act certificate on each side; a particular pair of target points
can need more. (6) The pair of records is the product in the precise sense: for any
machine mapping into both, preserving records, there’s exactly one map into the
pair that does both jobs.

Proof. (1) A move of the pair is a lever of one box. It moves that box’s component by
that box’s step, leaves the other component alone, and costs what that box charges
for it. So the pair’s run is the pair of the two boxes’ runs along the projections of the
trace, each box’s moves in the order they came, and the cost is the left projection’s
cost plus the right’s. Two interleavings with the same two projections end in the
same state at the same cost. (2) The toll prices a step that takes the record out of
the down-set of where it stood. A pair is at or below another when both sides are,
so the down-set of a pair is the two down-sets side by side, and a move of the left
box leaves the pair’s down-set exactly when it leaves the left down-set, the right
side not having moved. So the pair’s exits are the left exits and the right exits, each
priced by its own box, and the pair pays the toll exactly when both parts do; for
the converse, an exit at zero marks on one side is an exit at zero marks of the pair
with any state at all on the other. (3) Read through “either flag is up,” a step from
neither to either raises one side’s flag, and that side charges it at least one, so the
pair is a Thiele machine with floor one. Read through “both flags are up,” a run
from both down to both up raises each side’s flag on some step, no move touches
both, and each such step costs at least one; when each part can certify for one, the
two certificates one after the other cost two. (4) Give the pair the interface that
reads a move as its own box reads it, takes a claim to be a claim of one side, about
that side’s component and unchanged when that component is unchanged, with
both sides clean as clean, both sides loaded as loaded, the sum of the ledgers as
ledger, and the left box’s window as window. Clause (a) is the left box’s clause (a),
since a left base move acts on the left window as its instruction does and a right
move doesn’t touch the left component, and no base move of either side changes
either record. Clause (c) is the two price lists added. Clause (d) is the left box’s
witness claim with the right box idle. Clause (b) is the one with work in it. Take a
run from both clean that ends with the pair’s record raised, not at or below where it
began. Pairs compare side by side, so on one side the record ends not at or below
546   F Built from parts


               where that side began. Project the run onto that side: a run from clean that ends
               with that side’s record raised, so by that side’s clause (b) it contains that side’s chain,
               a passing CHECK of a claim c, a COMMIT of c with c’s component unchanged in
               between, and a CERTIFY. Put the other side’s moves back where they were. None of
               them touches the component c is about, so the chain is a chain of the interleaved
               run. (5) If a side ends at or above a point that isn’t at or below its floor, its record
               ends not at or below its floor either, or the point would be at or below the floor by
               passing through it. The clean start puts that side at its floor, so the projection onto
               that side is a run from clean with its record raised, which by that side’s clause (b)
               has three record moves of its own, a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY. The two
               sides’ moves are different moves, so six record moves at least, and by (c) a ledger
               rise of at least six; a three-act certificate on each side, from loaded starts where each
               side’s witness claim holds, makes exactly six. (6) A record-preserving map from a
               machine Z into a box is a map of states with a monotone map of records, the record
               of the image being the image of the record, and every move of Z simulated by some
               run of the box. Given one into each box, send a state of Z to the pair of its images.
               The record of the pair is the pair of the records, and a move of Z is simulated by the
               left box’s run followed by the right box’s, which is a run of the pair by (1). That map
               followed by either projection is the map you started with, and any map into the pair
               with those two projections agrees with it on every state, which is what equal maps
               means here.
                  Most of that is what you’d guess from the bench. Each box keeps its own ledger
               and nobody else pulls its levers, so the bills add, and it can’t matter which box you
               happened to work on first. The six in (5) is two certifications of three marks each,
               one per box, with no discount for doing them on the same bench.
                  Machines, with maps that keep the record, form a category, and item (6) says
               these pairs are its products. Ask the maps to keep the bill too and the pair stops
               being a product: a machine mapped into both boxes would pay its bill once on each
               side, twice in all. What survives is a symmetric monoidal structure, which is all that
               side by side needs. Its pentagon, triangle and hexagon laws say that regrouping
               four boxes, inserting an idle box, or exchanging groups of boxes gives the same final
               wiring whichever permitted route you take. Label the boxes and follow each wire:
               every rewiring only moves boxes around, so both routes put each wire at the same
               labelled terminal, at the same cost.
                  That paragraph is the most formal way I know of saying “side by side composes,
               and nothing about the order of the parts matters.” It’s a lot of category theory to
               confirm what the bench told me in a glance, and I’m glad to have it anyway. A
               glance is where I’d have missed something.
                                                                           F.2 One after the other   547


F.2 One after the other
Now wire them end to end. Run the first box, and when it’s done, tip its two bins
into the second box’s start, at no charge on the ledger, and run the second. That’s
how programs get chained everywhere, and my first thought was that the tipping
couldn’t matter. It’s plumbing. Pebbles go from one bin into another, nobody checks
anything, and plumbing has no business on a record. That turned out to be half
right, and the wrong half is item (4).


Theorem F.2 (One after the other). (1) Running one certified Thiele-complete
machine and then handing its two counters to another through loads that cost no
marks gives a certified Thiele-complete machine. (2) For any two programs of the
two-counter machine, it computes the composite: some schedule leaves the first
machine’s window where the first program takes the input, and the second’s where
the second program takes that result. (3) The hand-off keeps the toll when every
state it can load into sits at one level of the second machine’s record. (4) If some
load lands the second machine at a record that isn’t at or below another load’s, the
hand-off loses the toll: it’s a certification nobody paid a mark for.

Proof. (1) Give the second machine a loadable form. A state is either pristine,
holding the second machine’s loaded state for some ( a, b), or running, a state of the
second machine. A move LOAD ( a, b) turns a pristine state into the pristine state for
( a, b) and does nothing to a running one; the second machine’s own moves move a
running state as before and turn a pristine state into a running one. LOAD is a base
move and costs no marks. When the second machine is certified Thiele-complete its
loaded states are clean and stand at the floor, so a LOAD leaves the record alone;
the base, the toll and the witness claim are the second machine’s; and the chain
in front of a raise lies after the last LOAD before the second machine’s first move,
so it lifts through the projection onto the second machine’s own moves. So the
loadable form is certified Thiele-complete, and the composite, the first machine
side by side with it, is certified Thiele-complete by Theorem F.1(4). (2) A wired
schedule is the first machine’s moves, then a LOAD of the two counters its window
shows at that moment, then the second machine’s moves. The first stretch runs the
first program on the first window; the LOAD puts the second window at (1, a, b) for
the counters ( a, b) the first stretch left; the last stretch runs the second program on
it. If both programs halt, the two windows after the schedule are the two halting
configurations, the second’s on the first’s output, and the wire cost no marks. (3)
and (4) are one fact read two ways. A LOAD from the pristine state for one input to
the pristine state for another costs no marks, and carries the record from where the
first loaded state stands to where the second stands. If every loaded state stands at
548   F Built from parts


               one level, no LOAD moves the record, the composite’s exits are the two machines’
               own, and the toll is kept by Theorem F.1(2). If some loaded state stands at a record
               not at or below another’s, the LOAD from that other one to it, at zero marks, leaves
               a down-set, which is an exit nobody paid for, and the toll fails.
                  Item (4) is the one to remember. The tipping costs no marks, so it had better
               not tip in anything that counts as established. If pouring pebbles into the second
               box can land its panel somewhere that isn’t at or below where some other pouring
               would land it, the second machine gets a raised record without ever having checked
               anything. That’s a forged certificate wearing the costume of plumbing. My first
               thought was right about the pebbles. It was wrong about where they land.


               F.3 What doesn’t compose

               Here’s the list of things I tried to build on the bench that fell apart, each with a proof
               that it does. Every one of them started as a reasonable-looking wiring job.


               Theorem F.3 (What breaks). (1) Read the pair through “both flags are up” as a
               single flag, and any run that raises it from a clean start makes at least six record
               moves; the definition of certified Thiele-complete asks for a claim that three moves
               can certify, so through the pair’s own interface that reading fails the non-vacuity
               clause. (2) Two clocks side by side obey the toll with a two-counter machine inside.
               They aren’t Thiele-complete, so composing that easy bar composes nothing. (3)
               Give the small machine a second writer that changes counter A without raising its
               version, and the run “check that A is 0, let the other writer change A, commit, certify”
               raises the flag, so the earned-record clause fails when the machine is read the small
               machine’s way, with the second writer as a base move. (4) Two windows that each
               price their own machine exactly can collide as a pair, so exact pricing isn’t preserved
               by putting machines together. (5) Count the pair’s certifications with one number,
               and the count can’t tell which side certified. The pair of records can.

               Proof. (1) Through the pair’s interface, a run from a clean start that raises “both flags
               are up” ends with each side’s record raised, and by Theorem F.1(5) that takes at least
               six record moves. Clause (d) asks for a claim whose CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY,
               those three moves alone, raise the record from a loaded state. Three moves aren’t six,
               so (d) fails for that reading. (2) A clock is the two-counter machine with every move
               priced at one and a reading over it (Observation 15.22). Two side by side have a two-
               counter machine running inside, the left’s, and pay the toll by Theorem F.1(2); and
               every move of the pair is a move of one clock, costing one, while a Thiele-complete
               machine has a move that costs no marks (Theorem 10.12(5)). (3) Add to the small
                                                                         F.3 What doesn’t compose   549


machine a writer that changes counter A and leaves its version alone, read as a
base move. The run CHECK (A is 0), the writer’s move, COMMIT (A is 0), CERTIFY,
from a start with A at 0, passes its CHECK, finds its fact at the unchanged version
at the COMMIT, and raises the flag at the CERTIFY. The base and toll clauses still
hold, and so does the checker’s promise. What fails is clause (b). The small machine
reads “unchanged” as same value and same version, and the only chain in that run
has the writer’s move between its CHECK and its COMMIT, where counter A, the
thing the claim is about, changed its value. The COMMIT didn’t notice, because
it looks only at the version, and the version didn’t move. So a run from a clean
start raises the record with no earned chain in it. (4) Take a left box whose only
step its window doesn’t see is a certifying one, so the window still prices it exactly,
charging that unseen transition one; and a right box whose only step is a stutter, at
zero marks, leaving its down-set alone and its window unchanged, priced exactly
at zero. In the pair, the left box’s unseen certifying step and the right box’s stutter
show the same pair of windows before and after. One costs at least one and leaves
the pair’s down-set; the other costs no marks and doesn’t. So a price computed from
the pair of windows is short on the first or over on the second. (5) Replace the pair
of records by the number of sides that have certified. A run in which only the left
side certifies and one in which only the right side does both reach the count one,
with the left record raised in the first and at its floor in the second. The count can’t
tell them apart; the pair of records can.
    Item (1) is one flag for two boxes. It costs what two certifications cost, six record
moves, and the definition wants a claim that three can settle, so a single flag over
both panels, read through the pair’s interface, is too expensive to meet the definition.
That’s this interface. Nothing here shows that no other interface on the pair could
meet it, and Theorem F.1(4) shows the pair meeting it through a richer record. Item
(4) says that a window exact for each box alone can be fooled by the pair: two pair
states with different costs can show the same pair of readings.
    Item (3) is the one with the most teeth, because it’s the bug from Section 14, the
file checked and then swapped. On the bench it’s a second hand reaching into a bin
while the box isn’t looking. Two writers, one value, and a check that’s out of date
by the time anybody leans on it. The small machine’s version rule is exactly the fix,
and this is what happens without it: the commitment goes through on a claim about
a thing that changed underneath it. Database people and the people who build
processors have been fighting this one since at least Kung and Robinson’s paper of
1981 and the Livermore report of 1987, and that section gave it the security people’s
name, time of check to time of use. Here it’s a theorem about the record, and the
version number is what makes it go away. The second hand can still reach in. With
the version, its reach shows on the tally, and the COMMIT traps.
550   F Built from parts


                  Item (5) is my first guess from the side-by-side wiring, coming back to fail on
               schedule. It’s why the pair’s record compares one side at a time. Squash the two
               records into one number and the record forgets who did the work, and a record that
               forgets who did the work isn’t one anybody can lean on.


               F.4 One inside another

               The last way to wire the bench: put one box inside the other, as a guest on a
               host. Part of this the book already has. The appendix on the universal machines
               (Appendix D.2) showed the fixed program UP runs any computably presented Thiele
               machine, and the small machine’s own programs, with the record earned again by
               the host. What’s new is putting those links in a row, a box in a box in a box, and
               asking what the outermost one pays.
                  My first guess was that it could pay less. A host that’s clever about how it runs
               the guest might skip some of the guest’s bills. The first item below puts a floor under
               that: the host pays at least one for each step where the guest’s record went up. It’s a
               floor on rises, and it doesn’t keep the guest’s whole bill.


               Theorem F.4 (Nesting). (1) Let a host that pays the toll simulate a guest faithfully,
               with a record map that reflects the order. Say a run of the host follows a run of
               the guest when it splits into one stretch of host moves for each guest step, each
               stretch carrying the image of the state before that step to the image of the state after
               it. Every run of the guest has a host run that follows it, every such host run ends
               on the image of the guest’s end state, and every host run that follows a guest run
               costs at least the number of the guest’s steps that turned a cup over. A host run that
               only ends on the image of the guest’s end state can cost less. (2) In each link the
               surcharge is 0 while the guest’s record is down, and the bounds below hold at the
               points where it’s up. A small-machine guest on UP is carried with surcharge exactly
               0. A computably presented machine whose reading starts at no is carried, through
               its compiled guest, with surcharge at most 2, and, when every move costs at most
               one, exactly 2 once its reading has first said yes. One whose reading starts at yes is
               carried with surcharge exactly 3. (3) Links compose, and their surcharges add: a
               tower of k links has surcharge between the sums of their lower and upper bounds.
               (4) A tower of presented machines, each level running the next on UP , adds exactly
               2 for every level above the first, on top of the first level’s own surcharge, provided
               every level’s host run is itself presented by the next.
                                                                           F.4 One inside another   551


Proof. (1) The simulation gives, for each guest move, a list of host moves carrying
the image of the state before it to the image of the state after it. String those lists
together along the guest run: that host run follows it, and it ends on the image of
the guest’s end state, because each stretch ends where the next begins. Now take
any host run that follows the guest run, and a guest step that turned a cup over,
leaving the down-set of its record. Its stretch carries the image of the state before to
the image of the state after, and since the record map reflects the order, the image
after isn’t at or below the image before, or the guest’s record after would be at or
below the record before. If every host move in that stretch ended at or below where
it started, then chaining them, the end of the stretch would be at or below its start;
so some host move in it ends not at or below where it started, leaving the down-set
of where it stood, and the host, paying the toll, charges that move at least one.
Different guest steps have different stretches, so the charges add up to at least the
number of such steps. The end alone isn’t enough: a guest on one cup that turns
it over and turns it back has one rise and ends where it started, and the host run
that does nothing reaches the image of the end state at no marks. (2) A link from a
guest to a host matches every point of the guest’s run with a point of the host’s, with
the record bits equal there and the host’s ledger the guest’s plus a surcharge, the
surcharge 0 while the record is down and between the link’s two bounds once it’s
up, and halting and the record’s first rising matching. A small-machine guest run by
UP is a link with surcharge exactly 0: that is the ledger equality of Appendix D.1,
carried to UP . A computably presented machine run as its compiled guest is a link
with surcharge at most 2 from a reading that starts at no and exactly 3 from one
that starts at yes, which is Theorem D.8; once the reading has first said yes the
surcharge is the larger of 3 − c and 0, with c what the raising move cost, since the
host pays the larger of c and 3 there, and when every move costs at most one, c is
exactly one, the toll making it at least one, so the surcharge is exactly 2. (3) Match
the points through the middle: a point of the bottom run has a matching point of
the middle run, which has a matching point of the top run; the record bits agree
along the way; the top ledger is the bottom ledger plus both surcharges, which is 0
while the record is down and between the sum of the lower bounds and the sum
of the upper bounds once it’s up; halting and the first rising pass through. A tower
of k links is that, k − 1 times. (4) Each level above the first is, by the hypothesis, a
presented machine whose run is the level below’s host run, carried as its compiled
guest on UP . Its moves are the host’s moves, which cost 0 or 1 marks, so by (2) that
link adds exactly 2 once the record is up, and by (3) the additions stack on the first
level’s own surcharge.
  Item (1) is the cleanest sentence in the appendix. However you build the outer
box, as long as it pays its own toll and doesn’t lie about the inner box’s record, it
552   F Built from parts


               pays at least one for every step where the inner record climbed, on every run that
               keeps pace with the inner box step by step. The keeping pace is needed. A guest
               that turns a cup over and then turns it back ends where it started, and the host can
               reach that image by doing nothing at all, at no charge on its ledger. The step by step
               floor is the guest’s rises paid one by one; the end alone can’t see them. That’s a floor
               on the climbs, and it isn’t the inner box’s whole bill. A guest can charge a hundred
               for one rise while a host charges one for the matching rise, and both pay their tolls.
               Keeping the whole bill takes a further demand on the simulation, that it carry the
               guest’s costs too, and for UP that’s the separate ledger theorem of Appendix D.2,
               with its surcharge.
                   The premise in (4) is a real limit, and I want to say exactly what it is. Two links
               are unconditional: from a presented machine to its compiled guest, and from that
               guest to UP running it. Going deeper needs the host’s own run, at each level, to be
               presented as a machine the next level up can run, and the host keeps a register for
               every whole number, which doesn’t have a one-to-one code in a single number the
               way a presented machine needs. So the box that has to fit inside the next one has
               more states than there are numbers to name them. For three levels and more, the
               theorem says what happens if each level is presented. It doesn’t claim that it always
               is.


               F.5 What this adds up to
              Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a Thiele machine on the
              bench stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What breaks,
              breaks for reasons you could name before you saw the proof: a single flag for two
              claims costs two claims’ worth, a clock is still a clock, a shared value without a
              version can’t be trusted, and a hand-off that costs no marks can’t be allowed to carry
              a certificate. None of those is a surprise in hindsight. All of them are now theorems,
              and the composition question from Section 2 has an answer. Two Thiele machines
              side by side are one under both readings I tried, “either flag” and “both flags.” The
              “both flags” reading still fails the definition of certified Thiele-complete through the
              pair’s interface, the second writer breaks the earned-record clause through the small
              machine’s own reading, the clocks and the two counterexamples fail outright, and
              simulation in general has a proved floor.
                 Three of my first guesses on this bench were wrong: the single count, the
              harmless tipping, and the clever host that pays less. The last two leaned toward a
              record that says more than anybody paid for, and the first toward one that says less
              than it should. I didn’t see any of the three coming. The proofs did.
APPENDIX G




Running it

Everything so far is definitions and proofs about them. Does any of it run? This
appendix is me finding out. I built the small machine twice, once straight out of the
definitions and once by hand from the same description, ran both, and compared
the whole state after every step. Then I ran the universal programs on guests small
enough to finish, and real programs through the part of the compiler that executes.
   One rule for the whole appendix. The runs test the builds, and the proofs carry
the theorems. A run shows what a build did on the inputs it was given, and no
theorem in the book leans on one: every theorem in it stands on its argument, on
the page.
   Two counts to keep apart as you read. The ledger counts what the price list
charges. The number of interpreter steps counts the work this particular build does
to carry the run out. One guest step can take millions of host steps and add one
mark to the ledger. Every one of those host steps gives off heat on the hardware that
runs it, and the ledger counts none of that heat. The times only tell you which runs
are practical on this build. Here’s what ran and what didn’t.

              G.1 Taking the coat off
              The first executable is generated straight from the formal definitions, the way you’d
              strip the coat off a proof and keep the program underneath. The second was written
              separately, by hand, from the same description. Both implement the small machine,
              the host with a register for every whole number, the host with PAY, the universal
              programs and the loaders. The compiler below has an executable runner too.
                  Whole numbers matter here. A machine word in one build is 63 bits wide, and the
              guest codes U reads go up past 2100 , so ordinary fixed-width arithmetic would wrap
              around and lie. The mathematical machine never overflows, so its executable uses
              integers of any size, with the arithmetic chosen to match the definitions: subtraction
              stops at zero and division by zero gives zero. What sits between the definitions and
              the running code, the mappings, the compilers and the routines that read input and
              write output, is code I had to trust.


              G.2 A second machine, written by hand, to check the first
              Comparing two builds step by step catches one of them disagreeing with the descrip-
              tion, on the runs I tried. They’re compared on the whole state after every step: the
              program line, every counter and register and its version, the fact table in order, the
              channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag. The comparison covers exhaustive
              sets of short programs, random programs and both hosts, and they agree on every
              tested step. U and UP on tiny guests are compared at checkpoints spaced along the
              run instead of after every step, and the longer runs below against a separate guest
              implementation, once per pass of the loop and at the stop. I also broke the machine
              on purpose, giving it a fact table one too small, a CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY
              that cost no marks, a commitment that ignores versions, and a write that doesn’t
              bump the version, and each break gets caught. A second set pins the boundaries this
              book draws in words, and those runs come out as the words say: two runs that end
              in the same state with different first certifications, a check that can’t fail certifying
              from every start, a CHECK and six commitments billing seven without a flag, a write
              after the commitment and a flag over a claim that’s now false, sixteen copies of one
              CHECK filling the table, a CERTIFY costing one at a ledger already at two, and a
              merge between two yes-states that leaves the entering state alone.
                  A mistake both builds share gets past the comparison, and so does a mistake in
              the definitions themselves, since both builds follow them.


              G.3 U on a real guest
              Now the universal program, which is where I expected trouble. The guest I wanted
              to run first was the obvious one, a guest that goes the whole way: CHECK, COMMIT,
                                                                          G.3 U on a real guest   555


CERTIFY, flag up, run inside U on the built machine. Here’s why that’s not what
ran. U keeps the whole guest program as one number, a number that grows like
two raised to the sum of the codes for the guest’s instructions (for a guest of one
instruction it’s exactly a power of two), and it reads that number the only way a
counter can, one unit at a time. So its speed depends on the code, and the code
grows fast: a guest with one CHECK in it has code 224 , and a guest with the whole
chain has a code near 2106 .
    So I came down to what could finish. Here’s what ran, on the executable host,
compared against a separate guest implementation at every pass of the loop and at
the stop: the host stopped exactly when the guest did, and at the stop showed the
guest’s counters, trap latch, ledger and flag.

about 650,000 steps a second it would take something like twenty-two hours, nearly

been run. Runs this long only fit in memory at all because the build can repack the
host’s register store in the middle of a run; repacking changes how the registers are
stored, not what they hold.
    What a run that long can be is counted. All of U’s time goes into four loop shapes
from Appendix L, the ones that empty a register, copy it, copy it twice and halve it,
and each repeats one pass a known number of times: for a register at v, emptying
takes v + 1 steps, copying 2v + 1, copying twice 3v + 1, and halving three for every
two in v. Replace each loop by its count, step every other instruction one at a time
with the host’s own step, and the counts are exact as long as the four closed forms
are. The script scripts/count_universal_run.py does that, checks the four forms

              G.4 From source programs to the host

              Running guests one CHECK at a time doesn’t tell you whether the built machine
              can do anything you’d recognise as a program. You’d want to hand it gcd, or a
              sort, written the way people write them, and get the answer out, and writing gcd
              by hand in INC and DEC is no way to find out. So the last piece of the build
              is a compiler. The source is a small language you could write by hand: whole-
              number variables, addition, subtraction that stops at zero, comparisons, if, while,
              and procedures that return several results, with the rule that a procedure can only
              call ones defined before it, so there’s no recursion. Each translation stage has a
              proof that it preserves the program’s result: the procedures are inlined, the result is
              flattened to assignments and jumps, that is compiled to Minsky’s counter machine
              through the counter-machine compiler, that to a program for the host machine, that
              to a two-counter guest, and the guest to a run of UP .


              Theorem G.1 (The compiler is correct). For every source program with no recursion,
              and every input: the program computes y exactly when the runner (the bounded
              evaluator of the compiled host program) halts with y for some amount of fuel;
              exactly when the compiled host program halts with y; exactly when the two-counter
              guest halts with y; and exactly when UP running that guest halts with y, with its first
              counter at 0, its ledger at 0 and its flag down. So a terminating compiled program
              delivers its answer and certifies nothing. To certify a claim about that answer, a
              target program must add a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY; this compiler does
                                                             G.4 From source programs to the host   557


not insert that chain. The runner also takes exactly as many steps as the host
program does, with the rest of its fuel left over, and a run that doesn’t halt has used
all its fuel.

Proof. Six arrows and a runner, each argued below, and the statement is their
composition. Four of the arrows are between machines that take steps, and for those
one argument does both directions, so I give it first.
    The simulation argument. Take two machines S and T, each deterministic, where
S has a next state from every state inside its program, and a relation ∼ between
their states such that: a state of S inside its program is related only to states of T
inside its program, and a state of S outside it only to states of T outside it; and
from any related pair with S inside its program, one step of S is matched by one or
more steps of T that land related to S’s next state. Then from related starts, S halts
exactly when T does, and they halt related. Forward: induction on the length of S’s
run, one matched stretch per step, gives a run of T ending related to S’s last state,
which is outside S’s program, so T’s is outside its own. Backward: suppose T halts
after k steps and S doesn’t halt. Then S takes at least k + 1 steps without leaving
its program, the matched stretches give T a run of at least k + 1 steps all of whose
stretch ends are inside its program, and T, being deterministic, has only one run
from its start, which halted at step k. That’s a contradiction, so S halts, and by the
forward direction it halts related to where T did.
    Unfolding the calls. A procedure may only call procedures with smaller numbers,
so unfold them in order of number: procedure 0 calls nothing, and the unfolded
body of procedure i is built from the already unfolded bodies of the procedures
below i. The construction ends. The variables live in one global space. The main
program’s frame is variables 0 to n0 − 1, and a call made in a frame that starts
at b and has n variables becomes four pieces: assignments that put the argument
values into the callee’s frame, which starts at b + n; assignments that set the callee’s
other locals to 0; the callee’s unfolded body, with each of its variables x read as
global variable b + n + x; and assignments that copy its results into the caller’s
variables. Say a global state G carries a source state e in the frame at b when
G (b + x ) = e( x ) for every x of the frame. Forward, by induction on the source
derivation: an assignment, a sequence, a test and a loop are the same statement in
both programs, read in the frame; for a call, the source derivation runs the callee’s
body from the frame of parameters and zeros, the first two pieces build exactly that
frame at b + n, the induction hypothesis on the callee’s (shorter) derivation runs
the unfolded body to a state carrying the callee’s final frame, and the copy writes
the results where the source call writes them. Every assignment in the compiled
statement writes in its own frame or the frames above it, so variables below b are
never touched. Backward, by induction on the derivation of the compiled statement:
558   G Running it


              the compiled statement has the source statement’s shape everywhere except at calls,
              and the derivation of a compiled call is a derivation of its four pieces in sequence,
              which the induction hypothesis turns back into a derivation of the callee’s body from
              the frame the source call would build. So the unfolded program has a derivation
              ending with y in the answer variable exactly when the original does, and neither
              has one when the program doesn’t terminate.
                  Flattening. The flat code of a statement placed at address a: an assignment is one
              assignment; a sequence is the first statement’s code followed by the second’s; if b is
              a jump on false to the else part, the then part, a jump past the else part, and the
              else part; and while b with a body of l instructions is a jump on false to a + l + 2,
              the body at a + 1, and a jump back to a. Every jump in the code of a statement
              lands inside that code or at its end, the address just past it. Forward, by induction
              on the derivation: a derivation from e to e1 gives a flat run from a with variables e
              to the end of the code with variables e1 . For a loop that runs its body once more,
              the test falls through, the body’s code takes the run to a + l + 1, the jump returns
              it to a, and the induction hypothesis on the rest of the loop’s derivation finishes.
              Backward, by induction on the statement and, inside that, on the length of the run:
              a flat run from a that ends anywhere outside the code passes through the end of the
              code, and the part up to its first visit there has a derivation of the statement. For a
              loop, the run’s first step is the test. If it is false, the run jumps to the end, and the
              loop’s derivation is the one with a false test. If it is true, the run enters the body’s
              code, which it can leave only through its end at a + l + 1 (the body’s own backward
              statement), where the jump returns it to a with a strictly shorter run left, to which
              the inner induction applies. So the flat program at address 1 halts exactly when the
              structured statement has a derivation, with the same final variables.
                  Counter machine. Here a DEC jumps when its register is zero and goes on
              otherwise. Variable x lives in register x + 1, register 0 is kept at 0, so DEC 0 j is a
              plain jump to j, and registers above the variables are working space. The relation:
              register 0 is 0, registers 1 to n hold the flat variables, and every register above is
              0. Each flat instruction becomes a block, and each block is built from small loops,
              each argued by induction on the number of passes. Emptying a register: each pass
              takes one off, and the loop exits at zero. Moving s into d: each pass takes one off s
              and adds one to d, so s + d never changes, and at exit s is 0 and d holds the old sum.
              Copying: move s into two registers at once, then move one of them back. Cut-off
              subtraction t − u: take one off each while both are positive; at exit one of them
              is 0, and the other holds the difference, or 0. Comparison: take one off each in
              step; whichever reaches zero first, or both together, decides < and =, and the block
              empties both. The code of an expression, by induction on the expression, leaves its
              value in a working register t and returns every register above t to 0, and leaves every
              register below t as it found it. The code of a test, by induction on the test, goes to its
                                                              G.4 From source programs to the host   559


true or false address and leaves every register as it found it. So an assignment block
computes the value into the first working register, empties register x + 1, moves
the value in, and lands related; a jump on false runs the test’s code with the true
exit at the next block and the false exit at the block of j; a jump is DEC 0 j. The
linker places the blocks one after another and sends every jump to the start of its
target’s block. That’s the one-step matching. The flat machine has a next state from
every address in its program, and an instruction that names a variable outside the
frame just advances, so the step is total. The counter machine is deterministic. The
simulation argument gives both directions: the counter program from the loaded
inputs leaves its code with register out + 1 equal to y exactly when the flat program
halts with y in out.
     Host. The host’s DEC is the other way round: it jumps when its register is positive,
taking one off, and goes on at zero. An INC x stays INC x. A DEC x j at host address
a becomes three instructions: DEC x ( a + 3), then INC 0, then DEC 0 j′ , where j′
is the host address of j’s block. If register x is positive, the first takes one off and
jumps to a + 3, the start of the next block, which is what the counter machine does.
If it is 0, the run goes on to INC 0, which raises register 0 to one more than it held,
and DEC 0 j′ finds it positive, takes the one back off and jumps to j′ , which is the
counter machine’s jump at zero, with register 0 as it was. The relation: the same
registers, at corresponding addresses. Each counter-machine step is matched by one
or three host steps. The host program has no CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY or PAY,
and INC and DEC change only a register and the line, at no marks, so every host
state in the run has the start’s facts, channel, trap latch, ledger and flag. The counter
machine’s step is total, the host is deterministic, and the simulation argument gives:
the host program halts with register out + 1 equal to y exactly when the counter
program leaves its code with that register equal to y.
     Guest. The host program’s registers r0 , . . . , rk−1 are packed into the guest’s
                     r
counter B as ∏i pi i , one prime pi per register, with counter A the spare. That is the
packing of Appendix K.3, with the two counters’ jobs swapped. The relation: the
guest is at the start of the block for the matching instruction, B holds the code of
the registers, and A is 0. An INC on register i is the stretch that multiplies B by
pi ; a DEC on register i is the stretch that divides B by pi with remainder and takes
the positive branch when the remainder is 0, the zero branch otherwise, restoring
B. The appendix argues each stretch: it ends, because each of its loops empties
the counter it counts down; it lands with A at 0; and, by unique factorisation, it
changes the exponent of pi alone, by the right amount. The host’s step is total on
these programs and the guest is deterministic, so the simulation argument gives:
the guest halts with B coding registers whose register out + 1 is y, that is, with y
the exponent of that register’s prime in B, exactly when the host program halts with
560   G Running it


              that register at y. The guest has no record instruction, so its ledger stays 0 and its
              flag down.
                  UP . UP is U with one more branch, for a guest PAY, and this guest has no PAY
              and no record instruction, so on it UP runs only branches U has. Theorem D.2
              gives the one-step matching from a freshly loaded host, and Theorem D.3: UP halts
              exactly when the guest does, with its registers 0 and 1 holding the guest’s A and B,
              and its ledger and flag equal to the guest’s. So it halts with register 0 at 0, register 1
              the code with y in it, ledger 0 and flag down.
                  The runner. The runner keeps the host program and the registers in binary tries,
              a tree indexed by the bits of a number. Looking up an index and storing at one
              give what the finite map they stand for gives: induction on the bits of the index. So
              each round of the runner’s loop does exactly what one host step does to the same
              registers, and the runner stops when the line leaves the program or the fuel is spent.
              If it halts after k rounds, the host run of k steps is halted at the end of the program
              with the runner’s registers, and the fuel left is the fuel given less k. If the source
              program has a derivation, the arrows above give a halting host run, of some length
              k, and the host, being deterministic, has only that run; any fuel of at least k makes
              the runner take those k steps and stop. If the runner hasn’t halted, it used every
              unit of fuel on host steps that stayed inside the program, so the host is still running
              after that many steps, and a derivation, which would give a halting host run of some
              length k, would need k larger than the fuel.
                  Composing: the program computes y exactly when the unfolded program does,
              exactly when the flat program halts with y, exactly when the counter program does,
              exactly when the host program does, exactly when the guest halts with y coded in B,
              exactly when UP halts as stated, and exactly when the runner halts with y on some
              fuel.
                 The theorem says nothing about how many steps the compiled program takes
              next to the source. It’s about answers.
                 The runner and the compiler are implemented, and the build has been run on
              a set of programs I picked to be annoying: gcd, factorial, a primality program
              written with procedures, an Ackermann tower, a sorting network on a list packed
              into one number, and a tiny interpreter for another machine written in the source
              language. Then 220 random programs that halt, 160 random programs with loops
              that might not, programs that never halt run for a fixed budget, and programs
              mutated on purpose to make sure the comparison notices. Answers are compared
              with direct arithmetic and separate interpreters of the source and compiled programs.
              Ackermann’s function at (3, 5) is 253; the source program takes 64,768 operations
              to get there, and the compiled host program takes about 119 million steps. The
              executable runner does a few million host steps a second, so that’s under a minute.
                                                                          G.5 What wasn’t built   561


   That’s about 1,800 host steps per source operation for Ackermann, and up to
about a hundred thousand for multiplication by repeated addition, because every
addition copies a running total one unit at a time. On this build the work grows
with the size of the numbers being handled, because every operation is one pebble
at a time. How it grows with the size of the program I haven’t measured. The last
two stages, the two-counter guest and UP running it, are proved and have never
been run, and UP on a compiled guest would be slow for the same reason U on a
certifying guest is. Still, I like that 253. It came out of nothing but INC and DEC,
and a proof that they mean what the source meant.


G.5 What wasn’t built
No chip. The design was never cut into metal: there’s no circuit for the small
machine, no simulation of one at the level of gates, and no board ever ran any
of this. The small machine exists as mathematical definitions and executable
implementations that agree on every tested step. That’s the whole of what “it runs”
means in this book.
   I’d love to see it in metal some day. But builds that can be held against each other
on every step are worth a lot to me. A board with nothing to hold it up against isn’t,
and that’s the trade I made.
APPENDIX H




The CHSH check

The small machine checks whether a number is zero, even, or at least something.
That’s a fine way to show the chain, and a dull thing to certify. Here’s a check worth
earning, built from zero, and then the one thing the small machine’s host does
with it, which is smaller and more exact than “it checks for quantum behaviour,” a
sentence that’s tempting and wrong. In brief, so you know where this is going: the
check never computes the famous number and never writes down the famous bound.
It tests seven facts about integers in eight counts. If they pass, a certain five-by-five
table has a property called positive semidefinite, and that property forces the famous
number under the famous bound. The wall is a consequence of the check. It never
goes into it. Everything else is explaining those sentences.
    Why put it in the book? Because it pulls four things apart that the small examples
keep bunched together: the counts, the relation the counts satisfy, the act of checking
that relation, and the record kept of the act. Writing a tally down costs no marks on
this machine. The checker decides a real condition about a matrix, using nothing
but integer arithmetic. The step ties the passing check to this edition of the tally,
and the earned chain costs three marks, the same three it costs for “A is zero.” How
deep the condition is and what the three acts cost are different numbers, and here
you can see them apart.
    And the tally on its own carries no history of where it came from. A tally
somebody made up passes the same arithmetic as one that was played. What’s
claimed here is about the numbers and what the machine does with them, and the
guarantee paragraph below says exactly how far that goes.


H.1 The game
Two players, Alice and Bob, in separate rooms. A referee flips two independent fair
coins, independent also of the players’ plan, and hands Alice a question x, zero or
one, and Bob a question y, zero or one. Alice answers a, zero or one; Bob answers b.
No talking during the game. They may agree on a plan beforehand, as detailed as
they like. They win a round when their answers differ exactly when both questions
were one. In words: if either question is zero, match; if both are one, differ.
   Try to win every time. A plan is a list: what Alice says to x equals zero, what
she says to x equals one, and the same two for Bob. Four bits. Now write the four

                                  562
                                                                                   H.1 The game   563


requirements the rounds impose: a0 equals b0 (both asked zero); a0 equals b1; a1
equals b0; a1 differs from b1. Chain the first three: a0 equals b0 equals a1, and a0
equals b1, so b0 equals b1. But the fourth says a1 differs from b1, and a1 equals b0
equals b1. Contradiction. One of the four must break. So any plan loses at least one
of the four question pairs, and if the referee asks all four equally often, the best a
plan can do is three out of four. Seventy-five percent. Do it the long way too: there
are sixteen plans (four bits), and if you write them all out and count wins you’ll
find eight win three rounds and eight win one, and none wins four (the broken
requirements always come in odd numbers, which you can see by adding up the four
equations and keeping only whether the totals come out even or odd, with “equal”
as 0 and “differ” as 1: each of the four answers appears twice on the left, so the left
sides add to an even number, and the right sides add to one). Sharing a coin before
the game to pick a plan at random doesn’t help; a mixture of numbers no larger
than three-quarters is no larger than three-quarters. Arthur Fine, a philosopher of
physics at the University of Washington, much of whose work is on the physicist
Albert Einstein and the quantum theory, proved in 1982 that the whole “pre-agreed
answers, no influence between rooms” story is exactly the mixtures of those sixteen
lists, one scoreboard for all four questions at once; the sixteen are the whole classical
story. That one I don’t have to take on his word: the form of his theorem that speaks
of the four averages is proved in this book, and the end of this appendix says where.
    The number. Recode answers zero and one as plus one and minus one. For each
question pair, let E be the average, over many rounds, of Alice’s answer times Bob’s.
The CHSH quantity is S equals E00 plus E01 plus E10 minus E11. For one fixed
plan each win adds one to S and each loss subtracts one, so S is wins minus losses:
a three-win plan has S equal to two, a one-win plan has minus two. With equal
question frequencies, the win rate is one half plus S over eight. So “seventy-five
percent” and “S at most two” are the same fact, and the second is the one that got
the name.
    The ceiling is easy to reach and costs no marks to write down. Tally one round
per question pair with both players answering zero every time: after the recoding
every answer is plus one, so all four correlators are one. That’s the plan that answers
zero to everything, which matches on every pair and so wins the three pairs that ask
for a match, S = 1 + 1 + 1 − 1 = 2. On the small machine’s host a tally like that is
a few INCs on counters, and INC costs no marks. Nothing in it says the rounds were
played; anybody can tally anything at no charge on the ledger. The other side, that
no finite mixture of plans beats two, is Theorem I.2 in Appendix I, one direction
of Fine’s result. The full equivalence, in the form that speaks of the four averages,
appears in the last subsection of this appendix.
564   H The CHSH check


             H.2 Where it came from, and why anyone cared
             So who started this, and why would anybody care whether two rooms can win a
             coin game? The names come in a line, and the line didn’t mean much to me until
             I saw that each of them moved the same thing a notch: from an argument about
             what’s real, which you can only agree with or not, toward a pile of counts a referee
             can judge. Each one rests on a different piece of the game above.
                 The trail starts in 1935, with Einstein, by then at the Institute for Advanced Study
             in Princeton, and two younger colleagues there, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen,
             asking whether quantum mechanics describes everything that’s real about a pair
             of particles. Their argument: if measuring one particle lets you predict the other’s
             result with certainty, the result must already have been fixed, and the theory leaves
             that out. What they rest on is the plan in each player’s pocket, a pre-agreed list of
             answers, the plan above. And the first thing worth checking is whether the paper
             even says what Einstein meant. By his own account, not quite. Podolsky did the
             writing, and that June Einstein wrote to Erwin Schrödinger, the Austrian physicist
             whose 1926 wave equation is at the heart of quantum mechanics, that the essential
             thing had been “smothered by formalism.” The person who lays that letter out is
             Arthur Fine, the same Fine whose theorem closed the sixteen plans above, in his
             encyclopedia entry on the argument. So Fine stands at both ends of the line: he
             checked the founding paper against what its author meant, and he proved exactly
             what the plans can do. Even the founding paper is a lead to check. It isn’t a verdict.
                 For thirty years that was philosophy. In 1964 John Bell turned it into arithmetic:
             if each particle carries pre-agreed answers and nothing travels between the rooms,
             certain averages can’t exceed a fixed number, and quantum theory predicts they
             do. What that rests on took me a few reads. His inequality rules out the pair of
             assumptions together, called local realism (answers exist before you ask, and no
             influence across the gap). Either one alone survives it. And where does a paper like
             that get published? In a brand-new journal called Physics Physique Fizika, which
             charged authors no page fees and in fact paid them by the word, ten cents a word,
             and which folded in 1968 after four volumes, or three. I went looking for that
             count, and the sources don’t agree on it: four is the number the American Physical
             Society’s archive of the journal gives, and Iulia Georgescu, writing about the journal
             in Physics World in 2026, says three. She’s also where the ten cents comes from.
             As Andrew Whitaker tells it in his biography of Bell, the journal gave out no free
             copies, so Bell spent his payment buying copies of his own paper to mail to other
             physicists. A result nobody else holds a copy of hasn’t left the room yet, and Bell paid
             to send his across. In 1969 four physicists, John Clauser, then a graduate student
             at Columbia, Michael Horne and Abner Shimony at Boston University, and Richard
             Holt at Harvard, rewrote it as the four-average form above, S at most two, which
                                                    H.2 Where it came from, and why anyone cared   565


could be tried in a lab with imperfect equipment. It’s called the CHSH inequality,
after their initials. That notch rests on what a real lab can deliver. Shimony was in
philosophy and in physics at Boston University both, which is the whole line in one
man.
    Then the obvious next question: did anybody actually try it? Stuart Freedman,
a graduate student at Berkeley, and Clauser, by then a postdoc there too, tried
it in 1972. The physicist Alain Aspect’s group at the Institut d’Optique in Orsay,
with two colleagues there, Jean Dalibard and Gérard Roger, did it in 1982 with the
measurement settings switched while the photons were in flight, which in the game’s
terms, as I read it, is the referee handing out the questions too late for any note
about them to cross between the rooms. Before that, in 1975, Aspect went to see
Bell at CERN to tell him what he planned, and by Aspect’s own account Bell heard
him out in silence and then asked, first thing, whether he had a permanent position.
Aspect did. Bell’s reason, as Aspect tells it, was that most physicists would take the
experiment for a waste of time, or take him for a crackpot. I read that as the toll
in its oldest form: a check that could have come out the other way costs somebody
something to run, and Bell wanted to know who’d pay. And in 2015 three groups
of experimental physicists (Bas Hensen’s in Delft, with electrons 1.3 kilometres
apart; Marissa Giustina’s in Vienna; Lynden Shalm’s at NIST, the National Institute
of Standards and Technology, in Boulder) closed the two main escape routes at once.
In 2022 Clauser, Aspect and the Austrian physicist Anton Zeilinger shared the Nobel
Prize “for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell
inequalities and pioneering quantum information science.” The 2015 tests came out
of that line of work, and Zeilinger was one of the authors of the Vienna one. So
in under fifty years the subject went from a question you needed a permanent job
to risk to a Nobel. The lab number sits above two. A remaining escape, that the
referee’s coins were secretly correlated with the particles, is a philosophical one and
I’m not going to pretend it’s closed.
    Now put this book’s check on the same line, because that’s where my position
gives. It sits past the far end, at the counts. Those fifty years went into making the
counts worth judging, rooms really apart, questions really late, escape routes really
shut, and my check starts after all of it. It’s handed eight counts and can’t tell a
lab’s tally from one somebody wrote down at no charge. So the check is a referee of
counts, and everything that made these counts worth refereeing happened upstream
of it.
    What quantum play does: if the players share an entangled pair and choose what
to measure from their question, the best they can do is S equals two times the square
root of two, about 2.83, a win rate of about eighty-five percent. Boris Tsirelson,
a Soviet mathematician who later taught at Tel Aviv University, in a 1980 paper
called “Quantum generalizations of Bell’s inequality,” proved that that’s a ceiling:
566   H The CHSH check


             quantum correlations violate Bell, but only up to there. I prove that ceiling below,
             and show the state that reaches it, with real amplitudes and with complex ones, in
             any dimension at all, infinitely many levels included (the last subsections of this
             appendix say how). The first thing proved is the algebra.
                 And the wall above that, which is the one I find most instructive. In 1994 the
             physicists Sandu Popescu and Daniel Rohrlich asked: what if you only demand that
             nothing can be signalled, that Alice’s answers on their own have the same odds
             whatever Bob is asked, and the other way round? Then you can write down a “box”
             (the PR box, after their initials) that wins every round (its answers differ exactly
             when both questions are one, by fiat, each answer alone a fair coin), S equals four,
             and nothing about it lets either room send a message. So no-signalling on its own
             doesn’t explain the quantum ceiling; the PR box meets that condition and beats 2.83.
             (A box isn’t a physical theory, and nobody is claiming one that meets everything
             relativity asks.) The order is: two for plans, 2.83 for quantum, four for no-signalling.
                 And the box has the same kind of history as everything else in this book: some-
             body got there first. Popescu and Rohrlich’s initials stuck, but the big review of the
             field by Nicolas Brunner and four coauthors credits boxes like it to Peter Rastall,
             whose 1985 paper on locality and Bell’s theorem appeared in Foundations of Physics,
             and, separately, to Leonid Khalfin, a physicist at the Steklov Institute’s Leningrad
             branch, and Tsirelson himself, both in 1985, nine years before. Then the question
             that really matters: if relativity isn’t what stops things at 2.83, what is? People have
             tried candidates. In 2005 the computer scientist Wim van Dam, who works on the
             theory of quantum computing, argued, in a paper on the implausible consequences
             of such boxes, that with enough PR boxes, Bob could work out any yes-or-no func-
             tion of both their inputs after Alice sends him a single bit, which would make the
             whole question of how much two parties need to talk collapse, and that’s a strong
             hint the boxes are too good to be real. In 2009 Marcin Pawłowski, a physicist
             at the University of Gdańsk, and five coauthors proposed a principle they called
             information causality: Bob can’t get more information about Alice’s data than the
             bits she actually sends him. They argue that ordinary and quantum physics both
             obey it, and that any theory that beats 2.83 breaks it. How much of the rest of the
             quantum boundary it reaches is something I haven’t checked. Which principle fixes
             the whole quantum boundary, if any one does, this book won’t answer. The check
             below is a fence at the middle step.


             H.3 Five sentences that are easy to say by accident

             Here they are, each with what I can stand behind beside it.
                “Faster than light.” Nothing travels. Each room alone sees fair coins; the
             correlation shows up only when you lay the two columns side by side afterward.
                                                   H.3 Five sentences that are easy to say by accident   567


“Quantum means random.” The average S is fixed by the state; what’s random is
each single answer; the plans are the less random side. “A Bell violation proves
nonlocality.” It rules out local realism, both assumptions together, and every real
test has loopholes with names. “A tally above two proves nonlocality.” No: S is a
population average, and one finite tally can land above two by luck. Four rounds,
one per question pair, with coin-flip answers, reach S equals four one time in sixteen.
That gap between a population bound and a finite sample is the problem Yanbao
Zhang, Scott Glancy and Emanuel Knill, at NIST in Boulder, work through for real
Bell tests (Physical Review A, 2011 and 2013), and the book doesn’t solve it. The
way they solve it is worth knowing, because it has the shape of this book’s record.
Turn each round into a small bet that no local plan can expect to win, even a plan
that remembers every earlier round, multiply the bets as the rounds come in, and the
French mathematician Jean Ville’s inequality, from his 1939 thesis, one of the works
that started the theory of martingales, says the chance the product ever climbs past
one over δ is at most δ. So a flag can go up for good the moment the product crosses,
with its error stated up front. It needs one thing the small machine doesn’t have:
settings drawn underneath the program, where the program can’t choose them. And
how much can one round tell you? Wim van Dam, Richard Gill, a mathematical
statistician who later held the chair in that subject at Leiden, and Peter Grünwald
(2005) measured exactly that, in bits of evidence against every local plan. Of the
two-party proofs they compare, CHSH comes out the strongest, “much stronger”
than the others in their words, at about 0.046 of a bit per round, a few hundredths,
so a convincing record takes hundreds of rounds. Four won’t do. About a finite
tally, this book proves only the narrow thing, that a tally above two is not explained
by one fixed plan replayed every round, and that narrow thing is what the sentence
has to stay. The bound for a finite local model is a separate theorem, and it says
nothing about one tally. And “the PSD test proves the data is quantum.” (PSD is
short for positive semidefinite, the property of the five-by-five table from the opening
of this appendix; the next subsection builds both.) It doesn’t, and the direction
matters. Passing implies the five-by-five table, pinned in a way the next subsection
explains, is PSD, and that implies S squared is at most eight; both are proved. The
correlators of a PSD table like that are the correlators of some quantum strategy.
That’s Tsirelson’s representation theorem, and it’s proved here: the strategy is built
on two systems of eight levels each. The exact edge of the quantum set for this game
was found by Lawrence Landau, whose 1969 Berkeley thesis was on the quantum
theory of local observables, and Lluís Masanes, then at the University of Barcelona
(next subsection), and that’s proved here too. Failing says nothing about whether
the play was quantum: the check is complete for the pinned matrix, the quantum
set is wider than that, and quantum behaviour can fail it. Every one of the sixteen
568   H The CHSH check


             plans fails it, and I’ll show you why. What it guarantees is in one paragraph, once
             the check is on the host machine.


             H.4 The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means
             Here’s the mathematics the check rests on, and it’s one idea: a table of numbers
             could be a table of dot products. Take a two-by-two symmetric table with a and c on
             the diagonal and b off it. It’s positive semidefinite (PSD) when a and c are at least
             zero and a times c minus b squared is at least zero. Check two by hand: ones on
             the diagonal and one half off, the determinant is three quarters, passes; ones on the
             diagonal and 1.2 off, the determinant is negative, fails. The reading: PSD means the
             table could be the dot products of some arrows, and 1.2 is too big a dot product for
             two arrows of length one. That’s the whole idea, generalised to bigger tables.
                 Now the table. Rows and columns labelled I, A0, A1, B0, B1 (the identity, Alice’s
             two questions, Bob’s two). Diagonal all ones. The I row and column zero off the
             diagonal (that’s “zero marginals”: the table takes each answer alone to average to
             zero, a fair coin; the counts record no marginals and the check doesn’t test this).
             A0 with A1 zero, B0 with B1 zero (no round asks Alice both questions, so no tally
             holds that average, and the table sets it to zero). Those zeros are choices. They pin
             the table to one slice, and I’ll come back to what they cost. And the four Alice-Bob
             cells hold the four correlators E. That’s a five-by-five with four free numbers in it. It
             splits into the one in the corner and a four-by-four block made of an identity and
             the two-by-two grid E of correlators, and PSD of that block is the same as saying
             E shrinks every vector (E is a contraction), which is three inequalities: one minus
             E00 squared minus E10 squared at least zero; one minus E01 squared minus E11
             squared at least zero; and their product at least the square of (E00 E01 plus E10
             E11).
                 Run it. All four correlators 0.6 except E11 at minus 0.6, S equals 2.4: the two
             diagonal terms are 0.28 and 0.28, the cross term zero, passes; above two, below
             2.83. All four at one over root two (E11 negative): diagonals zero, cross term zero,
             passes with no slack, S equals two root two exactly, the 2.83; nudge any entry’s
             size up and a diagonal goes negative. The all-ones plan (one, one, one, one): first
             diagonal is one minus one minus one, negative, fails, though S equals two and it’s
             a perfectly legal classical play. The PR box (one, one, one, minus one): fails the
             same way. A fence at the middle step, and a fence that keeps out every one of the
             sixteen plans: each has all four correlators at plus or minus one, so the first diagonal
             is always one minus one minus one. Of the classical plays, only diluted mixtures of
             plans get through.
                 That point, one over root two in size in every entry, is four real numbers, and no
             tally of rounds ever lands on it. A tally’s correlators are ratios of whole numbers,
                                           H.4 The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means   569


and the point needs each of them to be one over root two, which would make root
two a fraction, and you killed that fraction with a pencil in Section 5. That point
and its mirror image, every sign flipped, are the only places the bound is reached
(Remark I.2 in the appendix). So a passing tally always has S squared strictly below
eight. It can get as close as you like: the (17, 3) tally in the five examples below
has S squared equal to 7.84, and tallies of the same shape with a fraction nearer
one over root two get nearer still. Two root two is the least bound the check can
promise, and no tally the check accepts ever reaches it. Hold on to that corner; it
comes back.
    Picture what quantum play can reach as a field, and every test as a fence. In 2007
Miguel Navascués, Stefano Pironio and Antonio Acín, in a paper called “Bounding
the Set of Quantum Correlations” (NPA, after their initials), came at the edge from
outside, resting on necessary conditions. In their terms a table like this one is the
first rung of a ladder: bigger tables of expected products, each PSD, each a necessary
condition for quantum behaviour when its entries are left free, each rung tighter, and
(their 2008 paper) converging to the quantum set (strictly, the set from commuting
operators, which can differ from the tensor-product set in general scenarios). Each
rung is a fence with the whole field inside it. The check’s table is the first rung
with the marginals and the two within-party entries pinned to zero. Pinning is a
stronger demand than the rung makes, so passing puts you inside the first rung, and
a quantum point can still fail. My fence cuts across the field. Lawrence Landau in
1988 and Lluís Masanes in 2003 came at the edge itself, for this two-questions-each
case only. I’d have drawn a flat wall at 2.83. The exact boundary they found is a
curved surface (the arc-sine form) touching 2.83 at one point. It’s proved here: a
table has a PSD completion exactly when its entries lie between minus one and one
and their arcsines pass four inequalities, so those are exactly the quantum tables.
    So the obvious next question: if every rung is tighter than the last, does some
rung finally land exactly on the quantum set and stop? My first guess was yes,
at least here. A 2026 preprint by Anubhav Chaturvedi, a quantum-information
theorist at the University of Gdańsk, says no: no finite rung of the ladder captures
the whole quantum set even in this simplest case. And for the four correlators
alone, a 2008 paper by the same Navascués, Pironio and Acín works out that the
first rung already lands on Landau and Masanes’s curved edge. That looked like a
contradiction until I saw what each one fences. Landau and Masanes draw the edge
for the four correlators alone. Chaturvedi’s is the full behaviours, each room’s own
odds included. So there’s the corner again from the other side: tallies never reach
it, and, if his proof holds, rungs never close on the field. I wanted that to be one
fact. It’s two. Mine is root two again, about which points a count can hit. His is
about the fences. His result backs, from outside, the caution this book keeps about
the ladder, that no finite rung may close on the whole quantum set. It says nothing
570   H The CHSH check


             about my own check, though. My check’s caution, that a quantum point can fail it,
             comes from the pinning, and his paper never pins anything.


             H.5 The check, in integers
             Eight counts: for each of the four question pairs, one counting rounds where the
             answers matched and one where they differed. A round is one bump to one count;
             nothing about the round is tested, and no marginals are recorded. Then the check
             reads the eight and tests seven integer facts. For each pair, let N be same plus
             different and D be same minus different (so E is D over N). The seven: the four N are
             strictly positive (every pair was sampled; a pair with no rounds is rejected outright,
             and never read as a correlator of zero); A, which is N00 squared N10 squared minus
             D00 squared N10 squared minus D10 squared N00 squared, is at least zero; B, the
             same with the other column, is at least zero; and with C equal to D00 D01 N10
             N11 plus D10 D11 N00 N01, C squared is at most A times B. Those are the three
             contraction inequalities with the denominators cleared. No division, no reals, no
             square root, no S. Try it: counts (same, different) of (4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) give
             E of 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, minus 0.6; N is five and D is three (minus three for the last); A is
             175, B is 175, C is zero; passes. That’s the first example above, the S equals 2.4 one,
             in integers.
                 The theorem chain, in words: a passed check gives PSD of the five-by-five built
             from the counts; contraction and PSD are equivalent, both directions; and PSD forces
             S squared at most eight. The names are in the statements below. The underlying
             algebra is one identity: four times the sum of the four correlators squared, minus S
             squared, is a sum of six squares, so if the row sums of squares are at most one, S
             squared is at most eight, and the point one over root two reaches it. That’s Tsirelson’s
             bound as algebra, with no Hilbert space (the mathematical home of quantum states)
             in it.
                 Here is the chain as three statements. The derivations are in Appendix I; this is
             what they prove.

             Definition H.1 (Correlators from the counts; the pinned matrix). For eight counts
             and a question pair xy, let Exy = (samexy − diffxy )/(samexy + diffxy ), read as
             0 when both are 0. For reals Exy , M ( E) is the symmetric five-by-five matrix on
             I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 with ones on the diagonal, Exy in the cells ( A x , By ) and ( By , A x ),
             and zero everywhere else (Definition I.5). M is PSD when vT Mv ≥ 0 for every real
             vector v, and S( E) = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .
                                                                       H.5 The check, in integers   571




Theorem H.1 (The integer check implies the pinned matrix is PSD). If eight counts
pass the seven integer facts, then M ( E) for their correlators is symmetric and PSD.

Proof. The four positivity facts make every denominator positive, so each Exy is
Dxy /Nxy , and dividing the other three facts by positive squares turns them into the
three contraction inequalities (Lemma I.15). Contraction is equivalent to PSD of
M ( E) by a Schur complement on the four-by-four block (Corollary I.13).
   In the appendix this is Theorem I.16, and Corollary I.13 gives the equivalence of
contraction and PSD in both directions.


Theorem H.2 (PSD forces the Tsirelson bound). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 : if
M ( E) is symmetric and PSD, then S( E)2 ≤ 8.

Proof. A PSD matrix with unit diagonal has every three-by-three principal minor at
